prompt: You have a resource group named RG-Production. A team member needs to spin up and manage IaaS compute resources and their disks in this resource group. The team member must not be able to modify networks or storage accounts connected to these resources, and must not be able to grant access to other users. Which built-in role should you assign at the resource group scope?

options.text: Owner
Contributor
Virtual Machine Contributor
Reader

explanation:
Virtual Machine Contributor grants the ability to create and manage VMs and their disks, including resetting the root password and managing local user accounts using VM extensions, but it does not grant access to the connected virtual network or storage account and does not allow assigning roles in Azure RBAC. This satisfies the requirement to manage compute resources without access to networks or storage, and without the ability to grant access to other users.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Owner: Owner grants full access to all resources, including the ability to assign roles in Azure RBAC, which violates the requirement that the team member must not be able to grant access to other users.
- Contributor: Contributor grants full access to manage all resources, including networks and storage accounts, which violates the requirement that the team member must not modify the networks or storage accounts connected to the resources.
- Reader: Reader is read-only and does not allow the team member to create or manage any compute resources at all.

prompt: A security operations team must be able to grant users and groups privileges to Azure resources by assigning built-in definitions at any scope in your tenant, including subscriptions added in the future. The team must not be able to create or modify Azure resources themselves, and must only manage access through Azure RBAC (not via other paths such as Azure Policy). Which built-in definition and scope should you assign?

options.text: Owner at the root scope (/)
User Access Administrator at the root scope (/)
Role Based Access Control Administrator at the root scope (/)
Contributor at the root scope (/)

explanation:
Role Based Access Control Administrator manages access to Azure resources by assigning roles using Azure RBAC, and is scoped at the root so it applies to all current and future subscriptions. It is restricted to RBAC only and does not allow managing access via other mechanisms such as Azure Policy, and it does not permit creating or modifying Azure resources.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Owner at the root scope (/): Owner grants full access to all resources plus the ability to assign roles in Azure RBAC. This violates the requirement that the team must not create or modify Azure resources.
- User Access Administrator at the root scope (/): User Access Administrator lets you manage user access to Azure resources, but it is broader than RBAC and can include other access management paths, whereas the requirement is to only manage access through Azure RBAC.
- Contributor at the root scope (/): Contributor grants full access to manage all resources but does not allow assigning roles in Azure RBAC, so the team could not grant users access.

prompt: A company wants to grant an external contractor view-only access to blob data in a specific storage account, using Microsoft Entra authentication. The contractor needs to view containers and list blobs. The contractor must NOT be able to write, delete, or modify any blobs. Which built-in role should be assigned at the storage account scope?

options.text: Storage Blob Data Contributor
Storage Blob Data Reader
Storage Blob Data Owner
Storage Account Contributor

explanation:
Storage Blob Data Reader grants read and list access to Azure Storage containers and blobs. It is a data-plane role used through Microsoft Entra authentication and does not allow writing, deleting, or modifying any blob data, which matches the view-only contractor requirement.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Storage Blob Data Contributor: Storage Blob Data Contributor allows read, write, and delete on containers and blobs. This violates the requirement that the contractor must not write, delete, or modify blobs.
- Storage Blob Data Owner: Storage Blob Data Owner provides full access to blob containers and data including assigning POSIX access control. This grants write and delete permissions and goes well beyond view-only access.
- Storage Account Contributor: Storage Account Contributor permits management of the storage account itself and provides access to the account key, which can be used to access data via Shared Key authorization rather than through Microsoft Entra authentication.

The team also needs to be able to remove backed up data when retention policies require it. The team must NOT be able to create new backup vaults or grant access to other users. Which built-in role should be assigned?

options.text: Backup Contributor
Backup Operator
Backup Reader
Owner

explanation:
Backup Contributor lets you manage the backup service, including creating, restoring, and removing backed up data, but cannot create vaults or grant access to other users. This matches the requirement for the team to perform daily backup operations and also remove backed up data on demand.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Backup Operator: Backup Operator lets you manage backup services except for the removal of backup data, in addition to the same restrictions on vault creation and granting access. It cannot remove backed up data, so it does not satisfy the retention-removal requirement.
- Backup Reader: Backup Reader can only view backup services and cannot make changes, so it does not allow the team to perform any backup or restore actions.
- Owner: Owner grants full access to all resources and the ability to assign roles in Azure RBAC, including the ability to create vaults and give access to others, which violates two of the stated restrictions.

prompt: A user, alice@contoso.com, has the Contributor definition assigned at the subscription scope and the Reader definition assigned at a specific resource group within that subscription. According to how Azure's access system handles privileges across overlapping scopes, what is the user's effective privilege within the resource group?

options.text: Only Contributor actions, because the subscription-scope definition supersedes resource group-scope definitions.
Only Reader actions, because the more specific resource group scope overrides the higher-scope definition.
The combined actions of both definitions under the additive Azure RBAC model.
No actions, because two definitions at different scopes are in conflict and cancel each other out.

explanation:
Azure RBAC is an additive model, so the user's effective privileges are the sum of the role assignments that apply. Both the subscription-scope Contributor definition and the resource group-scope Reader definition apply, so the user has the combined actions available to them inside the resource group.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Only Contributor actions, because the subscription-scope definition supersedes resource group-scope definitions: Subscriptions-scoped assignments do not supersede more specific scopes, and Azure RBAC does not work by having a higher scope override lower scopes.
- Only Reader actions, because the more specific resource group scope overrides the higher-scope definition: A more specific scope does not replace or override a higher-scope definition in Azure RBAC. Both assignments apply additively.
- No actions, because two definitions at different scopes are in conflict and cancel each other out: Azure RBAC does not cancel assignments when scopes overlap; overlapping assignments are combined, not subtracted.

prompt: You have a landing-zone team that owns the virtual networks in the resource group rg-platform. As demand changes they must reconfigure addressing and adjust the security rules of those networks, but virtual machines are delivered by a separate operations team and handing out permissions belongs to the security team. This tenant has been fully migrated to Azure Resource Manager, so no legacy networking resources exist. Which built-in role should you assign to the landing-zone team at the scope of rg-platform?

options.text: Network Contributor
Virtual Machine Contributor
Classic Network Contributor
Contributor

explanation:
Network Contributor lets a principal manage networks but not access to them, and the built-in role explicitly does not grant permission to deploy or manage virtual machines, so the team can create the virtual network, add subnets, adjust network security rules and attach network interfaces while being stopped from deploying VMs. It also contains no permission to grant access to others.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Virtual Machine Contributor: Virtual Machine Contributor creates and manages virtual machines, disks and VM extensions, but it explicitly does not grant management access to the virtual network or storage account the virtual machines connect to, so the landing-zone team would not be able to create subnets or change network security rules.
- Classic Network Contributor: Classic Network Contributor only covers classic (legacy) networks, and this scenario is entirely built on current resource-manager virtual networks, subnets and network interfaces.
- Contributor: Contributor grants full access to manage all resources, which would let the team deploy virtual machines as well, contradicting the requirement. It only withholds the right to assign roles.

The security team requires that this identity never uploads new images and never removes existing repositories, tags, or manifests. Which built-in role should you assign to the identity at the scope of that registry?

options.text: AcrPull
AcrPush
AcrQuarantineReader
AcrQuarantineWriter

explanation:
AcrPull is the built-in definition for pulling artifacts from a container registry. It lets the pipeline enumerate repositories, read tags and download images, and it carries no write permissions on the registry content, so the identity cannot upload images or delete repositories, tags or manifests, which is what the security team requires.

Why the other options are wrong:
- AcrPush: AcrPush grants the ability to push artifacts to a registry (as well as pulling them). Uploading images is precisely what the security team prohibits, so this definition is too broad.
- AcrQuarantineReader: AcrQuarantineReader only pulls quarantined images. The pipeline needs the ordinary, non-quarantined images in fabrikamregistry, so this role doesn't meet the functional requirement.
- AcrQuarantineWriter: AcrQuarantineWriter pushes artifacts to a registry (quarantined ones) and pulls quarantined images. It permits uploading, which violates the security requirement, and it doesn't cover the normal images the pipeline uses.

prompt: You have a storage platform team that works from a runbook in the resource group rg-storage-prod. They stand up accounts, tighten their firewall configuration, change access tiers, and switch on diagnostic settings as part of normal operations. Company policy states that this team must never receive the permissions that reach container or blob content through Microsoft Entra authentication. Which built-in role should you assign to the team at the scope of rg-storage-prod?

options.text: Storage Account Contributor
Reader and Data Access
Storage Blob Data Contributor
Storage Account Key Operator Service Role

explanation:
Storage Account Contributor permits management of storage accounts, which covers provisioning accounts and changing their configuration such as firewall rules, container access tier and diagnostic settings. The definition contains none of the container or blob data-plane permissions, so the team can't enumerate containers or upload and delete blobs with Microsoft Entra authorization, matching company policy.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Reader and Data Access: Reader and Data Access lets you view everything but not create or delete a storage account or a resource contained in one, so the platform team couldn't stand up accounts or reconfigure them. It also grants read/write access to all data in a storage account through account keys, which the policy forbids.
- Storage Blob Data Contributor: Storage Blob Data Contributor grants read, write and delete on storage containers and blobs, exactly the data-plane permissions policy prohibits, and it doesn't cover managing the accounts and their configuration.
- Storage Account Key Operator Service Role: Storage Account Key Operator Service Role only permits listing and regenerating storage account access keys; it can't create accounts, change firewall rules, adjust access tiers or enable diagnostics, so it doesn't satisfy the runbook.

context:
Every business application in your company runs on Azure App Service, and all of them sit in the resource group rg-apps. Two teams work there side by side. The infrastructure team owns the hosting configuration that sits underneath the applications — how many instances run, how large each instance is, and the thresholds at which the service grows or shrinks by itself — but it never publishes or edits the business applications themselves, which are the application team's responsibility. The application team publishes and maintains those applications and must leave the hosting configuration alone. Both groups hold only view access in rg-apps today. Which built-in roles should you assign at the scope of rg-apps?

- Principal: Infra-WebTeam; Definition assigned today: Reader; Scope: /subscriptions/8f21…/resourceGroups/rg-apps
- Principal: App-DevTeam; Definition assigned today: Reader; Scope: /subscriptions/8f21…/resourceGroups/rg-apps
prompt: The infrastructure team should receive _____, and the application team should receive [...].

options.text: Web Plan Contributor
Website Contributor
Contributor
Reader

explanation:
App Service separates the hosting construct that holds the shared infrastructure for a group of apps from the individual apps themselves, and Azure splits its built-in definitions along exactly that line. Web Plan Contributor covers the web plans for websites — the object that decides instance count, instance size, and autoscale behaviour — and it lets the infrastructure team change those settings without giving it any way to touch the business applications or to assign roles. Website Contributor is the mirror image: it covers the apps (code deployments, app settings, connection strings, and the like) while explicitly excluding the plans, so the application team gets what it needs and keeps its hands off the hosting configuration. Together the two narrow Contributor definitions give each team exactly its own slice of the resource group.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Website Contributor: Website Contributor covers the individual applications and deliberately leaves out the plans that hold them, so the infrastructure team would still be unable to change instance counts, instance sizes, or autoscale thresholds.
- Contributor: Contributor grants management of everything in the resource group, including the hosting configuration and the applications owned by the other team, so it is broader than this team's remit and the least-privilege test fails.
- Reader: Reader only permits viewing: the team could inspect the hosting configuration but could not change instance counts or sizes.

context:
A media company mounts the renders container of its storage account stmedia01 as a shared Linux filesystem for a rendering farm. The team that supports the farm must be able to create and delete containers, upload and remove blobs, and also set the read, write and execute permission bits that the farm's processes run under. The current state of the account and the team's grants is shown below. Which built-in role should you assign to the team?

- Setting: Storage account; Value: stmedia01, in subscription sub-fabrikam
- Setting: Shared directory; Value: renders container, mounted by the rendering farm over CIFS
- Setting: Supporting principal; Value: fabrikam-renderfarm-admins, a Microsoft Entra group
- Setting: Grants today; Value: Storage Blob Data Contributor at /subscriptions/sub-fabrikam/resourceGroups/rg-media/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/stmedia01
- Setting: Open change request; Value: Let the rendering service account have full control of the container's POSIX permission bits
prompt: You should assign the _____ built-in role to fabrikam-renderfarm-admins at the scope of the stmedia01 storage account.

options.text: Storage Blob Data Reader
Storage Blob Data Contributor
Storage Blob Data Owner
Storage Blob Delegator

explanation:
The team needs full management of containers and blob content, plus the ability to control POSIX access control on containers so the rendering farm's processes get the permission bits they run under. Storage Blob Data Owner is the built-in role that combines full access to blob containers and data with assigning POSIX access control, so it satisfies both parts of the change request. Assigning it at the scope of the stmedia01 storage account keeps the grant bounded to that account.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Storage Blob Data Reader: Storage Blob Data Reader only lists containers and reads blob content. It cannot create or delete containers, upload or remove blobs, or change container permissions, so it fails both parts of the requirement.
- Storage Blob Data Contributor: This role already covers creating and deleting containers and uploading and deleting blobs, but it does not include assigning POSIX access control, so the team still could not set the container permission bits the farm relies on.
- Storage Blob Delegator: Storage Blob Delegator only grants permission to obtain a user delegation key, which is used to mint a short-lived shared access signature for a container or blob. It gives no container or blob management rights and no control over container permissions.

The table lists the assignments currently shown on stcontosoprod01. Which of them will already cover the new storage account?

options.text: Only the assignment marked (Inherited), because it was recorded at the parent level
Only the three assignments marked This resource, because they were recorded against stcontosoprod01
All four assignments, because each one is inherited by every resource in the same resource group
None of the assignments, because access only reaches resources that already exist when the record is created

explanation:
An assignment shown as (Inherited) was created higher in the hierarchy — here at rg-contoso-prod — and permissions granted at a parent level flow down to everything inside that level, including resources added later. The three entries marked This resource were recorded against stcontosoprod01 itself, so they apply to that one storage account only and do not spread sideways to a different storage account in the same resource group.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Only the three assignments marked This resource, because they were recorded against stcontosoprod01: A record marked This resource is bound to the individual resource named in the assignment. Granting a job function role at a resource group level is what makes the access cover every resource in that group; a record attached to one storage account never reaches a sibling resource.
- All four assignments, because each one is inherited by every resource in the same resource group: Inheritance works downwards, not sideways. A record attached to a single resource does not grant the same access to the other resources sitting next to it in the resource group; only records made at the resource group level (the (Inherited) row here) do that.
- None of the assignments, because access only reaches resources that already exist when the record is created: Access does propagate to resources created later: an assignment made at the resource group level applies to all resources of that resource group, so the next storage account added to rg-contoso-prod is covered automatically.

prompt: You open Access control (IAM) on rg-contoso-prod, select Check access, pick Dana Whitfield, and the pane returns two Azure role assignments and one Deny assignment that came from Azure Blueprints. Dana insists that a group she belongs to gives her access to a storage account inside that resource group, yet it does not appear. What should you do?

options.text: Open the storage account itself: the pane lists the scope you selected plus the grants it inherits from higher scopes, but not grants made on resources below that scope
Open the group in Microsoft Entra ID: the pane lists the scope you selected plus the grants it inherits from higher scopes, but it does not resolve group grants onto individual members
Leave the Deny assignment in place: the pane lists the scope you selected plus the grants it inherits from higher scopes, and the Deny assignment is what is hiding the missing grant
Ask an Owner of the storage account to repeat the check: the pane lists the scope you selected plus the grants it inherits from higher scopes, and grants on resources below are shown only to Owners

explanation:
The Check access pane shows the access a principal holds at the scope you selected plus everything inherited into that scope from a higher level; assignments that were created on resources below the selected scope are not listed there. Dana's group membership on the storage account is recorded on the storage account itself, so repeat the same check on that resource.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Open the group in Microsoft Entra ID: the pane lists the scope you selected plus the grants it inherits from higher scopes, but it does not resolve group grants onto individual members: Group grants work the opposite way: a role assigned to a group is held by every member of that group, and those assignments do appear against the individual user in Check access. Looking at the group instead of Dana will not reveal anything extra about her effective access.
- Leave the Deny assignment in place: the pane lists the scope you selected plus the grants it inherits from higher scopes, and the Deny assignment is what is hiding the missing grant: The pane lists Deny assignments alongside Azure role assignments rather than using them to conceal Azure role assignments, so the Blueprints deny assignment is not what is filtering Dana's group grant out of the results.
- Ask an Owner of the storage account to repeat the check: the pane lists the scope you selected plus the grants it inherits from higher scopes, and grants on resources below are shown only to Owners: The pane only shows records at the selected scope, records inherited from above it, and records the signed-in account is allowed to read. Holding Owner on the subscription would not surface assignments created on a child resource, because assignments below the selected scope are never listed there.

Export in JSON rather than CSV, because the CSV writer leaves the identity columns out while the JSON writer keeps them
Start the download from the managed identity or group entry instead of the subscription, because the identity columns are filled in only when you begin from a principal

explanation:
When the identity running the download is not entitled to read the directory, the DisplayName, SignInName and ObjectType columns of the exported file are left blank. Granting that identity directory read permission, for example with the Directory Readers role, and downloading again fills those columns, while ObjectId stays populated because it comes from the assignment itself rather than from the directory.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Export in JSON rather than CSV, because the CSV writer leaves the identity columns out while the JSON writer keeps them: The file format is not the deciding factor. Both CSV and JSON are produced by the same download pane and resolve the identity columns in the same way, so switching format leaves the blank columns exactly as they are.
- Start the download from the managed identity or group entry instead of the subscription, because the identity columns are filled in only when you begin from a principal: The downloadable file is produced from a scope in the portal, and starting from a managed identity or group entry only changes the list you browse on screen — it does not populate identity columns that were left empty for lack of permission.
- Tick the Children checkbox so that role assignments below the scope you exported are included, because the missing identity data comes from records at child levels: The Inherited, At current scope and Children check boxes only decide which levels are included in the file. Records at child levels are present in an export and carry the same blank identity columns, so widening the selection does not resolve the missing names.

Storage Blob Data Contributor
Storage Blob Data Owner
Storage Account Contributor

explanation:

explanation:
The documentation states that when a Global Administrator elevates access with the Access management for Azure resources switch, that administrator receives the User Access Administrator role on all subscriptions in the tenant. Being an Azure role that manages user access to Azure resources and lets the holder assign roles, it restores the ability to hand out permissions across the tenant without waiting for someone else to create each assignment.

- User Administrator: User Administrator is a directory role covering things like creating and managing users and groups, changing passwords and managing licenses. It doesn't govern who can reach Azure resources, so it wouldn't restore the missing ability.

context: Your automation runs Azure CLI to hand out a role, but it passes a display name instead of the object identifier, and the request returns "Insufficient privileges to complete the operation." What explains the failure?
prompt: The request fails because _____.

options.text: the caller can't read Microsoft Entra ID, the lookup used to resolve the assignee
the caller can't read the subscription's resource groups, the lookup used to resolve the scope
the caller can't read the role definition, the lookup used to resolve the requested permissions
the caller can't read the policy assignments, the lookup used to resolve effective access

explanation:
Passing a display name makes Azure look the named account up in the directory. A caller such as a service principal has no permission to read Microsoft Entra ID by default, so that lookup fails and the command reports insufficient privileges. Granting the caller permission to read data in the directory fixes it, and with Azure CLI the same command can instead use the assignee object ID to skip the directory lookup altogether.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the caller can't read the subscription's resource groups, the lookup used to resolve the scope: The scope isn't resolved by a directory lookup, and failing to read resource groups doesn't produce this message. The failing step is the directory lookup for the account named on the command line.
- the caller can't read the role definition, the lookup used to resolve the requested permissions: The role definition isn't resolved from a directory lookup triggered by a display name. Naming the account sends the request to the directory first, and that is where it breaks.
- the caller can't read the policy assignments, the lookup used to resolve effective access: Policy assignments aren't consulted to resolve a named account, and they have nothing to do with this message. Only the directory lookup is involved, and supplying the object ID bypasses it.

options.text: put a condition on it

make it expire on a set date
swap it for a custom role definition

explanation:
The documentation describes two things you can do with a privileged assignment on that page: put a condition on it so the grant is constrained, or remove the assignment. Since the grant has to remain in place and simply stop covering everything beneath the scope, limiting the existing grant is the action to take.

Why the other options are wrong:
- move it to a narrower scope: Relocating a grant isn't one of the actions this page offers for a privileged assignment, and moving a subscription-level grant downward would change where it applies rather than trimming what it covers underneath.
- make it expire on a set date: Ending the grant on a date would stop it altogether, including for the resources that still need it, so it doesn't meet the requirement to keep the grant in place.
- swap it for a custom role definition: Replacing the role definition isn't offered on this page either. The two documented actions for an existing privileged assignment are to limit it with a condition or to remove it.

prompt: You manage a subscription that contains exactly three resource groups: web-rg, api-rg, and data-rg. The assignments shown in the table are the only ones that exist for this identity. The web team reports that the identity can still create and delete web apps in web-rg, but their policy allows only list and read actions there. Full management rights are still required in api-rg and data-rg. Which change should you make?

options.text: Remove the subscription-level Contributor assignment and create new Contributor assignments at api-rg and at data-rg, keeping the read-only assignment at web-rg
Keep the subscription-level Contributor assignment and add another Reader assignment at web-rg, so the narrower scope governs that resource group
Change the subscription-level Contributor assignment to point at api-rg, then create a second Contributor assignment for data-rg
Create a deny assignment at the subscription scope that blocks this identity from deleting resources anywhere in the subscription

explanation:
Azure RBAC is additive: the effective permissions of a principal are the sum of every role assignment that applies to it, and the scope hierarchy is parent-child, so the subscription-level assignment still contributes all of its actions for resources inside web-rg. Narrowing access therefore means taking the broad assignment away and recreating the permissions only where they are still needed. Deleting the subscription-level Contributor assignment and creating new Contributor assignments at api-rg and data-rg leaves web-rg governed solely by its read-only assignment.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Keep the subscription-level Contributor assignment and add another Reader assignment at web-rg, so the narrower scope governs that resource group: Adding another read-only assignment at web-rg cannot subtract anything: the subscription-level Contributor assignment still applies inside web-rg and its actions remain part of the effective permissions, so the identity keeps full management rights there.
- Change the subscription-level Contributor assignment to point at api-rg, then create a second Contributor assignment for data-rg: The scope of a role assignment is fixed when the assignment is created; it isn't repointed in place. To move the rights you would have to delete the subscription-level assignment and create new ones, which is what the keyed option does.
- Create a deny assignment at the subscription scope that blocks this identity from deleting resources anywhere in the subscription: A deny assignment blocks the listed action for every resource in its scope. Created at the subscription scope it would also block deletes in api-rg and data-rg, where full management is required, and it would leave the identity's other write rights inside web-rg intact.

Without a scope on the role assignment, the assignment inherits the level of the deployment, so a resource group deployment produces an assignment covering everything in pay-rg. When the assignment has to sit at the level of an individual resource, the role assignment must carry the scope that points at that resource, so setting it to stpayprod001 limits the readers to that single account and leaves the rest of pay-rg untouched.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Nest the role assignment resource inside the stpayprod001 resource block in the template: The documented way to assign a role at the level of a resource is to set the scope property on the role assignment. Moving the block inside the storage account does not replace it, and the assignment still takes its level from the deployment.
- Rename the role assignment resource to the resource ID of stpayprod001: The name identifies the assignment itself. Role assignment names are typically a GUID, and a name that looks like a resource ID does not redirect where the assignment applies.
- Put the role assignment resource in a separate template file and deploy that file against stpayprod001: Deployments target a tenant, management group, subscription, or resource group, never an individual resource. A second template deployed to that resource group produces another assignment at the same broad level.

prompt: Alice was granted the Reader role at the scope of one virtual machine that lives in a resource group named 'hr-rg'. She has no other role assignments anywhere in the tenant. She is curious about how this grant applies to a second virtual machine that also lives in the same resource group 'hr-rg'. What is Alice's effective access to the second virtual machine?

options.text: She has full access because both resources live in the same resource group and resource-scope role assignments automatically extend to peer resources.
She has Reader access because Reader role assignments always extend to every resource in the parent container regardless of the original scope.
She has Reader access only to the targeted virtual machine because role assignments at the resource scope do not extend to peer resources in the same resource group.
She has no access to any virtual machine because the Reader role cannot be assigned at the resource scope and only works at subscription or resource-group scope.

explanation:
This is the correct option because role assignments apply strictly to the scope at which they are created. A role assignment at the resource scope covers that one specific resource only; it does not extend laterally to peer resources that share the same parent container. Each peer resource needs its own separate role assignment before the principal can act on it.

Why the other options are wrong:
- She has full access because both resources live in the same resource group and resource-scope role assignments automatically extend to peer resources: This option is incorrect because role assignments do not propagate laterally between peer resources. Inheritance in Azure RBAC flows downward through the scope hierarchy (parent to child), so a grant at one resource does not reach the other resources in the same resource group.
- She has Reader access because Reader role assignments always extend to every resource in the parent container regardless of the original scope: This option is incorrect because the scope of a role assignment determines exactly what it covers; it does not automatically widen to every other resource in the parent container. Only an assignment written at the parent scope, such as the resource group itself, would reach every resource inside it.
- She has no access to any virtual machine because the Reader role cannot be assigned at the resource scope and only works at subscription or resource-group scope: This option is incorrect because Reader is a built-in role that can be assigned at any of the four scope levels: management group, subscription, resource group, or individual resource. Azure RBAC places no restriction on using Reader at the resource scope.

options.text: Permissions granted at a broad scope are inherited by every resource and group underneath it
Permissions from several grants are summed, so an extra assignment at a smaller scope cannot remove anything
Membership is transitive: being inside one group that is inside another carries the enclosing group's permissions

explanation: Azure RBAC combines four effects that the four reports are each showing: permissions flow down the parent-child scope hierarchy, permissions from several assignments are added together rather than cancelled out, group membership is transitive, and access exists only for as long as the assignment that grants it. context: Your tenant has a Microsoft Entra ID P2 license. The service desk team must be able to request elevation for a limited period, with their manager's approval, but only for the virtual machines that run in prod-app-rg. When you open the Add role assignment page for a single virtual machine, the options that would let you mark the grant as eligible or time bound are not shown. Which scope should the service desk assignment be created at?
prompt: The service desk assignment should be created at _____.

options.text: the resource group that holds the virtual machines
the subscription that holds the resource group
the individual virtual machine resource
the management group that holds the subscription

explanation:
The assignment type choices - eligible, or active with a permanent or time-bound duration - are only offered for management group, subscription, and resource group scopes. Because the service desk must reach nothing beyond the virtual machines in prod-app-rg, the resource group is the only scope that both offers those choices and keeps the grant inside the stated requirement.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the subscription that holds the resource group: The subscription scope also offers the eligible and time-bound options, but an assignment there would let the service desk activate the role over every resource in the subscription, including those outside prod-app-rg.
- the individual virtual machine resource: At the scope of a single resource such as one virtual machine, the portal does not offer the assignment type or duration options, which is exactly why they were missing on the page you opened.
- the management group that holds the subscription: A management group assignment does offer those options, but it would reach every subscription placed under that management group, well beyond what the service desk team needs.

context:
A junior administrator follows the documented steps for granting Azure access. On the Access control (IAM) page, the Role assignments tab works, but the Add role assignment command is greyed out and nothing happens when it is clicked. The security team checks which actions the junior administrator's group is authorized for. Which action must that group hold before the command becomes available?

- Observation: Role assignments tab opened at the level of pay-rg; Result: Lists the assignments created for pay-rg
- Observation: Add > Add role assignment clicked; Result: Option greyed out, page never opens
- Observation: Action audit for the junior administrator's group; Result: No entry for Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/write
prompt: Before that command can be used, the group has to be authorized for _____.

options.text: Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write
Microsoft.Authorization/policyAssignments/write
Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/write
Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/write

explanation:
Creating a role assignment is itself an authorized operation, so the person doing it needs Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write at the scope where the assignment is created, or at a higher scope. Built-in roles such as Role Based Access Control Administrator and User Access Administrator include this action. Without it the portal greys out the Add role assignment option, which is the behaviour described here.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Microsoft.Authorization/policyAssignments/write: That action covers creating policy assignments, not role assignments. It grants nothing over who can be given which role, so the Add role assignment option stays unavailable.
- Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/write: This action manages virtual machines. It says nothing about creating role assignments, which is the operation the junior administrator is trying to perform.
- Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/write: This action manages storage accounts. Like the virtual machine action, it belongs to the resource provider of a service and does not enable role assignment creation.

context:
The storage account stpay001 holds the payroll data the auditors must read. An ARM read-only lock is in place on that account, and every attempt to create their assignment against the account itself, or against a container inside it, fails with an authorization error. The auditors need read-only reach into blob data, with no ability to change or delete anything. Which scope should their assignment be created at?

- Attempt: 1; Target used: stpay001; Outcome: AuthorizationFailed
- Attempt: 2; Target used: Container exports in stpay001; Outcome: AuthorizationFailed
- Attempt: 3; Target used: pay-rg; Outcome: Not tried yet
prompt: The auditors' assignment should be created at _____.

options.text: the resource group pay-rg
the storage account stpay001
the blob container named exports
the subscription that owns pay-rg

explanation:
When a storage account carries an Azure Resource Manager read-only lock, the lock blocks role assignments that are scoped to the storage account or to a container within it. Creating the assignment one level higher, at pay-rg, is therefore the way to get the grant in place, and choosing a data-reader role definition keeps the reach limited to reading blob data rather than any management rights.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the storage account stpay001: This is one of the two scopes the read-only lock blocks, which is why attempt 1 returned AuthorizationFailed. An assignment scoped to the account cannot be created while the lock is in place.
- the blob container named exports: A container inside the account is the other blocked scope, as attempt 2 shows. Scoping the assignment to a single container fails for the same reason as the account-level attempt.
- the subscription that owns pay-rg: A subscription-scoped assignment would be created without hitting the lock, but it would hand the auditors reach over blob data in every storage account in the subscription, which is wider than they need.

- Principal: fin-grp; Scope used: /subscriptions/11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555/resourceGroups/pay-rg; Command finished: 23:15, no errors; Result 30 minutes later: Blob listing succeeded
prompt: The explanation to give the auditors is that _____.

options.text: a grant created at a management group scope can take much longer to become effective than one created at a narrower scope, so the auditors should keep retrying
a grant created at a management group scope becomes effective within the same short window as every other grant, so the command must have targeted the wrong scope
a grant created at a management group scope never reaches the data inside an object, so a separate data access role must be added at each subscription
a grant created at a management group scope is honoured only by the management plane, so the auditors have to create it from the portal instead

explanation:
Creating or removing role assignments can take up to ten minutes to take effect, and the documentation warns that an assignment created at the management group scope can take much longer. Both commands finished cleanly and the assignment created against pay-rg already works, so the remaining denial is the propagation delay, not a mistake in the scope value.

Why the other options are wrong:
- a grant created at a management group scope becomes effective within the same short window as every other grant, so the command must have targeted the wrong scope: The short window applies to assignments at narrower scopes. Treating a management group assignment as already effective sends you hunting for a wrong scope value when the real cause is propagation time.
- a grant created at a management group scope never reaches the data inside an object, so a separate data access role must be added at each subscription: Nothing in the documentation says a data access role created at the management group scope fails to reach data; it only notes that such an assignment takes longer to propagate. Adding roles at each subscription is not the remedy.
- a grant created at a management group scope is honoured only by the management plane, so the auditors have to create it from the portal instead: The command line tool is the documented way to create a data access role, including at narrow scopes such as a container, and the same propagation behaviour applies whatever tool is used. Switching to the portal does not speed anything up.

context:
The data team holds the Contributor role on the ml-rg resource group, and that is the only assignment any of its members has across the whole tenant. Tomorrow a new virtual machine is deployed to ml-rg. What happens to the data team's access to that new virtual machine?

- Item: Principal; Value: data-team
- Item: Role; Value: Contributor
- Item: Scope; Value: /subscriptions/11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555/resourceGroups/ml-rg
- Item: Any other assignment for this principal; Value:
prompt: Without adding anything new, _____.

options.text: They can work with it the same way they already work with everything else inside that resource group
They get no access to it, because a grant reaches only the resources that already existed when it was created
They can read it but not change it, because anything created later arrives without any access
They can act on it only after a fresh assignment is created for that resource group

explanation:
Scopes sit in a parent-child relationship and lower levels inherit the permissions granted at higher levels, so the Contributor assignment created on ml-rg flows down to everything contained in ml-rg. A virtual machine deployed there afterwards is covered by the existing assignment exactly like the resources already there.

Why the other options are wrong:
- They get no access to it, because a grant reaches only the resources that already existed when it was created: This is the opposite of how scopes behave. Permissions granted on a resource group flow down to the resources inside it, so something deployed there later is covered rather than excluded, and the assignment does not freeze at the moment it was created.
- They can read it but not change it, because anything created later arrives without any access: Nothing inside ml-rg is read-only by default. The single Contributor assignment already carries full management permissions over everything in that resource group, including the new virtual machine.
- They can act on it only after a fresh assignment is created for that resource group: No second assignment is required. The permissions are already granted on ml-rg, and the contents of ml-rg inherit them, so nothing has to be recreated when the new virtual machine appears.

The security policy states that the team must reach nothing else in the tenant, and those two resource groups sit in different subscriptions. You may add as many grants as the change process allows. Which approach should you take?

- Target: pay-rg; Kind: Resource group in sub-billing; Operations team requirement: Manage everything in it
- Target: inv-rg; Kind: Resource group in sub-inventory; Operations team requirement: Manage everything in it
- Target: platform-rg; Kind: Resource group in sub-billing; Operations team requirement: No access

- Target: sub-billing; Kind: Subscription; Operations team requirement: No access beyond pay-rg
- Target: sub-inventory; Kind: Subscription; Operations team requirement: No access beyond inv-rg
- Target: corp-mg; Kind: Management group containing sub-billing and sub-inventory; Operations team requirement: No access
prompt: To satisfy the policy, you should _____.

options.text: assign the Contributor role at the scope of each listed resource group
assign the Contributor role at the scope of each listed subscription
assign the Contributor role at the scope of the management group above both subscriptions
assign the Contributor role at the scope of a single listed resource group

explanation:
A role assignment takes effect at exactly the scope where it is created, and a resource group is a valid scope on its own. Creating one Contributor assignment at the scope of pay-rg and another at the scope of inv-rg gives the team management rights over the contents of both areas and nothing outside them, because every wider scope in the exhibit (the two subscriptions and the management group above them) also contains targets the policy excludes.

Why the other options are wrong:
- assign the Contributor role at the scope of each listed subscription: The exhibit shows platform-rg inside sub-billing and warehouse-rg inside sub-inventory. An assignment created at subscription scope reaches every resource in that subscription, so it would hand the team management rights over areas marked as no access.
- assign the Contributor role at the scope of the management group above both subscriptions: A management group is a scope above subscriptions, and an assignment there applies throughout every subscription beneath it, which is wider than the two resource groups the team owns.
- assign the Contributor role at the scope of a single listed resource group: An assignment applies only at the scope it was created at, so covering just one of the two resource groups leaves the team's other area unreachable.

prompt: Your team has deployed a container group into a subnet of an Azure virtual network so that the workload keeps a private IP address. Clients inside the corporate network reach the group's port 8080 successfully, but every outbound HTTPS call the container makes to an external partner API times out. You need to restore the container's outbound connectivity without exposing it publicly. Which component should you add to the subnet?

options.text: NAT gateway
Application Gateway
Azure Bastion
Azure Firewall

explanation:
A container group placed in a virtual network subnet requires a NAT gateway for its outbound traffic; it is the only outbound arrangement the Azure Container Instances service supports for subnet placement. Without it the group has no outbound path, which matches the symptom in the exhibit: inbound calls to port 8080 succeed while outbound HTTPS calls time out. Adding a NAT gateway to the subnet restores outbound connectivity while the group keeps its private IP.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Application Gateway: Application Gateway is a front-end (ingress) component. It can sit in front of a container group to provide a stable public address, but it does not provide the outbound path for a group deployed into a subnet, so it does not fix the timed-out outbound calls.
- Azure Bastion: Azure Bastion gives administrators browser-based RDP/SSH access to virtual machines without exposing public ports on them. It does not provide outbound connectivity for a container group running in a subnet.
- Azure Firewall: Azure Firewall is a network security appliance for inspecting and filtering traffic, and it is not the outbound arrangement supported by the Azure Container Instances service for groups deployed in a virtual network; that role belongs to the NAT gateway.

prompt: You have deployed a container group that runs a nightly batch job. The job exits with code 0 when it finishes successfully and with code 1 when it hits a transient failure. You need the group to retry a batch that ended with an error, while a batch that has already completed successfully must not be started again. Which restart policy should you configure for this container group?

options.text: Always
Never
OnFailure
Leave the restart policy unset so the service applies its default

explanation:
OnFailure restarts the container only when the process inside it fails, meaning it terminates with a nonzero exit code, and the container is always run at least once. That is exactly the behavior needed here: the batch that exited with code 1 is retried, while the batch that exited with code 0 is left alone, so a completed batch is not run again.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Always: Always restarts the container every time it stops, including after a clean exit with code 0, so a batch that already succeeded would be executed again and again.
- Never: Never only guarantees that the container is not restarted after a clean exit with code 0. After a nonzero exit code the platform might still restart the container, so this setting does not deliver the deliberate retry-after-error behavior the scenario calls for.
- Leave the restart policy unset so the service applies its default: When no restart policy is specified at container creation, the service applies Always as the default, which repeats the container after every exit, including successful ones, so completed batches would run again.

prompt: You have created the container group shown below to run the order-processing application. The application must save each day's results to an Azure Files share, and you also want a log shipper to run next to the application inside that same container group. The image is published for every operating system that Azure Container Instances can schedule. Which change should you make?

options.text: Recreate the container group with the OS type set to Linux.
Add the log shipper as a second container to the existing container group and keep its current OS type.
Mount the Azure Files share into the existing container group and keep its current OS type.
Deploy the log shipper as a separate container group with the same OS type and mount the same Azure Files share.

explanation:
Two of the capabilities this workload needs are restricted to Linux container groups in Azure Container Instances: running multiple containers in one container group and mounting volumes such as Azure Files shares. Because the group must hold both the application and the log shipper sidecar and must have the share mounted, the group has to be deployed with the OS type preference set to Linux, which is the operating system you indicate when creating the container group.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add the log shipper as a second container to the existing container group and keep its current OS type: Running several containers inside a single group (for example an application plus a logging sidecar) is only offered for Linux container groups, so the extra container cannot be added while the group keeps its current OS type.
- Mount the Azure Files share into the existing container group and keep its current OS type: Volume mounting, including Azure Files shares, is restricted to Linux container groups, so the share cannot be mounted into a group that keeps its current OS type.
- Deploy the log shipper as a separate container group with the same OS type and mount the same Azure Files share: A second, separate container group does not satisfy the requirement that the log shipper run inside the same group as the application: containers only share a container host, local network, storage and lifecycle when they belong to one group, and two groups do not share those resources.

prompt: You have deployed a container group to Azure Container Instances from your own Azure Container Registry with the command shown below. The pull currently relies on a shared registry user name and password, and your security team requires the group to authenticate to the registry with no user name or password kept in its definition, while the same application image continues to be pulled. Which change should you make?

options.text: Assign a managed identity to the container group and authorize it to pull images in the registry
Assign a managed identity to the container group but keep the registry user name and password so the pull of the images still uses the shared secret
Pass the registry user name and password to the container group as environment variables and let the image pull authenticate with them
Create a private endpoint for the registry and place the container group in a delegated subnet of the same virtual network

explanation:
Azure Container Instances supports managed identity, which lets a container group authenticate to any service that supports Microsoft Entra authentication without credentials in the container code, and the same identity can be used for an authenticated image pull against Azure Container Registry so that no user name or password has to be included in the container group definition. Assigning the identity to the group and giving it rights to pull from the registry therefore removes the embedded shared secret shown in the command while the same image continues to be pulled.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Assign a managed identity to the container group but keep the registry user name and password so the pull of the images still uses the shared secret: Assigning an identity is only half of the change: keeping --registry-username and --registry-password means the pull still authenticates with the shared secret, and those credentials remain in the group definition and in the deployment command, which is exactly what the requirement forbids.
- Pass the registry user name and password to the container group as environment variables and let the image pull authenticate with them: Environment variables still place the registry user name and password inside the container group definition, and the pull still authenticates as a shared secret rather than as the group itself. Moving the secret to a variable hides it on the command line but does not remove the stored credentials, so the stated requirement is not met.
- Create a private endpoint for the registry and place the container group in a delegated subnet of the same virtual network: A private endpoint and a delegated subnet control network reachability to the registry, not authentication. With this change the group would still need the registry user name and password to perform the pull, so the credentials remain in the definition.

You have deployed a container group to Azure Container Instances to run an image-processing pipeline. Each job pulls a message from a queue, writes its output to Azure Storage and then exits; if a job is stopped partway, the queue hands the message to another worker, so no work is lost. Finance wants the smallest compute bill for this workload, and the operations team has confirmed that cutting the pipeline short and retrying it later has no business impact. The group was created with the command below and is running today.

You need the container group to run under the deployment option that gives the lowest cost for this workload while tolerating interruption. Which change should you make to the container group?

options.text: Deploy the container group as a Spot container so that it uses unused Azure capacity and may be evicted
Deploy the container group with the Confidential SKU so that it can be hardware-isolated and its memory is encrypted by Azure
Deploy the container group with a standby pool so that new containers start faster and the group scales out in Azure
Deploy the container group as part of an NGroup in Azure so that a target count is maintained and upgrades roll across groups

explanation:
The Spot variant places a container group on spare Azure capacity, is priced up to 70% below regular-priority containers, and is billed per second of memory and core usage. Azure is allowed to preempt such a group whenever it needs the room back. In this pipeline every job is independent, its output is already persisted and the queue redelivers the message, so being stopped early costs nothing in business terms and the group can be re-created later. That makes the Spot variant the cheapest deployment option for this workload. The group's CPU, memory and restart policy have no effect on this price difference; the group shown is currently a regular-priority Standard deployment, so it should be redeployed with the Spot variant.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Deploy the container group with the Confidential SKU so that it can be hardware-isolated and its memory is encrypted by Azure: Choosing the Confidential SKU protects data while it is in memory and provides hardware-level isolation and integrity through a trusted execution environment. It does not change the price model, so it does not deliver the lowest cost for this workload.
- Deploy the container group with a standby pool so that new containers start faster and the group scales out in Azure: A standby pool keeps pre-warmed instances so that new containers start faster, which helps latency for scale-out. It keeps regular pricing and does not make the workload evictable, so it does not lower the bill in the way this pipeline needs.
- Deploy the container group as part of an NGroup in Azure so that a target count is maintained and upgrades roll across groups: NGroups provide fleet-level control over several linked groups: a maintained target count, coordinated rolling upgrades, placement across zones and load-balanced ingress. That suits a set of related long-running groups, but it does not offer the discounted, interruptible pricing this workload is after.

ACI NGroups with an ingress load balancer in front of several related groups

- A single Azure Container Instances container group that runs the application image directly: A single container group is an isolated container on ACI with no Kubernetes API, no cluster scheduling, and no support for applying the Deployment and HorizontalPodAutoscaler objects shown, so the application's rollout and scaling process would not work.

prompt: Payments API

options.text: Confidential SKU for the container group
Standby pool for the container group
Application Gateway in front of the container group
NGroups fleet for the container group

explanation: The four rows call for four different service capabilities. A container group's IP address can change when the group is replaced or bounced by platform maintenance, so the Payments API needs Application Gateway in front of the group to give clients a fixed public address. The video encoder needs the shortest delay before a new group can serve traffic, which standby pools deliver by keeping prepared capacity ready in advance. The claims processor must keep data in use protected from the host, which the Confidential SKU provides by running the workload in a trusted execution environment with hardware-based protections and memory encryption. The reporting estate needs coordinated rolling upgrades and a maintained target number of running groups across many related groups, which is exactly what NGroups delivers.

Your team runs container groups on Azure Container Instances, and you are writing the runbook that the support engineers follow. Each row of the table describes one action that must be possible. You need to attach the right command or portal step to each row. Drag the command or portal step that carries out each action into the matching row.

- Task: T1; Action the runbook must make possible: Deploy a new container group from a picture published in a public registry, for a job that should run once and then stop.
- Task: T2; Action the runbook must make possible: Confirm that a job container which has already finished is reported as stopped, and capture the exit code it returned.
- Task: T3; Action the runbook must make possible: Read back the text that the container's application printed to standard output, so the results can be pasted into the runbook.
- Task: T4; Action the runbook must make possible: Remove a container group that is no longer needed, and answer the prompt that appears afterwards.
prompt: Task T1

options.text: az container create
az container show
az container logs
Overview > Delete

explanation: Each row is handled by a different step. T1 is the deployment of the group, which is done with az container create; the same command carries the --restart-policy parameter (Always, Never or OnFailure) that decides what happens to a job once its process ends. context:
You have deployed a container group on Azure Container Instances that serves a partner-facing web workload. The partner's clients resolve the group's public hostname once and cache the resulting IP address for several hours. After Azure carried out a maintenance restart of the group, those clients could no longer connect, even though the container was healthy and none of its settings had changed. You need the partner to keep using a single public address that stays valid when the container group restarts, and your team does not want to manage any virtual machines. Which Azure service should you place in front of the container group?

- Observation: Before the maintenance restart; DNS name label: partnerapi; Public IP address of the container group: 20.62.190.5
- Observation: After the maintenance restart; DNS name label: partnerapi; Public IP address of the container group: 20.51.64.18
prompt: The Azure service that should front the container group so the partner keeps one unchanged public address is _____.

options.text: Application Gateway
Front Door
Traffic Manager
API Management

explanation:
A container group's own address is not guaranteed to stay the same: when the group restarts, its IP address can change, which is what the exhibit shows, so the address the partner cached no longer reaches the workload. For a static public IP address in this situation, the Azure Container Instances guidance specifies putting Application Gateway in front of the container group, so clients keep one unchanged front-end address without the team provisioning or maintaining virtual machines.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Front Door: Front Door is a global edge and content-delivery service for web experiences. It is not the component named in the Azure Container Instances guidance for giving a container group a stable public address.
- Traffic Manager: Traffic Manager routes traffic at the DNS level to endpoints in different regions and does not act as the component that fronts the container group with one fixed address.
- API Management: API Management adds API publishing, policies, and subscriptions on top of an existing endpoint; for a container group whose address changes on restart, the guidance points to Application Gateway as the component placed in front of the group.

The group runs one Linux container whose image comes from the company's own registry, and it mounts an Azure Files share to keep each day's output. The provider's security addendum requires that patient records stay protected while the application is reading them in memory, and that no other customer's workload share the same physical hardware as this group. The image and the one-container layout cannot change. You need the running group to meet the addendum. Which deployment option should you choose for this container group?

prompt: The container group should be deployed as _____.

options.text: Confidential containers
Regular containers
Spot containers

explanation:
Confidential containers on ACI run inside a trusted execution environment that provides hardware-based confidentiality and integrity protection for the workload; they protect data in use and encrypt the data being processed in memory, and they are selected as a SKU when you deploy the workload. The provider's addendum demands protection for the records while the application is using them in memory and hardware-level isolation from other customers, so the group must be deployed as Confidential containers.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Regular containers: Regular containers are the standard variant of the service: a container on ACI is isolated at the hypervisor level, about as strongly as it would be inside a virtual machine, but the group adds no trusted execution environment and no encryption of data held in memory, so it does not satisfy the addendum.
- Spot containers: Spot containers run interruptible workloads on unused Azure capacity at a discount of up to 70% and may be preempted whenever Azure is short on spare capacity. What they change is price and eviction behaviour; they add no protection for data held in memory, so they do not satisfy the addendum.

The command below creates a container group for an internal service. Our company operates several Azure subscriptions under one organization, and a published naming standard requires that every container group we create in any of those subscriptions uses the same public hostname label, so that a service can be re-created in a different subscription without changing the address its clients call. Our auditors also require that no workload outside the company can register the same label, because the group's fully qualified domain name depends on a generated hash that guards against malicious subdomain takeover. Which value should you use for the DNS name label scope reuse of this container group?

`az container create \
  --resource-group rg-contoso-platform \
  --name contoso-api \
  --image mcr.microsoft.com/azuredocs/aci-helloworld:latest \

prompt: You should set the DNS name label scope reuse of the container group to _____.

options.text: Tenant
Subscription
Resource Group
Any reuse

explanation:
The Tenant scope lets groups created anywhere in the company's own directory claim the same label, including groups placed in different subscriptions, while keeping the label out of reach of workloads from other organizations. That satisfies both halves of the requirement: the naming standard must hold across all of the company's subscriptions, and the label must not be registerable from outside the company, which preserves the protection that the generated hash in the fully qualified domain name gives against malicious subdomain takeover. The Subscription and Resource Group scopes are too narrow for a standard that must hold across every subscription the company owns, and Any reuse opens the label to every workload on the service.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Subscription: Subscription: This scope only permits reuse among groups that live in the same Azure subscription, so a group re-created in one of the company's other subscriptions could not register the same label and the naming standard would break.
- Resource Group: Resource Group: This scope only permits reuse among groups in the same resource group, which is narrower than the Subscription scope and therefore even less able to satisfy a naming standard that must hold across all of the company's subscriptions.
- Any reuse: Any reuse: This is the least secure option, because any group from any organization could register the same label; that broad reuse weakens the protection that the generated hash in the fully qualified domain name provides against malicious subdomain takeover.

The script runs unattended, and a colleague who can read the container group in the portal was able to print that credential in clear text. You need the credential to stop being readable that way, while the container still has to receive the value when it starts. Which change should you make to the deployment?

`az container create \
  --resource-group rg-payments-prod \

prompt: To satisfy the security requirement without changing what the running container receives, the deployment should _____.

options.text: pass the credential in a CLI environment variable
pass the credential base64-encoded on the command line
pass the credential in the container group's environment settings
pass the credential as a plain argument on the command line

explanation:
Credentials that are handed to the tool on the command line are kept as plain text in the backend, which is exactly what the portal reader exploited. Microsoft advises keeping user credentials in CLI environment variables so that they are encrypted or transformed when they are written to the backend. Changing the script so the partner credential is supplied through a CLI environment variable therefore removes the recoverable plain-text copy while the container still gets the secret at start-up.

Why the other options are wrong:
- pass the credential base64-encoded on the command line: Base64 is an encoding, not encryption, so the value that reaches the backend can still be decoded by anyone who can read the group's stored configuration; the credential stays recoverable.
- pass the credential in the container group's environment settings: Values entered as part of the container group's own environment settings become part of the group's definition and stay visible to anyone who can read the resource, so the credential remains readable in clear text.
- pass the credential as a plain argument on the command line: This is the behaviour the security team flagged: a credential typed on the command line is stored as plain text in the backend, so changing nothing here leaves the exposure in place.

Your team runs a nightly data-import job as a container group on Azure Container Instances, created with the command shown below. When it starts, the job fetches its database connection string from Azure Key Vault, and it prints a summary of every record it imported to standard output before it exits. Company policy states that no credential may be written into the container group definition or into the job's environment variables, and the support team must be able to read what the job printed after the run has finished. You need the container group to sign in to Microsoft Entra-supported services without any embedded credential, and you need the command that returns what the job printed.

Service principal with a client secret
Shared access key
User name and password

explanation:
Enabling a managed identity on the container group gives the group its own identity in Microsoft Entra, so it can authenticate to Azure Key Vault and to any other service that supports Microsoft Entra authentication without a user name, password or secret held in the container group definition or in environment variables. The job writes its summary to the standard output stream, and the az container logs command returns that stdout stream for the named container group, so it is the command the support team should run once the run has finished.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Service principal with a client secret: A service principal only authenticates when you also supply a secret or certificate, so a credential would have to be stored with the group, which the company policy forbids. A managed identity is created and rotated by the platform, so nothing has to be stored for the group to sign in.
- Shared access key: A shared access key is a static secret the group would have to carry with it, so it fails the requirement that no credential is kept with the deployment.
- User name and password: A user name and password are exactly the kind of stored credential the policy prohibits, and the service does not issue them to the container group.

A container group can be pinned to an availability zone that you choose yourself, and the zone is decided one group at a time. On the Basics tab, the Availability zones setting is where you pick that zone, so setting it to the zone that the owning team named places the workload in the same zone as its storage account. Spreading a fleet of related groups across zones is a fleet-level capability (NGroups multi-zone placement), not a per-group setting.
- Set Availability zones to the zone where the resource group was created: Resource groups are not tied to availability zones, so the zone of a resource group is not a valid choice. The zone for a group comes from the Availability zones setting on the group's creation page.
