prompt: You have a container registry on the Standard pricing plan in West Europe. Two CI agents and the Kubernetes cluster's image puller sign in with the registry's built-in administrator account to pull and push images, and an internal catalogue serves the same images to partners without signing in. During yesterday's release window, `docker pull` and `docker push` began failing with `429 Too Many Requests`, and the measurements collected during the failures are shown below. You need the release pipeline to finish reliably without running into the registry's limits, and the pricing plan cannot change this quarter. Which change should you make?

options.text: Sign in each CI agent and the cluster puller with separate Microsoft Entra ID service principals, and grant each principal only the registry permissions needed for that workload
Sign in each CI agent and the cluster puller with the shared administrator account, and raise the number of parallel pull and push operations

Sign in each CI agent and the cluster puller with one new Microsoft Entra ID service principal that has the built-in administrator role and registry permissions at the registry scope, and keep the administrator account for setup only
Sign in each CI agent and the cluster puller with separate Microsoft Entra ID service principals, and raise the number of parallel pull and push operations at the same time

explanation:
The registry-wide allowances on the Standard plan (10,000 requests/min for DataplaneRead, 4,000 for MetadataRead, 2,000 for DataplaneWrite) are all higher than the totals in the exhibit, so the registry as a whole is not the constraint. The failing traffic comes from one identity: the built-in administrator account's password and password2 share a single identity bucket, and on Standard a single identity is capped at 5,000 requests/min for reads (MetadataRead calls also consume that read capacity) and 1,000 for writes. The measurements put that identity at roughly 7,120 read-equivalent requests/min and 1,010 writes/min, so it is over its allowance while the registry-wide totals stay under the caps. Moving each CI agent and the cluster puller onto its own Microsoft Entra ID service principal puts each one in its own per-identity bucket, and RBAC lets you assign each principal only the permissions it needs; total traffic still fits inside the plan's registry-wide caps, so the release can complete without changing the plan.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Sign in each CI agent and the cluster puller with the shared administrator account, and raise the number of parallel pull and push operations: All components keep authenticating with the built-in administrator account, so every request stays in the one identity bucket the measurements show is already past its per-identity read and write allowances. Raising the number of parallel pull and push operations only pushes more requests into that same exhausted bucket and makes the failures more likely.
- Sign in each CI agent and the cluster puller with one new Microsoft Entra ID service principal that has the built-in administrator role and registry permissions at the registry scope, and keep the administrator account for setup only: A single new service principal is still a single identity, so all pipeline traffic is metered against one per-identity bucket instead of being spread across several; the registry-wide totals shown are not the constraint, so nothing improves. The built-in administrator role at the registry scope also grants far more access than the pipeline requires.
- Sign in each CI agent and the cluster puller with separate Microsoft Entra ID service principals, and raise the number of parallel pull and push operations at the same time: Separate service principals do spread the traffic across per-identity buckets, but raising the number of parallel pull and push operations pushes the combined request rate at the registry-wide allowances and at the continuously refilling token bucket, which can keep requests throttled for up to a minute. Working around throttling means lowering concurrency and staggering deployments, not increasing concurrency.

prompt: You have a container registry that stores the images for a shared internal API service. Every pod that starts fails with `manifest unknown`, although the image tags are visible in the portal under the registry's repositories. You need the new cluster to pull the images that are already stored in this registry. Which change should you make?

options.text: Update the image reference in the pull secret to the login server of the registry
Change the Domain Name Label scope of the registry to Unsecure and update the image reference in the pull secret to the plain login server address
Enable the admin account of the registry, re-push the image to the plain login server address, and rewrite the pull secret
Enable anonymous pull access on the registry so that the cluster pulls the image reference in the pull secret without credentials

explanation:
The registry's Domain Name Label scope is not Unsecure, so it publishes under a protected address (contosoapi-9c1d4f7a.azurecr.io) that carries a unique suffix instead of the plain contosoapi.azurecr.io name. The portal's Login server is that protected address, and every downstream reference — Dockerfiles, Kubernetes YAML, Helm charts and Docker commands — must use that fully qualified name exactly. The pull secret still names the plain address, which does not host the repository, so the pull fails with 'manifest unknown' even though the tags exist. Pointing the image reference at the registry's login server makes the cluster pull the images already stored in the registry.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Change the Domain Name Label scope of the registry to Unsecure and update the image reference in the pull secret to the plain login server address: The Domain Name Label scope is chosen when the registry is created and is permanent, so an existing registry cannot be switched to the Unsecure scope; that scope only leaves the plain name.azurecr.io address unprotected when it was selected at creation time. For this registry the fix is to reference its actual login server, not to alter the scope.
- Enable the admin account of the registry, re-push the image to the plain login server address, and rewrite the pull secret: Enabling the admin account changes how a client authenticates, not which address hosts the repository, and re-pushing under the plain login server address would fail for the same reason as the current pull, because the plain name does not point to this registry. The observed error is an address mismatch, not an authentication failure.
- Enable anonymous pull access on the registry so that the cluster pulls the image reference in the pull secret without credentials: Anonymous pull access only removes the need for credentials; it does not change the address the pull secret uses, so the pods would still fail with 'manifest unknown'. It is supported on Standard and Premium (not Basic) and would only be relevant once the image reference points at the correct host.

explanation:
The shared image shown in the exhibit (contosoapp.azurecr.io/python:3.12) is the image the application image is built from, and it lives in the same registry. Azure Container Registry tasks can be configured to rebuild dependent application images automatically when their base images are updated, so adding a base-image update trigger turns today's on-demand build into a reaction to the dependency you actually care about: each newly published version of the shared image immediately produces a rebuilt and pushed application image, with nobody running a command.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add a source-code commit trigger so the task rebuilds and pushes the application image automatically: A source-code commit trigger automates image builds when your team commits code to a Git repository, and setting one up requires a personal access token for that repository. The task's context here is a local directory uploaded by a developer, and the shared image is republished on its own schedule, so a commit trigger would not rebuild the application image when the shared image changes.
- Add a pull-request trigger so the task rebuilds and pushes the application image automatically: A pull-request trigger reacts to pull request activity in the configured Git repository rather than to the shared image. It would also need a personal access token for that repository, and nothing in the scenario ties new pull requests to the publication of a new shared image, so the application image would still be built from an out-of-date shared image.
- Add a timer trigger so the task rebuilds and pushes the application image automatically: A timer trigger runs the task on a fixed schedule whether or not the shared image changed. It therefore cannot guarantee a rebuild within minutes of each newly published version of the shared image, and it also spends build time producing identical images when nothing has changed.

The platform team wants the engineers who own the payments service to push only to the payments repository, and only when the image tag follows the approved release naming pattern; the runtime services that pull images from this registry must keep the rights they hold today. You need the registry itself to enforce that tag restriction, without removing the Microsoft Entra ID assignments that already exist. The registry's current configuration and assignments are shown below.

Which change should you make?

options.text: Keep the RBAC role assignment permissions mode as it is and widen the engineers' assignment to registry scope.
Set the role assignment permissions mode to RBAC Registry + ABAC Repository Permissions, applying a condition to repository-level access while the existing assignments stay in force.
Keep the RBAC role assignment permissions mode as it is and add the tag pattern as a condition on the existing repository-scoped role assignment, leaving the assignments as they are.
Keep the RBAC role assignment permissions mode as it is and enforce the approved tag pattern inside the release pipeline that builds and pushes the images.

explanation:
The permissions mode named RBAC Registry + ABAC Repository Permissions is the one that retains the standard Microsoft Entra ID RBAC role assignments while optionally applying Microsoft Entra attribute-based conditions for fine-grained, repository-level access control. Switching the registry to that mode is the only way to express the tag restriction on the payments repository without discarding the registry-scoped pull assignment that the runtime services rely on, so it satisfies both halves of the requirement.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Keep the RBAC role assignment permissions mode as it is and widen the engineers' assignment to registry scope: Widening the engineers' assignment to registry scope grants them push rights on every repository in the registry, which is broader than what the platform team asked for, and leaving the mode purely role-based means nothing ties those rights to the tag naming pattern. The requirement is a narrower, tag-conditioned grant, not a broader one.
- Keep the RBAC role assignment permissions mode as it is and add the tag pattern as a condition on the existing repository-scoped role assignment, leaving the assignments as they are: Repository-level attribute-based conditions are provided by the combined permissions mode. With the role-based mode left in place, attaching a condition to the repository-scoped assignment does not turn it into a conditional grant, so the engineers would keep unrestricted push rights on that repository and the tag restriction would not be enforced.
- Keep the RBAC role assignment permissions mode as it is and enforce the approved tag pattern inside the release pipeline that builds and pushes the images: The release pipeline is not part of the registry's access model. An engineer who holds push rights can still push an image with any tag directly to the registry, so the tag restriction is not enforced by the registry itself and the requirement is not met.

IP access rule configuration

You have three container registries to deploy, each with the requirements shown below. You need every registry to run on the pricing plan that satisfies its requirements at the lowest cost. Which pricing plan should you assign to each registry?

- Registry: A; Purpose and requirements: Course labs for students. Only a handful of test images are pushed and pulled, and each registry is deleted when the course ends.
- Registry: B; Purpose and requirements: A partner catalogue of sample applications. People who do not sign in must be able to retrieve the published images, and the platform also relies on artifact cache rules to avoid repeated downloads.
- Registry: C; Purpose and requirements: Release images for services running in two Azure regions. The registry must be reachable only from the company network over Azure private link, and the same images must keep serving clients in the second region.
prompt: Registry A

options.text: Basic
Standard
Premium

explanation: Registry A only has to push and pull a few test images for learning and development, so the cheapest tier, which is aimed at learning and test workloads, is enough. Registry B needs unauthenticated pulls and artifact cache rules: neither is offered on Basic, and Standard supports both, so Standard is the least expensive plan that meets its requirements. Registry C needs Azure private link with private endpoints and the same images served from a second region; private endpoints and geo-replication are available only on the top tier, so that tier is the only choice for Registry C.

You have an Azure Container Registry that stores the release images for your Kubernetes platform, and a quarterly change window is approaching in which the registry must also serve a locked-down network segment. The registry's current configuration is shown below. During the window, a release engineer works from a workstation that has the Azure CLI and the Docker client installed; the freshly built application image is already on that workstation, already named with the registry's address and the release label v2.

Four jobs have to be completed during the window. The list of commands below contains several commands that are not part of this work. Match each job to the command that performs it.

- Property: Registry name; Value: contosoapp
- Property: Resource group; Value: rg-apps
- Property: Location; Value: East US
- Property: Pricing plan; Value: Standard
- Property: Domain Name Label scope; Value: Subscription Reuse
- Property: Login server; Value: contosoapp-9f3a.azurecr.io
prompt: Authorize the workstation's client so that it can talk to the registry before any images are transferred

options.text: az acr login --name contosoapp
docker push contosoapp-9f3a.azurecr.io/paymentsapi:v2
az acr show-usage --name contosoapp
az acr update --name contosoapp --sku Premium
docker rmi contosoapp-9f3a.azurecr.io/paymentsapi:v2
az acr login --name contosoapp-9f3a.azurecr.io
docker tag paymentsapi:build contosoapp-9f3a.azurecr.io/paymentsapi:v2
docker push contosoapp.azurecr.io/paymentsapi:v2

explanation: Each job maps onto exactly one of the listed commands. Signing in to the registry is done with the registry resource name only, so `az acr login --name contosoapp` is the right form; the login server is never passed to that command. Transferring the locally built image into the registry requires the registry's login server exactly as shown for this registry, and because the Domain Name Label scope is a protected one the address carries the DNS hash, so `docker push contosoapp-9f3a.azurecr.io/paymentsapi:v2` puts the image where the cluster can retrieve it. Current consumption of storage and other plan allowances is reported by `az acr show-usage --name contosoapp`. Finally, private link with private endpoints and the network rules are only part of the Premium pricing plan, and `az acr update --name contosoapp --sku Premium` is the documented way to move a registry onto that plan, which is allowed from Standard without downtime.

You manage the container registry described below, which stores release images for several internal services. During the release window your support channel collected the observations listed here. You need to route each observation to the owner who can act on it, together with the underlying reason for it; two of the observations are not explained by any of the reasons.

Match each observation to the reason that best explains it.

- Property: Registry name; Value: contosoapp
- Property: Pricing plan; Value: Premium
- Property: Location; Value: West Europe
- Property: Geo-replication; Value: East US, Sweden Central
- Property: Admin account; Value: Enabled
prompt: Rate limit exhausted for that caller

options.text: Pushing and pulling during the release window returned 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header; the errors stopped once the release paused.
The storage total shown for the registry has stayed at 480 GiB for two days, while the team pushed an estimated 1.4 TiB of images in total.
Two scheduled jobs authenticate with the registry's built-in administrator account, the first with the primary password and the second with the other password; each is throttled at the same level.
A client that only enumerates image metadata and tags is rejected with 429, while the registry's overall traffic stays far below its published capacity.
Webhook creation fails with a message that the pricing plan does not permit that many.
A push of a very large image is refused with a message about the maximum size permitted for a single layer.

explanation: Each of the four observations maps to a documented behavior of the service. x1: exceeding a request rate limit returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header; limits are enforced with a token bucket that refills continuously, tolerates short bursts, and can keep rejecting requests for up to a minute after a burst empties it, which matches errors that clear when the release pauses (c1). x2: in a geo-replicated registry, storage usage is reported for the home region only, so the figure must be multiplied by the number of replicas - 480 GiB x 3 regions = 1,440 GiB, about 1.4 TiB (c2). x3: the admin account has two passwords, password and password2, but both share the same identity for throttling, so all admin-credential requests are throttled together as a single identity (c3). x4: MetadataRead requests, such as listing repositories, tags and manifests, also count against the DataplaneRead limit, so a client that only enumerates metadata can be throttled while overall traffic stays well below the allowance (c4). The webhook quota and the maximum single layer and manifest sizes are separate plan limits and explain none of the four observations (x5, x6).

context: You have a platform team that is about to create five Azure Container Registry instances for different purposes, and the team wants a deliberate rule for the suffix that Azure appends to the registry name. You need to pick that rule for each of the five creation situations below, and the pick is permanent once the registry exists. Which Domain Name Label scope should you choose for each situation?
prompt: A disposable lab registry that should keep its plain azurecr.io address

options.text: Unsecure
Tenant Reuse
Subscription Reuse
Resource Group Reuse
No Reuse

explanation: Each Domain Name Label scope fixes how the suffix is derived when a registry is created, and the scope cannot be changed afterwards. The plain-address choice keeps the registry reachable as name.azurecr.io with no takeover protection. The three sharing choices each reuse one hash within their own boundary: across the Entra tenant, across the subscription, and across the resource group. The last choice produces a fresh hash at every creation, so each registry gets a suffix of its own. Because Dockerfiles, Kubernetes manifests, and Helm charts must reference the resulting hashed address, each creation situation has to be matched to the scope that defines its sharing boundary.

context:
You have a container registry on the Premium pricing plan. It was created in East US, and its content is also served from West Europe and Southeast Asia. Since last Thursday's release, some image pulls from the West Europe cluster have been rejected with HTTP 429 responses, and the finance team has asked for the registry's storage total ahead of the next budget review. You have access to the registry's metrics and logs in Azure Monitor. Which Azure Monitor filter should you apply to find the requests that were rejected, and what storage total should you report to the finance team?

`PROPERTY                                 VALUE
Pricing plan                            Premium
Region where the registry was created    East US
Additional replication regions           West Europe, Southeast Asia
Maximum storage for the pricing plan    100 TiB
Storage reported by the registry        2.4 TiB`
prompt: Apply _____ to isolate the rejected requests, and report [...] to the finance team as the registry's storage total.

options.text: Transactions filtered on ResponseType = Throttled, split by ApiName and Region
DataTransfer filtered on ResponseType = Throttled, split by ApiName and Region
StorageUsed split by ApiName and Region
Transactions split by ApiName and Region with no filter applied

explanation:
Two separate facts drive the answer. First, to find the rejected requests, the registry's request records carry a response type, so filtering Transactions on ResponseType = Throttled and splitting by ApiName and Region shows exactly which operations and which regions were turned away; DataTransfer measures bytes moved rather than rejections, the StorageUsed metric tracks storage, and unfiltered Transactions mixes successful calls into the result. Second, for a registry that replicates to more than one region, the storage figure the registry reports covers only the region where it was created, so the whole registry holds 2.4 TiB times three regions = 7.2 TiB.

Why the other options are wrong:
- DataTransfer filtered on ResponseType = Throttled, split by ApiName and Region: DataTransfer records how much data was transferred for each operation; it holds no rejected-call detail, so filtering it cannot reveal which requests the registry turned away.
- StorageUsed split by ApiName and Region: The StorageUsed metric reports how much storage the registry holds; it carries no response type and no per-operation breakdown, so it cannot isolate rejected requests.
- Transactions split by ApiName and Region with no filter applied: Without a filter, Transactions returns every call, including the successful pulls and pushes, so it does not isolate the requests that were rejected.

context:
You own an Azure Container Registry that stores the delivery images for your organisation. The pipeline that produces those images is described below; today it runs on an external build server where an engineer starts each step in turn, so a full run takes more than an hour and nothing happens when nobody is watching. You want the registry to carry out the whole sequence on its own inside Azure, as one job, with the steps that do not depend on each other performed at the same time so that a run finishes far sooner. Which ACR Tasks feature should the platform team use?

`Step | Work carried out
1    | Compile the shared image from the common sources
2    | Run the integration test suite inside the compiled image (needs step 1)
3    | Compile a patched variant of the shared image
4    | Push the compiled and patched images into the registry (needs steps 1 and 3)`
prompt: The platform team should use _____.

options.text: A multi-step task
A single-step task
A base-image trigger
A source-code commit trigger

explanation:
The requirement is that the registry itself runs the whole sequence — compile, test, patched variant, push — as one job in Azure, with the parts that do not depend on each other performed at the same time. Azure Container Registry tasks cover exactly this: tasks build images in Azure on demand, and a multi-step task builds, tests and patches images in parallel in the cloud, so the independent steps of the sequence run simultaneously and the whole run happens inside the registry service rather than on an external server.

Why the other options are wrong:
- A single-step task: A single-step task performs one operation per run, so it cannot carry out the compile, test, patched-variant and push steps as one job, and it offers no mechanism for running independent steps at the same time.
- A base-image trigger: A base-image trigger only determines when a task is invoked, for example when a referenced base image receives a new version. It says nothing about how several steps of a pipeline are composed and executed within one task run, so it does not meet the requirement.
- A source-code commit trigger: A source-code commit trigger likewise decides when a task starts based on commits made to the source repository. It does not provide a way to run the several steps of the pipeline together in one task, so it does not meet the requirement.

context:
Your data-science team builds a training tool together with its model weights into a container image and pushes it to the Azure Container Registry that already holds the platform's other images. Every push attempt is refused, and the message returned by the registry points at the 240 GiB layer inside that image as the reason. The registry's current state is shown below. You need the analytics image stored in this same registry alongside the others, and the platform team does not want to run a second registry for it. Which change should you make?

`Property              | Value
----------------------|-----------------
Pricing plan          | Standard
Region                | West Europe
Storage consumed      | 35 TiB
Repositories          | 46
Webhooks configured   | 5
Anonymous pull access | Enabled`
prompt: You should _____.

options.text: repackage the image so that each layer stays under the per-layer ceiling the registry applies
move the registry to the Premium pricing plan, which permits larger layers
ask Azure Support to raise the registry's storage ceiling so the image can be pushed as it is
enable zone redundancy on the registry so the large layer is kept across availability zones

explanation:
The registry applies the same maximum image layer size of 195 GiB (and a maximum manifest size of 4 MiB) on Basic, Standard and Premium, so the refusal is caused by the 240 GiB layer in the image and not by anything a different plan would change. Repackaging the image so that no layer goes over that per-layer ceiling is the change that lets the push succeed; changing the pricing plan or asking for more storage leaves the layer ceiling exactly where it is.

Why the other options are wrong:
- move the registry to the Premium pricing plan, which permits larger layers: Moving to Premium leaves the per-layer ceiling unchanged at 195 GiB, because every pricing plan enforces the same maximum image layer size and manifest size. Premium mainly adds included storage, higher throughput, geo-replication and private link, none of which widens the layer limit.
- ask Azure Support to raise the registry's storage ceiling so the image can be pushed as it is: Azure Support can raise a registry's storage limit, its private endpoint count and its push/pull performance limits, but the per-layer and per-manifest size ceilings are not among the limits that can be increased, and this push is failing because of layer size rather than because storage ran out.
- enable zone redundancy on the registry so the large layer is kept across availability zones: Zone redundancy concerns how the registry's storage is replicated across availability zones in the region; it does not change how large an individual layer may be, and that ceiling is identical on every pricing plan.

context:
You sell containerized software to appliance manufacturers whose build farms run in their own data centers and have no identity in your directory. Compliance rules forbid registering the manufacturers' systems in your directory, so every build farm must be given a credential that the registry issues itself, restricted to pulling images from that manufacturer's own repository. Each farm must hold its own credential so that revoking one manufacturer's access does not disturb the others, and all of the manufacturers' images have to remain in this single registry. The registry and the credentials already issued are described below.

You need the registry to support every build farm with its own individual credential. Which change should you make?

`Registry name: contosoparts.azurecr.io
Location: West Europe
Pricing plan: Standard
Non-Microsoft Entra tokens issued: 470
Scope maps in use: 470
Manufacturer build farms that must sign in: 600
Repositories each credential may pull from: 1
Identities available to the manufacturers in the directory: None`
prompt: The registry should run on the _____ pricing plan so that every build farm can be given its own scoped credential.

options.text: Run the registry on the Premium pricing plan
Run the registry on the Standard pricing plan and request a higher token limit from Azure Support
Run the registry on the Standard pricing plan and let all build farms share a single scoped credential
Run the registry on the Standard pricing plan and give each build farm the registry's administrator credentials

explanation:
Each build farm needs its own credential issued by the registry itself, with permissions limited to one manufacturer repository, which is what a non-Microsoft Entra token bound to a scope map provides. The Standard plan allows only 500 such tokens, so the 600 individually revocable credentials the manufacturers need do not fit, and the number of tokens is one of the registry limits that Azure Support cannot raise. The Premium plan allows 50,000 non-Microsoft Entra tokens, so running the registry on Premium is the only way to issue one token per build farm. Repository-scoped permissions with non-Microsoft Entra tokens and scope maps remain supported there, and a Premium scope map can cover up to 500 repositories with up to 500 actions, so restricting each credential to a single manufacturer repository is fully achievable.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Run the registry on the Standard pricing plan and request a higher token limit from Azure Support: The maximum number of non-Microsoft Entra tokens is a fixed limit: only storage limits, private endpoint counts, and push/pull performance limits can be increased through an Azure Support request, while token and scope map counts cannot. The Standard plan also caps tokens at 500, which is fewer than the 600 separate credentials the build farms need, so neither half of this option satisfies the requirement.
- Run the registry on the Standard pricing plan and let all build farms share a single scoped credential: A single shared credential cannot be revoked for one manufacturer without affecting every other one, and it cannot limit each manufacturer to its own repository, so it breaks the stated requirement of individually revocable, per-partner credentials. It also does not give each build farm a credential of its own, which is the control the partners are being asked to accept.
- Run the registry on the Standard pricing plan and give each build farm the registry's administrator credentials: The built-in administrator account grants broad access to the whole registry and cannot be restricted to a single manufacturer's repository, so it fails the per-partner restriction. It would also mean every build farm shares one credential, which is exactly what must be avoided, and all of that traffic would count against a single identity for throttling.

context:
You are standing up a shared container registry for four product teams with an infrastructure pipeline. The creation step fails and nothing is deployed; the output below is everything the pipeline recorded. The team standard requires the registry name to carry the environment and the year, and the same name will be referenced from every Dockerfile and Helm chart once the registry exists. Which change should you make?

`$ az acr create --name fabrikam-2026-prod --resource-group rg-platform --sku Standard --location westeurope
ERROR: The registry name is invalid.`
prompt: The team should _____.

options.text: Create the registry with a name made up of letters and digits only
Create the registry with a name made up of letters, digits, and dashes
Create the registry with a name made up of letters and digits that is three characters long
Create the registry with the same name in a different resource group

explanation:
A registry name must be unique across Azure, must be 5 to 50 characters long, and may be built only from letters and digits, so dashes are not permitted (they are the delimiter used in the hashed DNS name of protected registries). The submitted name fabrikam-2026-prod is rejected because of the dashes it carries; its length is already within the permitted range and it is not too long. Removing the dashes keeps the environment and the year in the name, produces a name the service accepts, and that name then forms the registry's fully qualified DNS address used in Dockerfiles and Helm charts.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Create the registry with a name made up of letters, digits, and dashes: Dashes are excluded from a registry name because they are used as the delimiter in the hashed DNS name of protected registries, so a name that keeps them is refused again.
- Create the registry with a name made up of letters and digits that is three characters long: A name shorter than five characters is refused as well, and the submitted name was already inside the permitted 5-50 character range, so trimming it to three characters does not address the validation failure.
- Create the registry with the same name in a different resource group: The name is validated in the same way regardless of where the registry is placed, so deploying the identical name in another resource group leaves the dashes in place and the creation fails exactly as before.

context:
You have a container registry that stores the release images for three internal services. It runs on the Standard pricing plan in West Europe and currently holds 23.5 GiB of content. Finance has asked what the registry charges for keeping that content and how much content it could hold before it stops taking anything further. The registry's current configuration is shown below.

You need to answer finance with a single description. Which description should you give?

- Property: Pricing plan; Value: Standard
- Property: Location; Value: West Europe
- Property: Content stored; Value: 23.5 GiB
- Property: Repositories; Value: 7
- Property: Webhooks configured; Value: 6
prompt: The charge for the registry's stored content is _____, and the greatest amount of content this registry can hold is [...].

options.text: covered by the plan's charge up to the amount included with the plan, with storage above that billed per GiB
billed per GiB for every GiB stored, in addition to the amount included with the plan
covered by the plan's charge up to the amount included with the plan, with storage above that free of charge
covered by the plan's charge up to the amount included with the plan, with storage above that refused until the plan is changed

explanation:
The storage that comes with the plan is part of that plan's charge, so it is not billed again; anything stored above that included amount is charged per GiB until the tier's ceiling is reached, and going beyond the ceiling means opening an Azure Support request. On the Standard tier the ceiling for total stored content is 40 TiB, the same maximum as Basic — only the Premium tier goes higher, to 100 TiB.

Why the other options are wrong:
- billed per GiB for every GiB stored, in addition to the amount included with the plan: Billing every stored GiB on top of the plan's charge would also bill for the storage that the plan already includes; only the amount above the included storage is charged per GiB.
- covered by the plan's charge up to the amount included with the plan, with storage above that free of charge: Storage beyond the included amount is not free: once the included amount is used up, the excess is charged per GiB. Azure Support is only involved if the total would pass the tier's maximum.
- covered by the plan's charge up to the amount included with the plan, with storage above that refused until the plan is changed: The registry keeps accepting images past the amount included with the plan and charges the excess per GiB; pushes are not refused until the plan changes, because the tier's maximum sits far above the included storage.

Move the app to a Standard tier plan and restore the backup into the production slot.
Keep the app on the Basic tier plan and restore the backup into the production slot.
Keep the app on the Basic tier plan and restore the backup into a deployment slot, then swap the slot into production.

explanation:
Two conditions have to be satisfied here. First, the tier: backup and restore is offered on Basic, Standard, Premium and Isolated plans, but on the Basic tier only the production slot can be backed up or restored, so a slot-based restore workflow is not available there. The Standard tier supports backing up and restoring deployment slots. Second, the downtime goal: a restore stops the destination app or slot while it runs, so restoring into a separate deployment slot leaves production serving traffic during the operation, and the recovered slot can then be swapped into production. Placing the app on a Standard tier plan and restoring into a deployment slot meets both conditions.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Move the app to a Standard tier plan and restore the backup into the production slot: The tier is fine, but the restore target is not. Restoring into the production slot stops the destination app for the duration of the restore, so the live site is offline while the restore runs, which defeats the requirement that production keep serving traffic during the recovery.
- Keep the app on the Basic tier plan and restore the backup into the production slot: Restoring the production slot is allowed on Basic, but it stops the production app while the restore runs, so the site is unavailable for the recovery window. It therefore misses the minimal-downtime goal, and it also gives up the ability to restore into a slot later.
- Keep the app on the Basic tier plan and restore the backup into a deployment slot, then swap the slot into production: On the Basic tier only the production slot can be backed up or restored, so restoring into a deployment slot is not possible while the app stays on that tier. explanation:

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enable the app's automatic backup with a linked storage account, and keep copies until the records team releases them: Platform-managed automatic backups are created by the platform with no configuration: their hourly frequency and 30-day expiry are fixed and cannot be changed, they are not attached to a storage account, and they cannot be downloaded. They therefore fail the retention, export, and schedule requirements in the exhibit.
- Configure a scheduled backup against a linked storage account, with retention set to 30 days, and keep copies for the full 30-day window: Retention of 30 days is a valid value in the configurable range for a team-managed backup, but it reproduces the same fixed window that already applies today, so snapshots would still expire while the records team still needs them. prompt: You have an App Service web app on a Standard tier plan with the backup configuration shown in the exhibit. The operations team wants regular coverage of the app's on-disk content across the working day, and the team also takes on-demand copies on each release day. On release days the service refuses to accept the extra copies once the scheduled ones have run. They want the app adjusted so the number of copies taken in a day doesn't exceed what the service allows. Which configuration change should you make?

options.text: Change the schedule to run every three hours so the scheduled and on-demand copies stay inside the allowance of 12 backups a day
Keep the schedule at every 2 hours and rely on the daily allowance of 12 copies covering only scheduled copies, not on-demand copies
Change the schedule to run every 30 minutes so that a higher number of backups are taken each day
Set the retention period to indefinite so that stored copies are never deleted from the backup container

explanation:
A schedule of every 2 hours already produces 12 scheduled copies in a day, and the service allows at most 12 backups per day in total, counting on-demand and scheduled copies together. Adding the 2 on-demand copies taken on a release day pushes the total to 14, which is why the extra copies are refused. Running the schedule every three hours yields 8 scheduled copies, so 8 + 2 = 10 remains under the 12-per-day limit while keeping regular coverage, and three hours is a valid interval because the shortest supported interval is 2 hours.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Keep the schedule at every 2 hours and rely on the daily allowance of 12 copies covering only scheduled copies, not on-demand copies: Leaving the schedule at every 2 hours keeps 12 scheduled copies in a day, and on-demand copies draw from the same combined daily allowance, so the 2 on-demand copies on a release day cannot be taken. The allowance is not applied to scheduled copies alone.
- Change the schedule to run every 30 minutes so that a higher number of backups are taken each day: The shortest interval supported for a custom backup schedule is 2 hours, so a 30-minute schedule is not a valid setting. It would also produce far more than 12 copies in a day, exceeding the daily limit.
- Set the retention period to indefinite so that stored copies are never deleted from the backup container: Retention controls how long copies that already exist are kept, not how many copies may be created in a day. Making the retention period indefinite leaves the daily allowance unchanged, so the on-demand copies on release days would still be rejected.

After a corrupted release the team must put a copy of the app back, keep production traffic flowing throughout the recovery, and keep the customer uploads currently sitting in the existing staging deployment slot. Which restore configuration should you use?

options.text: Restore the backup into the existing staging deployment slot, then swap that slot into production.
Restore the backup into the production deployment slot of the app, then swap that slot into production.
Restore the backup into a new deployment slot, then swap that slot into production.
Restore the backup into a new App Service app, then swap that app into production.

explanation:
Point the restore at a deployment slot created for the recovery, then swap it into production. The service stops the target app or target slot while a restore runs, so restoring into a separate slot keeps the production site answering traffic during the recovery, and swapping that slot into production afterwards makes the recovered content live. Because the target slot is created for this purpose, its file system holds nothing to erase, so the uploads in the existing staging slot are left intact.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Restore the backup into the existing staging deployment slot, then swap that slot into production: Restoring over an existing slot erases everything in that slot's file system and overwrites it with the backup contents, so the customer uploads currently stored in staging would be lost. The restore must target a slot created for the recovery, not one that already holds data.
- Restore the backup into the production deployment slot of the app, then swap that slot into production: The production slot carries the same name as the app, so a restore aimed at it overwrites production itself instead of a side slot, and the app is stopped for the duration of the restore. That is exactly the production outage the team wants to avoid.
- Restore the backup into a new App Service app, then swap that app into production: Restoring into a separate App Service app yields a recovered copy that stays independent of the original app and its slots. A swap only moves a slot within the app it belongs to, so the recovered content would never take over the production site.

Leave it out of the custom backup and use the product's native backup and restore tools now
Add it to the custom backup and treat that arrangement as permanent, with no expiry
Let the platform's own hourly copies handle it, with nothing for anyone to set up

You have an App Service app named ContosoWeb that runs on a Standard tier plan. The app's custom backup captures the app content together with a linked Azure SQL Database, as shown in the exhibit. The product team wants the app content and the database data to be covered by backups for the next three years, and the platform team needs a dependable way to protect the database data across that whole period. Which configuration change should you make?

- Property: App name; Current value: ContosoWeb
- Property: Plan tier; Current value: Standard
- Property: Backup type in use; Current value: Custom backup
- Property: Content captured; Current value: App content and linked database
- Property: Linked database; Current value: Azure SQL Database (ContosoOrders)
- Property: Backup storage account; Current value: contosobackups
- Property: Retention; Current value: 30 days
- Property: Schedule; Current value: Every 4 hours
prompt: The configuration change that satisfies the product team's goal is _____.

options.text: Remove the linked database from the custom backup and switch database recovery to native backup and restore tooling built into the database itself before March 31, 2028
Keep the linked database in the custom backup and set the retention period to indefinite
Keep the linked database in the custom backup and move the app to an Isolated tier plan
Keep the linked database in the custom backup and shorten the schedule to one run every 2 hours

explanation:
Custom backups can capture a linked database only until March 31, 2028; from that date they stop supporting linked databases, and protecting the database data belongs to that database product's own native backup and restore tooling. That end date is fixed and cannot be pushed out by changing the tier, the retention window, or the schedule. Because the product team wants the app content and the database data to stay covered for the next three years, the linked database has to be taken out of the custom backup and the database's own backup and restore tooling has to be put in charge of the data.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Keep the linked database in the custom backup and set the retention period to indefinite: Retention controls only how long each custom backup is kept, and indefinite is a valid value, but it does not change which capabilities the service offers. The database stops being captured on the same date, leaving its data unprotected.
- Keep the linked database in the custom backup and shorten the schedule to one run every 2 hours: Changing how often the custom backup runs affects only the number of copies taken each day. It has no effect on the end of linked database support in custom backups, so the database data would still lose its copy after that date.

The business wants the site to keep serving requests, and the customer files to remain reachable, during an outage that disables the entire East US area. - Setting: App location; Current value: East US
- Setting: Instances; Current value: 3
- Setting: Zone redundancy; Current value: Off

prompt: The configuration change to make is _____.

options.text: Enable zone redundancy with two instances on the current plan
Turn on automatic backups and keep the copies for 30 days
Deploy a plan in another region with traffic failover and data replication
Turn on custom backups in a Storage account with indefinite retention

explanation:
App Service is a single-region service, so an outage that disables the whole region takes the app offline. To keep serving requests and keep the stored files reachable through such an outage, the app needs plans in more than one region, with traffic directed to the healthy copy and the stored files copied between the regions. Backups only help recover content after the fact; a backup by itself does not keep the app running in another region, so the team's proposal is not sufficient.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enable zone redundancy with two instances on the current plan: Zone redundancy spreads the instances of a plan across availability zones, so it addresses a single-zone failure rather than the loss of an entire region. It also requires Premium v2, Premium v3, or Premium v4 with at least two instances, so it is not offered on this Standard plan.
- Turn on automatic backups and keep the copies for 30 days: Automatic backups run every hour and expire after 30 days on a schedule that cannot be changed. They help recover the app content afterwards, but they neither keep the site serving requests nor keep the stored files reachable while the region is unavailable.
- Turn on custom backups in a Storage account with indefinite retention: Custom backups let the team control when copies are taken and how long they are kept, and they can include a linked database, but a restored copy is still placed in the same single region. Backups alone therefore do not keep the site running in another region during an outage of that region.

You have an App Service web app named ContosoWeb whose plan is shown in the exhibit. The business wants the site to keep serving requests if one availability zone in the region fails, and the operations group has so far been treating the app's backup copies as their answer to that risk. Which configuration change should you make?

`App name:          ContosoWeb
Plan pricing tier: Standard
Plan instance count: 1
Backup arrangement: Custom backups on a daily schedule, written to an attached storage account
Deployment slots in use: None`
prompt: The configuration change you should make is to _____.

options.text: Move the app to a Premium v3 plan, turn on zone redundancy for that plan, and run at least two instances on it
Move the app to a Premium v3 plan, turn on zone redundancy for that plan, and run a single instance on it
Keep the app on its Standard plan, turn on zone redundancy for that plan, and run at least two instances on it
Keep the app on its Standard plan and schedule extra custom backups each day so that copies are taken more often

explanation:
The requirement is that the app keeps serving requests when an availability zone in the region fails. Backups do not deliver that: a copy is a recovery artifact for app content, not a running copy of the site, so the operations group's proposal cannot satisfy the business goal. Zone redundancy is the setting that addresses this risk, and it is only offered on Premium v2, Premium v3 and Premium v4 plans, is applied at the plan level (so it covers every app hosted on the plan), and requires the plan to run at least two instances so the plan's instances can be spread across zones. ContosoWeb therefore needs to move onto an eligible tier (Premium v3 works, as do Premium v2 and Premium v4), have zone redundancy turned on for that plan, and run at least two instances. Backups should still be kept for recovering on-disk content, but they complement this setting rather than substitute for it.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Move the app to a Premium v3 plan, turn on zone redundancy for that plan, and run a single instance on it: Zone redundancy cannot do its job on a single instance, because the service requires the plan to run at least two instances for the plan's instances to be spread across availability zones. With one instance, the app would still be lost when the zone hosting that instance fails.
- Keep the app on its Standard plan, turn on zone redundancy for that plan, and run at least two instances on it: Zone redundancy is only available on Premium v2, Premium v3 and Premium v4 plans, so it cannot be turned on for a Standard plan no matter how many instances that plan runs.
- Keep the app on its Standard plan and schedule extra custom backups each day so that copies are taken more often: Taking more copies does not keep the site serving requests during an availability-zone failure; a backup is a stored copy of app content used for recovery, not a second running instance in another zone. Adding scheduled copies therefore does not meet the stated requirement.

The business wants the on-disk files and the contents of the linked Azure SQL Database to be recoverable after a failure, and it is willing to use more than one mechanism for that. Which configuration change should you make?

- Setting: Backup type; Value: Custom, scheduled every 6 hours
- Setting: Storage account; Value: contosobackups (West Europe)

prompt: The operations team should _____.

Move the app to a Premium v3 plan and keep the linked database in the custom backup so the whole database is captured
Reduce the retention to 0 days and keep the linked database in the custom backup so the whole database fits inside every copy
Switch the app to automatic backups so the platform captures the linked database for you

explanation:
A custom backup can hold up to 10 GB in total, and inside that ceiling no more than 4 GB may be taken up by the linked database. The exhibit's linked database is 6 GB, so it cannot ride along in the custom backup even though the combined size (2 GB of app content + 6 GB of database = 8 GB) sits under the overall 10 GB ceiling. The database therefore has to be unlinked from the custom backup, and its contents covered with the database product's own native backup and restore tooling, while the custom backup keeps protecting the app's on-disk files. Moving to a higher plan tier does not raise the allowance for the linked database portion, shortening retention only controls how long copies are kept rather than their size, and platform-made automatic backups do not include a linked database at all.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Move the app to a Premium v3 plan and keep the linked database in the custom backup so the whole database is captured: Plan tier has no effect on how much of a linked database a custom backup may carry: the 4 GB allowance for the database portion applies on every tier, so the 6 GB database still cannot be captured in full and the setup would leave the database unprotected.
- Reduce the retention to 0 days and keep the linked database in the custom backup so the whole database fits inside every copy: Retention decides how long each copy is kept, not how much it can hold. Shortening retention to 0 days only makes copies expire sooner, and the linked database portion of every copy stays capped at 4 GB, so the 6 GB database still cannot travel with the copy.
- Switch the app to automatic backups so the platform captures the linked database for you: Automatic backups are produced by the platform and do not include a linked database, so the Azure SQL Database contents would not be captured at all. The on-disk files would still be copied hourly, but the database would be left with none of the coverage the business asked for.

prompt: You have a .NET web app running on Azure App Service on a Linux worker. The team wants the production configuration to be supplied by App Service configuration instead of the appsettings.json file that ships with the deployment package, and the app must keep resolving the same keys from environment variables at runtime. The configuration file that is currently deployed contains nested entries, as shown below. Which two App Service setting names should you create so the application receives the same values?

options.text: Telemetry:InstrumentationKey and Custom:Api.Endpoint
Telemetry__InstrumentationKey and Custom__Api_Endpoint
Telemetry_InstrumentationKey and Custom_Api_Endpoint
Telemetry__InstrumentationKey and Custom_Api_Endpoint

explanation:
In a default Linux App Service app (and in a custom Linux container), the nested names taken from a JSON configuration file are expressed in App Service setting names by replacing every colon with two underscores and every period with a single underscore. The entry Telemetry:InstrumentationKey therefore becomes Telemetry__InstrumentationKey, and the entry Custom:Api.Endpoint becomes Custom__Api_Endpoint, so the correct option supplies both values under the names the application resolves from its environment.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Telemetry:InstrumentationKey and Custom:Api.Endpoint: Colons are not permitted in an App Service setting name, because names may contain only letters, digits, periods, and underscores. Keeping the colons here therefore breaks the naming rule as well as leaving the nested structure of the JSON file unmapped for the Linux app.
- Telemetry_InstrumentationKey and Custom_Api_Endpoint: This pair applies the period-to-single-underscore rule but also uses one underscore for the colon. On Linux, the colon in a nested name has to become two underscores, so Telemetry_InstrumentationKey would be treated as a flat name and would not deliver the value held under the nested Telemetry entry.
- Telemetry__InstrumentationKey and Custom_Api_Endpoint: The first name is correct, but the second one collapses both separators into single underscores. The colon in Custom:Api.Endpoint has to become two underscores while the period becomes one, giving Custom__Api_Endpoint, so this pair does not map both nested entries.

Managed Instance
App Service environment (ASE)
App Service plan hosting a custom Linux container

explanation:
The workload depends on Windows operating-system internals: COM calls, registry manipulation, MSI package installation, and a mapped drive. Managed Instance is the offering intended for legacy Windows applications tied to those internals, and its plan-scoped isolation fits this kind of workload; startup scripts can install dependencies, update COM, registry, IIS and ACL configuration, and execute MSI packages, so the machine state can be reproduced on every startup. The other three choices cannot satisfy the listed characteristics.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Standard App Service plan on a Windows SKU: A standard App Service plan is the right choice when the app must run on Linux or as a container, or when Azure should apply operating-system and runtime updates across many runtimes. It does not give the app the plan-scoped access to host internals that COM calls, registry writes, MSI installation and mapped drives require, so this legacy workload would break on it.
- App Service environment (ASE): An App Service environment is for isolated deployment of many applications on dedicated networking and virtual machines. It delivers isolation and network separation at that scale, but it does not provide the per-application Windows internals access (COM, registry, MSI) that this workload depends on, and only one application is being hosted here.
- App Service plan hosting a custom Linux container: Managed Instance explicitly excludes Linux workloads and container deployment, and a container cannot call a host COM component or install an MSI package against the host operating system, so this choice cannot run the application at all.

prompt: You have an ASP.NET Core web application running on Azure App Service that connects to a production SQL database. The database does not support Entra ID authentication, so the application must present a shared credential. Security policy forbids keeping that credential as a literal value in the app configuration, and the operations team needs it to live in a central store that supports rotation. The current state of the app configuration is shown below. Which approach should you use?

options.text: Store the password directly in the app setting value, because Azure already encrypts every app setting value while it is stored at rest.
Store the secret in Azure Key Vault and put a reference to it in the app setting value, granting the app permission to retrieve it.
Store the password in the appsettings.json file that ships inside the deployment package, and remove it from the app setting.
Store the password in the app setting value, and update that value from the portal each time the credential is rotated in Azure Key Vault.

explanation:
For production credentials, the recommended pattern is to keep the secret itself in Azure Key Vault and place a vault reference in the App Service setting, so the setting no longer holds the credential in plain form and the app is authorized to fetch the current value at runtime. That satisfies both constraints in the scenario: the literal password is out of the app configuration, and the credential is centrally stored and rotatable without changing the setting.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Store the password directly in the app setting value, because Azure already encrypts every app setting value while it is stored at rest: Values are encrypted while stored, but that protection only covers whatever you decide to place in the setting; the credential still sits in the app configuration, which the policy forbids, and there is no central copy to rotate.
- Store the password in the appsettings.json file that ships inside the deployment package, and remove it from the app setting: The packaged configuration file travels with the deployment artifact and is normally tracked alongside the source code, so the credential still exists outside a central store, and rotating it would mean rebuilding the package instead of updating one value in Azure.
- Store the password in the app setting value, and update that value from the portal each time the credential is rotated in Azure Key Vault: This keeps a copy of the credential in the setting and requires a manual portal edit on every rotation, so the setting does not point at the centrally stored copy and the two can drift out of sync.

You need to explain each recorded event by choosing the configuration setting or service behavior that accounts for it. Which option should you place in each target?

- Row: A; Recorded event: The application stopped answering requests for a few seconds immediately after the team changed one of its configuration records.
- Row: B; Recorded event: During a release, one parameter stayed on the test site instead of traveling to the live site.
- Row: C; Recorded event: The team tried to save a parameter whose identifier includes a hyphen, but the service rejected it.
- Row: D; Recorded event: An engineer confirmed that the new data was still missing from the overview screen even after closing the editor.
- Row: E; Recorded event: A security reviewer asked whether the text kept on disk can be recovered by someone who bypasses the portal.
prompt: Recorded event A

options.text: The platform cycles the running instance whenever an app setting is added, removed, or edited.
Mark the app setting as sticky to the current deployment slot.
Setting names may contain only letters, digits, periods, and underscores.
Apply in the setting dialog and then apply again on the Environment variables page.
App setting values are encrypted while stored at rest.
Use a Key Vault reference so the secret stays outside the entry itself.
Receive configured values as an environment variable at runtime.

explanation: Each recorded event has a matching platform behavior or configuration option. A brief loss of service right after an edit corresponds to the restart that occurs when an app setting is added, removed, or edited (A). A parameter that remains on the test site during a release corresponds to a setting marked sticky to the current deployment slot (B). A rejected identifier containing a hyphen corresponds to the restricted character set allowed for setting names, namely letters, digits, periods, and underscores (C). Data still missing after the editor is closed corresponds to the two-step save, applying in the setting dialog and then applying again on the Environment variables page (D). A reviewer asking whether the on-disk text can be read back corresponds to app setting values being encrypted while stored at rest (E).

context:
You are creating a new web site in Azure App Service for an internal team service. The facts the developers reported are listed below, and the creation form in the Azure portal asks you to choose one value for each field. Drag each value into the field where it belongs.

- Fact: Current implementation; What the developers reported: An internal service already written with the Flask framework; the team does not want to rewrite it
- Fact: Delivery; What the developers reported: The release pipeline packages the service with Docker and pushes it to the company's private artifact store
- Fact: Native dependency; What the developers reported: The service calls a native library that the team compiles and ships only for Unix-like targets
- Fact: Expected load; What the developers reported: About 30 concurrent internal users
- Fact: Isolation; What the developers reported: No requirement for dedicated networking or separate virtual machines for each deployment
prompt: Runtime stack for the web app

options.text: Windows
Linux
Node.js
Python
Code from a repository
Container image from a registry
App Service plan
App Service environment

explanation: The reported facts determine one value per creation field. The service is an existing Flask application, and Flask runs on Python, so the runtime stack field takes Python rather than Node.js. The native library is only built for Unix-like targets, so the worker must run on Linux rather than Windows. The release pipeline produces a Docker package that the team stores privately and that the platform pulls at start-up, so the publish method is a container image from a registry rather than code from a repository. Finally, with roughly 30 concurrent internal users and no requirement for dedicated networking or separate virtual machines per deployment, a standard App Service plan is the right compute resource; it supports Linux and custom container workloads while Azure maintains the operating system and runtime updates. An App Service environment is reserved for isolated deployment of many applications on dedicated networking and virtual machines, which this team does not need.

You have a legacy Windows business application running on Azure App Service with Managed Instance. The operations team has listed what this environment must support so the app can be operated day to day. Two of the capabilities listed below are not offered by this hosting option, so they belong in none of the slots. Drag each capability into the slot where it applies.

`Application attributes
----------------------
Operating system .... Windows
Plan ................ Managed Instance plan, SKU PMV4

Dependencies ........ Calls COM components and keeps its settings in the registry
`
prompt: The team must be able to open a desktop session on one of the app's instances to troubleshoot, without that instance being exposed to the public Internet.

options.text: Azure Bastion
Azure Key Vault
a startup PowerShell script
mapped drives
plan-scoped isolation
remote debugging
a Linux worker

explanation: Azure Bastion supplies the RDP route that lets operators reach a Managed Instance for troubleshooting rather than exposing the instance directly, so it fits the first slot. At plan level, registry definitions may reference secrets held in Azure Key Vault, which covers the secret-store requirement. Startup PowerShell scripts for Managed Instance can install dependencies, update COM, registry, IIS and ACL configuration and execute MSI packages, which covers the requirement to configure the machine on every boot. Supported SMB/UNC paths can be mapped or referenced through drive-letter access, so mapped drives covers the corporate file share requirement. Plan-scoped isolation gives tighter network boundaries between applications that share the same plan, which covers the separation requirement. Remote debugging and Linux workloads are both excluded from Managed Instance, so those two capabilities fit no slot.
