prompt: You have the App Service plan and the apps that run on it shown below for the Contoso order platform. During traffic spikes visitors must get fast responses without an engineer maintaining thresholds or schedules, and each web app must be able to cap how far it grows so that one busy app does not drive the cost for the others. Which action should you take?

options.text: Move Contoso-OrdersFn to its own plan on the Functions Premium tier, turn on automatic scaling for ASP-Orders, set the plan's Maximum burst, and set Always ready instances plus a Maximum scale limit for each web app.
Move Contoso-OrdersFn to its own plan on the Functions Premium tier, create an Azure Monitor autoscale setting with a CPU Percentage rule for ASP-Orders, and raise the maximum instance count.
Keep Contoso-OrdersFn on the ASP-Orders plan, turn on automatic scaling for the plan, and set the Maximum burst to 30 along with Always ready instances of 2 for each web app.
Keep Contoso-OrdersFn on the ASP-Orders plan, create an Azure Monitor autoscale setting with a scale condition that runs on weekdays, and set the maximum instance count for the plan to 30.

explanation:
The two goals — reacting to incoming HTTP traffic instead of to a metric or a clock, and letting each web app grow up to a ceiling of its own — are only met by automatic scaling: it is driven by HTTP traffic, it supports always-ready instances and a plan-wide Maximum burst, and its Maximum scale limit caps a single app's growth. The plan as it stands cannot use that method, because the CLI output shows Contoso-OrdersFn (kind: functionapp) running in the same plan as the two web apps, and automatic scaling is disabled on any plan that mixes web apps and Functions apps. The function app therefore has to be relocated first, and the Functions Premium tier is the recommended home for it. With only web apps left, automatic scaling can be turned on for ASP-Orders (the plan is already on a tier that supports it), the Maximum burst set at the plan level, and each web app given its Always ready instances value and its own Maximum scale limit.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Move Contoso-OrdersFn to its own plan on the Functions Premium tier, create an Azure Monitor autoscale setting with a CPU Percentage rule for ASP-Orders, and raise the maximum instance count: Moving the function app off the plan is right, but autoscale is the wrong method for the stated goals. Autoscale acts on metric and schedule rules rather than on the incoming HTTP traffic itself, and its rules apply to the entire App Service plan, so every app in the plan grows and shrinks together. It also offers no always-ready instances, no prewarmed instances and no per-app maximum, so it cannot give each web app its own ceiling.
- Keep Contoso-OrdersFn on the ASP-Orders plan, turn on automatic scaling for the plan, and set the Maximum burst to 30 along with Always ready instances of 2 for each web app: Automatic scaling is unavailable while web apps and an Azure Functions app share the plan — the plan shown hosts Contoso-OrdersFn as a functionapp alongside the two web apps. Adjusting the Maximum burst or the Always ready instances values does not remove that restriction, so the method cannot simply be switched on with everything left in place.
- Keep Contoso-OrdersFn on the ASP-Orders plan, create an Azure Monitor autoscale setting with a scale condition that runs on weekdays, and set the maximum instance count for the plan to 30: A schedule-driven autoscale condition scales the whole plan on a clock rather than in response to arriving visitors, and autoscale provides no per-app maximum, so one web app cannot cap its own growth. Leaving the function app in the plan also keeps the traffic-driven method, which does support per-app ceilings, out of reach.

prompt: You have the App Service plan and the web app shown below for the Contoso storefront. During the holiday campaign the site must handle peak traffic that requires 8 instances running at the same time, and the release team needs a staging slot to rehearse the next release before it reaches customers. Once the campaign work is done, the platform team also wants to be able to configure Azure Monitor autoscale metric and schedule rules on this same plan. The application code must not change, and no additional App Service plan may be created. Which action should you take?

options.text: Scale out the App Service plan on its current Basic tier until it runs 8 instances.
Enable automatic scaling on the App Service plan and set the maximum burst to 8 instances.
Add autoscale rules to the App Service plan that add an instance when CPU stays above 70 percent.
Scale up the App Service plan to the Standard tier.

explanation:
The plan is on the Basic tier, and a Basic plan scales out to at most 3 instances, so the campaign requirement of 8 instances running simultaneously cannot be met by changing the instance count alone; the pricing tier of the plan has to change. Standard plans scale out to as many as 10 instances, which covers the 8 required, and changing the pricing tier is what delivers the extra capabilities the release team needs, such as staging slots and custom domains and certificates. A Standard plan also meets the prerequisite for Azure Monitor autoscale, which requires a plan on Standard tier or higher. The tier change applies within seconds, affects all apps in the plan, and needs no code change or redeploy.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Scale out the App Service plan on its current Basic tier until it runs 8 instances: Keeping the plan on the Basic tier means the plan can scale out to only 3 instances, so 8 instances at once is unreachable no matter how the instance count is edited; the extra plan capabilities the release team needs also come from a pricing-tier change, not from a larger instance count.
- Enable automatic scaling on the App Service plan and set the maximum burst to 8 instances: Automatic scaling is offered only on Premium v2 to v4 plans, so it cannot be enabled for a Basic plan, and it is configured per app from the app's Scale-out (App Service plan) settings rather than being a tier capability. It also does not provide a staging slot.
- Add autoscale rules to the App Service plan that add an instance when CPU stays above 70 percent: Azure Monitor autoscale requires an App Service plan on Standard tier or higher, plus the Owner or Contributor role (or a custom role with Microsoft.Insights/autoscaleSettings/* permissions) on the plan; on a Basic plan no autoscale setting can be created, and metric rules alone would not give the app a staging slot.

options.text: Remove the spending limit in Cost Management + Billing, then change the plan's pricing tier to Standard tier or higher on the Scale up page.

explanation:
The plan is on the Free tier and the subscription still has a spending limit in place. A plan cannot leave the Free tier while a spending limit is active, so the limit has to be cleared in Cost Management + Billing before anything else. Once that is done, changing the pricing tier through the Scale up page is what delivers the three things the portal team needs: dedicated VMs, custom domains with certificates, staging slots, and autoscaling support. Moving to Standard tier or higher also satisfies the tier prerequisite for Azure Monitor autoscale rules and for deployment slots. Doing both in this order means one action chain achieves the requirement without touching application code or creating another plan.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Change the plan's pricing tier to Standard tier or higher on the Scale up page, then remove the spending limit in Cost Management + Billing: This reverses the required order. While the spending limit is still active, the plan is blocked from leaving the Free tier, so the pricing tier change cannot complete until the limit is removed. The limit has to be cleared first, not afterwards.
- Remove the spending limit in Cost Management + Billing, then raise the plan's instance count on the Scale out page so the portal handles more load: Clearing the spending limit is the right first step, but scaling out only runs additional instances of the app that already exists on the plan. It does not deliver deployment slots, a custom domain with a certificate, or autoscaling support — those arrive by moving the plan to a higher pricing tier.
- Change the plan's pricing tier to Standard tier or higher on the Scale up page and add Azure Monitor autoscale rules to the plan, leaving the spending limit in place: The pricing tier change and the autoscale rules are appropriate on their own, but the spending limit is left in place. Because a plan cannot leave the Free tier while a spending limit is active, the tier change will not take effect, so the plan stays where it is and none of the requested capabilities are unlocked.

prompt: You have the App Service plan and the web app shown below for the Contoso shopping-cart service. The plan runs on the Premium v3 tier with automatic scaling active, and Contoso-Cart was added to the plan after that switch was made. Every weekday evening the request volume rises sharply, yet the plan never grows beyond a single instance, the backlog of pending requests keeps growing, and users report that each request is served by the same instance. The service must add instances by itself when traffic arrives, with no engineer maintaining thresholds or schedules. Which action should you take?

options.text: For Contoso-Cart, open Settings > Configuration > General settings, set Session affinity to Off, and save.
For Contoso-Cart, open Settings > Configuration > General settings, set Session affinity to On, and save.
For Contoso-Cart, open Settings > Configuration > General settings, set Health check to Off, and save.
For Contoso-Cart, open Settings > Scale-out (App Service plan), raise Maximum burst from 10 to 20, and save.

explanation:
Automatic scaling is already active on this plan and its Maximum burst of 10 leaves plenty of headroom, so the ceiling is not the blocker. The blocker is the app's Session affinity (ARR affinity): those cookies pin requests to one specific instance, which restricts scaling and stops the plan from adding instances when traffic arrives. Setting Session affinity to Off for Contoso-Cart in Settings > Configuration > General settings and saving removes the pinning, so automatic scaling can then add instances up to the Maximum burst. Health check does not interfere with automatic scaling, and the app was added after the plan switched to automatic scaling, so its affinity setting was never cleared for it.

Why the other options are wrong:
- For Contoso-Cart, open Settings > Configuration > General settings, set Session affinity to On, and save: Session affinity is on by default and it is the affinity cookies, not the tier or the burst value, that hold traffic on a single instance. Leaving it On or setting it On keeps the plan pinned to one instance, so the service still cannot add instances on its own when requests arrive.
- For Contoso-Cart, open Settings > Configuration > General settings, set Health check to Off, and save: Health check does not have to be turned off; it can run alongside automatic scaling and it reports on app health. Disabling it removes a useful signal while leaving in place the affinity setting that keeps every request on the same instance, so the plan still never grows.
- For Contoso-Cart, open Settings > Scale-out (App Service plan), raise Maximum burst from 10 to 20, and save: Maximum burst is only the highest instance count the plan may reach once it decides to scale out. Raising it from 10 to 20 changes nothing while the app's requests are pinned to one instance, so the plan still stays at a single instance during the evening peak.

prompt: You have the App Service plan and the autoscale setting shown below for the Contoso order-tracking site, which runs on the Standard tier. Several times a day the plan adds an instance and then takes it away again a few minutes later, so response times swing between fast and slow and customers complain about slow pages. The plan must keep growing under sustained load using the CPU trigger that is configured today, and it must also be able to return to the minimum instance count when traffic drops, without the instance count oscillating. Which change should you make?

options.text: Add a scale-in rule with operator Less than and threshold 20 and keep the 5-minute cool-down period on the rules.
Add a scale-out rule with operator Greater than and threshold 90 and keep the 5-minute cool-down period on the rules.
Change the threshold of the existing scale-out rule from 70 to 90 and keep the 5-minute cool-down period on the rules.
Raise the Maximum instance count in the autoscale setting from 10 to 20 and keep the 5-minute cool-down period on the rules.

explanation:
The plan is flapping: an instance is added under load, the platform then removes it, CPU on the remaining instances rises again, and the scale-out rule adds one back. The documented remedy is to pair the scale-out rule with a scale-in rule and to use cool-down periods. A scale-in rule with operator Less than, metric threshold 20 and an operation that decreases the instance count gives the plan a metric-driven way to return to its minimum instance count when traffic falls, while the 5-minute cool-down stops the two rules from acting back-to-back. The existing CPU trigger (above 70 percent for 10 minutes, one instance at a time) and the maximum instance count of 10 stay exactly as they are, so the plan still grows under sustained load as required.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add a scale-out rule with operator Greater than and threshold 90 and keep the 5-minute cool-down period on the rules: This adds another reason for the plan to add instances and gives it no metric-driven way to remove them, so the plan still cannot settle back at its minimum instance count and the add/remove cycle continues. It does not address the oscillation at all.
- Change the threshold of the existing scale-out rule from 70 to 90 and keep the 5-minute cool-down period on the rules: This only makes the plan add instances less often; it does not give the plan any way to remove instances when traffic drops, and it weakens the growth behaviour the site must keep. The oscillating add/remove cycle remains unresolved.
- Raise the Maximum instance count in the autoscale setting from 10 to 20 and keep the 5-minute cool-down period on the rules: Raising the ceiling for growth changes nothing about when instances are added or removed, so the plan keeps adding and removing instances in the same cycle and never settles at its minimum count. It is also not achievable on this plan: the Standard tier caps a plan at 10 instances, so a maximum of 20 cannot be configured there.

- Plan: Contoso-Reporting plan; Pricing tier: Standard; Apps hosted: Contoso-Reporting; Configuration observed today: A CPU rule adds 1 worker when CPU stays above 70 percent for 10 minutes; at most 10 workers run and otherwise 1 worker runs

prompt: Contoso-Storefront must stay responsive to staff overnight and at weekends, without waiting for extra workers to be created.

options.text: Set Always ready instances
Change the prewarmed instance count with the Azure CLI
Turn on Enforce scale-out limit
Remove the spending limit on the subscription
Turn Health Check back on
Add a scale condition for repeated days with a start time and an end time

explanation: Each issue matches exactly one action. Keeping the site answerable during quiet hours is done by the per-app minimum that automatic scaling maintains, which is set with Always ready instances. The cold-boot delay when traffic arrives is solved by the spare warm capacity held for scale-out and activation events, whose size can only be adjusted with the Azure CLI. Stopping one site at a chosen number of workers while another site continues to grow needs the per-app cap provided by the Enforce scale-out limit option, whose value can sit anywhere between 1 and the plan's Maximum burst. Leaving the Free tier is blocked while a spending limit is still active on the subscription, so that limit has to be removed in Cost Management + Billing first. The probe that withdraws unhealthy workers can simply be switched back on, because Health Check works together with the platform-driven growth used on the Premium v3 plan. Finally, holding a fixed worker count inside a weekly Monday window requires a rule with repeated days plus a start time and an end time, with the default condition applying outside that window.

options.text: Move the Function app to its own plan on the Azure Functions Premium tier
Move the web app to its own plan and leave the Function app on the current plan

explanation:
The request-driven scaling option that grows a plan as HTTP requests arrive applies to App Service web apps only, and it is disabled whenever one plan hosts both web apps and function apps, which is exactly why the portal reports it as unavailable for Contoso-Plan. Relocating Contoso-Orders onto its own plan on the Azure Functions Premium tier, the plan type recommended for function workloads, removes the mix from Contoso-Plan. Contoso-Store then remains alone on the current plan with its custom domain and deployment slot untouched, and the traffic-driven scaling option becomes selectable for that plan, with no application code change and no second plan for the web app.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Move the web app to its own plan and leave the Function app on the current plan: Wrong because it leaves Contoso-Orders on the plan that also hosts the web app, so the function app never lands on a plan type intended for function workloads, and it also moves Contoso-Store off the plan the business requires it to stay on. It is the function app that has to be relocated for the mixed-plan restriction to be lifted.
- Move both apps to separate plans on the Azure Functions Premium tier: Wrong because a web app does not belong on the Azure Functions Premium plan, and the requirement is that Contoso-Store remain on the current plan so its custom domain and deployment slot keep working. Only the function app needs to be placed on a different plan.
- Keep both apps on the current plan and enable Azure Monitor autoscale rules on it: Wrong because leaving both apps on one plan keeps the request-driven scaling option unavailable for that plan. Azure Monitor autoscale is also not what was asked for: it is driven by metric thresholds or schedules that an engineer maintains, and its rules apply to the whole plan, so every app in the plan scales together instead of reacting to its own request volume.

options.text: set Maximum burst to 25 in Scale-out (App Service plan)
set Maximum burst to 40 in Scale-out (App Service plan)
set the pricing tier to a higher level in App Service plan -> Scale up
set the plan's Instance limits maximum to 25 in the autoscale setting

explanation:
The plan-wide limit on how many instances request traffic may add is the Maximum burst value, configured under Scale-out (App Service plan). On Premium v3 this value can be set up to 30, and it must be at least the plan's instance count; with 12 assigned instances, raising it from 14 to 25 is valid and lets the whole plan reach 25 instances. The per-app limit is a different control: the Enforce scale-out limit option on Contoso-Search, whose value must be between 1 and the plan's maximum burst, so 18 is acceptable once the burst is 25. Always ready instances fixes a floor rather than a ceiling, and the autoscale Instance limits maximum belongs to a different scaling method that should not be active alongside the one already in use.

Why the other options are wrong:
- set Maximum burst to 40 in Scale-out (App Service plan): A maximum burst of 40 exceeds the highest value that can be specified on Premium v2, v3 and v4, which is 30, so this value would not be accepted.
- set the pricing tier to a higher level in App Service plan -> Scale up: Changing the pricing tier changes the size and capacity of each instance and unlocks tier features; it does not set how many instances the plan may add in response to incoming requests, which is controlled by the Maximum burst value.
- set the plan's Instance limits maximum to 25 in the autoscale setting: Instance limits maximum is part of the Azure Monitor autoscale setting. Only one scaling method should be active for a plan, and this plan already grows from request traffic, so adding autoscale rules would conflict with the method in use; it would also cap every app in the plan instead of one app.

The plan must also be able to run as many as 10 instances during busy periods. Nothing on the plan currently changes its instance count, and the team's automation account already holds the Owner role on it. Which change should the team make?

- Property: App Service plan; Value: Basic B1
- Property: Apps hosted on the plan; Value: Contoso-Tools (web app)
- Property: Autoscale setting status; Value: Not configured
- Property: Scaling method in use; Value: Manual
prompt: The operations team should _____.

options.text: Move the plan up to the Standard tier
Add the CPU percentage rule to the plan's autoscale setting in the Azure Monitor portal
Turn on automatic scaling in the app's Scale-out (App Service plan) settings
Give the automation account the Contributor role on the plan and then add the CPU percentage rule

explanation:
Autoscale settings for an App Service plan are only supported when the plan is on the Standard tier or higher and has at least one app, and the person configuring them holds the Owner role, the Contributor role, or a custom role with Microsoft.Insights/autoscaleSettings/* permissions on the plan. Contoso-Tools' plan is Basic B1, so the plan must be moved to the Standard tier before any CPU percentage rule can be created; Basic also caps a plan at three instances, which is short of the ten the portal team needs. The Owner role is already in place and no other scaling method is configured, so nothing has to be disabled first.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add the CPU percentage rule to the plan's autoscale setting in the Azure Monitor portal: The rule itself is what the team wants, but a Basic B1 plan cannot carry an autoscale setting at all. The plan has to sit on the Standard tier or higher first, so adding the rule on its own cannot work.
- Turn on automatic scaling in the app's Scale-out (App Service plan) settings: Automatic scaling is a separate, request-traffic-driven option that requires a Premium v2, v3 or v4 plan, and it reacts to incoming HTTP traffic rather than to the CPU percentage. It is also unavailable on a Basic plan, so it cannot deliver the required behaviour.
- Give the automation account the Contributor role on the plan and then add the CPU percentage rule: The automation account already holds the Owner role, which is one of the accepted permissions for creating autoscale settings, and granting Contributor adds nothing. The real blocker is that the plan is below the pricing level where autoscale is supported, so this option leaves the requirement unmet.

Ahead of the annual partner summit the plan must be able to run more than 25 instances at the same time, while the shared front-end app must never occupy more than 12 of them. Which two changes should the platform team make?

- Setting: App Service plan; Value: contoso-public-api
- Setting: Pricing tier; Value: Premium v3
- Setting: Apps hosted; Value: Contoso-API, Contoso-Public

- Setting: Always ready instances (Contoso-Public); Value: 4

prompt: The platform team should apply _____ for the plan and [...] for Contoso-Public.

options.text: Maximum burst to 30
Autoscale instance limit to 30
Always ready instances to 30
Pricing tier to Premium v4

explanation:
Because the plan already grows as requests arrive, the plan-wide ceiling for that growth is the Maximum burst value, which on the Premium v3 tier can be set to at most 30 instances; 30 is the only value that covers the requirement of more than 25 concurrent instances, and it is also at or above the plan's current instance count of 4 as the platform requires. The cap for a single app inside that plan is the Maximum scale limit, which has to be turned on with the Enforce scale-out limit option and given a value between 1 and the plan's Maximum burst, so 12 is valid once the burst is 30.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Autoscale instance limit to 30: Azure Monitor autoscale reacts to a metric or to a schedule and its rules apply to the whole plan; it does not react to incoming request traffic. Only one growth method should be active on a plan at a time, and this plan already reacts to request volume, so an autoscale instance limit is not what raises the traffic-driven ceiling.
- Always ready instances to 30: Always ready instances fixes the number of instances an app keeps running as its floor, not a ceiling. Setting it to 30 would keep 30 instances running and billed around the clock instead of letting the plan react to demand, so it does not deliver the requested on-demand ceiling.
- Pricing tier to Premium v4: Changing the pricing tier changes the capacity of each instance, not how many instances the plan runs, and Premium v4 still tops out at 30 instances; the tier change is also not the control that lets a plan carry more than 25 instances at once.

The platform team has since switched the plan to grow on its own as requests arrive, set a ceiling of 20 instances on the plan, and given Contoso-Shop a personal ceiling of 8 instances. The plan still grows and shrinks in lockstep for all three apps whenever processor load crosses the old threshold, and Contoso-Shop regularly runs on more than 8 instances. No application code may change and no second App Service plan may be created. Which change should the platform team make?

prompt: The platform team should _____.

options.text: Remove the autoscale setting from the plan
Raise the plan's instance ceiling to 30
Delete only the scale-in rule from the autoscale setting
Lower the processor-load threshold on the autoscale setting

explanation:
Only one scaling method should be active on an App Service plan at a time. This plan still carries the earlier Azure Monitor autoscale setting (Enabled, CPU-based scale-out and scale-in rules, up to 12 instances), so two scaling methods act on the plan at once: the rules-based one keeps scaling the entire plan in lockstep and can take the plan past the per-app ceiling of 8, while the traffic-driven method is meant to grow the plan on its own up to the plan ceiling of 20. Deleting the autoscale setting from the plan (in the portal, choosing Manual scale on the plan strips the autoscale rules) leaves the traffic-driven method as the only configured method, after which the plan ceiling of 20 and Contoso-Shop's ceiling of 8 govern growth on their own.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Raise the plan's instance ceiling to 30: The plan already has a ceiling of 20 instances, which is a valid value on this tier, and raising it changes nothing about the conflict: while the earlier rules-based setting stays on the plan it keeps scaling all apps together and can still run Contoso-Shop on more than 8 instances.
- Delete only the scale-in rule from the autoscale setting: Deleting only the scale-in rule leaves the autoscale setting on the plan with its scale-out rule, so the plan still grows in lockstep for every app and still runs Contoso-Shop above its 8-instance ceiling; the whole setting has to go, not just one of its rules.
- Lower the processor-load threshold on the autoscale setting: Lowering the threshold only changes when the old rules-based method reacts. That method stays configured alongside the traffic-driven one, so the two keep conflicting and the entire plan keeps growing and shrinking together.

You have the Contoso media portal App Service plan shown below. It hosts a single Windows web app on the Free tier, and the subscription reports that a spending limit is in place. Ahead of the December premiere the portal must be able to run 30 instances at the same time, the release team needs a deployment slot to rehearse the new player, and the portal has to be served from its own domain with a TLS certificate. No application code may change and no second App Service plan may be created. Which action should the team take?

`App Service plan : Contoso-Media-Plan  (resource group contoso-media-rg)
Pricing tier     : Free
Web app on plan  : Contoso-Media  (Windows)
Subscription spending limit : On  -  1,000 USD per month
Scale-out method : Manual`
prompt: The team must _____.

options.text: remove the spending limit on the subscription in Cost Management + Billing, then change the plan's pricing tier to Premium
change the plan's pricing tier to Premium, then remove the spending limit on the subscription in Cost Management + Billing
remove the spending limit on the subscription in Cost Management + Billing, then change the plan's pricing tier to Standard
remove the spending limit in the plan's Scale up blade, then change the plan's pricing tier to Premium

explanation:
A plan cannot be moved off the Free tier while a spending limit is still in place for the subscription, so the limit has to be removed first in Cost Management + Billing; only after that does the scale-up to a higher pricing tier succeed. The target tier follows from the December requirement: Basic plans scale out to at most 3 instances, Standard plans to 10, and Premium plans to 30, so only Premium can run the 30 instances the premiere needs. Moving up to Premium is also what makes dedicated capacity, custom domains with certificates, and staging slots available, and the tier change applies within seconds to the apps in the plan without any code change or redeploy.

Why the other options are wrong:
- change the plan's pricing tier to Premium, then remove the spending limit on the subscription in Cost Management + Billing: The order is wrong. While the subscription still has a spending limit in place, the plan cannot leave the Free tier, so the pricing-tier change is rejected and can only be attempted after the limit is removed.
- remove the spending limit on the subscription in Cost Management + Billing, then change the plan's pricing tier to Standard: Standard plans scale out to at most 10 instances, so they cannot deliver the 30 simultaneous instances required for the premiere. Premium is the tier whose scale-out ceiling reaches 30.
- remove the spending limit in the plan's Scale up blade, then change the plan's pricing tier to Premium: The spending limit is a subscription-level setting managed in Cost Management + Billing, not a setting on the plan's Scale up blade, so removing it there leaves the scale-up blocked and the plan on the Free tier.

prompt: You have an App Service web app with the configuration shown in the exhibit. A validated build is sitting in the staging slot, and the promotion is carried out by hand after the smoke tests pass. When the staged build is promoted, the app becomes unresponsive and requests time out until the promotion completes. Which swap option should the release engineer select?

options.text: Swap with warm up
Stop/Reset during swap
Auto swap with warm up
Deploy the validated build to the production slot directly and leave the staging slot unchanged

explanation:
The app hangs precisely because its configuration is replaced underneath a running process that holds a SQL connection for its whole lifetime. Stop/Reset during swap is the documented option for apps that become unresponsive when settings change, including apps with database connections: the source slot is stopped and restarted so the configuration change applies to a fresh process. The trade-off is a slower cold start and greater downtime risk, which is acceptable here because the app is unresponsive during the promotion anyway. The promotion also stays a manual step, so the release engineer still approves the release after the smoke tests.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Swap with warm up: Swap with warm up is the default behavior: it prepares and warms the source instances before traffic is redirected so no requests are dropped during the transition. It does not shut the source slot down, so the configuration is still replaced underneath the running process and the app stays unresponsive — it does not address the symptom in the exhibit.
- Auto swap with warm up: Auto swap promotes the staged build automatically as soon as a deployment occurs, which removes the manual approval gate that the release process depends on. Warm up also leaves the source slot running, so the same hang would occur during the automatic promotion.
- Deploy the validated build to the production slot directly and leave the staging slot unchanged: Deploying straight to the production slot removes the staged copy of the release from the promotion path, so there is no validated environment to exchange with production and no quick way to promote or roll back by exchanging slots. It also contradicts the team's deploy-validate-promote process.

prompt: You have the App Service plan shown in the exhibit, and a request to move the app to the Standard tier to reduce cost. You need to determine the sequence of changes that lets the tier change succeed while the app keeps serving its current environments. Which action should you take?

options.text: Delete two of the seven slots, then scale the plan down to Standard
Scale the plan down to Standard, then delete any slots the plan no longer supports
Scale the plan down to Standard and keep all seven slots, because deployment slots are not billed separately
Move the app to a new Standard-tier plan that carries all seven slots, because a new plan applies its allowance from scratch

explanation:
The Standard tier permits at most five deployment slots, and a plan can only be moved to a tier that accommodates the app's current slot count. The app here uses seven slots, so the plan cannot be scaled down to Standard while all seven exist; the slot count must first be reduced to what Standard allows. Deleting two of the slots and then scaling the plan down is therefore the sequence that works. The fact that slots carry no separate charge does not remove the tier's slot quota, and the no-extra-charge rule doesn't remove the quota when scaling.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Scale the plan down to Standard, then delete any slots the plan no longer supports: The order is reversed. While the app still holds more slots than the target tier allows, the scale-down to Standard is blocked, so the scale-down has to come after the surplus slots are removed rather than before.
- Scale the plan down to Standard and keep all seven slots, because deployment slots are not billed separately: Slots have no separate charge, but each tier still caps how many slots an app may use. Keeping all seven slots in place therefore prevents the plan from being scaled down to Standard.
- Move the app to a new Standard-tier plan that carries all seven slots, because a new plan applies its allowance from scratch: The slot count belongs to the app and travels with it when the app is moved to another plan, so a fresh Standard-tier plan doesn't reset the allowance. Moving the app with seven slots to Standard would still fail, because Standard permits at most five slots.

prompt: You have the App Service web app and its deployment slots configured as shown in the exhibit. The team promotes a validated release by swapping the staging slot with the production slot. You need to know exactly what the production slot will be running and which configuration values it will use after the promotion. Which statement is correct?

options.text: After the swap, the production slot runs build 2026.10.25 with FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT = true, and its SqlDatabase connection string still points at prod-sql.
After the swap, the production slot runs build 2026.10.25 with FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT = true, and its SqlDatabase connection string now points at stg-sql.
After the swap, the production slot runs build 2026.10.01 with FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT = false, and its SqlDatabase connection string still points at prod-sql.
After the swap, the production slot runs build 2026.10.01 with FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT = false, and its SqlDatabase connection string now points at stg-sql.

explanation:
A swap exchanges the application content and the eligible configuration between the two slots. The staged build 2026.10.25 therefore becomes the production build, and FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT, which is not flagged as a slot setting, travels with the app, so production runs it as true. Items flagged as slot settings (sticky settings) are the exceptions: they remain with the slot they belong to, and slot-specific connection strings are not exchanged by a swap. SqlDatabase is flagged that way, so production keeps its own value, Server=prod-sql.database.windows.net.

Why the other options are wrong:
- After the swap, the production slot runs build 2026.10.25 with FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT = true, and its SqlDatabase connection string now points at stg-sql: The build and the app setting are right, but the connection string is not. SqlDatabase is flagged as a slot setting, so it stays with the slot it was defined in: production keeps prod-sql and the staged stg-sql value does not move across during the swap.
- After the swap, the production slot runs build 2026.10.01 with FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT = false, and its SqlDatabase connection string still points at prod-sql: The connection string is right, but the build and the app setting are not. The application content and the eligible configuration are exchanged between the slots during a swap, so production ends up running the staged build 2026.10.25 with FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT = true.
- After the swap, the production slot runs build 2026.10.01 with FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT = false, and its SqlDatabase connection string now points at stg-sql: Both parts are wrong. The staged build and the app setting that is not flagged as a slot setting are exchanged with production during the swap, while the SqlDatabase connection string, being a slot setting, stays with its own slot instead of moving to production.

prompt: You have an App Service web app and the release pipeline shown in the exhibit. You need each new build deployed to the staging environment to reach production on its own as soon as the deployment finishes, because this app has no pre-release validation gate. Which change should you make?

options.text: Enable auto swap for the staging slot so each deployment to that slot is promoted to the production slot
Perform a manual swap of the staging slot with the production slot after every deployment
Set the traffic percentage of the staging slot to 100 and the production slot to 0 so that requests reach the new build
Point the continuous deployment of the main branch at the production slot so that every commit is deployed there

explanation:
The requirement is that each build delivered to the staging slot reaches production by itself once the deployment finishes, with no human step and no validation gate. Auto swap on the staging slot does exactly this: the pipeline deploys to the slot and the platform promotes that content and its eligible configuration to production. The plan tier (Standard) already allows slots, so no tier change is needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Perform a manual swap of the staging slot with the production slot after every deployment: A hand-run swap still needs an engineer to trigger it after each deployment, so builds would not reach production on their own. Manual swapping is the right pattern only when a candidate build must be reviewed and smoke-tested before it goes live.
- Set the traffic percentage of the staging slot to 100 and the production slot to 0 so that requests reach the new build: Traffic percentage only divides incoming requests among slots that are already running; it does not move a newly deployed build into production. Sending 100% of traffic to staging would expose users to an unvalidated build while the old build stayed in production.
- Point the continuous deployment of the main branch at the production slot so that every commit is deployed there: Deploying the main branch straight to the production slot removes the staging environment from the release path and skips the review of a candidate build, which is the opposite of the recommended pattern of deploying to a nonproduction slot and then promoting the accepted build.

prompt: You have an App Service web app on the Premium tier whose configuration was copied into a new staging slot. A build deployed to that slot fails because the internal API host cannot be resolved, and the team wants the staging slot to reach that API exactly as production does. Which action should you take?

options.text: Add a private endpoint for the staging slot and add a DNS name for the slot's hostname.
Copy the production configuration to the staging slot again so that the private endpoint and its DNS name come with it.
Mark the private endpoint and DNS name as a slot setting on the staging slot so they are not exchanged during a swap.
Enable auto swap with warm up on the staging slot so the private endpoint and DNS name move to production on their own.

explanation:
Cloning configuration from one slot copies app settings, connection strings, language and framework versions, WebSockets, HTTP version and platform bitness, but a private endpoint is not cloned between slots. The staging slot therefore has no private endpoint, so the internal API host cannot resolve inside that environment and the deployment fails. You must set up the private endpoint for the staging slot yourself, together with the DNS name that resolves the slot's hostname in the private zone, so the staging slot reaches the API the same way production does.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Copy the production configuration to the staging slot again so that the private endpoint and its DNS name come with it: Repeating the configuration copy does not help: private endpoints are excluded from cloned configuration, so the staging slot would still have no private endpoint and the same DNS resolution failure would occur.
- Mark the private endpoint and DNS name as a slot setting on the staging slot so they are not exchanged during a swap: Slot settings (sticky settings) only decide whether configuration values are exchanged when slots are swapped. They do not create networking resources, so marking the endpoint and DNS name this way leaves the staging slot without a private endpoint.
- Enable auto swap with warm up on the staging slot so the private endpoint and DNS name move to production on their own: Auto swap promotes content and eligible configuration from a slot into production; it neither creates nor transfers private endpoints. The failure happens in the staging slot before any promotion, and swapping would not give that slot a private endpoint.

prompt: You have an App Service web app that runs a container image, and the release pipeline that moves builds into its deployment slots is shown in the exhibit. The team must be able to trace any customer report back to the exact build that was running at that moment, and the pipeline currently reuses one changeable label for every release. Which change should you make?

options.text: Tag the image with a traceable value that identifies the exact build, push it to the registry, then write the tag into the target slot
Tag the image with the same changeable label for every release, push it to the registry, then write the tag into the target slot
Tag the image with a traceable value that identifies the exact build, push it to the registry, then write the tag into the App Service plan
Tag the image with a traceable value that identifies the exact build, push it to the registry, then leave the target slot pointing at its current image

explanation:
Each release needs its own tag that ties the image to one specific build (for example the git commit ID or a timestamp). A label that changes from release to release makes it impossible to tell which code is actually running, which is exactly the debugging problem the guidance warns about. The container release flow for a slot has three steps: build and tag the image, push the tagged image to the container registry, and then write that tag into the target slot so the slot pulls the new image. The correct option performs all three in that order.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Tag the image with the same changeable label for every release, push it to the registry, then write the tag into the target slot: Reusing one changeable label for every release is the pattern to avoid: because the label moves on, nothing in the registry or the slot points back to the code that was running when the report was filed, so the exact build cannot be determined.
- Tag the image with a traceable value that identifies the exact build, push it to the registry, then write the tag into the App Service plan: The new image tag belongs to the configuration of the target slot, which is what makes that slot restart and pull the image. Writing the tag into the App Service plan instead leaves the slot with no indication of which image to run.
- Tag the image with a traceable value that identifies the exact build, push it to the registry, then leave the target slot pointing at its current image: The slot must be updated with the new tag so it restarts and pulls the newly tagged image. Leaving the slot pointing at its current image means the new build never reaches that environment at all.

prompt: You have the App Service web app and its deployment slots shown in the exhibit. Forty minutes ago the team promoted a new release to customers, and since then the production slot has been returning failed checkouts and elevated error rates. You need customers to be served the previous release again, and the team must not rebuild or redeploy the code. Which action should the release engineer take?

options.text: Swap the production slot with the staging slot so that the production slot is running the previous release again.
Redeploy the previous release artifact from the build pipeline to the production slot so that the production slot is running the previous code again.
Stop the production slot, copy the files from the staging slot into the production wwwroot folder, and restart the instances.
Set the traffic percentage of the production slot to 0 and of the staging slot to 100, so that the staging slot is running the previous release for all customer requests.

explanation:
An exchange between two slots is reversible. The promotion 40 minutes ago moved the content that production was running into the staging slot, so the staging slot still holds the last release that worked. Performing the same exchange again puts that release back into the production slot and moves the failed release into the staging slot, so customers return to the previous release with no rebuild, no new deployment, and a fast turnaround.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Redeploy the previous release artifact from the build pipeline to the production slot so that the production slot is running the previous code again: This is excluded by the stated requirement that the code must not be rebuilt or redeployed, and it also adds pipeline time and risk. The documentation describes the exchange between slots as reversible, so the last-known-good release can be restored without pushing artifacts again.
- Stop the production slot, copy the files from the staging slot into the production wwwroot folder, and restart the instances: Copying files by hand is not an exchange between slots: the configuration that travels with the app does not move with the copied files, and the two slot environments are left inconsistent with each other. The supported way to bring the previous release back into production is to exchange the two slots.
- Set the traffic percentage of the production slot to 0 and of the staging slot to 100, so that the staging slot is running the previous release for all customer requests: Changing the traffic percentages only changes where requests are sent; the failed release stays deployed in the production slot and keeps running there, and the slot that holds the previous release is a separate environment with its own hostname and configuration. The documented recovery from a bad promotion is another exchange of the slots.

prompt: You have an App Service web app whose release pipeline uploads a Node.js package that was already built by a separate build service to the staging deployment slot. The deployment fails because Kudu attempts to run npm install without access to the private package registry. You need the uploaded package to be deployed as supplied. Which action should you take?

options.text: Set SCM_DO_BUILD_DURING_DEPLOYMENT to false in the staging slot.
Set SCM_DO_BUILD_DURING_DEPLOYMENT to true in the staging slot.
Set SCM_DO_BUILD_DURING_DEPLOYMENT to false in the production slot.
Remove SCM_DO_BUILD_DURING_DEPLOYMENT from the staging slot.

explanation:
The pipeline uploads an artifact that was already compiled by an external build service, so Kudu should not build it again. Setting SCM_DO_BUILD_DURING_DEPLOYMENT to false in the staging slot, which is where the pipeline deploys and where the failure occurs, stops Kudu from running npm install during deployment and lets the supplied package be used as-is.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Set SCM_DO_BUILD_DURING_DEPLOYMENT to true in the staging slot: This keeps the build-during-deployment behavior that is already causing the failure, so Kudu continues to run npm install during the deployment to the staging slot.
- Set SCM_DO_BUILD_DURING_DEPLOYMENT to false in the production slot: The pipeline deploys to the staging slot, and each slot keeps its own configuration. Changing this setting only in the production slot leaves the failing staging deployment unchanged.
- Remove SCM_DO_BUILD_DURING_DEPLOYMENT from the staging slot: Deleting the setting does not disable the build step; it reverts the slot to the default behavior in which Kudu runs npm install for a Node.js deployment.

options.text: App Service access restrictions
App Service private endpoint
Auto swap for the deployment slot
Local cache for the deployment slot

explanation:
A deployment slot is a separate, live App Service environment with its own hostname, so it is reachable independently of the production hostname. Because the slot hostname must not be open to the general internet, the release engineer should apply App Service access restrictions on the slot so that only the validation team's addresses can reach it. Access restrictions are the documented way to keep a slot's hostname from being publicly accessible while still allowing approved callers.

Why the other options are wrong:
- App Service private endpoint: A private endpoint gives the slot a private IP for private-link traffic; it does not by itself keep internet callers from reaching the slot's own public hostname, so it does not satisfy the requirement to restrict who can reach that hostname.
- Auto swap for the deployment slot: Auto swap controls whether a new deployment in the slot is promoted to production automatically. It has no effect on who can reach the slot's hostname.
- Local cache for the deployment slot: Local cache improves response times for cached content and is recommended to be paired with deployment slots to avoid deployment downtime; it does not restrict network callers to the slot.

You have an App Service web app with a production slot and a staging slot on the same plan, as shown in the exhibit. The release team has deployed the next release candidate to the staging slot and wants that build to be judged against live customer traffic before it is promoted to everyone, while the live app keeps serving customers during the comparison. Which action should the release engineer take?

`Slot         Traffic %   Auto swap   Swap with warm up
production       100         Off        Enabled
staging           0         Off        Enabled`
prompt: The release engineer should _____.

options.text: set the Traffic % of the staging slot to 25.
set the Traffic % of the production slot to 25 and leave the staging slot at 0.
set the Traffic % of the staging slot to 100.
set the Traffic % of the staging slot to 0.

explanation:
A slot that has just been added starts with Traffic % set to 0, which is why all customer traffic currently reaches the production slot and the release candidate in the staging slot sees no live traffic. The Traffic % value of the staging slot is the control that decides how much of the customer traffic is routed to it, so raising it to an intermediate value sends live traffic to the staging slot for the comparison while the production slot continues to serve the remainder. Among the options, only raising the staging slot to an intermediate value (25) satisfies both requirements: the staging build meets live traffic and production keeps serving customers.

Why the other options are wrong:
- set the Traffic % of the production slot to 25 and leave the staging slot at 0: Lowering the Traffic % on the production slot does not send anything to the staging slot; the staging slot would stay at 0 and keep receiving no customer traffic, so the release candidate would still never be evaluated under live load.
- set the Traffic % of the staging slot to 100: Setting the staging slot to 100 routes every customer request to the staging slot and takes the production slot out of the traffic path, so there would be no live production traffic left to compare the release candidate against, and the candidate would effectively already be promoted.
- set the Traffic % of the staging slot to 0: Setting the staging slot to 0 is the state it already has: all customer traffic continues to go to the production slot and the release candidate in the staging slot never receives live traffic, so the intended comparison cannot happen.

- Plan property: Deployment slots in use; Value: production, staging
- Plan property: Average CPU utilization, last hour; Value: 94%
- Plan property: Average memory utilization, last hour; Value: 91%
- Plan property: Outcome of the last three promotions; Value: Each failed before the traffic switch completed
prompt: The release engineer should _____.

options.text: Temporarily increase the instance count, then return the plan to its earlier count after the promotion completes
Switch the promotion to Stop/Reset during swap so the source slot restarts before it takes traffic
Enable auto swap on the staging slot so each build reaches production without a manual promotion
Move the app to the Premium tier so the promotion runs on a higher-capacity plan

explanation:
The plan is running at 94% CPU and 91% memory, above the 90% level at which deployments may struggle to finish. The recommended remedy is to add instances to the plan temporarily so the deployment can complete, and then go back to the count the plan had before the release, which leaves the plan's footprint and monthly cost unchanged once the release is live.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Switch the promotion to Stop/Reset during swap so the source slot restarts before it takes traffic: Stop/Reset during swap is meant for apps that stop responding when their settings change. It stops and restarts the source slot, which introduces a slower cold start and greater downtime, and it does nothing to relieve the CPU and memory pressure on the plan.
- Enable auto swap on the staging slot so each build reaches production without a manual promotion: Auto swap only removes the manual promotion step. The promotion still runs on the same plan that is already at its resource limits, so it does not address why the promotions are failing.
- Move the app to the Premium tier so the promotion runs on a higher-capacity plan: Moving the app to the Premium tier changes the plan's tier and its ongoing cost permanently, which conflicts with the requirement that the plan keep its current footprint and monthly cost once the release is live.

prompt: You have an App Service app named api-prod running on a Standard S1 plan, and a corporate firewall that admits inbound traffic only to the IP addresses currently assigned to this app. The service must not drop any incoming requests while you replace its certificate. A private PFX certificate named cert-2024 is bound to the custom domain api.contoso.com and stops being valid in nine days, and you have a replacement PFX file named cert-2026 in hand. Which sequence of steps should you take?

options.text: Upload cert-2026, then use Update binding on the api.contoso.com SNI SSL binding so it serves cert-2026, and afterwards delete cert-2024.
Upload cert-2026, then delete the api.contoso.com SNI SSL binding, add a new SNI SSL binding that serves cert-2026, and afterwards delete cert-2024.
Upload cert-2026 and delete cert-2024 immediately, because App Service renews the site's certificates on its own.
Import cert-2026 from Key Vault, wait for the automatic sync to finish, then delete cert-2024 and the api.contoso.com SNI SSL binding.

explanation:
Two things are needed for HTTPS on a custom domain: the certificate must exist on the app, and a binding must attach it to the domain. Upload cert-2026 first so the app holds it, then switch the existing SNI SSL binding over with Update binding, which swaps the certificate served by that binding without removing the binding itself. Because the binding is never deleted, clients see no interruption and the app keeps the same inbound IP addresses that the corporate firewall admits. Once no binding references cert-2024, that certificate can be deleted from the app.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Upload cert-2026, then delete the api.contoso.com SNI SSL binding, add a new SNI SSL binding that serves cert-2026, and afterwards delete cert-2024: Removing the binding before the new one is in place creates a window in which api.contoso.com has no TLS configuration, so requests fail. In addition, deleting a binding can change the app's inbound IP addresses, which would invalidate the firewall rule and break access for clients that pin those addresses. This is exactly the risk when a certificate in use is replaced by rebuilding the binding from scratch.
- Upload cert-2026 and delete cert-2024 immediately, because App Service renews the site's certificates on its own: Automatic renewal only applies to certificates that Azure issues and manages on your behalf, such as the free managed certificate or an App Service certificate. A private PFX file you upload yourself is never renewed for you, so cert-2024 must be replaced manually. Deleting it before cert-2026 is serving traffic would break TLS for the site.
- Import cert-2026 from Key Vault, wait for the automatic sync to finish, then delete cert-2024 and the api.contoso.com SNI SSL binding: Import from Key Vault only works when the certificate lives in the vault, and cert-2026 was supplied to you as a PFX file. Even if the certificate came from a vault, the last step removes the binding instead of updating it, which both breaks the site and can change the app's inbound IP addresses, invalidating the firewall allowlist.

prompt: You have an App Service app named shop-web on a Standard S1 plan, and it must serve HTTPS for the custom domain shop.contoso.com with no certificate warnings in browsers. Your company already owns a certificate for that domain that was issued by a public CA, and you merged the certificate chain on a build host before exporting the PFX that you then tried to add to the app. Which action should you take?

options.text: Re-export the PFX with OpenSSL using `-keypbe PBE-SHA1-3DES -certpbe PBE-SHA1-3DES -macalg SHA1`, then upload the new file.
Re-export the PFX with OpenSSL using `-keypbe AES-256-CBC -certpbe AES-256-CBC -macalg SHA256`, then upload the new file.
Re-export the PFX with OpenSSL from server.crt instead of mergedcertificate.crt, using `-keypbe PBE-SHA1-3DES -certpbe PBE-SHA1-3DES -macalg SHA1`, then upload the new file.
Upload mergedcertificate.crt under Public key certificates (.cer), then add an SNI SSL binding for shop.contoso.com that uses that certificate.

explanation:
App Service accepts PFX files whose key and certificate bags are protected with the older 3DES algorithm, and OpenSSL 3 changed its default bag cipher to AES256, which the platform does not accept. The file on the export host therefore fails when it is added. Re-exporting with PBE-SHA1-3DES for both bags and SHA1 for the MAC produces a PFX that App Service can take, and because the merged chain (server certificate, intermediates and root) is the export input and the certificate was issued by a trusted CA, the resulting binding is validated by browsers and the domain shows the Secured state.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Re-export the PFX with OpenSSL using `-keypbe AES-256-CBC -certpbe AES-256-CBC -macalg SHA256`, then upload the new file: These are the OpenSSL 3 defaults that produced the file in the first place, and a PFX whose bags are protected with AES256 is exactly what App Service refuses. Re-exporting this way yields another unusable file. OpenSSL v1 defaults produce an acceptable file, or the 3DES and SHA1 settings can be passed explicitly.
- Re-export the PFX with OpenSSL from server.crt instead of mergedcertificate.crt, using `-keypbe PBE-SHA1-3DES -certpbe PBE-SHA1-3DES -macalg SHA1`, then upload the new file: The protection settings are right, but exporting only server.crt leaves the intermediate and root certificates out of the PFX. Such a file may be accepted by the platform, yet browsers cannot build the chain to the trusted CA and report a certificate validation error, so the domain still isn't served cleanly over HTTPS. The merged chain file has to be the input to the export.
- Upload mergedcertificate.crt under Public key certificates (.cer), then add an SNI SSL binding for shop.contoso.com that uses that certificate: Certificates uploaded as Public key certificates (.cer) are never used to secure custom domains; they exist so that the app's own code can present a certificate when calling remote resources. A TLS binding for shop.contoso.com requires a private certificate that carries the full chain and is signed by a trusted CA, so the .cer upload cannot secure the domain.

- Item: Existing role assignment on kv-cert; Value: Key Vault Secrets User for the system-assigned managed identity of billing-api

prompt: You have an App Service app named billing-api on a Premium P1V3 plan that must serve HTTPS for the custom domain billing.contoso.com. The certificate for that domain already lives in the Azure Key Vault kv-cert, and you want that vault to stay the only place where the certificate is stored, so that a renewed version reaches the app without manual work. When you configure the app to take its certificate from the vault, the operation fails with an authorization error. Which change should you make?

options.text: Assign the Key Vault Certificate User role to the Microsoft.Web service principal on kv-cert.
Assign the Key Vault Certificate User role to the system-assigned managed identity of billing-api on kv-cert.
Assign the Key Vault Secrets User role to the Microsoft.Web service principal on kv-cert.
Assign the Key Vault Reader role to the system-assigned managed identity of billing-api on kv-cert.

explanation:
The vault is the source of truth for this certificate, and App Service pulls the certificate material from Key Vault as the platform resource provider, so that provider identity needs data-plane read access to certificates. Assigning the Key Vault Certificate User role to the Microsoft.Web service principal (app/client ID abfa0a7c-a6b6-4736-8310-5855508787cd in Azure Cloud, 6a02c803-dafd-4136-b4c3-5a6f318b4714 in Government) on kv-cert authorizes the import. The client ID works with tooling such as the Azure CLI role assignment command, while ARM templates and Bicep normally use the service principal object ID of the enterprise application. With this permission in place, the app syncs a renewed certificate from the vault automatically (within about 24 hours) and updates the binding, and the permission must not be removed afterwards or the sync stops working.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Assign the Key Vault Certificate User role to the system-assigned managed identity of billing-api on kv-cert: The identity that performs the vault import is the App Service resource provider (Microsoft.Web), not the app's own system-assigned managed identity. Granting the certificate role to the app identity therefore leaves the import unauthorized, because the platform is the party reading the certificate out of the vault.
- Assign the Key Vault Secrets User role to the Microsoft.Web service principal on kv-cert: Key Vault Secrets User grants access to secrets, not to certificate objects. The App Service resource provider still cannot read the certificate material from kv-cert, so the import keeps failing with an authorization error.
- Assign the Key Vault Reader role to the system-assigned managed identity of billing-api on kv-cert: Key Vault Reader only allows management-plane metadata to be listed; it does not grant data-plane read access to certificate material, and the principal that needs it is the Microsoft.Web service provider identity rather than the app's managed identity.

You want contoso.com protected by the certificate that App Service issues for you and renews automatically at no cost, but every attempt to issue it fails and the domain still serves no certificate. Which action should you take?

Remove the IP restrictions on contoso-portal, then create the free App Service managed certificate for contoso.com and bind it to the domain.

explanation:
For a root domain such as contoso.com, the free App Service managed certificate can only be created - and later renewed - while the app is reachable from the internet, so the app must have no IP restrictions configured. contoso-portal currently allows only 203.0.113.0/24 and denies everything else, which blocks that validation, so the IP restrictions are what must be dealt with first. The other prerequisites are already satisfied: certificates need a Basic, Standard, Premium or Isolated plan (Basic B1 qualifies), and the A record already points at the app's inbound IP. Once the certificate is created, a TLS binding must still be added for contoso.com so the domain actually serves HTTPS.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Keep the IP restrictions on contoso-portal and add a DNS Certification Authority Authorization record for contoso.com with the value 0 issue digicert.com, then create the free App Service managed certificate for contoso.com and bind it to the domain: A DNS Certification Authority Authorization record with the value 0 issue digicert.com is only needed for some domains and merely controls which issuer may issue for the domain; it has no effect on whether the app can be validated. Here the request still fails because the app accepts traffic only from 203.0.113.0/24, and both creation and periodic renewal of the certificate for a root domain depend on the app being reachable from the internet.
- Keep the IP restrictions on contoso-portal and scale the plan up to a Premium P1V3 tier, then create the free App Service managed certificate for contoso.com and bind it to the domain: The app's plan tier is not the problem: certificates require the plan to be in the Basic, Standard, Premium or Isolated tier, so Basic B1 already qualifies and scaling up changes nothing. Leaving the IP restrictions in place keeps the app unreachable from the internet, which is the condition that stops the certificate for the root domain from being issued and renewed.
- Import a PKCS12 certificate for contoso.com from the Key Vault kv-contoso into contoso-portal and bind it to the domain, leaving the IP restrictions in place: Importing from Key Vault means the certificate is stored and maintained by your organization in kv-contoso and is a customer-managed option, so it does not meet the requirement of the certificate that App Service issues and renews automatically at no cost. You need the app to keep answering that system on the address it uses today, and shop.contoso.com must keep resolving to the address it uses today as well. Which change should you make?

options.text: Add an IP based SSL binding for legacy.contoso.com on a dedicated public IP, repoint that domain's A record to the new address, and leave the shop.contoso.com SNI SSL binding unchanged.
Add an IP based SSL binding for shop.contoso.com on a dedicated public IP, repoint both domains' A records to that address, and leave legacy.contoso.com on SNI SSL.
Change the legacy.contoso.com binding from SNI SSL to IP based SSL so that it reuses the inbound address the two domains currently share.
Add an IP based SSL binding for legacy.contoso.com on a dedicated public IP but leave the legacy.contoso.com A record pointing at the shared inbound address.

explanation:
A client that connects by IP address alone never sends a host name, so it cannot benefit from SNI, which selects the site certificate by host name. The TLS/SSL type that serves a site certificate to such a client is IP based SSL: it holds one binding and one certificate on a dedicated public IP that App Service creates, and the domain's A record is then repointed to that new address shown on the Custom domains page. Because IP based SSL allows only a single binding and certificate, the app keeps its existing SNI SSL binding for shop.contoso.com on the shared address, so that domain keeps resolving to the same IP as today. The Standard S1 plan already satisfies the requirement that IP based SSL needs the Standard tier or higher.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add an IP based SSL binding for shop.contoso.com on a dedicated public IP, repoint both domains' A records to that address, and leave legacy.contoso.com on SNI SSL: IP based SSL permits only one binding and one certificate, so the app cannot carry two of them. Putting shop.contoso.com on the dedicated address would also move that domain off the shared inbound IP, which breaks the requirement that it keeps resolving to its current address, and the IP-only client would arrive at the dedicated address where no certificate for legacy.contoso.com is presented.
- Change the legacy.contoso.com binding from SNI SSL to IP based SSL so that it reuses the inbound address the two domains currently share: IP based SSL cannot reuse the shared inbound address; App Service creates a dedicated public IP for that binding. Swapping the SNI SSL binding for an IP based one on legacy.contoso.com can change the app's inbound IP address, and the domain's A record would still point at an address that no longer presents its certificate.
- Add an IP based SSL binding for legacy.contoso.com on a dedicated public IP but leave the legacy.contoso.com A record pointing at the shared inbound address: After an IP based SSL binding is created, the domain's A record must be repointed to the new dedicated IP shown on the Custom domains page. If the A record keeps pointing at the shared address, the on-premises client never reaches the binding that holds the legacy.contoso.com certificate, so the symptom persists.

prompt: You have an App Service Environment v3 that hosts a single app, secure-api, on a Premium v3 plan. The security team wants the cipher suites offered to this app to be controlled from one place only, because changes made to the two cipher configurations listed below sometimes seem to have no effect. Clients of this app must keep negotiating TLS 1.3. Which change should you make?

options.text: Remove the Minimum TLS Cipher Suite setting from the app and keep the FrontEndSSLCipherSuiteOrder cluster setting as the single place where the cipher order is managed.
Remove the FrontEndSSLCipherSuiteOrder cluster setting from the App Service Environment and keep the Minimum TLS Cipher Suite setting on the app as the single place where the cipher order is managed.
Keep both settings and set the app's Minimum TLS Cipher Suite to the same value as the first suite in the FrontEndSSLCipherSuiteOrder cluster setting.
Keep both settings, add the two TLS 1.3 cipher suites to the app's Minimum TLS Cipher Suite selection, and restart the front end so that both changes take effect.

explanation:
Cipher suite preferences should be configured in exactly one place. In an App Service Environment, the FrontEndSSLCipherSuiteOrder cluster setting is the mechanism that governs the cipher order offered by the front ends, and the documentation explicitly advises not to also enable the Minimum TLS Cipher Suite for a web app in that situation, because the result can be conflicting configurations, which matches the symptom the team reports. The cluster setting shown in the exhibit already lists both TLS 1.3 suites (TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 and TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256), so deleting the app-level Minimum TLS Cipher Suite setting leaves TLS 1.3 negotiable and keeps the cipher order defined in one place. Because the cluster setting itself is not being changed, no front end restart is required; a restart is only needed after editing FrontEndSSLCipherSuiteOrder.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Remove the FrontEndSSLCipherSuiteOrder cluster setting from the App Service Environment and keep the Minimum TLS Cipher Suite setting on the app as the single place where the cipher order is managed: FrontEndSSLCipherSuiteOrder is the control that governs cipher order for an App Service Environment; it must contain both TLS 1.3 suites and any change to it requires a front end restart. The app-level Minimum TLS Cipher Suite setting is documented for multitenant App Service on Basic SKU or higher, so deleting the environment-level setting removes the control the environment relies on rather than the conflicting one, and it would leave the environment without the required TLS 1.3 suites.
- Keep both settings and set the app's Minimum TLS Cipher Suite to the same value as the first suite in the FrontEndSSLCipherSuiteOrder cluster setting: Matching one suite value in the two scopes still leaves two separate configurations in place, and the documentation warns that using both can result in conflicting configurations. The app-level list also carries its own fixed priority order that you can't reorder to match the environment-level list, so the two scopes still do not define one predictable cipher order.
- Keep both settings, add the two TLS 1.3 cipher suites to the app's Minimum TLS Cipher Suite selection, and restart the front end so that both changes take effect: The Minimum TLS Cipher Suite list is fixed: you can't add new or different cipher suites to it, and the TLS 1.3 suites are not selectable that way. A front end restart applies only after you change the FrontEndSSLCipherSuiteOrder cluster setting, and leaving both configurations enabled can still produce conflicting behavior, so this does not deliver a single place to manage cipher preferences.

prompt: You have an App Service app named hr-portal that runs on a Linux Premium v3 plan (see the exhibit). You need only company clients that present a certificate issued by the corporate certificate authority to be able to use the app, and the app itself must be able to read which client connected. Which action should you take?

options.text: Enable mutual TLS (mTLS) and configure the trusted certificate authority chain that validates client certificates
Enable end-to-end TLS (E2E) and upload the corporate certificate authority certificates as client certificates
Add a TLS binding for the custom domain and configure the corporate certificate authority certificates as the bound certificates
Upload the corporate certificate authority certificates as public key certificates (.cer) and turn on HTTPS Only

explanation:
Mutual TLS (mTLS) is supported on both Linux and Windows App Service plans. With mTLS enabled and a trusted certificate authority chain configured, clients must present certificates that are validated against that chain, and the client certificate details are exposed to the app code through request headers. That is exactly what this scenario requires: restricting access to clients holding a certificate issued by the corporate certificate authority and letting the app read who connected.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enable end-to-end TLS (E2E) and upload the corporate certificate authority certificates as client certificates: End-to-end TLS encrypts the traffic between the App Service front end and the app worker inside Azure, so that traffic is not unencrypted after it leaves the load balancer. It does not authenticate inbound callers against a certificate authority, and merely uploading the corporate authority certificates as client certificates does not restrict who can reach the app or expose client certificate details to the code.
- Add a TLS binding for the custom domain and configure the corporate certificate authority certificates as the bound certificates: A TLS binding attaches a server certificate to a custom domain so the domain serves HTTPS; it says nothing about the certificates presented by callers. Binding the corporate certificate authority certificates to the domain does not make the app request and check client certificates, so callers without a corporate-issued certificate would still be accepted.
- Upload the corporate certificate authority certificates as public key certificates (.cer) and turn on HTTPS Only: Public key certificates (.cer) are uploaded so that app code can present a public certificate when calling a remote resource; they are never used to secure custom domains or to authenticate incoming callers. HTTPS Only only forces inbound HTTP requests to be redirected to HTTPS and does not check client certificates either.
