prompt: You have an App Service app named payments-api that runs on a Basic B1 plan. Your organization's security baseline states that every inbound connection to the app and to its SCM endpoint must use the newest transport protocol version that App Service supports, and that clients offering only older versions must be turned away. The exhibit shows the app's current configuration and its latest compliance evaluation. Which change should you make?

options.text: Set the Minimum Inbound TLS Version setting to TLS 1.3
Set the Minimum Inbound TLS Version setting to TLS 1.2
Set the Minimum Inbound TLS Version setting to TLS 1.1
Set the Minimum TLS Cipher Suite setting to TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256

explanation:
Raising the Minimum Inbound TLS Version to TLS 1.3 makes that version the floor for inbound traffic to the app and its SCM endpoint, so a client that can only offer an older version is refused. TLS 1.3 is the newest inbound version App Service supports, and the built-in Azure Policy definition 'App Service apps should use the latest TLS version' audits exactly this setting, which is why the app is currently reported as NonCompliant.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Set the Minimum Inbound TLS Version setting to TLS 1.2: TLS 1.2 is the default minimum for new web apps and their SCM endpoints. Keeping that value leaves the app accepting clients that negotiate an older protocol, so it does not satisfy the baseline and does not clear the NonCompliant result.
- Set the Minimum Inbound TLS Version setting to TLS 1.1: TLS 1.1 is a legacy version that is no longer considered secure. Using it as the floor weakens the app's posture instead of enforcing the newest supported protocol version.
- Set the Minimum TLS Cipher Suite setting to TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256: The Minimum TLS Cipher Suite setting controls which cipher algorithms are offered for the protocol versions that are allowed; it does not raise the minimum protocol version, so clients that negotiate TLS 1.2 would still be accepted.

- App: hr-web; Plan: Linux Premium v3; Reported problem: Only devices holding a certificate issued by the company certificate authority may open a session, and the application must show which device connected.
- App: orders-api; Plan: Premium P1V3; Reported problem: Traffic between the platform front end and the worker that runs the application must be encrypted inside Azure, not only between the browser and the front end.
- App: finance-app; Plan: Standard S1; Reported problem: Only the suite named in the corporate standard may be negotiated, and the order of the allowed suites must be the one the platform publishes.

options.text: Set Minimum Inbound TLS Version to TLS 1.2
Set Minimum Inbound TLS Version to TLS 1.3
Enable the Minimum TLS Cipher Suite on the app
Enable mutual TLS and upload the trusted client certificate CA chain
Enable end-to-end TLS encryption for the front-end-to-worker traffic
Read the X-Forwarded-Proto and x-appservice-proto request headers in app code
Set the FrontEndSSLCipherSuiteOrder cluster setting and restart the front end

explanation: checkout-web needs a TLS 1.2 floor (Minimum Inbound TLS Version = TLS 1.2): TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 are legacy protocols that are no longer considered secure, while TLS 1.2 is the default minimum for new web apps and SCM endpoints and keeps broad client compatibility. partner-api needs Minimum Inbound TLS Version = TLS 1.3, the newest fully supported version whose two fixed suites (TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 and TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256) remain available. survey-app must read the X-Forwarded-Proto and x-appservice-proto headers, because TLS is terminated at the App Service network load balancers and the worker receives plain HTTP while the original protocol is reported through those headers. hr-web needs mutual TLS, which is supported on Linux and Windows plans, validates client certificates against a trusted CA chain you configure, and exposes client certificate details to the app through request headers. orders-api needs end-to-end TLS encryption, offered on Premium plans, so traffic between the front end and the worker is encrypted inside Azure. finance-app needs the app-level Minimum TLS Cipher Suite, supported on Basic SKU or higher on multitenant App Service, whose fixed list and priority order cannot be changed and which blocks every less-secure suite once a minimum is selected. The FrontEndSSLCipherSuiteOrder cluster setting belongs to an App Service Environment, so it fits none of these apps.

context:
You have an App Service app named ledger-api that runs on a Premium v3 plan (see the exhibit). The corporate security policy states that the traffic between the Azure network load balancer that accepts the incoming connection and the worker process that runs the app code must not be readable on the network inside Azure. Which change should you make to the app?

`App Service property            Current value
------------------------------  -----------------------------------
App Service plan                Premium v3
Minimum inbound TLS version     TLS 1.2
HTTPS Only                      On
Minimum TLS cipher suite        Not configured
Client certificate auth         Off
Custom domain binding           SNI SSL for ledger.contoso.com`
prompt: To satisfy the policy, you should _____.

options.text: Enable end-to-end TLS encryption for the app
Require TLS 1.3 as the minimum inbound version for the app
Assign a dedicated public IP with an IP based SSL binding for the app
Require client certificates with mutual TLS for the app

explanation:
End-to-end (E2E) TLS encryption is the App Service feature that also protects the front-end-to-worker traffic inside Azure, not just the client-to-front-end connection, and it is offered on Premium plans (recommended for new deployments) and legacy Standard plans. Because ledger-api runs on a Premium v3 plan, turning it on for the app is the change that satisfies the policy requirement that traffic between the Azure network load balancer and the worker process must not be readable on the internal network.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Require TLS 1.3 as the minimum inbound version for the app: Setting the minimum inbound TLS version only decides which protocol versions clients may negotiate with the front end of the app; the app still receives requests as plain HTTP from the front end, so the internal front-end-to-worker path is not protected and the policy is not met.
- Assign a dedicated public IP with an IP based SSL binding for the app: An IP based SSL binding gives the app a dedicated public IP address and its own certificate; it changes how the app is reached from the internet but leaves the traffic between the load balancer and the worker unprotected inside Azure.
- Require client certificates with mutual TLS for the app: Mutual TLS makes callers present a certificate that is validated against a trusted chain, which authenticates the clients; it does not protect the connection between the Azure network load balancer and the worker process.

context:
You have an App Service app that must serve HTTPS on a custom domain (see the exhibit). Corporate policy for this internal service requires the domain to be protected with a certificate issued by your organization's internal certificate authority instead of a publicly trusted one, and that certificate has already been exported as a password-protected PFX that contains the full chain. Which action should you take?

- Property: App name; Value: claims-api
- Property: Plan tier; Value: Standard S1
- Property: Deployment; Value: Multitenant (shared) service
- Property: Custom domain; Value: claims.contoso.com
- Property: TLS/SSL binding for claims.contoso.com; Value: None yet
- Property: Certificate issuer; Value: Internal certificate authority
- Property: Certificate file; Value: Password-protected PFX, full chain included
prompt: You should _____.

options.text: Move the app into an App Service Environment v3 and bind the internal certificate authority certificate for the custom domain
Upload the PFX under Bring your own certificates (.pfx) in App Service and add a TLS/SSL binding for the custom domain
Import the PFX from an Azure Key Vault and add a TLS/SSL binding for the custom domain
Enable mutual TLS on the App Service app so that clients must present a certificate signed by the internal certificate authority

explanation:
A certificate issued by a private (internal) certificate authority can be used for inbound TLS only in App Service Environment v3 — that isn't possible in App Service (multitenant). Because policy requires this internal CA certificate for claims.contoso.com, the app has to run in an App Service Environment v3 and the certificate must be bound to the custom domain there. The Standard S1 tier itself isn't the blocker: private certificates are supported on Basic, Standard, Premium and Isolated plans, and the PFX format already satisfies the private certificate requirements (password-protected, full chain). What blocks the current deployment is that it runs on the shared multitenant service.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Upload the PFX under Bring your own certificates (.pfx) in App Service and add a TLS/SSL binding for the custom domain: Uploading a password-protected PFX is the right mechanism for a certificate issued by a publicly trusted CA, but a certificate from an internal CA can't be used for inbound TLS on the shared multitenant service, so the custom domain would still not be protected by a certificate the clients can validate.
- Import the PFX from an Azure Key Vault and add a TLS/SSL binding for the custom domain: Importing the certificate from a Key Vault only changes where the certificate comes from and how renewals are synced. The certificate is still issued by an internal CA, and such a certificate can't be used for inbound TLS in multitenant App Service, so this doesn't secure the custom domain.
- Enable mutual TLS on the App Service app so that clients must present a certificate signed by the internal certificate authority: Mutual TLS validates the certificates that clients present to the app against a trusted CA chain that you configure; it doesn't allow the app to serve an internal-CA-issued server certificate that clients will accept for inbound HTTPS.

context:
You have an App Service app named travel-site that runs on a Standard S1 plan. It must serve HTTPS for the custom domain www.travelcontoso.com with the App Service managed certificate, which is issued and renewed automatically at no cost. The travelcontoso.com DNS zone is managed by the corporate DNS team, and only approved certificate authorities may act for company domains. Every attempt to create the managed certificate for www.travelcontoso.com fails, and the domain still serves no certificate of its own (see the exhibit). Which action should you take?

- Property: App name; Value: travel-site
- Property: App Service plan; Value: Standard S1
- Property: Custom domain; Value: www.travelcontoso.com
- Property: Where www.travelcontoso.com currently resolves; Value: The travel-site app
- Property: Certificate requested; Value: App Service managed certificate (no cost, renewed automatically)
- Property: Outcome of the creation attempts; Value: Failed - the domain still serves no certificate of its own
- Property: Who controls the travelcontoso.com zone; Value: The corporate DNS team; only approved certificate authorities may act for company domains
prompt: To make the App Service managed certificate available for www.travelcontoso.com, you should _____.

options.text: Create a CAA record for the domain with the value 0 issue digicert.com
Create a CAA record for the domain with the value 0 issue internalcorp-ca.com
Create an A record for the domain that points it to the app's IP address
Create an App Service certificate for the domain in the Azure Key Vault

explanation:
The App Service managed certificate is issued by DigiCert, and for some domains the DNS zone must explicitly allow that authority to act for the domain. A certificate authority authorization (CAA) record holding the value 0 issue digicert.com is what allows DigiCert to issue, and later renew, the managed certificate for www.travelcontoso.com, so the creation attempts start to succeed. Nothing about the app's plan, tier or address records needs to change, since the domain already resolves to the app and the failure comes from the zone's issuer policy.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Create a CAA record for the domain with the value 0 issue internalcorp-ca.com: Only the authority that issues the App Service managed certificate can be listed for that certificate to be created and renewed. Authorizing the internal authority instead leaves the managed certificate blocked, so the attempts keep failing.
- Create an A record for the domain that points it to the app's IP address: The address record for www.travelcontoso.com already points to the travel-site app, and an address record says nothing about which authorities the zone may let act; the failure comes from the zone's issuer policy, not from where the domain points.
- Create an App Service certificate for the domain in the Azure Key Vault: The App Service certificate is a different offering: it is a paid certificate issued by GoDaddy and kept in your Key Vault, exportable and usable outside App Service. It is not the no-cost certificate that App Service provides and renews automatically.

prompt: The app code should _____ so that the absolute URLs it generates use the protocol that the client actually sent.

options.text: Read the `X-Forwarded-Proto` request header and use its value as the URL scheme
Read the `X-Forwarded-For` request header and use its value as the URL scheme
Read the `X-Forwarded-Host` request header and use its value as the URL scheme
Read the `X-Forwarded-Port` request header and use its value as the URL scheme

explanation:
App Service terminates TLS at its network load balancers, so a request that arrived over HTTPS reaches the worker process as unencrypted HTTP and the in-process request object reports the "http" scheme. To learn the protocol the client really used, the code must inspect the `X-Forwarded-Proto` request header (App Service also exposes the original protocol in the `x-appservice-proto` header, whose value is `http` or `https`). Reading the header and using its value as the scheme produces correct absolute URLs for both browsers and the payment provider.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Read the `X-Forwarded-For` request header and use its value as the URL scheme: The `X-Forwarded-For` header carries the IP address of the original client (plus any proxy addresses), not the protocol, so building the URL from it cannot tell HTTP from HTTPS.
- Read the `X-Forwarded-Host` request header and use its value as the URL scheme: The `X-Forwarded-Host` header carries the host name the client requested; the app already knows its own host name, and this header says nothing about whether the client used HTTP or HTTPS.
- Read the `X-Forwarded-Port` request header and use its value as the URL scheme: The `X-Forwarded-Port` header carries the port of the original request; a port number alone cannot be used to choose between an http:// and an https:// URL.

context:
You have an App Service app named secure-portal that runs on a Standard S1 plan. The custom domain portal.contoso.com is mapped to the app, and the certificate that your organization bought from a public certificate authority is already stored on the app (see the exhibit). The domain currently answers over plain HTTP only, and requests to https://portal.contoso.com fail. The same certificate is installed on other company systems, so the app has to serve that exact certificate, and its key material must stay under your organization's control. Which action should you take?

- Item: App Service app; Value: secure-portal (Standard S1 plan)
- Item: Custom domain; Value: portal.contoso.com (A record points to the app's inbound IP)
- Item: Certificate on the app; Value: portal-cert, issued by a public CA, valid for portal.contoso.com until 2027-06-30
- Item: Certificate source; Value: Bring your own certificates (.pfx)
- Item: Public key certificates (.cer); Value: None
- Item: HTTPS on the custom domain; Value: Not working - the domain responds over plain HTTP only
prompt: The action you should take is to _____.

options.text: add a TLS binding for portal.contoso.com that uses the certificate stored on the app
add a TLS binding for portal.contoso.com that uses the public key certificate (.cer) stored on the app
add a TLS binding for portal.contoso.com that uses the App Service certificate (ASC) held in Azure Key Vault
add a TLS binding for portal.contoso.com that uses the App Service managed certificate

explanation:
Serving HTTPS on a custom domain takes two separate steps: the certificate must exist on the app, and a binding must attach that certificate to the domain. secure-portal already has the purchased certificate (portal-cert) stored on the app, but nothing attaches it to portal.contoso.com, which is why the domain still answers over plain HTTP only. Adding a TLS binding that uses the stored certificate completes the setup, and it keeps the app presenting exactly the certificate the organization installed on its other systems, with key material the organization controls. Two related reminders: a domain that shows the state Secured on the Custom domains page still does not prove the certificate is trusted, because App Service never checks whether a bound certificate is self-signed or expired, and the certificate renewal should be done by uploading the new file and updating the binding without deleting the old binding first, so the app keeps serving traffic throughout.

Why the other options are wrong:
- add a TLS binding for portal.contoso.com that uses the public key certificate (.cer) stored on the app: A public key certificate (.cer) holds only the public key and is uploaded under Public key certificates (.cer) when your code has to present a public certificate to reach a remote resource. It is never used to secure a custom domain, and this app has no .cer stored anyway, so it cannot serve HTTPS for portal.contoso.com.
- add a TLS binding for portal.contoso.com that uses the App Service certificate (ASC) held in Azure Key Vault: An App Service certificate (ASC) is a separate certificate issued by GoDaddy and kept in your key vault. It is not the certificate your organization purchased and installed on its other systems, so binding it would make the app present a different certificate than the one the requirement calls for.
- add a TLS binding for portal.contoso.com that uses the App Service managed certificate: The App Service managed certificate is issued and renewed by the platform. Its issuer, public key and private key can change at any time outside your control and it cannot be exported, so it cannot satisfy the requirement that the app present the organization's purchased certificate with key material under the organization's control.

context:
You have an App Service app named checkout-web on a Standard S1 plan that must serve HTTPS for the custom domain checkout.contoso.com with a publicly trusted certificate your organization already owns. A colleague prepared the PFX file on the team's Linux build host from the private key and the merged chain and protected it with a password, but the portal rejects the file every time the team tries to add it under Bring your own certificates (.pfx). The build host and the command that produced the file are shown in the exhibit. Which change should you make to the PFX file?

`$ openssl version
OpenSSL 3.0.13 30 Jan 2024

$ openssl pkcs12 -export -out checkout.pfx -inkey checkout.key -in mergedcertificate.crt
Enter Export Pass Phrase:`
prompt: The team should _____.

options.text: re-create the PFX with 3DES-based encryption for the key and the certificate and a SHA1 message authentication code
re-create the PFX with AES256-based encryption for the key and the certificate and a SHA256 message authentication code
re-create the PFX with 3DES-based encryption for the key, AES256-based encryption for the certificate, and a SHA1 message authentication code
re-create the PFX with 3DES-based encryption for the key and the certificate and a SHA256 message authentication code

explanation:
OpenSSL v3 changed the default PFX cipher from 3DES to AES256, and App Service doesn't accept a PFX produced with those v3 defaults, which is why the file is rejected even though the chain is complete and the file is password protected. Rebuilding the file with 3DES-based encryption for both the key and the certificate and a SHA1 message authentication code (openssl pkcs12 -export -out checkout.pfx -inkey checkout.key -in mergedcertificate.crt -keypbe PBE-SHA1-3DES -certpbe PBE-SHA1-3DES -macalg SHA1) produces the combination App Service accepts, which is the behavior OpenSSL v1 gave by default.

Why the other options are wrong:
- re-create the PFX with AES256-based encryption for the key and the certificate and a SHA256 message authentication code: This is the OpenSSL v3 default (AES256 with a SHA256 message authentication code), and App Service doesn't accept a PFX built that way. The key and the certificate must both be encrypted with PBE-SHA1-3DES and the MAC algorithm set to SHA1.
- re-create the PFX with 3DES-based encryption for the key, AES256-based encryption for the certificate, and a SHA1 message authentication code: The private key and the certificate must both use PBE-SHA1-3DES encryption, so leaving the certificate at the OpenSSL v3 AES256 default still yields a file App Service rejects. Use -keypbe PBE-SHA1-3DES and -certpbe PBE-SHA1-3DES together.
- re-create the PFX with 3DES-based encryption for the key and the certificate and a SHA256 message authentication code: The supported override pairs the 3DES encryption of the key and the certificate with -macalg SHA1. Keeping 3DES encryption but producing the file with a SHA256 message authentication code doesn't reproduce the PFX combination App Service accepts.

prompt: You maintain an ARM template that creates a storage account, and your team deploys the saved file azuredeploy.json with New-AzResourceGroupDeployment against a resource group that already exists. You need to revise the template so that only the storage SKUs your company licenses can be requested, and so that the deployment still completes when the caller does not pass a SKU value at all. Which entry should you place in the template's parameters section for that SKU?

options.text: "skuName": { "type": "string", "defaultValue": "Standard_LRS", "allowedValues": [ "Standard_LRS", "Standard_GRS", "Premium_LRS" ] }
"skuName": { "type": "string", "allowedValues": [ "Standard_LRS", "Standard_GRS", "Premium_LRS" ] }
"skuName": { "type": "string", "defaultValue": "Standard_LRS" }
"skuName": { "type": "int", "defaultValue": 1, "minValue": 1, "maxValue": 3 }

explanation:
The keyed entry combines the two constraints the requirement needs on one string parameter. The allowedValues array holds the permitted values, and a deployment is rejected during validation when the supplied value is not among them; the defaultValue is applied only when the caller supplies no value at all. The two properties can be declared together on the same parameter, so editing the existing skuName entry this way restricts the SKU to the licensed set while still letting a caller omit it.

Why the other options are wrong:
- "skuName": { "type": "string", "allowedValues": [ "Standard_LRS", "Standard_GRS", "Premium_LRS" ] }: The permitted-value list is present, but the parameter has no fallback, so a deployment that omits the SKU fails instead of completing with a sensible value.
- "skuName": { "type": "string", "defaultValue": "Standard_LRS" }: The fallback is present, but with no list of permitted values any string is accepted, so an unapproved or mistyped SKU passes validation and is carried through to the storage account resource.
- "skuName": { "type": "int", "defaultValue": 1, "minValue": 1, "maxValue": 3 }: minValue and maxValue constrain numeric parameters, while the storage account SKU is a name string, and this entry also drops the list of licensed tiers so an arbitrary name would still be accepted.

prompt: You maintain an ARM template for a virtual machine scale set that the platform team deploys with New-AzResourceGroupDeployment. The template takes a single object parameter that carries the instance count, the administrator login name and the image publisher. Your change advisory board wants any request that carries a setting outside that approved list to be stopped before anything is deployed, while the three approved settings must still have to be supplied on every deployment. Which change should you make to the saved template?

options.text: Set "additionalProperties": false on the object parameter and leave the existing "properties" map unchanged
Set "additionalProperties": true on the object parameter and leave the existing "properties" map unchanged
Set "additionalProperties" to a string type definition on the object parameter and leave the existing "properties" map unchanged
Set "items": false on the object parameter and leave the existing "properties" map unchanged

explanation:
The template already declares languageVersion 2.0, which enables the aggregate type validation constraints on parameters, and the object's "properties" map already makes instanceCount, adminLogin and imagePublisher mandatory, because every listed property is required unless its type definition sets "nullable": true. What is missing is a restriction on extra keys: when no additionalProperties constraint is given, the default is true, so an object parameter silently accepts undeclared keys. Adding "additionalProperties": false means no properties beyond those defined in the "properties" map may be supplied, so a request carrying a setting outside the approved list fails during validation, while the three listed settings remain required.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Set "additionalProperties": true on the object parameter and leave the existing "properties" map unchanged: Setting the constraint to true is what already happens by default: any property that is not listed in the "properties" map is accepted with any value, so a request carrying an unapproved setting would still go through.
- Set "additionalProperties" to a string type definition on the object parameter and leave the existing "properties" map unchanged: A type definition describes the schema that applies to the extra properties, so it only constrains the values those extra settings may take. Keys outside the approved list are still accepted, so the request would not be stopped.
- Set "items": false on the object parameter and leave the existing "properties" map unchanged: "items" is an array constraint used to validate elements of an array parameter; it does not apply to an object parameter and would not restrict the keys of the object.

prompt: You maintain an ARM template that creates a storage account in a resource group that already exists, and the platform team deploys the saved file with New-AzResourceGroupDeployment. After a recent edit, every run stops during validation with an error about a language expression, before a single resource is created. You need the deployment to complete again, and you still need the team to read the storage account's blob endpoint back from the deployment once the run succeeds. Which change should you make to the saved template?

options.text: Store the reference() expression in the outputs section of the template instead of in a parameter defaultValue.
Keep the reference() expression in the parameters section of the template and change that parameter to the secureObject type.
Keep the reference() expression in the parameters section of the template and replace it with a fixed defaultValue that someone types in by hand.
Replace the parameter with a variable in the variables section of the template so that the reference() expression is evaluated after the deployment starts.

explanation:
Resource Manager resolves parameter values before it starts the deployment operations, and reference() needs the runtime state of a resource, so it cannot be used in the parameters section; that is exactly why the run now fails during validation before anything is created. The place to define a value taken from a deployed resource, such as a storage account's primaryEndpoints.blob, and to return it to whoever ran the deployment is the outputs section of the template, so the reference() expression belongs there and the parameter that carries it should be removed.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Keep the reference() expression in the parameters section of the template and change that parameter to the secureObject type: Marking the parameter as secureObject only controls whether the value is kept out of deployment history and logs. It does not change the point at which the parameter is resolved, so a reference() expression declared in the parameters section still fails before the deployment starts.
- Keep the reference() expression in the parameters section of the template and replace it with a fixed defaultValue that someone types in by hand: Typing a fixed defaultValue by hand would let the validation pass, but the value would be hard-coded and could drift from the real storage account, and it still would not be returned to the team in the deployment results, so it does not satisfy the requirement.
- Replace the parameter with a variable in the variables section of the template so that the reference() expression is evaluated after the deployment starts: A variable's value can be reused inside the template, but its content is not returned to the caller in the deployment results, so the team still could not read the blob endpoint back from the deployment even though the template would run.

prompt: You maintain an ARM template that the platform team deploys with New-AzResourceGroupDeployment against a resource group that already exists. A change request adds one more setting that the operator must choose at deployment time, and a test run of that change stopped during validation before any resource was created. You need the deployment to succeed again with the new setting supplied by the caller on every run. Which change should you make to the saved template?

options.text: Combine the related inputs into one object parameter and read the entries with parameters('name').memberName
Declare the new setting as one more string parameter, giving the template 257 parameters
Move the inputs into the variables section and read them with variables('name')
Declare the new setting in the outputs section and read it back after the deployment finishes

explanation:
A single template may declare at most 256 parameters, and the saved file already contains 256 declarations, so one extra declaration pushes it past that limit and the run fails during validation before any resource is created. Grouping the related settings into one parameter of type object keeps the declaration count under the limit while still letting the caller supply the values: the deployment passes a single object and the template reads each entry with parameters('name').memberName. Because the file uses languageVersion 2.0, the object's properties can also be listed, and every listed property is required unless its type definition sets "nullable": true, so the new setting has to be supplied by the caller on every run. Setting additionalProperties to false on that object rejects keys that are not part of the approved list.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Declare the new setting as one more string parameter, giving the template 257 parameters: The template already declares 256 parameters, the maximum one template may contain, so adding one more string declaration takes it over the limit and the deployment fails during validation. The limit counts declarations, not the number of settings the virtual machine can receive, so the new setting has to arrive through a declaration that replaces existing ones rather than through an extra one.
- Move the inputs into the variables section and read them with variables('name'): Variables are values defined inside the template and are resolved before the deployment operations start; they are never supplied by the caller. Moving the settings into the variables section would mean the operator could no longer choose the new setting at deployment time, and those declarations would have to fit under the separate limit that applies to the variables section.
- Declare the new setting in the outputs section and read it back after the deployment finishes: Outputs are the values the deployment returns once it finishes, and they are shown next to the inputs in the deployment summary in the portal; they are not inputs. Declaring the new setting there would not let the caller supply it, and the number of parameters would stay at the limit, so the validation failure would remain.

prompt: You maintain an ARM template for a virtual machine scale set that the platform team deploys with New-AzResourceGroupDeployment against a resource group that already exists. The saved file azuredeploy.json currently accepts the scale set capacity as free-form text, so a run can ask for a count of 99 or send a value such as many. Your change request requires the deployment to turn down any count below 2 or above 10 before it touches a resource, while counts inside that range keep deploying as before. Which change should you make to the saved template?

options.text: Change the parameter's type to int and add minValue: 2 plus maxValue: 10
Keep the parameter's type as string and add minLength: 2 plus maxLength: 10
Change the parameter's type to int and add minLength: 2 plus maxLength: 10
Keep the parameter's type as string and add minValue: 2 plus maxValue: 10

explanation:
To enforce an inclusive numeric range, the count must be declared as an integer parameter, because minValue and maxValue are the constraints that apply to int parameters in ARM templates. Changing the capacity parameter's type to int and adding minValue: 2 and maxValue: 10 makes any request below 2 or above 10 fail during validation, before any resource in the group is created, while counts from 2 through 10 continue to deploy exactly as before.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Keep the parameter's type as string and add minLength: 2 plus maxLength: 10: minLength and maxLength are the constraints for string and array parameters, where they measure character count or item count; they are not numeric range checks. With the parameter left as string, a request of 99 has only two characters, so it would satisfy a length of 2 and still be accepted.
- Change the parameter's type to int and add minLength: 2 plus maxLength: 10: The length constraints apply to string and array parameters, so once the type is int, minLength and maxLength do nothing for the value. That change leaves the 2 to 10 range unenforced and any integer, such as 99, would still be accepted.
- Keep the parameter's type as string and add minValue: 2 plus maxValue: 10: The numeric range constraints are only enforced on integer parameters. Leaving the type as string means minValue and maxValue do not check the supplied value, so a request of 99 or many would still pass validation and reach the deployment.

prompt: You have an ARM template saved as azuredeploy.json. Its configuration is currently declared as many parameters, as shown below. The operations team must still be able to supply every setting on each deployment run, and the deployment is currently rejected before it creates anything. Which change should you make to the saved template?

options.text: Replace the separate parameters with one object parameter that carries the settings, and read each setting from that parameter in the resources section.
Change the type of each parameter from string to int and keep the same number of parameter declarations.
Move the settings into the variables section and reference variables() instead of parameters().
Delete the separate parameter definitions and write each setting value directly into the resources section.

explanation:
A template may declare at most 256 parameters, and the counts in the exhibit add up to 118 + 96 + 50 = 264, which is why the deployment is rejected before any resource is created. Consolidating the related settings into one object parameter lowers the number of declarations below the ceiling, keeps every setting reachable from the resources section through that parameter's properties (for example parameters('networkSettings').name), and still lets the operations team supply the values on each run.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Change the type of each parameter from string to int and keep the same number of parameter declarations: Changing a parameter's data type does not change how many parameters the template declares, so the count remains above the ceiling and the deployment is still rejected; it also stops non-numeric settings such as names from being supplied at all.
- Move the settings into the variables section and reference variables() instead of parameters(): Values placed in variables are fixed inside the template and cannot be supplied by the caller when a deployment runs, so the operations team would lose the ability to choose these settings for each run. Organizing related values into an object parameter is the documented way to cut the parameter count while keeping deployment-time input.
- Delete the separate parameter definitions and write each setting value directly into the resources section: Writing the values straight into the resources section removes the deployment-time inputs altogether, so the operations team can no longer supply the settings on each run, which the scenario requires.

prompt: You have an ARM template saved as azuredeploy.json that asks the operator for a network rule configuration on every deployment. You need each run to carry exactly two entries in a fixed order — the protocol name as text first, then the port as a whole number — and you need any run with the wrong number of entries or a value of the wrong kind to be turned down during validation, before anything is deployed. Which change should you make to the saved template?

options.text: In the ruleSettings parameter definition, add "prefixItems" with a schema for a text entry followed by a schema for a whole-number entry, and set "items" to false.
In the ruleSettings parameter definition, add "prefixItems" with a schema for a text entry followed by a schema for a whole-number entry, and leave "items" unset.
In the ruleSettings parameter definition, add a single "items" schema that allows a text entry or a whole-number entry.
Change the ruleSettings parameter definition to "type": "object" with a "properties" block for the protocol and the port, and add "additionalProperties": false.

explanation:
With "languageVersion": "2.0" in the template, "prefixItems" assigns a schema to each fixed position of the array, so the first position can require text and the second a whole number. Adding "items": false pins the collection to exactly those two prefix schemas, so a run carrying one entry, a third entry, or a value of the wrong kind is rejected during validation before any resource is touched.

Why the other options are wrong:
- In the ruleSettings parameter definition, add "prefixItems" with a schema for a text entry followed by a schema for a whole-number entry, and leave "items" unset: Leaving "items" unset means it defaults to true, and "items" governs elements beyond the last index covered by "prefixItems", so a third entry would still pass validation and fail later instead of being turned down before deployment.
- In the ruleSettings parameter definition, add a single "items" schema that allows a text entry or a whole-number entry: A single "items" schema applies to every element and does not distinguish positions, so text and whole numbers can be swapped and the number of entries is not pinned; the bad request would reach the deployment rather than being rejected during validation.
- Change the ruleSettings parameter definition to "type": "object" with a "properties" block for the protocol and the port, and add "additionalProperties": false: An object parameter with "properties" and "additionalProperties": false validates named members of an object, but this template reads the input as a two-entry collection through indexed positions, so changing the shape breaks the deployment instead of rejecting the bad requests.

prompt: Your team maintains an ARM template that provisions a SQL server and its database, and the platform group deploys the saved file with New-AzResourceGroupDeployment against a resource group that already exists. The current parameters section and the resource that consumes them are shown below. A recent audit reported that the administrator password that operators type into the deployment form ends up stored in the deployment record and printed in the deployment log. You need to revise the saved template so that the deployment still runs exactly as before, while that password value is no longer written into the deployment record or the log. Which change should you make to the saved template?

options.text: Declare the administratorPassword parameter with the type secureString.
Declare the administratorPassword parameter with the type secureObject.
Declare the administratorPassword parameter with the type string, and add a metadata description telling operators to rotate the password after every deployment.
Declare the administratorPassword parameter with the type string, and add allowedValues so that only the three passwords used by the test environment can be supplied.

explanation:
ARM templates offer two parameter types that mark a value as sensitive: secureString for a standalone secret such as this SQL administrator password, and secureObject when the secret is carried inside an object parameter. When a parameter is declared as secureString, Resource Manager still resolves the operator's value and hands it to the resource exactly as before, but the value is not saved to the deployment history and is not logged. So changing only the type of administratorPassword from string to secureString keeps the deployment working while keeping the password out of the deployment record and the log. Keep in mind the trade-off: because no copy of the value is kept, nobody can read the password back from the deployment afterwards, so the platform team must store it somewhere else (for example in Key Vault) if it is needed later.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Declare the administratorPassword parameter with the type secureObject: secureObject is meant for a secret that travels inside an object parameter, where the value is an object with named properties. Here the administrator password is a single standalone value that the resource reads directly through parameters('administratorPassword'), so an object type is the wrong fit: it changes the shape of the value the caller must supply and would no longer match how the resource consumes it. secureString is the type that marks a single sensitive string.
- Declare the administratorPassword parameter with the type string, and add a metadata description telling operators to rotate the password after every deployment: A metadata description only adds help text that the portal shows as a tip for that parameter in the deployment form; it has no effect on how the value is stored or logged. Leaving the type as string means the password is still written to the deployment history and still printed in the deployment log, so the audit finding stays open.
- Declare the administratorPassword parameter with the type string, and add allowedValues so that only the three passwords used by the test environment can be supplied: allowedValues merely restricts the supplied value to a fixed list and fails validation for anything else. It does not change whether the value is saved in the deployment history or logged, and it would also break the real workflow, because operators would be limited to the three test environment passwords. Keeping the type as string leaves the password readable in the deployment record and the log.

context:
You keep a shared Azure Resource Manager template saved as azuredeploy.json. It creates a storage account, an Azure App Service plan and web app, and a key vault inside a resource group that already exists, and the platform team deploys the saved file with New-AzResourceGroupDeployment against that group. You are now extending the file so the same template can run in many environments, and so later steps in the same run can use what it produced. Five entries still have to be written, and the open work is shown below. Match each open entry to the template function that carries it out.

- Entry in azuredeploy.json: variables.planName; What that entry has to produce: A plan name made by putting a fixed prefix in front of the site name the operator types on the deployment form
- Entry in azuredeploy.json: variables.nameSuffix; What that entry has to produce: A short tail that keeps two copies of the template in one group from producing identical names, and that a second run in the same group reproduces the same way
- Entry in azuredeploy.json: variables.planSku; What that entry has to produce: The SKU to give the plan, picked at run time from the tier value the operator supplies
- Entry in azuredeploy.json: outputs.webAppAddress; What that entry has to produce: The address the web app can be reached at, taken from the web app that the same run creates
- Entry in azuredeploy.json: web app setting for the administrator password; What that entry has to produce: The administrator password that the same run stores in the key vault
prompt: variables.planName

options.text: uniqueString()
concat()
if()
reference()
listSecrets()

explanation: Each open entry needs the function whose job matches it. concat joins the fixed prefix and the site name the operator typed into one plan name, so it fills variables.planName. uniqueString derives the same short value from the same inputs on every run, which is exactly what variables.nameSuffix needs so repeated runs in one group never produce identical names. if evaluates a condition and returns one of two values, which is how variables.planSku follows the tier the operator supplied. reference returns the runtime state of a resource, so outputs.webAppAddress can report the address of the web app that the same run creates. listSecrets returns the secret values held in a key vault, so the web app setting can be given the administrator password the same run stored there.

prompt: The revision reaches the resource group by _____, the re-run is given [...], and the outcome of the run is read from [...].

options.text: changing the tier in the plan that the file specifies
adding an output in the file that reports the plan's tier
adding a parameter in the file whose default value specifies the plan's tier
changing the version marker in the file to record the tier change

explanation:
The plan and the web app are already in the resource group because an earlier run of the same file created them, and the resources section of a template holds the resources you deploy or update, so saving the revised file and running it again re-applies the changed properties to what is already in the group. That is why the tier change belongs in the plan's own definition in the file: an output or a parameter default would carry no configuration into the deployment, and the version marker only labels the revision of the template. Each run is named by the operator so it can be picked out in the deployment history, so the new run must carry a name of its own; reusing the earlier name, or using a value that stays the same on every run such as the resource group name or the file name, means later runs overwrite earlier records instead of appearing side by side. Finally, the command returns the result of the run, and ProvisioningState is the value that tells you whether the deployment succeeded; the verbose switch adds per-resource detail and debug adds deeper troubleshooting information when a run fails.

Why the other options are wrong:
- adding an output in the file that reports the plan's tier: An output only publishes a value once the run has finished; it carries no configuration into the deployment, so the plan that is already in the group would keep the tier it has now.
- adding a parameter in the file whose default value specifies the plan's tier: A parameter supplies an input to a run, so while the plan's own definition still carries the old tier, the re-run keeps applying the old tier to the plan already in the group.
- changing the version marker in the file to record the tier change: The version marker only labels which revision of the template file was used; it does not carry the new tier, so the running plan is left on its current tier.

prompt: The saved template should take that location from _____ so that the same file completes successfully from both the resource group level and the management group level.

options.text: resourceGroup()
subscription()
tenant()
managementGroup()

explanation:
The same saved file has to complete from two different deployment levels, so the function it uses must be valid in both. Of the four scope functions, tenant() is the one that can be used at any scope, so it resolves in a resource group deployment and in a management group deployment alike. The other three each work only in a limited set of scopes, so each of them breaks one of the two runs you need.

Why the other options are wrong:
- resourceGroup(): resourceGroup() is limited to resource group deployments and raises an error in a subscription or management group deployment, so the run from the upper level would still fail.
- subscription(): subscription() is usable in resource group or subscription deployments, but it is not usable in a management group deployment, so it does not satisfy the upper-level run either.
- managementGroup(): managementGroup() works only in a management group deployment, so the runs against the individual resource group would fail after the change.

prompt: The change to make is to _____.

options.text: keep the expression as the fallback value of the parameter and remove the list of permitted values.
keep the expression as the fallback value of the parameter and reduce the list of permitted values to a single entry.
remove the expression, replace it with a fixed name, and keep the list of permitted values.
keep the list of permitted values and move the expression into a variable that the parameter reads.

explanation:
A parameter may use an expression in its defaultValue, but an expression is not allowed together with other properties on that parameter. In the file shown, vaultName pairs the defaultValue expression [format('keyVault{0}', uniqueString(resourceGroup().id))] with an allowedValues list, so Resource Manager rejects the template during validation before any resource is created; the location parameter shows the working form, where the expression stands alone with only the type. The requirement that a blank name still produces the generated one means the expression has to stay, and every parameter still needs its type declared, so the permitted-values list is the property that must go. With it removed the template validates, an omitted name still yields the generated key vault name, and the operator can still supply a name.

Why the other options are wrong:
- keep the expression as the fallback value of the parameter and reduce the list of permitted values to a single entry: The failure is not caused by how many names the list holds or by the generated name missing from that list; an expression cannot be combined with any other property on the same parameter, so shortening the list still leaves the template invalid.
- remove the expression, replace it with a fixed name, and keep the list of permitted values: Replacing the expression with a fixed name clears the conflict, but the deployment would then fall back to one of the listed names instead of the name generated from the target resource group when the operator leaves the box blank, which the requirement forbids.
- keep the list of permitted values and move the expression into a variable that the parameter reads: A variable cannot be used as a default value for a parameter, so pointing the default at a variable leaves the parameter in error; the expression and the permitted-values list still cannot live on the same parameter.

options.text: type, apiVersion, name, properties

explanation:
An entry in the template's resources array carries the resource kind, the REST API version to use when creating it, the resource's name and the resource's own settings block, so the Key Vault declaration must be written with type, apiVersion, name and properties. Separately, the command-line deployment steps in the template walkthrough only run on Azure CLI 2.37.0 or later, so the workstation still sitting on 2.30.0 has to be brought up to that release before the platform group redeploys the saved file.

Why the other options are wrong:
- type, apiVersion, location, tags: location and tags are optional per-resource settings rather than the fields every entry in the resources array carries; a declaration built from this list would still leave out the resource's name and its own settings, so the vault would not be described well enough to be created.
- kind, sku, location, dependsOn: kind, sku and dependsOn describe particular resource definitions or the ordering between resources; they are not the set of fields that every entry in the resources array carries.
- apiVersion, kind, location, plan: kind, location and plan apply only to specific resource definitions; an entry in the resources array is built from the resource kind, the API version, the resource's name and the resource's own settings.

prompt: Which change should you make to the saved file? Call _____ in place of the retired helper, and declare the connection configuration parameter with the type [...].

options.text: resourceId
extensionResourceId
subscriptionResourceId
tenantResourceId

explanation:
The retired helper providers() should be swapped for resourceId(), the supported function that builds the identifier of a resource nested inside a resource group deployment; the sibling identifier builders produce values for other scopes or for resources that extend other resources, so they would change what the template hands to the web app. Because the administrator password travels inside one configuration parameter, that parameter has to be declared with the secure object type, which keeps the whole value out of the deployment history and out of the log; a plain object or a plain string is recorded there, and a secure string applies to a single standalone text value rather than to a parameter carrying several named members.

Why the other options are wrong:
- extensionResourceId: That function builds the identifier of a resource that extends another resource, such as a role assignment or a lock, not of a child resource declared in the template, so it would not hand the web app the identifier of the nested networking resource it expects.
- subscriptionResourceId: That function builds identifiers for resources deployed at subscription scope. The resources in this template are deployed into a resource group, so the value it produces would not point at the deployed nested networking resource.
- tenantResourceId: That function builds identifiers for resources deployed at tenant scope, which sits above the level this template is deployed at, so it cannot describe the nested networking resource of this resource group deployment.

prompt: You have a Bicep file that creates a network interface and a virtual machine in a resource group. You need the deployment team to be able to supply the virtual machine's name when they run the deployment, and when they supply nothing the deployment must still create the same virtual machine the file creates today. The file must keep the prefix spelled out in only one place: the fallback has to be computed from the prefix declaration that is already there, so a later change to that declaration also changes the fallback. Which change should you apply to the file?

options.text: Change `var vmNamePrefix` into `param vmNamePrefix string = 'vm-${environmentName}'`, add `param vmName string = '${vmNamePrefix}-01'`, and set the virtual machine's `name` to `vmName`.
Make no change to `var vmNamePrefix` and add `param vmName string = '${vmNamePrefix}-01'`, and set the virtual machine's `name` to `vmName`.
Make no change to `var vmNamePrefix` and add `param vmName string = 'vm-${environmentName}-01'`, and set the virtual machine's `name` to `vmName`.
Make no change to `var vmNamePrefix` and add `param vmName string = vmNamePrefix`, and set the virtual machine's `name` to `vmName`.

explanation:
A parameter default value may be an expression or may be built from another parameter, but it can never reference a variable. Turning the prefix declaration into a parameter is what makes it usable inside the new parameter's default, so `vmName` falls back to the name the file produces today (with the shown defaults, 'vm-dev-01') while still allowing an override at deployment time. Assigning the resource's `name` from `vmName` then wires the new input to the virtual machine, and the prefix stays written down in exactly one place, so a later change to the prefix declaration also changes the fallback.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Make no change to `var vmNamePrefix` and add `param vmName string = '${vmNamePrefix}-01'`, and set the virtual machine's `name` to `vmName`: The default value reads `${vmNamePrefix}`, and a parameter default may never point at a variable. While the prefix is declared as a variable the file fails to compile, so the prefix declaration has to become a parameter before a default value can build on it.
- Make no change to `var vmNamePrefix` and add `param vmName string = 'vm-${environmentName}-01'`, and set the virtual machine's `name` to `vmName`: This compiles, but it writes a second copy of the prefix expression ('vm-${environmentName}') inside the new default instead of computing the fallback from the prefix declaration that is already in the file. The prefix is then spelled out in two places, so a later change to the declaration would leave the fallback stale.
- Make no change to `var vmNamePrefix` and add `param vmName string = vmNamePrefix`, and set the virtual machine's `name` to `vmName`: Two problems here: a default value cannot reference the variable `vmNamePrefix` at all, so the file would not compile, and even if it did, the fallback would be the prefix alone ('vm-dev') instead of the full name the file builds today.

prompt: You have a Bicep file that creates a key vault and one secret inside it, and the secret currently holds a placeholder value written directly in the file. You need the deployment team to supply the real value when they run the deployment, and that value must not be recoverable afterwards from the deployment's history or from command-line output. Which change should you apply to the file?

options.text: Add a `param secretValue string` declaration with the `@secure()` decorator and reference it in the secret's `properties.value` property.
Add a `var secretValue string` declaration and reference it in the secret's `properties.value` property.
Add a `param secretValue string` declaration without any decorator and reference it in the secret's `properties.value` property.
Add a `param secretValue int` declaration with the `@secure()` decorator and reference it in the secret's `properties.value` property.

explanation:
The file needs a new deployment-time input for the secret value, and that input must be a `string` (the secret's `properties.value` carries text) carrying the `@secure()` decorator, which keeps the supplied value out of deployment history, the portal and command-line output. Declaring `param secretValue string` with `@secure()` and referencing it in the secret's `properties.value` meets both requirements: the team supplies the value when they deploy, and the value is not recoverable afterwards, while the rest of the file stays as it is.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add a `var secretValue string` declaration and reference it in the secret's `properties.value` property: A `var` stores a value that is computed inside the file and its contents are fixed in the template, so the deployment team cannot supply the secret value when they run the deployment. The `@secure()` decorator also applies to parameters only, not to variables, so the value could not be kept out of deployment history this way.
- Add a `param secretValue string` declaration without any decorator and reference it in the secret's `properties.value` property: A `param` of type `string` with no decorator is valid and can be supplied at deployment time, but without `@secure()` the value is recorded in the deployment's history and returned in command-line output, so it fails the requirement that the value not be recoverable afterwards.
- Add a `param secretValue int` declaration with the `@secure()` decorator and reference it in the secret's `properties.value` property: The `@secure()` decorator is allowed only on `string` and `object` parameters, so it cannot be applied to an `int` parameter; an integer also cannot carry the text value that the secret's `properties.value` expects.

prompt: You have a Bicep file that creates a resource group and then calls a module that holds the application's networking resources. The file is written at subscription scope, and the deployment fails because the resources declared inside the module need a resource group. You need every resource the module defines to be created inside the resource group that this same deployment creates. Which change should you apply to the file?

options.text: Add `scope: newRG` to the module declaration
Add `scope: subscription()` to the module declaration
Add `scope: newRG` to the resource group declaration
Add `parent: newRG` to the module declaration

explanation:
A module that carries no `scope` property is deployed at the target scope of the file that declares it, so this module inherits the file's subscription scope and its resource-group-scoped resources fail. The `scope` property on a module overrides that default for that module alone, and a valid scope object can be the symbolic name of a resource group declared in the same file, so `scope: newRG` places everything the module defines inside the group the deployment creates.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add `scope: subscription()` to the module declaration: `scope: subscription()` names the subscription as the module's target, which is exactly the scope the module already inherits from this file, so the module's resources are still left without a resource group and the failure remains.
- Add `scope: newRG` to the resource group declaration: `scope` is a property of a module declaration; a resource declaration does not accept one. In this subscription-scoped file the resource group is already created at the subscription level, so there is nothing to scope there — a child resource is tied to its parent with the `parent` property instead.
- Add `parent: newRG` to the module declaration: `parent` is the property that binds a child resource to its parent resource declaration; it is not part of a module declaration, so the file would not compile this way and the module would remain on the file's own scope.

prompt: You have a Bicep file that creates one virtual machine in a resource group and reports that machine's size at the end of the deployment. The operations team keeps an approved catalogue of three sizes - Standard_D2s_v5, Standard_D4s_v5 and Standard_D8s_v5 - and a deployment that passes any other size has to be rejected. The size that comes back in the deployment's outputs must also stay inside that approved catalogue. Which change should you apply to the file?

options.text: Add a user-defined type whose union lists the three approved sizes, make it the type of the `vmSize` parameter, and give the `deployedVmSize` output the same type.
Add the `@allowed` decorator listing the three approved sizes to the existing `vmSize` parameter and leave the `deployedVmSize` output as `string`.
Add a `var` holding the three approved sizes and set the default value of the `vmSize` parameter to reference that variable.
Change the `vmSize` parameter to an `object` parameter with an `approvedSizes` property and add an `if` expression on the virtual machine so it is skipped when the supplied size is outside the list.

explanation:
A user-defined type can hold a union of literal values, and the same type can be used for a parameter and for an output. Declaring it with the three approved sizes, using it as the type of `vmSize` and as the type of the `deployedVmSize` output means a value outside the catalogue fails validation, and the value reported at the end of the deployment is held to the same catalogue. The union form is the right choice here because the restriction has to hold for the output as well as for the input.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add the `@allowed` decorator listing the three approved sizes to the existing `vmSize` parameter and leave the `deployedVmSize` output as `string`: `@allowed` pins a parameter to a fixed list of values and fails validation when a different value is supplied, but it is permitted only on `param` statements, so it cannot be attached to the `deployedVmSize` output. The reported size would remain an unconstrained string.
- Add a `var` holding the three approved sizes and set the default value of the `vmSize` parameter to reference that variable: A variable stores a computed or repeated expression for reuse inside the file, and a parameter's default value can never be built from a variable, so this change would not compile. Even if it did, a variable does not validate the value a caller supplies at deployment time.
- Change the `vmSize` parameter to an `object` parameter with an `approvedSizes` property and add an `if` expression on the virtual machine so it is skipped when the supplied size is outside the list: An `if` expression only decides whether a resource is created; it is not a validation mechanism. It would leave the deployment with no virtual machine rather than rejecting an unapproved size, and it cannot hold the reported output to the catalogue either.

prompt: You have a Bicep file that creates an application environment in a resource group: one virtual network, one network interface and a set of Windows Server virtual machines produced by a loop. The operations team wants the Azure Monitor agent extension attached to those servers so their telemetry reaches Log Analytics, but only the servers listed for monitoring should receive the extension, and the deployment must report the id of every extension it created so the dashboards can be wired up. The file contains no extension yet. Which change should you apply to the file?

options.text: Declare the extension as its own resource at the top level of the file with a `for` expression over the virtual machines, set `parent` to the virtual machine that each instance belongs to, add `if` inside the loop expression so only the monitored indexes receive it, and publish the extension id in the outputs.

Declare the extension as its own resource at the top level of the file with a `for` expression over the virtual machines, set `parent` to the virtual machine that each instance belongs to, and publish the extension id in the outputs, but leave `if` out so that every virtual machine in the loop receives the extension.

Nest the extension inside the virtual machine resource body so the hierarchy stays in one block, add `if` inside the loop expression so only the monitored indexes receive it, and publish the extension id in the outputs.

Move the extension into a separate module file, pass the virtual machine resource id to that module as a parameter, add `if` inside the loop expression so only the monitored indexes receive it, and publish the extension id in the outputs.

explanation:
The extension is a child of the virtual machine, and it has to be produced once for every server the loop creates and only for the servers on the monitoring list. A child that is created in a loop is declared on its own at the top level of the file with a `for` expression, and the `parent` property ties each instance to the virtual machine it belongs to; in that separate form the whole type must be spelled out, for example `Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/extensions@2024-07-01`, because the parent type is no longer implied by the surrounding block. The `if` inside the loop expression is evaluated during deployment and decides per instance whether that extension is created - conditional deployment does not cascade to child resources, so the condition has to sit on the extension itself. Because the child is now a named resource of the file, its id can also be published in an output for the monitoring team.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Declare the extension as its own resource at the top level of the file with a `for` expression over the virtual machines, set `parent` to the virtual machine that each instance belongs to, and publish the extension id in the outputs, but leave `if` out so that every virtual machine in the loop receives the extension: This attaches the extension to every server the loop produces, including the ones that are not listed for monitoring, so it fails the requirement that only the listed servers receive it. A `for` expression on its own creates one instance per loop item and applies to all of them; the condition has to be part of the loop expression for it to be evaluated per instance.
- Nest the extension inside the virtual machine resource body so the hierarchy stays in one block, add `if` inside the loop expression so only the monitored indexes receive it, and publish the extension id in the outputs: Nesting keeps the hierarchy visible in a single block, which is the right form for a child that always exists under its parent and is not produced per loop iteration or referenced on its own. A child that is produced for each member of a loop, and only for some of them, has to be declared at the top level of the file and attached with the `parent` property. The `if` expression can only be applied to a whole resource or module declaration, so it cannot be placed on a resource nested inside the loop body.
- Move the extension into a separate module file, pass the virtual machine resource id to that module as a parameter, add `if` inside the loop expression so only the monitored indexes receive it, and publish the extension id in the outputs: A module is compiled into a nested deployment with its own scope, and a child resource declared inside a module can only be attached to a parent that is declared in that same module. Passing the virtual machine id in as a parameter therefore cannot create the extension as a child of the virtual machines that this file declares; the parent relationship has to be expressed in this file with the `parent` property.

prompt: You have a Bicep file that deploys six Linux virtual machines for an application, driven by a loop over a parameter that holds the machine names. Deployments of this file are rejected intermittently because the compute service receives too many virtual machine create requests at the same moment. You need the machines produced by that loop to be created one after another, in sequence, while the loop keeps working from the same list of names. Which change should you apply to the file?

options.text: Add `@batchSize(1)` to the resource declaration that produces the virtual machines.
Add `@batchSize(1)` to the resource declaration that produces the network interfaces used by the virtual machines.
Add `@batchSize(1)` to the `param vmNames` declaration.
Replace the `for` expression with six separate resource declarations, one per machine.

explanation:
The instances produced by a `for` loop are deployed in parallel by default, which is why all six create requests reach the compute service at the same moment and some deployments are throttled. The `batchSize` decorator can be applied to a resource or module declaration that uses a `for` expression, and with a value of 1 its loop instances are deployed one after another rather than all at the same time. Putting it on the resource declaration that produces the virtual machines therefore makes the machines come up in sequence, while the loop keeps reading the same `vmNames` parameter.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add `@batchSize(1)` to the resource declaration that produces the network interfaces used by the virtual machines: The decorator would also be accepted on that declaration, because the network interface resource uses a `for` expression too, but it would only control the order in which the network interfaces are created. The virtual machines would still be requested in parallel - and each machine already waits for its own network interface to exist - so the burst of create requests would remain.
- Add `@batchSize(1)` to the `param vmNames` declaration: `batchSize` may only be applied to a resource or module declaration that uses a `for` expression; it cannot be attached to a `param` declaration, so the file would not compile with that change.
- Replace the `for` expression with six separate resource declarations, one per machine: Listing the machines as six separate resource declarations removes the loop but does not slow anything down. Resources that have no dependency between them are still deployed in parallel, so the same burst of create requests would reach the compute service, and the names would no longer come from the parameter.

prompt: You have a Bicep file that deploys an application's networking by calling a shared module that your platform team publishes to the organization's container registry. Last week the build agent's Bicep CLI was upgraded, and since then every build of the file fails. The shared module has to keep coming from the registry where the platform team publishes it - you are not allowed to publish it anywhere else - and the build has to succeed again. Which change should you apply to the file?

options.text: Rewrite the module path in the file to `br:fabrikammodules.azurecr.io/networking/hub:2.1.0`, delete the cached copy, and run `bicep restore` before compiling it again.
Rewrite the module path in the file to `br:fabrikammodules.azurecr.io/networking/hub:2.1.0` and run `bicep build` again, leaving the local cache untouched.
Rewrite the module path in the file to the public registry form `br/public:networking/hub:2.1.0` and run `bicep restore` before compiling it again.
Leave the module path in the file unchanged and add `#disable-next-line BCP446` above the module declaration to silence the reported error.

explanation:
Since Bicep CLI v0.43.1 the CLI rejects module references that use a custom domain and raises diagnostic BCP446; the hostname in the reference has to be one the CLI accepts (the built-in allowlist covers *.azurecr.io, *.azurecr.cn, *.azurecr.us, mcr.microsoft.com, mcr.azure.cn and ghcr.io). The shared module lives in the registry named fabrikammodules, so the private-registry path form br:<registry-name>.azurecr.io/<file-path>:<tag> yields br:fabrikammodules.azurecr.io/networking/hub:2.1.0. A module pulled from a registry must be fetched into the local cache with `bicep restore` before the file can use it, and because the reference was rewritten the stale cached entry has to be removed and the restore run again so the module is fetched through the corrected hostname.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Rewrite the module path in the file to `br:fabrikammodules.azurecr.io/networking/hub:2.1.0` and run `bicep build` again, leaving the local cache untouched: Rewriting the hostname clears the BCP446 error, but a module that comes from a registry is not usable until `bicep restore` has pulled it into the local cache. Because the reference changed, the entry cached under the old path has to be removed and the restore re-run; otherwise the build keeps working from the stale cached copy and the module is never fetched through the corrected hostname.
- Rewrite the module path in the file to the public registry form `br/public:networking/hub:2.1.0` and run `bicep restore` before compiling it again: The public registry form br/public:<file-path>:<tag> points at Microsoft's published module registry, where this organization's shared networking module does not exist. It would also mean republishing the module somewhere else, which the stated requirement rules out.
- Leave the module path in the file unchanged and add `#disable-next-line BCP446` above the module declaration to silence the reported error: A disable directive only silences the reported diagnostic; it does not make the custom hostname usable, and the CLI still blocks that registry when it tries to fetch the module. The documented fix is to update the references to use a supported hostname, and such directives are meant to be used sparingly, only after reviewing the diagnostic.

prompt: You have a Bicep file that creates a storage account and a blob container for an application. The file does not compile: the build fails because the default value of the storage account name parameter points at something that cannot be used there. Two things must remain true once you fix it: the deployment team must still be able to supply the storage account name when they run the deployment, and the name fragment that ends the resource names must stay written in exactly one place, so that changing it later also changes every name that depends on it. Which change should you apply to the file?

options.text: Declare the fragment as a parameter with a default value and let the storage account name parameter take its default from that parameter.

Keep the fragment as a variable and write the fragment's value directly into the default value of the storage account name parameter.
Keep the fragment as a variable and declare the storage account name parameter with a default value that is that variable.

A later edit to the variable would leave the derived names stale, so the fragment is no longer maintained in one place as required.
- Keep the fragment as a variable and declare the storage account name parameter with a default value that is that variable: A parameter default value can never point at a variable. Parameter values are resolved before any deployment operation starts, so leaving the storage account name parameter's default built from the variable keeps the file from compiling.
