prompt: You must _____ and [...].

options.text: delete the parameter and let the deployment produce the value
keep the parameter and let the deployment team supply the value
keep the parameter and change its type so the value is accepted
keep the parameter and add an allowed list for the value

explanation:
Two independent edits are needed. First, the default value of dataEndpoint calls reference(), which reads a resource's runtime state; Azure Resource Manager resolves parameter values before any deployment operation starts, so that call cannot appear in the parameters section and the build fails. Because the endpoint must come from the account this same deployment creates and nobody is to supply it, the parameter is removed and the endpoint is taken from the created storage account instead - for example `output blobEndpoint string = stg.properties.primaryEndpoints.blob`. Second, the two module calls share one static name; deploying modules with the same static name at the same scope can make one deployment report the wrong output, so each call is given its own name (for example 'reportsDeploy' and 'auditDeploy') and every invocation is recorded under a label that names the workload it deployed.

Why the other options are wrong:
- keep the parameter and let the deployment team supply the value: Asking the deployment team for the endpoint contradicts the requirement that nobody supplies it, and the offending expression stays in the file, so the build keeps failing on the same line.
- keep the parameter and change its type so the value is accepted: Changing the declared type has no effect: the default value calls a function that reads runtime state, and such calls are not allowed in the parameters section whatever type the parameter declares.
- keep the parameter and add an allowed list for the value: An allowed list only restricts which values may be passed for the parameter at deployment time; it does not make the expression in the default value legal, so the build still fails.

prompt: The monitoring agent must be rolled out only in the environments where the monitoring flag is true, and the deployment must still complete successfully when it is false — _____; and the agent's resources must be created in the shared group whose name the pipeline supplies rather than in the group where this file runs — [...].

options.text: Add an `if` condition to the module declaration in this file.
Add an `if` condition to each resource inside the shared module's own file.
Add a `for` loop over the flag to the module declaration in this file.
Add a `for` loop over the flag to each resource inside the shared module's own file.

explanation:
Two edits are needed. First, put the condition on the module call in this file: Bicep evaluates a condition placed on a module during deployment, so the module is created only when the flag is true and the remaining deployment still finishes when the flag is false. Because the shared module belongs to the platform team and cannot be edited, the conditional has to live in the file you own. Second, redirect the module: a module's scope may be a scope object or the result of one of the scope functions, so handing the supplied group name to the built-in resource group function makes the module's resources land in that shared group instead of the group where the file itself runs. The scope cannot be written as plain text, and a subscription or management group scope sits too high for the agent's resource-group resources.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add an `if` condition to each resource inside the shared module's own file: Conditioning each resource inside the shared module would mean editing the platform team's file, which is out of scope here; the conditional has to be applied to the module call in the file you own.
- Add a `for` loop over the flag to the module declaration in this file: A loop produces one or more copies of an item from an array or a range; it does not decide whether the item is created, so the agent would still be installed when the flag is false.
- Add a `for` loop over the flag to each resource inside the shared module's own file: Same two problems as the previous option: it changes a module this file does not own, and a loop over a flag cannot switch the installation off.

prompt: The change to make is to _____.

options.text: add `@secure()` to the output declaration in the module file
add `@secure()` to the output declaration in the parent file
add `@secure()` to a parameter declaration in the parent file and pass the module's output value into it
add `@secure()` to a variable declaration in the parent file and store the module's output value in it

explanation:
The password is published by the module's own output, so that is where the sensitivity has to be applied. With Bicep 0.35.1 or later you can put the `@secure()` decorator on a module output, which makes Azure Resource Manager treat the returned value as sensitive so it is not saved to the deployment history and is not logged in the portal or in command-line output. The build agent already runs Bicep CLI 0.36.2, so the decorator is available. The parent file then consumes the sensitive value where it belongs - writing it into the key vault secret - without the password being published anywhere.

Why the other options are wrong:
- add `@secure()` to the output declaration in the parent file: The decorator belongs on the output inside the module file, because that output is the value the nested deployment publishes and records. Marking an output in the parent file cannot withdraw it from the deployment history or the command-line output, and the parent file does not publish the password today.
- add `@secure()` to a parameter declaration in the parent file and pass the module's output value into it: `@secure()` on a parameter protects a value that the deployment team supplies at deployment time. The module's output only exists once the deployment is running, and parameter values are resolved before any deployment operation starts, so the module's value cannot be supplied as a parameter value; securing that parameter would also leave the published value unprotected.
- add `@secure()` to a variable declaration in the parent file and store the module's output value in it: `@secure()` can only decorate parameters and outputs - it is not valid on a variable. Storing the module's value in a variable also leaves the value published by the module unprotected, so it would still reach the deployment history and the command-line output.

prompt: To fix the two build failures, you should _____ and [...].

options.text: declare an output that returns the storage account's endpoint
declare a variable that stores the storage account's endpoint
keep the parameter but replace its default expression with a literal value
keep the parameter but change its type to an object

explanation:
Request 1: a parameter's value is resolved before any deployment operation starts, and reference() reads a resource's runtime state, so the expression in the 'blobEndpoint' parameter cannot be evaluated there and the build is rejected. Moving that expression into the outputs section fixes the build error and publishes the storage account's endpoint to the caller when the deployment finishes, which is what the pipeline needs for the application configuration.

Request 2: a local module path is resolved relative to the file that declares it and must be written with the forward slash separator; the Windows backslash is not supported. The path in the file uses backslashes, so rewriting it with forward slashes makes the build find the module that sits beside the template in the repository, while keeping the module where the platform team maintains it.

Why the other options are wrong:
- declare a variable that stores the storage account's endpoint: A variable is evaluated inside the file, so the build error disappears, but the value stays inside the deployment and the pipeline still cannot read the endpoint once the run finishes. Only a declaration in the outputs section hands the value back to the caller.
- keep the parameter but replace its default expression with a literal value: The file would compile, but the endpoint would become a hard-coded string instead of the value the storage account actually returns, so the pipeline would receive the wrong value.
- keep the parameter but change its type to an object: Changing the declared type does not help: reference() is still evaluated in the parameters section, which is resolved before the deployment begins, so the same build error remains.

prompt: You should _____.

options.text: change the input's type to object, carry the port inside it, and keep the secure marking
change the input's type to array, carry the port inside it, and keep the secure marking
keep the input's type as int and keep the secure marking
keep the input's type as int and drop the secure marking

explanation:
The secure marking (the decorator that hides a value) can only be applied to inputs whose type is string or object, so it cannot sit on an int input - that is exactly why the build fails. To pass a numeric value to a deployment while keeping it out of deployment history, the portal and command-line output, the number has to travel inside a secure object: declare the input as an object and carry the port as one of its values, then read it where the firewall rule needs it (for example string(dbPort.port)). The port stays a number for the rule, so the pipeline can keep supplying a number and no value has to be turned into text.

Why the other options are wrong:
- change the input's type to array, carry the port inside it, and keep the secure marking: The secure marking is not accepted on array inputs either, so declaring the input as an array and carrying the port inside it leaves the same compiler error. A number that must stay hidden has to travel inside a secure object (or be serialized as a secure string), not inside an array.
- keep the input's type as int and keep the secure marking: This is what the file already does, and it is the reason the build fails: the secure marking is only valid on string and object inputs, so keeping the input as int with that decorator cannot compile.
- keep the input's type as int and drop the secure marking: Removing the secure marking makes the file compile, but the port would then be recorded in the deployment's history and printed in the pipeline's console output, which the platform team explicitly forbids.

prompt: To meet both requirements, the subnet name input needs the _____ decorator so that a name outside the platform team's catalogue is rejected, and the same input needs the [...] decorator so the deployment catalogue can index the deployment.

options.text: @allowed(['alpha','beta','gamma'])
@minLength(1)
@maxLength(3)
@minValue(1)

explanation:
The subnet name input must carry @allowed([...]) and @metadata({ ... }).

For the catalogue rule, @allowed lists the accepted values in an array; the deployment fails during validation if a value that is not one of them is passed, and for an array-typed parameter the supplied value may be any subset of the listed values. That is exactly the required behaviour: a name outside the platform team's catalogue is rejected before any resource is created, while a deployment that names only approved subnets still succeeds. This decorator is permitted only on param statements, so the subnetNames parameter is the correct place for it. The length and integer decorators cannot express the rule: @minLength and @maxLength only constrain the number of items in an array (or characters in a string), and @minValue/@maxValue apply to integer parameters.

For the cataloguing rule, @metadata({ ... }) attaches arbitrary custom properties to the declaration, such as source or contact, which tooling can read; that is the machine-readable information the deployment catalogue needs. @description and its namespace-qualified form @sys.description produce only the tip text that the portal shows on the deployment form, so neither one carries the machine-readable custom properties, and the sys-qualified form is needed only when the file already declares an item named description.

Why the other options are wrong:
- @minLength(1): @minLength constrains the number of items in an array (here at least one); it never compares the content of the items against a fixed list, so a subnet name outside the platform team's catalogue would still be deployed.
- @maxLength(3): @maxLength caps the number of items in the array at three; it does not restrict which names may be supplied, so an unapproved name would still be accepted.
- @minValue(1): @minValue applies to integer parameters; the subnet name input is an array of strings, and an integer bound cannot express a fixed list of accepted names in any case.

prompt: You have a container app running on the Consumption plan in Azure Container Apps. You want the app to shut down completely during the hours when no requests arrive, so that you stop paying for idle compute, while still adding replicas during busy periods. Which scaling configuration should you apply to the app?

options.text: A scale rule based on HTTP traffic with a minimum replica count of 0
A scale rule based on CPU utilization with a minimum replica count of 0
A scale rule based on memory utilization with a minimum replica count of 0
A scale rule based on CPU utilization with a minimum replica count of 1

explanation:
Most applications can scale to zero, and the documented exception is apps that scale on CPU or memory load, which can never reach zero replicas. HTTP traffic is one of the supported scale triggers, so pairing a rule driven by incoming requests with a minimum replica count of 0 is the configuration that lets the app shut down completely when nothing is arriving and restart automatically when requests resume. Scale rules can be edited after the app is deployed, and scaling changes are applied through the app's revision model.

Why the other options are wrong:
- A scale rule based on CPU utilization with a minimum replica count of 0: CPU utilization is a valid scale trigger, but apps that scale on CPU or memory load are the exception to scale-to-zero: the platform keeps at least one replica running for them, so they never reach zero replicas even when the minimum replica count is 0 and idle compute is still billed.
- A scale rule based on memory utilization with a minimum replica count of 0: Memory load behaves the same way as CPU load here: an app whose scaling is driven by memory utilization can never scale to zero, so one replica remains running and continues to cost you during the idle hours.
- A scale rule based on CPU utilization with a minimum replica count of 1: This keeps both obstacles in place: a CPU-based trigger already prevents the app from reaching zero replicas, and a minimum replica count of 1 additionally guarantees that one replica stays running and billable at all times, including overnight.

The two apps also have to keep exchanging calls through the Dapr service invocation API. Which change should you make to the environment and its apps?

options.text: Keep the environment as a workload profiles environment, and assign orders-api to a Dedicated workload profile and report-worker to a Consumption workload profile.
Convert the environment to a consumption only environment, then assign orders-api to a Dedicated workload profile and report-worker to a Consumption workload profile.

explanation:
A workload profiles environment can host apps on either the Consumption plan or the Dedicated plan, but each plan is reached through its own workload profile, so the two apps have to sit on different profiles. Putting orders-api on a Dedicated workload profile gives it the customized hardware and the steadier, more predictable cost, and putting report-worker on a Consumption workload profile preserves serverless scale-to-zero with pay-per-use billing. Because both apps remain inside one environment, the built-in Dapr service invocation path between them keeps working.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Convert the environment to a consumption only environment, then assign orders-api to a Dedicated workload profile and report-worker to a Consumption workload profile: Consumption only environments are the legacy option and support only the Consumption plan, so a Dedicated workload profile cannot be used in them at all. Since orders-api requires specialized hardware and steadier cost, the environment has to be a workload profiles environment.
- Keep the environment as a workload profiles environment, and assign both orders-api and report-worker to the same Dedicated workload profile rather than giving report-worker a Consumption workload profile of its own: Placing both apps on one Dedicated workload profile means report-worker is charged per instance and the environment carries a fixed management fee, instead of the pay-per-use billing that was required. The Consumption plan inside a workload profiles environment is what provides that billing model for report-worker.
- Keep the environment as a workload profiles environment, but create a second environment for report-worker on a Consumption workload profile and leave orders-api on a Dedicated workload profile in the first environment: Splitting the apps across two environments breaks the stated requirement, because the built-in Dapr service invocation does not cross environment boundaries out of the box and reaching across them would require third-party solutions. It also spreads two tightly coupled apps across two environments instead of one shared boundary.

prompt: You operate a Container Apps environment that hosts five container apps, and one of them has Dapr enabled. Your operations team needs the container output, the container app scaling events, and the Dapr sidecar logs produced in that environment to be searchable together in the Log Analytics workspace they already use for other services, and the Dapr sidecar traces have to be correlated with the Application Insights instance managed by your platform team. Which change should you make to the environment?

options.text: Set properties.appLogsConfiguration so it points at the Log Analytics workspace, and set properties.containerAppsConfiguration.daprAIInstrumentationKey to the Application Insights instrumentation key.
Set properties.appLogsConfiguration so it points at the Application Insights instance, and set properties.containerAppsConfiguration.daprAIInstrumentationKey to the Log Analytics shared key.
Set properties.appLogsConfiguration so it points at the Log Analytics workspace, and set properties.containerAppsConfiguration.daprAIInstrumentationKey to the Log Analytics workspace ID.

Set properties.appLogsConfiguration so it points at the Log Analytics workspace, and store the Dapr instrumentation key as a secret in each container app instead of setting properties.containerAppsConfiguration.daprAIInstrumentationKey.

explanation:
Both requirements are handled by environment-level properties. Environment-level log routing is controlled by properties.appLogsConfiguration, which points at the Log Analytics workspace that receives the logs of all apps in the environment; the data collected there covers container stdout/stderr output, container app scaling events and Dapr sidecar logs when Dapr is enabled. Dapr tracing is configured separately through properties.containerAppsConfiguration.daprAIInstrumentationKey, whose value is the App Insights instrumentation key that is handed to the Dapr sidecar. So the environment must reference the Log Analytics workspace in properties.appLogsConfiguration and the Application Insights instrumentation key in properties.containerAppsConfiguration.daprAIInstrumentationKey.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Set properties.appLogsConfiguration so it points at the Application Insights instance, and set properties.containerAppsConfiguration.daprAIInstrumentationKey to the Log Analytics shared key: The two targets are reversed. properties.appLogsConfiguration must reference the Log Analytics workspace that stores the environment's logs, and the value of properties.containerAppsConfiguration.daprAIInstrumentationKey is an Application Insights instrumentation key, not the Log Analytics shared key, which is a credential used to write to the workspace.
- Set properties.appLogsConfiguration so it points at the Log Analytics workspace, and set properties.containerAppsConfiguration.daprAIInstrumentationKey to the Log Analytics workspace ID: The Log Analytics workspace ID is not an instrumentation key. The value placed in properties.containerAppsConfiguration.daprAIInstrumentationKey must be the Application Insights instrumentation key that gets handed to Dapr; a workspace identifier would not give the sidecar a valid target.
- Set properties.appLogsConfiguration so it points at the Log Analytics workspace, and store the Dapr instrumentation key as a secret in each container app instead of setting properties.containerAppsConfiguration.daprAIInstrumentationKey: Dapr tracing is configured at the environment level through properties.containerAppsConfiguration.daprAIInstrumentationKey, which is how the App Insights instrumentation key reaches the Dapr sidecar. Storing a value as a secret inside each container app does not hand it to the sidecar, and the same reasoning means log routing stays in properties.appLogsConfiguration for every app in the environment.

prompt: You have a container app named checkout in Azure Container Apps. You have deployed a new image for it, which is now available as an additional revision, while the earlier revision still handles every incoming request. You need the newer image to take a small portion of live requests so that you can compare how it behaves against the current version before rolling it out more widely. Which action should you take?

options.text: Split traffic between the revisions so that checkout-v1 receives 90% of requests and checkout-v2 receives 10%.
Split traffic between the revisions so that checkout-v1 receives 90% of requests, checkout-v2 receives 0%, and a new revision cloned from checkout-v1 receives 10%.
Split traffic between the container apps so that the app running checkout-v1 receives 90% of requests and the app running checkout-v2 receives 10%.
Split traffic between the revisions so that checkout-v1 receives 0% of requests and checkout-v2 receives 100%.

explanation:
Every deployed version of a container app is a revision, and Azure Container Apps can split traffic across the versions of an application for Blue/Green and A/B testing scenarios. Because checkout-v2 already exists as a revision of the checkout app, assigning 90% of the requests to checkout-v1 and 10% to checkout-v2 keeps a single app in place, exposes the newly deployed image to a small share of live traffic, and keeps the current version running for comparison.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Split traffic between the revisions so that checkout-v1 receives 90% of requests, checkout-v2 receives 0%, and a new revision cloned from checkout-v1 receives 10%: The 10% here goes to a copy of checkout-v1, so the newly deployed image checkout-v2 continues to receive no requests and the intended comparison never happens. Traffic weights belong to the revisions that already exist for the deployed images.
- Split traffic between the container apps so that the app running checkout-v1 receives 90% of requests and the app running checkout-v2 receives 10%: This treats the two images as two separate container apps. Weighting in Azure Container Apps is applied across the multiple versions of one application, so dividing requests between two distinct apps would require extra routing infrastructure outside the app's own revision configuration.
- Split traffic between the revisions so that checkout-v1 receives 0% of requests and checkout-v2 receives 100%: This sends all live requests to checkout-v2, which is a full rollout rather than the small exposure that was requested. With checkout-v1 at 0%, the two versions never run side by side under live traffic.

explanation:
Azure Container Apps lets you hold sensitive values as secrets on the container app and reference them from the app's configuration, so the credential is resolved by the platform instead of being baked into the container image or written out in the revision definition. The application keeps picking the key up from its environment, so no code change or image rebuild is needed, which satisfies all three conditions from the security team.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Store the payment API key in a shared configuration in the container app environment and configure the app to reference that configuration: A Container Apps environment's own properties cover log routing to Log Analytics and Dapr instrumentation, not per-application credentials, so there is no shared environment-level place where an individual app's credential belongs. You have four sets of containerized services that will run in Azure Container Apps. You need to organize them so that every requirement in the exhibit is satisfied. Which arrangement should be assigned to each group?

- Group: A; Apps: checkout-api, payment-worker; Requirement: The apps must exchange calls with one another through the built-in Dapr service invocation API, and they must write to the same log destination.
- Group: B; Apps: web-prod, web-test; Requirement: The apps must never share compute resources, and the platform owner wants them isolated by usage, for example test versus production.
- Group: C; Apps: gpu-inference, bursty-api; Requirement: The apps must sit in one environment. One of them needs specialized hardware with steadier cost predictability; the other must shut down completely when idle and be charged only while it is running.
- Group: D; Apps: api-hub; Requirement: The security team must define the address allocation and routing rules for the environment's traffic, because the setup that the platform generates automatically cannot accommodate them.
prompt: Group A

options.text: Put both apps in one environment
Place the two apps in separate environments
Use the default workload profiles environment, with one app on the Consumption plan and the other on the Dedicated plan
Bring your own virtual network into the environment

explanation: Group A's apps talk to each other through the Dapr service invocation API and share a log destination, so they belong together in a single environment. Group B's apps must never share compute resources and must be isolated by usage, so each one goes into its own environment. Group C needs one app on customized hardware with steadier cost predictability and the other scaling to zero and being charged only while running, inside one environment, which the default workload profiles environment supports by hosting the apps on separate workload profiles under the Dedicated and Consumption plans. Group D needs control over address allocation and routing, so an existing virtual network is supplied instead of the one the platform generates.

context:
Your platform team is moving four workloads onto Azure Container Apps, and each of them has to keep the way it is started today once the move is finished. Match each workload in the exhibit to the option that should run it.

- Workload: Ledger rollup; What it does: Aggregates the day's transactions into a monthly accounting ledger; How it is started today: A Windows virtual machine starts it by itself at 02:00 every night; Typical run length: About 15 minutes
- Workload: Mail helper; What it does: Sends a confirmation e-mail for each item that lands in a storage queue; How it is started today: A worker process watches the queue and acts whenever something new appears; Typical run length: A few seconds per item
- Workload: Orphan cleanup; What it does: Deletes orphaned blobs older than one year; How it is started today: An engineer runs a script by hand whenever they decide it is needed; Typical run length: Up to an hour
- Workload: Customer API; What it does: Answers customer requests over HTTPS and must stay reachable at all times; How it is started today: A web server behind a load balancer receives inbound requests; Typical run length: Continuously
prompt: A cleanup that an engineer starts by hand from a command line, runs a single time, and never repeats by itself

options.text: On-demand job
Scheduled job
Event-triggered job
Container app

explanation: The Orphan cleanup is run deliberately by an engineer whenever they choose, which is exactly what an on-demand job provides: it runs only when someone explicitly asks for it and then finishes. The Ledger rollup must begin by itself at 02:00 every night, which matches a scheduled job that runs on a recurring timetable. The Mail helper reacts to each new item that appears in a storage queue, which matches an event-triggered job that starts when an event arrives and processes it. The Customer API must stay reachable at all times and answer inbound requests, so it is a continuously running container app rather than work that runs and completes; deploying API endpoints is a typical container app workload, while jobs exist for background processing that runs to completion.

context:
You have four containerized services running in Azure Container Apps, and the platform team wants each one to add or remove replicas in response to a different signal. You need to decide what drives each service's replica count. Match each service in the exhibit to the trigger that should be configured for it.

`Service          Signal the platform team observed
storefront-api   Callers reach it through the web endpoint published for the app, and the number of requests follows the shopping season.
sync-worker      It consumes messages that appear in an Azure Service Bus queue, and the team wants a replica to start as soon as work is waiting there.
render-service   The team watches how much of the host's compute the container uses, and wants the number of replicas to follow that measurement.
telemetry-proxy  Its number of replicas has to follow a metric published by a third-party monitoring system, and the platform team has already wired that metric source into the environment's configuration.`
prompt: storefront-api

options.text: HTTP traffic
Event-driven processing
CPU or memory load
KEDA-supported scaler

explanation: Container Apps decides the replica count from declarative scaling rules, and the trigger category must match the signal that actually drives the workload. storefront-api is reached through the endpoint the platform publishes, so its demand is inbound requests and it uses the HTTP trigger (concurrent requests). sync-worker reacts to messages sitting in an Azure Service Bus queue, which is event-driven processing. render-service follows the container's own consumption of the host's resources, so it uses CPU or memory load; note that an app with this trigger can never scale to zero, so at least one instance stays running and is billed. telemetry-proxy follows a metric produced by a third-party monitoring system, which is neither inbound requests, nor a queue of messages, nor the container's own resource usage, so it needs a scaler from the KEDA ecosystem.

context:
You are standing up the first Azure Container Apps environment for Fabrikam, and the first workload is a fraud-detection model that has to run on a GPU. Two more containerized HTTP APIs are planned for the same environment next quarter; they receive no traffic for hours at a time, so they must be able to shut down when idle and cost nothing while they are down, while the fraud model's monthly spend must not rise and fall with request volume. The network team owns every network in the company and will not allow Azure to create new networking resources for this deployment, so the environment must land on the network the team already runs. Which environment and app-hosting setup should you choose?

`First workload      : contoso.azurecr.io/fraud-model:4.1.0  (needs a GPU)
Spend for workload  : a monthly amount that does not rise and fall with request volume
Two APIs next quarter: no traffic for hours at a time; nothing to pay while they are down
Network             : must run on the corporate virtual network the network team already
                      operates; Azure must not create networking resources for this deployment`
prompt: The setup the platform team should choose is _____.

options.text: a workload profiles environment placed on the corporate virtual network, with the fraud model on a Dedicated workload profile
a consumption only environment placed on the corporate virtual network, with the fraud model on a Consumption workload profile
a workload profiles environment placed on a generated virtual network, with the fraud model on a Dedicated workload profile
a consumption only environment placed on a generated virtual network, with the fraud model on a Consumption workload profile

explanation:
The workload profiles environment is the default environment type and it supports both the Consumption and Dedicated plans, and inside it apps can run on either plan or on both at once by sitting on separate workload profiles. That lets the GPU-based fraud model go on a Dedicated workload profile - the plan intended for workloads needing customized hardware and steadier cost prediction, where you pay per-instance charges plus a fixed environment management fee that does not grow or shrink with the number of workload profiles - while the two pay-per-use APIs planned for next quarter can later go on Consumption ones and shut down completely when idle. The environment also has to sit on the corporate virtual network the network team operates, which means the team supplies that network when the environment is created, because the network the platform generates on its own has only limited network capabilities and does not satisfy the requirement.

Why the other options are wrong:
- a consumption only environment placed on the corporate virtual network, with the fraud model on a Consumption workload profile: Consumption only environments (legacy) support only the Consumption plan, so they cannot offer the Dedicated plan that a GPU workload needs, and usage-based Consumption billing does not give the steady monthly amount the fraud model requires. The network choice is right here, but the environment type cannot host the first workload.
- a workload profiles environment placed on a generated virtual network, with the fraud model on a Dedicated workload profile: The environment type and the app-hosting choice are right, but the platform-generated virtual network does not meet the requirement: the environment must use the corporate virtual network that the network team owns and manages, and that network has to be supplied when the environment is created.
- a consumption only environment placed on a generated virtual network, with the fraud model on a Consumption workload profile: Both the environment type and the network are wrong. A consumption only environment supports only the Consumption plan and so cannot host the GPU workload, and a generated virtual network does not satisfy the requirement to run on the corporate virtual network.

Which change should you make to the environment, and what happens to the environment fee when that second profile is added?

prompt: The correct approach is to _____; additionally, [...].

options.text: enable the Dedicated plan on the existing consumption only environment and keep the app where it is
add a dedicated workload profile to the existing consumption only environment and move the app onto it
create a workload profiles environment and place the app on a dedicated workload profile
create a workload profiles environment and place the app on a consumption workload profile

explanation:
The environment in the exhibit is of the Consumption only (legacy) type, and the documentation states that consumption only environments support only the Consumption plan, so no dedicated workload profile can be added to it and the Dedicated plan cannot be enabled on it. The default environment type, a workload profiles environment, supports both the Consumption and Dedicated plans by placing apps on separate workload profiles, so the encoding app must be deployed into a new workload profiles environment on a dedicated workload profile, which is what provides the customized hardware and the steadier cost prediction the service needs. Once the environment runs on the Dedicated plan, it carries a fixed plan management cost for the environment as a whole, and that cost does not grow or shrink with the number of workload profiles, so adding the second profile leaves the environment fee unchanged; only the variable per-instance cost of the running workload profile instances changes.

Why the other options are wrong:
- enable the Dedicated plan on the existing consumption only environment and keep the app where it is: The Dedicated plan is available only in a workload profiles environment. A consumption only (legacy) environment supports the Consumption plan alone, so this environment cannot simply be switched over to the Dedicated plan.
- add a dedicated workload profile to the existing consumption only environment and move the app onto it: Consumption only environments have no dedicated workload profiles and support only the Consumption plan, so the app cannot be moved onto dedicated hardware inside the environment shown in the exhibit.
- create a workload profiles environment and place the app on a consumption workload profile: A consumption workload profile runs on the Consumption plan, which is billed per use as the upload volume changes and provides no customized or dedicated hardware, so it fails both the hardware and the predictable-cost requirement.

prompt: Apply _____ to the container app so the partner's client can connect.

options.text: TCP ingress
HTTP ingress
HTTPS ingress
Internal-only ingress

explanation:
Container Apps can publish an endpoint over HTTPS or TCP without any extra Azure infrastructure. Because the partner's client opens a raw socket connection and does not send HTTP or HTTPS requests, the endpoint needs TCP ingress, and that also satisfies the requirement to avoid managing a load balancer or other networking resources.

Why the other options are wrong:
- HTTP ingress: HTTP ingress expects HTTP requests, so the partner's raw-socket client could not use the endpoint.
- HTTPS ingress: HTTPS ingress also serves HTTP requests, so the partner's raw-socket client would not be able to communicate with the endpoint.
- Internal-only ingress: Internal-only ingress keeps the endpoint inside the environment, so a partner on the public internet could not reach it.

trigger         : Service Bus queue "orders"
binding         : Cosmos DB, collection "invoices"
target_env      : prod-env

prompt: The platform team should _____.

options.text: deploy the function app into the prod-env environment, keeping its triggers, bindings, and automatic scaling and placing it alongside the other apps in that environment
deploy the function app into a separate Container Apps environment, keeping its triggers, bindings, and automatic scaling but isolating it from the other apps in that environment
deploy the function app into the prod-env environment but convert it to a plain container app and replace the trigger and binding with custom scale rules
leave the function app on its current Function App plan and send its logs to the environment's log destination

explanation:
A Container Apps environment can host more than plain container apps: Azure Functions and Azure Spring Apps can be added to an existing environment for multi-service integration, and whatever runs in that environment shares the environment's virtual network and writes to the same logging destination. Deploying the function app into prod-env therefore puts it beside the existing apps on the same network and the same Log Analytics workspace, and because a function hosted this way keeps its triggers, bindings, and automatic scaling, the Service Bus trigger and the Cosmos DB binding need no rework.

Why the other options are wrong:
- deploy the function app into a separate Container Apps environment, keeping its triggers, bindings, and automatic scaling but isolating it from the other apps in that environment: A second environment gives the function its own virtual network and its own log destination, so the function would neither sit with the other apps in prod-env nor write to the Log Analytics workspace that prod-env uses.
- deploy the function app into the prod-env environment but convert it to a plain container app and replace the trigger and binding with custom scale rules: Converting the function into a plain container app and replacing the trigger and binding with custom scale rules throws away the trigger behavior, the binding behavior, and the automatic scaling that the requirement says must be kept.
- leave the function app on its current Function App plan and send its logs to the environment's log destination: Staying on the current Function App plan leaves the function outside prod-env, so it doesn't join the environment's virtual network; the environment's log configuration only routes logs for workloads hosted in that environment, so it can't substitute for hosting the function there.

context:
Your team runs three containerized APIs in one Azure Container Apps environment, and the order service they depend on runs today on Azure Spring Apps. The platform team wants the APIs to call the order service through the Dapr service invocation API without standing up any extra networking components, and wants to search all of the platform's container output in one place during troubleshooting. Which change should you make, and where do the order service's logs end up?

- Item: Order service; Detail: Runs on Azure Spring Apps as a standalone deployment
- Item: Containerized APIs; Detail: Three apps that run in one Azure Container Apps environment
- Item: Network path today; Detail: The APIs reach the order service through an Application Gateway and a public endpoint
- Item: Log destination for the environment; Detail: One Log Analytics workspace that receives the output of the apps in that environment
- Item: Required call style; Detail: Dapr service invocation from the APIs to the order service
prompt: The platform team should _____. After that change, the order service's logs go [...].

options.text: add the Azure Spring Apps service to the environment hosting the containerized APIs
add the Azure Spring Apps service to a separate environment and publish its endpoint to the internet
deploy the Spring service as a container image in a new revision of one of the containerized APIs
put the Spring service on its own virtual network and let the APIs reach it through a private endpoint

explanation:
Bringing the Azure Spring Apps service into the same Azure Container Apps environment as the containerized APIs is the right move. Azure Spring Apps can be added to an existing Container Apps environment for multi-service integration, and every app that runs in one environment shares that environment's virtual network, Dapr configuration and log destination. That is what allows the APIs to reach the order service through the built-in Dapr service invocation API with no extra networking components, and it avoids the public endpoint and Application Gateway path shown in the exhibit. Because all apps in an environment publish to the single Log Analytics workspace set for that environment through the environment's appLogsConfiguration property, the order service's logs arrive in the same workspace as the other apps' logs, giving the team one place to search all container output.

Why the other options are wrong:
- add the Azure Spring Apps service to a separate environment and publish its endpoint to the internet: A second environment cannot satisfy the requirement. Built-in Dapr service invocation does not cross environment boundaries out of the box, so the APIs in the first environment could not invoke the order service that way, and publishing an internet-facing endpoint contradicts the team's requirement.
- deploy the Spring service as a container image in a new revision of one of the containerized APIs: A revision redeploys a containerized app with a different image. The order service is an Azure Spring Apps service, which can be added to an existing Container Apps environment for multi-service integration, so it does not have to be rebuilt as a container image.
- put the Spring service on its own virtual network and let the APIs reach it through a private endpoint: Each Container Apps environment already sits on a virtual network that enforces its secure boundary, and internal-only ingress with DNS-based service discovery is built in, so app-to-app name resolution needs no private endpoint or additional network resources.

context: You administer the Container Apps environments for a company and you are preparing a capacity plan for the next year. Operations wants to hear automatically whenever one of the environments reports a change in its health or its status, and the capacity team has found that the two obvious portal pages show different numbers, so it needs the page that carries the authoritative, up-to-date ceiling on how many container apps and environments a tenant may host. Which pairing should you apply?
prompt: Set up _____ so that environment health and status changes raise a notification, and point the capacity team to [...] for the published ceiling.

options.text: Azure Monitor alerts
Azure Monitor dashboards
Azure Monitor workbooks
Azure Advisor recommendations

explanation:
Azure Monitor alerts are the Azure mechanism for being told automatically that a Container Apps environment's health or status changed; the portal and the CLI only let a person inspect that status on demand, so neither meets the "hear automatically" requirement. For the numbers, the quota values relevant to a given environment appear on the Quotas for Azure Container Apps page, but the authoritative and most up-to-date limits are published on the Azure subscription service limits page (the Container Apps section), so that is the page the capacity team should quote from when stating the ceiling on how many container apps and environments a tenant may host.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Azure Monitor dashboards: Azure Monitor dashboards are a visual view over collected metrics and logs for review on demand; they do not push a notification when an environment's health or status changes.
- Azure Monitor workbooks: Azure Monitor workbooks are saved, interactive queries and reports for exploring telemetry when someone opens them; they are not a channel that notifies the operations team about changes.
- Azure Advisor recommendations: Azure Advisor recommendations list suggested improvements to a customer's resources and configuration; they are not tied to a Container Apps environment reporting a change in health or status.

prompt: You have a container app named orders-worker on the Consumption workload profile that today reacts only to inbound HTTP requests. You need it to grow and shrink with the number of messages waiting in an Azure Service Bus queue, and you need at least one instance running at all times so a consumer is never cold. Which change should you apply to the app?

options.text: Add a custom scale rule that uses a KEDA ScaledObject targeting the Service Bus queue, and set minReplicas to 1.
Add an HTTP scale rule with concurrentRequests set to 10, and set minReplicas to 1.
Add a custom scale rule that uses a KEDA ScaledObject targeting the Service Bus queue, and set minReplicas to 0.
Add a TCP scale rule with concurrentConnections set to 10, and set minReplicas to 1.

explanation:
The autoscaling engine behind Azure Container Apps is KEDA, and custom scale rules built on a KEDA ScaledObject are the rule type used for event sources such as Azure Service Bus, so the app reacts to how many messages are queued rather than to request or connection counts. Setting minReplicas to 1 keeps one instance of the revision running at all times, so the app is never allowed to drop to zero replicas and a consumer stays warm. The ScaledObject-based rule combined with minReplicas of 1 therefore satisfies both parts of the requirement.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add an HTTP scale rule with concurrentRequests set to 10, and set minReplicas to 1: The rule type does not meet the requirement: an HTTP rule adds or removes replicas based on the number of concurrent inbound requests, which says nothing about the message backlog in the queue. Queue-driven sources such as Azure Service Bus need a custom rule based on a KEDA ScaledObject. The minReplicas value of 1 is appropriate, but on its own it does not deliver queue-based scaling.
- Add a custom scale rule that uses a KEDA ScaledObject targeting the Service Bus queue, and set minReplicas to 0: The rule type is right for a queue-driven workload, but minReplicas of 0 still permits the app to scale down to zero replicas whenever the metric falls away, which violates the requirement that an instance is always running. Keeping minReplicas at 1 is what guarantees a permanently available consumer.
- Add a TCP scale rule with concurrentConnections set to 10, and set minReplicas to 1: A TCP rule reacts to the number of concurrent connections to the app, not to the number of messages waiting in an Azure Service Bus queue, so the app would not scale out during a backlog. Event sources such as Service Bus require a custom rule based on a KEDA ScaledObject; the minReplicas value of 1 is correct but the rule type is not.

prompt: You have a Container Apps job that drains records arriving in an Azure Event Hubs stream and then stops. The team tried to make the job grow with the number of incoming records by adding an HTTP scale rule to the job definition, but every deployment of the job fails validation and the job never starts extra executions while a backlog builds up. You need the job to launch additional executions as records accumulate in the stream. Which change should you make to the job's configuration?

options.text: Replace the HTTP scale rule with a custom rule that uses a KEDA ScaledJob scaler.
Replace the HTTP scale rule with a TCP scale rule that counts concurrent connections.
Replace the HTTP scale rule with a custom rule that uses a KEDA ScaledObject scaler.
Remove the HTTP scale rule and set the minimum number of replicas to 1 so a single instance is always kept running.

explanation:
Container Apps jobs do not support HTTP or TCP scale rules, which is why the job definition shown here fails validation. Event-driven jobs build their scaling rules from KEDA ScaledJob scalers: replacing the HTTP rule with a custom rule based on a ScaledJob scaler (for example an Event Hubs scaler) makes the job start additional executions as records accumulate in the stream.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Replace the HTTP scale rule with a TCP scale rule that counts concurrent connections: TCP scale rules are unsupported on Container Apps jobs as well, so swapping the HTTP rule for a TCP rule would still fail validation. TCP rules fit long-running apps whose load is driven by concurrent connections, not jobs that run one execution per event.
- Replace the HTTP scale rule with a custom rule that uses a KEDA ScaledObject scaler: ScaledObject-based custom rules are the pattern for long-running services that continuously consume events. Jobs run one execution per event and therefore use ScaledJob-based scalers, so a ScaledObject rule is the wrong building block here and would not drive extra job executions.
- Remove the HTTP scale rule and set the minimum number of replicas to 1 so a single instance is always kept running: Removing the HTTP rule clears the validation failure, but the minimum number of replicas only keeps a single instance warm; it does not tie the number of executions to the backlog in the event source, so the job still would not start extra executions as records arrive.

prompt: You have a web API deployed as an Azure Container App that grows and shrinks based on inbound HTTP concurrency. During a traffic spike you collected the configuration and telemetry values shown below. You need to know how many container instances the platform will target for this revision with these values. Which instance count should you expect?

options.text: 2 replicas
3 replicas
4 replicas
8 replicas

explanation:
The desired count is calculated by rounding up the current metric value divided by the target metric value: ceil(55 ÷ 20) = ceil(2.75) = 3. The final target is then the smallest of the configured maximum, that desired count, and max(4, 2 × current instances): min(8, 3, max(4, 4)) = min(8, 3, 4) = 3. The configured minimum of 1 is already satisfied, so the platform targets 3 replicas.

Why the other options are wrong:
- 2 replicas: This is simply today's count, ignoring the request volume that drives the calculation, so it is not the value the platform will target.
- 4 replicas: The value max(4, 2 × current instances) is one input to the final minimum, not a floor applied afterward; because the desired count of 3 is lower than 4, the minimum of the three inputs is 3 rather than 4.
- 8 replicas: This is only the configured ceiling. The metric-derived desired count of 3 is below that ceiling, so the maximum is not what gets targeted.

The regional usage data collected for your subscription is shown below. You need this workload to run in that region as soon as possible. Which action should you take?

Deploy the same 36 vCPUs and 260 GB of memory request as a Spot container group in East US 2.
Keep the 36 vCPUs and 260 GB of memory request and retry the deployment in the same region after the capacity alert clears.

explanation:
A single Standard SKU container group deployment can use at most 31 vCPUs and 240 GB of memory, and these per-deployment ceilings can never be raised. The request for 36 vCPUs and 260 GB of memory sits above both ceilings, so it cannot be deployed as specified. Lowering the request to 30 vCPUs and 220 GB of memory keeps the same container group design inside the published maximums, and the regional quota usage in the exhibit shows plenty of subscription and regional capacity left, so no quota increase is involved.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Open an Azure support request with issue type Quota to raise the Standard SKU allowance for vCPUs and GB of memory in the region: A support request with issue type Quota can only raise the changeable quotas, such as the Standard SKU container group and core counts per region. The per-deployment maximums of 31 vCPUs and 240 GB of memory are hard limits that no request can raise, and the usage data shows the changeable quota is not exhausted.
- Deploy the same 36 vCPUs and 260 GB of memory request as a Spot container group in East US 2: Spot container groups support at most 4 vCPUs and 16 GB of memory, provide no virtual network support, and are available only in East US 2, West Europe and West US. A 36 vCPU and 260 GB of memory workload therefore cannot run as a Spot container group either.
- Keep the 36 vCPUs and 260 GB of memory request and retry the deployment in the same region after the capacity alert clears: Regional capacity pressure can indeed cause failures for larger groups, but retrying the identical request would not help here because the requested values exceed the published per-deployment maximums for a Standard SKU container group. The deployment stays invalid regardless of how much capacity the region has.

You need the deployment to succeed, the app must stay on the Consumption workload profile, and the log-forwarding sidecar must keep the CPU and memory it has today. options.text: Set the main container to 0.5 vCPU and 1.0Gi of memory
Set the main container to 0.5 vCPU and 1.25Gi of memory
Set the main container to 0.75 vCPU and 1.0Gi of memory
Set the main container to 1.5 vCPU and 2.5Gi of memory

explanation:
On the Consumption workload profile, the CPU and memory of all containers in the app are added together and that total must equal one of the supported vCPU/memory combinations (0.25 vCPU/0.5Gi, 0.5 vCPU/1.0Gi, 1.0 vCPU/2.0Gi, 2.0 vCPU/4.0Gi, 4.0 vCPU/8.0Gi). The sidecar already asks for 0.5 vCPU and 1.0Gi, so the main container has to be set to 0.5 vCPU and 1.0Gi, giving the app a total of 1.0 vCPU and 2.0Gi, which is a supported combination. With the current values the app asks for 1.5 vCPU and 2.25Gi in total, which is not one of the supported totals, so the deployment is rejected.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Set the main container to 0.5 vCPU and 1.25Gi of memory: Added to the sidecar's 0.5 vCPU and 1.0Gi, this would total 1.0 vCPU and 2.25Gi of memory. That total is not one of the supported vCPU/memory combinations for the Consumption workload profile, so the deployment would still fail.
- Set the main container to 0.75 vCPU and 1.0Gi of memory: Added to the sidecar's 0.5 vCPU and 1.0Gi, this would total 1.25 vCPU and 2.0Gi of memory. That pairing is not one of the supported combinations, so the deployment would still fail.
- Set the main container to 1.5 vCPU and 2.5Gi of memory: Added to the sidecar's 0.5 vCPU and 1.0Gi, this would total 2.0 vCPU and 3.5Gi of memory. That pairing is not one of the supported combinations, so the deployment would still fail.

prompt: You have an Azure Function deployed on Azure Container Apps that processes messages arriving in an Azure Storage queue. Its current configuration is shown below. In the portal, the control for defining your own scaling criteria is greyed out, so the app only reacts to the criteria the platform derives from the function's triggers. You want the app to also grow with the CPU load of processing those messages. Which change should you apply to the container app?

options.text: Set properties.configuration.allowScalingRuleOverride to true
Set properties.configuration.activeRevisionsMode to "single"
Set properties.configuration.scale.minReplicas to 1
Set properties.configuration.scale.maxReplicas to 100

explanation:
A function app running on Azure Container Apps is given scaling criteria that the platform derives from the function's triggers and bindings, and the portal's control for adding your own criteria is disabled. Customer-defined criteria — such as a CPU-based rule — are only accepted when allowScalingRuleOverride is enabled in the app's configuration, so turning that setting on lets the CPU rule be added alongside the generated ones.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Set properties.configuration.activeRevisionsMode to "single": activeRevisionsMode decides whether the app runs a single active revision or several revisions with traffic split between them; it has no effect on whether you are allowed to define your own scaling criteria.
- Set properties.configuration.scale.minReplicas to 1: minReplicas sets the floor of instances kept for the revision (0 is the lowest permitted value). Raising it to 1 keeps one instance warm, but it does not unlock the ability to add customer-defined criteria.
- Set properties.configuration.scale.maxReplicas to 100: maxReplicas sets the ceiling of instances for the revision (default 10, with 1,000 as the highest configurable value). Increasing the ceiling only allows more instances once scaling happens; it does not let you define new criteria.

prompt: You have a container app named checkout-api that runs two active revisions with different image versions, and inbound HTTP requests are distributed across those revisions. Each revision has an HTTP scale rule with concurrentRequests of 10 and maxReplicas of 5. You need the app to add instances for a larger burst of simultaneous requests, so you plan to add a scale rule that uses an HTTP criterion with a higher concurrentRequests value. Which approach should you take when applying that new scale rule?

options.text: Add the scale rule to the app: a new revision is produced that carries the new rule, the already active revisions continue with the scale rules they were created with, and the traffic split between revisions is changed from the Revision management page.

Add the scale rule to the app: a new revision is produced, and that revision automatically receives all of the traffic as soon as it becomes active, with no need to revisit the Revision management page.
Add the scale rule to the app and it is applied to the already active revisions in place, so the traffic split between the existing revisions is changed from the Revision management page.
Add the scale rule to the app and it is applied to the already active revisions in place, and the revision with the higher version automatically receives all of the traffic.

explanation:
In Azure Container Apps, adding or editing a scale rule produces a new revision, an immutable snapshot of the app that carries the rule you just added. Revisions that are already active are not rewritten, so each of them keeps the scale rule it was created with, and you decide how traffic is divided between revisions from the Revision management page. The correct option matches that behaviour exactly.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add the scale rule to the app: a new revision is produced, and that revision automatically receives all of the traffic as soon as it becomes active, with no need to revisit the Revision management page: A new revision does not capture the traffic on its own. Allocation across revisions is something you set yourself in the Revision management page, so the new revision starts with whatever weight you give it and receives traffic only in proportion to that weight.
- Add the scale rule to the app and it is applied to the already active revisions in place, so the traffic split between the existing revisions is changed from the Revision management page: Existing revisions are not patched in place when a rule is added. Adding a scale rule produces a new revision, and the revisions that are already active keep the scale rules they were created with, so the new criterion applies to the newly produced revision rather than being written into the running ones.
- Add the scale rule to the app and it is applied to the already active revisions in place, and the revision with the higher version automatically receives all of the traffic: This option is wrong twice over: a rule added at the app level is not applied in place to the revisions that are already active, and a new revision does not automatically absorb all of the traffic, since you assign the weights yourself.

prompt: You have a Standard SKU container group deployment in Azure Container Instances that requests the settings shown below. The service rejects the deployment and none of the containers start. Every container in the group mounts four data volumes, and the solution needs all of them mounted at run time. You need the complete solution running in that region. Which change should you apply?

options.text: Split the containers and volumes across two container groups so both groups stay within the volume limit
Ask Azure support to raise the volume limit for container groups, so that more volumes can be mounted in one group
Deploy the same containers and volumes in one group by switching the group to the Spot SKU
Deploy the containers and volumes in one group into a virtual network to get a higher volume limit

explanation:
The requested 24 volumes break the per-group ceiling, which is a hard limit for a single container group (60 containers, 20 volumes and 5 ports per IP are the published hard limits). Because that ceiling cannot be moved by any support request, the only way to keep every container and every required mount is to spread the workload over more than one group. Two groups of three containers with twelve volumes each are both inside the ceiling, and the subscription already has headroom (12 of 100 Standard SKU container groups used in the region), so the deployment is accepted and the whole solution runs.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Ask Azure support to raise the volume limit for container groups, so that more volumes can be mounted in one group: The number of volumes that a single group may mount is a hard limit, so a request to raise it is never approved; quota requests only apply to changeable quotas such as the number of Standard SKU container groups or cores per region per subscription.
- Deploy the same containers and volumes in one group by switching the group to the Spot SKU: The Spot SKU has far smaller maximums (4 vCPUs, 16 GB of memory, 50 GB of storage), is a preview feature offered only in East US 2, West Europe and West US, and it does not lift the per-group limit on mounted volumes, so this deployment would still be rejected.
- Deploy the containers and volumes in one group into a virtual network to get a higher volume limit: Deploying into a virtual network changes the CPU and memory maximums (31 vCPUs and 240 GB of memory, the same as a general deployment), but the per-group hard limits on containers, mounted volumes and ports per IP are unchanged, so the request is still rejected.

type: custom
minReplicas

explanation: The three built-in criterion types cover different signals, and the two replica limits control how many copies exist. options.text: Group A — Standard SKU, 12 vCPUs, 32 GB memory, 6 containers, 4 volumes, 2 ports on one IP address.
Group B — Standard SKU, 36 vCPUs, 120 GB memory, 4 containers, 2 volumes, 1 port on one IP address.

explanation: Group A stays inside every per-deployment maximum (31 vCPUs, 240 GB memory, 60 containers, 20 volumes, 5 ports per IP for a Standard SKU group), but its 12 vCPUs push the subscription's Standard SKU cores in East US from 95 to 107, above the 100-core regional allowance, so it is rejected until that allowance is raised through a support request with issue type Quota. Group B asks for 36 vCPUs, above the 31-vCPU hard maximum for a Standard SKU container group; hard limits can never be raised by a quota request, so it is rejected permanently. Group C is inside all hard limits and inside all regional quotas (cores 95+2=97, container groups 92+1=93, creates 285+1=286), so it is accepted and its containers start. Group D is within the hard limits and quotas, but its image is published only for linux/arm64 while Azure Container Instances supports only x64 (AMD64) images, so the group is created and the container fails to start.

prompt: The appropriate action is _____.

options.text: Update the container CPU and memory values in the app's template so a new revision uses the updated allocation.
Update the running revision's CPU and memory values in place so the new allocation applies immediately.
Increase maxReplicas in the app configuration so the existing revision receives more CPU and memory.
Add another container to the template with 0.5 vCPU and 1.0 GiB so the revision's total allocation increases.

explanation:
Azure Container Apps doesn't support vertical scaling, so the CPU and memory of a running revision cannot be resized in place. The container CPU and memory values live in the app's template, and any change to the template produces a new revision, so updating those values and letting the new revision take over is how the API container ends up running with 1.0 vCPU and 2.0 GiB while inbound requests keep being served. On the Consumption plan, the 1.0 vCPU / 2.0 GiB pairing is one of the supported vCPU and memory combinations.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Update the running revision's CPU and memory values in place so the new allocation applies immediately: Vertical scaling isn't supported in Azure Container Apps, so the CPU and memory of a running revision cannot be edited in place. Those values must be changed in the template, which creates a new revision.
- Increase maxReplicas in the app configuration so the existing revision receives more CPU and memory: maxReplicas controls how many replicas a revision runs, not how much CPU or memory each replica receives, so raising it does not enlarge the container.
- Add another container to the template with 0.5 vCPU and 1.0 GiB so the revision's total allocation increases: Adding a second container does not give the existing API container more CPU and memory. On the Consumption plan, all containers in an app share one fixed vCPU and memory allocation (1.0 vCPU / 2.0 GiB here) that would be divided between them, and it also changes the app's architecture.

Every deployment attempt fails with an error about the total size of the app's container images, so no instance of the app ever starts and inbound requests are refused. The team cannot compress the model file, replace it with a smaller format, or split it across several images, and the app must serve requests without any code change. You need the app to deploy and run in that region today. Which change should you apply?

- Property: Workload profile; Value: Consumption
- Property: Container image; Value: contoso.azurecr.io/vision-scorer:2026-10-20
- Property: Total size of the app's container images; Value: 9.5 GB
- Property: Container CPU and memory; Value: 1.0 vCPU / 2.0 GiB
- Property: minReplicas / maxReplicas; Value: 0 / 10
prompt: To make the deployment succeed, you should _____.

options.text: Assign the app to a Dedicated workload profile.
Keep the app on the Consumption workload profile and lower the container's CPU and memory requests.
Keep the app on the Consumption workload profile and raise the app's maxReplicas value.
Keep the app on the Consumption workload profile and pull the image with the app's managed identity.

explanation:
The Consumption workload profile supports container images totaling up to 8 GB for each app or job replica, and this app ships 9.5 GB of images, so the deployment is rejected before any instance starts. A Dedicated workload profile supports larger container images, so putting the app on a Dedicated workload profile lets the 9.5 GB image deploy. Note that a Dedicated workload profile can host several apps or jobs, so the images on it share the available disk space and the size that really fits depends on what else runs there.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Keep the app on the Consumption workload profile and lower the container's CPU and memory requests: The app is already on the Consumption workload profile, and that plan's image size ceiling is what the deployment is failing on. Lowering the container's CPU and memory requests changes the compute allocation, not the space the images occupy, so the same rejection occurs.
- Keep the app on the Consumption workload profile and raise the app's maxReplicas value: maxReplicas controls how many instances of a revision the platform keeps, not how much space the images need. Each replica on the Consumption workload profile is still held to the 8 GB image total, so raising this value does not let the 9.5 GB image deploy.
- Keep the app on the Consumption workload profile and pull the image with the app's managed identity: Using the app's managed identity with the acrPull role changes how the registry authenticates the pull, not how much space the images occupy. The Consumption workload profile image size ceiling still applies, so the deployment keeps failing.

context: You have an Azure Container App that is reached only by other services inside the environment, so its external endpoint has been turned off. The app defines no scale rule of its own, and after its last instance exited, the internal callers kept retrying but nothing came back. You need the app to keep serving those internal callers without any operator intervention. Which change should you make?
prompt: The team should _____.

options.text: Set minReplicas to 1.
Set maxReplicas to 20.
Add an HTTP scale rule with concurrentRequests of 10.
Set activeRevisionsMode to single.

explanation:
When ingress is disabled and the app has neither a minimum replica count nor a custom scale rule, the platform scales it down to zero and provides no way to bring it back, which is exactly the behavior observed here. Defining a minimum of one replica keeps a running instance available at all times, so the internal callers are served without any operator action.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Set maxReplicas to 20: This only raises the upper bound of the autoscaling range. The floor of the range is still zero, so the app can still drop to zero instances and stay there, and internal traffic still cannot revive it.
- Add an HTTP scale rule with concurrentRequests of 10: An HTTP rule is driven by inbound requests that arrive through the app's endpoint, and the endpoint is turned off in this environment, so the criterion never has a value to act on and the app remains with no instances.
- Set activeRevisionsMode to single: This property controls which revision is active for incoming traffic. It does not establish a floor for the number of running instances, so the app still ends up with nothing serving the internal callers.

context:
A container app named relay-worker reads messages from an Azure Service Bus queue and processes them. It grows and shrinks using a custom scale rule that watches how many messages are waiting in that queue. The operations team reports two separate problems with this app. First, when a backlog starts to build, the app does not add any instance for about half a minute, so messages wait longer than the team wants. Second, once the queue finally empties, the app's last instance keeps running for roughly five minutes before it goes away, and the team wants that released sooner. You need the app to react faster to a growing queue and to shut down its final instance sooner once the queue drains. Which two settings should you change?

- Property: Workload profile; Value: Consumption
- Property: Scale rule type; Value: Custom (KEDA ScaledObject) on Azure Service Bus queue length
- Property: Target queue length per replica; Value: 5 messages
- Property: Minimum replicas; Value: 0
- Property: Maximum replicas; Value: 10
- Property: Ingress; Value: Enabled
prompt: Set the _____ to 10 seconds so that a growing queue is noticed sooner, and set the [...] to 60 seconds so that the last instance is released sooner.

options.text: Cool down period
Polling interval
Scale down stabilization window
Scale up step

explanation:
The two symptoms map to two different scale-behavior settings. For a custom (KEDA ScaledObject) rule, the polling interval is how often the platform queries the event source, and it defaults to 30 seconds — exactly the half-minute delay before the growing queue is noticed, so lowering it makes the backlog detected and acted on sooner. (This setting has no effect on HTTP or TCP rules, but this app uses a custom rule.) The cool down period is how long the platform waits after the last event before taking the app down to its minimum replica count, and it defaults to 300 seconds — exactly the five minutes the final instance lingers, so lowering it releases that instance sooner. The cool down period applies to the move from the final replica to 0, which is the case here because the minimum is 0 replicas.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Cool down period: This setting governs how long the platform waits after the last event before taking the app down to zero; it does not affect how quickly a growing queue is inspected, so changing it wouldn't fix the first symptom.
- Scale down stabilization window: This setting only delays scale-down decisions once scale-down conditions are met; it has no effect on when the platform notices a growing queue or adds instances for it.
- Scale up step: This setting decides how many replicas are added once scaling out begins (1, then 4, 8, 16, 32 and onward); it does not change how often the queue is checked.
