prompt: The platform team should publish the shared rollout as a _____, and should add the certificate installation to the same file as a [...].

options.text: template spec
linked template
nested template
template parameter file

explanation:
The shared rollout belongs in a template spec: it stores the template as an Azure resource type whose access is managed with role-based access control, so users who only have read access can deploy it but cannot change it — exactly the 'application teams can start it, only the platform team can change it' goal. The certificate step belongs in a deployment script: deployment scripts add PowerShell or Bash to a template so end-to-end setup completes in a single deployment, and the code can be kept in an external source that the template references, which matches the team's separately maintained PowerShell file.

Why the other options are wrong:
- linked template: A linked template is only a reference from a parent template to another template location; it creates no shared catalog artifact with its own Azure role-based access control, so it cannot give readers run-only rights over a single approved copy.
- nested template: A nested template is a sub-deployment called from a parent template; it is a way to break a rollout into pieces, not a way to publish one shared copy that other teams can run without altering it.
- template parameter file: A parameter file only carries input values into a run; it does not store the rollout itself, publish it to a catalog, or control who may change it.

prompt: The identity object has to be added _____, and the platform team should run [...] to review the planned outcome before the tier reaches their production resource group.

options.text: to the root level of the resource declaration
to the properties section of the resource declaration
to the sku section of the resource declaration
to the tags section of the resource declaration

explanation:
A managed identity is declared beside type, apiVersion, name and location — directly in the resource declaration rather than inside the resource-specific settings — so the identity object has to be added there, next to those other properties. For the preview, the operation that compares the file with the live state of the environment and reports the resources that would be created, updated, or deleted plus any resource property changes, without altering anything, is the one the platform team needs before the tier reaches production.

Why the other options are wrong:
- to the properties section of the resource declaration: The properties section only accepts the settings defined for that resource type; an identity declaration is not one of those settings, so it cannot go there.
- to the sku section of the resource declaration: The sku section carries the size, tier, family and capacity of the resource and has no place for an identity declaration.
- to the tags section of the resource declaration: The tags section holds name and value pairs used for organizing and reporting resources; an identity declaration does not belong there.

context:
You have an ARM JSON template that a pipeline generates for the application team, and the generator emits a separate parameter for every tier setting. The generated file is rejected during validation before any resource is created, with a message saying that the file declares more parameters than the template format allows. You need the template to deploy successfully, while still letting whoever runs it supply every tier setting at deployment time and while each resource declaration keeps reading the one setting it needs. Which change should you make to the template?

- Section of the generated file: Parameters; What the generator emits: 312 declarations, one for each tier setting
- Section of the generated file: Variables; What the generator emits: 8 declarations
- Section of the generated file: Resources; What the generator emits: 23 declarations
- Section of the generated file: Outputs; What the generator emits: 4 declarations
prompt: The team should _____ so that the generated file passes validation and every tier setting can still be supplied when the deployment runs.

options.text: Group the tier settings into one parameter of type object
Group the tier settings into one parameter of type string
Group the tier settings into one variable of type object
Keep the tier settings as separate parameters and set a default value on each one

explanation:
A template may declare at most 256 parameters, and the generated file declares 312, so Resource Manager rejects it during validation before any resource is created (the variables, resources, and outputs in the file are all far below their own limits). The template format lets several related values travel together in a single parameter of type object, and the resource declarations then read the individual tier settings from that parameter's members. Grouping the settings that way drops the declared parameter count below the limit while keeping the settings as deployment-time input that the operator supplies and that each resource declaration can still read by name.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Group the tier settings into one parameter of type string: A parameter of type string carries one text value, so it cannot hold the several separately named tier settings that the resource declarations must each read; the settings would have to be packed into one opaque string instead of addressable members.
- Group the tier settings into one variable of type object: Variables are values defined inside the template file, not inputs supplied when the deployment runs. Moving the tier settings there would cut the parameter count, but the operator could no longer supply the settings at deployment time, which is exactly what the requirement asks for.
- Keep the tier settings as separate parameters and set a default value on each one: Giving each setting a default value does not change how many parameters the file declares. The validation complaint is about the number of declared parameters, so the file would still be rejected.

prompt: The build failure is resolved by _____.

options.text: putting the `if` expression on the same line as the assignment operator
putting the resource's opening brace on the same line as the assignment operator and leaving the `if` expression where it is
putting the `if` expression on the same line as the resource type and leaving the assignment operator where it is
putting the resource's opening brace on the same line as the `if` expression and leaving the assignment operator where it is

explanation:
Bicep ignores spaces and tabs but is sensitive to newlines, so a resource declaration cannot be split so that the `if` expression starts on the line after the assignment operator. Moving the `if` expression onto the same line as the '=' sign makes the declaration parse correctly, keeps the availability set tied to the boolean input, and leaves the rest of the file unchanged.

Why the other options are wrong:
- putting the resource's opening brace on the same line as the assignment operator and leaving the `if` expression where it is: This leaves the `if` expression starting on the line after the assignment operator, which is exactly the layout the compiler rejects. The conditional expression has to follow the '=' sign on the same line, and the opening brace comes after it.
- putting the `if` expression on the same line as the resource type and leaving the assignment operator where it is: The conditional expression has to follow the assignment operator in the declaration. Placing it beside the resource type puts it before the '=' sign, so the declaration is still not in a form the compiler accepts.
- putting the resource's opening brace on the same line as the `if` expression and leaving the assignment operator where it is: The assignment operator would still end one line, with the `if` expression starting on the next line, so the same build error is still raised. Moving the brace does not change where the conditional expression begins.

prompt: To make the rollout survive the turn-downs, the platform team needs to _____.

options.text: apply the retryOn decorator to the resource declarations, listing the error codes that trigger another submission and capping the number of extra submissions at 10
apply the batchSize decorator to the resource declarations, so the loop instances are deployed sequentially in batches of one
apply the secure decorator to the string parameters, so their values are kept out of the deployment history and the logs
apply the allowed decorator to the string parameters, so only the machine sizes on an approved list are accepted

explanation:
The requirement is that the file itself puts a resource deployment that the platform turned down forward again, waits longer before each repeated run, and stops after a bounded number of extra runs. In Bicep this is exactly what the retryOn decorator on a resource declaration does: it accepts a list of error code strings and an optional retry count (maximum 10, with exponential back-off). Putting it on the virtual machine and managed disk declarations makes the file re-submit the resource that was rejected, without the operators having to run the rollout by hand. The other decorators do not provide this behavior: batchSize only controls how many loop instances are deployed per batch (sequential deployment), secure only hides a parameter value from deployment history and the logs, and allowed only restricts a parameter to a fixed set of values.

Why the other options are wrong:
- apply the batchSize decorator to the resource declarations, so the loop instances are deployed sequentially in batches of one: batchSize sets up instances to deploy sequentially in batches, which controls how many loop instances run at a time. It never puts a resource deployment that the platform rejected forward again, so the rollout would still stop at the same point and the file would still have to be run by hand.
- apply the secure decorator to the string parameters, so their values are kept out of the deployment history and the logs: secure marks a string or object parameter as secure so its value is not saved to the deployment history and is not logged. It changes how a value is recorded, not what happens to a resource deployment that was turned down, so it does not satisfy the requirement.
- apply the allowed decorator to the string parameters, so only the machine sizes on an approved list are accepted: allowed makes sure the operator supplies one of an approved list of values for a parameter, and it is permitted only on param statements. It constrains input values before the run and has no effect on how the file handles a turned-down resource deployment.

prompt: To roll out the tier successfully, with every machine name still formed from the prefix held in the template's variables section and the instance number, you should _____.

options.text: Let the helper take the prefix as a parameter and join it with the index inside the helper.
Let the helper take the prefix as a literal string instead of a parameter, and join it with the index inside the helper.
Let the helper take the prefix as a template parameter, and join it with the index inside the helper.
Let the helper take the index as a template parameter, and join it with the prefix inside the helper.

explanation:
A user-defined function in an ARM JSON template can only use the parameters it declares itself; it has no access to the template's variables section and cannot call other user-defined functions. Declaring the prefix as a parameter of `nameFor` lets the helper build each machine name from the value it is handed plus the index it is called with, and the call sites can hand it the value held in the variables section.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Let the helper take the prefix as a literal string instead of a parameter, and join it with the index inside the helper: Hardcoding the prefix as a literal means the file no longer reads it from the variables section, so the tier prefix could not be changed in one place.
- Let the helper take the prefix as a template parameter, and join it with the index inside the helper: A template parameter is not visible inside a user-defined function body, because a function sees only the parameters declared on the function itself, so the helper would still be unable to read the prefix.
- Let the helper take the index as a template parameter, and join it with the prefix inside the helper: Moving the instance number to a template parameter does not reach the helper either, because a function body cannot see template parameters, so the per-call index would still be out of reach.

prompt: You have an availability set with the configuration shown below. You need to add a sixth virtual machine without changing the set's domain configuration. Which placement should you expect for the new virtual machine?

The same update domain as the second virtual machine
The same update domain as the third virtual machine
A new update domain beyond the configured five

explanation:
With five update domains, Azure cycles through the existing update-domain assignments as additional virtual machines are added. The sixth member therefore occupies the update domain assigned to the first member; the seventh would occupy the update domain assigned to the second member.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The same update domain as the second virtual machine: The second virtual machine's update domain is reused by the seventh member in a five-domain cycle, not by the sixth.
- The same update domain as the third virtual machine: The third virtual machine's update domain is reused later in the five-domain cycle, not by the sixth member.
- A new update domain beyond the configured five: The update-domain count is fixed when the availability set is created. Because this set has five update domains, an additional member reuses one of them instead of creating another domain.

prompt: You have an application tier made up of three virtual machines running in the West Europe region. Every machine is deployed as a regional resource with no zone selected, so when a datacenter in that region had an outage, the whole tier went offline. Corporate data residency rules keep this workload inside the current region. You need the tier to stay available if a single availability zone is lost. Which change should you make?

options.text: Add the instances to an availability set so the deployment is placed in separate fault domains and update domains.
Add instances with explicit zone placement so the deployment spans more than one availability zone.
Add a load balancer health probe with automatic failover so the deployment moves traffic to healthy instances.
Add a secondary region and replicate the instances with Azure Site Recovery so the deployment can fail over when a zone is unavailable.

explanation:
Availability zones are physically separate areas inside a region with independent power, network, and cooling. Because these three machines are deployed as regional resources with no zone selected, Azure may place them in any zone and a zone failure can interrupt all of them at once; a regional deployment can even have no zone placement at all. A deployment becomes zone-resilient when separate instances of a zonal resource occupy at least two zones, so the instances have to be placed on purpose in more than one availability zone, which is what the correct option does. West Europe supports three availability zones, so the instances can be split across them while staying inside the region required by the data residency rules. Availability sets would only give fault-domain and update-domain separation (the correct option, a load balancer health probe cannot help when every instance in the zone is down (the correct option, and Azure Site Recovery is a regional disaster recovery mechanism rather than in-region zone separation (the correct option.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add the instances to an availability set so the deployment is placed in separate fault domains and update domains: Availability sets arrange fault domains and update domains. That protects the tier against physical hardware, power, and network faults inside a datacenter, but the VMs of a set still sit in the zone they were deployed into, so a zone failure can take the whole tier down. It also does not answer the stated requirement, which is surviving the loss of an availability zone.
- Add a load balancer health probe with automatic failover so the deployment moves traffic to healthy instances: A health probe with automatic failover only redirects traffic between instances that are still healthy. Since all three instances are affected together by a zone failure, there is no healthy instance left to receive the traffic, so this change would not keep the tier available during a zone outage.
- Add a secondary region and replicate the instances with Azure Site Recovery so the deployment can fail over when a zone is unavailable: Azure Site Recovery replicates Azure VMs to a secondary location and supports failover and failback, which addresses a regional disaster rather than the loss of a single zone in the current region. It is also excluded here because data residency rules require the workload to stay in the current region.

prompt: You have an order API service built from three Linux virtual machines in the West Europe region, where this workload can be placed in three availability zones. The current configuration of the three machines is shown below. You need the service to keep serving customer requests if the zone that hosts it becomes unavailable. Which arrangement should you apply?

options.text: Move the three instances into an availability set with three fault domains inside one zone in the region.
Keep all three instances in one zone in the region and add a fourth instance there.
Spread the instances across more than one zone in the region so that separate copies run in different zones.
Reduce the service to a single instance in the region and let Azure move it to another zone automatically.

explanation:
All three virtual machines currently sit in Zone 1 of West Europe, so losing that zone removes every member of the service at once. West Europe offers three availability zones for this workload, so placing separate instances in more than one zone makes the deployment zone-resilient: when one zone fails, the instances in the remaining zones continue to serve requests. The machines already belong to an availability set, which separates them across fault domains for rack, power and network faults inside a datacenter, but it does not move them out of the zone they were placed in and therefore cannot carry the service through a zone outage.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Move the three instances into an availability set with three fault domains inside one zone in the region: An availability set assigns members separate fault and update domains so that hardware, power and network faults do not take down everything at once, but every member stays in the zone where the set was placed. The machines would keep sharing the fate of Zone 1, so the service would still go offline if that zone were lost.
- Keep all three instances in one zone in the region and add a fourth instance there: Adding a fourth machine in the same zone only adds another copy inside the same failure domain. Extra copies concentrated in one zone disappear together with that zone; zone resilience requires separate instances in at least two zones.
- Reduce the service to a single instance in the region and let Azure move it to another zone automatically: Azure does not automatically relocate a virtual machine to another zone when a zone fails, and a single instance removes the copy protection entirely. The workload has to be deliberately placed in more than one zone to survive the loss of one.

prompt: You are creating a new availability set for a stateless web tier. Two conditions apply: a maintenance restart must never take down more than one of the tier's virtual machines at a time, and the members must be distributed over the greatest number of fault domains the platform supports. The configuration that creates the set, and the size of the tier, are shown below. The deployment has to succeed on the first attempt, because the team will not rebuild the set later. Which values should you use?

options.text: Create the availability set with 3 fault domains and 12 update domains
Create the availability set with 5 fault domains and 12 update domains
Create the availability set with 3 fault domains and 5 update domains
Create the availability set with 2 fault domains and 20 update domains

explanation:
An availability set accepts no more than three fault domains and no more than twenty update domains, and both counts are locked in when the set is created, so the script has to carry valid values from the start. The tier contains twelve virtual machines, and update domains are the groupings of machines that Azure may restart together, so a count of twelve gives every machine a domain of its own and a maintenance restart affects a single machine only. Three fault domains is the highest number the platform allows, which meets the second condition, and twelve update domains stays well under the twenty-domain ceiling. The values requested in the script are therefore rejected: five fault domains is above the ceiling, and five update domains would force the sixth machine onward to share a domain with earlier members.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Create the availability set with 5 fault domains and 12 update domains: Five fault domains is above the limit of three fault domains per availability set, so the set cannot be created with that layout and the deployment fails before any machine is attached. The update domain count of twelve is acceptable, but the fault domain value still has to be brought within the ceiling.
- Create the availability set with 3 fault domains and 5 update domains: Three fault domains is acceptable, but twelve machines spread over only five update domains means the groups of machines that restart together are larger than one: the sixth machine shares the domain of the first, the seventh the second, and so on. A maintenance restart would then interrupt more than one machine at a time, which the first condition forbids.
- Create the availability set with 2 fault domains and 20 update domains: Twenty update domains is within the maximum of twenty, but only two fault domains leaves the members less separated from each other's shared power and network hardware than the platform allows, and the requirement calls for the greatest number of fault domains the platform supports, which is three. It also spreads twelve machines over twenty update domains, leaving eight groups with no member at all.

prompt: Your company has taken over a business that runs on its own Azure subscription. Both teams host the same web tier in the same region, and each team placed its instances in the zone that its own tooling labels as 1. Because the logical numbering is handed out to every subscription separately, the two zone 1 labels do not necessarily point at the same physical datacenter. The response below is what the first subscription returns for that region. You need one operation that shows how the zone numbering of the two subscriptions lines up, before the teams design a combined failover. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Use the Check Zone Peers API for both subscriptions, and enable the Microsoft.Resources/AvailabilityZonePeering feature on each subscription before calling it.
Use the Check Zone Peers API for both subscriptions, and call it without enabling the Microsoft.Resources/AvailabilityZonePeering feature, because that operation works on any subscription.
Use the List Locations API for both subscriptions, and enable the Microsoft.Resources/AvailabilityZonePeering feature on each subscription before calling it.
Use the List Locations API for one subscription only, and enable the Microsoft.Resources/AvailabilityZonePeering feature on each subscription before calling it.

explanation:
The Check Zone Peers API is the operation built for this job: it returns the zone mappings for multiple subscriptions so you can see how the logical numbering of each subscription lines up with the physical datacenters. Microsoft requires the Microsoft.Resources/AvailabilityZonePeering feature to be enabled on the subscriptions before this operation can be used, so the feature must be registered first. That is exactly what the correct option describes.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Use the Check Zone Peers API for both subscriptions, and call it without enabling the Microsoft.Resources/AvailabilityZonePeering feature, because that operation works on any subscription: The cross-subscription comparison operation is not available on any subscription by default: the Microsoft.Resources/AvailabilityZonePeering feature must be enabled on the subscriptions involved before the call succeeds. Skipping the registration makes the operation fail.
- Use the List Locations API for both subscriptions, and enable the Microsoft.Resources/AvailabilityZonePeering feature on each subscription before calling it: The List Locations API returns the zone mappings of a single Azure subscription per call. Calling it for both subscriptions gives you two separate per-subscription payloads that you would have to line up yourself, instead of one operation that compares the mappings across subscriptions.
- Use the List Locations API for one subscription only, and enable the Microsoft.Resources/AvailabilityZonePeering feature on each subscription before calling it: Two problems. First, the List Locations API reports the mappings of only the subscription you call it for, so it never shows how the second subscription is numbered. Second, you cannot assume the logical numbers line up: each subscription is assigned its own mapping when it is created, so logical zone 1 in one subscription can point at a different physical datacenter than logical zone 1 in another.

prompt: You have a storefront application that stores customer session state in a cache product. The details of the cache are shown below. You need the application to keep serving customers when the zone that hosts the cache becomes unavailable. Which change should you make?

options.text: Add an availability set around the existing cache instance so the platform spreads its hardware across fault domains.
Deploy a second cache instance in another zone of the same region.
Move the cache to a region that offers availability zones and keep it as a zonal instance.
Keep the cache instance in place but front it with a load balancer that has a zone-redundant configuration.

explanation:
The cache is a single instance pinned to one zone, so losing that zone takes the cache offline. A deployment becomes zone-resilient either by using a zone-redundant service or by running separate instances of a zonal resource in at least 2 zones. Adding a second cache instance in another zone of the same region meets that condition, and West Europe offers 3 zones so the new instance has a home. In practice the two instances sit behind the load balancer with health checking so traffic moves to whichever instance is healthy.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add an availability set around the existing cache instance so the platform spreads its hardware across fault domains: An availability set spreads its members over fault domains and update domains and limits hardware, power, and network failures, but it does not carry a deployment across availability zones; some shared-infrastructure failures still cross its fault domains. It therefore cannot keep the cache serving when the zone hosting it is lost.
- Move the cache to a region that offers availability zones and keep it as a zonal instance: Relocating the workload leaves the underlying exposure in place: one instance pinned to a single zone is lost whenever that zone is lost, in the new region as well. Zone resilience requires either a zone-redundant service or separate instances spread over at least 2 zones.
- Keep the cache instance in place but front it with a load balancer that has a zone-redundant configuration: A load balancer only distributes connections among healthy backends. With a single instance in one zone, the failure of that zone leaves no backend at all, so the front end stays reachable while the cache itself is gone.

- Request: A; Environment: West Europe; three availability zones; Required outcome: All members must stay pinned to the same availability zone to minimize network delay.
- Request: B; Environment: A region without availability zones; Required outcome: Members must be isolated from shared power and network failures.
- Request: C; Environment: Japan East; three availability zones; Required outcome: Loss of a facility must not stop the whole tier.
- Request: D; Environment: Canada Central; Required outcome: The service must remain available after a disruption that affects the entire region.
prompt: Request C

options.text: Place every instance in a selected availability zone
Group the instances in an availability set
Distribute the instances across several availability zones
Replicate to a secondary location with Azure Site Recovery

explanation: Request A calls for deliberately pinning the instances to one selected availability zone because the members need the shortest network distance; this placement does not by itself keep the service running if that zone is lost. Request B needs an availability set because the region has no availability zones, while fault domains and update domains separate members from correlated power and network failures. Request C needs instances distributed across several availability zones so that members outside the failed facility remain available. Request D needs Azure Site Recovery because using multiple zones cannot cover a complete regional disruption; Site Recovery replicates the VMs to a secondary location and supports failover.

context:
You have four workloads with the requirements recorded for each of them, shown below. You need to match every workload to the configuration that satisfies its requirement, so the operations team does not promise more protection than the platform delivers. Which configuration should you assign to each workload?

- Workload: Web tier; Recorded requirement: Its members must not sit behind the same power source and network switch, they must be spread over as many separate shared-hardware groups as the platform allows in this region, and a planned restart must never take down more than one member at a time.
- Workload: API tier; Recorded requirement: All of its members run in the same physically separate area inside the region, so losing that area stops the whole tier. The tier must remain available if that area is lost.
- Workload: Finance platform; Recorded requirement: All of its compute and data live in one region today, and the business has agreed that losing that whole region must not stop the service.
- Workload: Reporting fleet; Recorded requirement: The team wants a single place to configure many identical instances, push changes to them, and let capacity grow and shrink automatically as demand changes.
prompt: Web tier

options.text: An availability set with three fault domains and twenty update domains
Two virtual machines placed in two different availability zones
Azure Site Recovery replication to a secondary location
A virtual machine scale set in flexible orchestration mode

explanation: The web tier needs separation from shared power and network hardware plus staggered restarts, which is what an availability set with three fault domains and twenty update domains provides (three fault domains is the maximum and twenty update domains is the maximum; both counts are fixed when the set is created, and members are spread over the fault domains so no two share a power source and network switch, while maintenance restarts one update domain at a time). The API tier must survive the loss of the area of the region that hosts it, which requires separate instances in at least two availability zones, because a deployment is zone-resilient when zonal instances occupy two or more zones. The finance platform must survive the loss of a whole region, which availability zones cannot provide, so its virtual machines have to be replicated to a secondary location, and Azure Site Recovery does exactly that and supports failover and failback. The reporting fleet needs centralized configuration, change rollout, and automatic scaling of many identical instances, which a virtual machine scale set in flexible orchestration mode provides and which is the recommended option for high availability with the widest feature range.

context: You have a web service hosted by an availability set. You need to document how planned maintenance behaves so the operations team can update its runbook. Which statement should you use for each operational question?
prompt: Concurrency limit for a maintenance cycle

options.text: A single update domain is processed at any moment
The active update domain has 30 minutes to recover
Update domains are always visited in ascending numerical sequence
The next update domain is not required to follow an ascending sequence
All members of the active update domain restart together

explanation: Azure performs maintenance for only one update domain at a time. The domain undergoing maintenance has 30 minutes to recover before another restart begins. Azure may choose the remaining domains in an order that is not sequential, and virtual machines assigned to the same update domain can restart together. The statement that the domains are always visited in ascending numerical sequence does not match Azure's behavior.

context:
You are assembling the review notes that accompany every high availability deployment request in your company. Each note is one question an engineer must be able to answer about the platform, and the facts your team collected fill in those notes so that the design and the customer commitments stay accurate. The request under review and the collected facts are shown below. You need to file each fact under the question it answers.

`Deployment request under review
--------------------------------
Target region ....... East US 2
Compute instances .. Windows virtual machines with managed disks
Grouping per tier .. One availability set
Tier size .......... Up to five virtual machines per tier`
prompt: How many zones are offered in the region named in the request

options.text: Most regions in the published zone table list three zones, but East US 2 lists four.
Members spread over at least two zones keep serving when one zone is lost, while members confined to a single zone do not.
In a region that uses managed disks, the platform separates the virtual machines over either two or three fault domains.
A group created for high availability holds no more than twenty update domains, and that total is fixed once the group exists.
Two virtual machines in one group meet the 99.95% availability commitment, and the group adds no extra cost.

explanation: Each fact answers exactly one review question. The zone table fact (i1) belongs to the count of zones offered in the requested region, which is four in East US 2 while most regions offer three. The zone-spreading fact (i2) belongs to the question about losing one zone, because instances placed in at least two zones keep serving that failure while instances confined to a single zone do not. The managed-disk fact (i3) belongs to the count of groups that give each machine its own power and networking gear, because fault domains are exactly those groups and a region offers either two or three of them when managed disks are used. The update-domain fact (i4) belongs to the maintenance question, since an availability set allows at most twenty update domains and that count cannot be changed after the set is created. The service-level and cost fact (i5) belongs to the last question, because two virtual machines in an availability set meet the 99.95% SLA and the set itself is not charged for.

context:
You are re-architecting a stateless web tier that today runs as 12 Linux virtual machines in an availability set. After the change, the tier has to grow and shrink automatically with demand, has to let some instances start with their own command line instead of the shared one, and has to keep serving requests when one of the region's availability zones is lost. The design notes collected for the project are shown below. Which configuration should you create?

- Property: Target region; Value: West Europe
- Property: Availability zones offered by the region; Value: Three
- Property: Instances that need their own startup command; Value: Three of 12
- Property: Capacity changes today; Value: Requested by an engineer
- Property: Configuration and update rollout today; Value: Performed on each virtual machine
prompt: The team should create a Virtual Machine Scale Set using _____ and [...].

options.text: flexible orchestration mode
uniform orchestration mode

explanation:
Microsoft recommends virtual machine scale sets with flexible orchestration mode for high availability, because they centralize management, updates, configuration and automatic scaling and offer the widest feature range; flexible orchestration mode is also the mode that lets individual instances differ, which the three instances needing their own startup command require. For zone placement, a deployment only keeps serving after a zone is lost when its instances occupy at least two zones, so spreading the instances across the three availability zones offered by West Europe satisfies the requirement, while a single zone or letting the platform pick a zone does not. A scale set adds no separate resource charge; you pay for each virtual machine instance it creates.

Why the other options are wrong:
- uniform orchestration mode: Uniform orchestration mode creates every instance from a single image definition and applies the same configuration to all of them, so it cannot satisfy the requirement that three instances start with their own command line. Flexible orchestration mode is the configuration recommended for high availability, since it centralizes management, updates, configuration and automatic scaling and provides the widest feature range.

context:
You are designing the compute tier for an order-matching engine that runs on Linux virtual machines inside a single region. The engine keeps its working data on each machine, and the team measured how much delay the trading protocol can absorb between members of the tier. The business contract also commits the trading tier to a fixed availability level, and the finance team wants the tier built with the smallest configuration that satisfies that contract. The facts the team collected are shown below. You need to choose how the tier's virtual machines are grouped and how many members that grouping should hold. Which values should you use?

- Collected fact: Contractual availability commitment for the trading tier; Value: 99.95%
- Collected fact: Maximum delay the trading protocol tolerates between tier members; Value: Below 1 millisecond
- Collected fact: Round-trip delay measured between separate zones in the same region; Value: About 2 milliseconds
- Collected fact: Azure charge for traffic between zones inside one region; Value: None
- Collected fact: Zone-based placement offered for virtual machines in this region; Value: Yes
prompt: Deploy the trading tier as _____ that contains [...].

options.text: Availability set
Multiple availability zones
Single availability zone
Regional deployment with no zone selected

explanation:
The measured cross-zone round-trip delay of about 2 milliseconds is far above the sub-millisecond limit the trading protocol tolerates, so the tier must keep its members physically close rather than spread across separate zones. An availability set is the grouping that separates members across fault domains and update domains while leaving them in close proximity, and it adds no extra charge for the grouping itself. The contractual commitment of 99.95% requires at least two virtual machines in that grouping, so the smallest configuration that satisfies the contract is an availability set with two virtual machines.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Multiple availability zones: Placing members in multiple availability zones provides stronger protection against a zone outage, but the members end up in different datacenters roughly 2 milliseconds apart in round-trip terms, which exceeds the delay the trading protocol can absorb. The absence of an Azure transfer charge inside the region does not remove that latency penalty, so this choice breaks the protocol requirement.
- Single availability zone: A zonal deployment puts every member inside one zone, so losing that zone takes the whole tier offline, and members inside a single zone are not separated from each other across shared power and network equipment the way a grouping does.
- Regional deployment with no zone selected: With no zone chosen, Azure may place the machines anywhere in the region, so a single zone outage can interrupt the tier, and the members receive no separation from shared infrastructure faults or from maintenance restarts.

options.text: Convert the third machine's OS disk into a managed disk and add the machine to the existing managed availability set
Add the third machine to the existing managed availability set with its OS disk unchanged and let the platform place the disk
Move the third machine and its current OS disk into a separate unmanaged availability set and keep the other two machines where they are
Attach the page blob as a data disk to a new virtual machine with a managed OS disk and add that new machine to the existing managed availability set

explanation:
A managed availability set accepts only virtual machines whose disks are managed, so the page blob that still holds web-03's operating system content has to become a managed disk before the machine can join webset-northeurope. Once the disk is managed, web-03 joins the existing set, whose fault domain and update domain counts were fixed when it was created, so no new set has to be built and the members stay separated onto different shared power and network equipment with one maintenance restart at a time. The managed disks attached to each member follow that member's fault domain placement, so the converted disk is placed with web-03 rather than with another member.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add the third machine to the existing managed availability set with its OS disk unchanged and let the platform place the disk: The deployment cannot succeed this way. A managed availability set accepts only virtual machines with managed disks, so web-03 with its page blob operating system disk is refused, and the platform will not relocate or place that disk for you. The disk has to be managed before the machine is added.
- Move the third machine and its current OS disk into a separate unmanaged availability set and keep the other two machines where they are: This splits the tier into two separate groups, so the platform can no longer spread the three machines across the fault domains and update domains of one set. The new set would contain web-03 alone and give it no separation from the rest of the tier, and the two existing machines would keep the current set's protection only among themselves.
- Attach the page blob as a data disk to a new virtual machine with a managed OS disk and add that new machine to the existing managed availability set: The blob stays an unmanaged disk on the new machine, and the managed availability set accepts only virtual machines with managed disks, so attaching it as a data disk does not make the membership valid. It also leaves the original third member outside the tier instead of bringing it in.

options.text: hardware, power or network faults within the region
the loss of the whole region
operating system or application faults on the individual machines
a fault in one of the availability zones of the region

explanation:
An availability set is a logical grouping in which the platform assigns each member a fault domain and an update domain, so the set limits the impact of physical hardware failures, network outages and power interruptions inside the region; that is what the current grouping provides. It does not protect the application from operating-system or application-specific failures, and because all three members sit in availability zone 1 it does not protect them from a fault in that zone either. Neither availability sets nor availability zones protect against a full-region outage, so the contract requirement can only be met by adding Azure Site Recovery, which replicates the virtual machines to a secondary location and then supports failover to that location and failback.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the loss of the whole region: Fault domains and update domains only rearrange the members inside the region; nothing about the grouping carries the tier through the loss of the whole region.
- operating system or application faults on the individual machines: Members of an availability set can still fail together because of an operating-system or application-specific fault; the grouping only separates shared infrastructure such as power, cooling and networking.
- a fault in one of the availability zones of the region: All three members run in availability zone 1, so a fault in that zone takes the entire tier down; protection against a zone fault comes from placing members in several zones, not from the set itself.

prompt: You have created a Linux virtual machine in the Azure portal from the Ubuntu Server 22.04 LTS - Gen2 image. For the Administrator account you chose the SSH public key authentication type with the option to generate a new key pair, and the portal placed the new public key on the VM. The private key file was saved to the Downloads folder of your macOS workstation, and the VM has a public IP you can reach. You now need to sign in to the VM from that workstation with SSH. Which command should you run first?

options.text: chmod 644 ~/Downloads/myKey.pem
chown azureuser ~/Downloads/myKey.pem
chmod 400 ~/Downloads/myKey.pem
ssh -i ~/Downloads/myKey.pub azureuser@10.111.12.123

explanation:
The downloaded private key file was left with group and other read access (0664), so the SSH client refuses to use it and the sign-in fails with "Permission denied (publickey)". On macOS and Linux the key file must be restricted to the owner only, which is done with chmod 400 on the .pem file. After that, the same ssh command connects with the generated key pair, since Azure stores the matching public key on the VM and the private key stays on the workstation.

Why the other options are wrong:
- chmod 644 ~/Downloads/myKey.pem: chmod 644 still grants read access to the group and to other users, so the client continues to treat the key as too open and keeps ignoring it. The permission bits must allow access for the owner only.
- chown azureuser ~/Downloads/myKey.pem: Changing the file owner does not change the permission bits that the client reported as too open, and azureuser is the guest account name inside the VM rather than a local account on the workstation, so this command fails or changes nothing that matters.
- ssh -i ~/Downloads/myKey.pub azureuser@10.111.12.123: The .pub file contains only the public half of the key pair; the SSH client needs the private key file to authenticate. Passing the public key file with -i cannot establish the session.

Both instances currently sit in the same Availability Zone, and the tier was created with no infrastructure redundancy required. The business now requires the tier to keep at least 99.99% connectivity to at least one running instance while a single Availability Zone is serviced, and a data residency rule requires every instance to stay in the East US region. Which change should you make to the tier?

options.text: Move one of the two instances into a second Availability Zone in the East US region
Keep both instances in Availability Zone 1 in the East US region and add two more instances to that same Availability Zone
Move one of the two instances into a second region so the tier spans two regions
Replace the two instances with a single instance that uses the Availability Zones of the East US region

explanation:
Availability Zones are physically separated zones inside a single Azure region, and connectivity to at least one instance is guaranteed at least 99.99% of the time when two or more instances are deployed across two or more Availability Zones in the same region. Moving the second instance into a second Availability Zone in East US spreads the two existing instances over two zones while every instance stays in the region required by the residency rule, so the tier keeps serving when one zone is serviced.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Keep both instances in Availability Zone 1 in the East US region and add two more instances to that same Availability Zone: Adding more instances inside Availability Zone 1 leaves every instance in the same zone, so servicing that zone still interrupts the whole tier. The redundancy comes from running instances in more than one Availability Zone of the region, not from raising the instance count in a single zone.
- Move one of the two instances into a second region so the tier spans two regions: This breaks the data residency rule, which requires every instance to remain in the East US region, and it also does not satisfy the zone requirement, because the guarantee is defined for instances spread across two or more Availability Zones in the same region rather than for instances split across different regions.
- Replace the two instances with a single instance that uses the Availability Zones of the East US region: Collapsing the tier into a single instance removes the redundancy entirely. The connectivity guarantee depends on two or more instances deployed across two or more Availability Zones, so a lone instance would leave the service with nothing running during zone maintenance.

options.text: Virtual Machine Scale Sets
Availability Zones
Azure Site Recovery
Managed Premium SSD data disk
Local temporary storage
Register for Trusted Launch as default

explanation: Each choice maps to exactly one recorded outcome. A scale set supplies a load-balanced group whose instance count grows and shrinks with demand while configuration and updates are handled centrally for the group. Placing two or more instances in separate physical locations within one region (Availability Zones) is what keeps at least 99.99% connectivity to at least one instance while a single such location is down. Azure Site Recovery copies the workload to a region of your choosing, supports an automated failover plan, and lets you rehearse that failover before it is needed. A managed data disk holds business content separately from the instance so it can be detached from a failed machine and attached to its replacement. Local temporary storage is not charged for and suits caches and buffers that need not survive a deallocation. Registering for Trusted Launch as default makes every newly created Generation 2 instance boot with secure boot and vTPM already enabled, whichever client tool was used to create it.

context: You have a Windows virtual machine being created in the Azure portal with an Administrator account that uses password authentication. The password you entered is 11 characters long and otherwise follows the character rules. You need to know whether creation can proceed. Which result should you expect after you select Create?
prompt: After you select Create, _____

options.text: The deployment is rejected.
The VM is created without an Administrator password.
The VM is created and the portal generates a replacement password.
The VM is created with the 11-character password.

explanation:
For a Windows VM created in the portal, the Administrator password must contain at least 12 characters and satisfy the defined complexity requirements. An 11-character password is rejected when you select Create.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The VM is created without an Administrator password: The portal does not continue without the required Administrator credential; it validates the supplied password before creating the VM.
- The VM is created and the portal generates a replacement password: The portal does not generate a replacement password for a Windows Administrator account during this workflow.
- The VM is created with the 11-character password: The portal does not accept an Administrator password below the 12-character minimum, even if it otherwise satisfies the character rules.

context:
You have an Azure environment where the security standard requires that every new virtual machine comes up with hardware-rooted protections already switched on, and the standard must hold whether a machine is created in the portal, with the CLI, or with PowerShell. Engineers must not have to change extra values on each creation form. Which change should you make?

- Item: Operating system image for new machines; Detail: Ubuntu Server 22.04 LTS - Gen2
- Item: Clients used to create machines; Detail: Azure portal, Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell
- Item: Creation volume; Detail: About 40 machines per month across the team
- Item: Today's approach; Detail: Engineers choose extra values on each creation form
prompt: To meet the security standard, you should _____.

options.text: Register the subscription for Trusted Launch
Select the Trusted Launch security type on each machine in the portal
Assign an Azure Policy that requires a Premium SSD managed disk
Enroll the subscription in Azure Hybrid Benefit

explanation:
Trusted Launch as default (TLaD) is generally available for new Generation 2 virtual machines. Once you register for TLaD in the environment, any new Generation 2 VM created through any client tool comes up with secure boot and vTPM enabled automatically, so nothing extra has to be chosen on each creation form and the protection applies to portal, CLI, and PowerShell creations alike. It is a one-time, subscription-level setting, which is what the requirement asks for.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Select the Trusted Launch security type on each machine in the portal: Choosing the Trusted Launch security type by hand on each creation only affects machines built in the portal, and it still makes every engineer change extra values on the creation form, so it does not meet the requirement that the protection be automatic for CLI and PowerShell creations as well.
- Assign an Azure Policy that requires a Premium SSD managed disk: An Azure Policy that requires a Premium SSD managed disk governs which storage performance tier a machine may use. It has no effect on the hardware-rooted protections (secure boot and vTPM) that the security standard requires.
- Enroll the subscription in Azure Hybrid Benefit: Azure Hybrid Benefit reduces the operating system license cost for qualifying virtual machines; it does not enable hardware-rooted protections and has no bearing on the boot configuration of a new machine.

prompt: Regarding the charges for this deployment, _____.

options.text: compute is billed hourly by size and OS, and a partial hour is charged only for the minutes used, while storage is billed separately
compute is billed hourly by size and OS, and a partial hour is charged as a full hour, while storage is billed separately
compute is billed hourly by size and OS, and a partial hour is charged only for the minutes used, while storage is included in the compute charge
compute is billed monthly by size and OS, and a partial hour is charged only for the minutes used, while storage is billed separately

explanation:
Azure charges for virtual machine compute based on the size of the machine and its operating system, and when the machine runs for less than a full hour, only the minutes used are charged. Disk storage is billed on its own rather than being folded into the compute charge. The correct option therefore describes the charges correctly.

Why the other options are wrong:
- compute is billed hourly by size and OS, and a partial hour is charged as a full hour, while storage is billed separately: A partial hour is not charged as a full hour; only the minutes the virtual machine was used are billed, so this option overstates the compute cost.
- compute is billed hourly by size and OS, and a partial hour is charged only for the minutes used, while storage is included in the compute charge: Storage is not included in the compute charge; storage bills separately, so this option misstates how the disk charges are applied.
- compute is billed monthly by size and OS, and a partial hour is charged only for the minutes used, while storage is billed separately: Compute is billed hourly rather than monthly, so this option gives the wrong billing frequency for the virtual machine.

context:
You are creating a new Linux virtual machine for a customer-orders application. The order history must stay available after the current machine is replaced, and the replacement machine is deployed with its own operating system disk. The operations team wants to move the order history to that new machine without relying on the old instance booting successfully. You need to choose the storage that holds these records. Which option should you configure?

- Plan element: Operating system; Recorded value: Ubuntu Server 22.04 LTS - Gen2
- Plan element: Deployment type; Recorded value: New virtual machine, with no older disks to migrate
- Plan element: Storage objective; Recorded value: Order records stay with the application on whichever machine is serving it
- Plan element: Transfer constraint; Recorded value: The previous instance is not expected to boot after the move
prompt: You should configure _____ for the order records.

options.text: Managed data disk
Unmanaged data disk
Local temporary storage
OS disk only

explanation:
For new deployments the recommended storage is managed OS and data disks, and persistent data should sit on a separate data disk so it can be detached and attached to a replacement VM if the original fails. A managed data disk meets both requirements: the order history stays available after the machine is replaced and can be moved to the new machine without the old instance booting.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Unmanaged data disk: Unmanaged disks are the legacy choice that depends on a storage account and its blobs. For a brand-new virtual machine the recommended path is managed OS and data disks, and existing unmanaged-disk VMs are the ones that should be converted.
- Local temporary storage: Local temporary storage sits on the host rather than in remote Azure Storage. Its contents are discarded when the virtual machine is deallocated or deleted, so order records kept there would not survive the move to a replacement machine.
- OS disk only: Persistent data should be kept on a separate data disk that can be detached and attached to a replacement VM. Here the replacement machine is deployed with its own operating system disk, so the order records must be carried in a separate disk.

context:
You run your company's order-processing application on two virtual machines in the East US region, and the business wants those machines to keep serving if the entire region goes down. The table lists the requirements the business approved. You need to pick the service that meets them and the operation the operations team runs for the rehearsal. Which service should you configure, and which operation should the team run?

- Requirement: Continuity target; What the business approved: The workload must be brought up in a region the company selects; the selected region is not the designated paired region for East US
- Requirement: Rehearsal; What the business approved: The operations team must be able to rehearse the move on a schedule while the live workload keeps serving traffic
- Requirement: Workload state; What the business approved: The workload must carry its live state into the selected region rather than start from an older copy
prompt: Configure _____ for the two virtual machines and run [...] to rehearse the move without interrupting live traffic.

options.text: Azure Site Recovery
Availability Zones
Virtual Machine Scale Sets
Azure Backup

explanation:
Azure Site Recovery is the service that replicates virtual machines into a region of your choosing without being restricted to paired regions, and it supports a recovery plan that can automate the whole failover for an application spread across several machines. It is also the only one of these choices that lets a team rehearse the failover in advance without touching the running application or the ongoing replication, which is what the rehearsal requirement calls for. Running a test failover is the operation that exercises this without interrupting the live workload.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Availability Zones: Availability Zones are physically separate locations inside a single region. They keep a workload available while one zone is down, but they never copy the virtual machines into a region the company selects, so they cannot meet the continuity target.
- Virtual Machine Scale Sets: A scale set grows and shrinks a group of identical, load-balanced instances to follow demand and centralizes their configuration and updates. It does not copy the running workload into another region, so it does not meet the continuity target.
- Azure Backup: Azure Backup keeps scheduled copies of files and data in its own vault and restores them on demand. It does not stand up a replicated copy of the virtual machines in a selected region carrying their live state, so it does not meet the continuity target.

context:
Your platform team runs a Linux virtual machine that was created earlier today in the Azure portal from an Ubuntu Server 22.04 LTS image. The team now plans to roll out three more machines with the same sign-in behavior, and the platform owner has approved the requirements shown below.

`Requirement: Sign-in on the three new machines
Detail: Each new machine must accept the same key pair as the first machine, and no additional private key file may land on the engineer's laptop

Requirement: Nightly shutdown of the first machine
Detail: The machine must power itself off at 21:00 UTC every night, and the setting must be turned on for the machine after it has already been created`
prompt: For the three additional machines you select _____ as the SSH public key source, and for the existing machine you switch on the nightly shutdown from the VM's [...].

options.text: Use a key stored in Azure
Generate new key pair
Download a new key pair from Azure

explanation:
For the three follow-on Linux machines, 'Use a key stored in Azure' is the SSH public key source that satisfies the requirement: Azure already holds the public key for the team, the private key stays on the engineer's computer, and nothing is downloaded again, so the new machines accept the same key pair and no extra private key file lands on the laptop. Generating or downloading a new key pair would produce different credentials and add another file. For the nightly shutdown, the Linux creation flow has no auto-shutdown control, so you switch it on later from the VM's Operations section, select On, choose the shutdown time and time zone (UTC by default), and save. The Management tab is the Windows creation-time location and is not available for an existing Linux VM.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Generate new key pair: This creates a brand-new key pair for every machine and downloads a new private key file (myKey.pem) to the engineer's laptop, so the new machines would not accept the existing key pair and an additional file would be added.
- Download a new key pair from Azure: Pulling a new key pair from Azure again produces new credentials and another private key file on the engineer's laptop, which the requirement rules out; nothing needs to be downloaded when the existing pair is reused.

prompt: You are adding storage to an existing Windows virtual machine that hosts a tier-1 OLTP database. The new volume has to sustain at least 150,000 read/write operations per second and 3,000 MB/s of throughput, has to be adjustable in capacity and performance while it remains attached to the running VM, and has to use locally redundant storage because the database is pinned to a single datacenter. Which storage disk type should you create for the database?

options.text: Standard SSD disk (E-series)
Premium SSD v2 disk
Premium SSD disk (P-series)
Ultra Disk

explanation:
The required 150,000 IOPS and 3,000 MB/s sit above the ceiling of every other managed disk type, and only Ultra Disk can be provisioned that high: it supports up to 400,000 IOPS and 10,000 MB/s. It also matches the remaining conditions: capacity, throughput, and IOPS can be changed while the disk is attached and the VM is running (four resizes per 24-hour window, up to an hour to apply), it is offered with LRS redundancy, and it is a data-disk-only type, which is exactly the role required here. The 150,000 IOPS target is also below the VM's own 400,000 IOPS ceiling, so the disk can actually deliver it.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Standard SSD disk (E-series): Standard SSD (E-series) tops out at 6,000 IOPS and 750 MB/s and is aimed at web servers, lightly used applications, and dev/test scenarios, so it cannot reach the required 150,000 IOPS or 3,000 MB/s.
- Premium SSD v2 disk: Premium SSD v2 reaches at most 80,000 IOPS and 2,000 MB/s, below the 150,000 IOPS and 3,000 MB/s this database requires. It also has no host caching and can only be used as a data disk.
- Premium SSD disk (P-series): Premium SSD (P-series) delivers a maximum of 20,000 IOPS and 900 MB/s; even with unlimited on-demand bursting from P30 upward it reaches only 30,000 IOPS and 1,000 MB/s, still far below the target.

prompt: You have a Windows VM whose data disk is 4,096 GiB and was partitioned with MBR; the guest reports only 2,048 GiB of usable space on it. You have just attached a new blank 3,072 GiB data disk that has not been initialized in the guest. You need both volumes to expose their full capacity and to use one consistent partition style across the VM. What should you do?

options.text: Convert Disk 1 to GPT and initialize Disk 2 with GPT
Leave Disk 1 on MBR and initialize Disk 2 with MBR
Convert Disk 1 to GPT and initialize Disk 2 with MBR
Leave Disk 1 on MBR and initialize Disk 2 with GPT

explanation:
Both volumes sit at or above the 2 TiB mark, where GPT partitioning is required. Disk 1 is 4,096 GiB and is still partitioned with MBR, and an MBR layout can address only about 2 TiB of usable space, which explains why the guest reports only 2,048 GiB on a 4 TiB disk; converting it to GPT brings the missing capacity back into use. The newly attached 3,072 GiB disk is also larger than 2 TiB, so it must be initialized with GPT as well, keeping one partition style across the VM.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Leave Disk 1 on MBR and initialize Disk 2 with MBR: Leaving Disk 1 on MBR keeps its usable space capped at roughly 2 TiB, which is the exact symptom you are seeing, and MBR is not permitted on the 3,072 GiB disk because disks of 2 TiB or larger must use GPT.
- Convert Disk 1 to GPT and initialize Disk 2 with MBR: Converting Disk 1 to GPT is correct, but MBR cannot be used for the new 3,072 GiB disk, since disks of 2 TiB or larger require GPT partitioning.
- Leave Disk 1 on MBR and initialize Disk 2 with GPT: Initializing the new disk with GPT is correct, but keeping Disk 1 on MBR leaves about half of that 4 TiB volume unreachable, so the reported shortfall on drive D: would remain.

prompt: You run a transaction-heavy application on a Linux virtual machine. Its data disk was created with the configuration shown below and has not been changed since it was provisioned. The application team now needs the disk to sustain 60,000 read/write operations per second and at least 1,500 MB/s of throughput, and you want the least expensive configuration that reaches those numbers because the cost of a managed disk follows its provisioned size. What size should you set the data disk to?

options.text: 96 GiB
114 GiB
120 GiB
154 GiB

explanation:
Every Premium SSD v2 disk carries a free baseline of 3,000 IOPS, and past 6 GiB the IOPS ceiling rises by 500 for every additional GiB (a 160 GiB disk reaches the 80,000 IOPS maximum). That works out to an IOPS ceiling of 500 x size in GiB for any disk larger than 6 GiB, so the smallest disk that can be set to 60,000 IOPS is 60,000 / 500 = 120 GiB. At 120 GiB the disk can be provisioned with 60,000 IOPS and, because throughput grows 0.25 MB/s for each IOPS set above the baseline, up to the 2,000 MB/s maximum - comfortably above the 1,500 MB/s required, so the IOPS target is the binding constraint. The 6 GiB disk in the exhibit could never go above the 3,000 IOPS baseline no matter what was requested, and the tuning budget allows the change (four tuning operations per 24-hour window, one already used for the creation). Because the disk is billed on its provisioned size, 120 GiB is also the cheapest configuration that meets the requirement.

Why the other options are wrong:
- 96 GiB: At 96 GiB the IOPS ceiling is 500 x 96 = 48,000, which is 12,000 short of the 60,000 the application team asked for, so this disk cannot be provisioned to the target performance.
- 114 GiB: At 114 GiB the IOPS ceiling is 500 x 114 = 57,000. This size comes from taking the 57,000 IOPS needed on top of the baseline, dividing by 500 per GiB, and then forgetting to add the first 6 GiB, so the disk still delivers 3,000 IOPS less than required.
- 154 GiB: At 154 GiB the disk can be set to 77,000 IOPS, so it would run the workload fine, but it is bigger than the workload needs. Since managed disks are billed on the provisioned size, this configuration costs more than the 120 GiB disk that already satisfies the 60,000 IOPS target, so it is not the least expensive option.

prompt: You have a two-node Linux database cluster running on Azure virtual machines in a region where availability zones are supported. The data disk on each node and the targets the business signed off for the replacement tier are listed below. You need the data tier to keep serving traffic if one availability zone is lost, and you need each replacement disk to hit the agreed IOPS and throughput targets at the agreed provisioned size. Which managed disk configuration should you create for the data disks?

options.text: Premium SSD v2 with ZRS redundancy
Premium SSD v2 with LRS redundancy
Ultra Disk with ZRS redundancy
Ultra Disk with LRS redundancy

explanation:
Premium SSD v2 meets both requirements: it supports up to 80,000 IOPS and 2,000 MB/s, so 60,000 IOPS and 2,000 MB/s at 256 GiB are within its limits (a 256 GiB disk can be set well above 60,000 IOPS), and it supports zone-redundant storage, whose replicas span availability zones, so the volume survives the loss of one zone. It is a data-disk-only type, which matches the role required here, and the nodes are already pinned to zones, as Premium SSD v2 disks require in most zone-enabled regions.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Premium SSD v2 with LRS redundancy: Premium SSD v2 reaches the performance targets, but locally redundant storage keeps all three replicas inside one datacenter. If an availability zone is lost, the data volume goes offline with it, so this configuration does not satisfy the availability requirement.
- Ultra Disk with ZRS redundancy: Ultra Disk can far exceed the IOPS and throughput targets, but it is offered only with locally redundant storage — zone-redundant storage is not available for that type — so this combination cannot be created.
- Ultra Disk with LRS redundancy: This is the only redundancy option available for Ultra Disk, but locally redundant storage replicates within a single datacenter, so the volume would not remain available if one availability zone were lost. Ultra Disk is also a data-disk-only type and adds a per-vCPU reservation charge on capable VMs.

prompt: You are rolling out 40 identical application servers. Every instance must start from the same operating system and carry the same two application data volumes that the build machine holds today, and no instance may inherit the local sign-in accounts or the unique machine identity of the build machine. Which artifact should you produce from the build machine and use for the rollout?

options.text: Deallocate the build machine, generalize it with Sysprep, then capture the managed image and create all 40 VMs from it.
Capture the managed image from the build machine while it is still running and still signed in, with its local administrator password and SSH keys in place, then create all 40 VMs from it.
Take a snapshot of the build machine's OS disk, use it as the boot source for all 40 VMs, and attach two new empty data disks to each instance.
Take a snapshot of every disk on the build machine and attach the snapshots to all 40 VMs as their boot and data volumes.

explanation:
The artifact that can bootstrap many identical VMs and carry the whole set of application volumes is a managed image, and the only supported source for one is a generalized (Sysprep), deallocated VM. Generalizing is what removes the machine identity and the embedded local accounts so each instance gets its own, and the image contains every managed disk attached to the source — the OS disk plus both data disks — so a single artifact boots all 40 servers with the same application volumes. A snapshot cannot serve this purpose: it is a read-only, point-in-time copy of one disk, so it neither packages the two data volumes nor strips the identity and accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Capture the managed image from the build machine while it is still running and still signed in, with its local administrator password and SSH keys in place, then create all 40 VMs from it: Capturing while the source is still running and signed in, with the local administrator password and SSH keys still present, does not produce a deallocated and generalized VM, so every instance created from that artifact would inherit the build machine's identity and sign-in accounts — the exact outcome the rollout forbids.
- Take a snapshot of the build machine's OS disk, use it as the boot source for all 40 VMs, and attach two new empty data disks to each instance: A snapshot holds a copy of one managed disk only, so the instances would boot from the captured OS disk but start with two brand-new empty data disks rather than the application volumes already on the build machine. It also does not remove the build machine's identity or local accounts, so all 40 instances would share them.
- Take a snapshot of every disk on the build machine and attach the snapshots to all 40 VMs as their boot and data volumes: Each snapshot is an independent, read-only, point-in-time copy of a single disk, and snapshots taken one by one do not coordinate across disks. Used this way they neither strip the machine identity and accounts nor provide the reusable, all-disks template needed to launch 40 servers with working boot and data volumes.

prompt: You have a Windows build agent in Azure that keeps its npm package cache on the VM's local scratch volume so the shared file server is not saturated. The build team needs that cache to still be there after the scheduled maintenance work and after a redeploy of the VM. Which change should you make?

options.text: Move the cache to a managed disk attached to the VM so the cache survives a maintenance event or a redeploy.
Enable encryption at host on the VM so the cache on the local temporary disk is encrypted at rest after a maintenance event or a redeploy.
Set Azure Disk Encryption to cover the whole volume on the VM so the cache on the local temporary disk is restored after a maintenance event or a redeploy.
Take a scheduled managed disk snapshot of the local temporary disk on the VM so the cache data can be restored after a maintenance event or a redeploy.

explanation:
The scratch (temporary) disk is local ephemeral storage: its contents can be lost during a maintenance event, when the VM is redeployed, and when the VM is stopped; only a successful standard restart keeps them. That matches the exhibit, where the cache on D: is empty after both the maintenance event and the redeploy. A managed disk is provisioned as its own resource and is not re-created together with the VM instance, so relocating the cache to a managed disk that is attached to the VM is what makes the cache still present after a maintenance event or a redeploy.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enable encryption at host on the VM so the cache on the local temporary disk is encrypted at rest after a maintenance event or a redeploy: Encryption at host protects the VM's disk contents at rest; it says nothing about whether the files are still present. The local scratch volume is re-provisioned during a maintenance event and on a redeploy, so the cache would still be gone afterwards. Moreover, on a version 5 series VM such as Standard_D8s_v5 the temporary disk is already encrypted automatically, so this setting would not change anything for this workload.
- Set Azure Disk Encryption to cover the whole volume on the VM so the cache on the local temporary disk is restored after a maintenance event or a redeploy: Covering the whole volume with Azure Disk Encryption (VolumeType set to All on Windows, or EncryptFormatAll on Linux) encrypts the local scratch volume at rest, but the files are still wiped when that volume is re-created during maintenance or a redeploy. Encryption addresses confidentiality, not retention.
- Take a scheduled managed disk snapshot of the local temporary disk on the VM so the cache data can be restored after a maintenance event or a redeploy: A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of a managed disk resource, and the local scratch volume is not a managed disk, so there is no disk resource to snapshot for it. Even for a managed disk, a scheduled snapshot stores a copy rather than restoring the cache automatically after an event, so it does not meet the requirement.
