prompt: You run a line-of-business application on a Windows virtual machine. During normal hours the workload needs only a few hundred read/write operations per second, but the nightly batch job has to sustain 12,000 read/write operations per second for roughly two hours without being throttled. The application data sits on the managed disk listed below, and the virtual machine must stay up while you address this. What should you do with that disk?

options.text: Change the data disk's size tier to P30 and enable on-demand bursting.
Change the data disk's size tier to P20 and enable on-demand bursting.
Keep the data disk's size tier at P10 and enable on-demand bursting.
Attach a second data disk with size tier P20 and enable on-demand bursting on the VM, and run the batch job from it.

explanation:
The batch window requires 12,000 read/write operations per second held for about two hours. In the P1 through P20 range, a Premium SSD can burst only to 3,500 IOPS and 170 MB/s, and only for a maximum of 30 minutes, so no tier below P30 can carry that window. From P30 upward, a Premium SSD can reach 30,000 IOPS and 1,000 MB/s with unlimited duration once on-demand bursting is enabled, which covers a two-hour batch run. The disk is already attached to the running VM, so moving it to the P30 tier and switching on-demand bursting on is what has to change.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Change the data disk's size tier to P20 and enable on-demand bursting: P20 sits inside the P1-P20 range, where bursting tops out at 3,500 IOPS and 170 MB/s for at most 30 minutes. That is far below the 12,000 IOPS the batch window needs, and the window lasts longer than the allowed burst duration.
- Keep the data disk's size tier at P10 and enable on-demand bursting: P10 is also within the P1-P20 range, so turning on on-demand bursting still only lifts it to 3,500 IOPS for at most 30 minutes. The provisioned and burst limits of that tier cannot cover the batch window.
- Attach a second data disk with size tier P20 and enable on-demand bursting on the VM, and run the batch job from it: A separate disk on the P20 tier carries exactly the same 3,500 IOPS and 30-minute burst ceiling as the current disk, so hosting the batch job on it still cannot deliver 12,000 IOPS for two hours, and it adds cost rather than solving the problem.

prompt: You have four Windows virtual machines that run SQL Server instances, and all four instances must use one shared volume that holds the database files. The volume is a 1 TiB Premium SSD with LRS redundancy that today sits connected only to the first virtual machine, so the other three instances find no database files at all. What should you do to provision this shared volume correctly?

options.text: Attach one managed disk to all four virtual machines and bring them under WSFC (or Pacemaker) so the nodes coordinate access and lock writes
Attach one managed disk to all four virtual machines and install a shared-filesystem agent on each machine to coordinate access and lock writes, with no host-level clustering software
Create four separate managed disks, attach one to each virtual machine, and place the virtual machines in an availability set
Create four separate managed disks using ZRS, attach one to each virtual machine, and place the virtual machines in separate availability zones

explanation:
A single managed disk can be attached to several virtual machines at the same time for cluster applications, but that pattern requires a cluster manager such as WSFC or Pacemaker so the nodes can talk to each other and serialize writes. The existing 1 TiB Premium SSD already holds the data, so the fix is to attach that same disk to sql02, sql03 and sql04 as well and place the four machines under WSFC (or Pacemaker). Creating one disk per machine would produce four independent volumes instead of the single shared volume the application requires.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Attach one managed disk to all four virtual machines and install a shared-filesystem agent on each machine to coordinate access and lock writes, with no host-level clustering software: A shared-filesystem agent cannot replace the host-level component that this multi-attach pattern depends on: when one managed disk is mounted by several VMs for a cluster application, node communication and write locking must be handled by a cluster manager such as WSFC or Pacemaker. Without it, concurrent writes from the four instances are not coordinated and the data can be corrupted.
- Create four separate managed disks, attach one to each virtual machine, and place the virtual machines in an availability set: Four separate disks give every virtual machine its own private copy of the files, so the instances never see one shared volume and cannot fail over onto the same data. An availability set only spreads the member VM disks across storage scale units so that a single unit failure does not break the set; it does not create a shared volume across machines.
- Create four separate managed disks using ZRS, attach one to each virtual machine, and place the virtual machines in separate availability zones: ZRS replicates the content of one disk across availability zones for durability, but attaching one disk per virtual machine still yields four independent volumes rather than one shared volume, and the four instances would each work on different data. Zone redundancy is a property of a single disk, not a way of sharing one volume between VMs.

options.text: Charged as E15, the next offered tier, prorated hourly
Charged for the content the copy actually stores
Charged per 16 KiB block read or written
Charged per read or write of up to 256 KiB
Billable transactions per hour are capped

explanation: Each charge statement belongs to the storage object whose billing rules it reflects. The provisioned size of a managed disk is rounded up to the next offered tier and prorated hourly, so the 200 GiB Standard SSD behind the reporting database is billed as E15, the 256 GiB tier. A snapshot is billed only for the data it actually holds, so the nightly copy of a 64 GiB disk that holds 10 GiB is billed for 10 GiB. Transaction accounting differs by tier: on a Standard HDD every 16 KiB read or write counts as one billable transaction, which suits the seldom-read archive files, while on a Premium SSD each read or write of up to 256 KiB counts as a single billable operation, which is what the order-processing database produces. Both Standard tiers cap billable transactions per hour, so the web front-end Standard SSD, whose workload issues a very large number of small operations, is billed under that hourly ceiling.

context:
You have a fleet of Azure virtual machines and a list of storage problems that the operations team reported for the disks attached to them. You need to close every problem with one change to the disk, the virtual machine, or the surrounding configuration. Which change should you make in each case? Drag the change into the slot for its case.

`Case 1
  A new 512 GiB managed disk was attached to a running Windows virtual machine. In Disk Management the disk is listed with 0 bytes and no volume, and the guest shows no new drive for it.

Case 2
  A new Ultra Disk was created for a database virtual machine. The deployment pipeline refuses to boot the virtual machine from this disk, and the disk is rejected when the team publishes a virtual machine that uses it to the Azure Compute Gallery.

Case 3
  A virtual machine running Oracle Database 12.1 cannot mount a newly attached Ultra Disk. The database start-up log reports that the physical sector size of the disk is not supported.

Case 4
  A Premium SSD v2 data disk was created earlier today and the team has already adjusted its performance three times since it was created. The portal rejects a further performance change with an error, and the application is waiting for the higher performance.

Case 5
  A Premium SSD v2 data disk was created in a region that supports availability zones. Attaching it to a virtual machine that was created without a zone fails with an error, and the deployment of that virtual machine has to be retried.`
prompt: Case 1

options.text: Initialize the new disk in the guest, create a new simple volume, and format it so it comes online with a drive letter
Boot from a Premium SSD or Standard SSD and keep this disk for data only, outside the Azure Compute Gallery
Provision the disk with 512E sector size instead of the 4k default
Wait for the daily tuning allowance to reset, then submit the performance change
Create the virtual machine in the zone where the disk was provisioned

explanation: Case 1 is a disk that is attached but not yet prepared inside the guest: it must be initialized, a new simple volume added and the volume formatted so the guest brings it online with a drive letter. Case 2 uses an Ultra Disk, which can never serve as the OS disk and cannot be part of an Azure Compute Gallery image, so the boot volume has to be a Premium SSD or Standard SSD while the Ultra Disk stays a plain data disk outside gallery images. Case 3 is a sector-size mismatch: Ultra Disks default to a 4k physical sector size, and Oracle Database before release 12.2 needs 512E, so the disk has to be provisioned with 512E. Case 4 has already used up the tuning operations allowed in a 24-hour window (for Premium SSD v2 creating the disk counts as one of the four), so the requested performance change has to wait until the window resets. Case 5 is a placement problem: in most zone-enabled regions a Premium SSD v2 disk attaches only to a zonal virtual machine, so the virtual machine must be created in the zone the disk lives in.

You have a Windows virtual machine that runs a batch application, and the application team needs extra working space. You have to add storage to the virtual machine and then hand the application a drive it can write to. Put each action into the stage of the work where it belongs.

- Setting: Guest operating system; Value: Windows Server 2022
- Setting: Disk to add; Value: 512 GiB Premium SSD, named appdata01
- Setting: Drive letter the application expects; Value: F:
- Setting: Guest disks today; Value: osdisk holds the operating system, datadisk holds application data
prompt: Provision the storage in Azure and link it to the running instance

options.text: On the virtual machine's Disks pane, select Create and attach a new disk, choose the SKU and size, give it a name, and save.
In the guest, launch diskmgmt.msc, acknowledge the extra disk that appears with no volume on it, and compare its number and size with the disk you added.
Right-click that disk, choose New simple volume, and finish the wizard.
Select Format disk, then check that the disk shows Online and Healthy with a drive letter.

explanation: The work runs in four stages. First the disk has to exist in Azure and be connected to the virtual machine: on the VM's Disks pane you choose Create and attach a new disk, pick the SKU (Premium SSD) and size (512 GiB), name it (appdata01) and save. Only then does the guest see the hardware: in Disk Management (diskmgmt.msc) the new disk appears with no volume on it, and you acknowledge it and compare its number and size with the disk you added, so the next steps never point at datadisk, which already holds application data. Next you right-click that disk, choose New simple volume and finish the wizard, which carves out the partition and puts a file system in place. Finally you select Format disk and confirm the disk shows Online and Healthy with a drive letter, which is the drive (F:) the application can write to.

context:
You are rolling out a new Linux virtual machine that will run a production database. Its data disk is a Premium SSD v2 disk that stays attached to the running virtual machine while you adjust it, and the actions you took today are listed in the table. You need to know what happens to the request scheduled for 15:00, and you need to pick the managed disk type for the boot volume of the same virtual machine. The boot volume has to be a type the platform supports for operating system disks, and it must not be a type that the platform is retiring. Which statement should you place in each slot?

- Time: 07:00; Action on the Premium SSD v2 data disk: Disk created with 200 GiB, 3,000 IOPS, 125 MB/s
- Time: 09:00; Action on the Premium SSD v2 data disk: IOPS raised from 3,000 to 8,000
- Time: 11:00; Action on the Premium SSD v2 data disk: Throughput raised from 125 MB/s to 2,000 MB/s
- Time: 13:00; Action on the Premium SSD v2 data disk: IOPS raised from 8,000 to 12,000
- Time: 15:00; Action on the Premium SSD v2 data disk: Request to raise the throughput to 2,500 MB/s
prompt: The request submitted at 15:00 is _____, and the boot volume should be [...].

options.text: Rejected — the per-day tuning limit for the disk is reached
Accepted — the per-day tuning limit for the disk is not reached yet
Accepted — the per-day tuning limit does not apply to this disk type
Rejected — this disk type does not support tuning after creation

explanation:
Premium SSD v2 performance can be adjusted four times in a 24-hour period, and creating the disk counts as one of those four, so a newly created Premium SSD v2 can only be adjusted three times during its first day. Here the 07:00 creation plus the 09:00, 11:00 and 13:00 adjustments use all four operations, so the 15:00 request is rejected even though 2,500 MB/s is within the throughput that the current 12,000 IOPS setting permits. For the boot volume, only Premium SSD and Standard SSD are managed disk types the platform supports for operating system disks that are not being retired: Ultra Disk and Premium SSD v2 are data-disk-only types, and using a Standard HDD as an OS disk is retired on September 8, 2028.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Accepted — the per-day tuning limit for the disk is not reached yet: This counts only the three adjustments made at 09:00, 11:00 and 13:00. Creating the disk consumes one of the four allowed operations, so the limit is already reached when the 15:00 request arrives.
- Accepted — the per-day tuning limit does not apply to this disk type: The limit does apply to this disk type: Premium SSD v2 disks, like Ultra Disks, can be adjusted only four times in a 24-hour period, with the creation counting as one of them.
- Rejected — this disk type does not support tuning after creation: Premium SSD v2 disks are built for granular tuning after creation — capacity, IOPS and throughput can be changed at any time while the disk stays attached to the running virtual machine, with each change taking up to an hour to take effect.

You have a Windows virtual machine in Azure that runs a line-of-business application. Its 256 GiB disk volume currently stores 40 GiB of business records, and the compliance team needs an archived copy of that volume as it stands today. The archived copy must remain readable after the live volume is replaced with a 1 TiB volume next quarter, and finance needs to know how the archive will appear on the monthly bill. You need to produce the archive and explain its billing. Which option should you choose for the archived copy, and which statement describes its monthly bill?

- Property: Virtual machine; Value: Windows Server 2022, running continuously
- Property: Volume role; Value: Application workload volume attached to the virtual machine
- Property: Provisioned size; Value: 256 GiB
- Property: Used capacity; Value: 40 GiB
- Property: Planned change; Value: Volume replaced with a 1 TiB volume next quarter
- Property: Archive requirement; Value: Copy of the volume as it stands today, still readable after the replacement
prompt: You should _____, and [...].

options.text: Create a snapshot of the disk volume
Create a managed image of the generalized virtual machine
Create a managed disk and copy the contents of the volume with a file-copy tool
Create a second managed disk and attach it to the virtual machine

explanation:
Taking a snapshot of a managed disk yields an independent, read-only copy of that disk as of one moment in time; it is kept as a standard managed disk by default and it survives changes to the source, so it satisfies the compliance requirement for an archived copy of the volume that stays readable after the live volume is replaced. A managed image instead packages every disk of a deallocated, generalized VM and exists to launch many similar VMs, so it is the wrong artifact for archiving a single volume. Snapshots bill only for the data they contain, so this archive of a 256 GiB volume that stores 40 GiB is billed for 40 GiB; provisioned size is how managed disks themselves are billed.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Create a managed image of the generalized virtual machine: A managed image is built from a deallocated, generalized (Sysprep) VM and packages every disk that VM had, so it acts as a template for launching many similar VMs instead of as an archived copy of one volume at a single point in time.
- Create a managed disk and copy the contents of the volume with a file-copy tool: Copying files with a file-copy tool captures only what the application and file system expose and depends on the source volume remaining available, so it does not produce a consistent point-in-time copy of the managed disk.
- Create a second managed disk and attach it to the virtual machine: A newly created managed disk starts out empty, so attaching a second volume to the virtual machine does not duplicate the contents of the existing volume and does not preserve a copy of it.

- Object: Live application data disk; Current configuration: Standard SSD, 200 GiB provisioned, 120 GiB in use; Workload notes: Attached to the running VM and written and read continuously by the application
- Object: Archive copy volume; Current configuration: Not created yet; Workload notes: Weekly copies retained for two years, read only occasionally, and cost is the main concern
prompt: Create the archive copy volume as a _____ disk, and expect the monthly invoice to show the live application disk as [...].

options.text: Standard HDD
Standard SSD
Premium SSD
Premium SSD v2

explanation:
The archive holds weekly copies that are read only occasionally and kept for two years, so the cheapest acceptable managed disk type for infrequent, latency-tolerant storage is Standard HDD; the SSD and Premium families cost more and target web servers, general-purpose production, or fixed-size low-latency workloads. The live application disk is a Standard SSD with 200 GiB provisioned, and managed disk charges follow the provisioned size rounded up to the next offered size, so it is billed as the 256 GiB size (E15) on an hourly prorated basis, regardless of how much of that capacity the application currently uses.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Standard SSD: Standard SSD gives lower latency and more consistent performance for web servers and lightly used applications, but it costs more than the cheapest option and adds no benefit for copies that are read rarely.
- Premium SSD: Premium SSD targets fixed-size, low-latency production workloads and carries a higher price than the archive requires.
- Premium SSD v2: Premium SSD v2 is a tunable premium option with a free performance baseline, which is unnecessary for a rarely read, long-retained archive.

Your payment application runs on Linux virtual machines in a region where availability zones are supported. None of the nodes sits in a zone, and the application team has certified Premium SSD v2 as the only disk tier permitted for the database volumes, so the tier on these volumes stays fixed. A fresh Premium SSD v2 data disk per node is ready, and the operations team reports that attaching it to the current nodes is refused. The capacity plan for next year also has to record the highest performance that can be configured on the certified tier.

- Item: Region; Detail: Region A - availability zones supported
- Item: Node zone assignment; Detail: None
- Item: Certified disk tier for the database volumes; Detail: Premium SSD v2
- Item: Role of the new volume; Detail: Data disk
- Item: Tier change allowed; Detail: No
- Item: New volumes waiting; Detail: One per node
prompt: The storage team should _____. The certified tier can be configured up to [...].

options.text: Reprovision the virtual machine with a zone chosen at provisioning time, then attach the Premium SSD v2 disk to it
Provision a replacement Premium SSD v2 disk, then attach it to the current virtual machine, which has no zone
Enable host caching on the Premium SSD v2 disk, then attach it to the current virtual machine, which has no zone
Attach the Premium SSD v2 disk to the current virtual machine, which has no zone, and move the disk into a zone later

explanation:
In most regions that support availability zones, a Premium SSD v2 disk can only be attached to a zonal virtual machine, and the zone has to be picked when that virtual machine is created; only a subset of zone-enabled regions allows nonzonal disks on nonzonal VMs, with extra limitations, which is why the attachment to the current nodes is refused. Because the certified tier may not change, the remedy belongs on the virtual machine side: provision it again with a zone chosen up front and then attach the Premium SSD v2 disk to it. On the performance side, this tier reaches 80,000 IOPS and 2,000 MB/s per disk, on top of a baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s that every disk includes at no extra charge.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Provision a replacement Premium SSD v2 disk, then attach it to the current virtual machine, which has no zone: A freshly created disk of the same tier meets the same rule: in most zone-enabled regions this tier attaches only to zonal virtual machines. Replacing the disk leaves the nodes without a zone, so the attachment would still be refused.
- Enable host caching on the Premium SSD v2 disk, then attach it to the current virtual machine, which has no zone: This tier offers no host caching at all, and caching settings have no bearing on which virtual machines can take the disk. The refusal comes from the zone assignment of the virtual machine, not from any caching setting.
- Attach the Premium SSD v2 disk to the current virtual machine, which has no zone, and move the disk into a zone later: There is no later step that moves a disk into a zone, and the zone of a virtual machine is fixed when it is created. In most zone-enabled regions this tier attaches only to zonal virtual machines, so the current nodes cannot take the disk.

context:
Your team is moving an on-premises order-processing database into Azure in two phases, and the exhibit lists what the migration team has gathered. The 30 TiB data file has to exist in the target subscription as a managed disk before any virtual machine is created there, and the database virtual machines have to be created in phase one so that the Ultra Disks planned for phase two can be attached to them straight away instead of rebuilding the nodes later. Finance wants to know what the phase-one virtual machines will cost. Which option should you place in each slot?

`Migration plan  (target subscription: contoso-prod)

Source file   : VHD, 30 TiB, captured from the on-premises hypervisor
Workload      : transactional order-processing database, 30 TiB of data in total
VM quota      : request to create virtual machines in the target subscription is still being processed
Phase one     : create the database virtual machines (Standard_E32-8s_v3) so that Ultra Disks
                can be attached to them later without another change
Phase two     : attach Ultra Disks to those virtual machines for the transactional workload`
prompt: Bring the source file into Azure as a managed disk with _____, and tell finance that [...]

options.text: Direct upload
Managed image capture
Disk snapshot
Azure Elastic SAN volume

explanation:
Direct upload is the documented way to place a VHD into a managed disk without attaching it to a virtual machine, and it covers VHDs of up to 32 TiB, so the 30 TiB file qualifies while the virtual machine quota request in the target subscription is still pending. A managed image or a snapshot would not leave the file as a managed disk there, and an Elastic SAN volume is a consolidated storage back end rather than an import path. Separately, switching on the Ultra Disk capability on a virtual machine adds a per-vCPU reservation fee even when no Ultra Disk is attached (on the Standard_E32-8s_v3 size the fee is charged across 32 cores), so the phase-one virtual machines already carry that charge until an Ultra Disk is actually attached.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Managed image capture: A managed image is a reusable template built from a deallocated, generalized virtual machine, and it packages every disk that machine had; it does not leave the file as a managed disk in the target subscription, and the generalizing step needs a virtual machine that the pending quota request still prevents.
- Disk snapshot: A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of an existing managed disk, and the source file here is not yet a managed disk, so there is nothing for it to copy.
- Azure Elastic SAN volume: Azure Elastic SAN consolidates storage for many large-scale, I/O-intensive workloads and top-tier databases behind one block storage back end; it is not a mechanism that turns an external VHD file into a managed disk.

context:
Your team runs a columnar analytics platform on 12 Linux virtual machines in a single Azure region, and the plan is to serve the columnar store from Ultra Disks next quarter. The facts the platform team collected are in the table below. The infrastructure review has two open items: finance wants to know what switching the fleet over to Ultra Disk support will cost the subscription, and the platform team wants to know whether the planned data footprint is allowed as it stands. Which option should you place in each slot?

- Fact: Fleet; Detail: 12 Linux virtual machines of the size Standard_E32-8s_v3
- Fact: Planned data; Detail: One Ultra Disk of 20 TiB per virtual machine, all created in one subscription and in one region
- Fact: Current storage; Detail: The Premium SSD P30 data disks already attached to the fleet stay in place for the first quarter
prompt: Switching the fleet over to Ultra Disk support brings _____, while the planned data footprint [...].

options.text: a per-vCPU reservation fee for every virtual machine in the fleet
a per-gigabyte fee for every virtual machine in the fleet, based on the provisioned capacity of its Ultra Disks
a per-IOPS fee for every virtual machine in the fleet, based on the provisioned performance of its Ultra Disks
a per-disk fee for every virtual machine in the fleet, based on the number of Ultra Disks attached to it

explanation:
Two separate Ultra Disk facts decide this. First, turning on Ultra Disk support for a virtual machine adds a per-vCPU reservation fee to the subscription, and that fee is charged even on machines that carry no Ultra Disk, so the switch costs a reservation fee for every virtual machine in the fleet rather than a per-gigabyte, per-IOPS or per-disk amount. Second, the planned footprint is 12 virtual machines multiplied by one 20 TiB Ultra Disk each, which is 240 TiB created in a single subscription and a single region. The default Ultra Disk capacity allowance is 100 TiB per subscription per region, so the plan goes past it and a quota increase has to be requested before those disks can be created.

Why the other options are wrong:
- a per-gigabyte fee for every virtual machine in the fleet, based on the provisioned capacity of its Ultra Disks: The cost of switching on Ultra Disk support is not calculated per gigabyte. A managed disk's own price follows its provisioned size, but the capability charge is a reservation fee based on the number of virtual CPUs of each machine, so a per-gigabyte model does not describe it.
- a per-IOPS fee for every virtual machine in the fleet, based on the provisioned performance of its Ultra Disks: There is no per-IOPS charge for enabling the capability. Ultra Disk performance is provisioned per disk through its own IOPS and throughput settings, and those settings are not billed as a capability fee on the virtual machine.
- a per-disk fee for every virtual machine in the fleet, based on the number of Ultra Disks attached to it: The charge is not levied per attached Ultra Disk. Enabling the capability produces a per-vCPU reservation fee on the virtual machine even when no Ultra Disk is attached to it, so a per-disk model does not match.

- Item: In-guest disk encryption extension; Current state: Not installed
- Item: Azure Disk Encryption; Current state: Disabled on the OS disk and on all data disks
- Item: OS and data disks; Current state: Managed disks with server-side encryption at rest using a customer-managed key through a disk encryption set
- Item: Temporary / ephemeral disk; Current state: Not encrypted at rest
- Item: Disk cache; Current state: Not encrypted
- Item: Data path between compute and storage; Current state: Not encrypted

prompt: You have a Linux virtual machine vm-sales-01 whose temporary disk, disk cache, and data path between compute and storage must all be encrypted. You need this protection without installing an in-guest encryption extension and without consuming CPU on the VM, and you need Microsoft Defender for Cloud to report the disk encryption status as Healthy. Which option should you choose?

options.text: Enable encryption at host on the VM and keep the disk encryption set that supplies your customer-managed key
Enable Azure Disk Encryption on the VM with a key encryption key stored in your Key Vault
Enable confidential disk encryption on the VM and keep the disk encryption set for the data disks
Rely on the existing server-side encryption at rest with the customer-managed key and accept the Defender status

explanation:
Encryption at host is the Azure platform layer that adds exactly the coverage the VM is missing: temporary and ephemeral disks are encrypted at rest, disk caches are encrypted, and data travelling between compute and storage is encrypted. It needs no in-guest extension and consumes none of the VM's CPU. Because the managed disks already use a disk encryption set with a customer-managed key, the cache inherits the disk's encryption type (customer-managed key encrypted cache), while temporary and ephemeral disks remain encrypted with platform-managed keys. Defender for Cloud reports the disk encryption status as Healthy for encryption at host, so the current Unhealthy status also clears.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enable Azure Disk Encryption on the VM with a key encryption key stored in your Key Vault: Azure Disk Encryption encrypts OS and data disks from inside the guest operating system (BitLocker on Windows, DM-Crypt on Linux), so it requires the guest agent and it does consume VM CPU — it fails both stated constraints. It is also mutually exclusive with encryption at host: a VM that currently or ever had ADE can never have encryption at host switched on, and ADE cannot be enabled on disks that already use encryption at host.
- Enable confidential disk encryption on the VM and keep the disk encryption set for the data disks: Confidential disk encryption protects the OS disk and, when opted in, the confidential temp disk, with keys bound to the VM's TPM, so it requires a confidential-capable VM size and it does consume CPU. It therefore violates the requirement to protect the workload without taking CPU from the VM.
- Rely on the existing server-side encryption at rest with the customer-managed key and accept the Defender status: Server-side encryption at rest only covers data once it is persisted to the storage clusters; temp disks, disk caches and the compute-to-storage path stay unprotected. That gap is precisely why Defender for Cloud reports SSE-only VMs as Unhealthy, so accepting the current status does not meet the requirement.

For a Key Vault used to encrypt managed disks, soft delete and purge protection are mandatory rather than optional hardening, and a role assignment (Key Vault Administrator, Owner, or Contributor) must be added on the vault so the disk encryption set can use the key. Once those are in place, the VM is deployed with Encryption at host selected on the Disks pane and the customer-managed key chosen under Key management: temporary disks are then encrypted at rest with platform-managed keys, the OS and data disk caches follow the encryption type of the disk itself (customer-managed key here), and data flows encrypted between compute and storage, without any in-guest agent and without consuming VM CPU. As an extra step after the disk encryption set is deployed, open it and select the displayed alert so the vault is granted permissions to the set.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add a Reader role assignment to the Key Vault kv-orders so des-orders can use the key, then deploy vm-orders-05 with Encryption at host selected and the customer-managed key chosen under Key management; the vault's soft delete and purge protection settings do not need to change: Reader is not one of the roles that lets a disk encryption set use the vault's key (Key Vault Administrator, Owner, or Contributor are), and soft delete plus purge protection are mandatory for a vault that encrypts managed disks. The exhibit shows both vault settings disabled and no role assignment, so this path leaves the vault unusable for customer-managed key encryption.
- Recreate des-orders with the encryption type set to Encryption at-rest with a platform-managed key and add a Key Vault Contributor role assignment to kv-orders, then deploy vm-orders-05 with Encryption at host selected: Two problems: the stated goal is customer-managed key protection for the disk caches, and a disk encryption set created with a platform-managed encryption type would not deliver that; and the vault's soft delete and purge protection stay disabled, which is mandatory for a vault used to encrypt managed disks. (Changing the encryption type of an existing disk encryption set is in any case impossible — a brand-new set would be required.)
- Enable soft delete and purge protection on kv-orders, then deploy vm-orders-05 with Encryption at host selected and the customer-managed key chosen under Key management; the disk encryption set already holds the permissions needed for the key once it is deployed: Turning on soft delete and purge protection is necessary but not sufficient: the vault also needs an Azure RBAC role assignment so the disk encryption set can use the key. The disk encryption set does not obtain key access on its own, and the empty role assignment list in the exhibit shows this step is still missing.

prompt: You operate a Linux virtual machine scale set in the East US 2 subscription. Five instances are running today, and the security team requires that every instance — including the five that are already running — has its temporary disk, its disk cache, and the data path between compute and storage encrypted, with no in-guest extension installed. The provider feature registration for the subscription has already been completed. The current state of the scale set is shown below. Which action should you take?

options.text: Enable encryption at host for the scale set, then deallocate and reallocate the five running instances so that they come back with the new model in place.
Enable encryption at host for the scale set and leave the five running instances as they are, because instances created after the change pick it up on their own.
Deallocate and reallocate the five running instances first, and only after that enable encryption at host for the scale set.
Enable encryption at host for the scale set and let the platform recreate the five running instances during the next planned maintenance window.

explanation:
The setting lives in the scale set model, so turning it on affects only instances created from that point onward. Members that already exist must be deallocated and reallocated so the platform recreates them with the new setting. Doing the model change first and then deallocating and reallocating the five running members therefore covers both the current instances and every instance created later; the custom image and the Linux configuration are unaffected by the change.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enable encryption at host for the scale set and leave the five running instances as they are, because instances created after the change pick it up on their own: Instances created after the model change are the only ones that pick up the setting automatically; members that already exist keep running unchanged until they are deallocated and reallocated. Leaving the five running instances in place therefore fails the requirement.
- Deallocate and reallocate the five running instances first, and only after that enable encryption at host for the scale set: The order matters. Instances deallocated and reallocated while the setting is still off come back without it, because the setting takes effect only for instances created after it is enabled on the model. Enabling first and reallocating the existing members afterwards is what covers them.
- Enable encryption at host for the scale set and let the platform recreate the five running instances during the next planned maintenance window: The platform does not recreate existing members on its own when the model changes; there is no automatic maintenance step that rebuilds them. Deallocating and reallocating each existing member is an action you perform yourself.

prompt: You are creating a new Linux virtual machine scale set in the Contoso-Prod subscription. The security team requires that every instance have its temporary disk, its disk cache, and the data path between compute and storage encrypted, and that no in-guest encryption extension be installed. The PowerShell session you are working in is connected to Contoso-Prod, and the subscription capability check you ran returns the result shown below. Which action should you take first?

options.text: Register the EncryptionAtHost provider feature in the Contoso-Prod subscription and wait until it shows as Registered, then deploy the scale set
Register the EncryptionAtHost provider feature in the Contoso-Dev subscription, where it already shows as Registered, and deploy the scale set in that subscription instead
Deploy the scale set in the Contoso-Prod subscription first, register the EncryptionAtHost provider feature afterwards, and deallocate and reallocate the instances so they pick up the change
Install the Azure Disk Encryption extension on each instance of the scale set so the temporary disk and the disk cache are protected

explanation:
The host-side disk encryption capability is enabled per subscription: it must be registered in the subscription that hosts the virtual machine or scale set before the control on the Disks pane can be selected. The check in the exhibit shows the capability is NotRegistered for Contoso-Prod, so the first action is to run Register-AzProviderFeature (or az feature register) for the EncryptionAtHost feature in the Microsoft.Compute namespace against Contoso-Prod and confirm it reads Registered, which can take several minutes. Only after that can the scale set be deployed with the Disks pane option selected, which protects the temporary disk, the disk cache and the encrypted flow between compute and storage with no in-guest extension involved.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Register the EncryptionAtHost provider feature in the Contoso-Dev subscription, where it already shows as Registered, and deploy the scale set in that subscription instead: Registration is scoped to a single subscription. Registering the capability in Contoso-Dev leaves it unavailable in Contoso-Prod, and the workload has to stay in Contoso-Prod, so a scale set deployed there would still miss the required protection for the temporary disk, the cache and the compute-to-storage path.
- Deploy the scale set in the Contoso-Prod subscription first, register the EncryptionAtHost provider feature afterwards, and deallocate and reallocate the instances so they pick up the change: The registration is a deployment prerequisite, not a follow-up step: the control on the Disks pane is unavailable until the registration reads Registered, and registration itself can take several minutes, so a scale set created beforehand is created without the option. Deallocating and reallocating instances applies to members of an existing scale set that was enabled after creation, not to instances that were deployed without the option in the first place.
- Install the Azure Disk Encryption extension on each instance of the scale set so the temporary disk and the disk cache are protected: An in-guest extension is excluded by the stated requirement. Azure Disk Encryption encrypts from inside the guest operating system, consumes VM CPU, and cannot be combined with the host-side option, since a VM or scale set that currently or ever had Azure Disk Encryption can never use the host-side option; Azure Disk Encryption is also scheduled to retire on September 15, 2028.

prompt: You have Windows virtual machine vm-report-07 in the East US 2 subscription of Contoso-Prod. The compliance team has reviewed this virtual machine and decided that the extra protection layer that is switched on at the platform level is no longer required for this workload, so they asked you to turn that option off. The virtual machine has to be running again afterwards with the same disks and all data intact. The configuration collected by the platform team is shown below. Which action should you take?

options.text: Deallocate vm-report-07, then set Encryption at host to No under Additional settings on the Disks pane and save.
Restart vm-report-07, then set Encryption at host to No under Additional settings on the Disks pane and save.
Set Encryption at host to No under Additional settings on the Disks pane and save while vm-report-07 keeps running.
Enable Azure Disk Encryption on vm-report-07, then set Encryption at host to No under Additional settings on the Disks pane and save.

explanation:
The option cannot be changed while the virtual machine is running, so the compute resources have to be released first: deallocate vm-report-07, open the Disks pane, expand Additional settings, set Encryption at host to No and save. The disks, their contents and the guest OS are untouched, and the virtual machine can then be started again.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Restart vm-report-07, then set Encryption at host to No under Additional settings on the Disks pane and save: A restart only bounces the instance: the virtual machine stays running with its compute resources allocated, and the setting is refused while the virtual machine is running. The change is only accepted after the resources have been released (deallocated).
- Set Encryption at host to No under Additional settings on the Disks pane and save while vm-report-07 keeps running: Saving the Disks pane while the virtual machine is still running is rejected, because this option cannot be turned off on a running virtual machine. The virtual machine must be deallocated before the change is made.
- Enable Azure Disk Encryption on vm-report-07, then set Encryption at host to No under Additional settings on the Disks pane and save: Azure Disk Encryption is mutually exclusive with this option: a virtual machine that currently or in the past used Azure Disk Encryption can never have the host-level option switched on, and enabling Azure Disk Encryption also encrypts from inside the guest OS, consuming the virtual machine's CPU. It is not a way to remove the platform-level setting.

You now want to protect managed disks with this key, but every attempt to create the disk encryption set that references key-orders fails. options.text: Turn on purge protection for kv-contoso-prod and leave soft delete enabled.
Turn off soft delete for kv-contoso-prod and turn on purge protection.
Turn off soft delete for kv-contoso-prod and leave purge protection turned off.
Leave kv-contoso-prod exactly as it is now — soft delete enabled and purge protection turned off — and retry the disk encryption set deployment.

explanation:
A key vault that is used to encrypt managed disks must have both soft delete and purge protection turned on; the documentation states that these two settings are mandatory for that use rather than optional hardening. Reviewing the exhibit, everything else is already in order: the key is RSA with a 2048-bit size, the Key Vault Administrator role is assigned at the vault scope, and the planned disk encryption set sits in the same region (East US 2) and subscription as the vault and the future virtual machine. The one gap is purge protection, which is turned off, so the vault does not yet meet the requirements for encrypting managed disks and the disk encryption set that references key-orders cannot be created. Turning purge protection on while keeping soft delete enabled completes the required configuration.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Turn off soft delete for kv-contoso-prod and turn on purge protection: Turning soft delete off removes the retention of deleted keys, and both settings are required for a vault used to encrypt managed disks. Even with purge protection on, the vault would still not qualify, so this change does not unblock the deployment.
- Turn off soft delete for kv-contoso-prod and leave purge protection turned off: This removes both of the settings that a vault must have before its keys can be used to encrypt managed disks, so key-orders would still not be usable by the disk encryption set.
- Leave kv-contoso-prod exactly as it is now — soft delete enabled and purge protection turned off — and retry the disk encryption set deployment: The key type, the role assignment and the region alignment in the exhibit are all correct, so retrying without changing the vault simply reproduces the same failure. prompt: You are deploying a new Linux virtual machine vm-billing-12 in the East US 2 region of the Contoso-Prod subscription. The security policy requires the operating system disk and data disk caches of that virtual machine to be protected with the customer-managed key key-orders, and it also requires the temporary disk and the data path between compute and storage to be encrypted without installing anything inside the guest operating system. The resources prepared for this deployment are listed below. Which action should you take?

options.text: Create a new disk encryption set with the encryption type Encryption at-rest with a customer-managed key that references key-orders in kv-orders, then use it for the virtual machine's disks with Encryption at host enabled.

Update the encryption type of des-orders to Encryption at-rest with a customer-managed key that references key-orders in kv-orders, then use it for the virtual machine's disks with Encryption at host enabled.
Use des-orders for the virtual machine's disks with Encryption at host enabled and select key-orders in kv-orders under Key management.
Create a new disk encryption set with the encryption type Encryption at-rest with a platform-managed key, then use it for the virtual machine's disks with Encryption at host enabled.

explanation:
The encryption type of a disk encryption set is fixed at creation time, so des-orders, which was created with Encryption at-rest with a platform-managed key, can never be changed to use the customer-managed key key-orders. To meet the policy you must create a brand-new disk encryption set whose encryption type is Encryption at-rest with a customer-managed key, reference key-orders in kv-orders, and grant the set access to that key (by accepting the permission prompt on the set). Create the new set in the same region and subscription as the virtual machine and its disks, then select it under Key management on the Disks pane and enable Encryption at host. Because the disks are then protected with the customer-managed key, their caches are encrypted with that same key, and enabling Encryption at host additionally encrypts the temporary disk and the data path between compute and storage without any in-guest extension and without consuming VM CPU.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Update the encryption type of des-orders to Encryption at-rest with a customer-managed key that references key-orders in kv-orders, then use it for the virtual machine's disks with Encryption at host enabled: The encryption type of a disk encryption set is permanent. des-orders was created with Encryption at-rest with a platform-managed key, so it cannot be updated to a customer-managed key; a later change to that type means creating a brand-new disk encryption set.
- Use des-orders for the virtual machine's disks with Encryption at host enabled and select key-orders in kv-orders under Key management: Using des-orders as it is leaves the operating system and data disks on platform-managed encryption, so their caches would not be protected with key-orders. Choosing a key under Key management does not change the encryption type the set was created with.
- Create a new disk encryption set with the encryption type Encryption at-rest with a platform-managed key, then use it for the virtual machine's disks with Encryption at host enabled: A disk encryption set created with Encryption at-rest with a platform-managed key leaves the operating system and data disk caches encrypted with platform-managed keys, so it does not satisfy the requirement to protect those caches with the customer-managed key key-orders.

Encryption at host

Confidential disk encryption

explanation: Each requirement is met by exactly one of the four options. The requirement for a protected temporary disk and an encrypted path between compute and storage with no CPU cost on the virtual machine is satisfied by encryption at host, which adds temp disk protection, cache protection and encrypted traffic between compute and storage while leaving the VM's CPU untouched. The requirement for the operating system and data disks to be protected from inside the guest operating system is satisfied by Azure Disk Encryption, which runs BitLocker on Windows and DM-Crypt on Linux in the guest with keys held in Azure Key Vault. The requirement that the persisted disks stay protected with no option to switch the protection off is satisfied by server-side encryption at rest, which is always active for managed disks once they are written to the storage clusters.

`PS> Get-AzProviderFeature -FeatureName "EncryptionAtHost" -ProviderNamespace "Microsoft.Compute"

FeatureName       ProviderNamespace   State
-----------       -----------------   -----
EncryptionAtHost  Microsoft.Compute    Registered`
prompt: Position 1

options.text: Create the key vault with soft delete and purge protection enabled.
Generate or import the RSA 2048 key inside the vault.
Add the Key Vault Administrator role assignment to the vault in Access control (IAM).
Create the disk encryption set with Encryption at-rest with a customer-managed key, select the vault, key and key version, then select the displayed alert to grant the vault permissions.
Create the virtual machine, turn on Encryption at host and select the customer-managed key under Key management.

The subscription capability check in the exhibit shows the registration is already Registered, so registration takes no position in this sequence.

Server-side encryption with a disk encryption set
Confidential disk encryption with a disk encryption set
Encryption at host with a customer-managed key

Enable purge protection on the key vault
Grant the Key Vault Administrator role at the vault scope
Create the disk encryption set with the encryption type Encryption at-rest with a customer-managed key
Enable auto key rotation on the disk encryption set

explanation: Soft delete and purge protection are the two vault settings that must be enabled before a Key Vault can be used to encrypt managed disks: soft delete keeps a removed key recoverable for the retention period (90 days by default), while purge protection blocks permanent deletion until that retention period has lapses. The disk encryption set needs rights on the vault, which the documentation obtains by assigning the Key Vault Administrator, Owner, or Contributor role at the vault. Because the encryption type of a disk encryption set cannot be changed after it is created, a set that must rely on the organization's own key has to be created with the Encryption at-rest with a customer-managed key type, and automatic rotation of that customer-managed key is enabled on the disk encryption set so the disks follow the newest key version without manual edits.

context:
You have a Linux virtual machine vm-logs-01 in the East US 2 subscription Contoso-Prod. The provider feature registration for the subscription is already complete, and data disk disk-logs is currently attached to the virtual machine. The security team wants this virtual machine to run with encryption at host switched on, so that the temporary disk, the disk cache and the traffic between compute and storage are all protected. The existing content of disk-logs must be preserved, and the virtual machine has to stay available for its workloads. The configuration collected by the platform team is shown below.

What should you do?

`Subscription              : Contoso-Prod
Region                   : East US 2
Virtual machine          : vm-logs-01 (Linux)
Provider feature registration : Registered
Encryption at host       : Disabled
Attached data disk       : disk-logs
Data disk type           : Ultra Disk
Data disk sector size    : 512e
Data disk creation date  : April 20, 2023`
prompt: To meet the security requirement, you should _____.

options.text: Snapshot disk-logs and create a new disk using the snapshot, then attach the new disk to vm-logs-01
Snapshot disk-logs and attach the snapshot to vm-logs-01 as a data disk
Create a new Ultra Disk of the same size in the same resource group and attach it to vm-logs-01
Snapshot disk-logs and create a new disk using the snapshot, but leave disk-logs attached to vm-logs-01

explanation:
Ultra Disks and Premium SSD v2 carry an extra restriction: a disk that uses a 512e sector size must have been created after 5/13/2023, and a disk created earlier has to be snapshotted so that a new disk can be created using that snapshot. disk-logs is an Ultra Disk with a 512e sector size that was created on April 20, 2023, so as it stands it cannot be used on a virtual machine that has encryption at host switched on. Snapshotting disk-logs and creating a new disk using that snapshot produces a disk with a creation date after the cutoff while keeping the existing content, and attaching that new disk instead of the original lets encryption at host be switched on.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Snapshot disk-logs and attach the snapshot to vm-logs-01 as a data disk: A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of a disk and cannot be attached to a virtual machine as a data disk; a managed disk has to be created using the snapshot, and it is that new disk that satisfies the creation-date restriction.
- Create a new Ultra Disk of the same size in the same resource group and attach it to vm-logs-01: A brand-new empty Ultra Disk of the same size throws away the existing content of disk-logs, and the ineligible disk-logs would still be attached to the virtual machine, so the protection requirement would not be met. The existing content is preserved by snapshotting disk-logs and creating the new disk using that snapshot.
- Snapshot disk-logs and create a new disk using the snapshot, but leave disk-logs attached to vm-logs-01: The new disk created using the snapshot is eligible, but leaving disk-logs attached keeps a 512e disk that was created before 5/13/2023 on the virtual machine, and the option cannot be switched on while such a disk is attached. disk-logs has to be detached and replaced by the new disk.

context:
You look after the virtual machines in the Contoso-Prod subscription, and the security team requires that the temporary disk, the disk cache and the traffic between compute and storage of every machine be protected at the platform level, with nothing installed inside the guest operating system. The current state of virtual machine vm-legacy-03 is shown below. Which plan should you follow?

`Subscription: Contoso-Prod
Region: East US 2
Virtual machine: vm-legacy-03 (Linux)
Provider feature registration (Microsoft.Compute / EncryptionAtHost): Registered
Encryption at host on the virtual machine: Not enabled
Azure Disk Encryption on the virtual machine: Enabled in 2021 and never removed
Attached data disk: disk-legacy-03 (Ultra Disk, 512e sector size, created 2022-03-09)
Contents of the attached disk: Billing records that must be preserved`
prompt: The plan consists of _____ and [...].

options.text: build a replacement virtual machine, turn the disk protection option on, and move the workload onto it
turn the disk protection option on for the existing virtual machine and keep the workload there
reinstall the guest operating system on the existing virtual machine and turn the option on for it
add the Azure Disk Encryption extension to the existing virtual machine and leave the workload running

explanation:
Two independent blockers apply to vm-legacy-03. First, the machine has had Azure Disk Encryption enabled since 2021 and never removed, and the conflict with the platform-level disk protection option is permanent: a virtual machine that ever had Azure Disk Encryption enabled can never have encryption at host switched on. The workload therefore has to be moved onto a different virtual machine, where the option can be turned on. Second, the attached disk is an Ultra Disk that uses a 512e sector size and was created on 2022-03-09, which is before the 5/13/2023 cut-off, so it cannot be used as it is once encryption at host is enabled. The documented way forward is to take a snapshot of disk-legacy-03 and create a disk from that snapshot, which keeps the billing records intact and produces a disk that satisfies the rule, and that new disk is then attached to the replacement machine.

Why the other options are wrong:
- turn the disk protection option on for the existing virtual machine and keep the workload there: Switching the option on for the existing virtual machine is not possible: the exclusion applies to any machine that has ever had Azure Disk Encryption enabled, so vm-legacy-03 has to be replaced rather than reconfigured.
- reinstall the guest operating system on the existing virtual machine and turn the option on for it: Reinstalling the guest operating system does not clear the historical Azure Disk Encryption association recorded for the virtual machine, so the option still cannot be enabled for it.
- add the Azure Disk Encryption extension to the existing virtual machine and leave the workload running: Installing the Azure Disk Encryption extension keeps the workload in the category that is excluded from the platform-level option, and it also contradicts the requirement to install nothing inside the guest operating system.

enable Azure Disk Encryption on the virtual machine for the data disk first, then turn on encryption at host for the virtual machine

explanation:
The data disk disk-sql-data is an Ultra disk that uses the 512e sector size and was created on 2023-03-14, so it predates the 2023-05-13 cutoff that applies to 512e disks eligible for this host-level protection (only Ultra Disks and Premium SSD v2 qualify). The documented remedy for such an older disk is to take a copy of it and create a new disk from that copy, which carries the database files over onto a disk that meets the requirement; that new disk is then attached and the host-level option is switched on for the virtual machine. The provider feature registration already reads Registered, so registration is not the blocker here.

Why the other options are wrong:
- turn on encryption at host for the virtual machine while the data disk stays in place, because the platform option covers every disk of the machine: Switching the host-level option on does not pull a disk that fails the disk requirement into scope, and Azure does not migrate or re-encrypt an existing disk in place. disk-sql-data uses the 512e sector size and was created before 2023-05-13, so it has to be replaced by a disk created after that date before the virtual machine can run with this option enabled.
- create a brand-new empty disk of the same SKU and size, attach it in place of the old one, then turn on encryption at host for the virtual machine: A brand-new empty disk carries none of the database files, so the requirement that the existing content survives the change is not met. The supported way to keep the data is to base the new disk on a copy of the existing one.
- enable Azure Disk Encryption on the virtual machine for the data disk first, then turn on encryption at host for the virtual machine: Azure Disk Encryption and encryption at host are mutually exclusive on the same virtual machine: encryption at host can never be enabled on a machine that has Azure Disk Encryption, and Azure Disk Encryption also works from inside the guest operating system, consumes VM CPU and retires on September 15, 2028.

- Update the encryption type of disk encryption set des-1 on the new virtual machine to a customer-managed key: The encryption type of a disk encryption set is permanent, so des-1 cannot be edited to a customer-managed key encryption type; a change of type means creating a brand-new disk encryption set instead.

options.text: soft delete and purge protection
a private endpoint and network access rules
customer-managed key rotation and automatic key expiry
resource locks and diagnostic settings

explanation:
A key vault that is used to encrypt managed disks must have soft delete and purge protection enabled — these are mandatory settings, not optional hardening: soft delete keeps a key for a retention period and purge protection blocks permanent removal of it until that period has lapsed. Separately, the disk encryption set, the virtual machine, its disks and its snapshots must all be deployed in one region and one subscription, while the key vault may live in a different subscription as long as it sits in the same region as the disk encryption set. In the exhibit, the vault is already in East US 2 but in Contoso-Sec, so it can stay where it is, and the disk encryption set, virtual machine, disks and snapshots can all be created in East US 2 in Contoso-Prod.

Why the other options are wrong:
- a private endpoint and network access rules: A private endpoint and network access rules control how the vault is reached over the network. They are not among the settings that must be enabled before a key vault can be used to encrypt managed disks.
- customer-managed key rotation and automatic key expiry: Customer-managed key rotation and automatic key expiry are conveniences for managing the keys themselves. They are not the mandatory vault settings for managed disk encryption.
- resource locks and diagnostic settings: Resource locks and diagnostic settings help with governance and monitoring of the vault, but they are not required before the vault can be used with managed disks.

az vm encryption disable --resource-group rg-app --name vm-app01 --volume-type OS

explanation:
A virtual machine protected by Azure Disk Encryption must have encryption removed before it can be moved to a different subscription, and the documented way to do that is `az vm encryption disable --resource-group <rg> --name <vm> --volume-type all`. The VM here is already stopped and deallocated, so decryption is the remaining preparation step. After it completes, submit one move request that carries the VM and both of its managed disks together, because the disks are dependent resources that must reside in one resource group and travel in the same request to the destination subscription.

Why the other options are wrong:
- az vm encryption disable --resource-group rg-app --name vm-app01 --volume-type OS: Decrypting only the OS volume leaves the data disk encrypted, so the cross-subscription move is still refused. Every volume attached to the VM must be decrypted, which is why the documented command uses `--volume-type all` rather than a single volume type.
- az provider register --namespace Microsoft.Compute --subscription sub-billing-02: Registering Microsoft.Compute in the destination subscription is a general prerequisite for receiving resources, and the provider is already registered there, so this command changes nothing for this scenario. It also does nothing about the encrypted disks, and the move request is rejected while the disks remain encrypted.
- az resource move --destination-group rg-app --destination-subscription-id <sub-billing-02-id> --ids <vm-app01-id> <os-disk-id> <data-disk-id>: This is the move request itself rather than the preparation the move depends on. Running it while Azure Disk Encryption is still enabled fails the cross-subscription move; the disks must be decrypted first. The request shape is otherwise sound, since the VM and both managed disks must be included together in one request.

explanation:
A virtual machine that is protected by Azure Backup cannot be relocated until the restore point collection that belongs to it is deleted; deleting that collection removes only the instant recovery points and leaves the vault data intact. The backup protection on the VM must also be stopped temporarily while the move runs, and the backup configuration is then re-established in the resource group the VM ends up in (rg-erp-prod here).

Why the other options are wrong:
- Delete the recovery services vault rs-vault-01 that holds the backup of vm-erp01, and move the virtual machine into resource group rg-erp-prod afterwards: Deleting the recovery services vault is not required and destroys data. Only the restore point collection has to be removed, and removing it clears just the instant recovery points rather than the vault's stored backup data. The vault can stay where it is and keep serving the VM after the move.
- Re-protect the virtual machine with Azure Backup in resource group rg-erp-prod first, and start the move once that new backup configuration is active: The order is reversed. Backup is reconfigured once the VM already sits in its new resource group; while the VM is still in rg-erp there is no virtual machine in rg-erp-prod that could be protected. Instead, protection on the source VM is stopped temporarily so the move can proceed.
- Delete the restore point collection AzureBackup_vm-erp01_1729384756 and request the move while backup protection stays enabled on the VM: Deleting the collection is necessary but not sufficient on its own. A data-residency rule requires that workload to run in West Europe, so you create an Azure Resource Mover collection for the relocation and start adding the resources to it. options.text: Request an Owner role assignment at the source subscription, so the account can add resources to the collection and Resource Mover can create its system-assigned managed identity and grant it the required access.

Request a Reader role assignment at the source subscription, so the account can add resources to the collection and Resource Mover can create its system-assigned managed identity and grant it the required access.

explanation:
Azure Resource Mover requires the account that adds resources to the move collection to hold Owner on the subscription that contains the source resources. The first time a given source/destination pair is used in a subscription, Resource Mover creates a system-assigned managed identity in that subscription and has to grant it Contributor or User Access Administrator there, and creating that identity and assigning those roles requires ownership of the subscription. In this scenario the account only holds Reader at sub-prod-01 (plus Contributor at the resource group and at the destination subscription), so the add-resources step is rejected with access denied. Requesting an Owner assignment at sub-prod-01 resolves the failure and lets the collection proceed.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Request a Reader role assignment at the source subscription, so the account can add resources to the collection and Resource Mover can create its system-assigned managed identity and grant it the required access: Reader is read-only: it can neither create the managed identity in the source subscription nor assign roles to it, so the add-resources step would still be denied. The documented prerequisite for adding resources is ownership of the subscription that holds them, not read access.
- Request an Owner role assignment at the destination subscription, so the account can add resources to the collection and Resource Mover can create its system-assigned managed identity and grant it the required access: The scope is wrong. Owner at the destination subscription does not cover sub-prod-01, which is where the source resources live and where the managed identity has to be created and given the required access. The prerequisite applies to the subscription containing the resources being moved.
- Request a User Access Administrator role assignment at the destination subscription, so the account can add resources to the collection and Resource Mover can create its system-assigned managed identity and grant it the required access: Two problems: the assignment is made at the destination subscription rather than the subscription holding the source resources, and User Access Administrator is the kind of role Resource Mover grants to the managed identity it creates, not the role the adding account needs in order to create that identity and grant those roles.

explanation:
A virtual machine that uses Azure Disk Encryption cannot be moved to another subscription until encryption is turned off, and the documented way to do that decrypts every volume with `--volume-type all`. Because the destination is a different subscription, the VM and its dependent managed disks must then be relocated together in a single move request, which is exactly what the correct option does.

Leaving vm-fin01's managed disks behind in rg-fin breaks that dependency, so the relocation is rejected.
- Run `az vm encryption disable --resource-group rg-fin --name vm-fin01 --volume-type OS`, then move vm-fin01 and both of its managed disks to sub-fin-02 in one request: This decrypts only the OS volume. The published workaround for a cross-subscription relocation turns off encryption for all volumes (`--volume-type all`), so the encrypted data volumes would still prevent the VM from being moved.

explanation:
The request listed only the virtual machine and its managed OS disk. The network interface that is attached to vm-web03 was neither part of the request nor already present in rg-web-prod, which is what the MissingMoveDependentResources error reports. You have virtual machine vm-billing01 with Azure Disk Encryption turned on for its disks, and it is running in resource group rg-billing of subscription sub-fin-01. Finance wants this workload relocated into resource group rg-billing-prod, which sits in the same subscription, but every relocation attempt is refused by Azure. The operations team also reports that, once the relocation is done, the monitoring queries and automation templates that address the virtual machine by its resource ID stop returning data. Which action should you take, and what should you do about those queries and templates?

`Virtual machine          : vm-billing01
Current resource group   : rg-billing
Target resource group    : rg-billing-prod
Target subscription      : sub-fin-01 (same subscription)
Azure Disk Encryption    : Enabled
Power state              : Running
`
prompt: The correct approach is to _____, and then to [...].

options.text: Deallocate the virtual machine and then move it to the destination resource group.
Disable Azure Disk Encryption on the virtual machine and then move it to the destination resource group.
Move the virtual machine to the destination resource group and leave it running.
Delete the virtual machine and redeploy it from its managed disks in the destination resource group.

explanation:
A virtual machine that uses Azure Disk Encryption can be moved to another resource group only while it is in a deallocated state, so the first step is to stop the machine and then run the move into rg-billing-prod inside the same subscription; encryption does not have to be turned off for a move that stays within one subscription. Moving the workload rewrites its resource ID, so every monitoring query and automation template that references the old ID has to be pointed at the destination scope.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Disable Azure Disk Encryption on the virtual machine and then move it to the destination resource group: Turning encryption off is only required when the virtual machine is moved to a different subscription. Here the target group is in sub-fin-01 as well, and because the machine is still running the relocation would keep being refused.
- Move the virtual machine to the destination resource group and leave it running: The workload must be in a deallocated state before it can be moved to another resource group, so a move performed while the machine is running is refused.
- Delete the virtual machine and redeploy it from its managed disks in the destination resource group: Deleting and recreating the workload is not needed for a relocation inside a single subscription and would destroy the existing virtual machine and its disks; that pattern is the workaround for Marketplace-plan virtual machines that cannot be moved across subscriptions.

options.text: submit the move in several batches, each limited to no more than 800 resources, keeping each virtual machine with the resources it depends on
submit the move again as a single request after registering the Microsoft.Compute resource provider for virtual machines in the target subscription
submit the move again as a single request after raising the virtual machine quota in the target subscription so the incoming resources fit
submit a move of resource group rg-fleet itself into the target subscription so the virtual machines and their resources travel with the group

explanation:
A single move operation can carry at most 800 resources, and this request lists 1,240 virtual machines, so Resource Manager returns an error immediately and nothing is relocated. The work must therefore be separated into several smaller move operations, each with no more than 800 resources. Because this move crosses a subscription boundary, a virtual machine and the resources it depends on, such as its managed disks and network interface, must be located in the same resource group and travel together in the same request, so each batch should carry a complete workload rather than splitting a machine from its dependencies. Keep batches moderate in size, since even a move with fewer than 800 resources can fail by timing out. The other prerequisites are already satisfied here: both subscriptions are in the same tenant, Microsoft.Compute is registered in the target subscription, the target quota is sufficient, and neither group carries a read-only lock.

Why the other options are wrong:
- submit the move again as a single request after registering the Microsoft.Compute resource provider for virtual machines in the target subscription: Registering the Microsoft.Compute resource provider matters only when the target subscription has never hosted that resource type, and the exhibit shows the registration is already in place. The request was refused because it exceeded what one move operation can carry, so registering the provider and resubmitting the same oversized request is rejected again.
- submit the move again as a single request after raising the virtual machine quota in the target subscription so the incoming resources fit: Destination subscription quota must cover the incoming resources, but the quota here is already sufficient. Raising the quota does not resolve a rejection caused by the number of resources in a single request; the request has to be divided into smaller operations.
- submit a move of resource group rg-fleet itself into the target subscription so the virtual machines and their resources travel with the group: A resource group cannot be moved to another subscription. Its resources have to be moved into a resource group in the target subscription instead, and group-level settings such as tags, role assignments, and policies do not travel and must be re-created there.

prompt: The relocation succeeds once you _____, and the identity that runs the command must have [...].

options.text: Register the Microsoft.Network namespace in the destination subscription, wait for it to complete, then rerun the move.
Register the Microsoft.Network namespace in the source subscription, wait for it to complete, then rerun the move.
Register the Microsoft.Compute namespace in the destination subscription, wait for it to complete, then rerun the move.
Leave the network interface out of the request so the destination does not need the networking namespace, then rerun the move.

explanation:
The failure reported by the service is that the subscription receiving the resources is not registered for the Microsoft.Network resource type, so the move is rejected before anything relocates. The provider namespace must be registered in the destination subscription (for example with az provider register --namespace Microsoft.Network, then confirm the registration has completed) and the move retried; the source subscription already hosts the running workload, so its registration is in place. Independently of the registration, the identity that submits the move needs Microsoft.Resources/subscriptions/resourceGroups/moveResources/action on the source resource group and Microsoft.Resources/subscriptions/resourceGroups/write on the destination resource group.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Register the Microsoft.Network namespace in the source subscription, wait for it to complete, then rerun the move: This changes nothing: the source subscription already runs the virtual machine, so the provider is available there. The registration that is missing is in the subscription that will receive the resources, so registering it in the source leaves the move failing with the same error.
- Register the Microsoft.Compute namespace in the destination subscription, wait for it to complete, then rerun the move: The service message names Microsoft.Network as the namespace that is not registered, and the network interface travels with the virtual machine, so the destination must have the networking provider available. Registering Microsoft.Compute does not satisfy the check the service performs.
- Leave the network interface out of the request so the destination does not need the networking namespace, then rerun the move: Omitting a dependent does not remove the requirement, because the network interface and its settings are moved along with the virtual machine; a request that leaves out a required dependent fails with a missing-dependent error instead. The destination still needs the networking provider registered.
