The platform team wants the workload relocated into resource group rg-hub-new of the same subscription, which was created for a new deployment standard, but every relocation attempt is rejected. Tonight's change window requires the workload to keep answering customer requests while it is relocated. Which action should you take to let the relocation succeed, and what happens to the workload while it runs?

- Setting: Virtual machine; Value: vm-hub01 (running, East US)
- Setting: Current resource group; Value: rg-hub
- Setting: Group the workload must end up in; Value: rg-hub-new
- Setting: Lock on rg-hub-new; Value: Read-only
- Setting: Lock on rg-hub; Value: None

prompt: To let the relocation succeed you should _____, and while it runs the workload [...].

options.text: Remove the read-only lock from the destination resource group and resubmit the move.
Remove the read-only lock from the source resource group and resubmit the move.
Remove the read-only lock from the subscription that owns both groups and resubmit the move.
Wait for the four-hour limit to elapse so that Azure releases the group locks automatically, then resubmit the move.

explanation:
The rejection is caused by the read-only lock on rg-hub-new, the group the workload must end up in. Azure cannot move resources while a read-only lock exists on the source resource group, the destination resource group, or the subscription, so the read-only lock on rg-hub-new has to be removed and the move resubmitted; the exhibit shows no lock on rg-hub or on sub-prod-01. Once the relocation runs, both the source and the destination resource group are locked, which prevents creating, deleting or updating resources in them, including changing the virtual machine's size, yet the running machine continues to operate normally and the services that rely on it experience no downtime.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Remove the read-only lock from the source resource group and resubmit the move: rg-hub carries no lock, so removing one there changes nothing; the lock that stops the relocation is the read-only lock on rg-hub-new, the group the workload must end up in.
- Remove the read-only lock from the subscription that owns both groups and resubmit the move: There is no read-only lock on sub-prod-01, and a lock has to be removed at the scope where it was applied; the exhibit places the lock on rg-hub-new.
- Wait for the four-hour limit to elapse so that Azure releases the group locks automatically, then resubmit the move: The four-hour allowance and the automatic release govern the lock that the move operation itself places on the two groups. A read-only lock that you applied is not removed for you, and the request is refused before the move even starts, so waiting changes nothing.

prompt: Your conclusion about the request is that _____, and your next step is to [...].

options.text: the request is still running in the background and will keep rg-core and rg-core-new locked until every resource has been relocated
the service stopped the operation and released the locks on rg-core and rg-core-new; the resources that relocated are in rg-core-new and the resources that failed are in rg-core
the service rolled the operation back entirely, so every resource in the request is again in rg-core and none of them are in rg-core-new
the service released the locks on rg-core and rg-core-new after deleting the resources that failed, so rg-core now holds only the resources that relocated

explanation:
A single move can run for up to four hours, and the source and destination resource groups stay locked for that whole time. When that limit is reached, Resource Manager ends the operation and unlocks both groups: the resources that completed the move are in the destination group (rg-core-new), while the resources that hit an error stay in the source group (rg-core). Nothing is rolled back and nothing is deleted, so the remaining resources are still intact and can be relocated with a new move request that names them together with the resources they need.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the request is still running in the background and will keep rg-core and rg-core-new locked until every resource has been relocated: The request does not keep running in the background: four hours is the longest a single move may take, and at that point the service ends the operation and releases the locks on both groups, so there is nothing left to wait for.
- the service rolled the operation back entirely, so every resource in the request is again in rg-core and none of them are in rg-core-new: There is no automatic rollback when the time limit is reached. The service simply unlocks both groups and leaves the completed moves in place in the destination, so the resources that already relocated stay in rg-core-new.
- the service released the locks on rg-core and rg-core-new after deleting the resources that failed, so rg-core now holds only the resources that relocated: Ending a move never deletes resources. The ones that hit an error remain in the source group and stay usable, so the workload is not lost and the copy in the source must not be destroyed.

The virtual machine vm-a07 also runs a custom script extension, vm-a07/ConfigureMonitoring. The platform team wants this workload relocated into resource group rg-a07-new of the same subscription, with the extension still in place afterwards. You submit a move request that lists three entries, and the service refuses the request. Which entries should the request contain?

- Item: Source resource group; Value: rg-a07 (subscription sub-prod-01)
- Item: Target resource group; Value: rg-a07-new (subscription sub-prod-01)
- Item: Virtual machines; Value: vm-a07, vm-a08

options.text: the virtual machines vm-a07 and vm-a08 and the extension vm-a07/ConfigureMonitoring, but no availability set entry
the availability set as-a07 and the virtual machines vm-a07 and vm-a08, and no extension entry
the availability set as-a07 and the extension entry vm-a07/ConfigureMonitoring
only the virtual machine vm-a07, after removing it from the availability set as-a07 and submitting it on its own

explanation:
Two rules decide the content of the request. First, a virtual machine that belongs to an availability set cannot be moved on its own, so the availability set as-a07 and both of its virtual machines, vm-a07 and vm-a08, must travel in the same request. Second, a move request lists top-level resources only: Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines carries Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/extensions along with it, and a child resource such as vm-a07/ConfigureMonitoring cannot be requested on its own. The extension therefore stays out of the request and is relocated along with vm-a07 automatically, so the workload keeps its custom script extension in the target resource group.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the virtual machines vm-a07 and vm-a08 and the extension vm-a07/ConfigureMonitoring, but no availability set entry: This is the request that was already refused: it lists the child extension resource as a separate entry, which is not allowed, and it leaves the availability set behind, so the two virtual machines would still be moved individually out of an availability set.
- the availability set as-a07 and the extension entry vm-a07/ConfigureMonitoring: Listing the availability set together with the extension entry still requests the child resource separately, which the service rejects, and it omits the two virtual machines that actually have to be relocated.
- only the virtual machine vm-a07, after removing it from the availability set as-a07 and submitting it on its own: A virtual machine that is part of an availability set cannot be moved individually, removing it from the set is not a supported way to work around that, and the request also leaves vm-a08 and the extension behind.

options.text: Snapshot app-vm-01, create a managed disk from the snapshot, and deploy a VM on the target size using the disk.
Deallocate app-vm-01, resize it to the target size, and start it again.
Resize the running VM in the portal, since the reboot that follows handles the local temp disk difference.
Attach an extra Premium_LRS managed disk to app-vm-01 and resize the VM from its current size to the target size.

explanation:
A Windows VM can only be resized between sizes that share the same local temp disk setup: local temp disk to local temp disk, or no local temp disk to no local temp disk. app-vm-01 runs Standard_E4_v3, which has no local temp disk, while the target Standard_D8s_v5 has one, so a direct resize is refused no matter the power state. The supported path is to snapshot the VM, create a managed disk from that snapshot, and deploy the VM on the target size using the disk, then attach the Premium_LRS data disks to it.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Deallocate app-vm-01, resize it to the target size, and start it again: The deallocate-resize-start sequence only works when the temp disk situation is unchanged, or when the VM runs Linux. Linux VMs can be resized across the local temp disk boundary, but a Windows VM is limited to like-for-like changes, so the resize request would be rejected.
- Resize the running VM in the portal, since the reboot that follows handles the local temp disk difference: A reboot does not soften the like-for-like restriction for Windows VMs. Because the local temp disk setup differs between the current and target sizes, the size change is blocked while the VM is running and the machine keeps its present capacity.
- Attach an extra Premium_LRS managed disk to app-vm-01 and resize the VM from its current size to the target size: Attaching an additional managed data disk does not change whether the target size provides a local temp disk, and data disks are attached separately from the size choice. The mismatch therefore still blocks the resize.

options.text: Deallocate the VM, look at the size list again, then apply the new size and start it
Apply the new size with Update-AzVM while the VM is running and let the platform reboot it
Select Standard_D8s_v3, the only listed entry with 8 vCPUs, and apply it without stopping the VM
Create a replacement VM from a snapshot of the current OS disk and delete the original after cutover

explanation:
The configuration you need (8 vCPUs with 64 GiB of RAM, for example a memory-optimized size such as Standard_E8s_v3) is not among the reported targets: the only 8-vCPU entry listed, Standard_D8s_v3, offers just 32 GiB of RAM. The list produced by Get-AzVMSize contains only the sizes the VM's own hardware cluster allows, and a size that is missing while the machine runs can reappear once the VM is stopped, because a stopped machine exposes more choices. The documented order is therefore to deallocate the VM, review the size list again, apply the new size, and start it. Because deallocation releases any dynamic IP address while the OS and data disks stay untouched, plan for that and for the restart that any size change causes.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Apply the new size with Update-AzVM while the VM is running and let the platform reboot it: Changing the SKU in place while the VM is running only succeeds for a target the cluster already offers, and the size you need is missing from that list. If such a request cannot be allocated, the VM model still displays the requested size while the machine keeps running on its previous one, so GET calls would report a size the VM is not actually using. A running-VM resize also forces a restart, so it is a disruptive operation for stateful workloads.
- Select Standard_D8s_v3, the only listed entry with 8 vCPUs, and apply it without stopping the VM: Standard_D8s_v3 is indeed the only listed entry with 8 vCPUs, but it provides only 32 GiB of RAM and therefore misses the 64 GiB requirement. The list shown for a powered-on VM is itself restricted, so its contents do not prove that a suitable size does not exist.
- Create a replacement VM from a snapshot of the current OS disk and delete the original after cutover: Rebuilding from a snapshot is the work-around only for changes that cannot be done in place, such as moving a Windows VM from a size with a local temp disk to one without a local temp disk. Here the new size can be applied to the existing VM after deallocation, and copying the disk neither widens the set of sizes the cluster offers nor keeps the original VM as the target of the change.

options.text: Standard_E16s_v3
Standard_E16_v3
Standard_D16s_v3
Standard_B2ms

explanation:
The E family is the memory-optimized line, which suits big-data pipelines and workloads that keep large datasets in RAM. Its `s` variant is the one that supports Premium Storage, so `Standard_E16s_v3` satisfies both the in-memory workload and the requirement to keep the Premium_LRS disks.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Standard_E16_v3: This is the memory-focused family, but without the `s` variant the size cannot be used with Premium Storage, so it conflicts with the Premium_LRS disks; a Premium Storage workload needs the `s` version (for example `Standard_E4s_v3` instead of `Standard_E4_v3`).
- Standard_D16s_v3: The D line is general purpose: it spreads capacity between processor and memory and is aimed at development, test, compact databases and lightly loaded workloads rather than a RAM-heavy big-data pipeline.
- Standard_B2ms: The B line is burstable: it meters CPU with credits and is throttled back to base performance once credits are depleted, so it does not suit a sustained, memory-heavy pipeline.

You need the whole set to end up on Standard_E8s_v3, which provides 8 vCPUs and 64 GiB of RAM per instance, and all three instances must be serving traffic again once the work is finished. Which sequence should you use?

options.text: Deallocate the virtual machines in the availability set, set the required size on each member, and power the set back on.
Deallocate the virtual machines in the availability set, set the required size on one member only, and power the set back on.
Resize the virtual machines in the availability set one at a time while they keep running, and let the platform reboot each member after the change.
Deallocate the virtual machines in the availability set, move each member to a size the platform reports today, and power the set back on.

explanation:
Two facts drive the sequence. First, the target size is absent from the list the platform reports for a running instance; a size that is not offered for a powered-on VM has to be applied while the VM is deallocated, so each member must be stopped before the change. Second, an availability set requires every member to move to the new size, because resizing only one member leaves the remaining members on their previous size. The documented procedure is therefore to deallocate every VM in the set, apply the new size to each of them, and then start them all again — which is the correct option.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Deallocate the virtual machines in the availability set, set the required size on one member only, and power the set back on: Changing only one member leaves sql-b and sql-c on Standard_D2s_v5, so the set ends up with mixed sizes. Availability sets require every member to be moved to the new size, because a single resized member can leave the others on their previous size.
- Resize the virtual machines in the availability set one at a time while they keep running, and let the platform reboot each member after the change: Resizing a running virtual machine reboots it, so the instances would restart one after another, and doing it member by member leaves the set with mixed sizes. In addition, the target size is not offered for an instance that stays powered on, so it cannot be selected in this state.
- Deallocate the virtual machines in the availability set, move each member to a size the platform reports today, and power the set back on: The sizes the platform reports today top out at Standard_D8s_v5 with 8 vCPUs but 32 GiB of RAM, and Standard_E2s_v3 with only 2 vCPUs. None of them delivers the requested 8 vCPUs with 64 GiB of RAM, so this sequence cannot produce the target configuration.

prompt: You have a Windows virtual machine named fin-app-01 in resource group rg-fin that runs an in-house finance application. The team wants the application to run on the target size listed below, because that size adds local temp storage the application can use for caching. You need the application back on the target size with its operating system configuration and both attached data disks intact, and the machine serving traffic once the work is finished. Which sequence should you use?

options.text: Deallocate the Windows virtual machine so that the target size can be applied, resize it in place, and start it again.
Snapshot the Windows virtual machine, create a disk from that snapshot, and create a new virtual machine from that disk on the target size.
Resize the running Windows virtual machine from the current size to the target size; Azure restarts the instance and the attached data disks are kept.
Snapshot the data disks, create a new virtual machine on the target size with those disks attached, and then deallocate the original Windows virtual machine.

explanation:
The guest is Windows, and the current size (Standard_D4s_v5) has no local temp storage while the target size (Standard_D8ds_v5) has some, so this move crosses the local temp disk boundary. Windows virtual machines are restricted to like-for-like size changes: local temp disk to local temp disk, or no local temp disk to no local temp disk. The documented way to move a Windows VM that has no local temp disk onto a size that has one is to snapshot the VM, create a disk from that snapshot, and then create the new VM from that disk. That path carries the operating system configuration onto the target size and lets the existing data disks stay with the workload, and the new machine can then be started so the application serves traffic again.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Deallocate the Windows virtual machine so that the target size can be applied, resize it in place, and start it again: Powering the machine off first only addresses whether the target size is offered by the current hardware cluster; it does not remove the Windows like-for-like restriction, so an in-place resize from a size with no local temp disk to a size that has one is not the supported path for a Windows guest.
- Resize the running Windows virtual machine from the current size to the target size; Azure restarts the instance and the attached data disks are kept: Resizing a running machine is allowed in general and does reboot it, but the Windows restriction still blocks this particular move because the current size has no local temp storage and the target size has it; the fact that the data disks remain attached does not make the resize valid.
- Snapshot the data disks, create a new virtual machine on the target size with those disks attached, and then deallocate the original Windows virtual machine: Copying only the data disks carries the application data but not the operating system state and configuration of fin-app-01, so the replacement machine would not come back with its operating system configuration intact. The documented path captures the virtual machine itself, creates a disk from that snapshot, and creates the new virtual machine from that disk.

prompt: You have a Linux virtual machine named etl-01 in resource group rg-data that runs a nightly extract-transform-load job. Since the job was moved onto this machine, its runtime has tripled, and the slowdown shows up in bursts partway through each run rather than at one fixed point. You need the job to hold full processor speed for its entire six-hour window, keep the same balance of processor and memory it has today instead of buying capacity the job never uses, and keep the machine's managed disks on Premium_LRS. Which size should you select?

options.text: Standard_D2s_v5
Standard_B4ms
Standard_D2_v5
Standard_E2s_v5

explanation:
Standard_D2s_v5 is the only choice that meets all three requirements. It belongs to the D family, a general-purpose line that spreads capacity evenly between processor and memory, so it preserves the balanced profile the job has today instead of skewing it toward cores or toward RAM. It is not credit-metered, so the six-hour run keeps full processor speed for its entire window rather than being capped back to a base rate after an accumulated allowance is spent. Finally, the trailing s in the size string is what enables Premium Storage, so the Premium_LRS managed disks continue to work on it.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Standard_B4ms: Standard_B4ms stays in the B family, the only line that meters processor use with credits: it accumulates credits below a base threshold, spends them when the workload runs above it, and once they are exhausted it is limited back to base performance until they rebuild. That is the same bursty pattern already causing the slowdown, so the job would still lose speed partway through the run.
- Standard_D2_v5: Standard_D2_v5 sits in the same family and keeps the same processor-to-memory balance, but its size string lacks the s that enables Premium Storage, so the machine's Premium_LRS managed disks cannot keep running on it. The size string itself decides storage support, so this name is not interchangeable with the s variant.
- Standard_E2s_v5: Standard_E2s_v5 comes from the E family, which favors memory over cores. It would add memory capacity the workload never consumes and move the machine away from the even processor-to-memory balance the job has today, so it does not match the requirement of not buying capacity that goes unused.

Your team supports a group of Azure virtual machines, and colleagues have logged five resize outcomes that nobody can explain. The table below lists each machine with what was observed during the change. You need to pair every machine with the sizing constraint that accounts for its result, so that future size changes for this group can be planned correctly. Which constraint should you drag onto each machine?

- Machine: vm-report-01; What the team observed: Its managed disks must stay on Premium_LRS. After the machine was moved to Standard_E8_v3 the disks could no longer be used with Premium_LRS, and the same move to Standard_E8s_v3 worked without complaint.
- Machine: win-fin-07; What the team observed: This Windows machine has no local temp disk, and its resize to a target size that includes a local temp disk was refused.
- Machine: web-08; What the team observed: This Linux machine was moved from a size that has a local temp disk to one that has none, and later moved back to a size that has one, with no extra steps in between.
- Machine: burst-09; What the team observed: The machine is idle most of the day and runs short bursts of work. After a few minutes at full speed it fell back to base processor performance and stayed there, then returned to full speed after a period of idle time.
- Machine: calc-10; What the team observed: Its resize to the NVMe-capable size that the machine's own cluster offered was refused.
prompt: vm-report-01

options.text: Windows virtual machines can only be resized between sizes that both have a local temp disk or both lack one.
Linux virtual machines can be resized across the local temp disk boundary, from a size that has one to a size that does not and back again.
Disk tier support is decided by the size name: only the variant whose name carries the s suffix can host Premium Storage disks.
Burstable sizes meter processor time with credits, so a machine that has spent its credits is throttled back to base performance until they rebuild.
A size that is SCSI-based cannot be resized to a size that offers remote NVMe storage.

explanation: Each machine's outcome is produced by a distinct sizing rule: the size name alone decides whether Premium Storage disks can be attached (vm-report-01), Windows only allows like-for-like moves on local temp disk (win-fin-07), Linux can cross that boundary freely (web-08), the credit-metered burstable family throttles back to base performance after its credits are spent and recovers while they rebuild (burst-09), and a SCSI-based size cannot be resized to a remote NVMe-enabled size (calc-10). Pairing each machine with the rule that explains it lets the team predict which changes are possible before attempting them.

You are deploying a new Linux virtual machine, vm-api-01, for an internal API service in resource group rg-app. The service has to run on ARM-based silicon rather than on the processors your existing fleet uses, the machine must come from the fifth generation of the D line, and its managed disks must stay on Premium_LRS. The deployment brief below lists what the new machine needs, and you have four candidate size names to choose from, all giving the same vCPU and memory count. Which size should you select?

`Deployment brief - vm-api-01
----------------------------------------
Operating system      : Linux
Processor             : ARM-based (Microsoft Cobalt or Ampere Altra)
Family and generation : D line, fifth generation
Processor capacity    : 2 vCPUs, 8 GiB memory
Managed disk tier     : Premium_LRS
Candidate size names  : four names, all with the same vCPU and memory count`
prompt: The new Linux virtual machine should be created on _____.

options.text: Standard_D2ps_v5
Standard_D2as_v5
Standard_D2s_v5
Standard_D2_v5

explanation:
The name Standard_D2ps_v5 decodes as family D, 2 vCPUs, the letter p for an ARM-based CPU (Microsoft Cobalt or Ampere Altra), the letter s for Premium Storage support, and v5 for the fifth generation of the series, so it satisfies both the ARM processor requirement and the Premium_LRS disk requirement.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Standard_D2as_v5: The letter a in this name marks an AMD CPU, so the machine would run on AMD silicon rather than on the ARM-based processor the service requires.
- Standard_D2s_v5: This name has no processor letter before the s, so it runs on Intel x86-64 silicon and misses the ARM-based processor requirement.
- Standard_D2_v5: This name carries neither a processor letter nor the s feature letter, so it runs on Intel x86-64 and, without the s variant, it cannot provide Premium Storage support for the managed disks.

You have a Linux virtual machine named warehouse-01 in resource group rg-data that runs a data warehouse over large attached disks. The queries are I/O-bound, so the team wants more disk throughput rather than extra processor headroom. You need to move the machine onto a size whose main strength is fast access to its attached disks, while its managed disks stay on Premium_LRS. The size you have in mind is not offered by the VM's current hardware cluster, so the machine has to be deallocated before the change, and customers reach the service through a dynamic public IP address today. You need to pick the size and to know what the deallocation does to the disks and the address. Which size should you select, and what should you expect?

- Property: Operating system; Value: Linux
- Property: Managed disk tier; Value: Premium_LRS
- Property: Public IP address; Value: Dynamic
- Property: Target size offered by the current hardware cluster; Value: No
prompt: Select _____ for warehouse-01, and expect that [...].

options.text: Standard_L8s_v2
Standard_L8_v2
Standard_E8s_v3
Standard_D8s_v5

explanation:
Standard_L8s_v2 belongs to the L line, which is aimed at storage-heavy work by pairing large attached disks with high local disk throughput and I/O, so it matches the warehouse's I/O-bound demand. The s version of a size is the one that can use Premium Storage, so this choice keeps the managed disks on Premium_LRS. When a VM is deallocated, a dynamic IP address attached to it is released, while the OS disk and the data disks stay untouched. Deallocating first is also what makes a target size that the running machine's hardware cluster did not offer available for the change.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Standard_L8_v2: Standard_L8_v2 is not the s version of the size, and the s version is the one that can use Premium Storage, so this choice fails the Premium_LRS requirement for the managed disks.
- Standard_E8s_v3: Standard_E8s_v3 comes from the E line, which favors memory over cores for database servers, caching and analytics; it does not deliver the local-disk throughput focus that the I/O-bound warehouse needs.
- Standard_D8s_v5: Standard_D8s_v5 comes from the general-purpose D line, which trades quicker processors and more memory per core for balanced line-of-business, web and batch work rather than optimizing local disk I/O.

- Brief item: Data classification; Requirement: Personal health data
- Brief item: Isolation; Requirement: Records must stay unreadable outside the processor's own protected area while the service is working on them; protection implemented only inside the guest operating system was rejected by the audit

- Brief item: Region; Requirement: East US
prompt: The size that satisfies the brief is _____.

options.text: Standard_DC2ads_v5
Standard_D2ads_v5
Standard_E2ads_v5
Standard_DC2s_v3

explanation:
Standard_DC2ads_v5 satisfies all three conditions in the brief. The DC family is the one that adds confidential computing, where trusted execution environments run in hardware, which is what the audit demanded: the platform hardware itself keeps the records isolated while they are being processed. The 'a' character in the name marks AMD processors, and the 's' in the size marks the Premium Storage variant, so the managed disks can use Premium_LRS. The other three candidates each miss one condition.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Standard_D2ads_v5: Standard_D2ads_v5 covers the AMD processor and Premium_LRS requirements, but the D line is the general-purpose family and offers no hardware-level isolation of the data being processed, so it fails the audit condition.
- Standard_E2ads_v5: Standard_E2ads_v5 is the memory-optimized line, which suits large in-memory workloads but does not add the hardware isolation the audit required (only the EC subfamily layers that on top of E), so it fails.
- Standard_DC2s_v3: Standard_DC2s_v3 provides the hardware isolation and the Premium Storage variant, but its name carries no vendor letter, and a missing vendor letter means Intel x86-64 processors, so it fails the AMD requirement.

You have a Linux virtual machine named eda-01 in resource group rg-chip that runs a licensed electronic design automation simulation suite for a semiconductor design team. Every project is dominated by a single compilation thread, and the toolchain repeatedly stalls while waiting for data it expects to find close to the processor, which has pushed several builds past the deadline their licences allow. The team wants eda-01 moved onto a configuration that suits that kind of job, and it also wants to see exactly which configurations the platform currently offers for this machine before anything is changed. Which size family should you choose, and which PowerShell command should you run to list the configurations offered for eda-01?

- Property: Operating system; Value: Linux
- Property: Current size; Value: Standard_D16s_v5
- Property: Workload; Value: Licensed electronic design automation simulation
- Property: Concurrency per job; Value: One compilation thread
- Property: Observed symptom; Value: Builds stall on memory fetches and overrun the licensed runtime window
prompt: The size family that matches the workload is _____, and the PowerShell command that reports the configurations offered for this machine is [...].

options.text: FX-series
F-series
D-series
M-series

explanation:
FX is the family that pairs fast single-core speed with a large per-core cache on Intel Ice Lake silicon, and it is the family recommended for electronic design automation work, so it fits a licensed simulation suite whose jobs are dominated by one compilation thread that stalls on memory fetches. F-series only offers a processor-heavy balance for medium-load web servers, network appliances, batch queues, application servers, analytics and gaming, D-series is the general-purpose line for line-of-business applications, relational databases, web and application tiers, queued batch work and game servers, and M-series is the ultra memory-optimized family for extreme in-memory, data warehousing and HPC needs rather than cache-sensitive single-thread speed. For the second part, Get-AzVMSize called with the VM's resource group and name lists the sizes offered by the hardware cluster where that VM is hosted, so it returns exactly the configurations that are valid targets for eda-01.

Why the other options are wrong:
- F-series: F-series keeps a processor-heavy balance suited to medium-load web servers, network appliances, batch queues, application servers, analytics and gaming; it does not deliver the high single-core speed and large per-core cache that a cache-bound electronic design automation toolchain needs.
- D-series: D-series is the general-purpose line for line-of-business applications, relational databases, busy web and application tiers, queued batch work and game servers, so it is not the family targeted at single-threaded, cache-sensitive simulation jobs.
- M-series: M-series is the ultra memory-optimized family for enormous in-memory databases, data warehousing, HPC, heavy SQL Server and similar workloads; the shortfall on eda-01 is cache-sensitive single-thread performance rather than a lack of RAM capacity.

You are helping an aerospace research group in resource group rg-sim prepare its next three-year capacity commitment. The group runs computational fluid dynamics over large meshes and high-resolution weather modelling on the family described in the exhibit, and the exhibit also lists the sales position for that family. You need a family that is still purchasable on a three-year reserved plan, that remains available for the whole commitment, and that matches the simulations the group runs. You also want to know what happens to machines that are still on the old family once its end date passes. Which family should you select, and what should you expect?

- Item: Family in use today; Detail: HC-series - Intel Xeon Scalable processors, aimed at high-density compute for finite element analysis, molecular dynamics and computational chemistry
- Item: Reserved capacity sales; Detail: Sales of 1-year and 3-year reserved instances for this family ended on 2 April 2026
- Item: End of life; Detail: Instances of this family are retired on 31 May 2027
- Item: Simulations run by the group; Detail: Computational fluid dynamics over large meshes and high-resolution weather modelling
prompt: The new virtual machines should use the _____ family, and the team should plan for the fact that once the end date in the exhibit passes, [...].

options.text: HBv5-series
HC-series
HX-series
NP-series

explanation:
The family the group runs on today can no longer be bought on a one-year or three-year reserved plan, because those sales ended on 2 April 2026, and it is retired on 31 May 2027, so it cannot anchor the new three-year commitment. Of the candidates, HBv5-series is the HPC family built on AMD EPYC processors with high memory bandwidth, aimed at computational fluid dynamics, finite element analysis, weather modelling, seismic processing and genomics, and it is still on sale, so it both matches the simulations the group runs and can carry the reserved term. Azure points new HPC deployments at the HBv5 or HX lines in place of the retiring family, and HX is aimed at large-memory electronic design automation work rather than fluid dynamics and weather. Once 31 May 2027 passes, instances still on the retiring family are deallocated, stop running and no longer have SLA or support, so the replacement has to be in place before that date.

Why the other options are wrong:
- HC-series: One-year and three-year reserved instance sales for this family ended on 2 April 2026, and the family is retired on 31 May 2027, so it cannot anchor a new three-year commitment; its high-density compute focus also serves finite element analysis, molecular dynamics and computational chemistry rather than the fluid dynamics and weather modelling in this scenario.
- HX-series: This family supplies large memory capacity for electronic design automation workloads. It is still on sale, but the simulations described here sit in the high-memory-bandwidth HB family, not in the large-memory EDA line.
- NP-series: This is the FPGA-accelerated family, pairing AMD Xilinx Alveo U250 FPGA boards with Intel Xeon 8171M CPUs for inference, video transcoding, custom database acceleration and telecom signal handling, so it does not fit the group's simulations.

prompt: The recurring slowdown occurs because _____.

options.text: CPU credits are consumed and, once exhausted, the VM is held at its base CPU performance until the credits rebuild
CPU credits are consumed and, once exhausted, the VM keeps its full CPU performance while work backs up
CPU credits are consumed and, once exhausted, the VM stays at its base CPU performance permanently
CPU credits are consumed only while the VM is stopped, so a running VM keeps its full CPU performance

explanation:
The machine in the exhibit runs a burstable size, Standard_B2ms. The B family is the only Azure VM type that meters CPU with credits: credits accumulate while the workload stays below the base CPU threshold, are spent when the workload runs above it, and once the balance is depleted the VM is throttled back to its base CPU performance until the credits rebuild during lighter use. That matches the observed cycle in the exhibit, where throughput stops improving during the busy window and the earlier rate returns after an idle stretch, so the keyed explanation is correct.

Why the other options are wrong:
- CPU credits are consumed and, once exhausted, the VM keeps its full CPU performance while work backs up: Once the credits are spent the VM does not keep its full CPU performance; it is pulled down to its base CPU level, which is why the amount of work finished per minute stops improving during the busy window.
- CPU credits are consumed and, once exhausted, the VM stays at its base CPU performance permanently: The reduced performance is temporary. Credits accumulate again while the workload stays under the base CPU threshold, so the VM returns to its burst CPU performance rather than staying limited permanently.
- CPU credits are consumed only while the VM is stopped, so a running VM keeps its full CPU performance: Credits are consumed while the VM is running and the workload stays above the base CPU threshold; a running burstable VM does lose processing speed once its credit balance is spent.

prompt: You run the webSS scale set in resource group app-rg, and a seasonal traffic peak requires the fleet to grow to about 900 instances. Every attempt to scale out is refused by the platform well before that point, and the business deadline is close. Which change should you make?

options.text: Update the scale set's image to a marketplace image or a custom image stored in the Azure Compute Gallery, which supports 1,000 instances
Enable automatic instance repairs, which replaces an unhealthy instance with the same image or a golden copy, so the fleet scales up on its own
Spread the scale set across availability zones in Azure so a datacenter failure does not stop the workload
Add a virtual machine scaling profile to the scale set so autoscale can use the current image to create the additional instances

explanation:
Scale sets that run from a managed image are capped at 600 instances, which is why scale-out on webSS is refused before the fleet can reach 900. Marketplace images and custom images stored in the Azure Compute Gallery support up to 1,000 instances, so moving the scale set off the managed image onto one of those sources lifts the ceiling above the 900 instances the peak requires.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enable automatic instance repairs, which replaces an unhealthy instance with the same image or a golden copy, so the fleet scales up on its own: Automatic instance repairs deal with unhealthy instances; they do not change the image-based ceiling on how many instances a scale set may run. Turning them on leaves the scale set exactly as limited as before, so the scale-out request would still be refused.
- Spread the scale set across availability zones in Azure so a datacenter failure does not stop the workload: Availability Zones distribute the instances of a scale set across datacenters for failure protection. They have no bearing on the maximum instance count, which is determined by the kind of image the fleet runs from, so the scale-out refusals continue.
- Add a virtual machine scaling profile to the scale set so autoscale can use the current image to create the additional instances: A virtual machine scaling profile tells autoscale what configuration the added instances should have, and it must exist for autoscaling to work at all. It does not change the ceiling on total instance count, so defining one would not stop the platform from rejecting the scale-out.

prompt: You have the scale set and the autoscale rule shown in the exhibit running in resource group app-rg. The rule only reacts to platform counters, so the fleet grows even while end users are struggling, and it stays flat while they are struggling badly. You need the fleet to grow automatically when users experience slow page loads, long response times, or abnormal session counts, and the operations team will not accept a solution that relies on counters collected inside the guest with a storage account behind them. Which metric source should you configure for the rule?

options.text: Application Insights metrics
Azure diagnostics extension metrics
Host-based metrics from the scale set
Azure Service Bus queue metrics

explanation:
The rule needs a source that reports what end users experience. Application Insights is the documented source for end-user signals such as response time, page load performance and session counts, so pointing the rule's metric source at Application Insights makes the fleet grow on slow page loads and long response times instead of on platform counters alone. The Azure diagnostics extension (in-guest counters plus a storage account) and Service Bus queue sources are ruled out by the stated constraints, and host-based metrics carry no end-user signal at all.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Azure diagnostics extension metrics: The Azure diagnostics extension is an agent that runs inside the VM and publishes in-guest performance counters, for example AverageReadTime for disks and PercentIdleTime for CPU, to storage. It requires a storage account and configured performance counters, which the operations team has excluded, and it still exposes no page-load or response-time data.
- Host-based metrics from the scale set: Host-based metrics describe how the instances are performing at the platform level (Percentage CPU, Network In, Network Out, disk read/write counters, CPU credit counters) and need no agents, but they say nothing about page loads or response times, so the fleet would still ignore end-user experience.
- Azure Service Bus queue metrics: A Service Bus queue source scales on the number of messages the web tier posts to a queue, so it only works if that tier publishes such messages. Nothing is being posted to a queue here, and queue length would not reflect slow page loads or long response times.

It also makes the rule scale in more eagerly when load falls.
- Add a second autoscale rule based on the Network In metric that adds instances when traffic rises: A second metric-based rule is still reactive: instances are added only after traffic crosses the threshold and stays there for the configured period, so capacity is not ready when the load first increases and the early slowdown is unchanged.

prompt: You have the scale set shown in the exhibit running in resource group app-rg. Browsers cannot open the site over HTTPS because the instances serve plain HTTP and carry no certificate, and every request is handed to whichever instance happens to answer, so /api and /media traffic is mixed together. You need a single entry point that decrypts the HTTPS traffic before it reaches the instances and that directs each URL path to the right group of instances. Which change should you make?

options.text: Front the scale set with Azure Application Gateway, so it decrypts the HTTPS traffic and routes each URL path to the correct instance group.
Front the scale set with Azure load balancer, so it decrypts the HTTPS traffic and routes each URL path to the correct instance group.
Front the scale set with Azure Application Gateway, so it only passes connections through to the instances and leaves the HTTPS and URL path handling to them.
Front the scale set with Azure load balancer, so it only passes connections through to the instances and leaves the HTTPS and URL path handling to them.

explanation:
Azure Application Gateway is the component that can sit in front of a scale set and perform advanced layer-7 handling plus TLS termination: it decrypts the incoming HTTPS request before it reaches the instances, so the instances need no certificate, and it can send each URL path to a different backend pool, which matches the two instance groups (group A for /api, group B for /media). The Azure load balancer used today only offers basic layer-4 traffic distribution, so it cannot do either of those jobs.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Front the scale set with Azure load balancer, so it decrypts the HTTPS traffic and routes each URL path to the correct instance group: The Azure load balancer performs basic layer-4 traffic distribution only. It can forward connections to the instances, but it cannot decrypt the encrypted request on their behalf and it cannot inspect the URL path, so browsers would still fail on the HTTPS request and the two instance groups would keep receiving mixed traffic.
- Front the scale set with Azure Application Gateway, so it only passes connections through to the instances and leaves the HTTPS and URL path handling to them: Application Gateway is the right product, but this configuration only passes connections through and leaves the HTTPS and URL path handling to the instances. In this scale set the instances run plain HTTP with no certificate installed, so they cannot accept the encrypted request or split traffic by URL path on their own.
- Front the scale set with Azure load balancer, so it only passes connections through to the instances and leaves the HTTPS and URL path handling to them: This pairs the product that only offers basic layer-4 distribution with pass-through behaviour, so nothing in the request path decrypts the HTTPS traffic or separates the /api and /media requests.

prompt: You have the scale set shown in the exhibit running in resource group app-rg. Every instance currently runs in one zone of the westeurope region, so when that zone goes down the whole service stops answering requests. You need the workload to keep serving traffic when one zone fails. Which change should you make?

options.text: Turn on zone placement for the scale set so the instances are spread across the Availability Zones of the region and the fleet survives the loss of one zone.
Raise the platform fault domain count from 3 to 5 so the instances are spread over more fault domains inside the region.
Move the scale set to a different Availability Zone and keep every instance running in that one zone.
Add the instances to an Availability Set so the platform spreads them over separate fault domains inside the region.

explanation:
A scale set by itself does not protect against the loss of a data center; spreading the instances over the Availability Zones of the region (zone placement) is what does. With instances distributed over several zones, the failure of one zone's facility still leaves instances in the other zones to serve traffic. Fault domains and Availability Sets only isolate VMs from each other inside a region, so they cover host and rack failures but not the loss of a zone's data center.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Raise the platform fault domain count from 3 to 5 so the instances are spread over more fault domains inside the region: Fault domains isolate VMs from one another inside a region, which covers host, rack and similar platform failures. Adding more fault domains to spread across improves that isolation, but every instance still sits in one zone, so a zone-level data-center failure takes the whole fleet down.
- Move the scale set to a different Availability Zone and keep every instance running in that one zone: Relocating the scale set to another Availability Zone and keeping every instance there only moves the single point of failure to a different zone; the service still stops completely when that one zone fails.
- Add the instances to an Availability Set so the platform spreads them over separate fault domains inside the region: An Availability Set spreads VMs across fault domains within a region rather than across Availability Zones, and the instances of a scale set are not members of an Availability Set, so this change would not survive the loss of a zone's data center either.

options.text: Manual
Schedule-based
Metric-based
Predictive scaling
Host-based metrics
Azure Diagnostics extension
Application Insights

explanation: The Release team wants capacity set on demand by a person, which is the Manual way of changing the instance count (it updates the sku.capacity property). The Retail team needs the extra instances in place before a promotion that always begins at the same clock time, which is what Schedule-based rules do. The Performance team wants the fleet to react only after a monitored counter has remained beyond its limit for the configured period, which is the behaviour of Metric-based rules reacting to sustained load. The Forecasting team wants the fleet to react to demand shapes nobody on the team defines, which is what Predictive scaling does by acting on usage patterns it discovers. Host-based metrics, the Azure Diagnostics extension, and Application Insights are data sources that a rule can read, not mechanisms that drive the number of instances, so they fit no slot.

Match each team's request to the value that satisfies it.

- Team: Payments; Metric watched by the rule: Percentage CPU; Request from the team: React to the mean level of processor use across the whole five-minute window, so a single brief spike never adds capacity on its own.
- Team: Search; Metric watched by the rule: Network Out; Request from the team: React to the worst reading seen inside the window, so a brief but serious spike still adds capacity.

context:
You have the api-vmss scale set in resource group app-rg, and the single autoscale rule attached to it never changes the fleet size: the number of running members stays at 5 no matter how high the CPU reading goes, and the pool never grows. The trigger, the aggregation and the threshold on the rule are all the ones you intended, and the rule is visible on the scale set. You need the rule to grow the fleet on its own once the CPU reading stays above the threshold. Which change should you make?

`Scale set:            api-vmss
Resource group:       app-rg
Region:               westeurope
Current instance count: 5
Autoscale rules on the scale set: 1
Rule trigger:         Percentage CPU, aggregation Average, greater than 80 percent
Rule scale-out action: Increase count by 5`
prompt: You should _____ so that the rule reacts to the CPU reading the way you expect.

options.text: create a virtual machine scaling profile that defines the configuration of the servers the rule adds
add a recurring scaling profile that scales the fleet out at 08:00 on weekdays
raise the maximum instance count permitted by the autoscale setting
change the metric aggregation used by the rule from Average to Maximum

explanation:
Autoscaling stays inert on a scale set that has no virtual machine scaling profile describing what a newly added instance should look like. The api-vmss rule already carries a host-based CPU trigger, an aggregation, a threshold and a scale-out action, yet the fleet never changes size at all, which points at the missing instance profile rather than at the rule's trigger or its thresholds. Adding a virtual machine scaling profile that defines the configuration of instances to add gives autoscaling the definition it needs, and the saved rule can then add members when the Percentage CPU reading stays above 80 percent.

Why the other options are wrong:
- add a recurring scaling profile that scales the fleet out at 08:00 on weekdays: A recurring profile belongs to schedule-based autoscaling: it would grow the fleet at a fixed time of day rather than reacting to the CPU reading, so it does not satisfy the requirement, and it does not supply the instance definition that autoscaling needs before it can provision anything.
- raise the maximum instance count permitted by the autoscale setting: Changing the ceiling only alters how many members are permitted; because nothing in the scale set tells autoscaling what a new member should look like, the rule still cannot act on the CPU reading and the fleet stays at 5.
- change the metric aggregation used by the rule from Average to Maximum: The aggregation decides how the readings inside the window are combined into a single figure; switching it from Average to Maximum changes only that figure and leaves autoscaling without the instance profile it needs to provision new members.

The security baseline for this workload forbids any reusable administrator secret being stored with the deployment, and every instance the scale set creates - including the ones added later as load grows - must accept the same personal sign-in from the operations team, which the team already holds. Which administrator credential should you configure?

prompt: You should configure _____ as the administrator credential for this deployment.

options.text: SSH public key
Administrator password meeting the length and character-class rules
Administrator password shorter than 12 characters
SSH private key

explanation:
For a Linux OS disk image the Administrator account section of a scale set accepts an SSH public key instead of a password, and you can either supply a key pair you already hold or let the platform generate one for you. That gives the operations team a reusable sign-in credential that works on every instance the scale set creates, including instances added later, without storing a shared secret in the deployment, which is what the baseline in the scenario requires.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Administrator password meeting the length and character-class rules: A password is one of the two credentials the Administrator account section accepts, and one that satisfies the length and character-class rules would pass validation, but it would be a single reusable secret held for the whole fleet. That is exactly what the security baseline forbids, so the credential that meets the requirement is the key-based one.
- Administrator password shorter than 12 characters: A password shorter than 12 characters fails validation when the scale set is created, so this choice would not let the deployment succeed at all.
- SSH private key: The half of the pair that is handed over to the platform is the public one; the private half has to stay with whoever signs in. Handing over the private half would hand over the sign-in secret itself.

The operations team has written a long list of monitoring conditions that it wants the fleet to react to, and every condition on that list has to keep influencing how many instances run. When you load the whole list into the scale set's autoscale profile, the platform accepts only part of it, and the remaining conditions are dropped without warning. Which change should you make?

- Item: Scale set name; Value: api-vmss
- Item: Resource group; Value: app-rg
- Item: Monitoring conditions in the operations list; Value: 27
- Item: Rules currently attached to the autoscale profile; Value: 20
- Item: Conditions on the list with no rule attached; Value: 7
prompt: You should _____.

options.text: limit this scale set to 20 rules and move the extra rules to a second scale set
keep every rule on this scale set and request a quota increase to raise the cap
give every rule on the list its own scale set in the resource group
attach the first 20 rules and drop the rest of the list

explanation:
A single scale set accepts a maximum of 20 autoscale rules, so the 27 conditions in the operations list can never all live in one profile on this scale set. Because the ceiling is counted per scale set, the workable fix is to bring this profile down to 20 rules and place the rules that do not fit on another scale set, which has its own allowance of 20. That keeps every condition driving the fleet size without asking the platform for anything it does not grant.

Why the other options are wrong:
- keep every rule on this scale set and request a quota increase to raise the cap: The count of rules a scale set can carry is a fixed platform restriction rather than a quota that can be raised on request, so asking for an increase leaves the profile still unable to hold all 27 rules and the conditions beyond the accepted number remain unenforced.
- give every rule on the list its own scale set in the resource group: Nothing in the platform requires one scale set per monitoring condition; a single scale set holds up to 20 rules, so spinning up 27 scale sets in the resource group is unnecessary, expensive and leaves the original workload fragmented.
- attach the first 20 rules and drop the rest of the list: Silently discarding the seven conditions that have no rule means those conditions no longer influence the fleet size at all, which breaks the stated requirement that every monitoring condition keeps working.

context: You have the api-vmss scale set in resource group app-rg, whose four instances are scaled out by one autoscale rule. Each time the rule reacts, it adds only a fraction of the instances that are already running, so the fleet stays too small during a load spike. You need each reaction to add the same three extra instances, whatever the current fleet size is. Which scale-out action should the rule use?
prompt: The rule's scale-out action should be _____.

options.text: Increase count by
Increase percent by
Increase count to

explanation:
The rule must add the same three extra instances on every trigger, so the scale-out action has to be a fixed count change rather than a share of the running instances. On a four-instance fleet a proportional action adds only a fraction of an instance, so the service would still be short of capacity.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Increase percent by: This action scales the fleet by a share of the instances already running, so on a four-instance fleet each trigger adds only a fraction of an instance instead of the three extra instances the workload needs.
- Increase count to: This action moves the fleet to a chosen total number of instances instead of adding a constant increment, so the number of instances added would vary from one trigger to the next.

prompt: For Team A's request you should _____, and for Team B's request you should base the rule on [...].

options.text: Install the Azure diagnostics extension and point the rule at the storage account it writes to
Install Azure Application Insights and point the rule at the application telemetry it produces
Keep the current scale set and point the rule at another host-based reading
Post to an Azure Service Bus queue and let an external worker consume the messages it receives

explanation:
Team A needs a reading taken inside the virtual machine: how long it waits on its disks. That level of detail is produced only by the Azure diagnostics extension, which runs inside the virtual machine, writes its performance metrics (such as AverageReadTime for disks) to Azure storage, and needs storage accounts plus configured performance counters; the autoscale rule then consumes those readings from that storage account, so Team A's rule changes its metric source from the current scale set to the storage account fed by the extension. Team B needs the opposite: the amount of data the virtual machines read from their disks, measured by the platform itself with nothing installed on the machines. That is the host-based metric Disk Read Bytes, which requires no agent and no storage account, so Team B's rule keeps the current scale set as its metric source and simply watches Disk Read Bytes.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Install Azure Application Insights and point the rule at the application telemetry it produces: Application Insights supplies application-level telemetry - response times, page load performance and session counts - not the detailed in-virtual-machine disk readings Team A asked for. It fits a requirement about user-facing application behaviour, not about how long the machines wait on their disks.
- Keep the current scale set and point the rule at another host-based reading: Host-based readings cover only the built-in list (Percentage CPU, Network In, Network Out, Disk Read Bytes, Disk Write Bytes, Disk Read Operations/Sec, Disk Write Operations/Sec, CPU Credits Remaining, CPU Credits Consumed). The time a virtual machine spends waiting on its disks is not one of them, so choosing another host-based reading cannot satisfy Team A.
- Post to an Azure Service Bus queue and let an external worker consume the messages it receives: An Azure Service Bus queue lets an application or another component post messages that trigger rules; it is a different mechanism for feeding rules and it does not supply the in-virtual-machine disk readings Team A requires.

context:
You administer the api-vmss scale set in resource group app-rg. Its fleet has held eight instances for weeks, and the only times anybody changes that number are during incident calls. Demand on this workload is not flat: across the last eight weeks the same intra-day and intra-week shape has repeated, yet nobody on the team has ever written down the clock times or the counter levels that go with that shape, and they will not start now. You want the number of running instances to track the demand curve that is already visible in the workload's history, and you will not accept a solution where the sizing depends on a person or on conditions somebody has to keep in a table by hand. Which scaling method should you configure for the scale set?

- Property: Scale set name; Value: api-vmss
- Property: Resource group; Value: app-rg
- Property: Orchestration mode; Value: Flexible
- Property: Scaling; Value: Manual
- Property: Current instance count; Value: 8
- Property: Autoscale rules; Value: None
prompt: The team should configure _____ for the api-vmss scale set so that the instance count tracks the workload's demand without anyone keeping conditions up to date by hand.

options.text: Manual resizing
Schedule-based scaling rules
Metric-based scaling rules
Predictive AI

explanation:
The instance count of a scale set can be driven in four ways: by hand, by a set schedule, by rules that react to metric thresholds, or by predictive AI that discovers usage patterns and adjusts the fleet from what it detects. In this scenario the workload already shows a repeating demand shape in its own recent history, the team will not record peak times, and nobody will keep counter thresholds in a table, so the method that fits is predictive AI: the platform works the demand pattern out for itself and sizes the fleet accordingly. Manual resizing leaves the sizing with the team, schedule-based rules require the peak times to be written down, and metric rules require thresholds to be kept up to date.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Manual resizing: Manual resizing only changes the instance count when a person performs the action, for example by editing the capacity value in the portal or by running the scale command. The fleet would then stay at eight instances and would never follow the workload's demand curve on its own, which is exactly what the team has ruled out.
- Schedule-based scaling rules: Schedule-based rules pre-provision instances for peaks that someone has already recorded, such as the start of the working day or a promotion. The peak times for this workload have never been written down and the team will not start doing so, so a rule of this kind could not be relied on.
- Metric-based scaling rules: Metric rules react to a counter staying at or above a threshold for a configured period, so the team would have to keep counter levels and thresholds in step with the workload. No such conditions exist for this scale set and none are planned, and a threshold rule only reacts once load has already become heavy.

explanation:
With a quarterly reset period, the configured amount is spread evenly across the three months of the quarter, so 12,000 USD gives each month a share of 4,000 USD. The cost being tracked restarts at zero at the start of every new period, which is why the 80% threshold of this budget fires at 3,200 USD of monthly spend.

Why the other options are wrong:
- 12,000 USD: That is the total for the entire quarter. It is the figure the three monthly shares add up to, not the amount a single month is measured against.
- 1,000 USD: Spreading an amount across twelve months applies to an annual reset period. A quarterly budget divides its amount across the three months of the quarter, so this figure is too low.
- 6,000 USD: Nothing is split in half at the middle of a quarter; the amount is divided evenly across the three months, so no month is measured against this figure.

Action groups can be attached to budgets only at the management group scope
Action groups can be attached to budgets only at the billing account and enrollment account scopes
Action groups can be attached to budgets only at the billing profile and invoice section scopes

explanation:
Attaching an action group while you create or edit a budget is limited to subscription and resource group scopes. Because this budget sits at the management group level, the portal disables that control. Moving the budget to one of the supported scopes, or attaching the action group logic elsewhere, resolves it.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Action groups can be attached to budgets only at the management group scope: The opposite is true: action group support for budgets is not offered at the management group scope, which is why the control is disabled.
- Action groups can be attached to budgets only at the billing account and enrollment account scopes: Billing account and enrollment account scopes are valid scopes for budgets in an Enterprise Agreement, but action groups are not offered when budgets are created or edited at those levels.
- Action groups can be attached to budgets only at the billing profile and invoice section scopes: Billing profile and invoice section scopes are supported budget scopes under a Microsoft Customer Agreement, but they don't support attaching an action group to a budget.

prompt: You are setting up alerts on a new budget for a subscription in the portal. You need the alert configuration to be accepted exactly as you enter it, so the finance team hears from you before spending runs away. Which candidate should you submit?

options.text: Candidate A — a single actual cost threshold of 80% and one recipient email address
Candidate B — three actual cost thresholds of 50%, 80% and 120%, with no recipient email address
Candidate C — a single actual cost threshold of 2500% and one recipient email address
Candidate D — a forecast-based alert with no threshold value and one recipient email address

explanation:
A budget must carry at least one cost threshold, expressed as a percentage of the budget amount, together with a matching recipient email address, and alert thresholds are only supported from 0.01% to 1000%. Candidate A supplies exactly that: an in-range actual cost threshold of 80% plus an address to notify, so the portal accepts the configuration.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Candidate B — three actual cost thresholds of 50%, 80% and 120%, with no recipient email address: Three thresholds are within the allowed maximum of five per budget, but no recipient email address is supplied. Because a threshold needs a corresponding address to notify, this configuration can't be accepted as entered.
- Candidate C — a single actual cost threshold of 2500% and one recipient email address: The threshold is 2500% of the budget amount, far above the supported ceiling of 1000% for budget alerts. The presence of a valid address doesn't make an out-of-range value acceptable.
- Candidate D — a forecast-based alert with no threshold value and one recipient email address: A forecast-based alert only fires when predicted spend crosses a configured threshold, so leaving the threshold value unset gives Cost Management no condition to evaluate. At least one threshold and a corresponding email address are still required.

Priya, who owns the subscription, is away for two weeks and the finance director has approved a higher monthly limit for the budget she created. You need Sam, the platform engineer, to make that adjustment in place. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Yes — a Cost Management Contributor can change the amount of a budget another user created
No — a Cost Management Contributor can change the amount only of a budget they created themselves
No — a Cost Management Contributor can see budgets in the portal but cannot change any amount
Yes — a Cost Management Contributor can delete a budget another user created and create a replacement

explanation:
Budgets in Cost Management follow defined role behavior: Contributor and Cost Management Contributor can create, change, or delete their own budgets, and they can change the budget amount on budgets that other people created. Sam's role therefore lets Sam raise the amount on Priya's budget without deleting and recreating it.

Why the other options are wrong:
- No — a Cost Management Contributor can change the amount only of a budget they created themselves: That describes the rights over a user's own budgets. It isn't the whole picture: the same role may also change the amount on budgets created by other users, which is exactly what Sam needs here.
- No — a Cost Management Contributor can see budgets in the portal but cannot change any amount: Read-only visibility is what Reader and Cost Management Reader get on budgets they have permission to view. Cost Management Contributor has write access, so this restriction doesn't apply to Sam.
- Yes — a Cost Management Contributor can delete a budget another user created and create a replacement: Deleting is limited to a user's own budgets; removing a budget created by someone else is an Owner-level operation. That is why Sam must edit in place rather than replace it.

An action group is attached to a budget created at subscription scope
Five cost thresholds and five contact addresses are entered

explanation: A quarterly reset period works like a monthly one, except the amount for the quarter is divided evenly among its three months. Because a budget resets automatically at the end of a period for the same budget amount when you select an expiration date in the future, and because a budget is automatically deleted once it expires, the expiration-date choice matches the behavior about reusing the same amount and then being deleted automatically. Budget evaluation requires that all subscriptions within the scope, such as a management group, operate under a single currency, so a scope whose subscriptions bill in different currencies is the one where notifications can go missing. Action groups are supported for subscription and resource group scopes, and an attached action group performs actions such as mobile push notifications, webhook calls, or automation runs when the budget threshold is met. Finally, a budget requires at least one cost threshold and a corresponding email address and can optionally include up to five thresholds and five email addresses, so five of each is the ceiling rather than a value that can be increased.

context: Your platform team reviews the machine-sizing suggestions Advisor produces for virtual machines and virtual machine scale sets. Each slot below describes the signal behind one of those suggestions. Drag each suggestion to the signal that produces it.
prompt: The machine ran no activity at all over the last seven days, judged on processor and outbound network metrics

options.text: Shutdown recommendation
Resize SKU recommendation
Instance count recommendation
Burstable recommendation

explanation: A shutdown recommendation is made for resources that weren't used at all over the last seven days, and its criteria are based on processor and outbound network utilization, so it belongs with the idle-machine signal. A resize SKU recommendation is made when the current load can fit on a more appropriate, less expensive size, which may be in the same family (for example D3v2 to D2v2), a newer version (D3v2 to D2v3), or a different family (D3v2 to E3v2). An instance count recommendation applies to virtual machine scale sets where fewer machines of the same SKU would carry the load; Advisor prioritizes these over SKU change recommendations because they are easily actionable and deliver faster savings. A burstable recommendation is made when average processor utilization is below a burstable SKU's baseline performance and the burstable SKU credits would be sufficient to support the average utilization over seven days.

context: Your team is creating a budget in the Azure portal for a subscription that tracks one line of business. The finance team wants to hear from the service itself as spending climbs toward the agreed limit, so the notification settings must be accepted exactly as they are typed in.
prompt: Enter _____ as the smallest percentage of the budget amount a cost threshold can be set to, and enter [...] as the largest number of thresholds and contact email addresses a single budget supports.
explanation:
The alert limit for a budget supports a range of 0.01% to 1000% of the budget threshold, so 0.01% is the smallest cost threshold the portal accepts. A budget requires at least one cost threshold with a matching email address, and you can optionally include up to five thresholds and five email addresses in a single budget, so five of each is the maximum.

Why the other options are wrong:
- 0.001%: 0.001% sits below the documented range, whose lower bound is 0.01% of the budget threshold, so the portal would reject it.
- 1%: 1% is inside the supported range, but it is not the smallest value a threshold can be set to.
- 10%: 10% is accepted as a threshold value, but again it is not the lowest value in the supported range.

context:
Your finance team bought reserved capacity and a savings plan for a subscription, and both purchases were charged in full in a single month. The budget emails for that subscription report far less than the totals on the invoice, and the team wants to know why. Which statement accounts for the difference?

- Item: Reserved instance purchase; Amount charged this month: 12,000 in full, booked in one month
- Item: Saving plan purchase; Amount charged this month: 6,000 in full, booked in one month
- Item: Pay-as-you-go compute; Amount charged this month: 4,100
prompt: The discrepancy arises because _____.

options.text: Evaluations use actual cost and don't include amortization
Evaluations use actual cost and include amortization
Evaluations use amortized cost and include amortization
Evaluations use amortized cost and don't include amortization

explanation:
Budget cost evaluations are based on actual cost and explicitly don't include amortization. Reserved instance and purchase data are now part of what budgets evaluate, but the purchase is counted at its actual amount in the period it lands rather than being spread across the covered term, so the totals behind the budget emails are lower than the amortized view finance expects.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Evaluations use actual cost and include amortization: Amortization is never part of a budget evaluation, so pairing it with actual cost is not correct.
- Evaluations use amortized cost and include amortization: Budgets don't spread a purchase across its term, so neither half of this statement matches how evaluations work.
- Evaluations use amortized cost and don't include amortization: The second half is right, but evaluations aren't amortized; they are calculated from actual cost.
