Your organization holds an Enterprise Agreement, and its Azure Prepayment is being consumed faster than the finance director expected as new environments are provisioned. Nobody wants to maintain a budget for this agreement, but the director does want an automatic notification as the balance is drawn down, at the points the service itself uses. Which arrangement delivers that?

- Account property: Agreement type; Value: Enterprise Agreement
- Account property: Azure Prepayment balance (USD); Value: 78,000
- Account property: People who must be informed; Value: Account owners
prompt: Configure _____ for the agreement, and expect the service to notify the account owners at [...] of the Azure Prepayment balance.

options.text: Budget alert
Credit alert
Department spending quota alert
Cost anomaly alert

explanation:
Cost Management generates credit alerts automatically at 90% and at 100% of the organization's Azure Prepayment balance, which is the offering for organizations with an Enterprise Agreement. Each notification is reflected in the cost alerts list and emailed to the account owners, so no budget has to be maintained.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Budget alert: Budget alerts only fire when spending reaches a threshold someone defined on a budget, so they don't track consumption of the Azure Prepayment.
- Department spending quota alert: Department spending quota alerts depend on a spending quota configured in the portal and go to department owners; they are a different mechanism.
- Cost anomaly alert: A cost anomaly alert reports unusual consumption patterns that Cost Management detects; it doesn't report progress against the Azure Prepayment balance.

context: Your platform team works through the items listed in the Advisor dashboard. For one recommendation, a reviewer changed its state to completed by hand because the fix had already been applied outside the portal, and Advisor has not yet confirmed the change. You need to set the team's expectations about what happens next. Which statement is accurate?
prompt: Advisor can take _____ to recognize that the action was taken, and until it does, a recommendation a reviewer completed by hand is displayed as [...].

options.text: up to 24 hours
up to 48 hours
up to one hour
no time at all

explanation:
After you implement a recommendation, it can take up to a day, that is up to 24 hours, for Advisor to recognize the action and run its system verification. Until that verification takes place, a recommendation that a reviewer completed by hand is shown with the indication 'Marked completed', which distinguishes it from one Advisor verified on its own.

Why the other options are wrong:
- up to 48 hours: The 48-hour window belongs to the lookback period setting for virtual machine right-sizing recommendations; after that configuration changes, recommendations may take up to 48 hours to refresh. It isn't the delay for recognizing an implemented action.
- up to one hour: An hour is roughly how long a budget threshold notification takes after an evaluation, which is unrelated to Advisor verifying an implemented recommendation.
- no time at all: Advisor does perform system verification itself and updates the state once it does, so the action isn't recognized with no delay.

context:
Your tenant's management group holds subscriptions denominated in euros and others denominated in US dollars. The finance lead created a budget at that management group level, and the notifications configured on it never arrive. You need to restore them without changing the spending limit the team agreed on.

- Subscription: sub-web; Billing denomination: EUR
- Subscription: sub-data; Billing denomination: EUR
- Subscription: sub-analytics; Billing denomination: USD
- Subscription: sub-identity; Billing denomination: USD
prompt: Choose _____ so that the finance lead starts receiving the notifications again.

options.text: Narrow the budget to a scope whose subscriptions all use one currency
Add another budget at the same management group scope for subscriptions in the second currency
Change the reset period of the existing budget at that scope to the billing quarter
Add filters for publisher type Azure and charge type Usage to the existing budget at that scope

explanation:
For budget evaluation, all subscriptions inside the scope, such as a management group, must operate under a single currency. Multi-currency evaluation isn't supported, which is why the notifications for the management group budget are missed. Placing the budget on a scope whose subscriptions all use one currency restores the evaluation and its alerts.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add another budget at the same management group scope for subscriptions in the second currency: Adding a second budget at the same management group scope doesn't resolve anything: the limitation applies to the subscriptions inside the scope, not to the number of budgets defined there.
- Change the reset period of the existing budget at that scope to the billing quarter: The reset period only controls how the amount is divided across the months of a period; it has no bearing on the mixed currencies of the subscriptions being evaluated.
- Add filters for publisher type Azure and charge type Usage to the existing budget at that scope: Those filters restrict which charges count toward the evaluation, limiting it to first-party Azure consumption, but they don't address the mixed currencies that stop the notifications from being produced.

context:
Your team defined the budget shown below for the sub-prod-web subscription, and the finance director now wants a higher monthly limit to take effect next January. You need to tell the team what happens to this budget as time passes and what they would have to do to put the higher limit into effect. Which statement is accurate?

- Setting: Scope; Value: Subscription - sub-prod-web
- Setting: Monthly limit; Value: 5,000 USD
- Setting: Time grain; Value: Monthly
- Setting: Start date; Value: 2026-01-01
- Setting: Expiration date; Value: 2028-12-31
prompt: Because this budget _____ at the end of each period, you must [...] to apply a different limit from January, and when its expiration date arrives the budget [...].

options.text: resets with the same amount
resets with the latest forecast
resets with the highest month's cost
keeps its amount until edited by hand

explanation:
A budget that has a future expiration date resets at the end of every monthly, quarterly, or annual period for the same budget amount, so the cost being evaluated starts again from zero against the identical figure. Because it always comes back with the same value, changing the amount that applies to later periods means putting in a new budget rather than adjusting the existing one. Once the expiration date passes, the budget is automatically deleted rather than left in place.

Why the other options are wrong:
- resets with the latest forecast: The carried-over figure is not recalculated from a forecast. Forecasted cost predictions are used only to decide when forecasted alerts fire; the budget still returns to the amount that was entered.
- resets with the highest month's cost: Spending recorded earlier in the period does not change what the budget returns to. Only the accumulated cost restarts from zero, against the same budget figure each time.
- keeps its amount until edited by hand: No manual step is needed at a period boundary. The budget returns to the same figure by itself, and it stops being evaluated only when its expiration date is reached.

context:
- Scope: Subscription; Lock level: CanNotDelete
- Scope: Resource group; Lock level: ReadOnly
- Scope: Storage account; Lock level: (none)
prompt: You administer an Azure subscription that contains a resource group, which contains a storage account. The current lock configuration is shown in the following table. A user at the resource scope attempts to delete the storage account by using the Azure CLI. What is the outcome?

options.text: The delete succeeds because the storage account itself has no lock.
The delete fails because the lock at the resource-group scope is the most restrictive restriction in the inheritance chain.
The delete fails because the lock at the subscription scope is the only restriction in the inheritance chain.
The delete succeeds because the lock at the resource-group scope only prevents modifications, not deletions.

explanation:
Locks inherit from parent scopes. When a lock exists at a parent scope, all resources within that scope inherit the same lock. The most restrictive lock in the inheritance chain takes precedence. ReadOnly is more restrictive than CanNotDelete (because ReadOnly also blocks modifications), so the resource-group lock wins and the delete attempt is denied.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The delete succeeds because the storage account itself has no lock: Locks are inherited from parent scopes. Even though no lock is set directly on the storage account, the resource-group lock applies through inheritance.
- The delete fails because the lock at the subscription scope is the only restriction in the inheritance chain: The subscription lock does apply through inheritance, but both the subscription and resource-group locks are inherited. The most restrictive one (ReadOnly on the resource group) takes precedence over CanNotDelete, so the subscription scope is not the one that decides the outcome.
- The delete succeeds because the lock at the resource-group scope only prevents modifications, not deletions: A ReadOnly lock blocks both modifications and deletions. It is more restrictive than CanNotDelete, not less restrictive, so the delete is blocked.

prompt:
A security audit reveals that engineers routinely retrieve the access keys of an Azure storage account by calling a built-in operation. The security lead wants to stop that access while still allowing the team's applications to read and write blob content with their code. An administrator applies a Read-only lock on the storage account.

After the lock is in place, an engineer runs the commands shown in the following code block from a workstation with Contributor rights on the resource group.

options.text: The lock prevents both the list-keys call and the blob upload, so the team's applications cannot manage blobs anymore.
The lock prevents the list-keys call through the management endpoint, but the team's applications can still upload blobs through the storage account's data plane.
The lock prevents only blob operations, not the list-keys call, so the team can still retrieve the account keys.
The lock has no effect because locks cannot be applied at the storage-account scope.

explanation:
Locks only apply to control plane operations and not to data plane operations. The list-keys call goes through the management endpoint (control plane), so the Read-only lock blocks it. Blob operations performed through the storage account's data plane endpoint are unaffected, so the upload still succeeds.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The lock prevents both the list-keys call and the blob upload, so the team's applications cannot manage blobs anymore: The control plane list-keys call is blocked, but the data plane blob upload is not blocked by the lock. Locks apply only to control plane operations, not to data plane operations.
- The lock prevents only blob operations, not the list-keys call, so the team can still retrieve the account keys: Locks block control plane operations, including the list-keys call. Blob data operations go through the data plane and are not blocked by the lock.
- The lock has no effect because locks cannot be applied at the storage-account scope: Locks are fully supported at the storage-account scope. The list-keys error in the output confirms the lock is being enforced at that scope.

options.text: Delete and ReadOnly
CanNotDelete and ReadOnly
DenyDelete and DenyModify
None and Full

explanation:
The Azure portal uses the labels 'Delete' and 'Read-only', but the underlying Azure PowerShell parameter values for the LockLevel parameter are 'CanNotDelete' (matching the portal Delete behavior) and 'ReadOnly' (matching the portal Read-only behavior). New-AzResourceLock accepts those two values.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Delete and ReadOnly: 'Delete' is the Azure portal label, not a valid PowerShell LockLevel value. The portal label and the cmdlet parameter value differ; you must translate them when you script.
- DenyDelete and DenyModify: 'DenyDelete' and 'DenyModify' are not valid LockLevel values for New-AzResourceLock. The cmdlet accepts only CanNotDelete and ReadOnly.
- None and Full: 'None' and 'Full' are not valid LockLevel values for New-AzResourceLock. The cmdlet accepts only CanNotDelete and ReadOnly.

prompt: To meet a regulatory requirement, every subscription in the organization has a CanNotDelete restriction applied at the subscription scope. A director submits a request to cancel one of those subscriptions. What happens when the cancellation is processed?

options.text: The cancellation is blocked by the restriction, and the subscription remains active.
The cancellation proceeds; the resources are deactivated and then permanently deleted after a waiting period.
The cancellation proceeds and every resource is permanently removed immediately.
The restriction is first removed automatically, and then the cancellation proceeds with no waiting period.

explanation:
A resource lock does not block the cancellation of an Azure subscription. When you cancel a subscription that has a lock in place, Azure preserves the resources by deactivating them instead of deleting them right away, and only permanently removes them after a waiting period.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The cancellation is blocked by the restriction, and the subscription remains active: Resource locks do not block subscription cancellation, regardless of the lock level. The cancellation request is processed.
- The cancellation proceeds and every resource is permanently removed immediately: Resources are not deleted immediately on cancellation when a lock is involved. They are deactivated first and only permanently removed after a waiting period.
- The restriction is first removed automatically, and then the cancellation proceeds with no waiting period: The cancellation does not require the lock to be removed first. Locks do not block subscription cancellation, and the deactivation-then-permanent-deletion waiting period is still applied.

prompt:
An operations team deployed a solution that automatically provisioned two resource groups: an unlocked overview group (rg-overview-prod) and a locked infrastructure group (rg-infra-prod). The team tries to remove the lock on rg-infra-prod by using Remove-AzResourceLock. The command fails with an error indicating that the lock cannot be removed by user accounts. What should the team do to remove rg-infra-prod?

The current state of the two resource groups is shown in the following block.

options.text: Retry Remove-AzResourceLock while signed in with Owner scope at the subscription level, and pass the -Force switch to override the lock.
Open the rg-infra-prod blade in the Azure portal, find the lock entry under Settings, and click Delete to remove the lock.
Find the parent managed application in the Azure portal and delete it; deleting the application also deletes the locked rg-infra-prod resource group.
Submit a support request to Microsoft to remove the system-owned lock, and wait for the response before deleting the rg-infra-prod resource group.

explanation:
For services implemented through managed applications, the infrastructure resource group is locked by a system application and cannot be removed by deleting the lock itself. The documented approach is to locate the parent managed application service in the Azure portal and delete it; that action also removes the locked infrastructure resource group.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Retry Remove-AzResourceLock while signed in with Owner scope at the subscription level, and pass the -Force switch to override the lock: Lock ownership by a system application cannot be overridden by Owner scope or the -Force switch. The lock cannot be deleted through the cmdlet regardless of the operator's role.
- Open the rg-infra-prod blade in the Azure portal, find the lock entry under Settings, and click Delete to remove the lock: The lock entry cannot be removed from the portal because the system application owns it. Trying to delete the lock in the portal or through PowerShell produces the same ownership error.
- Submit a support request to Microsoft to remove the system-owned lock, and wait for the response before deleting the rg-infra-prod resource group: Support escalation is not the documented approach. The documented way to clean up the locked infrastructure is to delete the parent managed application service, which removes the resource group as part of the operation.

options.text: Management Group Contributor
Owner
Contributor
Management Group Reader

explanation:
The documented chart of supported actions on a management group shows Management Group Contributor as the only built-in role that supports create, rename, move and delete while offering neither assign access nor assign policy. That is exactly the delegated change-making task without access or policy rights. (Note that moving items still requires the extra permissions listed for move operations.)

Why the other options are wrong:
- Owner: Owner supports every action in the chart, including assign access and assign policy, so it hands the team far more than the reshaping task requires and lets it change governance conditions.
- Contributor: Contributor supports create, rename, move, delete and assign access. It would let the team change who has access, which is explicitly outside what the team should be allowed to do.
- Management Group Reader: Management Group Reader only supports the read action on the management group scope, so the team could not create, rename, move or delete management groups.

explanation:
This is the documented scenario where a subscription that carries a role assignment is moved outside the branch of the management group used in the custom role definition's assignable scope. The service rejects the move because the assignment can no longer reach the definition, and the documented fix is to remove the role assignment from the subscription before moving it to its new parent.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Remove the Owner role assignment on the target management group, then retry the request: The rejection is not caused by access permissions on the destination scope, so deleting an Owner role assignment there leaves the definition and the subscription assignment just as disconnected as before.
- Move the management group that holds the role definition so it remains the parent of both subscriptions in the new branch: Relocating the management group that holds the definition does not help the subscription that is being moved: its assignment would still point to a role definition it can no longer reach from its branch. The documented fixes concern the subscription's assignment or the definition's assignable scope.
- Grant Reader on the target management group, then retry the request: A built-in read-only role on the destination scope has no bearing on the relationship between a custom role definition and a subscription-level assignment, so the move keeps failing.

You need the portal label changed to 'Corporate Landing Zones' while the identifier stays exactly as it is so that automation scripts and existing role assignments keep working. Which command should you run?

options.text: Update-AzManagementGroup -GroupId 'contoso-landing-zones' -DisplayName 'Corporate Landing Zones'
New-AzManagementGroup -GroupId 'contoso-landing-zones' -DisplayName 'Corporate Landing Zones'
Update-AzManagementGroup -GroupId 'Landing Zones (old)' -DisplayName 'Corporate Landing Zones'
Remove-AzManagementGroup -GroupId 'contoso-landing-zones'

explanation:
Update-AzManagementGroup updates an existing management group, and -DisplayName changes only the label shown in the Azure portal. The identifier that scripts and role assignments depend on is supplied through -GroupId, which takes the directory-unique management group ID (for example Update-AzManagementGroup -GroupId 'ContosoIt' -DisplayName 'Contoso Group'). Because that identifier can't be edited after creation, changing the display name is the only way to relabel the container without disturbing references, and the children stay attached to the same group.

Why the other options are wrong:
- New-AzManagementGroup -GroupId 'contoso-landing-zones' -DisplayName 'Corporate Landing Zones': New-AzManagementGroup creates a brand-new container rather than relabelling an existing one. Creation requires a new unique identifier, and the identifier of an existing group can't be reused or changed, so this neither relabels contoso-landing-zones nor preserves its children.
- Update-AzManagementGroup -GroupId 'Landing Zones (old)' -DisplayName 'Corporate Landing Zones': -GroupId takes the directory-unique identifier of the management group, not the label shown in the portal. Passing 'Landing Zones (old)' means the command has no group to resolve, so the update never reaches the intended management group.
- Remove-AzManagementGroup -GroupId 'contoso-landing-zones': Remove-AzManagementGroup deletes the management group instead of renaming it. Deletion requires that no child management groups or subscriptions remain underneath, and this group still holds sub-prod-eu and sub-prod-us, so it can't be used to change the label.

prompt: The sandbox environment has been retired and contoso-sandbox must no longer appear in the hierarchy, while the subscriptions and management group sitting beneath it have to keep running under contoso-corp. Which action should be taken?

options.text: Move the child management group and the subscriptions under it to a different parent management group, and delete contoso-sandbox with write permission on that group
Delete contoso-sandbox immediately with Contributor permission, and let the subscriptions and the child management group underneath be cleaned up at the same time
Move contoso-sandbox itself under a different parent management group and leave its contents in place, so it no longer appears beneath contoso-corp
Ask a Microsoft Entra Global Administrator to remove contoso-sandbox and its subscriptions from the tenant root group, and then let the hierarchy settle

explanation:
A management group can be deleted only when it has no child management groups and no subscriptions under it, and when the requester holds write permissions on the group (Owner, Contributor, or Management Group Contributor). The account in this scenario already has Contributor on contoso-sandbox, so the blocking condition is the content underneath. Moving the child management group and its subscriptions to another parent management group empties contoso-sandbox, after which the group itself can be removed.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Delete contoso-sandbox immediately with Contributor permission, and let the subscriptions and the child management group underneath be cleaned up at the same time: Deletion isn't cascading. A management group that still contains child management groups or subscriptions can't be deleted, and the portal makes this explicit: if the Delete button is unavailable, hovering over it shows the reason. Content underneath must be moved out first.
- Move contoso-sandbox itself under a different parent management group and leave its contents in place, so it no longer appears beneath contoso-corp: Moving contoso-sandbox to a different parent management group changes where the group sits in the tree; it doesn't remove it, so contoso-sandbox still exists and still carries its children, and the goal of retiring the container isn't met.
- Ask a Microsoft Entra Global Administrator to remove contoso-sandbox and its subscriptions from the tenant root group, and then let the hierarchy settle: A Global Administrator role relates to elevating access to the root management group, and role assignments on that root apply to the whole directory. Removal of a management group isn't performed at the root level, and elevation there gives no shortcut past the requirement that the group be empty before deletion.

context:
Your tenant contains 420 Azure subscriptions, and every one of them sits directly beneath the directory's single top-level container. A security rule must block virtual machine creation in two regions across all of them, and it must also cover subscriptions the company adds next year. You need one assignment, made in a scope that new subscriptions inherit automatically. Which management group should you assign the policy to?

- Item: Region rule; Value: Virtual machine creation blocked in eastus and northeurope
- Item: Subscriptions today; Value: 420, each a direct child of the directory's single top-level container
- Item: Subscriptions arriving next quarter; Value: Automatically placed under that same top-level container
prompt: You should assign the policy at the _____ so that every subscription inherits it.

options.text: The root management group
Each subscription that hosts virtual machines
A separate management group per blocked region
The management group that holds the company's landing zones

explanation:
Every directory has one built-in top-level management group, and all other management groups and subscriptions fold up to it. Anything assigned there - policies, role assignments - cascades by inheritance to the whole tree, and new subscriptions are placed under it automatically, so a single assignment covers today's subscriptions and any created later.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Each subscription that hosts virtual machines: An assignment made on a subscription applies only to that subscription, so the rule would have to be repeated 420 times and each future subscription would need its own copy.
- A separate management group per blocked region: A new group per blocked region only covers the subscriptions placed beneath it, and placing subscriptions under those groups changes the governance hierarchy rather than covering everything at once.
- The management group that holds the company's landing zones: A group that holds only the landing zones covers just its own descendants, so subscriptions elsewhere in the directory, including future ones created at the top, would not inherit the rule.

context: In your Microsoft Entra directory, nobody holds a role on the single top-level management group, so no one can currently be given rights anywhere in the hierarchy. A member of the Microsoft Entra Global Administrators role has been asked to open that group and hand out role assignments to colleagues so they can shape the hierarchy. Which step must be taken first?
prompt: The Global Administrator must _____ before role assignments can be made on that group.

options.text: Elevate access, then assign roles from that group
Assign the Owner role on that group first
Assign the Management Group Contributor role on that group first
Create a child management group and assign roles there instead

explanation:
No one has permissions on the root management group by default, and Microsoft Entra Global Administrators are the only identities that can obtain them. They do this by elevating their access, which grants them the User Access Administrator role on the root management group; only then can they assign any Azure role to other users or groups to manage the hierarchy.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Assign the Owner role on that group first: Owner is just another role, and it cannot be self-assigned on the root management group because the person has no permissions there yet. The permission has to come from elevating access first.
- Assign the Management Group Contributor role on that group first: Management Group Contributor is also only a role that can be granted after the person already holds permissions on that group, so assigning it is a result of the first step rather than the first step itself.
- Create a child management group and assign roles there instead: Creating a child group and assigning roles there does nothing for the top-level group itself; the request here is about the directory-wide group, and access to it can only be obtained by elevating access.

context:
A platform team wants a single view that lists every networking resource in the tenant, even though those resources sit in many different subscriptions and resource groups, and the team must not change how policies or role assignments inherit down the hierarchy. The same resource must be able to appear in several of these views at the same time. Which type of container should the team create?

- Requirement: One view spanning many subscriptions; Notes: Networking resources sit in 40 subscriptions and 300 resource groups
- Requirement: Existing hierarchy must not change; Notes: Policy and role assignments are already in place and must keep inheriting as before
- Requirement: A resource in more than one view; Notes: Team, project and environment views over the same resources
- Requirement: Least privilege; Notes: Viewers must see the view without being able to change the resources in it
prompt: The team should create _____ for that view.

options.text: Service groups
Management groups
Resource groups
Azure tags

explanation:
Service groups are created at tenant level in the Microsoft.Management resource provider and let resources, resource groups and subscriptions from anywhere in the hierarchy be connected into a single group without reorganizing the existing hierarchy. A resource can belong to several groups at once, which supports the team, project and environment views, and permissions on a service group don't grant access to the resources it contains, which keeps the team on least privilege.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Management groups: Management groups build the governance hierarchy above subscriptions so that access and policies inherit downward. They are not a grouping for resources shared across scope boundaries, and every subscription can have only one parent.
- Resource groups: Resource groups exist inside a single subscription and are used for the deployment and lifecycle of closely related resources, so they can't span the 40 subscriptions in this scenario.
- Azure tags: Tags are metadata added to individual resources. They can be used as criteria in policy, but they don't create a container, don't aggregate resources into a view and carry no permission inheritance.

context:
A move of subscription sub-retail-01 out of contoso-sales and into contoso-eu was rejected this morning. Your role assignments on the three scopes involved are listed below. Which change would allow the move to succeed?

- Scope: sub-retail-01 (the subscription being moved); Your role assignments: Owner
- Scope: contoso-sales (its current parent management group); Your role assignments: Reader
- Scope: contoso-eu (the target parent management group); Your role assignments: Owner
prompt: To allow the move, you should _____.

options.text: Grant a role that includes Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/write on contoso-sales
Grant a role that includes Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write on contoso-eu
Grant a role that includes Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/subscriptions/write on contoso-sales
Grant a role that includes Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/write on contoso-eu

explanation:
A move is evaluated at three layers: the child subscription being moved, the target parent management group and the current parent management group. Each layer needs Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/write. Owner already gives you that on sub-retail-01 and on contoso-eu, but Reader on contoso-sales only reads, so write on the current parent is the missing piece.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Grant a role that includes Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write on contoso-eu: Owner on contoso-eu already includes Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write, and extra role assignment rights on the target parent aren't what's missing.
- Grant a role that includes Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/subscriptions/write on contoso-sales: Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/subscriptions/write is required on the child subscription, where you already hold Owner. Granting it on the current parent doesn't satisfy the current-parent requirement, which is Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/write.
- Grant a role that includes Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/write on contoso-eu: Owner on contoso-eu already includes Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/write, so granting it again on that scope changes nothing.

context:
Your security team must review every role assignment and policy assignment change recorded against contoso-corp in one place, including changes made outside the Azure portal, and must forward those records to their long-term monitoring platform for retention. Which approach should they configure?

- Requirement: One place to review changes; Notes: Role assignment and policy assignment events recorded against contoso-corp
- Requirement: Include events raised outside the portal; Notes: Automation, template deployments and CLI activity
- Requirement: Retention; Notes: Records must be kept for 400 days for compliance
- Requirement: Blast radius; Notes: Only contoso-corp is in scope, not the rest of the tenant
prompt: The team should configure _____.

options.text: Diagnostic settings that route its activity log entries to Log Analytics
A policy assignment that audits resources in every subscription beneath it
A role assignment that gives the security team the Monitoring Reader role on it
A scheduled Get-AzManagementGroup -GroupId contoso-corp script that exports the hierarchy

explanation:
Management groups are supported in Azure Monitor activity logs, so events such as role assignment and policy assignment changes made to contoso-corp can be queried in the same central place as other Azure resources, whether the change came from the portal or from automation. Using the Azure Resource Manager REST API, diagnostic settings can be enabled on the management group to send those activity log entries to a Log Analytics workspace, Azure Storage or Azure Event Hubs, which satisfies the retention requirement.

Why the other options are wrong:
- A policy assignment that audits resources in every subscription beneath it: A policy assignment defines the allowed or denied state of resources and doesn't capture a stream of historical events, so it can't satisfy a review or retention requirement.
- A role assignment that gives the security team the Monitoring Reader role on it: A role assignment only grants permissions. The Monitoring Reader role lets a team query monitoring data but creates no forwarding of that scope's records to another system.
- A scheduled Get-AzManagementGroup -GroupId contoso-corp script that exports the hierarchy: Get-AzManagementGroup returns the management group object and its hierarchy as it stands at the time it runs. It doesn't return the history of changes, and nothing forwards those records anywhere.

explanation:
With hierarchy protection not enabled, any user in the tenant can create a management group without already holding management group write permission. The new group is placed under the root management group (or the default management group), and the service automatically gives the creator an Owner role assignment on it, so no permission has to be granted beforehand.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the request is blocked until a Global Administrator elevates that person's access to the root management group: Elevating access at the root management group is what a Microsoft Entra Global Administrator does so they can start assigning roles to other people; it isn't a prerequisite for a user with no permissions to create a management group when hierarchy protection is off.
- no permission check blocks the request, and the creator receives a Reader role assignment: The role assignment the service creates for the account that creates the group is Owner, which grants full control over the new group. Reader is read-only and gives the person nothing they can administer with.
- no permission check blocks the request, and the creator receives a Management Group Contributor role assignment: Management Group Contributor permits creating, renaming and deleting child management groups, but it isn't the role the service grants automatically to the account that creates a management group.

prompt: You are rolling out a new tag policy across a subscription. You first want to see which existing resources are missing the required tag so you can communicate with resource owners, but you don't want to alter any resources or block new deployments yet. After the report is reviewed, you intend to switch to a stricter setting. Which effect should the initial policy assignment use?

options.text: audit
deny
modify
deployIfNotExists

explanation:
The audit effect records the compliance state of existing and new resources in the dashboard but does not change the resources or block new deployments. The Azure Policy overview recommends starting with an audit or auditIfNotExists effect so that you can see the impact on your environment before switching to an enforcement effect.

Why the other options are wrong:
- deny: deny blocks the resource action; it would prevent the resource from being created or updated, which is exactly what the scenario is trying to avoid for the initial assessment.
- modify: modify adds or updates fields (such as tags) on the resource at create or update time; it would alter resource state rather than just report on it.
- deployIfNotExists: deployIfNotExists deploys a related template (such as a diagnostic setting) when the condition matches; it changes the environment instead of only reporting on it.

prompt: Your team bundles multiple occurrences of the same built-in tag policy inside a single initiative so they can be assigned together. The policyReferences portion of the initiative definition appears below. Each occurrence should map to a different tag-name value at assignment time. Per the documentation, how does the initiative distinguish these two occurrences?

options.text: Each occurrence is given a unique reference ID that you supply when adding the policy to the initiative.
The initiative automatically appends a numeric suffix to the policy's displayName.
Azure Policy rejects the initiative because the same policy definition cannot be referenced twice.
The second occurrence silently overrides the first one during the assignment.

explanation:
When you add a policy definition to an initiative that already contains that policy, each occurrence is given a distinct reference ID you choose, which is also what you reference from the initiative's parameters. The create-and-manage tutorial describes this: when the same definition is added twice, each entry gets a different reference ID so the initiative can configure each occurrence with different parameter values during the assignment.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The initiative automatically appends a numeric suffix to the policy's displayName: Initiatives do not auto-rewrite the displayName of a member policy; they rely on the reference ID rather than displayName to disambiguate duplicate policies.
- Azure Policy rejects the initiative because the same policy definition cannot be referenced twice: Azure Policy does accept the same policy definition more than once inside an initiative; the create-and-manage tutorial explicitly adds the same tag policy twice and assigns each instance a different reference ID.
- The second occurrence silently overrides the first one during the assignment: The second entry is not silently dropped or merged. Both occurrences are kept in the initiative and each applies independently with its own reference ID and parameter values.

prompt: A developer authors a custom policy that requires every resource group in scope to carry a specific tag. The relevant portion of the policy definition JSON is shown below. The mode property was left blank by mistake. Per the documentation, which mode value should the developer set so that the rule also evaluates resource groups (and not only resources that support tags and locations)?

options.text: "all"
"Indexed"
"Microsoft.Kubernetes.Data"
"Microsoft.KeyVault.Data"

explanation:
The 'all' mode evaluates resource groups, subscriptions, and resource types. Per the definition-structure basics docs, policies that enforce location or tags on a resource group or subscription must set mode to 'all' and specifically target the Microsoft.Resources/subscriptions/resourceGroups or Microsoft.Resources/subscriptions type. Leaving mode blank in Azure CLI results in a null value that behaves like Indexed, which would not evaluate resource groups — so the developer needs to explicitly set 'all'.

Why the other options are wrong:
- "Indexed": The 'Indexed' mode only evaluates resource types that support tags and location; resource groups are skipped, which defeats the purpose of a policy that targets Microsoft.Resources/subscriptions/resourceGroups.
- "Microsoft.Kubernetes.Data": 'Microsoft.Kubernetes.Data' is a Resource Provider mode used for managing Kubernetes cluster components like pods, containers, and ingresses — not for resource group tag enforcement.
- "Microsoft.KeyVault.Data": 'Microsoft.KeyVault.Data' is a Resource Provider mode used for managing Key Vault vaults and certificates — not for resource group tag enforcement.

prompt: You assign a built-in policy whose rule applies a default tag and its value to resources that don't already carry it. The assignment is also set to create a remediation task so existing resources are updated. Per the documentation, what is automatically created and granted the necessary permissions so the assignment can apply those changes?

options.text: A system-assigned managed identity with the Contributor role on the assignment scope
A user-assigned managed identity with the Contributor role on the assignment scope
A system-assigned managed identity with the Reader role on the assignment scope
A Microsoft Entra application with a client secret and the Contributor role on the assignment scope

explanation:
Assignments that use the modify or deployIfNotExists effects require an identity so the assignment can alter or deploy resources. The create-and-manage tutorial walks through exactly this scenario: 'Create a Managed Identity is automatically checked since this policy definition uses the modify effect. Type of Managed Identity is set to System Assigned. Permissions is set to Contributor automatically based on the policy definition.' The system identity is created on the assignment and granted the Contributor role at the scope of the assignment.

Why the other options are wrong:
- A user-assigned managed identity with the Contributor role on the assignment scope: Azure Policy assignments do not create user-assigned managed identities; they only auto-provision a system-assigned identity. A user-assigned identity would need to be created separately and referenced.
- A system-assigned managed identity with the Reader role on the assignment scope: The Reader role only permits reading resources. The modify effect must write tags onto existing resources, which requires write permissions like Contributor.
- A Microsoft Entra application with a client secret and the Contributor role on the assignment scope: Azure Policy assignments do not register a Microsoft Entra application with a client secret. They provision a managed identity associated with the assignment itself.

prompt: Your organization has two policy assignments on overlapping scopes. Their definitions are shown below. A user attempts to deploy a new resource into the Finance scope using a location allowed by the Finance-rg row but blocked by the row on the subscription. According to the documentation, what is the result?

options.text: The deployment is prevented because both are evaluated and the parent's restriction also applies.
The deployment succeeds because the more specific child scope overrides the parent.
The deployment succeeds because the assignment created most recently takes precedence.
The deployment succeeds because the more permissive child rule overrides the parent.

explanation:
Azure Policy evaluates every assignment that applies to a resource scope, and the resulting behavior is cumulative-most-restrictive. From the policy effects page: 'If both policy 1 and policy 2 had a deny effect, a resource would be blocked by the overlapping and conflicting policy definitions... Each assignment is individually evaluated. As such, there isn't an opportunity for a resource to slip through a gap from differences in scope.' Because the subscription assignment still denies the requested location, the deployment is blocked even though the child resource group assignment would otherwise allow it. To let the Finance scope accept extra regions, the subscription assignment must be excluded or amended for that scope.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The deployment succeeds because the more specific child scope overrides the parent: A child-scope assignment does not override its parent. Both assignments are evaluated independently and the parent's restriction remains in force.
- The deployment succeeds because the assignment created most recently takes precedence: Azure Policy does not pick a winner by creation time. All assignments that match the resource scope are evaluated together, not just the newest one.
- The deployment succeeds because the more permissive child rule overrides the parent: A more permissive child assignment does not override a more restrictive parent. The union of applicable assignments is cumulative-most-restrictive, so the parent's deny still applies.

prompt: Your team needs to create a custom policy definition and assign it to resources across three different subscriptions in your organization. The three subscriptions are direct children of the same management group. Where should you save the policy definition so it can be assigned to resources in all three subscriptions?

options.text: In one of the three subscriptions
In a resource group inside one of the three subscriptions
In the management group that contains the three subscriptions
In a management group that does not contain the three subscriptions

explanation:
Per the documentation, the definition location determines which scopes the policy can be assigned to. A subscription-scoped definition can only be assigned within that same subscription. A management-group-scoped definition can only be assigned to child management groups and child subscriptions. To assign a policy definition to several subscriptions, the location must be a management group that contains each subscription. The shared parent management group contains all three subscriptions as children, so saving the definition there enables assignment to all three.

Why the other options are wrong:
- In one of the three subscriptions: A policy definition stored at the subscription scope can only be assigned to resources within that same subscription. Selecting one of the three subscriptions would prevent the definition from being assigned to the other two subscriptions.
- In a resource group inside one of the three subscriptions: A policy definition must be stored at the subscription or management group scope; resource group is not a valid definition location. Even if a resource group were valid, the definition must be reusable across all three subscriptions, not just one.
- In a management group that does not contain the three subscriptions: A management group that does not contain the target subscriptions cannot have the definition assigned to them, because the management group's assignments can only target its own child scopes.

prompt: You're authoring a custom policy definition to enforce pod-level settings in a managed container service on Azure. The JSON snippet below shows the policy structure with the mode field left blank. Per the documentation, which value should fill the blank?

options.text: all
indexed
Microsoft.Kubernetes.Data
Microsoft.KeyVault.Data

explanation:
Per the documentation, Microsoft.Kubernetes.Data is the Resource Provider mode for managing Kubernetes clusters and components such as pods, containers, and ingresses, supported for Azure Kubernetes Service clusters and Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes clusters. When a custom policy must evaluate pod-level properties (not general Resource Manager properties), the policy definition must specify this mode so the engine knows how to evaluate the resources.

Why the other options are wrong:
- all: The 'all' mode applies to general Resource Manager properties across subscriptions, resource groups, and resource types. It does not enable evaluation of pod-level Kubernetes components.
- indexed: The 'indexed' mode is restricted to resources that support tags and location. Pod-level Kubernetes components fall outside that scope.
- Microsoft.KeyVault.Data: Microsoft.KeyVault.Data is for managing vaults, certificates, and secrets in Azure Key Vault, not Kubernetes pods or cluster components.

prompt: Your organization has several service identities and user accounts that interact with Azure resources. You need to author a custom policy rule that distinguishes between these identity types so it can block resource deletions when they are initiated by a user account but still allow deletes triggered by an automated service identity. Per the documentation, which policy rule construct can be used to inspect the identity of the requestor?

options.text: principalType()
requestContext().identity
caller()
resourceGroup().identity

explanation:
Per the documentation, the requestContext().identity property in policy rules provides access to identity information about who is making the request. This enables identity-aware rules that can block or allow actions based on the calling principal (for example, blocking deletes initiated by a user account while allowing those initiated by an automated service principal).

Why the other options are wrong:
- principalType(): principalType() is not a documented Azure Policy rule construct for inspecting requestor identity; Azure Policy rules do not expose requestor information through a function with that name.
- caller(): caller() is not a documented Azure Policy rule construct for inspecting the calling identity. The documentation identifies requestContext().identity as the construct that exposes identity information.
- resourceGroup().identity: resourceGroup() in Azure Policy rules returns information about the resource group context, not the identity of the requestor. The .identity suffix on this construct does not retrieve requestor identity.

context: Your platform team is trialling a new assignment in the production subscription that deploys a diagnostic setting to storage accounts. During the trial, application teams must not have their deployments rejected or altered by the assignment, the compliance state of accounts that already exist still needs to be reported, and the team wants to launch a remediation task for the accounts that are already missing the setting. According to the documentation, which value should the assignment use for enforcementMode?
prompt: The assignment should use the enforcementMode value _____.

options.text: Default
DoNotEnforce
Enroll

explanation:
DoNotEnforce is the setting that leaves the assignment in place for evaluation without applying its effect when resources are created or updated, so application deployments are neither rejected nor altered while compliance is still reported for resources that already exist. The assignment-structure documentation also states that remediation tasks can still be started for deployIfNotExists policies when enforcementMode is set to DoNotEnforce, which is exactly what the team needs for the accounts already missing the setting.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Default: Default is the standard setting and enforces the policy effect for all resources in scope during creation or update, so deployments that don't satisfy the rule would be blocked or altered — the opposite of what this trial requires.
- Enroll: Enroll makes the assignment available for staged enforcement through policy enrollments, where the effect applies only once a scope owner creates an enrollment resource for a given scope. It isn't the setting that simply stops enforcement while leaving remediation tasks available.

context: A regulator granted your team a time-limited waiver for a single production resource group, and the waiver is recorded on an exception ticket with a scheduled end date. The resource group must still show up in compliance reporting with its waived state visible to auditors, and the rules assigned above it should no longer be assessed there. According to the documentation, which should you create?
prompt: To implement the waiver, you should create _____.

options.text: A policy exemption on the resource group
An exclusion in the assignment's notScopes array
A resource selector in the assignment
A policy group in the initiative definition

explanation:
A policy exemption is created on the resource hierarchy or individual resource as a child object, identifies a portion of an assignment that isn't evaluated, and leaves those resources showing as Exempted in compliance reports so they can still be tracked. It can also be configured to expire on a schedule through the expiresOn property, which matches the time-limited waiver with an end date, and it can be granted to a resource that is exempt from multiple assignments.

Why the other options are wrong:
- An exclusion in the assignment's notScopes array: notScopes removes the resource group from the assignment entirely, so its resources are neither evaluated nor counted in the compliance state — the waived resource would disappear from reporting rather than appear with a waived status. It also requires editing the policy assignment object rather than adding something at the resource group.
- A resource selector in the assignment: A resource selector narrows which resources an assignment is evaluated for based on characteristics such as resource location or resource type. It has no expiry behavior and doesn't record a reason for waiving assessment.
- A policy group in the initiative definition: A policy group inside an initiative definition only categorizes the policy definitions included in the initiative (the Regulatory Compliance feature uses these groups as controls). It doesn't stop evaluation for any resource group.

prompt: Azure Policy reads this definitionVersion value as _____.

options.text: It stays on the major.minor version the engineer selected and automatically takes every text-level fix
It always follows the latest major version of the definition and automatically takes new minor versions and text-level fixes
It stays on the major.minor version the engineer selected and never picks up anything further for the life of the assignment
It follows every major version of the definition, including ones Microsoft publishes after the assignment was created

explanation:
The '#.#.*' format holds the assignment to the chosen major and minor version path, and the trailing wildcard means updates at the remaining level are ingested automatically. The documentation states that all patch changes must be autoingested for security reasons, and that patch changes are limited to text changes and break glass scenarios — which is exactly the combination the team needs.

Why the other options are wrong:
- It always follows the latest major version of the definition and automatically takes new minor versions and text-level fixes: That describes the default behaviour of an assignment, where the latest major version is used and minor and patch changes are ingested automatically. Choosing it would move the assignment onto any new minor version as soon as one is released.
- It stays on the major.minor version the engineer selected and never picks up anything further for the life of the assignment: There's no way to use the wildcard to stop ingestion: text-level changes are always picked up automatically, so an assignment written this way doesn't freeze at the version it was pinned to.
- It follows every major version of the definition, including ones Microsoft publishes after the assignment was created: A wildcard never causes an assignment to follow future major versions. Moving to a later major version has to be an explicit choice made in the first number of the version string.

context: Your team wrote a custom deployIfNotExists definition in its own tenant that deploys a diagnostic setting to storage accounts. Remediation fails during deployment because the assignment's managed identity has no permission to create that setting, and built-in definitions aren't an option for this rule. According to the documentation, which property must the custom definition declare so that the identity can be given the access it needs?
prompt: The custom definition must declare _____.

options.text: details.roleDefinitionIds
metadata.roleDefinitionIds
parameters.roleDefinitionIds
identity.roleDefinitionIds

explanation:
For a custom deployIfNotExists or modify definition, the roles required to deploy the template or apply the change are declared in the roleDefinitionIds array inside the details property, and each entry is the full resource identifier of a role rather than the short role name. Once declared, the managed identity on the assignment must be granted those roles before a remediation task can run; built-in definitions already have these roles prepopulated.

- metadata.roleDefinitionIds: The metadata property stores descriptive values such as category, version, preview, or deprecated that drive how the definition is listed and displayed in the portal. It doesn't carry the roles the assignment identity needs.

options.text: Create two resource groups, splitting the four resources so each group holds resources with the same lifecycle and can be deployed, updated, and deleted as one unit.

explanation:
All resources in a resource group should share the same lifecycle - you deploy, update, and delete them together. In the exhibit, the two storefront resources change weekly with the release train and are replaced when the storefront is retired, while the two data resources change rarely and are retained for seven years for audit. Putting each pair in its own group keeps every group on one lifecycle, so each can be changed or removed as a unit without disturbing the other team's resources.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Create four resource groups, one per resource, so each resource has a lifecycle of its own and can be deployed, updated, and deleted as one unit: One group per resource gives every item a private lifecycle but gives up the main purpose of the container: resources that genuinely belong together can no longer be deployed, updated, or deleted together as a single unit.
- Create two resource groups, splitting by owning team, so each team's resources can be deployed, updated, and deleted as one unit even when their lifecycles differ: Team ownership isn't lifecycle. The Data team's two resources change on quite different cycles, and the Storefront team's two resources change together, so grouping by team mixes lifecycles in one group and separates matching ones across groups.
- Create one resource group per Azure region, so each region's resources can be deployed, updated, and deleted as one unit regardless of their lifecycle: Geographic grouping ignores lifecycle entirely. It splits resources that belong on the same schedule across separate groups, and it forces resources with very different schedules into one group, so a change or removal can't be handled as one coordinated operation.

- Aspect of the deployment: Resource group; Observed value: rg-commerce
- Aspect of the deployment: Value entered when the group was created; Observed value: East US
- Aspect of the deployment: Region hosting the web app and the storage account; Observed value: West Europe
- Aspect of the deployment: Traffic reaching the web app; Observed value: HTTPS requests sent to the app's own endpoint

prompt: Shaped by the value entered at creation time

options.text: Where the metadata about the group's resources is kept
How create, update, and delete requests that target the group's resources are routed
Rerouting calls to management.azure.com to a backup area when the group's own region is unavailable
Read and write calls sent straight to a storage account's data endpoint
Serving a web app to browsers over HTTPS
Keeping a storage account's data reachable when the location hosting that account fails

explanation: The location supplied when a resource group is created decides where the group's metadata about its resources is stored, and control plane operations (create, update, delete) that target resources in the group are routed through that location, so the metadata location, the routing of those calls, and the automatic rerouting of them to a backup region when the group's region is temporarily unavailable all follow the value entered at creation time. Data plane traffic - HTTPS requests to a web app's endpoint and read/write requests sent directly to a storage account - goes straight to the resource endpoints, so the group's location has no bearing on it. When the region that actually hosts a resource fails, data plane access to that resource is affected no matter where its resource group is located, which is outside the rerouting Resource Manager performs for control plane operations.

context:
You have prepared a single move request that lists more than 800 resources from `rg-legacy` to `rg-app` in the same subscription. Every submission is rejected before anything is relocated, and the operations lead wants the migration completed this week. You need to adjust your plan so the relocation succeeds. Which change should you make?

- Item: Entries in the request; Value: 812 resources, each given by its full resource ID
- Item: Source; Value: rg-legacy (subscription sub-retail)
- Item: Destination; Value: rg-app (subscription sub-retail)
- Item: Entries whose parent has child resources; Value: 37
- Item: Result of the last two submissions; Value: Rejected; nothing relocated
prompt: The change you make is to _____.

options.text: Split the work into several smaller batches.
Retry the same submission until the service accepts it.
Remove the entries for parent resources that have child resources.
Ask the owner of the destination subscription to raise its per-group instance limit.

explanation:
Resource Manager turns a move submission away straight away once it carries more than 800 resources, so a single oversized submission can never succeed no matter how it is re-sent. The documented remedy is to break a large migration into separate, smaller move operations, which also lowers the chance of one of them timing out.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Retry the same submission until the service accepts it: Repeating the identical oversized submission produces the same rejection; nothing about waiting changes the entry count that triggers the error.
- Remove the entries for parent resources that have child resources: Whether a parent or one of its children is listed doesn't change how many entries are counted against the limit, and child resources travel with their parent anyway. Removing those 37 entries leaves the submission well over the maximum, so it still fails.
- Ask the owner of the destination subscription to raise its per-group instance limit: The per-group instance limit is about how many instances of one resource type can live in a single resource group. Raising it says nothing about how many resources one move submission may carry, so the oversized request is still refused.

context:
Your team deploys everything for a retail solution through Azure Resource Manager, and the resource group `rg-sales` sits in the Sweden Central region. That region becomes temporarily unavailable. You need to explain to the operations team what happens to each type of request. Which statement should you give them?

- Item: Resource group; Detail: rg-sales
- Item: Region set when the group was created; Detail: Sweden Central
- Item: How the team deploys; Detail: Azure Resource Manager templates and SDKs
- Item: Status of the region; Detail: Temporarily unavailable
- Item: Endpoints the team calls directly; Detail: Application URL and storage endpoint
prompt: The guidance you give the team is: _____.

options.text: Control plane requests routed through the resource group are rerouted to a backup region, while data plane requests are not.
Control plane requests routed through the resource group are rerouted to a backup region, and data plane requests are too.
Control plane requests routed through the resource group are rerouted to a backup region, but every data plane request fails.
Control plane requests routed through the resource group are not rerouted, and data plane requests fail until the region recovers.

explanation:
When the region holding a resource group is unavailable, Azure Resource Manager sends control plane requests aimed at that group to a backup region without the client changing any endpoint, so deployments and other management calls keep working. That handling applies only to control plane traffic that passes through Resource Manager; requests the team sends straight to an application's URL or a storage endpoint are untouched by it.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Control plane requests routed through the resource group are rerouted to a backup region, and data plane requests are too: The automatic rerouting is limited to control plane operations handled by Resource Manager. Requests that go directly to a resource's own endpoint are outside its scope, so they are not rerouted along with the management calls.
- Control plane requests routed through the resource group are rerouted to a backup region, but every data plane request fails: Nothing in the resource group behaviour stops direct requests from working. They simply aren't part of the rerouting; that traffic is only affected if the region hosting the resource itself is unavailable.
- Control plane requests routed through the resource group are not rerouted, and data plane requests fail until the region recovers: This has the rerouting backwards. Resource Manager does send control plane requests for a resource group to a backup region when the group's region is unavailable, and it does so transparently, so the group does not go dark for the whole outage.

context:
Your team has a resource group of virtual machines and storage accounts in East US. A data residency rule now requires the workload to run in West Europe, and the group is in subscription `sub-prod`. You need to relocate everything. Which approach should you take?

- Item: Current resource group; Detail: rg-app, located in East US
- Item: Contents; Detail: 40 virtual machines and their storage accounts
- Item: Region the resources run in; Detail: East US
- Item: Required location; Detail: West Europe
prompt: The approach to take is to _____.

options.text: Use Azure Resource Mover to move the resources across regions from the resource group.
Use the Move button's Move to a new subscription option and target a subscription in the West Europe region.
Use the Move button's Move to a new resource group option and target a group in the West Europe region.
Move each resource one at a time into new resource groups that you create in the West Europe region.

explanation:
A standard relocation only changes the container a resource is associated with; the resource stays in the physical location it was deployed to. Changing where a workload runs is a separate capability, and the portal points this scenario at Azure Resource Mover for moving resources to a different region.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Use the Move button's Move to a new subscription option and target a subscription in the West Europe region: Choosing another subscription changes only which subscription holds the resources. Every virtual machine and storage account remains in the region it was deployed to.
- Use the Move button's Move to a new resource group option and target a group in the West Europe region: The same limitation applies: resources can sit in a different region than their group, so moving them into a group located in West Europe leaves them running in East US.
- Move each resource one at a time into new resource groups that you create in the West Europe region: Moving items one at a time repeats the same container change, and relocating a resource never alters the region it runs in, so nothing would serve from West Europe.

context:
You want a chargeback report that lists the assets belonging to the retail cost center. The value is already set on the subscription and on the resource group, yet the report returns none of the resources held in that group. You need the report to pick them up. Which action should you take?

- Scope: Subscription sub-retail; Tags currently set: CostCenter = 1420
- Scope: Resource group rg-retail; Tags currently set: CostCenter = 1420
- Scope: Storage account stdata (in rg-retail); Tags currently set: Env = prod
- Scope: Web app shop-prod (in rg-retail); Tags currently set: Env = prod
prompt: The action to take is to _____.

options.text: Add the tag to every resource inside the group.
Add the tag to the management group that sits above the subscription.
Add the tag to a policy assignment scoped to the resource group.
Add the tag to the resource group only and wait for the resources to pick it up.

explanation:

submit a request that names only the two attached extensions, because the parent stays in the current group
submit a request that names the parent virtual machine and both attached extensions, because each entry is processed on its own
submit three requests, one for the parent virtual machine and one for each attached extension

explanation:
A move request should list only the top-level (parent) resources. Child resources, such as the extensions of a virtual machine, follow their parent automatically and cannot be moved independently. Naming just the virtual machine therefore relocates the machine and both of its extensions in a single operation, which is what the consolidation needs.

Why the other options are wrong:
- submit a request that names only the two attached extensions, because the parent stays in the current group: The extensions are child resources of the virtual machine and can't be moved on their own. A request that names only the extensions is rejected, which is the failure you already hit.

explanation:

Why the other options are wrong:
- Your data is kept for a while and then permanently deleted 7 days after the cancellation, and you aren't charged for the kept data: Permanent deletion of the data happens 30 to 90 days after the cancellation, not 7 days.
- Your data is erased as soon as the cancellation completes, and you receive a refund for the unused days of the billing period: Azure doesn't erase your data as soon as you cancel; it keeps it temporarily in case you reactivate the subscription, and canceling doesn't give back the unused days of the billing period.

prompt: Your company records ownership with a costCenter tag on every resource group. The resources inside those groups carry no such metadata today, and you want the ones that already exist to pick it up along with anything deployed from now on. Which policy definition should you assign?

options.text: Inherit a tag from the resource group
Append a tag and its value from the resource group
Require a tag and its value on resources
Add or replace a tag on resource groups

explanation:
'Inherit a tag from the resource group' copies the tag name and its value from the parent resource group onto every resource in scope each time that resource is created or updated, and a remediation task can be run so resources deployed earlier pick the value up as well. That matches the exhibit: the groups already carry costCenter, while the virtual machine and storage account inside have nothing.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Append a tag and its value from the resource group: 'Append a tag and its value from the resource group' only supplies the pair to a resource that is missing the tag, so a resource already holding a different value keeps it, and it leaves resources created before the assignment untouched until they are changed. It would not push 4711 and 4712 onto the existing members.
- Require a tag and its value on resources: 'Require a tag and its value on resources' uses the deny effect, so it evaluates whether a resource carries the expected pair and blocks the deployment when it does not; it never supplies the value from the resource group, so the members shown in the exhibit would still go untagged and deployments would fail.
- Add or replace a tag on resource groups: 'Add or replace a tag on resource groups' targets resource groups only. The groups in the exhibit already hold the right value, and vm-web-01 and stwebprod01 would remain without costCenter.

For storage accounts the tag name may be at most 128 characters, and stappdata01 arrives with a 200-character name. That exceeds the limit imposed on that resource type, so the request carrying those pairs is the one that fails.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The storage account, because it carries more tag pairs than that resource type allows: Twelve pairs is well inside the ceiling that applies to a resource, a resource group or a subscription, which is 50 name-value pairs. The storage account is rejected because of the name length, not the count.
- The virtual machine, because its tag name is longer than the maximum length allowed for that resource type: Virtual machines accept tag names of up to 512 characters, and 480 characters is under that, so vm-sales01 is not the problem.
- The public IP address, because it carries more tag pairs than that resource type allows: Public IP addresses are not one of the resource types capped at 15 tags, and 20 pairs is also below the general ceiling of 50, so pip-sales01 is accepted.

Resource

options.text: The role grants Microsoft.Resources/tags write access but does not let the user apply tags on resources via the Azure portal
The Azure portal enforces a built-in Owner assignment on every resource before saving tag changes
The PowerShell cmdlet writes tags via a service principal that bypasses Azure role checks
Subscription-scope roles are not enforced during Azure portal sessions of the same user

explanation:
The Tag Contributor role grants write access to the Microsoft.Resources/tags resource type, which permits tag operations through Azure PowerShell and the REST API. The role, however, does not let you apply tags to resources or resource groups through the Azure portal; the portal requires a role on the resource itself (such as Contributor) for the Tags blade to save changes, which is why op2 in action 3 succeeds while op1 in action 2 is denied.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The Azure portal enforces a built-in Owner assignment on every resource before saving tag changes: Tag changes succeed from the portal when the operator has a role (such as Contributor) that grants write access on the resource. The portal does not require the built-in Owner role for tag operations.
- The PowerShell cmdlet writes tags via a service principal that bypasses Azure role checks: PowerShell does not bypass Azure role checks. The success of action 1 is the same Tag Contributor role that the portal rejects in action 2; the difference is the interface, not any privileged code path.
- Subscription-scope roles are not enforced during Azure portal sessions of the same user: Subscription-scope role assignments are honored during Azure portal sessions. The difference between action 2 and action 3 is the role assigned to each user, not any propagation or scope issue.

prompt: The code block below is a truncated response from the Azure unique tags API. The monitoring tool flags the response as malformed because the same key appears twice. What property of the API explains the repetition?

options.text: The API re-emits the key on a subsequent page when additional values for it remain to be returned
The unique tags API treats each case variant of the key as a separate entry
The cost report duplicates the key each time a new tag value is added
The PATCH operation duplicates the key in the response when the resource supports more than 15 tags

explanation:
The unique tags API has a per-page size limit. When a tag key has more unique values than fit on one page, the API returns additional values on subsequent pages and re-emits the key at the start of those pages to signal that the values are still under that key. This pattern is expected behavior for the API and the presence of nextLink in the response indicates more data follows.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The unique tags API treats each case variant of the key as a separate entry: Tag names are case-insensitive for operations. The unique tags API matches them that way, so different casings of the key do not produce separate entries under the same logical key.
- The cost report duplicates the key each time a new tag value is added: The duplication observed here is a property of the unique tags API itself. The cost report uses the values stored by the provider and is unrelated to how the API response is shaped.
- The PATCH operation duplicates the key in the response when the resource supports more than 15 tags: The PATCH operation is unrelated to the unique tags API. The 15-tag limit applies to specific resource types such as Azure Automation and Azure Front Door; it does not produce a repeated key in the unique tags API response.
