context: Your tenant still shows a list of verification options on the Password reset blade, but since 30 September 2025 you can no longer add, remove, or change that list in that place. You want those options to remain enforced for the tenant going forward. Which action should you take?
prompt: The correct action is to _____.

options.text: migrate the settings to the Authentication methods policy
migrate the settings to the legacy multifactor authentication policy
migrate the settings to the tenant authorization policy
migrate the settings to the password reset properties page

explanation:
The tutorial states that managing authentication methods in the legacy multifactor authentication and self-service password reset policies is deprecated, and that beginning 30 September 2025 they can no longer be managed there. Customers are told to use the manual migration control to move to the Authentication methods policy by the deprecation date, so the configuration on the legacy blade must be migrated there.

Why the other options are wrong:
- migrate the settings to the legacy multifactor authentication policy: The legacy multifactor authentication policy is deprecated at the same time as the legacy self-service password reset policy, so it is not a valid destination for the settings.
- migrate the settings to the tenant authorization policy: The tenant authorization policy stores the AllowedToUseSspr property that governs whether administrator accounts can use self-service password reset; it does not store the user verification options.
- migrate the settings to the password reset properties page: The password reset properties page is the same legacy surface where these options can no longer be added or changed.

context: A member of staff can no longer sign in after too many failed attempts and recovers the account through the self-service portal. When asked for a new password, the user types the same one they used immediately before the lockout, and the portal accepts it. You need to confirm that this matches expected behavior for the tenant. Which statement is correct?
prompt: The portal accepted the value because _____.

options.text: a voluntary change blocks reuse of the previous password but a recovery does not
a recovery blocks reuse of the previous password but a voluntary change does not
both a voluntary change and a recovery block reuse of the previous password
neither a voluntary change nor a recovery blocks reuse of the previous password

explanation:
The password policy settings list password change history and password reset history as separate properties. Password change history stops a user from reusing the previous password when they change a password, while password reset history allows the last password to be used again when a user resets a forgotten password. So accepting the previous password during a portal recovery is expected.

Why the other options are wrong:
- a recovery blocks reuse of the previous password but a voluntary change does not: This reverses the rule: reuse is blocked for a voluntary password change, not for a recovery of a forgotten password.
- both a voluntary change and a recovery block reuse of the previous password: Recovering a forgotten password can reuse the previous password, so it isn't blocked in both cases.
- neither a voluntary change nor a recovery blocks reuse of the previous password: A voluntary password change does stop the previous password from being used again, so at least one of the two cases is blocked.

context:
You disabled self-service password reset for administrator accounts in the tenant. The exhibit shows the resulting configuration. People who hold an administrator role still get an interruption during every interactive sign-in telling them they can't store any verification details. You need that interruption to stop appearing for them. Which change should you make?

- Item: Tenant authorization policy - AllowedToUseSspr; Value: false
- Item: Password reset - Self service password reset enabled; Value: Selected
- Item: Group chosen for the Selected scope; Value: SSPR-Test-Group
- Item: Membership of SSPR-Test-Group; Value: 4 accounts holding Microsoft Entra administrator roles and 40 accounts holding none
- Item: Registration - Require users to register when signing in; Value: Yes
prompt: To stop the prompt, the administrator should _____.

options.text: remove the administrator accounts from the group SSPR is enabled for
remove the non-administrator accounts from the group SSPR is enabled for
add the administrator accounts to the group SSPR is enabled for
remove the administrator accounts from the included group in the Authentication methods policy

explanation:
When the password reset policy for administrators is disabled through the tenant authorization policy (AllowedToUseSspr set to false), administrators can't reset their passwords through SSPR even if they fall inside the user password reset scope. If registration is required and they are in that scope, they are still interrupted at sign-in but see a message saying they can't register any methods. The documented remedy is to explicitly exclude administrators from the password reset policy for users, which in the admin center means the group the feature is enabled for.

Why the other options are wrong:
- remove the non-administrator accounts from the group SSPR is enabled for: The accounts without administrator roles are the ones who can still use the feature, so removing them would remove working functionality instead of stopping the administrator prompt.
- add the administrator accounts to the group SSPR is enabled for: The administrator accounts are already in the scope group, so adding them changes nothing and the interruption continues.
- remove the administrator accounts from the included group in the Authentication methods policy: The included group in the Authentication methods policy controls where the centralized policy applies; it doesn't determine the scope that drives this prompt on the Password reset blade.

context: You must roll out self-service password reset to two separate pilot groups, HR-Pilot and Finance-Pilot, and keep the rollout limited to those pilots. The group picker on the Password reset blade in the Microsoft Entra admin center takes a single group at a time. Which approach should you use?
prompt: The approach is to _____.

options.text: make one of the groups a member of the other
assign both groups to the same administrative unit
apply a dynamic membership rule to both groups
convert both groups into a single directory role

explanation:
The tutorial notes that the admin center can enable one Microsoft Entra group for self-service password reset, and that as part of a wider deployment the service supports nested groups. Putting one pilot group inside the other lets a single selection in the group picker cover both sets of users while keeping the rollout limited to them.

Why the other options are wrong:
- assign both groups to the same administrative unit: Administrative units organize directory objects for management purposes; they don't determine which users the self-service password reset setting applies to.
- apply a dynamic membership rule to both groups: Dynamic membership rules populate a group from directory attributes such as department, but each rule fills its own group and doesn't let a single selection cover two separate groups.
- convert both groups into a single directory role: Directory roles assign privileges to administrators; they have no effect on which users are in scope for self-service password reset.

context: Some accounts in your tenant authenticate against an external directory, and their passwords are synchronized to the cloud copy. After one of these users recovers an account through the self-service portal, the page reports success, but the new value is rejected at sign-in for roughly two minutes. You need to explain the delay. Which statement explains it?
prompt: The delay happens because _____.

options.text: the change only updates the external directory and copying back into Microsoft Entra ID runs on a fixed interval
the portal waits for the user's phone to confirm the second factor before the change is applied
the change is queued until an administrator approves it in the admin center
the delay ends once the user's group membership is copied from the external directory

explanation:
For federated accounts whose passwords are synchronized, the source of authority stays in the external directory, so the portal updates the password only there. Synchronization back to Microsoft Entra ID is scheduled every two minutes, which is why the new value isn't accepted right away.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the portal waits for the user's phone to confirm the second factor before the change is applied: The second factor proves identity before the change; it isn't a step that runs afterwards, so it causes no delay.
- the change is queued until an administrator approves it in the admin center: Self-service password reset finishes without an administrator approval step, so nothing waits in a queue.
- the delay ends once the user's group membership is copied from the external directory: Membership data doesn't carry the new password to the cloud; the wait comes from the fixed interval for copying password changes.

context: Your company uses Microsoft Entra ID with an on-premises Active Directory synchronized through Microsoft Entra Connect. Password writeback is enabled and SSPR is turned on for the HR-Pilot group. Locked-out employees report that the SSPR portal forces them to pick a new password each time they try to recover access. You need a configuration change so employees can recover access while keeping the existing password.
prompt: To achieve this, set the _____ option to [...] on the Password reset blade.

options.text: Allow users to unlock accounts without resetting their password
Notify users on password resets
Write back passwords to on-premises
Number of authentication methods required

explanation:
The 'Allow users to unlock accounts without resetting their password' option, when set to Yes, gives users a separate choice to unlock their on-premises account without going through a password reset. The No value combines unlock with a forced password reset, which is the symptom the locked-out employees describe.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Notify users on password resets: Notify users on password resets controls email notifications sent to the user's primary and alternate addresses when a reset happens; it does not affect whether an unlock can happen independently of a reset.
- Write back passwords to on-premises: Write back passwords to on-premises enables cloud-to-on-premises password synchronization and is already enabled in the scenario; it does not separate unlock from reset.
- Number of authentication methods required: Number of authentication methods required sets how many challenge methods the user must complete during a reset or unlock; it does not control whether an unlock can occur without a reset.

context:
`User properties supported in dynamic membership rules:
- user.objectId : GUID of the user object (null check selects all users)
- user.userType  : member | guest
- user.accountEnabled : true | false

Operators: -eq, -ne, -and, -or`
prompt: You create a new security group with a Dynamic User membership type in Microsoft Entra ID. The group must include every member user in the tenant while excluding every guest user. The membership should update on its own whenever user accounts change. Which rule should you enter?

options.text: user.objectId -ne null
(user.objectId -ne null) -and (user.userType -eq "Member")
user.accountEnabled -eq true
(user.objectId -ne null) -or (user.userType -eq "Member")

explanation:
Per the Microsoft Entra documentation on dynamic membership groups, to include every member user while excluding guest users, combine a non-null objectId check with a userType equality check joined with -and.

Why the other options are wrong:
- user.objectId -ne null: user.objectId -ne null returns every user object in the directory regardless of userType, so guest users would still be included.
- user.accountEnabled -eq true: user.accountEnabled -eq true returns every enabled user, which includes enabled guest accounts; it does not filter by user type.
- (user.objectId -ne null) -or (user.userType -eq "Member"): The -or operator makes either condition sufficient. Because user.objectId -ne null is true for every user, this rule includes both members and guests.

On the All Users page, select the users in groups of 60 or fewer, and run the Edit action for each group

explanation:
The Microsoft Entra documentation states that on the All Users page you can select up to 60 users at a time and update their attributes at once. With 150 users to update, you batch them in groups of 60 (or fewer) and run the Edit action for each group.

Why the other options are wrong:

User principal name
Display name
Job title

However, you can update Microsoft Entra ID attributes directly in the Microsoft Entra admin center, and Usage Location is given as the explicit example of such an attribute.

Why the other options are wrong:

context:
- Item: Metric alert rule 'CPU high'; Details: Scope: virtual machine scale set vmss-prod in resource group RG1. Attached action groups: ag-ops
- Item: Metric alert rule 'Disk queue high'; Details: Scope: virtual machine scale set vmss-worker in resource group RG1. Attached action groups: ag-ops
- Item: Azure Backup alerts for storage account stg-prod; Details: Raised by the Azure Backup service. No action groups are attached.
- Item: Patching window; Details: Every Saturday 22:00 to 02:00, repeating while the rollout continues
prompt: Your company runs a weekly patching window for a virtual machine scale set. While the window is open, on-call staff must stop getting SMS and email notifications for high CPU readings on that scale set, and the same must apply to backup job failures on a storage account in the same resource group, because those failures come from the Azure Backup service rather than from a rule you own. Alerts for slow disk queues on other virtual machines in that resource group must keep paging on-call, and every alert raised during the window must stay listed in the portal so the change can be audited afterwards. Which configuration should you use?

options.text: Create an alert processing rule scoped to the resource group that removes the action groups from the alerts matching the filter, during the maintenance window
Disable the 'CPU high' metric alert rule for the duration of the maintenance window so that no alerts are produced
Detach the SMS and email actions from the 'ag-ops' action group for the duration of the maintenance window
Create an alert processing rule scoped to the subscription that removes all action groups from every alert in the resource group, during the maintenance window

explanation:
An alert processing rule is the object that fits this requirement, because it changes alerts that have already fired instead of creating new ones: its suppression action removes the action groups from the affected fired alerts, its scope can run from a single resource up to a whole subscription in the same subscription, its filters (for example alert rule name, monitor service, resource type) narrow down which alerts it affects, and its scheduling tab can be set to a one-time or recurring window such as the weekly patching slot. Filtering on the 'CPU high' rule and on the Azure Backup alerts leaves 'Disk queue high' paging as the business requires, and because only the action groups are stripped, the fired alerts remain visible in the portal, Azure Resource Graph, the API and PowerShell, preserving the audit trail. Processing rules are also the documented way to act on alert sources such as Azure Backup that cannot select their own action groups. Keep in mind that a new or updated processing rule can take up to 30 minutes to take effect, and suppressed alerts skip the end-of-window resolved notification.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Disable the 'CPU high' metric alert rule for the duration of the maintenance window so that no alerts are produced: Turning the metric alert rule off means the rule never fires, so no alert instance is created for the CPU readings and nothing appears in the portal for the audit. It also has no effect on the backup job failures, because those alerts are not produced by that rule, and disabling and re-enabling a rule by hand every week is impractical when many rules cover the resource.
- Detach the SMS and email actions from the 'ag-ops' action group for the duration of the maintenance window: Action group edits are not time-bound: once the SMS and email actions are detached, every rule that uses 'ag-ops' stops notifying, including the disk queue rule that must keep paging, and re-attaching them by hand when the window closes is error-prone. Action group actions offer no schedule, so they cannot be limited to a recurring window.
- Create an alert processing rule scoped to the subscription that removes all action groups from every alert in the resource group, during the maintenance window: This is too broad. Scoping the rule to the subscription and stripping the action groups from every alert in the resource group also silences the disk queue alerts, so the on-call team would no longer be paged for a condition the business wants reported. The scope and filters need to be narrowed to the intended alerts so the remaining rules keep notifying.

context:
`Action group ........................ ag-payments
Action type ........................ Webhook
Endpoint ........................... https://tickets.contoso.example/azure-monitor-hook
Credentials ........................ basic auth passed in the URI
Endpoint reply ..................... HTTP 500 Internal Server Error
Second action in same group
  (SMS page to on-call engineer) ..... Delivered successfully`
prompt: You have an action group that opens a ticket in the company's ticketing system and pages the on-call engineer whenever the payment API breaches its latency threshold. After running the built-in test for the group, the ticketing endpoint answers every request with a server error while the page reaches the engineer. You need to know what happens to the ticketing call each time an alert fires. Which behavior should you expect?

options.text: The endpoint is called again up to five times, with delays of 5, 20, 5, 40 and 5 seconds, because an HTTP 500 response is among the failures that Azure Monitor retries.
The webhook action fails and the endpoint is not called again, since an HTTP 500 response is not among the failures Azure Monitor retries.

The webhook action fails on the first call, but the endpoint is called again five times after that because an HTTP 500 response is among the failures that Azure Monitor retries; the endpoint is then left alone for 15 minutes.

The webhook action is retried on every alert evaluation until the endpoint returns a success code; an HTTP 500 response is among the failures that Azure Monitor retries, so the notification keeps failing and is not dropped.

explanation:
Azure Monitor only retries a webhook call for a specific set of failures: the status codes 408, 429, 503 and 504, or the HttpRequestException, WebException and TaskCancellationException exceptions. A 500 response is not in that list, so the webhook action fails on the single call that was made and the endpoint is not contacted again for that notification. The multi-attempt schedule (up to five retries with delays of 5, 20, 5, 40 and 5 seconds, followed by no calls to the endpoint for 15 minutes) applies only to the failures that Azure Monitor can retry, so it does not apply here.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The endpoint is called again up to five times, with delays of 5, 20, 5, 40 and 5 seconds, because an HTTP 500 response is among the failures that Azure Monitor retries: The retry schedule itself is described correctly (up to five further attempts with delays of 5, 20, 5, 40 and 5 seconds), but it only applies to the failures that Azure Monitor can retry: status codes 408, 429, 503 and 504, or HttpRequestException, WebException and TaskCancellationException. An HTTP 500 response is outside that list, so the endpoint is not called again.
- The webhook action fails on the first call, but the endpoint is called again five times after that because an HTTP 500 response is among the failures that Azure Monitor retries; the endpoint is then left alone for 15 minutes: The five retries and the subsequent 15-minute pause belong to the failures that Azure Monitor can retry. Since a 500 response is not one of them, the webhook action fails on the first call and no further calls are made to the endpoint for that notification.
- The webhook action is retried on every alert evaluation until the endpoint returns a success code; an HTTP 500 response is among the failures that Azure Monitor retries, so the notification keeps failing and is not dropped: There is no repeating retry loop for a 500 response. Only the listed status codes and exceptions allow another call, so the action is simply failed for that notification instead of being retried until the endpoint recovers.

prompt: You have a metric alert rule that watches the percentage CPU metric on a production virtual machine, and the on-call rotation wants to know how many pings they will get during a long CPU spike, plus what the portal will display for the alert. The rule configuration is shown below. Which behavior should the on-call engineer expect?

options.text: Each check interval in which the CPU reading is above the learned band produces its own alert instance and its own notification, so the on-call engineer receives a repeating ping somewhere between one and six minutes.

The alert fires once, stays in the fired state while the condition keeps being met, and becomes resolved after the condition fails for three consecutive checks, at which point a resolved notification is sent.
The alert instance is removed from the portal 30 days after it was created even though the CPU reading is still above the learned band, and the rule then fires the same alert again.

Changing the user response from New to Acknowledged or Closed in the portal marks the alert as resolved and clears the alert condition, so the rule can fire again for the same CPU spike without any other action.

explanation:
The rule has Automatically resolve alerts enabled, so it is stateful: it fires a single time, its alert condition stays fired for as long as the CPU reading remains outside the learned band, and no further actions run in the meantime. For metric alerts the alert is treated as resolved only once the condition has failed on three checks in a row, and at that point the rule emits a resolved notification and the alert condition changes to resolved.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Each check interval in which the CPU reading is above the learned band produces its own alert instance and its own notification, so the on-call engineer receives a repeating ping somewhere between one and six minutes: This describes a stateless rule. Because Automatically resolve alerts is enabled, the rule fires one time and stops triggering actions until the alert is resolved, so the engineer gets a single notification rather than a repeating stream. The one-to-six-minute repetition cadence belongs to stateless metric rules whose frequency is under five minutes.
- The alert instance is removed from the portal 30 days after it was created even though the CPU reading is still above the learned band, and the rule then fires the same alert again: Alert instances are dropped from the portal after the 30-day retention window, but for a stateful alert the condition is retained until the alert resolves, precisely so the rule cannot fire the same alert again. The instance can disappear while the rule still refuses to re-fire for that condition, so the conclusion in this option is wrong.
- Changing the user response from New to Acknowledged or Closed in the portal marks the alert as resolved and clears the alert condition, so the rule can fire again for the same CPU spike without any other action: The user response (New, Acknowledged, or Closed) is maintained separately from the alert condition and only changes when someone changes it. Changing it neither resolves the alert nor resets the rule; a metric alert ends on its own once the condition has failed for three checks in a row.

prompt: You have an action group that must notify the order-processing service described below whenever an alert fires. The service has no public endpoint, and the notification must travel over the service's private network path. You need an action type that can deliver the notification to that service without making it reachable from the public internet. Which action type should you configure?

Secure webhook
Event hubs
Logic apps

explanation:
Event hubs is the only action type that supports Azure Private Link (and network security perimeter), so it is the way to deliver a notification to a target that is reachable only over a private network path and has no public endpoint. The target accepts the default Azure Monitor payload, so no payload reshaping is required.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Webhook: A Webhook calls an endpoint over the public internet and carries basic auth in the URI. Because the order-processing service has no public endpoint, a Webhook cannot deliver the notification to it.
- Secure webhook: A Secure webhook authenticates to a protected API with a Microsoft Entra ID service principal and does not use basic auth in the URI, but it does not support Azure Private Link, so it cannot reach a service available only over a private network path.
- Logic apps: Logic apps is appropriate when the payload has to be reshaped into a schema the target expects. Here the default Azure Monitor payload is accepted, and Logic apps does not provide Private Link support for delivering to the target.

context:
`Rule type                : Metric alert
Target                   : vm-prod-web-01 (Virtual Machine)
Signal                   : Percentage CPU
Condition                : Average greater than 90%
Check every              : 5 minutes
Lookback period          : 5 minutes
Enable upon creation     : Yes
Automatically resolve alerts : Yes`
prompt: You have a metric alert rule that watches the percentage CPU metric on a production virtual machine, configured as shown below. The rule already fired earlier today, and the average CPU dropped back under the threshold at 14:20 and stayed there. The on-call rotation wants to know when the portal will flip this alert over to a resolved state and send the resolved notification, so they can size the follow-up window. Which timing should they expect?

options.text: After one check finds the condition unmet — about 5 minutes later, at 14:25
After three consecutive checks find the condition unmet — about 15 minutes later, at 14:35
After two checks find the condition unmet — about 10 minutes later, at 14:30
After the lookback window closes with no further checks — about 5 minutes later, at 14:25

explanation:
Because Automatically resolve alerts is enabled, this metric rule is stateful: it fires once, stays in the Fired state, and only clears once the condition is no longer met. A metric alert resolves after three consecutive checks that find the condition unmet. With Check every set to 5 minutes, that covers about three evaluation intervals, so the alert moves to Resolved and the resolved notification is sent at roughly 14:35, about 15 minutes after the condition stopped being met at 14:20.

Why the other options are wrong:
- After one check finds the condition unmet — about 5 minutes later, at 14:25: One evaluation that no longer meets the condition does not clear a stateful metric alert. The alert remains fired until the condition has stayed unmet across three consecutive checks, so it would still be open at 14:25.
- After two checks find the condition unmet — about 10 minutes later, at 14:30: Two evaluations are not enough for a metric alert to resolve; the documented behavior is that it stays fired until the condition is unmet for three consecutive checks, which at a 5-minute interval lands at about 14:35, not 14:30.
- After the lookback window closes with no further checks — about 5 minutes later, at 14:25: The lookback period only determines which data points each evaluation considers — it does not terminate an alert. The alert still has to pass through the consecutive-check requirement before it is marked resolved and the resolved notification is sent.

context:
- Condition: 1; Signal: Blob service latency; Dimension filter: ApiName = GetBlob; Threshold: 200 ms; Operator: Greater than
- Condition: 2; Signal: Blob service latency; Dimension filter: ApiName = PutBlob; Threshold: 200 ms; Operator: Greater than
prompt: You have an alert rule on a storage account that must page on-call when the latency of either the GetBlob or the PutBlob operation exceeds 200 ms. You added a condition for each operation and filtered the ApiName dimension to the matching operation in each condition, but the portal refuses to save the rule. You need the paging to cover both operations, and you do not want the rule to evaluate operations that the team does not own. Which change should you make?

options.text: Create a separate alert rule for each operation value
Keep both conditions in the same alert rule and remove the ApiName dimension filter so the rule covers alerts for every operation
Keep both conditions in the same alert rule, set the ApiName dimension to GetBlob in both conditions, and add the wildcard value for all current and future values
Keep both conditions in the same alert rule and switch to a dynamic threshold so each condition can use a different dimension value

explanation:
A metric alert rule can carry only one value per dimension, and when two conditions share a dimension, both conditions must use the same value for it. GetBlob in the first condition and PutBlob in the second therefore cannot be saved together. Giving each operation its own alert rule with a single condition keeps the 200 ms threshold for that operation value, avoids paging for operations the team does not own, and both rules can carry the same action groups so paging is unchanged.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Keep both conditions in the same alert rule and remove the ApiName dimension filter so the rule covers alerts for every operation: Dropping the ApiName dimension leaves both conditions scoped to the blob latency signal as a whole, so the rule can no longer target the GetBlob or PutBlob operation specifically and the two conditions become duplicates. Paging would then cover every blob operation, including ones outside the team's scope.
- Keep both conditions in the same alert rule, set the ApiName dimension to GetBlob in both conditions, and add the wildcard value for all current and future values: The wildcard that stands for all current and future values cannot be used on a rule that has multiple conditions, and the shared ApiName dimension still has to carry one identical value in both conditions, so this configuration is not accepted.
- Keep both conditions in the same alert rule and switch to a dynamic threshold so each condition can use a different dimension value: Dynamic thresholds cannot be used on a rule with multiple conditions, and even with a static threshold the shared dimension must carry the same value in both conditions, so changing the threshold type does not remove the restriction that caused the rejection.

context:
- Setting: Subscription; Value: Contoso-Payments-Prod (Microsoft Azure public cloud)
- Setting: Workload deployment region; Value: Germany West Central
- Setting: Data-residency policy; Value: Notifications raised for workloads in this subscription must be processed inside Germany
- Setting: Platform events to notify on; Value: Azure Service Health subscription alerts
- Setting: Regional processing locations offered; Value: East US, West US, East US2, West US2, South Central US, North Central US, Sweden Central, Germany West Central, India Central, India South
prompt: You have an Azure subscription in the Microsoft Azure public cloud that hosts the company's payment platform in Germany, and a policy that every notification raised for those workloads has to be processed inside Germany. The subscription owner also wants to be told about Azure Service Health events affecting the subscription. You need a set of action groups that satisfies both requirements. Which configuration should you create?

options.text: Two action groups: one Regional in Germany West Central for the subscription's workloads, and one Global for the Service Health events.
One action group Regional in Germany West Central, handling both the subscription's workloads and the Service Health events.
One action group Global, handling both the subscription's workloads and the Service Health events.
Two action groups Regional in Germany West Central and East US, handling both the subscription's workloads and the Service Health events.

explanation:
An action group's region is fixed when the group is created, and the two requirements pull it in opposite directions. The residency rule means the notifications for the German workloads must be handled by a group whose processing stays inside that geography, which is the Regional option in Germany West Central (a location where Regional processing is offered). Service Health alerts, on the other hand, only respond properly when the action group's region is set to Global, and they exist only in the public cloud. One group cannot be both Regional in Germany and Global, so two groups are required: a Regional one in Germany West Central for the workload alerts and a Global one for the Service Health events.

Why the other options are wrong:
- One action group Regional in Germany West Central, handling both the subscription's workloads and the Service Health events: A single group set to Regional in Germany West Central keeps workload notifications inside the required geography, but Service Health alerts only respond properly when the action group's region is set to Global, so the platform events would not be handled as required.
- One action group Global, handling both the subscription's workloads and the Service Health events: A single Global group would handle the Service Health events correctly, but a Global group is persisted in at least two regions and processed anywhere, so notifications for the German workloads could be processed outside Germany, violating the data-residency policy.
- Two action groups Regional in Germany West Central and East US, handling both the subscription's workloads and the Service Health events: Both groups are Regional, so no group has the Global region that Service Health alerts require, and East US lies outside the geography the policy mandates, so the second group adds nothing useful.

context:

prompt: You have two alert processing rules in subscription SUB1 that both match alerts raised for the payments resource group. Their current settings are shown in the exhibit. A Critical metric alert fires in that resource group, and the on-call engineer is expected to be reached by the action group AG-PAY-ONCALL. You need to know whether the on-call engineer is actually contacted and whether the raised alert can still be audited afterwards. Which outcome should you expect?

options.text: Notifications are suppressed and the action group AG-PAY-ONCALL is skipped.
Notifications are delivered and the action group AG-PAY-ONCALL is run as well.
The action group AG-PAY-ONCALL is run, and notifications are suppressed only until the next alert fires.
Both rules take effect, so the action group AG-PAY-ONCALL is run and notifications are delivered.

explanation:
When a fired alert matches both a rule that suppresses notifications and a rule that applies an action group, suppression wins on priority. The suppress rule strips the action groups from the fired alert, so AG-PAY-ONCALL is not invoked and the on-call engineer is not contacted. The alert itself is still raised and stays visible in the portal, Azure Resource Graph, the API, and PowerShell, so it can still be audited afterwards; because every action group was removed, the end-of-maintenance resolved notification is skipped as well.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Notifications are delivered and the action group AG-PAY-ONCALL is run as well: This outcome assumes the applied action group runs and the notifications go out, but when the same fired alert matches a suppress-notifications rule and an apply-action-group rule, suppression takes priority, so the added group is not invoked.
- The action group AG-PAY-ONCALL is run, and notifications are suppressed only until the next alert fires: Suppressing notifications is not a one-alert or short-lived effect: when the suppress rule matches, every action group is removed from the fired alert, so AG-PAY-ONCALL is not invoked for this alert or for later alerts that match the same rule.
- Both rules take effect, so the action group AG-PAY-ONCALL is run and notifications are delivered: The two rules do not both take effect on the same fired alert. Suppression takes priority over applying an action group, so the notifications are suppressed instead of AG-PAY-ONCALL being applied.

context: A bank operates a payments platform and is assembling a single action group that all of its monitoring rules will share. Five separate targets have to be reached from that group, and for each one there is a constraint on how the request must be delivered. Drag the element you would configure in the group onto each requirement so that the constraint is met.
prompt: A ticket-system API on the public internet that expects the caller to present a username and password inside the request address

options.text: Webhook
Secure webhook
Logic apps
Automation Runbook
SMS
Event hubs
ITSM
Functions

explanation: Each requirement maps to a different element of the action group. The publicly reachable ticket-system API that expects a username and password in the request address takes the Webhook action, because that action can carry basic authentication in the URI. The partner API that refuses basic authentication and authenticates with a Microsoft Entra ID service principal takes the Secure webhook action, which signs the request as the service principal and never uses basic auth. The team chat endpoint that only accepts its own message format takes Logic apps, which reshape the payload into the schema the endpoint expects before delivery. The prepared remediation workflow that must start unattended on every fired alert takes the Automation Runbook action, which runs a stored workflow in an Automation account and that workflow can also be started manually. context: You have a production subscription in the public cloud where the operations team wants Azure Monitor to behave in five different ways, and several of those behaviors have to come from a different part of the alerting setup rather than from the same one. You need to know which Azure Monitor component delivers each behavior, so you can build the right configuration the first time. Drag each component onto the requirement it satisfies.
prompt: One alert for every row a saved workspace query returns, delivered as close to real time as the platform allows

options.text: Metric alert rule
Log search alert rule
Simple log search alert
Activity log alert rule
Action group
Alert processing rule

explanation: The row-by-row requirement belongs to a simple log search alert, because a simple log search alert evaluates each row a Log Analytics query returns individually, which supports near-real-time alerting at scale. The per-machine numeric requirement belongs to a metric alert rule: one metric alert rule can monitor resources of the same type that exist in the same Azure region, and an individual notification is sent for each monitored resource. The repeat-on-every-write-operation requirement belongs to an activity log alert rule, which is triggered when a new activity log event matches the conditions, and all activity log alerts are stateless, so they fire each time the condition is met. Deciding who is told when something is raised and what runs automatically belongs to an action group, the reusable collection of notification methods and automated actions that runs with the alert. Changing alerts that have already been raised, without editing the definition that raised them, belongs to an alert processing rule, which modifies fired alerts as they are being fired, for example by adding or suppressing action groups.

context:
You have a subscription that runs a customer-facing web tier on about forty Linux virtual machines, and the operations team is building a new metric rule for that tier in the Azure portal. The lead on the rota has written down six separate expectations about how the rule must behave, and several of them are decided by fields on the same page of the creation wizard. You need to configure the rule so that every expectation is met. Drag each setting you would configure onto the expectation it satisfies.

- Context: Workload; Detail: Customer-facing web tier on about forty Linux virtual machines
- Context: Signal; Detail: Percentage CPU reported by the platform for each machine
- Context: Paging destination; Detail: AG-WEB-ONCALL, which emails and texts the on-call rota
- Context: Demand pattern; Detail: Two predictable spikes each day, otherwise a flat baseline
- Context: Incident definition; Detail: A sustained CPU reading above 85 percent is treated as a customer incident
- Context: Coverage today; Detail: No metric rule watches this tier
prompt: The rule should raise a single notification the first time the condition is met and later report that the condition has cleared.

options.text: Automatically resolve alerts: On
Enable upon creation: On
Threshold: Static, threshold value 85, aggregation type Average
Threshold: Dynamic, threshold sensitivity High
Threshold: Dynamic, threshold sensitivity Medium
Threshold: Dynamic, threshold sensitivity Low

explanation: Each expectation lines up with one field of the metric rule wizard. 'Automatically resolve alerts' makes the rule stateful, so it fires once, stays fired while the condition holds and then sends a resolved notification. 'Enable upon creation' starts the rule running as soon as the wizard is finished, with no later action needed. The expectation about a number the business agreed on in advance is met by a static threshold, which evaluates the aggregated reading against the configured threshold value (85 percent, with Average as the aggregation function). The three remaining expectations compare the reading with the metric's own recent behaviour, so they need a dynamic threshold, and the amount of deviation tolerated decides the sensitivity level: High triggers on the smallest deviation, Medium is the balanced default that still fires on a noticeable departure, and Low fires only on large deviations, so small swings are ignored.

context:
You have a metric alert rule on the percentage CPU metric of vm-prod-web-03 that pages the on-call engineer by SMS through the action group attached to it. The platform team now wants the same rule to reach an internal chat integration as well, and it wants that machine-to-machine call to carry two extra values, the change ticket number and the service owner, that the standard alert data does not include. The rule and the planned recipient are described below. You need to know how many action groups the rule can carry and how they run, and which recipients actually receive the two extra values. Which behavior should you expect?

`Rule target               : vm-prod-web-03
Signal                   : Percentage CPU, Average over 5 minutes, greater than 80
Action groups attached   : AG-ONCALL
Notification in AG-ONCALL: SMS to the on-call engineer
Recipient to add         : Internal chat integration, reached by a Webhook action that posts to its public endpoint
Values to carry          : Change ticket number and service owner`
prompt: The rule can carry _____, and [...] will receive the two extra values.

options.text: up to five action groups, which then run concurrently with no defined order
up to three action groups, which then run one after another in the order listed
up to five action groups, which then run one after another in the order listed
up to ten action groups, which then run concurrently with no defined order

explanation:
A single alert rule can have up to five action groups attached to it, and those groups execute concurrently in no defined order, so AG-ONCALL and a second group holding the chat integration call can both sit on the same rule without either waiting on the other. The two extra values are set as custom properties on the rule, and custom properties are carried in the payloads delivered by the Webhook, Logic Apps, Azure Functions and Automation runbook actions, but not in email, SMS or Azure app push notifications. So the chat integration receives the ticket number and service owner, while the on-call engineer's SMS message does not.

Why the other options are wrong:
- up to three action groups, which then run one after another in the order listed: The ceiling is five action groups per rule, not three, and the attached groups run concurrently with no defined order rather than sequentially in the order they are listed.
- up to five action groups, which then run one after another in the order listed: The limit of five is right, but attached groups run concurrently in no defined order; they are not executed one after another in the order listed.
- up to ten action groups, which then run concurrently with no defined order: A rule may carry at most five action groups, not ten, although the concurrent and unordered execution described here is correct.

context:
You have a metric alert rule on the production API of a retail platform, and it is connected to an action group configured as shown below. During a traffic spike last night the rule fired 412 times in about two hours. The on-call engineer received only the first handful of emails and text messages, but the incident-tracking Logic App and the Jira webhook each handled all 412 alerts. You need to explain why the two paths that reach the engineer behaved differently from the other two. Which explanation should you give?

- Action configured in the group: Email on-call@contoso.com; What it does: Delivers an alert email to the on-call engineer
- Action configured in the group: Text message to the on-call engineer's number; What it does: Delivers an alert text message to the on-call engineer
- Action configured in the group: Start the incident-tracking Logic App; What it does: Records the alert in the incident tracker
- Action configured in the group: Webhook to the Jira connector; What it does: Opens a ticket for the alert

options.text: Rate limiting suspends email, SMS, voice, and push notifications per phone number, address, or device across all subscriptions, while other action types continue to run.
Rate limiting suspends email, SMS, voice, and push notifications per alert rule, while other action types continue to run.
Rate limiting suspends email, SMS, voice, and push notifications per phone number, address, or device across all subscriptions, and other action types are suspended as well.
The email and messaging providers suspend delivery per phone number, address, or device across all subscriptions, while other action types continue to run.

explanation:
Azure Monitor applies rate limiting to the notification elements of an action group. When the limit is reached, email, SMS, voice, and push notifications are suspended per phone number, address, or device, and that suspension spans all subscriptions, which is why the on-call engineer stopped receiving emails and text messages during the spike. Other action types are not rate limited, so the incident-tracking Logic App and the Jira webhook kept processing every one of the 412 alerts.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Rate limiting suspends email, SMS, voice, and push notifications per alert rule, while other action types continue to run: The suspension is not counted per alert rule. Rate limiting is applied per recipient endpoint (phone number, address, or device) across all subscriptions, so every rule that targets the same engineer draws on one shared budget.
- Rate limiting suspends email, SMS, voice, and push notifications per phone number, address, or device across all subscriptions, and other action types are suspended as well: Only the notification elements - email, SMS, voice, and push - are subject to rate limiting. Other action types such as webhooks, Logic apps, Automation runbooks, Event hubs, Functions, and ITSM are not rate limited, which is why the incident tracker and the ticket webhook still processed every alert.
- The email and messaging providers suspend delivery per phone number, address, or device across all subscriptions, while other action types continue to run: The suspension is carried out by Azure Monitor's rate limiting, not by the email or messaging providers. The effect applies to email, SMS, voice, and push notifications per phone number, address, or device across all subscriptions.

Second, the drafted short name is longer than the deployment accepts, so you need the limit in order to correct it. Which notification type should you add to the action group, and what is the maximum number of characters its short name may contain?

`Action group name: AG-PAY-OPS
Drafted short name: AG-PAY-OPS-ALERTS
Notifications already defined:
  - Text message to the on-call mobile numbers
  - Voice call to the escalation number
  - Email to a shared payments distribution list that is maintained by hand

prompt: The action group should carry _____ so that recipients are reached according to the assignment they hold in the subscription with no one-time verification step, and its short name may contain at most [...].

options.text: Email
Email Azure Resource Manager role
SMS
Azure app push notifications

explanation:
The action group needs the 'Email Azure Resource Manager role' notification. That notification mails the members of the assignment a person holds in the subscription, and Monitoring Contributor is one of the built-in assignments it supports, so the recipient list follows staffing changes without anyone typing addresses in by hand. Unlike plain email notifications, recipients of an ARM-role email do not have to confirm their address with a code before the first message is delivered, which matches the requirement that nobody performs a one-time verification. For the second slot, an action group declared in an ARM template is a Microsoft.Insights/actionGroups resource whose groupShortName may be at most 12 characters, so the drafted AG-PAY-OPS-ALERTS (18 characters) must be shortened to 12 characters or fewer.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Email: Plain email notifications only reach the addresses typed into the group, so the list of recipients has to be maintained by hand, and every newly added recipient has to confirm their address with a code within 30 minutes of the group being saved. That fails both the 'no manual recipient list' and the 'no one-time verification' parts of the requirement.
- SMS: Text messages go only to the phone numbers stored in the group and are rate limited per number across all subscriptions; they are never derived from the assignment a person holds in the subscription, so this cannot satisfy the requirement.
- Azure app push notifications: Push notifications are delivered to devices registered for the application and are rate limited per device, so they do not reach people identified by the assignment they hold in the subscription.

context:
Your team is adding two alert processing rules in subscription SUB1 to quiet night-shift noise. The first one is meant to silence notifications for alerts about the marketing analytics cluster, which is registered in subscription SUB2. The second one silences notifications for the CPU alerts raised in resource group RG-OPS in subscription SUB1. You need to know whether the first rule will affect the notifications for that cluster, and when the second rule will start acting on newly raised alerts. Which outcome should you expect?

`Rule 1 - ClusterNoiseOff
  Created in subscription: SUB1
  Target: Marketing analytics cluster (registered in SUB2)
  Filter: Alert rule name = MarketingAnalytics-HighCPU
  Action: Suppress notifications

Rule 2 - OpsCpuNoiseOff
  Created in subscription: SUB1
  Target: Resource group RG-OPS (in SUB1)
  Filter: Alert rule name = OpsWorker-HighCPU
  Action: Suppress notifications`
prompt: The notifications for the cluster in the other subscription _____, and the rule that targets resource group RG-OPS takes effect [...].

options.text: keep coming through, because coverage stays inside the subscription where the rule is created
stop, because the rule reaches resources in every subscription of the tenant
stop, but only after the rule is also created in the subscription that owns the cluster

explanation:
Two separate facts decide the outcome. First, a processing rule can only act on resources that belong to the same subscription as the rule, so the rule created in SUB1 has no effect on the marketing analytics cluster that is registered in SUB2 — that cluster's notifications keep coming through, and only a rule created in the subscription that owns the cluster could suppress them. Second, a newly created or updated processing rule can take up to 30 minutes to take effect, and alerts raised during that window may escape it, so the rule for RG-OPS begins acting up to 30 minutes after it is saved rather than instantly.

Why the other options are wrong:
- stop, because the rule reaches resources in every subscription of the tenant: A processing rule never reaches across subscriptions; it applies only to resources in its own subscription, so the rule in SUB1 leaves the cluster's alerts untouched and their notifications keep coming through.
- stop, but only after the rule is also created in the subscription that owns the cluster: Creating an additional rule in the cluster's own subscription would be the way to suppress those notifications, but it does not change the fact that the rule created in SUB1 has no effect there, so the notifications keep coming through.

During a noisy release window the payments team must go quiet while the web, data, and security teams keep receiving their pages, and once the release finishes the payments team must start receiving pages again. Nobody wants to edit the alert rule or the group definition to achieve this, so the engineer replies from the phone instead. The group details are in the exhibit. options.text: DISABLE AG-PAY
STOP AG-PAY
PAUSE AG-PAY
MUTE AG-PAY

explanation:
The engineer controls notifications from the phone because the action group accepts reply texts on the text message channel: DISABLE followed by the short name of one action group silences that group only, ENABLE followed by the same short name turns that group's notifications back on, and HELP returns the list of replies the service accepts. Because the requirement is to affect only the payments group (AG-PAY) and leave the web, data, and security groups untouched, the per-group commands carrying that group's short name are the right ones.

Why the other options are wrong:
- STOP AG-PAY: STOP is the reply that silences notifications for every action group at once and it takes no group name, so sending it with a group name is not a valid way to target only the payments group.
- PAUSE AG-PAY: PAUSE is not one of the reply texts the service recognises; the accepted per-group command for silencing notifications is DISABLE.
- MUTE AG-PAY: MUTE is not an accepted reply text; the recognised command that silences one action group is DISABLE.

You maintain the alerting for an order-processing platform that runs in subscription SUB1. An action group named AG-OPS is attached to a metric alert rule, and one of the actions in that group calls an Azure Function named ProcessPayments so that a ticket is raised in the ticketing system. Last week the platform team regenerated that function's access key, and since then the action has failed on every alert, so no ticket is created any more. You need to get this notification path working again without changing the alert rule, and you also want to confirm that the target function is set up in a way this kind of action can actually use. Which action should you take, and what must the target function support?

- Property: Action group; Value: AG-OPS, attached to the metric rule CPU-High-PROD
- Property: Failing action; Value: Open ticket — Azure Function ProcessPayments
- Property: What the action holds; Value: The function's HTTP trigger URL and the function's access key
- Property: Recent change; Value: The access key for ProcessPayments was regenerated on 12 October
- Property: Observed result; Value: The action returns an error every time an alert fires and no ticket is created
prompt: To fix the failing notification, you should _____ in the action group, and the target function must [...].

options.text: Remove and re-create the action so it stores the function's current endpoint and access key
Change the short name of the action group so the action is rebuilt with the function's new endpoint and access key
Move the action group to the Global region so the action picks up the function's new endpoint and access key
Add a second action of the same type to the action group so the function's new endpoint and access key are used

explanation:
The Functions action stores the function's HTTP trigger endpoint and access key inside the action definition (for example https://azfunctionurl.azurewebsites.net/api/httptrigger?code=<access_key>), so the values are captured when the action is defined. When the access key for ProcessPayments was regenerated, the copy held by the action became stale and every invocation fails. Because those values are baked into the action definition, the action has to be removed and re-created so it picks up the function's present endpoint and key; editing the alert rule is neither needed nor helpful. The target function also has to meet two conditions for this action to work at all: its endpoint must support the HTTP POST method, and the function must have access to its storage account — without storage account access the keys aren't available and the function URI isn't reachable, so the action still fails.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Change the short name of the action group so the action is rebuilt with the function's new endpoint and access key: The short name of an action group is only a short display label; changing it doesn't rebuild the actions inside the group, so the action keeps the stale key and continues to fail.
- Move the action group to the Global region so the action picks up the function's new endpoint and access key: The processing region of an action group controls where notifications are processed. Moving the group between Global and a regional option doesn't update the endpoint and key embedded in its actions, so the failing call remains.
- Add a second action of the same type to the action group so the function's new endpoint and access key are used: Adding a second action of the same type leaves the original action with the stale key in place, so the group still attempts the broken call on every alert.

`Recovery Services vault                : rsv-prod-01
Protected item                        : vm-app-01 (Linux, Trusted Launch image)
Attached data disks                   : 2 x Ultra Disk (512 GiB each), 1 x Premium SSD v2
Policy subtype                        : Standard
Backup frequency                      : Daily
Retention range (daily recovery pts)  : 180 days
Instant Restore snapshot retention    : 7 days`
prompt: You have a Recovery Services vault that protects a production Linux virtual machine with an Azure Virtual Machine backup policy. The VM was created from a Trusted Launch image and has Ultra Disk and Premium SSD v2 data disks attached; the scheduled backup jobs are failing because those disk types are not supported by the current configuration. The business wants the workload protected more than once a day and wants rapid restore points to remain available for a full week. You need to update the backup policy in the vault. Which change should you make?

options.text: Change the policy subtype to Enhanced and change the backup frequency to Hourly
Change the policy subtype to Enhanced and change the Instant Restore snapshot retention to 1 day
Keep the policy subtype as Standard and change the backup frequency to Hourly
Keep the policy subtype as Standard and change the retention range for daily recovery points to 10 years

explanation:
The failing jobs are caused by the disk types on the VM: the Standard policy subtype cannot protect Ultra Disk or Premium SSD v2, while the Enhanced subtype adds support for Ultra Disks, Premium SSD v2 and Trusted Launch VMs, and it also brings zone-redundant Instant Restore snapshots plus the ability to schedule backups as often as every 4 hours. Moving the frequency to Hourly therefore both clears the unsupported-disk failures and delivers more than one backup per day, and it leaves the existing 7-day Instant Restore snapshot retention untouched, which already satisfies the one-week rapid restore requirement. Note also that once a VM is protected with the Enhanced subtype, it cannot be moved back to Standard.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Change the policy subtype to Enhanced and change the Instant Restore snapshot retention to 1 day: Changing the subtype to Enhanced fixes the unsupported disk types, but shortening the Instant Restore snapshot retention from 7 days to 1 day breaks the requirement that rapid restore points stay available for a week, and the frequency is left unchanged, so the workload is still protected only once a day. Instant Restore snapshot retention can be set anywhere from 1 to 30 days and already defaults to 7 days, so no reduction is needed here.
- Keep the policy subtype as Standard and change the backup frequency to Hourly: Keeping the Standard subtype leaves the backup jobs failing, because Standard cannot protect Ultra Disk or Premium SSD v2. Backing up Trusted Launch VMs with Standard is only possible through Azure CLI 2.73.0 or later, PowerShell Az 14.0.0 or later, or the REST API 2025-01-01 or later, and none of that changes the unsupported disk types. Changing the frequency alone does not resolve the failures.
- Keep the policy subtype as Standard and change the retention range for daily recovery points to 10 years: Retention length governs how long recovery points are kept; it does not change which disk types can be protected. With the Standard subtype the Ultra Disk and Premium SSD v2 remain uncovered and the jobs keep failing, and the once-a-day schedule is left in place. Longer retention also does not create extra backup runs per day.

prompt: You have a Recovery Services vault that protects several Azure virtual machines with an Azure Virtual Machine backup policy. The business rule for this workload requires that daily recovery points are kept for three months, and the application team wants the recovery points that support a fast restore to remain available for two weeks after each backup. You need to update the policy in the vault so that both requirements are met. Which change should you make?

options.text: Raise the retention range for daily recovery points to 90 days and then set Instant Restore retention to 14 days.
Set Instant Restore retention to 14 days while leaving the retention range for daily recovery points at 7 days.
Raise the retention range for daily recovery points to 90 days and set Instant Restore retention to 45 days.
Raise the retention range for daily recovery points to 14 days and leave Instant Restore retention at 7 days.

explanation:
For an Enhanced policy the Instant Restore snapshot retention can be set from 1 to 30 days (default 7 days), but it can never exceed the vault retention duration. The retention range for the daily recovery points is currently only 7 days, so it has to be raised to 90 days (three months) first, and only then can the Instant Restore retention be raised to the 14 days the application team needs for fast restores. Lengthening the retention range also applies retroactively, so the recovery points already stored in the vault keep the longer retention instead of being pruned.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Set Instant Restore retention to 14 days while leaving the retention range for daily recovery points at 7 days: While the retention range for the daily recovery points stays at 7 days, an Instant Restore retention of 14 days is not allowed, because the Instant Restore retention duration can never exceed the vault retention duration. It also leaves the workload short of the required three months of daily recovery points.
- Raise the retention range for daily recovery points to 90 days and set Instant Restore retention to 45 days: The Enhanced policy allows an Instant Restore retention of 1 to 30 days, so a value of 45 days is outside the supported range even though the daily point retention of 90 days would otherwise cover it.
- Raise the retention range for daily recovery points to 14 days and leave Instant Restore retention at 7 days: This combination is a valid configuration, but it does not satisfy the requirements: daily recovery points would be kept for only 14 days instead of three months, and fast restores would remain available for only the 7 days that are already configured.

Change the backup frequency from Daily to Weekly and keep the 180-day retention
Enable Long Term Retention for monthly recovery points and keep the daily retention at 180 days

Lowering the retention for daily recovery points from 180 days to 90 days therefore cleans up the points that are older than 90 days, while the schedule stays at Daily so the workload is still backed up every day.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Set the Instant Restore retention to 90 days and leave the 180-day retention for daily recovery points unchanged: Instant Restore retention controls how long the zone-redundant snapshot copies that support fast restores are kept; it does not determine how long the recovery points stored in the vault are kept. With the daily retention left at 180 days, the points older than 90 days would remain in the vault.
- Change the backup frequency from Daily to Weekly and keep the 180-day retention: Switching the schedule from daily to weekly removes the existing daily recovery points, including the ones that are still inside the allowed 90-day window, and it stops the daily backup runs that this workload still requires.
- Enable Long Term Retention for monthly recovery points and keep the daily retention at 180 days: Long Term Retention governs the monthly and yearly backup points. It does not cap the daily points, so the daily recovery points older than 90 days would still be kept in the vault.

prompt: You have a Recovery Services vault that protects a production Linux virtual machine named app-prod-01 with an Azure Virtual Machine backup policy. The policy takes one backup every day at 02:00 and keeps recovery points for 180 days, and the vault already holds a series of daily recovery points for that machine. The workload owner has decided that a single backup each week is enough and asks you to switch the policy to a weekly schedule. You need to modify the backup policy in the vault and report to the owner what happens to the recovery points that are already stored. Which option correctly describes the result of saving this change?

options.text: The daily recovery points already stored in the vault are cleaned up when the policy is changed to a weekly frequency.
The daily recovery points already stored in the vault are kept until they expire under the current retention range when the policy is changed to a weekly frequency.
The daily recovery points already stored in the vault are moved into long-term retention when the policy is changed to a weekly frequency.
The daily recovery points already stored in the vault are converted into weekly recovery points when the policy is changed to a weekly frequency.

explanation:
Switching the backup frequency of an Azure Virtual Machine policy from daily to weekly cleans up the daily recovery points that are already stored in the vault. They are not carried over to the new schedule, so the VM can no longer be restored to any of those earlier daily dates, and after the change only the new weekly runs create recovery points. This is a destructive consequence the owner must be told about before the policy is saved.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The daily recovery points already stored in the vault are kept until they expire under the current retention range when the policy is changed to a weekly frequency: Letting the stored points age out under the current retention range is the behavior that applies when only the schedule days or tags change while the retention range stays the same, and when a policy moves from weekly to daily. A move from daily to weekly instead cleans up the existing daily recovery points rather than letting them expire gradually.
- The daily recovery points already stored in the vault are moved into long-term retention when the policy is changed to a weekly frequency: Long Term Retention is the concept used for monthly and yearly recovery points. Changing the backup frequency does not move the stored daily recovery points into long-term retention; they are cleaned up when the schedule moves from daily to weekly.
- The daily recovery points already stored in the vault are converted into weekly recovery points when the policy is changed to a weekly frequency: Azure Backup never converts existing daily recovery points into weekly ones. After the frequency change, the vault holds only the recovery points that the new weekly runs create, so the earlier daily dates are lost.

The business wants app-vm-01 protected every 6 hours with recovery points kept for 30 days, while every other virtual machine in the vault must keep the schedule and retention it runs today. You need to change the backup policy applied to app-vm-01 only. Which option should you take?

options.text: Create an Azure Virtual Machine policy with an hourly interval of 6 hours and a retention of 30 days, then assign it to app-vm-01 from the vault item dashboard and choose Save, which applies the schedule immediately.

Open the HourlyBackup policy with Modify, change its hourly interval to 6 hours and its retention to 30 days, and save it, which applies the schedule immediately to app-vm-01 and to the other virtual machines assigned to HourlyBackup.
Assign the existing NightlyCore Azure Virtual Machine policy to app-vm-01 from the vault item dashboard and then choose Save, which applies the schedule immediately to that machine.
Run Backup Now for app-vm-01 and set Retain Backup Till to 30 days to create an extra recovery point with the required retention, which applies the schedule immediately to that machine.

explanation:
app-vm-01 currently shares the HourlyBackup policy with app-vm-03 and app-vm-07, so changing that policy in place would alter the schedule and retention of machines that must stay as they are. The right move is to set up a separate Azure Virtual Machine policy carrying the hourly 6-hour interval and the 30-day retention, then assign it to app-vm-01 from the vault item dashboard and select Save, which applies the assignment immediately to that machine only.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Open the HourlyBackup policy with Modify, change its hourly interval to 6 hours and its retention to 30 days, and save it, which applies the schedule immediately to app-vm-01 and to the other virtual machines assigned to HourlyBackup: Modify edits the existing policy itself, so every virtual machine assigned to HourlyBackup (app-vm-01, app-vm-03 and app-vm-07) would start running the 6-hour interval with 30-day retention. That violates the requirement that the other machines keep their current schedule and retention.
- Assign the existing NightlyCore Azure Virtual Machine policy to app-vm-01 from the vault item dashboard and then choose Save, which applies the schedule immediately to that machine: The NightlyCore policy is a daily policy that runs at 02:00, so assigning it to app-vm-01 would produce one backup per day rather than one every 6 hours. Its 30-day retention matches the requirement, but its frequency does not, and the change would still not deliver the required 6-hour schedule.
- Run Backup Now for app-vm-01 and set Retain Backup Till to 30 days to create an extra recovery point with the required retention, which applies the schedule immediately to that machine: Backup Now runs an extra on-demand job and the Retain Backup Till field sets the retention of that single on-demand recovery point only. Neither of them changes the schedule or the retention of the policy assigned to app-vm-01, so the machine would keep running every 4 hours with 90-day retention.
