prompt: You have a Recovery Services vault named rsvault-prod that protects a group of Azure virtual machines with an Enhanced Azure Virtual Machine backup policy called CorpPolicy. The audit team now requires the policy to produce a recovery point on a specific day of every month that is kept for seven years and a recovery point on a specific day of every year that is kept for ten years, in addition to the daily points the policy produces today. You need to update the backup policy in the vault so that both requirements are met. Which change should you make?

options.text: Add a monthly retention rule that runs on a chosen day of the month with a retention range of 84 months, and a yearly retention rule that runs on a chosen day of the year with a retention range of 10 years, keeping the daily schedule and its 180-day retention as they are.

Add a monthly retention rule that runs on a chosen day of the month with a retention range of 60 months, and a yearly retention rule that runs on a chosen day of the year with a retention range of 10 years, keeping the daily schedule and its 180-day retention as they are.

Add a monthly retention rule that runs on a chosen day of the month with a retention range of 84 months, and a yearly retention rule that runs on a chosen day of the year with a retention range of 5 years, keeping the daily schedule and its 180-day retention as they are.
Extend the daily retention range to 2,555 days and add a yearly retention rule that runs on a chosen day of the year with a retention range of 10 years, without adding a monthly rule.

explanation:
Retention can be defined separately for daily, weekly, monthly and yearly backup points, and the monthly and yearly ones are the long-term retention rules: a monthly rule fires on a chosen day of the month and a yearly rule on a chosen day of the year. Both ranges are editable, and their defaults are 60 months for monthly points and 10 years for yearly points. Seven years of monthly points therefore needs the monthly rule set to 84 months, and the ten-year audit requirement is met by a yearly rule of 10 years, while the daily schedule and its 180-day retention stay untouched so the daily points the policy produces today are unaffected.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add a monthly retention rule that runs on a chosen day of the month with a retention range of 60 months, and a yearly retention rule that runs on a chosen day of the year with a retention range of 10 years, keeping the daily schedule and its 180-day retention as they are: 60 months is only five years - it is the default for monthly points - so the monthly points would be cleaned up after five years instead of the required seven. The yearly rule in this option is right, but the monthly rule is not.
- Add a monthly retention rule that runs on a chosen day of the month with a retention range of 84 months, and a yearly retention rule that runs on a chosen day of the year with a retention range of 5 years, keeping the daily schedule and its 180-day retention as they are: The monthly rule of 84 months satisfies the seven-year requirement, but the yearly rule of 5 years keeps the yearly point for only half of the ten years the audit team asked for.
- Extend the daily retention range to 2,555 days and add a yearly retention rule that runs on a chosen day of the year with a retention range of 10 years, without adding a monthly rule: Lengthening the daily retention range only changes how long the daily points are kept; it adds no rule that fires on a chosen day of the month, so the monthly requirement is not met. It would also store every daily point for seven years, which increases vault storage cost.

prompt: You have a Recovery Services vault named rsvault-westus that protects a Windows virtual machine named svc-vm-14 with the Azure Virtual Machine backup policy shown below. The business wants the per-snapshot cost for this virtual machine lowered, the read-only reference data that is mounted by eight other virtual machines and the scratch logs that are regenerated every hour left out of the recovery points produced from now on, and the customer and order records on Data disk 1 still protected. You need to update how this workload is backed up in the vault. Which change should you make?

options.text: Enable selective disk backup for the Azure Virtual Machine backup policy and deselect Data disk 2 and Data disk 3
Enable selective disk backup for the Azure Virtual Machine backup policy in the MARS console so that Data disk 2 and Data disk 3 are skipped
Raise the Instant Restore snapshot retention of the Azure Virtual Machine backup policy to 30 days and set the daily retention range to 30 days
Keep the Azure Virtual Machine backup policy as it is and detach Data disk 2 and Data disk 3 from the virtual machine before every scheduled backup, reattaching them when the job ends

explanation:
Selective disk backup is the documented way to protect only a subset of the data disks attached to a virtual machine: noncritical or shared disks are left out of the backup, the snapshot cost is cut, and each recovery point then contains only the included disks, which can be restored from Instant Restore or from the vault tier. Turning it on for the Azure Virtual Machine backup policy and deselecting Data disk 2 (the read-only data mounted by eight other virtual machines) and Data disk 3 (the hourly scratch logs) leaves Data disk 1 with the customer and order records, along with the OS disk, as the protected content of every new recovery point.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enable selective disk backup for the Azure Virtual Machine backup policy in the MARS console so that Data disk 2 and Data disk 3 are skipped: The file and folder settings for the MARS agent are specified in the MARS console, and the MARS agent covers files, folders and system state on on-premises Windows servers and on Azure VMs. It has no knowledge of which disks are attached to an Azure virtual machine, so a MARS configuration cannot decide which of those disks are written into the recovery points of svc-vm-14.
- Raise the Instant Restore snapshot retention of the Azure Virtual Machine backup policy to 30 days and set the daily retention range to 30 days: Extending the Instant Restore snapshot retention only keeps more snapshots in the snapshot tier and adds to the cost of the policy; it removes nothing from the recovery points. Data disk 2 and Data disk 3 would still be captured in every backup, so the snapshot cost would not fall.
- Keep the Azure Virtual Machine backup policy as it is and detach Data disk 2 and Data disk 3 from the virtual machine before every scheduled backup, reattaching them when the job ends: The backup service does not detach or reattach data disks for you, and taking the shared reference data and the scratch disk offline around every job would disrupt the workload that reads them and still require manual work each night. The disks stay attached and are kept out of the recovery points by the backup configuration itself.

The policy runs on the schedule shown in the exhibit. You need to update the backup policy so that both requirements are met. Which change should you make?

Keep the backup frequency on Hourly, set the repeat interval to 12 hours, and set Instant Restore retention to 30 days.

The hourly frequency can use a repeat interval of 4, 6, 8, 12 or 24 hours, and the recovery point objective on an hourly schedule ranges from a 4-hour floor to a 24-hour ceiling. The workload owner tolerates at most half a day of loss, so the 24-hour interval is out. The number of snapshots taken per day also caps the allowed Instant Restore retention: every 4 hours over a 24-hour duration means six scheduled snapshots, and the more snapshots per day, the fewer days of retention are permitted. That rules out the 4-hour and 6-hour intervals when the requirement is the full 30 days the vault holds recovery points. The 12-hour interval is the one that lets snapshot retention rise to 30 days, and 30 days is both the maximum Instant Restore retention and equal to the vault's retention duration, which it can never exceed.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Keep the backup frequency on Hourly, set the repeat interval to 4 hours, and set Instant Restore retention to 30 days: Six scheduled snapshots a day (every 4 hours across the 24-hour duration) reduce the maximum allowed Instant Restore retention below the full 30 days the vault keeps its recovery points, so the required window is not delivered even though the recovery point objective is the tightest of the four.
- Keep the backup frequency on Hourly, set the repeat interval to 6 hours, and set Instant Restore retention to 30 days: A 6-hour interval still schedules four snapshots a day, more than the 12-hour interval, so the maximum allowed Instant Restore retention stays below 30 days and the requirement for the whole vault retention period is not met.
- Keep the backup frequency on Hourly, set the repeat interval to 24 hours, and set Instant Restore retention to 30 days: A 24-hour repeat interval pushes the recovery point objective to the 24-hour ceiling, which exceeds the half-day loss the workload owner accepts, even though it produces the fewest snapshots and therefore the most generous retention allowance.

options.text: LRS
GRS
ZRS

explanation: Each requirement maps to one Azure Backup option. A whole-region outage is covered by GRS, which keeps a copy in a paired secondary region. Surviving the loss of one availability zone while every copy stays in the same region calls for ZRS. You have a Recovery Services vault named rsvault-prod that protects a Linux virtual machine running an order-processing database with an Azure Virtual Machine backup policy. After the last restore of that machine, the database had to be put through crash recovery by hand and its write-ahead log replayed before the service would start. The business now wants each recovery point for this workload to be application-consistent, so that a restore brings the database up without any manual repair work. You need to change how this workload is protected in the vault. Which change should you make?

`Recovery Services vault : rsvault-prod (East US)
Protected workload    : orders-vm-03 (Azure Virtual Machine)
Operating system      : Ubuntu 22.04 LTS
Backup policy name    : OrdersPolicy
Policy subtype        : Standard
Backup schedule       : Daily at 01:00
Recovery point retention : 30 days
Snapshot copies kept for fast restore : 7 days
Guest backup extension : VMSnapshotLinux
Restore result reported by operations : database required crash recovery by hand and write-ahead log replay before the service started`
prompt: The change to make is _____.

options.text: Configure pre-backup and post-backup scripts so the database is quiesced during the snapshot
Configure the Enhanced policy subtype so the backup captures all attached disks together during a single crash-consistent snapshot
Configure VSS integration so the guest is able to create an application-consistent snapshot of the running database
Configure the MARS agent and use the MARS console to capture the database files and folders

explanation:
On a Linux virtual machine, Azure Backup takes a file-consistent backup, and application-consistent recovery points are obtained only by manually customizing pre/post scripts. Adding pre-backup and post-backup scripts lets the database be quiesced (for example, flushed and frozen) around the snapshot, so the recovery point is application-consistent and the restored database starts without manual crash recovery or write-ahead log replay. That is exactly the symptom the operations team reported, so the scripts are the change that fixes it.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Configure the Enhanced policy subtype so the backup captures all attached disks together during a single crash-consistent snapshot: This workload runs Linux, so the Enhanced subtype buys zone-redundant Instant Restore storage, shorter intervals between backups, Trusted Launch support, Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disk support, and snapshots that capture several disks together, but those snapshots are crash-consistent. A restored database still has to be crash-recovered by hand, so the manual repair work the business wants removed remains. Enhanced is also a one-way move: a virtual machine already protected with Enhanced cannot be switched back to Standard.
- Configure VSS integration so the guest is able to create an application-consistent snapshot of the running database: Coordinating with VSS is the Windows mechanism: for running Windows virtual machines, Azure Backup coordinates with the Volume Shadow Copy Service to take an app-consistent snapshot (full VSS backup by default, with a file-consistent fallback when an app-consistent snapshot cannot be taken). A Linux guest does not use VSS, so this setting does not apply to the machine in the scenario and would not change the consistency of its recovery points.
- Configure the MARS agent and use the MARS console to capture the database files and folders: The MARS agent covers files, folders and system state, and its file/folder settings are configured in the MARS console rather than in the Azure Virtual Machine backup policy. Because it does not use application VSS writers, it does not capture app-consistent snapshots, so switching this workload to the MARS agent would still leave the database needing crash recovery after a restore. On-premises Linux machines also cannot be backed up directly with the MARS agent.

explanation:
Two different pieces of work are needed. For the new policy, the schedule must be Hourly, the first run has to start at 20:00, the repeat interval has to be 12 hours — the intervals that can be chosen are 4, 6, 8, 12 and 24 hours, and only 12 hours gives the two runs per day the request asks for — and the duration has to be 24 hours so the window covers the entire day. For app-vm-12, the extra point is produced with the Backup Now operation, and the Retain Backup Till field in that pane sets the retention of the on-demand backup itself: the retention range of an on-demand backup is the value you specify when you trigger it. Entering a date three years out therefore keeps that single point available long after the 90-day retention of CorpPolicy would have removed it.

- Hourly schedule with a start time of 20:00, a repeat interval of 4 hours and a duration of 24 hours: Repeating every 4 hours across a 24-hour window produces six runs per day, not the two the request calls for; 4 hours is a valid interval but the wrong one for this workload.

new-vm-22                     : Created today at 09:15 and protected with the same policy;

prompt: The on-demand run requested for new-vm-22 results in _____, and the hourly runs of app-vm-07 reach the vault as follows: [...].

options.text: the whole virtual machine being transferred to the vault, because the first scheduled backup is still running
only the blocks that changed since the previous run being transferred to the vault, because the first scheduled backup has already produced the baseline
the job waiting for the first scheduled backup to finish and then transferring only the changed blocks to the vault
the job failing and being retried later, because a backup of the virtual machine is already running

explanation:
For the on-demand run on new-vm-22, the initial backup is still pending, and when the initial backup is pending an on-demand backup creates a full copy of the virtual machine in the Recovery Services vault; only once the initial backup is complete does an on-demand run send just the changes since the previous snapshot, because every backup to Azure after the first one is incremental. For the hourly runs of app-vm-07, only the last backup of the day is transferred to the vault, and if that run fails the first backup of the next day is transferred instead. That is why six successful runs inside one 24-hour period (a 4-hour interval over a 24-hour duration produces six scheduled snapshots) leave only one recovery point in the vault.

Why the other options are wrong:
- only the blocks that changed since the previous run being transferred to the vault, because the first scheduled backup has already produced the baseline: This describes the behaviour once the initial backup has already completed, where an on-demand run transfers only the blocks that changed since the previous snapshot. new-vm-22's initial backup has not finished yet, so the requested run does not behave this way.
- the job waiting for the first scheduled backup to finish and then transferring only the changed blocks to the vault: The job is not queued behind the pending initial backup. When the initial backup is pending, the on-demand run creates a full copy of the virtual machine in the vault rather than waiting and then sending only changed blocks.
- the job failing and being retried later, because a backup of the virtual machine is already running: The run does not fail because another backup is in progress; an on-demand backup can be triggered while the initial backup is pending, and in that situation it creates a full copy of the virtual machine in the vault.

The company operates only in the East US region, and two new Recovery Services vaults plus one new Azure Virtual Machine backup policy are being set up. The exhibit lists what has already been decided. The business requires that the recovery points held in the payroll vault survive the loss of an availability zone while never being copied outside the East US region, that the new policy protect the payroll workload several times a day with the tightest spacing between recovery points that the service supports, and that no single administrator be able to remove recovery points from the analytics vault unless a second administrator has approved the operation first. You need to complete the configuration so that every requirement is met. Which setting should you use for each requirement?

- Item: Subscription; Value: contoso-prod
- Item: Region; Value: East US
- Item: Vault rsvault-payroll; Value: New vault that will hold the recovery points of the payroll platform
- Item: Vault rsvault-analytics; Value: New vault owned by the analytics team

prompt: To meet all three requirements, configure rsvault-payroll with _____ redundancy, run PayPolicy with [...], and [...] for rsvault-analytics.

options.text: LRS
GRS
ZRS

explanation:
The payroll vault needs ZRS, because zone-redundant storage replicates the recovery points across availability zones and guarantees data residency and resiliency in the same region, which is exactly what the East US zone-failure requirement asks for; LRS only protects against server rack and drive failures, and GRS copies the data to a paired region, which would break the residency requirement. PayPolicy must run hourly backups every 4 hours: with the Enhanced policy subtype Azure Backup can be scheduled as often as every 4 hours, and that is the shortest interval it supports, so this is the tightest spacing that still produces several recovery points per day. The analytics vault needs Multi-User Authorization with Azure Resource Guard, which adds the approval layer in front of critical operations such as deleting recovery points so a second administrator can sign off; soft delete only keeps deleted recovery points recoverable for a while and adds no approval step, and cross-region restore only changes where a restore can be performed.

Why the other options are wrong:
- LRS: Locally redundant storage keeps three copies of the data in a single datacenter and protects against rack and drive failures only, so it gives no protection against the loss of an availability zone and does not meet the requirement.
- GRS: Geo-redundant storage replicates the data to a paired region, which is what protects against a region-wide outage, but it copies the recovery points outside the East US region and provides no in-region zone resilience.

prompt: Your team opens the Azure Backup workbooks in Log Analytics workspace la-backup. The tiles and grids that cover the workloads protected in the Recovery Services vault come back empty, while the same workbook returns rows for the workloads in the Backup vault over the same period. Both vaults have been sending logs to this workspace for several weeks, so ingestion lag does not explain the gap. You want the reports to populate for the Recovery Services vault. Which change should you make?

options.text: Republish prod-rsv's rsv-diag setting so the six Azure Backup events are sent in Resource specific mode instead of Azure diagnostics mode.
Add the legacy Azure Backup Reporting Data event to prod-rsv's rsv-diag setting so it keeps being sent in Azure diagnostics mode.
Republish prod-bv's bv-diag setting so the six Azure Backup events are sent in Azure diagnostics mode instead of Resource specific mode.
Remove Addon Azure Backup Storage Data from prod-bv's bv-diag setting and add the legacy Azure Backup Reporting Data event to it in Resource specific mode.

explanation:
For a Recovery Services vault, the six Azure Backup events reach the Backup reports only when they are sent in Resource specific mode; when they are sent in Azure diagnostics mode, no data appears in the reports. prod-rsv currently sends those events in Azure diagnostics mode, which is exactly why its tiles and grids are empty, whereas prod-bv (a Backup vault) already uses Resource specific mode and therefore returns rows. Republishing rsv-diag with the same six events under Resource specific mode creates the dedicated per-event tables in la-backup (for example CoreAzureBackup and the Addon tables) that the workbooks query, and that is the recommended target mode for new settings.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add the legacy Azure Backup Reporting Data event to prod-rsv's rsv-diag setting so it keeps being sent in Azure diagnostics mode: The legacy Azure Backup Reporting Data event is supported only in Azure diagnostics mode, so adding it to that setting would indeed flow data, but the Log Analytics reporting solution is moving off the legacy event: it is on a deprecation path and the reports will cease to support data from it. The workbooks read the new per-event tables, so this change does not fill the empty tiles and keeps the estate on the route that is being retired.
- Republish prod-bv's bv-diag setting so the six Azure Backup events are sent in Azure diagnostics mode instead of Resource specific mode: prod-bv is already returning data, and for Backup vaults all diagnostics events are sent to the resource-specific tables only, so there is nothing to migrate there. Republishing that setting to Azure diagnostics mode would put a working feed at risk and would not affect prod-rsv, which is the vault with the empty tiles.
- Remove Addon Azure Backup Storage Data from prod-bv's bv-diag setting and add the legacy Azure Backup Reporting Data event to it in Resource specific mode: A diagnostic setting carries a single log mode, and the legacy Azure Backup Reporting Data event flows no data at all when it is sent in Resource specific mode, so the second half of this change cannot work. Addon Azure Backup Storage Data is also not applicable to a Backup vault, because storage consumed and frontend size already arrive through Core Azure Backup Data and Addon Azure Backup Protected Instance Data, so removing it changes nothing. prompt: You have a Recovery Services vault that protects a group of Azure VMs, and its backup logs already reach a Log Analytics workspace where the workbook tiles show job outcomes. You need the on-call rotation to be notified whenever Azure Backup raises an alert about a protected item, using a notification path that remains supported going forward. Which change should you make?

options.text: Create an Azure Monitor alert and route the fired alert through an alert processing rule and an action group that targets a logic app, webhook, or runbook.
Enable the Addon Azure Backup Alerts category in the vault's existing diagnostic setting and let the classic alerts solution notify the on-call rotation.
Enable the Addon Azure Backup Alerts category in the vault's existing diagnostic setting and pair it with an Azure Monitor action group that targets a logic app.
Create an Azure Monitor alert that queries the Addon Azure Backup Alerts table in the workspace every five minutes, without an alert processing rule or action group.

explanation:
The classic alerts solution has been deprecated in favour of Azure Monitor-based alerting, so the Addon Azure Backup Alerts category should not be selected for this. The supported pattern is to create an Azure Monitor alert, then use an alert processing rule to route the fired alert and an action group that invokes a logic app, webhook, or runbook to reach the on-call rotation.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enable the Addon Azure Backup Alerts category in the vault's existing diagnostic setting and let the classic alerts solution notify the on-call rotation: This depends on the classic alerts solution, which is deprecated; the Addon Azure Backup Alerts category should not be selected. Notification should come from an Azure Monitor alert combined with an alert processing rule and an action group.
- Enable the Addon Azure Backup Alerts category in the vault's existing diagnostic setting and pair it with an Azure Monitor action group that targets a logic app: Selecting the deprecated Addon Azure Backup Alerts category is the part to avoid, even though an action group is attached to it. An action group alone does not replace the deprecated event; the alert should be created in Azure Monitor and passed through an alert processing rule to an action group.
- Create an Azure Monitor alert that queries the Addon Azure Backup Alerts table in the workspace every five minutes, without an alert processing rule or action group: The query depends on data from the Addon Azure Backup Alerts category, which is deprecated and is not among the categories enabled in the vault's diagnostic setting, so the query would return no usable data. On top of that, omitting both an alert processing rule and an action group leaves no target that can notify the on-call rotation.

The vault's current diagnostic setting is shown below. You need the workbook to keep reporting storage consumption while the vault does not send the same information to the workspace twice. Which change should you make?

options.text: Remove Addon Azure Backup Storage Data from the diagnostic setting; the storage consumed and frontend size already arrive through Core Azure Backup Data and Addon Azure Backup Protected Instance Data.

Remove Core Azure Backup Data from the diagnostic setting; the storage consumed and frontend size already arrive through Addon Azure Backup Storage Data and Addon Azure Backup Protected Instance Data.

explanation:
For a Backup vault, the frontend size and the backup storage consumed are already part of Core Azure Backup Data and Addon Azure Backup Protected Instance Data, so the Addon Azure Backup Storage Data event is not applicable to Backup vaults and selecting it only produces a redundant table. Removing that event leaves the workbook's storage figures intact while avoiding a second copy of the same numbers.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Remove Core Azure Backup Data from the diagnostic setting; the storage consumed and frontend size already arrive through Addon Azure Backup Storage Data and Addon Azure Backup Protected Instance Data: The Addon Azure Backup Storage Data event does not apply to a Backup vault, and Core Azure Backup Data is the main event that carries the baseline vault data; dropping it would remove information the reports rely on rather than a duplicate of it.
- Remove Addon Azure Backup Protected Instance Data from the diagnostic setting; the storage consumed and frontend size already arrive through Core Azure Backup Data and Addon Azure Backup Storage Data: Addon Azure Backup Protected Instance Data carries the frontend size figures, so removing it would lose values the workbook displays; the event that does not apply to a Backup vault is Addon Azure Backup Storage Data.
- Keep all six events in the diagnostic setting; the storage consumed and frontend size arrive through separate tables for each of the six events: Leaving all six events selected keeps the Addon Azure Backup Storage Data table in place for a Backup vault, where that event is not applicable and yields a redundant table next to the data already delivered by Core Azure Backup Data and Addon Azure Backup Protected Instance Data.

prompt: You have a Recovery Services vault that ships its backup diagnostics to a Log Analytics workspace through a single diagnostic setting, and your operations team still has custom Kusto queries that read the vault data from the shared diagnostics table. You want the Azure Backup workbooks to begin returning job information while those custom queries keep returning rows during the changeover. Which change should you make?

options.text: Change the existing diagnostic setting to enable Resource specific and select the six new Azure Backup events, removing the Azure diagnostics mode.
Add a second diagnostic setting to enable Azure diagnostics and select the six new Azure Backup events, and keep the existing diagnostic setting until the custom queries are migrated.
Add a second diagnostic setting to enable Resource specific and select the six new Azure Backup events, and keep the existing diagnostic setting until the custom queries are migrated.
Remove the existing diagnostic setting and add one that enables Resource specific with the six new Azure Backup events selected.

explanation:
For a Recovery Services vault, the Backup reports only pick up the six new Azure Backup events when they are sent in Resource specific mode, so a setting in that mode is required before the workbook can show job information. The legacy Azure Backup Reporting Data event, by contrast, carries data only in Azure diagnostics mode, so the existing setting has to stay in place while the custom queries that read the shared diagnostics table are rewritten against the new per-event tables. Keeping one setting for the legacy event and a second setting for the six new events lets both operate during the changeover, and the legacy setting can be retired once the queries are migrated.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Change the existing diagnostic setting to enable Resource specific and select the six new Azure Backup events, removing the Azure diagnostics mode: Switching the existing setting over to Resource specific withdraws the Azure diagnostics path that the legacy Azure Backup Reporting Data event depends on, so the custom queries that read the shared diagnostics table stop returning rows as soon as the change is applied instead of after a planned migration.
- Add a second diagnostic setting to enable Azure diagnostics and select the six new Azure Backup events, and keep the existing diagnostic setting until the custom queries are migrated: The six new Azure Backup events are honoured by the Backup reports only when they are sent in Resource specific mode. A second setting that uses Azure diagnostics mode therefore leaves the workbook without job data.
- Remove the existing diagnostic setting and add one that enables Resource specific with the six new Azure Backup events selected: Removing the existing setting cuts off the only supported route for the legacy Azure Backup Reporting Data event, which works solely in Azure diagnostics mode, so the custom queries break before they have been rewritten against the new tables.

prompt: You have a Recovery Services vault that protects 420 Azure VMs, and your analysts read the Backup Reports workbook in a Log Analytics workspace. The Cloud Storage and Protected Instances tiles return identical figures whichever time range the analysts pick, and they have concluded that the range filter has no effect on the report. You need to correct their understanding of how these two tiles are produced. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The values are point-in-time snapshots taken at the end of the selected time range, so narrowing the range does not change them.
The values are point-in-time snapshots taken at the start of the selected time range, so narrowing the range does not change them.
The values are the sum of the daily values across the selected time range, so narrowing the range should reduce them.
The values are the daily average across the selected time range, so narrowing the range should reduce them.

explanation:
In the Backup Reports workbook, the Cloud Storage and Protected Instances figures are point-in-time readings captured at the close of the selected time range, not totals accumulated across that range. That is why the exhibit shows the same 2.41 TB and the same 418 items for every range the analysts pick: the tiles reflect the state of the estate at one moment, while job, schedule and policy-adherence widgets re-aggregate the underlying records for each range.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The values are point-in-time snapshots taken at the start of the selected time range, so narrowing the range does not change them: This option describes a reading taken when the range opens. The report captures the storage and protected-instance values once, at the close of the selected range, so a start-of-range reading is not what the tiles contain, and a start-of-range value would normally shift when the range is moved.
- The values are the sum of the daily values across the selected time range, so narrowing the range should reduce them: A sum would grow as the range widens and shrink as it is narrowed, so the exhibit's constant 2.41 TB could not be a sum. These two tiles report the value as it stands at the close of the selected range rather than a total over the period.
- The values are the daily average across the selected time range, so narrowing the range should reduce them: An average would also vary with the range that is selected, which contradicts the constant figures shown for the Protected Instances tile. The tile reads the instance count once, at the close of the selected range, and repeats that reading for every range.

prompt: You have a Recovery Services vault that protects Azure VMs with Azure Site Recovery and also uses a recovery plan, and your analysts open the Azure Site Recovery Job History report in the Backup Reports workbook. The table below shows the operations that were recorded in the vault on 12 April. You need to identify which of these operations the report is expected to list. Which set of operations should you expect?

options.text: The failover test of the estate triggered from the recovery plan and the failover of the single VM triggered on the replicated item.
Only the failover test of the estate triggered from the recovery plan; the failover of the single VM triggered on the replicated item is excluded.
Only the failover of the single VM triggered on the replicated item; the failover test of the estate triggered from the recovery plan is excluded.
All four operations, including the nightly backup of the application VMs and the backup of the Azure File share along with the failover test of the estate and the failover of the single VM.

explanation:
The Azure Site Recovery Job History report lists only the jobs that were triggered on replicated items and recovery plans. In the exhibit, the failover test of the estate was triggered from the recovery plan and the failover of the single VM was triggered on the replicated item, so both operations belong in this report. The scheduled backups of the application VMs and the Azure File share are backup operations rather than Azure Site Recovery jobs, so they are not listed by this report.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Only the failover test of the estate triggered from the recovery plan; the failover of the single VM triggered on the replicated item is excluded: This drops the failover of the single VM, but that job was triggered on a replicated item, and jobs triggered on replicated items are included in the Azure Site Recovery Job History report alongside the recovery plan operations.
- Only the failover of the single VM triggered on the replicated item; the failover test of the estate triggered from the recovery plan is excluded: This drops the failover test triggered from the recovery plan, yet jobs triggered on recovery plans are also included in the Azure Site Recovery Job History report, so the estate failover test belongs in the results.
- All four operations, including the nightly backup of the application VMs and the backup of the Azure File share along with the failover test of the estate and the failover of the single VM: This pulls in the scheduled backup jobs for the application VMs and the Azure File share. Those are backup operations recorded by the vault, and this report covers only the Azure Site Recovery jobs triggered on replicated items and recovery plans.

You are reviewing how backup data from a set of Recovery Services vaults reaches the Azure Backup workbooks in Log Analytics. The notes below list the five points that are still open from that review, and the list of steps that follows holds the moves your team has drafted to close them. You need to attach one step to each open point, and any step that settles none of them should be left out. Drag each step to the matching point.

`Point 1: rsv-we runs in West Europe. Every event record it produces must be kept for seven years in a storage account, and the workbook data keeps coming from the workspace la-backup in East US 2.

Point 2: Twelve vaults in the subscription have no diagnostics setting. They must all reach the workspace, and the operations team does not want to open each vault one by one.

Point 3: Compliance has asked for the names of the vaults that are still sending the older event instead of the current one.

Point 4: Governance compares items on a weekly schedule with items on a daily schedule in the policy adherence grids and wants to know how the period buckets behave.

Point 5: The BI team still runs the old template app that read backup data from a storage account; the platform group has said that route will stop being supported.`
prompt: Point 1 — archival of the seven-year event records

options.text: Create the storage account in the same region as the Recovery Services vault.
Replace the Power BI template app and the V1 schema with the Azure Backup workbooks in Log Analytics, because that route is on a deprecation path.
Assign the built-in Azure Policy definition that adds diagnostics settings to the vaults in scope, with Owner access on each subscription.
Run the documented Kusto query that unions AzureDiagnostics with CoreAzureBackup and returns the vaults found only under AzureBackupReport.
Treat a month in the policy adherence grids as four weeks, and expect the items on a weekly policy to have no daily view.
Point the stored copy at a storage account in a different region, since the vault's location does not limit where the copy is written.
Enable the Azure Backup Reporting Data event on the remaining vaults so that their rows appear in the reports.
Add the Addon Azure Backup Alerts event to the diagnostics setting so that the workspace receives the backup alerts.

explanation: Each open point is settled by exactly one of the drafted steps. The archival requirement for rsv-we is met by creating the storage account in the vault's own region, because a Recovery Services vault can only send diagnostic logs to a storage account in the same region, while the Log Analytics workspace may sit in another region or subscription. Bulk coverage of the twelve vaults with no diagnostics setting is met by the built-in Azure Policy definition that adds a diagnostics setting to the vaults in scope, which can be assigned to a subscription or a resource group and requires Owner access on each subscription. The compliance request for names is met by the documented Kusto query that unions AzureDiagnostics with CoreAzureBackup and returns the vaults found only under AzureBackupReport. The policy adherence question is met by treating a month as four weeks (28 days, so partial weeks drop out) and by knowing that items on a weekly policy have no daily view. The retirement of the team's tooling is met by moving onto the Azure Backup workbooks in Log Analytics, since the Power BI template app that sourced data from a storage account and the V1 schema are on a deprecation path. The remaining three steps settle no point: a storage account in another region is not allowed for a Recovery Services vault, the legacy Azure Backup Reporting Data event is honoured only in Azure diagnostics mode and therefore does not populate the backup reports for a Recovery Services vault, and the classic backup alerts event should not be selected at all.

an hourly and a daily view

explanation:
The Policy Adherence grids follow an aggregation logic similar to the report charts, with two differences for items whose backup policy runs on a weekly schedule: there is no daily breakdown for those items, so only the weekly and monthly views are available, and a 'month' in those grids is counted as a four-week period (28 days) rather than 30 days, which keeps partial weeks out of the results. vm-group-b is on a weekly policy, so the analysts get the weekly and monthly views, and each monthly bucket spans 28 days.

- Component: Archive destination; Detail: storage account sa-backup-archive - region not yet chosen

prompt: The correct placement is _____.

The Log Analytics workspace must match the vault's region; the storage account need not.
Both destinations may sit in any region.
Both destinations must match the vault's region.

explanation:
A Recovery Services vault can send its diagnostic logs only to a storage account that sits in the same region as the vault itself, so sa-backup-archive would have to be created in North Europe. The Log Analytics workspace is the flexible one: it may live in the vault's region or in another region (and even in another subscription), so la-backup can be placed elsewhere and still receive rsv-prod's data and populate the Azure Backup workbooks.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The Log Analytics workspace must match the vault's region; the storage account need not: This reverses the two constraints. It is the storage account that is tied to the vault's own region; the Log Analytics workspace is the destination that is allowed to sit in another region.
- Both destinations may sit in any region: Neither destination is unconstrained. Because a Recovery Services vault can only archive its diagnostic logs to a storage account in the vault's own region, both cannot be placed in any region.
- Both destinations must match the vault's region: This is too strict on the reporting side. A Log Analytics workspace in another region still receives the vault's diagnostic logs, so the two destinations are not both forced into the vault's region.

The changes in the exhibit were made in that vault during March, and your analysts set the Time Range to 1-31 March. You need to know what the workbook shows for that range. - Object in the vault: Backup item for virtual machine "vm-app-03"; Change made during March: Deleted on 20 March, when the virtual machine was unregistered from the vault
prompt: For the 1-31 March range, the workbook's grids _____.

list the deleted backup item for the virtual machine only for 1-19 March and the deleted backup policy only for 1-9 March
list the deleted backup policy for the whole range but omit the deleted backup item for the virtual machine throughout
list both the deleted backup policy and the deleted backup item for the virtual machine for the whole range

explanation:
The report displays the backup items and the backup policies that still exist at the end of the selected time range, and the same convention applies to policies as to items. Anything deleted part-way through the range is therefore not displayed at all for that range, rather than appearing up to its deletion date. The policy was deleted on 10 March and the virtual machine's backup item on 20 March, so at the end of the 1-31 March range neither object exists, and both are absent from the grids.

Why the other options are wrong:
- list the deleted backup item for the virtual machine only for 1-19 March and the deleted backup policy only for 1-9 March: This option assumes the workbook keeps a day-by-day history of the range. The grids are built from the backup items and policies that exist at the end of the selected range, so an object deleted during the range drops out entirely instead of being shown up to the day it was deleted.
- list the deleted backup policy for the whole range but omit the deleted backup item for the virtual machine throughout: A backup policy follows the same rule as a backup item: once it has been deleted, it is not listed for the range in which the deletion happened, even for the days on which it existed. The policy is therefore absent from the March grids along with the virtual machine's backup item.
- list both the deleted backup policy and the deleted backup item for the virtual machine for the whole range: This option treats a mid-range deletion as if the objects had survived for the whole range. Both objects were deleted before 31 March, so both are left out of the 1-31 March grids.

You support twelve Recovery Services vaults, and the backup data they send lands in the workspace la-backup, where your operations analysts look for job history. You plan to move the remaining vaults off the older single-event stream that carried all of a vault's backup data in one place, and the first step is to produce the list of vaults that still send that stream. The Microsoft-documented audit query works with two sets of rows, one for the older stream and one for the current per-event data, and it returns the vault identifiers that are present only in the older set. You need to fill in those two row sets correctly.

- Vault: rsv-prod; What reaches la-backup today: Legacy combined event only
- Vault: rsv-finance; What reaches la-backup today: Legacy combined event only
- Vault: rsv-web; What reaches la-backup today: Six per-event tables, one per event
- Vault: rsv-hr; What reaches la-backup today: Legacy combined event only
prompt: To build that list, the audit query reads _____ and compares them with [...].

options.text: the AzureDiagnostics rows where Category is AzureBackupReport, OperationName is Vault and SchemaVersion_s is V2
the CoreAzureBackup rows where Category is AzureBackupReport, OperationName is Vault and SchemaVersion_s is V2
the AzureDiagnostics rows where Category is AzureBackupReport, OperationName is Job and SchemaVersion_s is V2
the AddonAzureBackupJobs rows where Category is AzureBackupReport, OperationName is Vault and SchemaVersion_s is V2

explanation:
The documented audit for finding vaults that still send the legacy single event unions the rows that the legacy stream wrote into the shared diagnostics table, filtered to Category AzureBackupReport with OperationName Vault and SchemaVersion_s V2, with the rows in the CoreAzureBackup table, and then keeps the vault identifiers found only under the legacy category. The first row set therefore has to come from AzureDiagnostics with exactly those three filters, and the second row set has to come from CoreAzureBackup, which carries the vault-level records of the current per-event data.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the CoreAzureBackup rows where Category is AzureBackupReport, OperationName is Vault and SchemaVersion_s is V2: CoreAzureBackup is the resource-specific table that the current per-event data lands in, so it holds no rows for the older combined stream. The legacy rows live in the shared diagnostics table under Category AzureBackupReport, which is what the documented audit query filters on.
- the AzureDiagnostics rows where Category is AzureBackupReport, OperationName is Job and SchemaVersion_s is V2: The documented audit query filters the legacy rows down to OperationName Vault, because the vault-level records are what identify which vault sent the data. Filtering to Job returns job records instead of vault records, so the vault identifiers can no longer be derived from the result.
- the AddonAzureBackupJobs rows where Category is AzureBackupReport, OperationName is Vault and SchemaVersion_s is V2: AddonAzureBackupJobs is one of the per-event tables created by the current six events, so it never contains the older combined stream. The legacy rows are the ones under Category AzureBackupReport in the shared diagnostics table.

prompt: You accidentally deleted the Windows Server virtual machine vm-erp-01. You have to bring it back with exactly the network setup and the licensing arrangement it had, as recorded in the exhibit, and it must run in the same Azure region where it was running. Which Azure Backup operation should you use?

options.text: Restore disk
Create a new VM
Replace existing
Cross Region Restore

explanation:
Restore disk is the operation that covers this configuration. The documented cases it handles include machines with multiple NICs, internal or external load balancing, multiple reserved IP addresses, and Hybrid Use Benefit licensing where the license type is set to Windows_Server - vm-erp-01 matches every one of them. The job copies the virtual hard disks into the staging account and produces a template you can edit and deploy (or drive with PowerShell), so the machine can be rebuilt with the same load balancing, multiple NICs, reserved IPs and Windows_Server licensing.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Create a new VM: Create a new VM quickly brings up a basic machine from the recovery point and places it in the same region as the source, but the special cases that belong to this VM (multiple NICs, internal load balancing, reserved IPs and the Windows_Server license type) are exactly the ones handled by Restore disk, and a machine created this way comes back with no availability set and no way to pick one.
- Replace existing: Replace existing restores a recovery point over a disk on a machine that is still present: Azure Backup snapshots that machine first, stores the snapshot in the vault under the retention policy, then swaps the disks and leaves the original disk in the resource group. vm-erp-01 has already been deleted, so this operation cannot be used.
- Cross Region Restore: Cross Region Restore copies vault-tier data into the region the vault treats as secondary and is intended for a full or partial outage of the primary region; the primary region in this scenario is fully operational. It also offers only Create a VM and Restore Disks and does not support replacing an existing machine.

options.text: Change the vault storage redundancy to ZRS
Change the vault storage redundancy to GRS
Change the vault storage redundancy to LRS
Keep the vault storage redundancy as it is and enable cross-region restore on the vault

explanation:
Restoring a zone-pinned virtual machine into another zone of the same region is only offered when the Recovery Services vault stores its data with zone-redundant storage. Every other condition shown in the exhibit is already satisfied: managed disks, a zone-pinned and unencrypted source, a recovery point held in the vault tier, and the Create new restore option. The vault therefore has to be switched to zone-redundant storage so that the restore configuration lets you pick the zone to restore into.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Change the vault storage redundancy to GRS: Changing the vault storage redundancy to GRS keeps the vault's copies in the paired region but provides no zone redundancy inside the region, so the restore still cannot offer a zone target for an in-region restore.
- Change the vault storage redundancy to LRS: Changing the vault storage redundancy to LRS leaves the vault in the state it is already in, and locally redundant storage does not meet the redundancy requirement for restoring into a different zone in the same region.
- Keep the vault storage redundancy as it is and enable cross-region restore on the vault: Cross-region restore only opens a zone choice when the virtual machine or disks are created in the vault's paired region, and it additionally requires that paired region to support zones. It does nothing for a restore that stays inside the vault's own region, so the zone target stays unavailable.

prompt: You have used the Azure Backup file-recovery capability to pull a single configuration file out of a recovery point of vm-hr-01 onto a helper machine, and that session is still open on the helper. The next scheduled backup of vm-hr-01 then failed. You need vm-hr-01's scheduled backups to succeed again without discarding any of its recovery points. Which action should you take?

options.text: Leave the mounted volumes in place and close the File Recovery session without detaching them
Run `mount -a` on the script host to reattach every logical volume, then close the File Recovery session
Run the File Recovery script's clean command on the Linux host to clear orphaned mount points, but keep the mounted volumes available
Select Unmount Disks in the File Recovery menu and run the File Recovery script's clean command on the Linux host to clear orphaned mount points

explanation:
A file-recovery session that is left mounted keeps the backup agent from opening the source volumes, which is exactly what the UserErrorUnableToOpenMount failure on the following backup job indicates. The remedy documented for Azure Backup is to finish the session by choosing Unmount Disks in the File Recovery menu, and because the helper machine in this scenario runs Linux, to also run the recovery script's clean command (python scriptName.py clean) to clear orphaned mount points. Doing both lets the next scheduled backup of vm-hr-01 complete while every existing recovery point is retained.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Leave the mounted volumes in place and close the File Recovery session without detaching them: Closing the session while the volumes are still mounted is what caused the follow-up backup job to fail with UserErrorUnableToOpenMount. The session must be ended by detaching the mounted volumes, not by simply closing it.
- Run `mount -a` on the script host to reattach every logical volume, then close the File Recovery session: `mount -a` is explicitly called out as the wrong way to work with these mounts; each logical volume should be mounted individually with `sudo mount <LV path> <mountpath>`. In any case, reattaching volumes without detaching them from the session leaves the original failure condition in place.
- Run the File Recovery script's clean command on the Linux host to clear orphaned mount points, but keep the mounted volumes available: Running the clean command on a Linux helper only clears orphaned mount points left over from earlier runs; it does not release the volumes that are still attached by the open session. The mounted volumes also have to be detached through the File Recovery menu before the next backup can succeed.

prompt: Your team protects the Linux virtual machine vm-sales-01 with the Recovery Services vault rsvault-sales using the backup policy shown in the exhibit. The business now requires that a recovery point exist every four hours, while the daily recovery points are still kept for 30 days. Which change should you make?

options.text: Change the policy sub type to Enhanced
Keep the policy sub type as Standard and change the schedule frequency to every four hours
Keep the policy sub type as Standard and trigger an on-demand backup every four hours
Keep the policy sub type as Standard and change the daily backup point retention to 90 days

explanation:
The sub type of the backup policy is what sets the cadence. With Standard, the virtual machine is backed up once a day at the time you choose and recovery points are kept for 30 days; with Enhanced, a backup runs every four hours at that time and the daily backup points are kept for 30 days. The exhibit shows the policy still uses the Standard sub type with a once-daily schedule, so the change that satisfies the requirement is to edit the policy in the vault and switch its sub type to Enhanced, which yields a recovery point every four hours while keeping 30 days of daily points.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Keep the policy sub type as Standard and change the schedule frequency to every four hours: The sub type, not a free-form schedule field, determines how often recovery points are created: Standard runs one backup a day at the time you pick, and only the Enhanced sub type adds the every-four-hours runs. Changing the frequency while the sub type stays Standard leaves the daily cadence in place.
- Keep the policy sub type as Standard and trigger an on-demand backup every four hours: An on-demand backup (Backup now) creates a recovery point only when someone triggers it and sets its retention with the calendar control. Nothing in the policy runs it on a schedule, so the machine would still have just the one daily scheduled recovery point for most of the day.
- Keep the policy sub type as Standard and change the daily backup point retention to 90 days: Retention controls how long a recovery point is kept, not how often backups run. The exhibit shows the machine already keeps 30 days of daily points, and widening that window would still leave a single recovery point per day rather than one every four hours.

- Edit the Recovery Services vault in the exhibit, and then change its region to West Europe and its resource group to RG-Compliance: Editing the vault's properties will not work here: a vault generated by enabling backup from the virtual machine blade takes the VM's region and resource group, and neither of them can be changed once backup is enabled that way.

prompt: You have a Linux virtual machine vm-db-02 that is protected by the Recovery Services vault rsvault-db. Its file system is corrupted, and clients connect to it through the private IP address that is already registered with them. The virtual machine is still deployed, and you need to bring the machine back to a good state on that same instance, in the same subscription and region, without changing its address. The exhibit lists what is known about the workload. Which Azure Backup operation should you use?

options.text: Create a new VM from the recovery point
Replace existing
Restore disk
Cross Subscription Restore

explanation:
Replace existing is the operation that brings a virtual machine back in place: Azure Backup first captures a snapshot of the machine and stores it in the vault under the retention policy, then swaps the disks of the virtual machine that is still deployed, so the network interface, private IP address, resource group, and subscription stay as they were. The previous disk is left in the resource group for you to delete once the machine is verified. The exhibit confirms this workload is eligible, because it is a Resource Manager virtual machine using managed disks and its image is not generalized. Continue only after the job's "Transfer Data to Vault" subtask reports success; otherwise bring the latest recovery point back with Create a new VM.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Create a new VM from the recovery point: Create a new VM builds a separate machine from the recovery point and leaves the corrupted virtual machine and its private IP address in place, so the clients that already point at that address would still reach the broken instance. The new machine also has to be created in the source region and would need its own address.
- Restore disk: Restore disk writes the recovered disks plus an editable ARM template into the staging storage account for you to deploy yourself, typically for configurations such as multiple NICs, reserved IPs, availability sets, or a specific licensing arrangement. It does not put the recovered disks back into the deployed virtual machine, so the machine would have to be rebuilt.
- Cross Subscription Restore: Cross Subscription Restore is used when the target subscription differs from the subscription that holds the protected virtual machine. It does not swap the disks of the running virtual machine, and the requirement here is to recover the instance inside its own subscription and region, so this operation does not meet the goal.

options.text: Install the Azure VM agent on the protected virtual machine
Choose a helper whose operating system generation matches the protected virtual machine
Give the helper direct outbound access to the recovery endpoint
Add the open-iscsi and lshw packages to the Linux helper and switch its locale to English
Run the script on a separate D2v3 virtual machine
Regenerate the script and use the credential it shows at that moment
Restore the virtual machine from the recovery point and copy the document from the restored operating system
Use mount -a on the Linux helper so that every logical volume is attached at once

explanation: Each request is blocked by one specific precondition. srv-mon-04 was built from a custom image, and a machine without the Azure VM agent cannot have the backup extension deployed on it, so the agent has to be added to that machine first. For file extraction, the host that runs the generated script must run the same operating system generation as the protected machine, which rules out helper-win-01 (Server 2022) for srv-web-01 (Server 2019) and makes a generation-matching helper the answer. helper-win-01 reaches the internet only through a corporate filtering service, and proxies commonly break the iSCSI/3260 path, so the script needs direct outbound access for the srv-erp-02 extraction. The Linux helper needs the open-iscsi and lshw packages, and because the script is English-only the system locale should be English. srv-fs-03 stores its data on an LVM volume group across striped disks, and such layouts must be handled by running the script on another machine, with a separate D2v3 virtual machine recommended. Finally, the script is valid for only 12 hours and its password is shown only at the moment it is generated, so the expired copy for srv-web-01 must be replaced by a newly produced script.

context:
Your company reorganized its Azure subscriptions. The virtual machine vm-fin-02 is protected by the Recovery Services vault rsvault-fin, and the recovery points recorded for it are held at the vault tier. After the reorganization the machine has to come back inside subscription Sub-B instead of subscription Sub-A, and you want to work from the recovery points that already exist for it. The exhibit lists the current state of the vault and of the protected item. What should you do?

- Property: Vault name; Value: rsvault-fin
- Property: Vault subscription; Value: Sub-A
- Property: Protected virtual machine; Value: vm-fin-02 (subscription Sub-A)
- Property: Recovery point tier; Value: Vault tier
- Property: Cross Subscription Restore; Value: Off
- Property: How the setting was changed; Value: Ordinary switch, not the permanent one
prompt: To bring vm-fin-02 back into subscription Sub-B using the recovery points that already exist for it, you should _____.

options.text: Re-enable the Cross Subscription Restore setting on the vault
Grant the owners of subscription Sub-B the Backup Operator role on the vault and keep the Cross Subscription Restore setting off
Move the vault into subscription Sub-B and restore from there, relying on the Cross Subscription Restore setting remaining off
Create a new vault in subscription Sub-B, re-protect vm-fin-02 there and restore it from there, keeping the Cross Subscription Restore setting off on the original vault

explanation:
A vault-tier recovery point can be restored into a subscription other than the one hosting the protected virtual machine only when Cross Subscription Restore is switched on for the vault; snapshot-tier points always stay in the protected machine's subscription. That control lives under Vault > Properties and can be switched on, switched off, or permanently disabled, with only the permanent variant being irreversible. The vault here was switched off with the ordinary switch, so the setting can be turned back on, which allows vm-fin-02 to be restored into subscription Sub-B from the recovery points that already exist.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Grant the owners of subscription Sub-B the Backup Operator role on the vault and keep the Cross Subscription Restore setting off: Granting the Backup Operator role controls who may manage backups in the vault, but it does not change the vault's cross-subscription restore behaviour. With the setting off, a vault-tier point still cannot be restored into subscription Sub-B.
- Move the vault into subscription Sub-B and restore from there, relying on the Cross Subscription Restore setting remaining off: Moving the vault does not satisfy the requirement, because the protected machine stays in subscription Sub-A, so restoring into Sub-B is still a restore into a subscription other than the protected machine's and therefore still needs the setting turned on. Moving a vault while the setting is off also breaks restores back into the original subscription.
- Create a new vault in subscription Sub-B, re-protect vm-fin-02 there and restore it from there, keeping the Cross Subscription Restore setting off on the original vault: A second vault starts with new recovery points rather than the ones that already exist for vm-fin-02, so it does not meet the stated requirement, and the original vault's setting would still be off for any later restore.

explanation:
A restore that runs with a managed identity needs two things: the identity must already be associated with the Recovery Services vault, which id-web-restore is here, and the VM restore operator role must be assigned on the staging location (the storage account) and on the target resource group where the restore creates its resources. In this scenario that means the assignment must cover stgweb01 and RG-Web-Restore, so the identity can write the restore output and create the restored disks.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add the VM restore operator role assignment on the Recovery Services vault and the target resource group: This places the assignment on the vault instead of on the staging storage account. The vault is where the identity must already be associated; the staging storage account is the location the restore job writes its template and VHD files to, so the role must be granted there for the job to succeed.
- Add the VM restore operator role assignment on the staging storage account and the protected VM's resource group: The restored disks are created in RG-Web-Restore, so the permissions have to cover that resource group. RG-Web-Prod only holds the original protected VM, and the restore job does not create or modify resources there.
- Add the Storage Blob Data Contributor role assignment on the staging storage account and the target resource group: Storage Blob Data Contributor grants blob data access only. In addition to the storage account, the restore creates and manages disks and other resources in the target resource group, and the VM restore operator role is the role that covers those restore permissions.

context:
You have to bring back the deleted virtual machine vm-api-02, which is protected by the Recovery Services vault rsvault-orders, and the machine has to end up in the availability set AS-PROD next to the other API servers that front the internal load balancer. The exhibit lists what is on record for this workload. Which Azure Backup operation should you use?

`PROPERTY                          VALUE
Protected item                   vm-api-02
Recovery Services vault          rsvault-orders
Region                           East US 2
Availability set to join         AS-PROD
Other members of AS-PROD         vm-api-01, vm-api-03, vm-api-04
Original vm-api-02 instance      Deleted; no instance remains`
prompt: The operation to use is _____.

options.text: Restore disk
Create a new VM
Replace existing
File recovery

explanation:
Restore disk is the operation intended for special machine configurations such as membership of an availability set: it produces the machine's storage together with a downloadable ARM template that you can edit and deploy, or you can build the virtual machine with PowerShell, and that is the supported way to place vm-api-02 into AS-PROD. The other catalogue entries cannot satisfy the requirement: a machine rebuilt with Create a new VM in the portal comes back with no availability set and offers no way to choose one, and Replace existing can only be used while the original instance still exists, which it does not here.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Create a new VM: Create a new VM is the quickest way to get a running machine from a recovery point, but a virtual machine rebuilt that way in the portal has no availability set and gives you no way to pick one, so it cannot be joined to AS-PROD.
- Replace existing: Replace existing swaps the protected storage onto the original virtual machine, so it requires that instance to still exist; vm-api-02 has been deleted, and the operation also cannot be pointed at a different availability set.
- File recovery: File recovery mounts a recovery point read-only on a helper machine so that individual files can be copied out; it never produces a running virtual machine and therefore cannot place vm-api-02 in AS-PROD.

context:
You have just brought a new virtual machine back online from one of the existing recovery points of vm-chg-01 with the Create a new VM operation, and that job wrote its output to the storage account stgacct-chg. The job has now finished, and the invoice for stgacct-chg carries charges that the finance team does not recognize and wants gone. Your compliance rules forbid discarding any of the recovery points that vm-chg-01 already has, and stgacct-chg is shared with other recovery jobs, so it has to remain in place. The exhibit lists what is on record for this workload. Which action should you take?

- Item: Protected virtual machine; Value: vm-chg-01
- Item: Restore operation used; Value: Create a new VM
- Item: Tier of the recovery point that was used; Value: Vault tier (Vault-Standard)
- Item: Data disks attached to the virtual machine; Value: 2
- Item: Largest data disk; Value: 600 GB
- Item: Account that received the restore output; Value: stgacct-chg (Standard LRS, East US 2)
prompt: To clear the charges that the finance team does not recognize, you should _____.

options.text: delete the VHD files that the restore copied into the storage account
delete the recovery points that the restore left in the vault tier for vm-chg-01
delete the storage account that the restore used and register a replacement for it
change the backup policy of vm-chg-01 so that its recovery points are kept in the snapshot tier

explanation:
When you create a virtual machine from a recovery point that is held at the vault tier (Vault-Standard), Azure Backup also copies the VHD files of the disks into the staging storage account for machines whose disks are under 4 TB or that have fewer than 16 disks. vm-chg-01 has two data disks with a largest disk of 600 GB, so that condition is met, and the extra items billed on stgacct-chg are those copies. The copies are handed over to managed storage, so deleting them from the staging storage account stops the extra charges. The recovery points that the machine already has in the vault and the registered staging account itself both stay in place, which is what the compliance rule and the shared usage of stgacct-chg require.

Why the other options are wrong:
- delete the recovery points that the restore left in the vault tier for vm-chg-01: Discarding the recovery points breaks the protection that vm-chg-01 already has and violates the compliance rule, and it would not remove the copies already sitting in stgacct-chg, so the extra charges would remain.
- delete the storage account that the restore used and register a replacement for it: stgacct-chg is the staging account registered with the vault and is shared with other recovery jobs; deleting it breaks those jobs and contradicts the requirement that the account stays in place.
- change the backup policy of vm-chg-01 so that its recovery points are kept in the snapshot tier: A policy change only affects where recovery points created from now on are kept; it does not remove the copies that the finished restore already wrote into stgacct-chg, so the charges on the current invoice stay.

context:
Your team protects the Linux virtual machine vm-app-09 with Azure Backup. The machine was created from a custom image, and every backup job fails right away with an error saying the backup extension could not be installed. What should you do to get the backups running again?

`Protected machine : vm-app-09
Image source      : custom, built in-house from vm-app-09-image.vhd
Marketplace image : No
VM agent          : missing from the machine
Backup extension  : could not be installed
Policy sub type   : Standard
Last backup status: Failed`
prompt: To get the backups running again, you should _____.

options.text: Install the VM agent on the protected machine so the backup extension can install
Install the backup extension manually on the protected machine from the Extensions blade
Install a new backup policy in the vault and enable it for the protected machine
Rebuild the custom image with the VM agent included, then protect a new machine built from it

explanation:
Azure Backup deploys its own extension on top of the VM agent. Marketplace images already contain the agent, but a custom image such as the one used for vm-app-09 does not, so the extension has nothing to install onto and every backup job fails. Installing the VM agent on the protected machine is the prerequisite step; once the agent is present the backup extension installs by itself and Azure Backup keeps it patched afterwards.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Install the backup extension manually on the protected machine from the Extensions blade: The backup extension is placed and maintained by Azure Backup itself on the VM agent, not deployed by hand from the Extensions blade. With no agent on the machine the extension cannot be installed, so installing the agent first is the required step.
- Install a new backup policy in the vault and enable it for the protected machine: The failure is in the extension installation on the machine rather than in the policy that drives the schedule, so creating and enabling a different policy in the vault leaves the same error in place.
- Rebuild the custom image with the VM agent included, then protect a new machine built from it: Nothing requires the image to be rebuilt: the agent can be installed on the existing machine, and protecting a newly built machine would not restore backups for vm-app-09.

You need the session to complete so that you can retrieve the quarterly report file from the protected machine. The exhibit lists what is known about both machines. prompt: On the helper machine, add _____ so the session can reach the recovery endpoint, and make sure the helper is running [...] so that the recovery script can run there.

options.text: Allow outbound to the AzureBackup service tag on TCP port 3260
Allow outbound to the AzureBackup service tag on TCP port 443
Allow outbound to the AzureFrontDoor.FirstParty service tag on TCP port 3260
Allow outbound to the Microsoft.Storage service tag on TCP port 3260

explanation:
The file-recovery session reads the recovery point data from the recovery endpoint, and the documented way to allow that traffic is the AzureBackup service tag on TCP port 3260; the script itself already downloads over port 443, so the missing rule is the one for port 3260. The script host must also run the operating system generation that pairs with the protected machine, and a protected machine on Windows Server 2016 pairs with a Windows 10 script host.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Allow outbound to the AzureBackup service tag on TCP port 443: This points at port 443, which is the port used to fetch the recovery script itself; that download already succeeds, and the data connection to the recovery endpoint is made on TCP port 3260.
- Allow outbound to the AzureFrontDoor.FirstParty service tag on TCP port 3260: This service tag is listed for port 443 for obtaining the script. The service tag documented for reaching the recovery endpoint on port 3260 is AzureBackup, so this rule does not open the path the session needs.
- Allow outbound to the Microsoft.Storage service tag on TCP port 3260: Microsoft.Storage is not the service tag documented for the recovery endpoint traffic. The file-recovery data path is allowed with the AzureBackup service tag on TCP port 3260.
