- Requirement or context: Continuity requirement; Value: Recovery points must remain available if an entire region is lost
- Requirement or context: Rehearsal requirement; Value: Recover from the paired region during scheduled drills while the primary region is healthy
- Requirement or context: Cost acceptance; Value: Billing at RA-GRS rates for the PostgreSQL backups held in the vault is acceptable
- Requirement or context: Timing of the choice; Value: The redundancy value must be settled at creation time and cannot be changed once items are protected
prompt: Your team is creating a Backup vault in the Azure portal for an Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server, and you are on the Instance details tab of the create wizard. Business continuity requires the recovery points to survive the loss of an entire Azure region, and the team must be able to rehearse a regional recovery during planned drills without waiting for an outage declaration. Which storage redundancy setting and companion toggle should you select?

options.text: Geo-redundant (GRS) with Cross Region Restore enabled
Geo-redundant (GRS) only, keeping the paired region sealed until an outage is declared
Zone-redundant (ZRS) with Cross Region Restore enabled
Locally redundant (LRS) with Cross Region Restore enabled

explanation:
Geo-redundant (GRS) keeps a second copy of the recovery points in the Azure paired region, which is what protects against loss of an entire primary region; it is also the recommended setting when Azure holds the primary copy of the data. Turning on Cross Region Restore then makes those secondary-region recovery points available for restores and regional resiliency drills at any time, with no outage declared in the primary region. Enabling Cross Region Restore is billed automatically at RA-GRS rates for the PostgreSQL backups stored in the vault, which the scenario accepts.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Geo-redundant (GRS) only, keeping the paired region sealed until an outage is declared: With Geo-redundant (GRS) alone the backups in the paired region become accessible only after Microsoft declares an outage in the primary region, so the scheduled drill during a healthy primary region cannot be performed. This setting satisfies the regional-outage requirement but not the rehearsal requirement.
- Zone-redundant (ZRS) with Cross Region Restore enabled: Zone-redundant (ZRS) keeps the redundant copies inside the primary region, spread across availability zones. It does not maintain a copy in the Azure paired region, so it satisfies neither the loss-of-region requirement nor restores from the paired region.
- Locally redundant (LRS) with Cross Region Restore enabled: Locally redundant (LRS) stores copies within the region only and is the recommended choice when Azure is not the primary backup storage endpoint, because it reduces Azure storage cost. It offers no protection against loss of the region and no paired-region recovery points to restore from.

prompt: You have an Azure Backup vault named prod-vault in the East US region that protects an Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server. The vault is protected by a key that your organization keeps in the Azure Key Vault kv-backup-keys, and the only principal listed with a role on that Key Vault is the vault's own identity. Since the last key rotation, every scheduled and on-demand backup job fails with a key retrieval error. You need the backup jobs to succeed again while keeping the key under your own control in Azure Key Vault. Which access change should you make?

options.text: Grant the vault's System Assigned Managed Identity access to the Key Vault so it can read the key.
Grant the Backup Management Service access to the Key Vault so it can read the key.
Grant the vault's User Assigned Managed Identity access to the Key Vault so it can read the key.
Grant the Backup vault resource itself access to the Key Vault so it can read the key.

explanation:
When a Backup vault uses Customer Managed Keys, the key read against Azure Key Vault is performed by the Backup Management Service; the vault's managed identity is not the actor that reaches into the Key Vault. The exhibit shows that only the vault's System Assigned Managed Identity holds a role on kv-backup-keys and that jobs still fail with a key retrieval error, so the missing piece is access for the Backup Management Service. Granting that service access to the Key Vault lets the key be used for the vault's encryption while the key stays under your own control.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Grant the vault's System Assigned Managed Identity access to the Key Vault so it can read the key: The vault's System Assigned Managed Identity already holds Key Vault Crypto User on that Key Vault, and permissions given to a vault's managed identity are not what make Customer Managed Keys work, because the key read is carried out by the Backup Management Service.
- Grant the vault's User Assigned Managed Identity access to the Key Vault so it can read the key: A User Assigned Managed Identity can be attached to a vault and outlives the vault, but it is not the principal that reads the encryption key, so granting it a role on kv-backup-keys leaves the failing jobs unchanged; the Backup Management Service needs the access instead.
- Grant the Backup vault resource itself access to the Key Vault so it can read the key: The vault resource itself is not the principal that performs the key read either. Only the Backup Management Service reads the key for Customer Managed Keys, so granting the vault resource access in the Key Vault does not resolve the failures.

prompt:
You have a Backup vault named fin-vault in resource group rg-backup of the Contoso-prod subscription. It protects an Azure Disk named data-finance01, which sits in resource group rg-data. A backup policy runs from an automation account whose run-as identity is svc-backup-runner, and every attempt to back up the disk ends with an authorization error reporting that access to data-finance01 was denied. The access configuration that is in place today is listed below.

You need the disk backups to complete with the smallest possible permission footprint, and the automation account must not receive any write or delete permission on data-finance01. Which change should you make?

options.text: Grant the fin-vault System Assigned Managed Identity the Reader role on the Azure Disk data-finance01.
Grant the svc-backup-runner run-as identity the Reader role on the Azure Disk data-finance01.
Grant the svc-backup-runner run-as identity the Owner role on the resource group rg-data.
Grant the svc-backup-runner run-as identity the Key Vault Reader role on the Key Vault kv-backup-keys.

explanation:
Whoever creates or updates a backup instance must be able to read the source resources, and that grant has to sit with the user or service identity that performs the work rather than with the vault's managed identity. In this scenario svc-backup-runner is the run-as identity that creates and updates the backup instance for the disk, so handing it the Reader role on data-finance01 is the minimal change that removes the authorization error, and Reader grants no write or delete permission on the disk.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Grant the fin-vault System Assigned Managed Identity the Reader role on the Azure Disk data-finance01: The vault's managed identity is not the party that creates or updates the backup instance. The documentation is explicit that the read grant on the source belongs to the user or service identity doing that work, not to the vault's managed identity, so granting Reader to the fin-vault identity does not clear the denial.
- Grant the svc-backup-runner run-as identity the Owner role on the resource group rg-data: Owner on rg-data hands the automation account full control over every resource in the group, including write and delete rights on the protected disk, which breaks the requirement to keep the footprint minimal and read-only.
- Grant the svc-backup-runner run-as identity the Key Vault Reader role on the Key Vault kv-backup-keys: Key Vault Reader on kv-backup-keys governs access to key material stored in that Key Vault. The protected disk lives in rg-data, so this assignment grants nothing on data-finance01 and the backup continues to be denied.

prompt: You are creating two Azure Backup vaults in the Contoso-prod subscription — prod-vault in rg-blue and test-vault in rg-green. The platform team wants one managed identity to carry the access grants for prod-vault and for test-vault, so that the grants are administered in a single place. During the Q1 migration, prod-vault will be deleted and re-created, and the identity that carries the grants must still be usable afterwards. Which managed identity configuration should you use?

options.text: System Assigned Managed Identity, created with each vault and removed with that vault
User Assigned Managed Identity, created independently and referenced by both vaults
User Assigned Managed Identity, created once for each vault, so each of the vaults keeps a separate identity
System Assigned Managed Identity, created for one vault and reused by the other vault

explanation:
A User Assigned Managed Identity is a standalone object whose lifecycle is separate from the vaults it is attached to: it can be attached to one or several vaults, it can be shared across vaults, and it outlives the deletion or re-creation of a vault. That lets a single identity and a single set of role assignments serve prod-vault and test-vault, and it keeps working after prod-vault is deleted and re-created during the Q1 migration.

Why the other options are wrong:
- System Assigned Managed Identity, created with each vault and removed with that vault: The System Assigned Managed Identity is generated together with the vault and is bound to that vault's lifecycle. Each vault would therefore need its own identity and its own set of grants, and the identity of prod-vault would disappear with the vault during the migration, leaving the grants dangling.
- User Assigned Managed Identity, created once for each vault, so each of the vaults keeps a separate identity: Creating one identity per vault produces two identity objects and two sets of grants, which does not meet the requirement of a single identity and a single set of role assignments covering prod-vault and test-vault. It also states that the identity is removed with its vault, which is not how a user-assigned identity behaves — such an identity survives deletion and re-creation of the vault it is attached to.
- System Assigned Managed Identity, created for one vault and reused by the other vault: A System Assigned Managed Identity belongs to the vault that generated it and is bound to that vault's lifecycle, so it cannot be attached to a second vault and cannot be reused by test-vault. It also disappears when prod-vault is deleted, so it would not satisfy the requirement that the grants remain usable after the vault is re-created.

prompt:
You are retiring the Backup vault pg-vault in resource group rg-backup of the Contoso-prod subscription. Every attempt to remove it from the portal is refused, and the vault must be gone by the end of the change window. The state reported for the vault is shown below.

You need the vault removed together with everything it holds, and no backup data may survive in the subscription afterwards. Which change should you make?

options.text: Remove all backup policies from the vault but leave the backup instances in place, then delete the vault.
Remove all backup instances and backup policies from the vault, then delete the vault.
Remove all backup instances from the vault but leave the backup policies in place, then delete the vault.
Change the vault's storage redundancy to Locally redundant and detach the vault's managed identity, then delete the vault.

explanation:
A vault is refused for deletion while it still holds protected data sources or backup data, and a Backup vault can hold both backup instances and backup policies, so both kinds of object have to go before the vault itself can be removed. This vault still carries the protected items pg-fin-01 and data-disk-01 together with the policies pg-daily-90d and disk-daily-30d, so the correct change is to remove every entry from the Backup Instances view and every remaining backup policy, then delete the vault. When hunting for leftovers, work through each Datasource type filter, because a single instance or policy hidden under one filter value keeps the vault undeletable. Remember that removal cannot be undone: the recovery points of the protected servers disappear permanently, which matches the requirement that no backup data survive the decommission.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Remove all backup policies from the vault but leave the backup instances in place, then delete the vault: Removing only the backup policies leaves the backup instances and the protected data sources with their recovery points inside the vault. The delete request is still refused while any backup instance or backup data remains, so the operation fails.
- Remove all backup instances from the vault but leave the backup policies in place, then delete the vault: Removing only the backup instances leaves the backup policies in the vault. Both backup instances and backup policies must be gone before the vault can be deleted, so the portal keeps refusing the delete request.
- Change the vault's storage redundancy to Locally redundant and detach the vault's managed identity, then delete the vault: Neither part of this change releases anything: the redundancy level is in fact locked once items are protected, and detaching the vault's managed identity leaves the protected items and their stored recovery points untouched. The vault therefore stays undeletable.

prompt:
You have a Backup vault named contoso-vault in resource group rg-backup of the Contoso-prod subscription, and it protects an Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server. A separate company runs its own Microsoft Entra tenant, and after a ransomware incident locks the Contoso side out, that company must bring the PostgreSQL server's vaulted backup data into fabrikam-vault, which it owns and administers. The partner must be able to do this without holding any account in the Contoso-prod subscription, and the Contoso team must not expose the stored backup data to partner users.

You need the partner to be able to work with the PostgreSQL server's vaulted backup data through fabrikam-vault. Which change should you make?

options.text: Configure Cross Tenant Restore (preview) on contoso-vault and create a mapping from contoso-vault to fabrikam-vault
Configure Cross Region Restore on contoso-vault so the partner can pull the PostgreSQL recovery points from the paired region to a new server

Create and configure a second Geo-redundant Backup vault named fabrikam-vault inside the Contoso-prod subscription, re-protect the PostgreSQL server with it, and add the partner's guest account as Owner on it
Configure a guest account for the partner in the Contoso-prod tenant with Owner on contoso-vault so their administrators can copy the recovery points into fabrikam-vault themselves

explanation:
Cross-tenant restore (preview) is the supported way to bring vaulted data from a source vault into a vault that lives in a different tenant: it recovers the vaulted backup data from the source tenant into the target vault by mapping the source Backup vault to that target vault. You configure it on the source vault (contoso-vault) and create the mapping to the partner's vault (fabrikam-vault), after which the protected items and their recovery points can be worked with from fabrikam-vault. The exhibit fits this capability: Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server is one of the workloads the preview feature covers, and fabrikam-vault is owned by the partner in a separate tenant, so it can act as the target vault. Ordinary restores stay inside one tenant, so nothing else in the current configuration brings the data across.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Configure Cross Region Restore on contoso-vault so the partner can pull the PostgreSQL recovery points from the paired region to a new server: Cross Region Restore only replicates the PostgreSQL backups to the paired Azure region and opens the secondary copy so you can rehearse recovery there; it keeps the data within the same tenant, so it cannot make the protected data available through fabrikam-vault in the partner's tenant.
- Create and configure a second Geo-redundant Backup vault named fabrikam-vault inside the Contoso-prod subscription, re-protect the PostgreSQL server with it, and add the partner's guest account as Owner on it: A second vault created inside the Contoso-prod subscription remains in the same tenant as the source data, and a guest account on it is still an account in the Contoso-prod subscription. Only the cross-tenant capability brings vaulted data into a vault in another tenant.
- Configure a guest account for the partner in the Contoso-prod tenant with Owner on contoso-vault so their administrators can copy the recovery points into fabrikam-vault themselves: The vaulted backup data is kept in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant, so partner guests have no direct route to that storage even if they are given an Owner role on contoso-vault. Role assignments made inside the Contoso-prod tenant cannot be used to copy the data into fabrikam-vault themselves.

prompt: You have a new Azure Backup vault named blob-vault that the platform team is creating in the Contoso-prod subscription to hold vaulted backups for an Azure Blob container. The blob data's primary copy is kept on an on-premises NAS appliance outside Azure, finance has capped the vault's monthly storage charge at the cheapest tier the platform team approves, and the stated recovery objective covers restoring in the same Azure region only. You need the vault's storage footprint chosen correctly while the vault is being created so that the monthly charge stays within the approved cap. Which storage redundancy setting should you select?

options.text: Locally redundant (LRS)
Zone-redundant (ZRS)
Geo-redundant (GRS)
Geo-redundant (GRS) with Cross Region Restore enabled

explanation:
Because Azure is not where the primary copy of the backed-up data lives, the documented guidance is to choose Locally redundant (LRS) for the vault, which reduces Azure storage cost. The vault currently holds no protected items, so this is the point at which the setting can still be chosen — once items are protected, a vault's storage redundancy cannot be changed.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Zone-redundant (ZRS): Zone-redundant (ZRS) spreads copies across availability zones and is the costlier option, so it does not match a vault whose approved charge is capped at the cheapest tier, and the recovery objective does not require surviving the loss of an availability zone.

You have a new Azure Backup vault that the platform team is creating in the Contoso-prod subscription to hold vaulted backups for an Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server. Contoso's security policy requires that the key protecting the vaulted backup data be generated, stored, rotated and revoked by Contoso's own security team inside Contoso's own Azure Key Vault. The same policy requires that role-based control over backup and restore operations on the vault, including which workloads the vault is allowed to back up, stays enforced. This vault serves a single team and is not shared with any other vault. The configuration decided so far is listed below.

You need the new vault configured so that both parts of the policy hold. Which change should you make?

options.text: Under Encryption settings select Customer Managed Keys and point the vault at the key in kv-contoso-crypto, but leave the vault's System Assigned Managed Identity disabled.
Under Encryption settings select Customer Managed Keys and point the vault at the key in kv-contoso-crypto, and turn on the vault's System Assigned Managed Identity.
Under Encryption settings select Microsoft managed keys and turn on the vault's System Assigned Managed Identity, leaving the key lifecycle with the platform service.

Under Encryption settings select Customer Managed Keys and point the vault at the key in kv-contoso-crypto, but replace the Backup Management Service app's key read access with key read access for the vault's System Assigned Managed Identity.

explanation:
Two separate requirements are in play, and this option satisfies both. First, Contoso's requirement to own the encryption key is met by selecting Customer Managed Keys under the vault's Encryption settings and pointing the vault at contoso-backup-key in kv-contoso-crypto; with Microsoft managed keys the key stays under the platform service's control, so Contoso could not rotate or revoke it on its own authority. The key read for that arrangement is performed by the Backup Management Service app, which per the exhibit already holds Key Vault Crypto User on kv-contoso-crypto, so no permission change in the key vault is required. Second, access to backup and restore operations, including which workloads the vault may back up, is enforced through the managed identities associated with the vault. With the System Assigned Managed Identity disabled and no User Assigned Managed Identity attached, the vault currently has no identity carrying those grants. Because this vault serves a single team and is not shared, the System Assigned Managed Identity is the simplest choice to bring back.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Under Encryption settings select Customer Managed Keys and point the vault at the key in kv-contoso-crypto, but leave the vault's System Assigned Managed Identity disabled: The encryption half is right, but the identity half is not. With the System Assigned Managed Identity disabled and no User Assigned Managed Identity attached, the vault has no managed identity at all, and it is through those identities that the vault's role-based access control, including the grants that decide which workloads it may back up, is enforced. Turning the System Assigned Managed Identity on is the simple fix for a vault used by a single team.
- Under Encryption settings select Microsoft managed keys and turn on the vault's System Assigned Managed Identity, leaving the key lifecycle with the platform service: Selecting Microsoft managed keys leaves the encryption key under the platform service's control, so Contoso cannot generate, rotate or revoke it on its own authority and the key-ownership part of the policy is not met. Turning on the identity only addresses the access side, and it also has to be paired with the customer-managed option.
- Under Encryption settings select Customer Managed Keys and point the vault at the key in kv-contoso-crypto, but replace the Backup Management Service app's key read access with key read access for the vault's System Assigned Managed Identity: The key read for a vault that encrypts its data with a customer-managed key is performed by the Backup Management Service app, not by the vault's own managed identity; permissions given to the vault's identity in the key vault are not what makes that option work. Removing the app's access and giving it to the vault's identity instead takes away the access that the service actually needs, so backup jobs would fail with a key retrieval error.

The security and operations teams have attached four guarantees to the sign-off for this vault, and each guarantee below is met by one characteristic of the Backup vault model. The team wants every guarantee recorded against the characteristic that delivers it.

Match each guarantee to the characteristic of the Backup vault that provides it.

- Guarantee: Copies held where no guest, outside partner or source-server intruder has a direct route into them; What the business requires: The copies must sit in a subscription and tenant that Contoso does not administer, so a compromised source environment cannot tamper with them or wipe them out.
- Guarantee: Recovery that survives a compromise of the production environment and the servers holding the copies; What the business requires: Even if the production environment and the servers that hold the copies are both taken over, the recovery points must stay recoverable.
- Guarantee: Different reach for different teams, down to the sources each may back up and the key stores each may use; What the business requires: One team may protect only the databases it owns, while another may additionally use the organization's own key stores for the keys that protect the copies.
- Guarantee: One place to follow every job and alert, with matching reporting; What the business requires: Every job and every alert raised for the resources in the vault must be traceable from a single place, and reporting for the same must be available there too.
prompt: Copies held where no guest, outside partner or source-server intruder has a direct route into them

options.text: Data isolation
Enhanced capabilities to help secure backup data
Fine-grained control over which workloads the vault can access
Central monitoring of the V2 workloads

explanation: Each guarantee lines up with exactly one characteristic of the Backup vault model. Data isolation puts the vaulted copies in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant, so guests and outside partners have no direct route into them and a compromised source environment cannot tamper with or wipe them. The enhanced capabilities are what allow data to be recovered safely even when production and backup servers are both compromised. Fine-grained control over which workloads the vault can access is what separates the two teams, letting one be limited to the sources it owns while another additionally reaches the key stores used for encryption key management. Central monitoring of the V2 workloads is what puts backup jobs and alerts together in one place, with the matching reporting available in the Resiliency.

You are building a new Azure Backup vault for the Contoso-prod subscription, and the design review recorded five obligations for the vault. The context for the new vault is shown below.

You need each obligation to be met by one of the configuration changes listed for dragging. Match each obligation to the configuration change that satisfies it.

- Context item: Resources to be protected; Recorded situation: One Blob container (vaulted backup) and one Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server
- Context item: Azure region for the vault; Recorded situation: East US
- Context item: Company's own copy of the blob data; Recorded situation: On-premises NAS appliance outside Azure
- Context item: Recovery exercise; Recorded situation: Quarterly, run from the copies in the paired area with no failure declared in the primary area
- Context item: Key custody; Recorded situation: Contoso's own security team generates, rotates and revokes the key material
- Context item: Grant administration; Recorded situation: Two platform teams administer the vault's grants; the vault will be deleted and rebuilt in June
- Context item: Approved protected resources; Recorded situation: Two storage volumes, one database instance, one Azure Key Vault
prompt: The company's own copy of the data sits on-premises, recovery is carried out inside the vault's own area, and finance wants the smallest monthly Azure bill for the vault.

options.text: Create the Azure Backup vault with Locally redundant storage redundancy.
Create the Azure Backup vault with Geo-redundant storage redundancy and enable Cross Region Restore.
Create the Azure Backup vault with Geo-redundant storage redundancy and keep Cross Region Restore disabled.
Select Customer Managed Keys under Encryption settings on the Azure Backup vault.
Apply role assignments through the vault's managed identity so that it covers only the named workloads and the Azure Key Vault used for key management.

explanation: Each obligation maps to the vault configuration change that delivers it. An on-premises primary copy with same-area recovery and the smallest Azure bill points to Locally redundant storage redundancy chosen at creation, because that is the documented way to cut Azure storage spend when the original data is not held in Azure. Restoring from the copies held in the paired area on a scheduled date, while nothing has failed in the primary area, needs Geo-redundant storage plus Cross Region Restore turned on, because GRS replicates the backups to the paired region and Cross Region Restore allows restores from those secondary recovery points at any time without a declared outage. Surviving the loss of an entire region from an Azure-hosted primary copy while refusing the higher rate that the rehearsal capability brings points to Geo-redundant storage with Cross Region Restore left off, since a vault with Cross Region Restore enabled is billed automatically at RA-GRS rates. Generating, rotating and revoking the key material in the company's own Azure Key Vault points to the Customer Managed Keys option under Encryption settings, since the default Microsoft managed keys need no key-management effort by the customer. Finally, limiting the vault to the approved storage volumes, database instances and the chosen Azure Key Vault points to role assignments carried by the vault's managed identity, because RBAC on the vault can be tuned per workload, including which Azure Disks or PostgreSQL servers may be backed up and which Key Vaults are used for encryption key management.

You are finalizing the access design for contoso-vault, a new Azure Backup vault in rg-backup of the Contoso-prod subscription. It will hold vaulted backups of an Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server named pg-fin, and Contoso brings its own encryption material for the vaulted data. The design decisions on record are shown below.

You need to record, for each requirement that came out of the security review, the scope in which the design grants or withholds the related access. Match each requirement to the correct scope.

- Design decision: Vault; Recorded value: contoso-vault in rg-backup, subscription Contoso-prod
- Design decision: Protected workload; Recorded value: Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server named pg-fin
- Design decision: Scheduled job; Recorded value: Runs as svc-backup-runner, the run-as identity of an automation account
- Design decision: Encryption material; Recorded value: Supplied by Contoso rather than generated by the service
prompt: The Backup vault

options.text: Only engineers who hold the helpdesk role may start a restore of the stored recovery points.
The identity that runs the scheduled job must be able to read the server it protects.
Contoso's own encryption material, generated and rotated by its security team, must be usable by the service that protects the stored copies.
Guests and other external users must not be able to open the stored copies directly, even if the production environment is compromised.

explanation: Each requirement lands on a different scope of the Backup vault model. Limiting restores to the helpdesk role is enforced by the role assignments made on the vault itself, because Backup vaults work with Azure RBAC and only the roles assigned there can reach backup and restore operations. Letting the scheduled job read the server it protects requires read permission on that source resource, held by the identity that creates or updates the backup instance rather than by the vault's managed identity. Using Contoso's own encryption material involves the Backup Management Service app reaching into Azure Key Vault to read the key, so the relevant permission is granted on the Key Vault that holds it, and the vault's own identity is not the actor. Finally, keeping guests and other external users away from the stored copies is achieved by the isolation of the backup storage in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant, where those external users have no direct route at all.

Delete the backup instance that covers the protected server, then edit the storage redundancy of the existing vault.
Leave the storage redundancy of the existing vault unchanged, because that value is fixed when the vault is created.

explanation:
Storage redundancy is the one storage choice a Backup vault team makes, and it is made when the vault is created. The documentation is explicit that once items are protected in a vault, the redundancy level is locked, so a choice that turns out to be wrong cannot be edited in place afterwards. pg-vault already protects a PostgreSQL server, so its Locally redundant setting stays exactly as it is and cannot be edited in the portal, by editing the policy, or by clearing out backup instances. Because the recovery points that already exist must not be destroyed, the team keeps this vault as it is and reaches regional resilience by putting a vault with the redundancy it wants in place from the start and protecting the server there.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Edit the storage redundancy of the existing vault in the Azure portal: The storage redundancy is not an editable property of a vault that already holds protected items: once items are protected the redundancy level is locked, so editing it in the portal does not turn this vault into a geographically redundant one.
- Edit the backup policy that is attached to the protected server in the existing vault: The backup policy controls when backups run and how long recovery points are kept; it does not control the redundancy of the vault's storage, so editing the policy leaves the Locally redundant setting in place.
- Delete the backup instance that covers the protected server, then edit the storage redundancy of the existing vault: Removing the backup instance destroys the recovery points that already exist, and the redundancy stays locked once items have been protected, so this route both loses data and still fails to change the setting.

explanation:
The Resiliency blade is the single place where the vault's V2 workloads can be watched from backup jobs up to alerts, with matching reporting. The behaviour described — restoring from the paired region at any time with no outage declared in the primary region — is the Cross Region Restore capability, and a vault with that capability enabled is billed automatically at RA-GRS rates for the PostgreSQL backups it holds, rather than at plain GRS rates.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Backup Instances page: The Backup Instances page lists the protected items and their backup instances, and it is the place the portal guidance points engineers to when emptying a vault before deleting it; it is not the surface that shows the running jobs and alerts with matching reporting.
- Backup Policies page: Backup policies hold the schedule, retention and protection settings that drive backups; they are configuration to be read or edited, not the place where jobs and alerts for the protected workload are watched.
- Encryption settings page: Encryption settings only carries the vault's encryption configuration, such as the choice between Microsoft managed keys and a customer managed key, and provides no view of backup jobs or alerts.

context:
You are creating an Azure Backup vault named sec-vault in the Contoso-prod subscription to hold vaulted backup data for an Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server named pg-fin. The security and audit teams have attached two conditions to the sign-off for this vault, and the conditions on record are shown below.

You need the vault to satisfy both conditions. Which statement correctly completes the description of the recovery points it holds?

`Condition | Requirement recorded by the audit team
C1        | A full compromise of the production PostgreSQL server, including its administrator credentials, must not let the stored recovery points be changed or destroyed.
C2        | The audit evidence must name every party that can open the storage that holds the recovery points, and people outside Contoso who assist with restore drills must not be listed.`
prompt: The recovery points that the Backup vault holds for the protected workload are kept _____, and [...].

options.text: in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant, where guest accounts and external users have no direct route to the storage
in Contoso's own subscription and resource group, with access restricted by the vault's Azure RBAC assignments
in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant, where principals with a backup role on the vault have direct reach to the storage
in Contoso's own subscription and resource group, with network rules leaving guest accounts and external users no direct route to the storage

explanation:
A Backup vault keeps the recovery points it accumulates in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant, and guests and other external users have no direct route to that storage or its contents. Because the copy of the backup data lives outside the customer's own subscription and outside the reach of the workload's administrators, a compromised source environment cannot be used to alter or wipe the recovery points that already exist. Role-based control on the vault governs which principals may run backup and restore operations; it does not hand out a path into the storage itself.

Why the other options are wrong:
- in Contoso's own subscription and resource group, with access restricted by the vault's Azure RBAC assignments: The recovery points are not stored in Contoso's own subscription and resource group; they are kept in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant. Role assignments on the vault control who may perform backup and restore operations; they are not a restriction applied to storage in the customer's own resource group.
- in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant, where principals with a backup role on the vault have direct reach to the storage: The location is right but the reach is wrong: holding one of the backup roles on the vault grants the ability to run backup and restore operations, not a direct path to the storage that holds the recovery points. Guests and other external users have no direct route to that storage at all.
- in Contoso's own subscription and resource group, with network rules leaving guest accounts and external users no direct route to the storage: The recovery points are not held in Contoso's own subscription and resource group, and network rules are not what protects them. The isolation comes from the data being kept in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant that guests and external users cannot route to.

sit in storage that Azure manages for you, and the redundancy set at creation can be changed later in the vault's storage settings
sit in a storage account that you create and administer, and the redundancy set at creation is the only storage choice you make
sit in a storage account that you create and administer, and the redundancy set at creation can be changed later in the vault's storage settings

explanation:
The Backup vault keeps its backup data in storage that the service manages on your behalf, so the Contoso platform team does not create, own or run a storage account for the recovery points. The one storage-related decision that remains theirs is the redundancy level chosen when the vault is created (Geo-redundant for store-vault). Because the vault already protects an Azure Blob container, that level is now locked and is not something the team can adjust afterwards.

Why the other options are wrong:
- sit in storage that Azure manages for you, and the redundancy set at creation can be changed later in the vault's storage settings: The first half is right, but the second half is not: the redundancy level is fixed once items are protected in the vault, so it cannot be raised later, and the vault does not expose a storage setting for changing it.
- sit in a storage account that you create and administer, and the redundancy set at creation is the only storage choice you make: The redundancy half is right, but the storage half is wrong: the vault's underlying storage is managed by the service for you, so there is no storage account for the team to create and administer.
- sit in a storage account that you create and administer, and the redundancy set at creation can be changed later in the vault's storage settings: Both halves are wrong: the recovery points live in storage that Azure manages for you rather than in a storage account the team owns, and the redundancy level chosen at creation cannot be changed once items are protected in the vault.

options.text: a subscription and tenant managed by Microsoft, where guests and other external users have no route to the stored data
the Contoso-prod subscription and tenant, where guests and other external users have no route to the stored data
a subscription and tenant managed by Microsoft, where any principal holding Owner on Contoso-prod can read the stored data directly

explanation:
Azure Backup holds the backup data of a Backup vault in a subscription and tenant that Microsoft manages, and guests and other external users have no route into that storage or its contents. That isolation is what stops a compromised source environment from being used to alter or wipe the recovery points already stored. The vault resource itself lives in Contoso-prod, but the data it holds does not, so the statement that pairs the Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant with the absence of any route for guests and external users is the accurate one.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the Contoso-prod subscription and tenant, where guests and other external users have no route to the stored data: The reachability half is right, but the location is wrong. Only the vault resource itself is created in the Contoso-prod subscription; the backup data it accumulates is kept in a subscription and tenant that Microsoft manages, not in Contoso's own subscription and tenant.
- a subscription and tenant managed by Microsoft, where any principal holding Owner on Contoso-prod can read the stored data directly: The location is right, but the reachability is wrong. Because the data is isolated in a subscription and tenant that Microsoft manages, holding Owner on Contoso-prod does not hand an identity direct read access to the raw stored contents.
- the Contoso-prod subscription and tenant, where any principal holding Contributor on rg-continuity can read the stored data directly: Both halves are wrong. The stored data is not kept in the Contoso-prod subscription, and holding Contributor on rg-continuity does not give direct read access to the stored contents either, because the data sits outside that subscription and tenant.

context:
Contoso is decommissioning the Azure Blob container that the vault blob-vault protects, and the platform team would like the vault to go away in the same change. The records compliance group has set a seven-year retrievability rule for the vaulted recovery points of that container, and no other copy of those points exists. The current situation is shown below.

You need an accurate statement for the change request. Which statement should you write?

- Setting: Vault; Value: blob-vault, an Azure Backup vault in rg-backup of the Contoso-prod subscription
- Setting: Protected workload; Value: Blob container contoso-archive, protected through vaulted backup
- Setting: Recovery points in the vault; Value: 12 points; the newest was taken three days ago
- Setting: Other copies of these points; Value: None
- Setting: Records compliance rule; Value: The points for this container must remain retrievable for seven years
prompt: The change request should state that _____.

options.text: the vault stays in place while the recovery points are still required, because removing a vault permanently destroys the backup items and the backup data the vault holds, and the removal cannot be reversed
the vault can be removed now, because the backup data is kept in the Microsoft-managed subscription and is retained independently of the vault
the vault can be removed now and re-created later in the same subscription, after which the earlier recovery points can be reached again
the vault can be removed now once the Blob container is decommissioned, because the recovery points are not tied to the protected workload

explanation:
Taking a vault out of service is a one-way operation: every backup item and all of the backup data for the protected servers are destroyed permanently, and the removal cannot be reversed. The vaulted recovery points for contoso-archive exist only inside blob-vault, so as long as the compliance rule keeps them retrievable for seven years, the vault has to stay where it is; removing it and later re-creating a vault with the same name would leave the container with no recovery points at all.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the vault can be removed now, because the backup data is kept in the Microsoft-managed subscription and is retained independently of the vault: This option mistakes the storage model for a retention guarantee. The vaulted data is kept in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant, which keeps it out of reach of guests and external users, but that isolation does not preserve the data once the vault itself is gone: removing the vault destroys the backup data it holds for good.
- the vault can be removed now and re-created later in the same subscription, after which the earlier recovery points can be reached again: A vault accumulates its own recovery points over time. A vault created later with the same name starts out with no recovery points of its own, so the earlier points cannot be reached again through it.
- the vault can be removed now once the Blob container is decommissioned, because the recovery points are not tied to the protected workload: The points are held by the vault, not by the protected workload. Once the Blob container is decommissioned the vault still holds them, and removing the vault destroys them, so the state of the workload itself has no bearing on whether they survive.

prompt:
You are using the current connection monitor experience to watch reachability and latency for your production application tier, and one monitor is already carrying part of that traffic.

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Connection monitor | cm-hub-prod |
| Monitor region | West Europe |
| Test group | tg-app-to-db |
| Source candidate | vm-app-01 (West Europe) |
| Source candidate | vm-app-02 (East US) |
| Destination | vm-db-01 (West Europe), TCP port 1433 |

The requirement is that both application servers probe the database server continuously, with the database server acting as the destination for each check, so that the East US server also shows up in the collected results.

Which action should you take?

options.text: Add vm-app-02 to the existing West Europe connection monitor as a source after installing the Network Watcher Agent extension on it
Provision a second connection monitor in the East US region and add vm-app-02 as its source
Move the connection monitor to the East US region and pick vm-app-01 as its source instead
Turn on a cross-region source setting for the test group so both source VMs are covered by one connection monitor

explanation:
A connection monitor is bound to a single region, and the Azure virtual machines and scale sets it can offer as sources are only those created in that same region — that is also why the Azure endpoints list only shows resources tied to the monitor's region. vm-app-02 is created in East US, so it is never offered as a source for a monitor that lives in West Europe, and no extension or test group setting can change that. Standing up a second connection monitor in the East US region lets vm-app-02 act as a source while vm-db-01 remains the destination for the checks, so both application servers end up reporting into the collected results.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add vm-app-02 to the existing West Europe connection monitor as a source after installing the Network Watcher Agent extension on it: Installing the Network Watcher Agent extension makes a virtual machine observable, but it does not override the region rule that decides which virtual machines may be chosen as sources. Because vm-app-02 sits in East US while cm-hub-prod is in West Europe, it will not appear in the monitor's Azure endpoints list even after the extension is installed.
- Move the connection monitor to the East US region and pick vm-app-01 as its source instead: Relocating the monitor simply moves the exclusion to the other server: vm-app-01 is created in West Europe, so after the move it would no longer be eligible as a source. The monitor's region has to line up with the region of the source virtual machines, which is why a monitor per region is needed rather than one relocated monitor.
- Turn on a cross-region source setting for the test group so both source VMs are covered by one connection monitor: There is no cross-region source switch on a test group. Source eligibility is filtered by the region chosen when the monitor was created, so test group configuration alone cannot make two virtual machines in different regions serve as sources of a single monitor.

explanation:
After the move to the current experience, connectivity data is published through the ChecksFailedPercent and RoundTripTimeMs metrics, and the previous ProbesFailedPercent and AverageRoundtripMs values are remapped onto those metrics (ProbesFailedPercent to ChecksFailedPercent, AverageRoundtripMs to RoundTripTimeMs). Alerts are migrated automatically, which is why the carried-over alert rule still fires, while dashboards and integrations that query the old metric names have to be edited by hand. Rewriting the two dashboard queries to the current metric names restores the trends.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Replace ProbesFailedPercent with AverageRoundtripMs and AverageRoundtripMs with ChecksFailedPercent in the dashboard queries: This pairs the wrong metrics together: the failed-check panel would query a latency metric and the latency panel a percentage metric, so the dashboard would still not show the intended values.
- Replace ChecksFailedPercent with ProbesFailedPercent and RoundTripTimeMs with AverageRoundtripMs in the dashboard queries: This turns the mapping around and points the panels at the legacy metric names, which the moved monitor no longer publishes, so the panels would remain empty.
- Re-create the moved monitor in Connection monitor (classic) so the dashboard queries keep returning rows: Connection monitor (classic) is deprecated and no longer available, so nothing can be re-created in it; the fix is to update the dashboard queries to the metric names the current experience publishes.

prompt: You have attached the Network Watcher Agent VM extension to a virtual machine scale set so that the set can act as a monitored source in a connection monitor, but the members of the set are still running the previously imaged model, so no checks originate from that source. You need the set to start generating the probes toward its destination, and the upgrade mode of the scale set has to stay as it is. Which action should you take?

options.text: Upgrade the scale set manually so the Network Watcher Agent extension is applied.
Change the scale set's upgrade mode to Automatic so the Network Watcher Agent extension is applied without a manual upgrade.
Remove the Network Watcher Agent extension from the scale set and keep the scale set only as a destination endpoint.
List the scale set's instance IP addresses as external address endpoints so that the probes are sent to them from the hybrid source.

explanation:
A virtual machine scale set that uses the Manual upgrade mode keeps running the previously imaged model until an upgrade is performed. Because the Network Watcher Agent extension was added to the model after creation, the running members do not carry it, the set cannot act as an observable source, and no probes are generated from it. The documented fix is to upgrade the scale set after the extension has been installed, which rolls out the new model and makes the extension effective. Scale sets configured for automatic upgrade need no extra step, and consenting to an auto upgrade at creation time would remove the manual task - but here the upgrade mode must remain as it is, so the scale set itself has to be upgraded.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Change the scale set's upgrade mode to Automatic so the Network Watcher Agent extension is applied without a manual upgrade: Automatic upgrade removes the extra step, but that change alters the scale set's upgrade strategy, which the requirement rules out. With the mode left as Manual, the extension that was added to the model only reaches the running members when the set is upgraded.
- Remove the Network Watcher Agent extension from the scale set and keep the scale set only as a destination endpoint: Destinations never need a monitoring extension, so a scale set can legitimately be used as a destination. Here, though, the set has to be the source that sends the checks toward vm-core-01, and deleting the extension removes exactly the capability needed for that role, leaving the test group with no observable source.
- List the scale set's instance IP addresses as external address endpoints so that the probes are sent to them from the hybrid source: External address endpoints are destination entries added by name plus a URL, IP, or FQDN. Listing the scale set's instance IPs there turns them into targets of checks that originate somewhere else, so the set still does not generate probes; those IPs also change whenever the set is reimaged.

prompt: You are watching the customer portal front end with a connection monitor, and one test group probes it from a virtual machine in the same region. The front end is served over TLS. The monitor's dashboard reports the check as passing, yet the portal has been answering with 503 Service Unavailable for the past hour and the on-call engineer was never notified. You need the check to report a failure whenever the front end answers with an error reply instead of a healthy one, while keeping the same source and destination endpoints and continuing to publish the round-trip-time metric. Which change should you make?

options.text: Set the test configuration protocol to HTTP and keep the destination port at 443
Set the test configuration protocol to HTTP and set the destination port to 80
Set the test configuration protocol to TCP and keep the destination port at 443, and enable Listen on port
Set the test configuration protocol to ICMP and remove the destination port

explanation:
A check that must judge what the endpoint answers has to run with the HTTP protocol, because that is the protocol whose success criteria are the response status codes the target returns; TCP only proves that the port accepts a connection, which is why the check reported Pass while the portal was returning 503 Service Unavailable. Because this front end is served over TLS, the HTTP check has to keep running against port 443, and the same sources, destinations, success thresholds and round-trip-time metric collection all stay as they are.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Set the test configuration protocol to HTTP and set the destination port to 80: The protocol is the right one, but port 80 is not where this TLS front end listens, so the check would no longer target the endpoint that is returning the error reply. Moving the port to 80 either finds nothing listening or tests a different, plaintext service, and either way the failing reply from the TLS endpoint stays invisible to the check.
- Set the test configuration protocol to TCP and keep the destination port at 443, and enable Listen on port: TCP keeps the check at port-level reachability: it confirms that the destination port accepts a connection but never inspects what the service replies, so a 503 reply would still be recorded as a successful check. Listen on port is a TCP-only setting that opens the destination port for the traffic; it does not make the check evaluate the reply returned by the application.
- Set the test configuration protocol to ICMP and remove the destination port: ICMP is the ping-style option: it measures reachability and latency for the packets themselves and never reads the reply of the service, so it cannot distinguish a healthy page from an error page. Removing the destination port also discards the endpoint information the check needs.

Install the Azure Monitor Agent on the datacenter server without enrolling it with the Azure Arc agent.

explanation:
A source has to be observable before the monitor can run checks from it. For a host in your own datacenter that means running the Azure Arc agent together with the Azure Monitor Agent. Once both are in place, the source picker lists Arc-enabled machines that already run the Azure Monitor Agent, so the server becomes selectable for the test group and its checks appear in the results.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Install the Log Analytics agent on the datacenter server, then reopen the source selection list: The Log Analytics agent is no longer accepted for on-premises sources. - Install the Network Watcher Agent VM extension on the datacenter server, then reopen the source selection list: The Network Watcher Agent VM extension is for virtual machines and scale sets in the cloud; it is not installed on on-premises servers and does not make a datacenter host an observable source.

On-premises sources also require the Azure Arc agent, so the machine would still not appear in the source selection list without it.

prompt: A support work item asks whether a particular virtual machine can reach a hostname that resolves to an address in another virtual network. Nothing that runs continuously covers this pair today, and the team needs the outcome for the work item now rather than a standing record. You need the quickest way to get that answer from the machine itself. Which action should you take?

options.text: Run Connection troubleshoot from vm-web-03 against the target and use the returned result.
Create a Connection monitor in West Europe with vm-web-03 as the source and the target as the destination, then read the first test result.
Run IP flow verify on vm-web-03 against the target to see whether the traffic would be allowed or denied.
Generate a Topology view for the virtual network that holds vm-web-03 and look for the path to the target.

explanation:
Connection troubleshoot is the Network Watcher tool that tests a connection at a point in time. It can be run from a virtual machine, a virtual machine scale set, an application gateway or a Bastion host against a virtual machine, an FQDN, a URI or an IPv4 address, and it returns output similar to a connection monitor's. This request matches that exactly: vm-web-03 (a virtual machine) probing a hostname, with a single outcome needed right now and no standing monitoring required.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Create a Connection monitor in West Europe with vm-web-03 as the source and the target as the destination, then read the first test result: Connection monitor is the continuous, end-to-end service: it needs a monitor resource with a test group, a Log Analytics workspace and an observable source (the Network Watcher Agent on the virtual machine), and it keeps running to trend latency and loss. Setting one up is not the quickest way to settle a single point-in-time question, and the work item does not need ongoing monitoring.
- Run IP flow verify on vm-web-03 against the target to see whether the traffic would be allowed or denied: IP flow verify is the one-shot filtering check. prompt: You have a connection monitor in West Europe, and its test group checks a server in East US. The test configuration protocol is TCP, the destination port is 443, and 'Listen on port' is enabled. The firewall team has already allowed the source address, yet the destination port is never opened by the checks, so the monitor never confirms the new rule works. You need the check to open the destination port on every run. Which change should you take?

options.text: Create a connection monitor whose region matches the destination's region and add the test group to it with a source from that region, so 'Listen on port' opens the destination port on every check.
Keep the connection monitor in West Europe and change the test configuration's protocol to HTTP with the destination port set to 443, so 'Listen on port' opens the port over the application protocol.

Keep the connection monitor in West Europe and add a virtual machine from the East US region as an additional source on a test group, so 'Listen on port' opens the port from a source inside the destination's region.
Keep the connection monitor in West Europe, leave the TCP protocol and 'Listen on port' as they are, and rely on the existing metric alert rule to notify the team on every failed check.

explanation:
'Listen on port' is a TCP-only capability, and it cannot work when the source and destination machines sit in different regions. In this case the source is in West Europe while the destination is in East US, so the port is never opened even though the firewall now permits the source address. Building the test group in a connection monitor whose region matches the destination's region and selecting a source from that region puts both ends in one region, which is what the setting requires. The region of a connection monitor also decides which Azure virtual machines and scale sets can be selected as sources, so the source has to come from the destination's region for this test group to work.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Keep the connection monitor in West Europe and change the test configuration's protocol to HTTP with the destination port set to 443, so 'Listen on port' opens the port over the application protocol: Port opening belongs to TCP test configurations only. With the protocol set to HTTP, 'Listen on port' is not offered, so the check would send application requests and evaluate response codes instead of opening the TCP port. That still validates the service path but does not meet the requirement to open the destination port.
- Keep the connection monitor in West Europe and add a virtual machine from the East US region as an additional source on a test group, so 'Listen on port' opens the port from a source inside the destination's region: A connection monitor can only take Azure virtual machines and scale sets that were created in the monitor's own region as sources, so a machine from the East US region cannot be added as a source to a monitor based in West Europe. The monitor's region has to change instead of the source list.
- Keep the connection monitor in West Europe, leave the TCP protocol and 'Listen on port' as they are, and rely on the existing metric alert rule to notify the team on every failed check: Leaving the protocol and the setting unchanged keeps the source and the destination in different regions, which is exactly the condition that stops 'Listen on port' from working. A metric alert rule only reports what the collected measurements show; it does not change which ports get opened or which regions the endpoints live in.

The datacenter host is enrolled with Azure Arc and the Azure Monitor Agent is running on it, and the host is already listed as a source in the test group. The checks seem to start, but the Log Analytics workspace that the monitor is configured with returns no records for the past two days, and the dashboard shows that source's tests with an Indeterminate status. You need the measurements from that site to be stored in the workspace and to appear on the monitor dashboard.

Which action should you take?

options.text: Enable Network Performance Monitor in the Log Analytics workspace that this connection monitor is configured with
Register the datacenter host with the Log Analytics agent instead of the Azure Monitor Agent, and point the monitor at a workspace where it reports
Attach the Network Watcher Agent VM extension to the datacenter host so that the monitor collects results into the same workspace
Create a new connection monitor in the datacenter's own region that targets a separate Log Analytics workspace

explanation:
Measurements produced by a connection monitor are uploaded into the Log Analytics workspace configured for that monitor, and that upload only succeeds once Network Performance Monitor is registered in the target workspace. Here the workspace holds only the core Log Analytics solution, so the probes from the Arc-enabled source run but their results never land in the workspace — which is what the 0-row query and the Indeterminate dashboard status show, since Indeterminate means the Log Analytics workspace holds no data. Register the component from Network Watcher > Monitoring > Connection monitor > + Enable Non-Azure, choosing the subscription and the workspace law-hybrid-ops, then confirm the new entry appears under Classic > Legacy solutions. The agents on the source are already the ones required for an on-premises host (Azure Arc plus Azure Monitor Agent), so no agent change is needed, and moving to another monitor or workspace would leave the current workspace empty as well.

- Register the datacenter host with the Log Analytics agent instead of the Azure Monitor Agent, and point the monitor at a workspace where it reports: On-premises sources require the Azure Arc agent followed by the Azure Monitor Agent; the Log Analytics agent is no longer accepted for on-premises sources, so re-registering the host with it would not create a valid source. Pointing the monitor at a different workspace also does not help, because that new workspace would be missing the same component.
- Attach the Network Watcher Agent VM extension to the datacenter host so that the monitor collects results into the same workspace: The Network Watcher Agent VM extension is what makes Azure virtual machines and scale sets observable as sources; an on-premises host cannot use it. The exhibit already shows the Arc agent and the Azure Monitor Agent present on the datacenter host, which is the required combination for that site, so the missing data is not an agent problem.
- Create a new connection monitor in the datacenter's own region that targets a separate Log Analytics workspace: Creating a new monitor in another region and a fresh workspace changes where the probes are defined but does not address why no records are uploaded; the newly targeted workspace would still need the same component registered before data could flow into it.

You have finished configuring a connection monitor in the Azure portal for an estate that spans Azure and an on-premises datacenter, and the operations team logged the effects that showed up in the collected data afterwards. You need to attribute each recorded effect to the single setup choice that produced it. Which setup choice belongs with each observation?

- Observation: A; Effect recorded on the monitor: The group's checks run far more often than once per minute, but each stored metric point covers a whole minute, with the individual probes inside it folded together.
- Observation: B; Effect recorded on the monitor: Every run over TCP leaves the destination service accepting the incoming connection, so the check's own traffic succeeds even though the firewall team had opened nothing for it.
- Observation: C; Effect recorded on the monitor: The results contain no path details and no per-hop timing values, even though the group's protocol is one of the two that are able to collect them.
- Observation: D; Effect recorded on the monitor: The group ends up holding two configurations, and the extra one repeats the same sources and destinations as the first and carries a name generated from the first one's.
prompt: Observation A

options.text: Test frequency set to 30 seconds
Listen on port enabled on a TCP configuration
Disable traceroute selected on an ICMP configuration
Create TCP test configuration selected

explanation: Each recorded effect traces back to one specific setup choice. A: a 30-second test frequency makes the checks run more often than the one-minute minimum granularity of the metrics store, so the sub-minute probes are aggregated into a single point. B: Listen on port is a TCP-only option that opens the destination port on each run, which is why the destination service starts accepting the probe's own traffic. C: Disable traceroute applies to TCP and ICMP only and suppresses both topology and hop-by-hop round-trip discovery, so no path or per-hop timings appear. D: Create TCP test configuration, offered when HTTP is the protocol, clones the same sources and destinations into a second configuration whose name is derived from the first one.

- ID: D; Observation: Immediately after the monitor was created in the portal, it did not appear on the dashboard for its region.

A newly created monitor takes about five minutes to appear on the dashboard.
Ingestion into Log Analytics and Azure Monitor alert charges still apply even though the portal shows no estimate.

A test group in your connection monitor checks the playback manifest of a video-on-demand service over TLS. The group holds two test configurations: tc-playback-http, whose protocol is HTTP and whose destination port is 443, and tc-playback-icmp, whose protocol is ICMP. The HTTP one is the configuration that confirms the service answers with a valid response, and the team also wants port-level results for the very same endpoints, without adding a further test configuration to the group by hand. Which action should you take?

| Setting | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Connection monitor | cm-vod (West Europe) |
| Test group | tg-playback |
| Test configuration | tc-playback-http |
| Protocol of that configuration | HTTP |
| Destination port of that configuration | 443 |
| Other test configuration in the group | tc-playback-icmp (protocol ICMP) |
| Sources in the group | vm-edge-01, vm-edge-02 |
| Destination in the group | cdn-playback.contoso.com |

- Setting: Connection monitor; Value: cm-vod (West Europe)
- Setting: Test group; Value: tg-playback
- Setting: Test configuration; Value: tc-playback-http
- Setting: Protocol of that configuration; Value: HTTP
- Setting: Destination port of that configuration; Value: 443
- Setting: Other test configuration in the group; Value: tc-playback-icmp (protocol ICMP)
- Setting: Sources in the group; Value: vm-edge-01, vm-edge-02
