prompt: To meet the requirement, you should _____.

options.text: Open tc-playback-http and turn on the Create TCP test configuration setting
Open tc-playback-icmp and turn on the Create TCP test configuration setting
Open tc-playback-http and turn on the Listen on port setting
Open tc-playback-http and change the protocol from HTTP to TCP

explanation:
The Create TCP test configuration setting is offered only on a test configuration whose protocol is HTTP. Turning it on for tc-playback-http clones the same sources and destinations into a second test configuration named tc-playback-http_networkTestConfig, so the port-level check is produced for the same endpoints without a further configuration being added to the group by hand, and the HTTP check that validates the service response stays exactly as it is.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Open tc-playback-icmp and turn on the Create TCP test configuration setting: This setting appears only when HTTP is selected. tc-playback-icmp uses ICMP, so the control is not offered on it, and editing the ICMP configuration would not add the port-level results to the HTTP configuration.
- Open tc-playback-http and turn on the Listen on port setting: Listen on port applies to TCP (and ICMP) configurations only, and it opens the destination port for the checks rather than producing a port-level companion from the HTTP configuration, so it is not the control that fits an HTTP configuration.
- Open tc-playback-http and change the protocol from HTTP to TCP: Changing the protocol to TCP replaces the HTTP check, so the validation of the service response is lost. The extra configuration that clones the sources and destinations is only produced from a configuration that is still set to HTTP.

context:
You have been running a connection monitor for the path between your branch office router and an Azure application gateway, and the operations team reviews the collected results in the platform's Azure Monitor Metrics view every day. That view only exposes about a month of history, but the compliance team now needs twelve months of history for the same link and must be able to analyze and export it well after that month has passed. Which action should you take?

`Connection monitor                        : cm-branch-to-gw
Monitor region                           : West Europe
Test group                               : tg-branch-gw
Source                                   : Branch office router (Azure Arc enabled, Azure Monitor Agent running)
Destination                              : app-gw-prod-01 (HTTP, destination port 443)
Data store configured for the monitor     : law-netops (West Europe)
Platform metric view                     : Azure Monitor Metrics - 30 days of history available
Compliance requirement                   : 12 months of history, analyzable and exportable from the platform`
prompt: To satisfy the compliance requirement, the team should _____.

options.text: Query the Log Analytics workspace and extend its retention so the twelve months of history stay available
Configure the Azure Monitor Metrics view and extend its retention so the twelve months of history stay available
Set the test frequency to 30 seconds with one-minute granularity so the twelve months of history stay available
Create an alert rule on the Test Result metric and enable the rule upon creation so the twelve months of history stay available

explanation:
The measurements produced by a connection monitor are delivered to the Log Analytics workspace that is configured for that monitor, and that store keeps the records for as long as its retention is set, which is where long-retention analysis, correlation and export belong. Azure Monitor Metrics is the right place for metric alerting, but its metric window is only 30 days by default, so it cannot be stretched to twelve months. Changing the test frequency or the aggregation granularity changes how many samples are produced, not how long they are kept, and an alert rule evaluates each check and notifies an action group instead of storing the measurement history. Because the compliance team needs twelve months of history that can still be analyzed and exported, the retention of the Log Analytics workspace holding the monitor's records is the setting that has to change.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Configure the Azure Monitor Metrics view and extend its retention so the twelve months of history stay available: Azure Monitor Metrics holds the metric series for a 30-day window by default, so configuring that view cannot produce the twelve months of history the compliance team asks for; the long-lived copy of the same measurements lives in the Log Analytics workspace.
- Set the test frequency to 30 seconds with one-minute granularity so the twelve months of history stay available: The test frequency and the granularity decide how often the checks run and how the samples are aggregated (the one-minute granularity actually folds sub-minute probes together), not how long the stored data is kept, so the history would still end at the configured retention of the data store.
- Create an alert rule on the Test Result metric and enable the rule upon creation so the twelve months of history stay available: An alert rule built on the Test Result metric evaluates every check and notifies the action group, but it does not retain the measurement records, so the team would still have no twelve months of data to analyze or export.

context:
You have designed a connection monitor for the West Europe region whose test group should use every one of the 240 virtual machines in a large compute pool as a probe origin. You need each machine in the pool to contribute measurements so that the operations team has one combined view of the path to the shared database. Which action should you take?

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Planned probe origins for the design | 240 virtual machines |
| Other test groups planned in the same connection monitor | 4 |
| Target region for the design | West Europe |
prompt: The action you should take is to _____.

options.text: Create extra connection monitors and place the machines across them
Keep one connection monitor and add extra test groups to hold the machines
Keep one connection monitor and move some machines into its destination list
Keep one connection monitor and reduce the number of test groups it contains

explanation:
The documented limit is 100 sources and destinations per connection monitor, and this design names 240 virtual machines as probe origins, so they cannot all be hosted on a single monitor. Putting the machines onto further connection monitors keeps every monitor within the cap, and because the monitors can all write to the same Log Analytics workspace, the operations team still gets one combined view of the path to the shared database.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Keep one connection monitor and add extra test groups to hold the machines: Adding test groups does not add capacity: the ceiling of 100 sources and destinations applies to the whole connection monitor rather than to each group, so 240 named probe origins still exceed it. Test groups carry a separate limit of 20 per monitor, which this design does not reach, so extra groups cannot solve the problem.
- Keep one connection monitor and move some machines into its destination list: The destination list holds the endpoints that are being probed, so shifting probe origins there changes what is being measured instead of raising capacity, and the 100 sources and destinations ceiling for the monitor still applies.
- Keep one connection monitor and reduce the number of test groups it contains: Reducing the number of test groups does not change the ceiling of 100 sources and destinations for the monitor, so the 240 named machines still overrun it. The planned four test groups are well inside the separate limit of 20 per monitor, so that count was never the obstacle.

context:
You have a connection monitor in West Europe that watches the path from two application servers to an internal order-processing API over TCP. The operations team has approved two changes to the measurement settings of the test configuration, and both changes must be applied without touching the sources, the destination, or the protocol.

First, the incident process expects each check to run 45 seconds after the previous one, so that a broken link surfaces well inside the team's one-minute response window.

Second, the team wants engineers to see a warning state as soon as the measured round-trip time goes above 600 ms, so that they get a heads-up rather than a hard failure at that point.

| Setting | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Connection monitor | cm-order-api (West Europe) |
| Test group | tg-order-api |
| Test configuration | tc-order-api |
| Protocol | TCP |
| Destination port | 443 |
| Sources | vm-order-a, vm-order-b |
| Destination | api-order.internal.contoso.com |
| Test frequency (current) | 1 minute |
| Success threshold - checks failed (current) | 10% |
| Success threshold - round trip time (current) | 500 ms |

Which two settings should you change?
prompt: The two changes are to set the test frequency to _____ and to set the round-trip-time success threshold to [...].

options.text: Custom
30 seconds
1 minute
5 minutes

explanation:
The test frequency is taken either from the fixed choices 30 seconds, 1 minute, 5 minutes, 15 minutes and 30 minutes, or from a user-entered value that may run from 30 seconds up to 30 minutes. A 45-second spacing is not one of the fixed choices, so it can only be held by a user-entered value; the fixed 30-second, 1-minute and 5-minute choices all produce the wrong spacing. For the round-trip-time limit, a test reports a warning once it passes 80% of the configured limit and reports a failure once it breaches that limit, so a 750 ms limit makes the warning appear from just above 600 ms while only readings above 750 ms count as failures. A 450 ms or a 600 ms limit would already be failing at or below the 600 ms point, and a 900 ms limit would not warn until past 720 ms.

Why the other options are wrong:
- 30 seconds: This is one of the fixed values, so the checks would repeat every 30 seconds instead of the 45-second spacing the incident process expects.
- 1 minute: This is one of the fixed values and is the value already in place; it repeats every 60 seconds, so a failure can take up to a minute to appear.
- 5 minutes: This is one of the fixed values, and its 5-minute spacing is far longer than the response window the incident process works to.

The finished design has to fit within the capacity that the platform documents for a single monitor, and no business unit's path may go unwatched.

Which action should you take?

- Item: Planned connection monitor; Value: cm-enterprise-we
- Item: Subscription; Value: sub-enterprise-prod
- Item: Azure region of the monitor; Value: West Europe
- Item: Test groups in the design; Value: 26 (one per business unit)
- Item: Sources per test group; Value: 1 virtual machine created in West Europe
- Item: Destinations per test group; Value: 2 endpoints
prompt: To keep every business unit's path under continuous observation while staying within the documented capacity, you should _____.

options.text: split the test groups across separate monitors in the same subscription and region
trim the sources and destinations in the test groups so that one monitor holds at most 10 of each
move the surplus test groups into monitors in another region of the same subscription so that each one stays within its documented capacity
create the monitors with the deprecated Connection monitor (classic) experience, which applies no limit on test groups

explanation:
A single connection monitor holds at most 20 test groups, so the 26 test groups in this design cannot all live in one monitor. The endpoint counts are not the constraint: the plan needs 26 sources and 52 destinations, both inside the limit of 100 sources and destinations per monitor. Placing the 26 test groups in two monitors in the same subscription and region leaves 13 test groups per monitor, keeps every business unit's path watched, and stays well below the limit of 100 connection monitors per subscription per region.

Why the other options are wrong:
- trim the sources and destinations in the test groups so that one monitor holds at most 10 of each: This design is not over capacity on endpoints: it needs 26 sources and 52 destinations, and a monitor allows 100 sources and destinations. Cutting them down to 10 each would leave endpoints unwatched and would not address the constraint that is actually exceeded, which is the number of test groups in one monitor.
- move the surplus test groups into monitors in another region of the same subscription so that each one stays within its documented capacity: The ceiling of 20 test groups applies to every connection monitor in every region, so relocating groups to another region does not let 26 groups fit into one resource. It would also break source selection, because only source virtual machines created in the region of the monitor can be chosen as sources, and all source virtual machines here are in West Europe.
- create the monitors with the deprecated Connection monitor (classic) experience, which applies no limit on test groups: Connection monitor (classic) is deprecated and no longer available, so no new monitor can be created with that experience, and it cannot be used to work around the capacity of the current one.

context:
You are tuning a connection monitor in West Europe that watches the path from a branch office router to an application gateway over TCP. The most recent check is shown with a warning status on the dashboard, even though the operations team still treats that path as healthy and does not want to be woken up for it. They want the warning to begin only once the measured round trip time passes the limit they consider healthy, and they want the check itself to keep counting as broken only when the link is clearly degraded, well above that limit. Which change should you make?

`Connection monitor:  cm-branch-link (West Europe)
Test group:          tg-branch-to-appgw
Test configuration:  tc-branch-tcp, protocol TCP, destination port 443
Round trip time threshold:                            750 ms
Checks failed threshold:                               10 percent
Round trip time the network team treats as healthy:   640 ms
Most recent measurement:                              620 ms round trip time, 0 percent checks failed
Status reported for that check:                       Warning`
prompt: The change you should apply to the test configuration is _____.

options.text: Set the round trip time threshold to 800 ms
Set the round trip time threshold to 640 ms
Set the checks failed threshold to 20 percent
Set the test frequency to 30 seconds

explanation:
A test is reported as failed once the measured round trip time breaches the configured threshold, while a warning is raised as soon as the measurement passes 80 percent of that threshold. The team wants the warning to start just above 640 ms, so the threshold has to be 640 divided by 0.8, which is 800 ms. With that value the warning begins above 640 ms and the check only fails above 800 ms, keeping the failure point well above the level the team still regards as healthy. The current 750 ms threshold is what produces the premature warning, because 80 percent of 750 ms is 600 ms, and the measured 620 ms therefore already lands in the warning band.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Set the round trip time threshold to 640 ms: With the round trip time threshold set to 640 ms, the warning would begin once the measurement passed 512 ms (80 percent of 640 ms) and the check would already be counted as broken at 640 ms, which is exactly the level the operations team still regards as healthy. It therefore warns too early and fails too early.
- Set the checks failed threshold to 20 percent: The checks failed threshold controls the tolerated share of unsuccessful probes. Raising it from the default 10 percent to 20 percent has no effect on when the round trip time warning starts or on the point at which the round trip time is treated as a breach.
- Set the test frequency to 30 seconds: The test frequency controls how often the checks run. Running them every 30 seconds instead of every minute collects more samples but leaves the round trip time threshold, and therefore the point at which the warning and the failure occur, unchanged.

In the Availability (%) (Thresholds + Formatted) column settings, set the maximum value to 85 and leave the minimum value at 90.

In the Availability (%) (Thresholds + Formatted) column settings, set the minimum value to 85 and the maximum value to 85.

explanation:
The availability thresholds in this workbook are configured as a minimum/maximum pair that ships as minimum 90 and maximum 99, producing Warning at 99% and Critical at 90%. The Critical health state is raised only when availability drops below the minimum value, and the value you edit for the Critical state is that minimum. Changing the minimum to 85 while keeping the maximum at 99 therefore makes an account critical below 85% and leaves the warning level at 99%. (In practice you switch the workbook to Edit mode, edit the Availability (%) (Thresholds + Formatted) column in the Availability by API name grid, then Save as and Done editing so the published default is not overwritten.)

Why the other options are wrong:
- In the Availability (%) (Thresholds + Formatted) column settings, set the maximum value to 85 and leave the minimum value at 90: The maximum value of the pair corresponds to the warning level, not to the critical boundary, and the critical state fires only below the minimum value. Changing the maximum to 85 moves the warning threshold while the critical boundary stays at 90%, so an account at 87% would still not be reported as critical.
- In the Availability (%) (Thresholds + Formatted) column settings, set the minimum value to 99 and the maximum value to 85: This swaps the two bounds, so the critical state would be raised only below 99% and the warning level would move down to 85%. That does not produce a critical state below 85% and changes the warning level in the wrong direction.
- In the Availability (%) (Thresholds + Formatted) column settings, set the minimum value to 85 and the maximum value to 85: Setting both values to 85 does move the critical boundary to 85%, but it also pulls the warning level down from 99% to 85%, so accounts between 85% and 99% would be flagged as warning and the requirement that warning still trigger at 99% is not satisfied.

prompt: You are troubleshooting the network traffic of a single virtual machine, and the two network charts in the table below disagree about how many bytes the machine sent in the last hour. You need to know which of the two figures reflects the traffic this VM exchanges with the other VMs in the same virtual network. Which statement explains the difference?

options.text: The overview chart is measured by the host and shows only billable traffic, while VM insights measures inside the guest and includes traffic between VMs.
The overview chart is measured inside the guest and includes traffic between VMs, while VM insights is measured by the host and shows only billable traffic.
Both charts are measured by the host, but the overview chart excludes traffic between VMs while VM insights includes it.
Both charts are measured inside the guest, and the difference comes from the sampling interval used to collect the counters.

explanation:
The network chart on the Azure VM overview page is drawn from the host's view of activity in the guest machine and covers only the traffic that gets billed, so traffic exchanged with other VMs in the virtual network never appears there. The VM insights Performance charts come from counters collected inside the guest VM itself and account for all inbound and outbound TCP/IP traffic, including inter-VM traffic. That is why the guest-based figure (48.7 GB) is far larger than the overview figure (12.4 GB), and why VM insights is the chart to trust for traffic between VMs.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The overview chart is measured inside the guest and includes traffic between VMs, while VM insights is measured by the host and shows only billable traffic: This reverses the two data sources. The overview page chart is the host-measured one that shows only billed traffic and omits inter-VM traffic, while VM insights is the guest-measured chart that includes it.
- Both charts are measured by the host, but the overview chart excludes traffic between VMs while VM insights includes it: This mixes up the two charts. VM insights is not host-measured; its data is gathered inside the guest VM. The gap between the two figures comes from what the overview chart counts (billed traffic only), not from two charts taken at the same measurement point.
- Both charts are measured inside the guest, and the difference comes from the sampling interval used to collect the counters: This is wrong because the overview chart is host-measured rather than guest-measured, and the difference is not caused by sampling intervals. It comes from the scope of the data each chart counts: billed traffic only versus all inbound and outbound traffic including inter-VM traffic.

The attached XFS data disk is exactly the kind of volume that does produce values, so this statement contradicts the populated chart for /mnt/data.
- On Linux VMs, guest disk counters are collected from every mounted volume, including network shared drives, as soon as the machine reports to Azure Monitor: Remote network shares do not contribute guest disk counters, and simply reporting to Azure Monitor does not change that. The empty chart for /mnt/share shows the volume is never sampled, so this statement cannot explain the result.
- On Linux VMs, guest disk counters are collected only from local data disks using XFS or the EXT family, and network shared drives are included as well: Network shared drives stay out of disk counter collection on Linux, so the CIFS-backed Azure Files mount cannot supply the missing values. This statement contradicts the chart that shows nothing for /mnt/share.

You support 120 Azure Storage accounts that are watched with Storage insights, and your team answers every customer ticket from the four workbooks that sit on a single account's Monitoring > Insights page. The account below is the subject of four open tickets. Drag each ticket to the workbook that answers it.

- Account detail: Storage account; Value: rgproddata01 (West Europe)
- Account detail: Time range inspected; Value: Last 4 hours
- Account detail: Average end-to-end request time; Value: 310 ms
- Account detail: Average time spent handling a request inside the service; Value: 240 ms
- Account detail: Requests answered with an error status; Value: 412, of which 301 were throttled
- Account detail: Share of the allotted space in use; Value: 78%
- Account detail: Data objects stored in the account; Value: 4.1 million
prompt: Availability workbook

options.text: Ticket 4812 — The customer wants to know whether a regional problem affected the storage service during last night's incident, and how the state of each data service in the account has changed across the selected window.
Ticket 4823 — The customer says their calls are slow and wants the end-to-end time compared with the time the service itself spent handling each request.
Ticket 4830 — The customer wants a breakdown of the responses their application received with an error status, including how many of those were throttled.
Ticket 4841 — The customer wants to know how much of the allotted space is in use and how many data objects the account is holding.

explanation: Each ticket asks for a different category of information, and each account-level workbook in Storage insights is tailored to one category. The request about a regional incident and the state of each data service over the selected window belongs with the Availability workbook, which opens with the health state of the storage service and shows a per-data-service trend line and trend chart. The request comparing end-to-end time with the time spent inside the service belongs with the Performance workbook, whose rollup tile and chart set contrast E2E latency with server latency and break latency of successful calls down by API. The request about error responses and throttled requests belongs with the Failures workbook, which carries tiles for client-side errors other than the named ones and for client-throttling errors plus tables of transactions by API name and by response type. The request about space in use and the number of objects held belongs with the Capacity workbook, which reports the amount of storage used per data object and how many data objects are stored.

You have 240 virtual machines onboarded to VM insights, and the on-call team raises the same three requests during every shift. You need each request answered from the multi-VM Performance view (Monitor > Solutions > Virtual Machines > Performance). Which tab should each request go to? Drag each request to the correct tab.

- Resource group: rg-app-prod; Virtual machines: 140; Guest performance counters: Collected by VM insights
- Resource group: rg-app-test; Virtual machines: 60; Guest performance counters: Collected by VM insights
- Resource group: rg-data; Virtual machines: 40; Guest performance counters: Collected by VM insights
prompt: Top N Charts

options.text: Show the five machines under the heaviest processor load and the five with the least free memory side by side, so the shift can eyeball the whole fleet in seconds.
Rank every machine in the fleet by available memory and keep extending the ranking until all of them are included, so the worst offender can be handed to a capacity owner.
Report the fleet-wide mean and 95th percentile of file system space consumed, so a single number can be trended week over week.

explanation: The three requests map one-to-one onto the three tabs of the multi-VM Performance view. The quick side-by-side glance at the five busiest machines by processor load and the five with the least free memory belongs to Top N Charts, because that tab renders five charts (CPU Utilization %, Available Memory, Logical Disk Space Used %, Bytes Sent Rate, Bytes Receive Rate) and each chart shows only its top five machines. The request to rank every individual machine and work through them one by one belongs to Top N List: it opens with 20 machines ordered by 95th-percentile CPU Utilization %, the Load More button extends the ranking up to 500 machines, and the Metric dropdown switches the ranking to Available Memory, so all 240 machines in the fleet can be covered. The request for a fleet-wide mean and 95th percentile of file system space consumed belongs to Aggregated Charts, which reports averages and percentiles across many machines and defaults Logical Disk Space Used % to average plus the 95th percentile.

- Resource: pip-app-prod (public IP address); Location: East US; Observed state: Attached to agw-app-prod
- Resource: agw-app-prod (application gateway); Location: East US; Observed state: Attached to pip-app-prod
- Resource: nsg-app-prod (network security group); Location: East US; Observed state: No flow log configuration present
- Resource: nsg-data-prod (network security group); Location: West US; Observed state: Flow log and analytics collection configured
- Resource: cm-branch (reachability test to the branch office); Location: East US; Observed state: Criteria: checks failed % = 10, RTT ms = 500
- Resource: vm-partner (virtual machine); Location: East US; Observed state: Calls to a partner API take about 8 seconds
prompt: Network health

options.text: Give me the inventory of the resources deployed in the production resource group, each type counted and sorted by name, and let a search for a public IP address also return the resources attached to it.
Work out which of the network security groups in the subscription are not publishing flow logs, and switch the collection on for those that are missing.

Check whether the reachability tests between the branch office and the virtual network are passing, and tighten the criteria for failed checks percentage and round-trip time so that a degraded link is reported sooner.
Find out why calls to a partner API from one virtual machine are slow: capture the packets that leave the machine and confirm the next hop along the route.

explanation: Each request belongs to the area of Network insights that carries its data or its controls. The inventory of deployed resources — filtered by subscription, resource group and type, sorted by name or resource count, with a search box that also returns associated resources — is the Network health area, which answers the request about a public IP address and the resources attached to it. The list of network security groups with their flow log configuration status, where the missing collection can be turned on, is the Traffic area. The results of the configured tests together with the criteria that decide their verdict (checks failed percentage and round-trip time) are the Connectivity area. The troubleshooting tools used to capture packets and confirm the next hop for one slow virtual machine are the Diagnostic Toolkit.

context:
You look after 210 Linux virtual machines whose guest counters reach a single Log Analytics workspace through a VM insights data collection rule. The capacity team has asked for one picture that covers the whole fleet and makes the machines closest to exhausting their memory visible. You open the multi-VM Performance view (Monitor > Solutions > Virtual Machines > Performance) to build it. Which tab do you take the chart from, and what does the memory chart on that tab show by default?

- Request from the capacity team: Measurement to chart; What is needed: How much memory each machine still has available
- Request from the capacity team: Scope of the picture; What is needed: One chart covering the whole fleet, not a list of individual machines
- Request from the capacity team: Low end of the measurement; What is needed: The smallest percentile bands, so near-exhausted machines stand out
- Request from the capacity team: Period covered; What is needed: The last 7 days
prompt: The chart comes from the _____ tab, where the memory chart reports [...] by default.

options.text: Aggregated Charts
Top N Charts
Top N List

explanation:
The Aggregated Charts tab of the multi-VM Performance view is the one that charts each guest metric across the whole fleet instead of ranking individual machines, and on that tab the Available Memory chart is shipped with the average plus the 5th and 10th percentile values. That combination is what exposes the machines sitting at the low end of the memory measurement, which is what the capacity team asked for. The average plus the 95th percentile pairing belongs to the CPU Utilization % and Logical Disk Space Used % charts on the same tab, and the average on its own is the default for the two byte-rate charts, so neither of those describes the memory chart.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Top N Charts: Top N Charts ranks the five worst machines for each of five metrics (CPU Utilization %, Available Memory, Logical Disk Space Used %, Bytes Sent Rate and Bytes Receive Rate); it produces a short per-metric ranking rather than one summary picture of the metric for the fleet.
- Top N List: Top N List is a table of individual machines ordered by a chosen metric, starting with 20 entries and extendable to 500, so it ranks machines instead of charting the metric across the fleet.

context:
The capacity team wants a detailed look at the disk activity of one database host, db-vm-07. For that host they need the disk operations per second, the disk throughput in MB per second, the largest share of space used on any of its logical disks, and a table that lists capacity, utilization and average for each logical disk volume. The analysts report that the fleet-wide charts they normally use show none of these measures. Where should they look?

- Requested for db-vm-07: Disk operations per second; Detail: One value per logical disk volume
- Requested for db-vm-07: Disk throughput; Detail: MB per second, one value per logical disk volume
- Requested for db-vm-07: Largest share of space used; Detail: Across all logical disk volumes of the host
- Requested for db-vm-07: Volume table; Detail: Capacity, utilization and average for each logical disk
prompt: The correct choice is _____.

options.text: Open the virtual machine and select Monitoring > Insights > Performance
Open Monitor > Solutions > Virtual Machines > Performance and stay on the Top N Charts tab
Open Monitor > Insights > Storage Accounts and select the account's Capacity workbook
Open Monitor > Solutions > Virtual Machines > Performance and stay on the Aggregated Charts tab

explanation:
The three extra measures the team needs — Logical Disk IOPS, Logical Disk MB/s and Max Logical Disk Used % — together with the per-logical-disk table showing capacity, utilization and average, are added only on the page scoped to a single machine, reached by opening the virtual machine and selecting Monitoring > Insights > Performance. The fleet-wide view under Monitor > Solutions exposes just the five capacity charts (CPU Utilization %, Available Memory, Logical Disk Space Used %, Bytes Sent Rate, Bytes Receive Rate) plus the Top N list, and the storage Capacity workbook reports account-level used capacity and object counts rather than the guest disk counters of a single host.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Open Monitor > Solutions > Virtual Machines > Performance and stay on the Top N Charts tab: The Top N Charts tab of the fleet-wide view only offers the five capacity charts (CPU Utilization %, Available Memory, Logical Disk Space Used %, Bytes Sent Rate, Bytes Receive Rate) with the top five machines each, so it cannot produce disk IOPS, disk MB/s, the maximum disk space used figure or a per-volume table.
- Open Monitor > Insights > Storage Accounts and select the account's Capacity workbook: The storage account Capacity workbook reports used capacity and object counts per data service for a storage account, and it does not expose the guest disk counters of a single host or a table broken down per logical disk volume.
- Open Monitor > Solutions > Virtual Machines > Performance and stay on the Aggregated Charts tab: Aggregated Charts show averages and percentiles for the same five fleet-wide capacity metrics, so this tab also lacks the per-machine disk IOPS, disk MB/s and maximum disk space used charts and the per-logical-disk table.

context:
Your network operations team works from the Network insights page in Azure Monitor, and analysts pin parts of it to the Azure dashboard that the on-call team watches. The exhibit shows the range each side is set to. Since the latest pin, the on-call team says the network figures on the dashboard cover a different period from the one the analysts picked, so the numbers no longer line up with what was seen in Network insights. Which statement explains this?

`Item                                              | Value
-------------------------------------------------|---------------
Range picked by the analysts in Network insights | Last 24 hours
Time range configured on the pinned dashboard    | Last 1 hour
Dashboard that holds the pin                     | net-ops-handover`
prompt: The most accurate explanation is that _____.

options.text: the Network insights workbook uses the Auto time grain derived from the selected time range, but once a chart is pinned the time range follows the dashboard settings
the Network insights workbook uses the Auto time grain derived from the selected time range, and pinning a chart copies that range to the Azure dashboard so the period shown there stays fixed
Network insights stores a fixed grain for every chart in the workbook, so whether or not a chart is pinned makes no difference to the range or the grain that is displayed
a pinned chart follows the dashboard settings for its time range, but the grain stays at the value used in Network insights instead of being derived from the range

explanation:
Network insights workbooks run with the Auto time grain, and that grain is derived from the selected time range. When any part of a workbook is pinned, however, the time range depends on the dashboard settings instead. The pinned view therefore shows the period configured on the dashboard (here the last hour) and the grain derived from that period, which is why the on-call team no longer sees the 24-hour period the analysts had chosen in Network insights.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the Network insights workbook uses the Auto time grain derived from the selected time range, and pinning a chart copies that range to the Azure dashboard so the period shown there stays fixed: Pinning does not copy the range chosen in Network insights onto the dashboard. Once a chart is pinned, the period displayed comes from the dashboard settings, so it follows the dashboard and can change with it rather than staying fixed at the range the analysts picked.
- Network insights stores a fixed grain for every chart in the workbook, so whether or not a chart is pinned makes no difference to the range or the grain that is displayed: Network insights does not use a fixed grain for its charts. It uses the Auto time grain, which is derived from the selected time range, so pinning a chart does change which period, and therefore which grain, is displayed.
- a pinned chart follows the dashboard settings for its time range, but the grain stays at the value used in Network insights instead of being derived from the range: The grain is not frozen at the value used in Network insights. The Auto time grain continues to be derived from the range in effect, and after pinning that range comes from the dashboard settings, so the grain changes along with the dashboard range instead of staying put.

context: You look after a storage estate that the platform team reviews with Storage insights. The team wants its own version of the storage reports, with 60 storage accounts in two subscriptions already preselected every time the report opens, so that all analysts work from identical figures. The published version that three other teams depend on must remain unchanged for them. You need to give the team the steps to build its own version, the place to open it from, and the scope it can lock in. Which statement is correct?
prompt: To give the team its own version of the report, you _____; the saved copy is then opened from [...], and it can be preconfigured to select [...].

options.text: select Edit, apply the changes, then choose Save as and Done editing
select Edit, apply the changes, then choose Save to overwrite the published configuration
select Edit, apply the changes, then choose Save and close
select the down-arrow icon next to the pushpin to export the results to Excel

explanation:
Storage insights keeps customizations separate from the published default: you put the workbook into edit mode, apply your changes, use Save as to store them as a copy, and finish with Done editing to return to reading mode. That copy is then launched from the workbook gallery, not from the storage pages or the dashboard, so every analyst opens the same customized version. A customized storage workbook can be scoped by default to up to 10 subscriptions and up to 200 storage accounts, which covers the 60 accounts in two subscriptions the platform team wants preselected, and the published configuration that the other three teams use is left untouched.

Why the other options are wrong:
- select Edit, apply the changes, then choose Save to overwrite the published configuration: Saving directly over the published configuration would replace the version the other teams depend on. Storage insights never overwrites the published default workbook; the customizations are kept in a separate copy created with Save as.
- select Edit, apply the changes, then choose Save and close: Save and close only commits an individual column-setting change while you are still in the edit session. It does not create the separate copy of the workbook, and it does not take you back to reading mode the way Done editing does.
- select the down-arrow icon next to the pushpin to export the results to Excel: The down-arrow icon beside the pushpin exports the grid results to Excel. Exporting does not persist any customization and does not produce a saved copy of the report.

context:
You have a Windows Server 2022 virtual machine, vm-billing-03 (Standard_D8s_v5), that repeatedly stalls under load for 10 to 15 minutes every afternoon and then recovers on its own. The machine produces no crash dump, and the Windows event log shows no service or driver faults. You need the Azure Monitor tooling that is meant for troubleshooting the performance of a single virtual machine, including the ways it can be run for this kind of investigation. Which capability should you use?

- Item: Virtual machine; Detail: vm-billing-03 (Windows Server 2022, Standard_D8s_v5)
- Item: Reported symptom; Detail: Freezes for 10 to 15 minutes every afternoon, then recovers on its own
- Item: Evidence available; Detail: No crash dump; Windows event log shows no service or driver faults
- Item: Team goal; Detail: Find the cause on the machine itself and fix the stall
prompt: The correct approach is to use _____ for this investigation.

options.text: Performance Diagnostics, with Continuous diagnostics and On-demand diagnostics modes
VM insights Performance charts, with Aggregated Charts, Top N Charts and Top N List tabs
Network Watcher Diagnostic Toolkit, with packet capture, next hop and IP flow verify
Storage insights Performance workbook, with Failures, Availability and Capacity workbooks

explanation:
Performance Diagnostics is the separate troubleshooting capability for Windows and Linux virtual machines, and it runs in two modes: Continuous diagnostics and On-demand diagnostics. The fault has to be investigated on the machine itself rather than through fleet-wide counter charts, so this capability, together with the two ways it can be run, is the right choice.

Why the other options are wrong:
- VM insights Performance charts, with Aggregated Charts, Top N Charts and Top N List tabs: The VM insights Performance charts are the monitoring view for guest counters, arranged into the Aggregated Charts, Top N Charts and Top N List tabs. They chart utilization over time and offer no diagnostics modes for investigating a fault on one machine.
- Network Watcher Diagnostic Toolkit, with packet capture, next hop and IP flow verify: The Network Watcher Diagnostic Toolkit is the network troubleshooting toolbox with packet capture, next hop and IP flow verify. It analyses network paths rather than guest performance and it has no diagnostics modes.
- Storage insights Performance workbook, with Failures, Availability and Capacity workbooks: The Storage insights Performance workbook reports storage service behaviour such as end-to-end versus server latency and successful-call latency by API. It is a storage report with no diagnostics modes and nothing that diagnoses a virtual machine.

- Item: Diagnostic settings on those accounts; Current state: None defined
- Item: Log Analytics workspace la-prod-eastus; Current state: Receives no storage account metrics

AppRequests | where DurationMs > 1000 | project name, url
AppRequests | where durationms > 1000 | project Name, Url

The schema lists the table as AppRequests and the columns as Name and Url, so only this query resolves every name correctly: the table is spelled as in the schema, the filter uses the DurationMs column, the projection keeps Name and Url, and the operators are lower case. - apprequests | where DurationMs > 1000 | project Name, Url: This query refers to the table as apprequests in lower case. Because table names are case sensitive, that name does not match the AppRequests table listed in the schema pane, so the query fails to prepare before it can return any rows; the table name must be written exactly as shown in the schema.

Why the other options are wrong:
- AppRequests | project DurationSeconds = DurationMs / 1000: project keeps only the columns you list, so this query returns the single DurationSeconds column and the original fields such as ResultCode and ClientCity are dropped from the output, which is exactly the symptom the team reported.
- AppRequests | summarize DurationSeconds = avg(DurationMs / 1000): summarize aggregates records into groups and applies an aggregation to each group, so this query returns one overall average row instead of one row per request, and the original request fields are not carried over.
- AppRequests | where DurationMs >= 1000 | extend DurationSeconds = DurationMs / 1000: The added field is computed correctly and the original columns survive, but the where filter discards every request that finished in under one second, so the report no longer lists all of the requests that arrived during the window.

A colleague's statement for this report is rejected by the portal, which says it cannot find one of the columns even though that column is listed in the pane. You need a statement that runs successfully and returns the Paris requests with their duration and no other fields. Which statement should you write?

- Table: AppRequests; Column: TimeGenerated
- Table: AppRequests; Column: Name
- Table: AppRequests; Column: Url
- Table: AppRequests; Column: DurationMs
- Table: AppRequests; Column: ResultCode

- Table: AppTraces; Column: SeverityLevel

options.text: AppRequests | where clientcity == "Paris" | project Name, DurationMs
AppRequests | where ClientCity == "Paris" | project Name, DurationMs
AppRequests | where ClientCity == "Paris" | project name, durationMs
AppRequests | where ClientCity = "Paris" | project Name, DurationMs

explanation:
Azure Monitor Logs runs KQL case-sensitively, so every table and column name has to be typed exactly as the schema pane shows it, while language keywords such as where and project are written in lowercase. The pane lists the city column as ClientCity and the duration column as DurationMs, so the filter has to read `where ClientCity == "Paris"` and the two fields that must survive in the output have to be listed as `project Name, DurationMs`. The double-equals operator tests equality, and project keeps only the columns you name, which matches the requirement that the report carry the request name and its duration and nothing else.

Why the other options are wrong:
- AppRequests | where clientcity == "Paris" | project Name, DurationMs: The schema pane spells the city column with a capital C, so the lowercase spelling used here matches no column and the portal cannot find it.
- AppRequests | where ClientCity == "Paris" | project name, durationMs: The columns kept in the output must match the schema spelling as well; the pane lists Name and DurationMs, so the lowercase spellings used here are not resolved.

You have a Log Analytics workspace that receives Windows security events from your virtual machines through the rule that the Azure Monitor Agent uses, and query results now show each event twice. The affected machines also run the Log Analytics agent, so both place the same records into the workspace. You need the duplication to stop while the events stay in the workspace. Which change should you make?

- TimeGenerated: 2026-11-05 09:14:22; Computer: web-01; EventID: 4624; Account: svc-backup
- TimeGenerated: 2026-11-05 09:14:22; Computer: web-01; EventID: 4624; Account: svc-backup
- TimeGenerated: 2026-11-05 09:14:23; Computer: web-01; EventID: 4672; Account: admin-ea
- TimeGenerated: 2026-11-05 09:14:23; Computer: web-01; EventID: 4672; Account: admin-ea
prompt: You should _____.

options.text: Update the data collection rule so that it no longer collects what the Log Analytics agent already sends.
Lower the retention period of the Log Analytics workspace so that the duplicated records age out of the workspace sooner.
Add a second data collection rule so that the Azure Monitor Agent writes its records to a different table in the same workspace.
Configure summary rules in the Log Analytics workspace so that the repeated records are collapsed into a single row when they are queried.

explanation:
When a virtual machine has both the Log Analytics agent and the Azure Monitor Agent installed, the same telemetry can reach the workspace twice, and the results then contain duplicate rows exactly like the ones in the exhibit. The documented remedy for this case is to keep the Log Analytics agent in place but adjust the collection configuration so that the rule used by the Azure Monitor Agent stops gathering data that the Log Analytics agent already delivers. That is precisely what this option does, and the events remain in the workspace for queries and alerts.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Lower the retention period of the Log Analytics workspace so that the duplicated records age out of the workspace sooner: Retention only controls how long records stay in the workspace; it does not prevent a second copy from arriving, so the duplicated rows continue to appear in every query until the retention window expires.
- Add a second data collection rule so that the Azure Monitor Agent writes its records to a different table in the same workspace: Adding another rule merely gives the incoming data another destination; the same telemetry is still written twice into the workspace, so a query still returns each event two times.
- Configure summary rules in the Log Analytics workspace so that the repeated records are collapsed into a single row when they are queried: Summary rules aggregate data at ingestion time into their own summary tables for efficient queries; they do not remove repeated rows from the original table, so the duplicated events would still be returned.

You have a Log Analytics workspace that collects Windows security events from your servers, and the security team must pull every record of the workspace's Windows security event table whose fields contain the phrase Cryptographic. The result must cover the last seven days, that window has to be written into the query text so that it travels with the query when the team reuses the query in a workbook, and the query has to finish in seconds rather than minutes. Which query should you use?

`Workspace tables in scope
  SecurityEvent   Windows security events collected from the servers
  SysEvent        Windows system events such as service state changes
  AppRequests     Application Insights request telemetry

Query in use today
  search "Cryptographic"
  | take 10

Outcome of the current query
  Elapsed time    2 min 41 sec
  Tables scanned  312
  Rows returned   10
`
prompt: You replace the query in use today with _____.

options.text: search in (SecurityEvent) "Cryptographic" | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
search "Cryptographic" | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
search in (SecurityEvent) "Cryptographic" | take 10
search in (SecurityEvent) "Cryptographic" | where TimeGenerated > ago(7h)

explanation:
The `in (SecurityEvent)` clause restricts the free-text search to the workspace's Windows security event table, so the engine no longer scans every table and the query finishes in seconds; `where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)` writes the seven-day window into the query text, and `d` is the suffix that means days, so the window travels with the query wherever it is reused, such as in a workbook.

Why the other options are wrong:
- search "Cryptographic" | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d): This statement omits the `in (SecurityEvent)` clause, so the phrase is looked for in every table in the workspace instead of the security event table alone. The search then has to process far more data, which is why the current query takes minutes, and the result can also contain matching records from tables other than the security event table.
- search in (SecurityEvent) "Cryptographic" | take 10: Scoping the search to the security event table is right, but `take 10` returns at most ten rows, so the output is still a sample rather than every matching record, and no window is written into the query text at all.
- search in (SecurityEvent) "Cryptographic" | where TimeGenerated > ago(7h): The search is scoped to the correct table, but `ago(7h)` expresses seven hours, not seven days, so only the last seven hours of events are returned. The `d` suffix is the one that means days.

You have an Application Insights workload whose request telemetry is stored in the AppRequests table of a Log Analytics workspace. The workspace returns the records shown below. You need the hourly service report to include every request that either reported the status code 500 or took longer than 10,000 milliseconds, and the health probe requests must be left out of the report entirely. Which statement should you write?

- Name: GET /api/orders; Url: /api/orders; DurationMs: 820; ResultCode: 200; ClientCity: Paris; TimeGenerated: 2026-11-05 09:05
- Name: GET /api/orders; Url: /api/orders; DurationMs: 14500; ResultCode: 200; ClientCity: Paris; TimeGenerated: 2026-11-05 09:07
- Name: POST /api/checkout; Url: /api/checkout; DurationMs: 3200; ResultCode: 500; ClientCity: Berlin; TimeGenerated: 2026-11-05 09:11
- Name: GET /api/health; Url: /api/health; DurationMs: 12500; ResultCode: 200; ClientCity: Paris; TimeGenerated: 2026-11-05 09:12
- Name: POST /api/checkout; Url: /api/checkout; DurationMs: 11800; ResultCode: 500; ClientCity: Paris; TimeGenerated: 2026-11-05 09:15
- Name: GET /api/orders; Url: /api/orders; DurationMs: 210; ResultCode: 503; ClientCity: Berlin; TimeGenerated: 2026-11-05 09:18
prompt: The query that produces exactly the rows you need for the report is _____.

options.text: AppRequests | where ResultCode == 500 and DurationMs > 10000 | where Url != "/api/health"
AppRequests | where ResultCode == 500 or DurationMs > 10000 | where Url != "/api/health"
AppRequests | where ResultCode == 500 or DurationMs > 10000 | where Url == "/api/health"
AppRequests | where ResultCode != 500 and DurationMs > 10000 | where Url != "/api/health"

explanation:
The query starts from the AppRequests table and chains two where operators, each of which filters the rows produced by the previous one. The first condition uses `or`, so a request qualifies on its own when it either reported the status code 500 or took longer than 10,000 milliseconds; with the sample records this keeps the slow successful orders request (14,500 ms), the failed checkout request (3,200 ms, code 500) and the slow failed checkout request (11,800 ms, code 500). The second condition uses the inequality operator on Url, which removes the health probe row (12,500 ms) that the first condition would otherwise have kept, while leaving every other URL untouched. The table and column names are written exactly as they appear in the workspace schema, because KQL in Azure Monitor is case sensitive.

Why the other options are wrong:
- AppRequests | where ResultCode == 500 and DurationMs > 10000 | where Url != "/api/health": Using `and` between the two conditions means a request must have failed with status code 500 and be slower than 10,000 milliseconds at the same time. On the sample data that returns only the 11,800 ms failed checkout row, so the slow successful request and the fast failed request both disappear from the report.
- AppRequests | where ResultCode == 500 or DurationMs > 10000 | where Url == "/api/health": The equality comparison on Url keeps only the rows whose URL is exactly "/api/health", which is the opposite of what is needed: the report would contain a single health probe row and lose every order and checkout request.
- AppRequests | where ResultCode != 500 and DurationMs > 10000 | where Url != "/api/health": Negating the status code comparison discards every failed request, so the two checkout rows that reported 500 never reach the report, and the surviving rows are only slow ones that succeeded. The requirement needs the failed requests included, not removed.

You have a Log Analytics workspace with the schema shown below, and you are rebuilding the queries that feed the support dashboards and the daily handover report. You need each of the four requests below to be met by one of the KQL fragments provided. Which fragment should you use for each request?

Request 1: A quick spot check of the request telemetry that returns a limited batch of records in no particular order.

Request 2: A breakdown of the request telemetry that gives one row for every pairing of where the visitor connected from and the status code the request returned, showing how many requests fall into each pairing.

Request 3: A view of the Windows audit records that keeps only the machine, the complete text describing what happened, and the first four characters of that text, discarding every other field.

Request 4: A sweep across the whole workspace that finds every record, in any table, whose fields contain the phrase 'Failed logon'.

- Table: AppRequests; Columns: Name, Url, DurationMs, ResultCode, ClientCity
- Table: SecurityEvent; Columns: TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, EventSourceName, Level, Activity, ObjectName
prompt: Request 1 - a limited batch of request records in no particular order

options.text: AppRequests | take 250
AppRequests | summarize count() by ClientCity, ResultCode
SecurityEvent | project Computer, Activity, First4 = substring(Activity, 0, 4)
search "Failed logon"

explanation: Request 1 needs an arbitrary, unordered slice of the request records, which is exactly what the take fragment returns, so it goes to Request 1. Request 2 needs one row per combination of two attributes with a tally of the requests in each combination, which the summarize count() by two columns fragment produces, so it goes to Request 2. Request 3 needs only a few columns from the audit records plus a shortened version of the long text, which the project fragment computes with substring while discarding the remaining fields, so it goes to Request 3. Request 4 needs a free-text sweep of every table in the workspace, which the bare search fragment performs because search without a table restriction sweeps all tables, so it goes to Request 4.

You have a workspace of log data in Azure Monitor that your operations team works with from the Azure portal and from a custom reporting utility, and new people join the team regularly. You need each of the four problems below to be resolved by one of the actions listed. Which action should you take for each problem?

- Property: Workspace contents; Value: Application Insights request records and Windows security events
- Property: Ad hoc analysis; Value: Queries are run in the Azure portal
- Property: People joining this month; Value: 4
- Property: Reporting integration; Value: A scheduled utility retrieves log events over REST and writes the output to a warehouse
prompt: A colleague opens the portal page for the workspace they are assigned to and receives a 'No access' message instead of any records.

options.text: Grant the Log Analytics Reader built-in role to the affected person.
Require TLS 1.2 or later on the program that fetches log entries from the endpoint.
Let trainees practise in the Log Analytics demo environment.
Use the Observability Agent so a developer can explore the telemetry in natural language.
Install the Log Analytics agent on every virtual machine that sends telemetry.

explanation: The 'No access' problem is fixed by granting the Log Analytics Reader built-in role, because querying a workspace needs the Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces/query/*/read permission that this role provides. The REST integration that broke on 1 July 2025 matches the requirement that log query endpoints demand TLS 1.2 or higher from that date. New joiners who have no Azure subscription can practise on the Log Analytics demo environment, which ships sample data for the tutorial queries. The team member who cannot write queries can explore the data with the Observability Agent, which runs the KQL on their behalf and surfaces the insights. Installing the Log Analytics agent on virtual machines only changes how telemetry is collected and solves none of the four problems.

You have a workspace of request telemetry for a customer-facing application, and the support team runs its morning query in the Logs blade of the Azure portal. The query they use is listed below. During the last sprint the team hit a string of puzzling behaviours and asked you to account for them. Match each observation to the reason behind it.

`AppRequests
| where ResultCode != 200
| project Name, Url, DurationMs, TimeGenerated`
prompt: The same number of entries appears before and after the analyst reduces the period.

options.text: The Show limit caps how many rows the browser receives, so the visible total does not fall when the window is shortened.
Reordering in the results pane happens on the browser side over rows already fetched, so a rerun restores the sequence the query produced.
The search box above the grid filters only what the browser is already displaying, so the query itself is never changed and nothing is fetched again.
Rows must be gathered into time buckets before they can be plotted, so a query that returns one row per record leaves nothing to draw.
In Simple mode the default filter operator is Select from list, which offers values taken from the records currently displayed.

explanation: Each observation is explained by the matching mechanism: the Show limit caps the rows that reach the browser, so the visible total need not fall when the period is shortened (i1 with s1); sorting and grouping in the results pane reorganise only the rows the query already returned, and a rerun replaces that arrangement (i2 with s2); the search box filters only what is already displayed in the browser and leaves the query untouched (i3 with s3); charting needs the rows summarised into time buckets, so one row per record gives nothing to draw (i4 with s4); and in Simple mode the default filter operator offers only values taken from the records in the current results (i5 with s5).

prompt: You created the diagnostic setting shown below so that an application's logs and metrics are archived in a storage account and streamed to an external SIEM through Event Hubs. Ninety minutes after creating it, neither destination has received any data. You need the setting to deliver data to both destinations. What should you do?

options.text: Enable 'Allow trusted Microsoft services' on diagstore and diaghubs.
Enable 'Allow trusted Microsoft services' on contoso-web only.
Move diagstore and diaghubs to East US and recreate contoso-web-diag there.
Add a Log Analytics workspace as an extra destination in contoso-web-diag and keep the current two destinations.

explanation:
The diagnostic setting can be created successfully and still deliver nothing when a destination Storage account or Event Hubs namespace has virtual network access enabled: those destination resources must allow 'Allow trusted Microsoft services', otherwise Azure Monitor cannot push data into them. Both diagstore and diaghubs are virtual-network enabled with public network access disabled, which is exactly the condition described. Enabling that exception on the two destination resources unblocks delivery of the allLogs and AllMetrics data to the archive and the SIEM stream. Nothing else is blocking the flow: both destinations already sit in West Europe, the same region as contoso-web, and the shared access policy on diaghubs already grants Manage, Send and Listen for streaming.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enable 'Allow trusted Microsoft services' on contoso-web only: Enabling the exception only on contoso-web does not help, because contoso-web is the monitored resource that pushes data out; the setting that permits delivery must be turned on for the destination resources (diagstore and diaghubs). With it left off on both destinations, neither would receive any records.
- Move diagstore and diaghubs to East US and recreate contoso-web-diag there: For a regional monitored resource, the Storage account and Event Hubs namespace destinations must be in the same region as that resource. Both destinations are already in West Europe with contoso-web, so relocating them to East US would break the same-region requirement instead of fixing delivery.
- Add a Log Analytics workspace as an extra destination in contoso-web-diag and keep the current two destinations: A Log Analytics workspace is a valid destination type and one of each type may be included, but adding it does not remove the network restriction on diagstore and diaghubs. Logs would reach the workspace while the two required destinations would still receive nothing.

prompt: You have a virtual machine app01 in resource group rg-app that must send its resource logs and platform metrics to the Log Analytics workspace law-central. You manage this environment with an infrastructure-as-code pipeline and deploy the ARM template shown below as part of it. The deployment fails and reports that the metric category 'Percentage CPU' isn't supported, so nothing gets configured for the machine. You need the deployment to succeed and the machine's platform metrics to reach law-central. Which change should you make to the template?

options.text: Replace the metric category in the template with AllMetrics and redeploy the template
Add a second metrics entry that uses AllMetrics while keeping the Percentage CPU entry, then redeploy the template
Remove the metrics array from the template and redeploy the template
Replace the metric category in the template with the allLogs category group and redeploy the template

explanation:
Diagnostic settings deployed through a Resource Manager template (likewise the REST API, Azure CLI, or Azure PowerShell) accept only the AllMetrics metric category, apart from a limited number of Azure services. The 'Percentage CPU' entry in the metrics array is what the deployment rejects, so replacing that entry with AllMetrics both fixes the deployment and causes the machine's platform metrics to be exported to law-central, while the two log categories continue to be collected as written.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add a second metrics entry that uses AllMetrics while keeping the Percentage CPU entry, then redeploy the template: Adding an extra entry leaves the unsupported 'Percentage CPU' category in the template, so the deployment still fails. Every metric category other than AllMetrics has to be removed from the metrics array, not merely supplemented.
- Remove the metrics array from the template and redeploy the template: Dropping the metrics array lets the deployment succeed, but the setting then requests no platform metrics at all, so nothing metric-related would ever arrive in law-central. The requirement is that the machine's platform metrics reach the workspace, so metric collection must stay in the setting.
- Replace the metric category in the template with the allLogs category group and redeploy the template: allLogs is a log category group used in the Logs section, not a valid metric category. A metrics entry named with a category group is still rejected, so the deployment would continue to fail and the platform metrics would not be sent.

prompt: You need the resource logs of a Linux virtual machine vm-report in resource group rg-ops to reach the corporate SIEM, which consumes events from Event Hubs. The diagnostic setting shown below is in place on the virtual machine, but the event hub holds no events at all and the SIEM dashboard stays empty. You need the Event Hubs destination to actually deliver the logs. Which change should you make?

options.text: Add the Manage right to the shared access policy siem-send and grant the ListKey right on the authorization rule hub-rule.
Add the Manage right to the shared access policy siem-send and leave the authorization rule hub-rule unchanged.
Add the Listen right to the shared access policy siem-send and grant the ListKey right on the authorization rule hub-rule.
Add the Send right to the shared access policy siem-send and grant the Listen right on the authorization rule hub-rule.

explanation:
Two separate permission gaps block this stream. The shared access policy on the namespace defines what the streaming mechanism may do, and streaming to Event Hubs through a diagnostic setting requires the Manage, Send, and Listen rights — siem-send currently grants only Send and Listen, so Manage is missing. In addition, updating a diagnostic setting so that it includes the Event Hubs stream requires the ListKey right on the Event Hubs authorization rule, and hub-rule grants no rights at all. Granting Manage on siem-send and ListKey on hub-rule clears both gaps, so the setting can be updated and the logs can flow. Region placement and firewall settings are already satisfied, so neither is the cause.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add the Manage right to the shared access policy siem-send and leave the authorization rule hub-rule unchanged: Adding Manage to the shared access policy only fixes the policy side. The authorization rule hub-rule still grants no rights, so the ListKey permission needed to add or update the Event Hubs stream in the diagnostic setting is still missing and the destination still can't be configured.
- Add the Listen right to the shared access policy siem-send and grant the ListKey right on the authorization rule hub-rule: Listen is already granted on siem-send, so granting it again changes nothing, and the right actually missing from that policy is Manage. Even with ListKey added to hub-rule, the streaming mechanism would still lack the permissions it needs.
- Add the Send right to the shared access policy siem-send and grant the Listen right on the authorization rule hub-rule: Send is already granted on siem-send, and granting Listen on the authorization rule doesn't satisfy the ListKey permission required to update the diagnostic setting with the Event Hubs stream. The policy would also still be missing Manage.

prompt: You have a Linux virtual machine vm-app01 in resource group rg-app. The resource logs of the machine must be queryable in two Log Analytics workspaces, law1 and law2, and the platform metrics must continue to be delivered to law1. The current configuration of the machine is shown below. Which change should you make?

options.text: Create a second diagnostic setting on vm-app01 that sends the resource logs to law2, and add the platform metrics to the existing diagnostic setting for law1.
Add law2 to the existing diagnostic setting that sends the resource logs and the platform metrics to both workspaces.
Create a second diagnostic setting on vm-app01 that sends the resource logs to law2, and move the platform metrics from the existing diagnostic setting to the new one.
Configure a workspace transformation rule on law1 that reshapes the incoming resource logs and routes a copy of them to law2.

explanation:
A diagnostic setting can carry no more than one destination of each type, so law1 and law2 have to be attached to separate diagnostic settings on vm-app01. A resource accepts up to five diagnostic settings, so adding a second one is within the limit. The new setting carries the resource log categories to law2, while the existing diag-law1 setting keeps its AllMetrics export, so law1 continues to receive the platform metrics and both workspaces hold the resource logs.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add law2 to the existing diagnostic setting that sends the resource logs and the platform metrics to both workspaces: A single diagnostic setting can reference only one Log Analytics workspace, one storage account and one Event Hubs namespace, so law2 cannot be added as a second workspace destination in diag-law1. The addition is rejected and law2 receives nothing.
- Create a second diagnostic setting on vm-app01 that sends the resource logs to law2, and move the platform metrics from the existing diagnostic setting to the new one: Moving the AllMetrics export into the new setting means law1 stops receiving the platform metrics, which the requirement still demands. Enabling metric export in both settings is allowed, but then the metrics are collected and billed twice.
- Configure a workspace transformation rule on law1 that reshapes the incoming resource logs and routes a copy of them to law2: A workspace transformation DCR filters or reshapes records per table for the sources that write to that table in that workspace; it cannot forward records into a different workspace. Since law2 would not be a destination of any diagnostic setting, its tables stay empty.

prompt: You have an Azure SQL Database sqlb-sales in resource group rg-data. To satisfy a compliance requirement you added a diagnostic setting to the database and routed it to the Log Analytics workspace law-sec, as shown below. The compliance team reports that the database captures no events at all, and the workspace holds nothing for this database. You need the database's auditing turned on so that its events are recorded and reach law-sec. Which action should you take?

options.text: Enable auditing from the auditing pane of the Azure SQL Database.
Enable the SQLAuditLogs category on the Azure SQL Database by adding a second diagnostic setting that sends the logs to a storage account instead of the workspace.
Change the diagnostic setting from the audit category group to allLogs so that every category of the Azure SQL Database is collected to law-sec.
Enable auditing in the transformation rules of the law-sec workspace so that audit entries from every source are preserved.

explanation:
Choosing the audit category group in a diagnostic setting only tells Azure Monitor which resource log categories to forward to the destinations you chose; it does not switch on the database's auditing feature. For Azure SQL Database, auditing must be enabled from the database's auditing pane, where the audit targets are configured. Because the database's auditing is currently off, it produces no audit records, so no destination, including law-sec, can receive anything. Once auditing is enabled, the audit records are collected as resource logs and the existing diagnostic setting forwards them to law-sec.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enable the SQLAuditLogs category on the Azure SQL Database by adding a second diagnostic setting that sends the logs to a storage account instead of the workspace: Adding a diagnostic setting that sends the SQLAuditLogs category to a storage account only chooses another route for logs the database already produces. With auditing switched off in the database there are no audit records to forward, so the compliance requirement still wouldn't be met.
- Change the diagnostic setting from the audit category group to allLogs so that every category of the Azure SQL Database is collected to law-sec: Switching the category group from audit to allLogs widens the set of categories that Azure Monitor forwards once the resource is producing data. It does not enable the database's auditing, so the database would still emit no audit events.
- Enable auditing in the transformation rules of the law-sec workspace so that audit entries from every source are preserved: Workspace transformation rules filter or reshape records that already arrive for a table in a workspace. They cannot switch on a resource feature or decide which categories a resource produces, and the audit category group is already selected in the diagnostic setting shown.

prompt: You have a Log Analytics workspace law-sec in resource group rg-sec that collects two high-volume tables from a Windows virtual machine fleet and a Linux web tier. The security operations center wants alerts raised on these logs as new events arrive, and auditors must be able to query the last 400 days of both tables interactively in Azure Monitor Logs. The current configuration of the workspace is shown below. Which change should you make?

options.text: Move both tables to the Analytics plan and set the analytics retention to 400 days.
Move both tables to the Basic plan and set the analytics retention to 400 days.
Keep both tables on the Auxiliary plan and set the analytics retention to 400 days.
Move both tables to the Analytics plan, leave the retention at 30 days, and copy older records to a storage account with an export rule.

explanation:
The two tables need both alerting on incoming events and a long window of interactively queryable data. Analytics is the table plan suited to continuous monitoring and real-time detection: it supports all table types, enables log alerts, and its analytics retention starts at 30 days and can be extended up to two years at a prorated monthly charge, so setting it to 400 days satisfies the audit requirement. Moving both tables to Analytics and raising the retention to 400 days therefore meets both goals.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Move both tables to the Basic plan and set the analytics retention to 400 days: Basic tables have no analytics retention at all, so no setting can make the last 400 days interactively queryable on that plan. Basic also allows only Simple Log Alerts, so it is aimed at medium-touch troubleshooting and incident response rather than continuous detection on verbose security data.
- Keep both tables on the Auxiliary plan and set the analytics retention to 400 days: Auxiliary is built for verbose audit and compliance archiving with minimal ingestion cost, but it has no alerts and no analytics retention. Keeping the tables there and asking for 400 days of analytics retention is not possible, so the SOC alerting goal and the auditor query goal both fail.
- Move both tables to the Analytics plan, leave the retention at 30 days, and copy older records to a storage account with an export rule: Moving the tables to the Analytics plan is the right direction, but leaving retention at 30 days keeps the interactive query window at its starting value. An export rule copies records to a storage account for long-term archiving; it does not make the last 400 days queryable in Azure Monitor Logs, so the auditors' requirement is still unmet.
