prompt: You have a web app app-portal in resource group rg-app, and you need its resource logs archived long term in a storage account and streamed to the corporate SIEM, which consumes events from Event Hubs. Your team prepared four candidate destinations, listed below, and chose stl-arch for the archive and eh-compact for the stream. When you try to save the diagnostic setting with that pair, the save fails with an error and the app ends up with no diagnostic setting at all, so nothing is routed to either destination. You need the diagnostic setting to be created and to deliver data to both a storage account and an Event Hubs namespace. Which pair of destinations should you select?

options.text: Use stl-std as the archive destination and eh-plain as the streaming destination in the diagnostic setting.
Use stl-arch as the archive destination and eh-plain as the streaming destination in the diagnostic setting.
Use stl-std as the archive destination and eh-compact as the streaming destination in the diagnostic setting.
Use stl-arch as the archive destination and eh-compact as the streaming destination in the diagnostic setting.

explanation:
Only Standard storage accounts are accepted as a Storage account destination in a diagnostic setting; Premium storage accounts are not supported destinations. Compacted Event Hubs namespaces are not supported destinations either, while a namespace without compaction is. In the candidate list, stl-std is the only Standard storage account and eh-plain is the only namespace that does not have compaction enabled, so selecting stl-std for the archive and eh-plain for the stream lets the setting be created and deliver logs to both destinations.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Use stl-arch as the archive destination and eh-plain as the streaming destination in the diagnostic setting: The streaming destination eh-plain is acceptable, but stl-arch is a Premium storage account, and Premium storage accounts are not supported diagnostic setting destinations, so the setting still cannot be created with this pair.
- Use stl-std as the archive destination and eh-compact as the streaming destination in the diagnostic setting: The archive destination stl-std is acceptable, but eh-compact has compaction enabled on its hubs, and compacted Event Hubs are not supported destinations, so this pair is rejected as well.
- Use stl-arch as the archive destination and eh-compact as the streaming destination in the diagnostic setting: Both candidates are unsuitable: stl-arch is a Premium storage account and eh-compact is a compacted Event Hubs namespace. Neither can be used as a diagnostic setting destination, so nothing gets configured.

prompt: You have an Azure SQL Database sqldb-orders in resource group rg-data (subscription sub-app) whose location is Sweden Central. A compliance rule requires the database's resource logs and platform metrics to be archived for seven years in a Storage account and streamed to the corporate SIEM through Event Hubs. Your team selected the two destinations listed below and attempted to save a single diagnostic setting on the database, but the portal refuses the save and reports an error about the location of a destination, so neither the archive nor the stream receives any data. You need the diagnostic setting to be created and to deliver the database's logs and metrics to both destinations. Which change should you make?

options.text: Create the archive storage account in Sweden Central and use it with ns-telemetry as the destinations.
Use the existing archive storage account stlogs-archive in West Europe with ns-telemetry in Sweden Central as the destinations.
Create an Event Hubs namespace in West Europe and use it with the existing archive storage account stlogs-archive as the destinations.
Move stlogs-archive into rg-data in sub-app and use the storage account with ns-telemetry as the destinations.

explanation:
For a regional monitored resource such as an Azure SQL Database, the Storage account and Event Hubs namespace used as diagnostic setting destinations must be located in the same region as the monitored resource. sqldb-orders sits in Sweden Central, so the archive Storage account has to be provisioned in Sweden Central; ns-telemetry is already there. With the account created in Sweden Central, the setting can be saved and both destinations receive the database's resource logs and platform metrics.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Use the existing archive storage account stlogs-archive in West Europe with ns-telemetry in Sweden Central as the destinations: stlogs-archive stays in West Europe, which is not the database's region, so the portal keeps rejecting the save and no logs or metrics reach either destination.
- Create an Event Hubs namespace in West Europe and use it with the existing archive storage account stlogs-archive as the destinations: A new Event Hubs namespace in West Europe still leaves the stream outside the database's Sweden Central region, and stlogs-archive is in West Europe as well, so the save would continue to fail.
- Move stlogs-archive into rg-data in sub-app and use the storage account with ns-telemetry as the destinations: Relocating stlogs-archive to a different resource group and subscription leaves it in West Europe; the constraint concerns the destination's region, not its subscription or resource group, so the setting would remain invalid.

audit category group
individual category types
AllMetrics metric category
Export activity log

explanation: Each clause is matched with the selection inside the diagnostic setting that satisfies it. The clause asking for every category the machine emits is met by the allLogs category group, which takes all categories in one selection and already includes the categories that record customer interactions with data and with service settings. The change request from the platform team lists four clauses that the setting has to satisfy, and everything the setting collects must end up in the Log Analytics workspace law-retail. Match each clause to the selection you make in the diagnostic setting that satisfies it.

`Clause | Applies to                                  | Requirement
PC-1   | Resource log categories of vm-orders          | Every category the virtual machine emits has to be captured.
PC-2   | Resource log categories of vm-orders          | Only the categories capturing how customers used the data and how the service configuration was changed may be collected.
PC-3   | Resource log categories of vm-orders          | Only the SecurityLog category may be captured.
PC-4   | Platform performance counters of vm-orders    | The machine's platform performance counters have to be forwarded to law-retail.`
prompt: PC-2 - only the categories capturing how customers used the data and how the service configuration was changed

options.text: allLogs category group
audit category group
individual category types
AllMetrics metric category
Export activity log

explanation: Each clause is matched with the selection inside the diagnostic setting that satisfies it. The clause asking for every category the machine emits is met by the allLogs category group, which takes all categories in one selection and already includes the categories that record customer interactions with data and with service settings. The clause that permits only the customer-interaction and service-configuration categories is met by the audit category group, which holds exactly those records and leaves the remaining categories out. The clause naming a single category is met by ticking individual category types, because once a category group is chosen the portal blocks picking categories one by one. The clause about the machine's platform performance counters is met by AllMetrics under the Metrics tab, the selection that forwards platform metrics to the chosen destinations.

You have two Azure Key Vaults, kv-prod and kv-billing, in resource group rg-sec (West Europe), and neither of them has any diagnostic setting yet. - Resource property: Destination resources available in rg-sec; Value: law-sec (Log Analytics workspace), law-ops (Log Analytics workspace), stl-archive (Storage account, West Europe, Standard), eh-siem (Event Hubs namespace, West Europe)
- Resource property: Existing diagnostic settings; Value: None on either vault
prompt: kv-prod: every log category the vault emits must be delivered, and the team should not tick categories one at a time

options.text: Under Logs, select the allLogs category group
Under Logs, select the audit category group
Under Metrics, select AllMetrics
Create a second diagnostic setting and give each setting one workspace
Under Logs, select AllMetrics
Under Metrics, select the audit category group
Add law-sec and law-ops as destinations in the same setting

explanation: For kv-prod, choosing the allLogs category group under Logs collects every category the vault emits without selecting categories one at a time, and choosing AllMetrics under Metrics is what forwards platform measurements to the selected destinations. The allLogs category group is not needed because ds-web-01 already sends every log category, and the HTTP Data Collector API is the superseded mechanism.

context:
You manage how data reaches a Log Analytics workspace from several places. The platform team has provided four requirements, and each requirement must be met by exactly one of the configuration changes listed below. Match each requirement to the change that satisfies it.

`Data path                                          How it reaches the workspace today
-----------------------------------------------   -----------------------------------------------
Software vendor application on vendor hardware    Telemetry delivered straight into the workspace
Virtual machine fleet vm-fleet                    Collected by the Azure Monitor agent with a data collection rule
Production resources that carry diagnostic settings   Records delivered by the diagnostic settings of each resource
Virtual machine platform metrics                  Most of them are included in the export, one is not`
prompt: A software vendor's on-premises application delivers telemetry into Azure; the team needs OAuth-based access and centrally managed schemas, and the vendor application cannot be modified.

options.text: Send the source records with the Logs Ingestion API through a data collection endpoint and rule
Extend the source-side data collection rule that the flow already uses, so its metrics keep flowing
Apply an ingestion-time transformation to the table that receives the records
Fetch the unsupported metrics with the Metrics REST API and write them into a table with the Logs Ingestion API

explanation: The vendor application is a custom, third-party source, so its records are pushed with the Logs Ingestion API together with a data collection endpoint and a data collection rule, which is what provides OAuth authentication and schema governance without touching the source system. The virtual machine fleet already runs under a data collection rule, and ingestion-time transformations are not applied to flows governed that way, so the filtering has to be added to the rule at the source. The data that arrives through diagnostic settings lands in a table and can be reshaped by an ingestion-time transformation for that table, which is where the noisy entries are dropped. The platform metric that is not exported cannot be reshaped into existence: unsupported metrics are read with the Metrics REST API and then loaded with the Logs Ingestion API so they become queryable.

context:
You are responsible for the telemetry paths in the retail Azure environment shown in the exhibit. The four requirements in the exhibit map one-to-one onto the approaches below, and each approach is applied once. Which approach belongs with each requirement?

- Request: R1; Approved requirement: Every entry recorded in the activity log of subscription sub-retail must be archived in the Storage account stl-retail.
- Request: R2; Approved requirement: Every entry recorded at the level of mg-retail must be searchable by the operations team in the Log Analytics workspace law-retail.
- Request: R3; Approved requirement: The resource logs and the platform metrics produced by virtual machine vm-retail must both arrive in law-retail, so the on-call team can query and alert on them together.
- Request: R4; Approved requirement: The custom logs emitted by the third-party application contoso-orders must reach law-retail through a currently supported collection path whose incoming schema the platform team can govern centrally.
prompt: Request R1

options.text: Configure a diagnostic setting on vm-retail that sends its resource logs and AllMetrics to law-retail.
Use the activity log export of subscription sub-retail to send its activity log entries to stl-retail.
Configure a diagnostic setting on mg-retail that sends its activity log entries to law-retail.
Create a data collection rule and a data collection endpoint, then send the custom records through the Logs Ingestion API.
Configure a workspace transformation data collection rule that filters records after they arrive in a supported table.

explanation: R1 asks for the subscription's activity log, which is gathered automatically and only has to be forwarded, so it is handled with the activity log export (Export activity log) pointing at stl-retail. R2 concerns entries recorded at the management group level, and management groups use their own management group diagnostic settings, so a diagnostic setting on mg-retail sends those entries to law-retail. R3 concerns a single resource's own telemetry, so a diagnostic setting is created on the virtual machine, with its log categories and AllMetrics selected so that platform metrics travel to law-retail as well. R4 comes from a third-party application, for which the recommended path is the Logs Ingestion API together with a data collection rule and data collection endpoint, replacing the old HTTP Data Collector API and adding OAuth authentication and schema governance. The workspace transformation rule only filters or reshapes records that other sources have already delivered to a supported table, so it starts no collection and satisfies none of the four requirements.

explanation:
For custom and third-party sources, the recommended path is the Logs Ingestion API used with a data collection rule and a data collection endpoint. It supersedes the legacy HTTP Data Collector API and adds OAuth-based authentication, DCR-governed schema control, and transformations. That satisfies both requirements at once: the vendor authenticates with a token instead of a long-lived shared secret, the data collection rule governs the schema and separates the record types into their own tables, and the records continue to land in the same workspace, law-vendor.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Send LedgerSync's records with the legacy HTTP Data Collector API, and use a shared key that the vendor holds: The HTTP Data Collector API is the older mechanism that the Logs Ingestion API replaces. It authenticates with a shared key and offers no schema governance, so it fails both requirements: dropping the long-lived shared secret and controlling the incoming record types in Azure.
- Send LedgerSync's records with the Azure Monitor agent, and use a data collection rule that targets the workspace: The Azure Monitor agent gathers telemetry from the machines where it is installed; it gives a hosted third-party application no way to push its own records into a workspace. LedgerSync's records originate outside Azure, so the agent is not the mechanism for this source.
- Send LedgerSync's records with Event Hubs streaming, and use an Event Hubs namespace and a shared access policy: Event Hubs streaming is used to forward data to external systems such as a SIEM. It gives the vendor neither token-based authentication for its connection nor a schema controlled in Azure for records landing directly in the workspace, so it does not satisfy the requirements for this source.

explanation:
Sum adds the values captured inside each interval, so with a 60-minute granularity every plotted point represents the entire hour's transaction volume (1045 + 1120 + 990 + 1180 = 4335 for the first hour, and 4305 for the second). That matches the reporting requirement of one point per hour showing all transactions handled during that hour.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Count: Count returns the number of measurements taken in the interval, not the total of their values, so the first hour would be plotted as 4 rather than the hour's volume. Count matches the added value only for metrics that are always captured as 1, and this metric is not one of them.
- Average: Average divides the interval's values by the number of measurements, so it yields a per-sampling-period figure (about 1084 for the first hour) instead of the hour's total volume.
- Max: Max returns only the largest single value captured in the interval (1180 for the first hour), which describes the busiest sampling period and leaves out the rest of the hour's transactions.

prompt: You have a shell script that collects platform metric data for every virtual machine in the company inventory by using the Metrics REST API, issuing one query per machine. The monthly report now takes roughly 40 minutes, and the script regularly receives HTTP 429 responses, so some machines are missing from the report. You need to finish the collection reliably without leaving any machine out. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Use the Azure Monitor Metrics Batch REST API to read a maximum of 50 resource IDs for one subscription and region in one call
Use the Metrics REST API to read one virtual machine at a time in a concurrent loop for a single subscription and region
Use the Prometheus HTTP API of an Azure Monitor workspace to read the same platform metric values in one query
Use the Metrics REST API to read every virtual machine at a coarser time granularity in a concurrent loop for a single subscription and region

explanation:
Azure Monitor provides a dedicated endpoint for high-volume metric queries: the Azure Monitor Metrics Batch REST API. A single batch request can carry up to 50 resource IDs, and all IDs in that request must belong to one subscription and one region. Using it improves throughput and reduces the throttling risk that is producing the HTTP 429 responses in your run. Since the inventory in the exhibit is spread over two subscriptions and three regions, you would group the machine IDs into sets that satisfy that one-subscription/one-region constraint and issue one batch request per group.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Use the Metrics REST API to read one virtual machine at a time in a concurrent loop for a single subscription and region: The standard Metrics REST API answers for one resource at a time. Firing many single-machine queries in parallel does not change the service's per-request limits, and high concurrency is a common cause of the HTTP 429 responses you are already seeing.
- Use the Prometheus HTTP API of an Azure Monitor workspace to read the same platform metric values in one query: The Prometheus HTTP API is the retrieval path for metrics stored in an Azure Monitor workspace, which holds Prometheus and OpenTelemetry data. The virtual machines' platform metrics are not stored there, so this endpoint returns nothing for them.
- Use the Metrics REST API to read every virtual machine at a coarser time granularity in a concurrent loop for a single subscription and region: A coarser granularity changes how many samples come back per machine, but the script still sends one query per virtual machine. The number of queries stays the same, so the throttling and the roughly 40-minute runtime remain.

explanation:
In Metrics explorer, a filter narrows the set of dimension values that contribute to the chart, while splitting decides whether each remaining value is merged into one line or drawn as its own line. Filtering IP down to the three requested addresses and splitting on Direction therefore produces one line per direction for each of the three addresses, which is exactly what the security team asked for.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add a filter on the Direction dimension, and apply splitting on the IP dimension: This applies the filter to the Direction dimension instead of the IP dimension, so every address in the range stays in scope and the chart is not limited to the three requested sources. Splitting on IP then draws a separate line per address, but the inbound and outbound values of each address are still merged together.
- Apply splitting on the IP and Direction dimensions, and add no filter: With no filter, all six IP values in the range remain in the chart, so the three requested addresses are never isolated and the legend grows far beyond the requested scope. Splitting on both dimensions alone cannot narrow the data.
- Add a filter on the IP dimension for the three addresses only, without applying splitting: This correctly restricts the chart to the three addresses, but without splitting the Inbound and Outbound values are combined, so you cannot see each direction on its own line as required.

Your compliance team wants the node CPU totals from your Kubernetes cluster for the last 400 days, and those readings reach your Azure Monitor workspace through the Prometheus collection path. Before you commit to delivering anything, you must confirm the history still exists and plan how the values come out of the workspace.

- Item: Metric the compliance team asked for; Value: node_cpu_seconds_total
- Item: Source cluster; Value: prod-aks-01 (Kubernetes)
- Item: How the readings reach Azure Monitor; Value: Prometheus collection path into the Azure Monitor workspace

prompt: Prometheus metrics in your Azure Monitor workspace _____, and to extract the readings for the compliance team you [...].

options.text: are retained for 18 months, which covers the 400-day reporting window
are retained for 93 days, which does not cover the 400-day reporting window
are retained for 32 days, which does not cover the 400-day reporting window
are retained for 30 days, which does not cover the 400-day reporting window

explanation:
Prometheus data held in an Azure Monitor workspace is retained for 18 months, so the 400-day reporting window the compliance team asked for is still inside the retention period. A single PromQL query is limited to a 32-day span, so the readings have to be gathered with several queries, each covering at most 32 days.

Why the other options are wrong:
- are retained for 93 days, which does not cover the 400-day reporting window: 93 days is the retention period for platform and custom metrics, not for Prometheus data kept in a workspace; a 400-day window would fall well outside it.
- are retained for 32 days, which does not cover the 400-day reporting window: 32 days is the maximum span of one PromQL query, not a retention period; Prometheus data in a workspace stays available for 18 months.
- are retained for 30 days, which does not cover the 400-day reporting window: 30 days is the longest range a single chart can query for platform and custom metrics; Prometheus data stored in an Azure Monitor workspace is retained for 18 months.

- Setting: Retention of the Application Insights logs; Value: 90 days
- Setting: Chart span required by the compliance team; Value: Last 60 days
prompt: In this situation, _____.

options.text: a chart for the compliance team can display the entire requested range because the 30-day query limit does not apply to log-based metrics
a chart for the compliance team can display the entire requested range because the 30-day query limit applies to log-based metrics
a chart for the compliance team can display only the most recent 30 days because the 30-day query limit applies to every metric stored in Azure Monitor Metrics including log-based metrics
a chart for the compliance team can display only the most recent 30 days because log-based metrics query the underlying log records which are kept for only 30 days

explanation:
Log-based metrics are backed by log queries rather than by the metric time series. The documentation states that while platform and custom metrics are stored for 93 days, a single chart can query only 30 days of them, and that this limitation does not apply to log-based metrics. Retention for log-based metrics follows the retention of the underlying log events, and the Application Insights logs behind this metric are stored for 90 days, so the 60-day span the compliance team asked for is both available in the logs and outside the 30-day chart window restriction.

Why the other options are wrong:
- a chart for the compliance team can display the entire requested range because the 30-day query limit applies to log-based metrics: The 30-day chart query window is not a blanket rule for log-based metrics. It is documented for platform and custom metrics stored in Azure Monitor Metrics, and the documentation explicitly states that this limitation doesn't apply to log-based metrics, so this reasoning is incorrect.
- a chart for the compliance team can display only the most recent 30 days because the 30-day query limit applies to every metric stored in Azure Monitor Metrics including log-based metrics: The 30-day query window does not cover every metric kept in Azure Monitor Metrics. It applies to platform and custom metrics, while log-based metrics are exempt because they are log queries underneath, so the chart is free to span the full requested period.
- a chart for the compliance team can display only the most recent 30 days because log-based metrics query the underlying log records which are kept for only 30 days: Availability of a log-based metric follows the retention of the underlying log events, which for this Application Insights resource is 90 days as shown in the exhibit. A 30-day log history is therefore not the limiting factor here; the restriction that could have truncated the chart, the 30-day query window, does not apply to this metric.

You monitor a busy Linux virtual machine's processor utilization with a chart in Metrics explorer. The readings normally sit at the very top of the scale, and a short dip during the afternoon matters to the on-call team, so a colleague narrowed the y-axis range until the dip became obvious. Today one of the analysts resized the browser window, the points on the chart were redrawn with different spacing, and the narrowed range no longer frames the data the way the team expects. The chart's current configuration is listed in the exhibit. You need the y-axis bounds the team chose to keep giving the same picture of the dip no matter how the browser window is sized. What should you change?

`Chart configuration - vm-web-01

Metric ................ Percentage CPU
Scope ................. vm-web-01 (Linux, West Europe)
Time range ............ Last 24 hours
Time granularity ...... Automatic
Aggregation ........... Maximum
Y-axis range .......... Minimum 99, Maximum 100
`
prompt: To keep the y-axis bounds the team chose giving the same picture of the dip for every viewer, you should _____.

options.text: set the time granularity to a fixed interval
keep the time granularity on automatic and re-apply the y-axis range whenever the chart is resized
set the time granularity to a fixed interval and reset the y-axis range to automatic
keep the time granularity on automatic and change the aggregation from maximum to average

explanation:
This chart has its y-axis boundaries narrowed around the readings and uses the Maximum aggregation, which is exactly the situation in which the time grain should not be left to the automatic choice. When the grain is selected automatically it can change as soon as a viewer resizes the browser window or changes screen resolution, and the redrawn points no longer match the axis bounds that were chosen, which is the symptom reported here. Pinning the time granularity to a fixed interval keeps the plotted points and the narrow axis bounds aligned for everyone who opens the chart.

Why the other options are wrong:
- keep the time granularity on automatic and re-apply the y-axis range whenever the chart is resized: Any viewer can resize the window at any time, so re-applying the bounds afterwards only repairs the chart after the fact; the automatically chosen grain can change again and invalidate the range once more.
- set the time granularity to a fixed interval and reset the y-axis range to automatic: Fixing the grain is the right part of the change, but clearing the y-axis range returns the chart to the default scale, which hides the small dip the team wanted to make visible.
- keep the time granularity on automatic and change the aggregation from maximum to average: Switching the aggregation does not stop the automatically selected grain from changing when the window is resized, so the selected axis bounds can still be invalidated; a fixed grain is the documented remedy for a chart with locked axis boundaries.

split by the dimension, set the display limit to 50, and change the sort order to Ascending

explanation:
Splitting the chart on the ContainerName dimension gives every container its own series instead of one merged line. The display limit that belongs to splitting (allowed values 1 to 50, 10 as the default) caps how many container series are actually drawn, so setting it to 6 delivers the 'no more than six lines' requirement. The sort order offered for the split segments is Descending by default, which already presents the containers with the largest counts first, so it should be left as it is; only the limit needs changing.

Why the other options are wrong:
- split by the dimension, set the display limit to 10, and keep the Descending sort order: The ordering is fine, but leaving the display limit at its default of 10 would draw ten container series, two more than the team allows.
- split by the dimension, set the display limit to 6, and change the sort order to Ascending: The limit of 6 is right, but switching the order to Ascending would list the containers with the smallest counts first, which is the opposite of what the team asked for.
- split by the dimension, set the display limit to 50, and change the sort order to Ascending: A limit of 50 would draw far more container series than the six the team allows, and the Ascending order would additionally place the smallest counts first.

context:
You maintain a Metrics explorer chart for the virtual machine vm-app-01. It was showing the Percentage CPU metric on its own, and you have now added the Network In Total metric so that both readings can be examined together. The CPU line has flattened into a straight line along the bottom of the graph because the byte counts are far larger than the percentage values, so nobody can read the CPU pattern any more. The chart's current configuration is shown in the exhibit. Your team needs both signals to keep a readable shape. What should you do?

`Resource ............. vm-app-01 (virtual machine)
Metrics on the chart . Percentage CPU, Network In Total
Chart type ........... Line chart
Y-axis range ......... Auto
`
prompt: You should _____.

options.text: Draw the metrics on separate charts, one chart per metric.
Stack the metrics on the current chart as an area.
Split the metrics on the current chart by dimension.
Fix the axis bounds on the current chart.

explanation:
Adding a second metric with a different unit to the same chart puts both series on one shared axis, and because byte counts are far larger than a percentage, the CPU line is squeezed flat and becomes unreadable. The documented guidance is not to mix units or very different scales on one chart but to use separate charts, and in Metrics explorer a second chart is started with the New chart control. Putting each signal on its own chart restores the readable shape of the CPU readings while the network series gets its own scale.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Stack the metrics on the current chart as an area: A stacked area chart draws each value plus a combined total. Adding a byte count to a percentage produces a meaningless combined total, and both series still share the single axis, so the flattened CPU line remains unreadable. Stacking suits values of the same kind that add up meaningfully.
- Split the metrics on the current chart by dimension: Splitting breaks a series into one line per dimension value, for example per source IP address. It changes how the data is broken up, not the shared axis, so two signals expressed in different units still cannot both be read on one chart.
- Fix the axis bounds on the current chart: Setting the axis bounds only rescales the values that are already plotted on that chart. It cannot make a percentage and a byte count comparable on one axis, so the CPU line stays flattened. A pinned range is also fragile, because an automatically chosen granularity can redraw the chart after a browser window resize and invalidate the chosen bounds.

Your platform team keeps two charts side by side for one workload: the first plots the CPU utilization of a virtual machine, taken from the platform metrics that Azure collects from that machine automatically, and the second plots the container CPU readings that a Kubernetes cluster's Prometheus pipeline sends to an Azure Monitor workspace. The values plotted for the minute 14:00 and the minutes that follow are listed in the exhibit below, and the service owners want to know why the two charts disagree and how to make the comparison dependable. Which explanation and follow-up action should the team take?

- Minute: 14:00; Virtual machine CPU (platform metrics): 61 %; Container CPU (Prometheus metrics in the workspace): 54 %
- Minute: 14:05; Virtual machine CPU (platform metrics): 63 %; Container CPU (Prometheus metrics in the workspace): 55 %
- Minute: 14:10; Virtual machine CPU (platform metrics): 60 %; Container CPU (Prometheus metrics in the workspace): 56 %
- Minute: 14:15; Virtual machine CPU (platform metrics): 62 %; Container CPU (Prometheus metrics in the workspace): 58 %
- Minute: 14:20; Virtual machine CPU (platform metrics): 62 %; Container CPU (Prometheus metrics in the workspace): 62 %
prompt: The two charts disagree because _____, and the team should [...].

options.text: Platform metrics are preaggregated, workspace metrics are kept as raw time series, and the two have different ingestion latency
Workspace metrics are preaggregated, platform metrics are kept as raw time series, and the two have different ingestion latency
Both series are kept as raw time series, and only the workspace series has an ingestion delay
Both series are preaggregated, and only the workspace series has an ingestion delay

explanation:
Platform metrics are preaggregated before they are stored, whereas metrics held in an Azure Monitor workspace, such as the Prometheus data scraped from the cluster, are kept as raw time series, and the two sources can also have different ingestion latency. That combination is why the value plotted for one minute can differ between the two charts, and it is why the gap in the exhibit narrows as the minutes pass. The difference disappears once the latency gap has settled and both series are examined at the same time granularity, which is exactly what the second slot asks the team to do.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Workspace metrics are preaggregated, platform metrics are kept as raw time series, and the two have different ingestion latency: This reverses how the two sources are stored. The series held in an Azure Monitor workspace are the ones kept as raw time series, while platform metrics are the ones that are preaggregated before they are stored, so the mismatch in the exhibit cannot be explained this way.
- Both series are kept as raw time series, and only the workspace series has an ingestion delay: This describes both series as raw, but platform metrics are preaggregated before storage, and the discrepancy comes from the combination of differing storage and differing latency rather than from a delay that affects only the workspace series.
- Both series are preaggregated, and only the workspace series has an ingestion delay: This describes both series as preaggregated, but the workspace series is stored as a raw time series, and the latency difference is a property of the two sources rather than a delay that applies only to the workspace series.

prompt: You have an Azure subscription that runs production virtual machines in the East US and West US regions. You need to protect those virtual machines with Azure Backup and run a scheduled audit in which the backup data is recovered from the paired region on demand, without waiting for a disaster to be declared. Which vault configuration should you create?

options.text: Create a separate vault in each protected region and enable Cross Region Restore with Geo-redundant storage
Create a single vault in one protected region and enable Cross Region Restore with Geo-redundant storage
Create a separate vault in each protected region and enable Cross Region Restore with Zone-redundant storage
Create a separate vault in each protected region and enable Cross Region Restore with Locally-redundant storage

explanation:
A vault's region must match the region of the data source it protects, so the East US and West US virtual machines require one vault per region, with the vault in the first location created before any other. Cross Region Restore is what makes the paired secondary region available for an on-demand restore during the audit, and that capability is offered only with Geo-redundant (GRS) replication, which is also the default replication type. Because replication settings are chosen before protection starts, this configuration should be settled before any virtual machine is added to a vault.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Create a single vault in one protected region and enable Cross Region Restore with Geo-redundant storage: One vault cannot cover sources in two different regions, because the vault's region must match the region of the data source it protects. With virtual machines in East US and West US, one vault per region is required, so a single vault in one region leaves the other batch unprotected.
- Create a separate vault in each protected region and enable Cross Region Restore with Zone-redundant storage: Zone-redundant storage keeps data available across availability zones within a region, but it does not provide the paired-region copy that Cross Region Restore depends on. The on-demand recovery in the paired region required by the audit is therefore not delivered by this configuration.
- Create a separate vault in each protected region and enable Cross Region Restore with Locally-redundant storage: Locally-redundant storage has no copy in the paired region and is intended for cases where Azure is not the primary backup storage endpoint and lower regional durability is accepted. Cross Region Restore is offered only with Geo-redundant replication, so this combination does not satisfy the audit requirement.

prompt: You have a Recovery Services vault that protects no items yet and an Azure Key Vault that already holds the RSA key you want the vault to use. You need the vault's backup data protected with that key, and you want to be able to revoke the vault's access to it later. You will also protect the virtual machines with Azure Backup once the key is in place. Which sequence of steps should you follow?

options.text: Enable the vault's managed identity, assign permissions so the vault can reach the key, enable soft delete and purge protection in the Key Vault, then assign the encryption key to the vault.
Assign the encryption key to the vault, then enable the vault's managed identity, assign permissions so the vault can reach the key, and enable soft delete and purge protection in the Key Vault.
Enable the vault's managed identity, assign the encryption key to the vault, then assign permissions so the vault can reach the key, and enable soft delete and purge protection in the Key Vault.

Enable the vault's managed identity, assign permissions so the vault can reach the key, and enable soft delete and purge protection in the Key Vault, but assign the encryption key to the vault only after the virtual machines are protected.

explanation:
The documented order for customer-managed key encryption is: enable the vault's managed identity, assign permissions so the vault can reach the key in Azure Key Vault, enable soft delete and purge protection in that Key Vault, and only then assign the encryption key to the vault. The exhibit shows that every prerequisite is still missing (managed identity disabled, no permission granted, Key Vault protections off) and that no items are protected, so the key can still be assigned; afterwards the key can be disabled or the vault's access to it revoked.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Assign the encryption key to the vault, then enable the vault's managed identity, assign permissions so the vault can reach the key, and enable soft delete and purge protection in the Key Vault: This assigns the encryption key first, which cannot work: the vault's managed identity is not enabled yet, it has no permissions to reach the key, and the Key Vault still lacks soft delete and purge protection. The identity, the permissions, and the Key Vault protections must all be in place before the key is assigned.
- Enable the vault's managed identity, assign the encryption key to the vault, then assign permissions so the vault can reach the key, and enable soft delete and purge protection in the Key Vault: This assigns the encryption key before the vault's managed identity has been granted permissions to reach it and before soft delete and purge protection are enabled in the Key Vault, which reverses the required order. Assigning the key is the final step, after the identity, the permissions, and the Key Vault protections.
- Enable the vault's managed identity, assign permissions so the vault can reach the key, and enable soft delete and purge protection in the Key Vault, but assign the encryption key to the vault only after the virtual machines are protected: Customer-managed key encryption cannot be enabled once items are protected, so postponing the key assignment until after the virtual machines are protected permanently rules out this configuration. The key has to be assigned while the vault still has no protected items.

prompt: You have a Recovery Services vault that protects several Azure virtual machines, and the storage cost of the backup data is now a concern. Leadership accepts that the backup data might not survive the loss of an entire Azure region, but the recovery points that are still inside their retention window must remain available for restore. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Stop protection with retained data on the current vault, restore the unexpired recovery points from it, and protect the virtual machines again in a new vault with locally redundant storage.
Disable soft delete on the current vault, then change the storage replication type to locally redundant in the Backup Configuration pane.
Delete the current protection and backup data from the geo-redundant vault, then protect the virtual machines again in a new locally redundant vault.
Stop protection with retained data on the current vault and change the storage replication type of that same vault to locally redundant, then restore the unexpired recovery points into it.

explanation:
Once a vault has backups configured, the portal no longer offers the choice to modify the storage replication type, so a geo-redundant vault cannot simply be switched to locally redundant in place. To keep the data, you stop protection on the existing vault with the data retained, which leaves the existing recovery points in that geo-redundant vault at ongoing cost, restore only the points that have not expired from it, and then protect the virtual machines again in a new vault that uses locally redundant storage, where the initial replica is created.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Disable soft delete on the current vault, then change the storage replication type to locally redundant in the Backup Configuration pane: The Backup Configuration pane stops offering a modify choice for the storage replication type after any backup has been configured, so the replication type of this vault cannot be edited in place. Turning soft delete off also belongs to the destructive conversion route, which permanently erases the protected server's backup data and backup items with no undo.
- Delete the current protection and backup data from the geo-redundant vault, then protect the virtual machines again in a new locally redundant vault: Deleting the current protection and backup data from the vault permanently discards the existing recovery points, so the points that are still inside the retention window could no longer be restored. That route is only appropriate when you are willing to discard the old data entirely.
- Stop protection with retained data on the current vault and change the storage replication type of that same vault to locally redundant, then restore the unexpired recovery points into it: Stopping protection with retained data is the correct starting point, but the storage replication type of the existing vault cannot be modified once backups are configured, and a virtual machine can be added to only one vault at a time. The locally redundant target therefore has to be a new vault that holds the restored points and the recreated protection.

One vault already exists and protects nothing yet, and the exhibit shows the current state. What should you do next?

options.text: Create a second vault in West US with Geo-redundant storage, enable Cross Region Restore in both vaults, and protect the virtual machines in each region with the vault in that region.
Enable Cross Region Restore in contoso-backup in East US and protect all three virtual machines with that single vault.
Create a second vault in West US with Geo-redundant storage, enable Cross Region Restore only in the new vault, and protect all three virtual machines with that new vault.
Create a second vault in West US with Locally-redundant storage, enable Cross Region Restore in both vaults, and protect the virtual machines in each region with the vault in that region.

explanation:
A vault must sit in the same region as the data source it protects, and when data sources span several regions you create one vault per region, creating the vault in the first location before any other. contoso-backup in East US already exists, so the West US vault is the second one to be created. The paired-region restore option is switched on at the vault level in Backup Configuration and is supported only for a vault that uses Geo-redundant storage, so the new vault must use Geo-redundant storage and the setting must be enabled in both vaults for the drill to reach the East US and the West US recovery points. Each region's virtual machines are then protected with the vault located in that same region.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enable Cross Region Restore in contoso-backup in East US and protect all three virtual machines with that single vault: web-vm-01 runs in West US, and a vault must be in the same region as the data source it protects, so the East US vault cannot hold the West US recovery points. When data sources are in several regions, you create one vault per region and create the vault in the first location before any other.
- Create a second vault in West US with Geo-redundant storage, enable Cross Region Restore only in the new vault, and protect all three virtual machines with that new vault: This breaks the rule that a vault must be in the same region as the data source it protects, since app-vm-01 and db-vm-01 are in East US and would be backed up by the West US vault. It also leaves the paired-region restore setting disabled in the vault that holds the East US recovery points, and that setting is switched on per vault, so each vault whose data must be recoverable from the paired region needs it enabled.
- Create a second vault in West US with Locally-redundant storage, enable Cross Region Restore in both vaults, and protect the virtual machines in each region with the vault in that region: The paired-region restore option is supported only for a vault that uses Geo-redundant storage. With Locally-redundant storage the backup data is held in the vault's own region, so it cannot be recovered from the paired region on demand. prompt: You have a Recovery Services vault in your production Microsoft Entra tenant that protects three Azure virtual machines. A ransomware attack has blocked every administrator sign-in in that tenant, and your company also controls a second Microsoft Entra tenant that has its own subscription and one new Recovery Services vault. You need the protected workloads running again in that second tenant, and you cannot wait for administrator access to be restored in the production tenant. What should you do?

options.text: Use the cross-tenant restore (preview) capability: create a mapping between the source vault and the vault in the second tenant, then restore the protected items from that vault.
Enable Cross Subscription Restore on the source vault and restore the backup data to a subscription of the second tenant.
Enable Cross Region Restore on the source vault and recover the backup data from the paired region, so the protected items can be restored in that region without waiting for a declared disaster.
Turn on Enhanced soft delete for the source vault so the deleted recovery points stay recoverable for a custom number of days and the setting cannot be switched off.

explanation:
The cross-tenant restore capability (currently in preview) is built for exactly this situation: it lets vaulted backup data be restored from a source tenant into a different tenant by mapping the vault that holds the data to a vault in the target tenant, and it is documented for tenant lockout and ransomware scenarios. Because the backup data itself is kept in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant, the protected items can be surfaced through the mapping and restored from the vault in the second tenant, even though no administrator can sign in to the production tenant. The other three approaches all remain inside the compromised tenant and therefore cannot deliver the workload into the tenant you control.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enable Cross Subscription Restore on the source vault and restore the backup data to a subscription of the second tenant: Cross Subscription Restore only restores into a different subscription within the same tenant as the source, so it cannot place the protected data in a second tenant. It is also enabled on the Properties pane of the source vault, which nobody can administer while every administrator sign-in is blocked.
- Enable Cross Region Restore on the source vault and recover the backup data from the paired region, so the protected items can be restored in that region without waiting for a declared disaster: Cross Region Restore recovers the replicated copy that sits in the Azure paired region, and that paired region belongs to the same tenant as the source vault. It is intended for drills, audit and regional outage scenarios rather than for moving protected data into a different tenant, and enabling the toggle on the Backup Configuration pane also requires access to the source vault.
- Turn on Enhanced soft delete for the source vault so the deleted recovery points stay recoverable for a custom number of days and the setting cannot be switched off: Enhanced soft delete keeps deleted recovery points recoverable for a customized number of days and makes the setting always-on so it cannot be disabled, but it only protects data that stays in the vault. It neither relocates backup data into another tenant nor restores access to the locked-out tenant.

One of the virtual machines has no recovery points at all, and you need it covered by Azure Backup while the recovery points you already hold stay available for restore. What should you do?

options.text: Create a second Recovery Services vault in the West Europe region and back up the West Europe virtual machines to that second vault.
Enable Cross Region Restore in the existing East US vault and back up the West Europe virtual machines to that vault.
Add the West Europe virtual machines to the existing East US vault so that one vault holds every recovery point.
Create a second Recovery Services vault in the East US region and back up the West Europe virtual machines to the existing East US vault.

explanation:
A vault only protects data sources that sit in the same region as the vault itself, and when workloads are spread across several regions you run one vault per region. The unprotected West Europe virtual machine therefore needs its own vault built in West Europe, while the existing East US vault continues to serve the East US virtual machines and keeps the recovery points that are already in it. Nothing has to be moved, deleted, or re-pointed.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enable Cross Region Restore in the existing East US vault and back up the West Europe virtual machines to that vault: Cross Region Restore is a restore capability of a geo-redundant vault: it lets you recover replicated data in the paired region on demand. It does not change which vault is allowed to hold the recovery points of a given workload, so switching it on does not let an East US vault protect a West Europe virtual machine.
- Add the West Europe virtual machines to the existing East US vault so that one vault holds every recovery point: Adding the West Europe virtual machines to the East US vault conflicts with the rule that a vault protects workloads located in its own region, so this configuration is not supported even though it would consolidate the backup policies in one place.
- Create a second Recovery Services vault in the East US region and back up the West Europe virtual machines to the existing East US vault: The region is the problem here, so creating another vault in East US repeats the mismatch, and pointing the West Europe virtual machines at the existing East US vault is not a valid arrangement. The vault that holds those recovery points has to be created in the region where the workloads run.

prompt: You have a Recovery Services vault in the West Europe region that protects three Azure virtual machines under a 90-day backup policy. During a review you found that a recovery point was removed inside its retention window by a person who holds owner rights on the vault. You need recovery points to stay in place for the whole retention window so that they cannot be removed at all, and you need that control to be impossible for a malicious insider to switch off. Which setting should you configure on the vault?

options.text: Enable immutability on the vault
Enable Enhanced soft delete on the vault
Enable Cross Region Restore on the vault
Enable Cross Subscription Restore on the vault

explanation:
The scenario needs a control that keeps recovery points from being deleted before their backup-policy expiry and that cannot be disabled by a malicious actor. Azure Backup immutable vaults do exactly this: once recovery points are created they cannot be deleted before their expiry according to the backup policy, and the immutability can be made irreversible to protect the backup data from threats such as ransomware and malicious actors. Applying that control on this vault addresses both the deletion found in the review and the requirement that the control itself be impossible to switch off.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enable Enhanced soft delete on the vault: Enhanced soft delete lets you customize the soft delete retention period and makes soft delete always-on so it cannot be disabled by a malicious actor, but it still allows a backup to be deleted and only keeps the deleted data recoverable for the chosen period. It therefore does not stop a recovery point from being removed inside its 90-day retention window, so it does not satisfy the requirement that recovery points stay in place and cannot be removed at all.
- Enable Cross Region Restore on the vault: Cross Region Restore is already enabled on this vault, and it is used to recover data from the Azure paired region on demand for audit, compliance, or outage scenarios. It changes where data can be restored from; it has no effect on whether a recovery point can be deleted or on the retention window of the protected items, so it cannot prevent the deletion seen in the review.
- Enable Cross Subscription Restore on the vault: Cross Subscription Restore is configured under Properties and allows data to be restored from the vault into a different subscription within the same tenant. It changes the destination of a restore rather than the ability to delete a recovery point, so it does nothing to protect recovery points from being removed inside their retention window.

prompt: You have a Recovery Services vault in your production Microsoft Entra tenant that protects six Azure virtual machines with Azure Backup. A subscription consolidation is planned, and the business wants those protected workloads to be available in a second subscription of the same tenant. You need the recovery points to stay usable so the virtual machines can be brought back there. Which change should you make to the vault?

options.text: Turn on Cross Region Restore in the vault's Backup Configuration and restore the protected virtual machines into the paired Azure region of the current subscription.
Turn on Cross-tenant restore (preview) for the source vault and map it to the Recovery Services vault in the other Microsoft Entra tenant.
Create a storage account in the second subscription of the same tenant and point the vault at it, so that the backup data for the protected virtual machines is written there.
Turn on Enable Cross Subscription Restore in the vault's Properties and select Update, then restore the protected virtual machines into the second subscription of the same Microsoft Entra tenant.

explanation:
Cross Subscription Restore is switched on from the vault's Settings > Properties pane, where you choose Update and then select Enable Cross Subscription Restore > Update. Once it is on, a recovery point can be restored into a subscription other than the one that holds the source vault, as long as the target subscription belongs to the same Microsoft Entra tenant. That matches this consolidation: prod-backup-vault keeps protecting the six virtual machines in sub-prod-001, while their data can be recovered into sub-dev-002, and no mapping across tenants is needed. The feature currently covers Azure VMs, SQL Server running in Azure VMs, SAP ASE and SAP HANA hosted in Azure VMs, and Azure Files, so the protected virtual machines are within scope.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Turn on Cross Region Restore in the vault's Backup Configuration and restore the protected virtual machines into the paired Azure region of the current subscription: Cross Region Restore pulls the replicated copy held in the Azure paired secondary region, so it recovers the workload into the paired region of the current subscription rather than into the second subscription of the same tenant. It also works only with Geo-redundant replication, and the exhibit shows that replication type is already in place with the toggle already on, so this setting is not what is missing.
- Turn on Cross-tenant restore (preview) for the source vault and map it to the Recovery Services vault in the other Microsoft Entra tenant: Cross-tenant restore (preview) maps the source vault to a target vault so that data can be restored into a different Microsoft Entra tenant, and it is aimed at situations such as tenant lockout or a ransomware attack. Here both subscriptions belong to contoso.onmicrosoft.com, so a mapping across tenants does not address the requirement.
- Create a storage account in the second subscription of the same tenant and point the vault at it, so that the backup data for the protected virtual machines is written there: Azure Backup provisions and manages the vault's backup storage itself, so you do not create or specify a storage account for backup data, and the data itself is kept in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant that guests and external users cannot reach directly. A customer-owned storage account cannot be used to make the protected workloads recoverable in the second subscription.

context:
You have a Recovery Services vault that uses Geo-redundant storage and that you switched on Cross Region Restore for this morning; you then protected two virtual machines with Azure Backup. You need the audit team to run a recovery drill in which both virtual machines are recovered from the paired region, and you want the copy that comes back to be as current as the service allows. Which wait time and policy should you plan for?

- Property: Storage replication type; Value: Geo-redundant
- Property: Cross Region Restore; Value: Enabled today
- Property: Items protected since it was enabled; Value: Two Azure virtual machines
- Property: Audit drill request; Value: Recover both virtual machines from the paired region
prompt: The drill team must allow _____ before the newly protected items can be used in the secondary region, and the vault's [...] should be configured so that the secondary copy is as current as the service allows.

options.text: up to 48 hours
up to 36 hours
up to 24 hours
up to 12 hours

explanation:
After Cross Region Restore is switched on, it can take up to 48 hours for the backup items to become available in the secondary region, so the drill must be planned with that wait. For Azure VM backups the secondary region recovery point objective can be up to 36 hours in the worst case; the Standard policy holds the primary region RPO to up to 24 hours and replication to the secondary region to up to 12 hours, while the Enhanced policy improves the best-case achievable secondary region RPO through more frequent local recovery point creation, with the worst case still at 36 hours. Because the audit team wants the freshest copy the service can deliver, the Enhanced policy is the right choice.

Why the other options are wrong:
- up to 36 hours: 36 hours is the worst-case amount by which the secondary region can trail the primary region for Azure VM backups; it is not how long newly protected items need before they can be used in the secondary region.
- up to 24 hours: 24 hours is the maximum primary region recovery point objective that the Standard policy provides; it does not describe the delay before backup items become usable in the secondary region.
- up to 12 hours: 12 hours is the longest replication interval to the secondary region allowed by the Standard policy; it is not the readiness delay for backup items in the secondary region.

context:
You use Azure Backup to protect a group of production virtual machines, and you are finalizing the Recovery Services vault that holds their recovery points. The exhibit lists the protected workload and the outcomes your team needs. Complete the configuration plan.

- Item: Protected workload; Detail: 20 Windows and Linux virtual machines running in the East US region
- Item: Paired-area drill; Detail: The audit team must recover the protected data from the Azure paired area on demand, without waiting for a disaster to be declared
- Item: Advisor follow-up; Detail: Some of the virtual machines are reported as having no protection, and you want to switch protection on directly from the recommendation
- Item: Storage replication today; Detail: Locally-redundant
prompt: Set the vault's storage replication to _____ so that the drill can run on demand, and, when acting on the Advisor recommendation, supply [...].

options.text: Geo-redundant
Locally-redundant
Zone-redundant

explanation:
Geo-redundant storage is the default replication type for a new vault and the only one that keeps a replicated copy in the Azure paired area, so it is the choice that allows recovery from the paired area on demand; the Cross Region Restore toggle in Backup Configuration works only with Geo-redundant, and it should be settled before any item is protected because the portal then stops offering the change. When you act on an Advisor recommendation for an unprotected virtual machine, you enable backup inline by naming the vault plus the backup policy that defines the schedule and retention; Azure Backup provisions and manages the vault's storage, so no storage account is part of that flow.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Locally-redundant: Locally-redundant keeps the recovery points in their own area only, so there is no copy in the Azure paired area to restore from and the on-demand drill cannot be served with it.
- Zone-redundant: Zone-redundant spreads the recovery points across availability zones inside one area, which helps availability and data residency, but it places no copy in the Azure paired area, so the drill cannot be run on demand from it.

context:
Your company stores the backup data of its production virtual machines in the vault described in the exhibit. The compliance team wants to run a drill in which that data is restored from the Azure region paired with the vault's own region, on demand, without waiting for Microsoft to declare a disaster. When you open the vault's Backup Configuration pane, the setting that allows such a restore is not listed, even though your account can reach the paired region. What should you do first?

`Recovery vault summary - contoso-prod-backup

  Location             : East US
  Storage replication  : Geo-redundant (GRS)
  Cross Region Restore : toggle not listed on the Backup Configuration pane
  Protected items      : 2 virtual machines
`
prompt: In the subscription's Resource provider pane, you should select _____ and then choose Re-register.

options.text: Microsoft.RecoveryServices
Microsoft.Storage
Microsoft.Compute
Microsoft.ManagedIdentity

explanation:
The exhibit shows that the vault already stores its backup data with Geo-redundant (GRS) storage, which is the replication type that supports restoring from the paired region, so the missing entry is not caused by the storage setting. When the paired-region restore setting is absent from the Backup Configuration pane even though the account can reach the paired region, the remedy is to re-register the resource provider that manages backup vaults, Microsoft.RecoveryServices, from the subscription's Resource provider pane; the setting then becomes available on the vault.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Microsoft.Storage: Microsoft.Storage registers the storage services used for disks and file shares. Re-registering it refreshes that provider only and does not restore the backup configuration entries that the vault's Backup Configuration pane is missing, so the paired-region restore option would still not be listed.
- Microsoft.Compute: Microsoft.Compute registers virtual machines and the compute resources built on them. Re-registering it has no effect on which settings a backup vault displays on its Backup Configuration pane.
- Microsoft.ManagedIdentity: Microsoft.ManagedIdentity is used for the identities that a vault relies on when it reaches keys and other resources. Re-registering it does not make the missing paired-region restore setting appear on the vault.

context:
You have an Azure subscription that hosts the virtual machines of a payments platform in the North Europe region. The platform runs in Germany, and German records law requires that every copy of the protected data stays inside Germany. The platform team also wants the recovery points to remain reachable if part of that region becomes unavailable. You are creating a Recovery Services vault for these machines and you have reached the Backup Configuration step of the creation flow. Which storage replication type should you select, and where does Azure Backup keep the protected data?

- Item: Protected workload; Value: Payments platform virtual machines
- Item: Region of the protected workload; Value: North Europe
- Item: Country the workload operates in; Value: Germany
- Item: Constraint on copies of the protected data; Value: Every copy must stay inside Germany
- Item: Availability goal for the recovery points; Value: Remain reachable if part of the region is unavailable
prompt: You should select _____ for this vault, and Azure Backup keeps the protected data [...].

options.text: Geo-redundant (GRS)
Locally-redundant (LRS)
Zone-redundant (ZRS)

explanation:
Zone-redundant (ZRS) spreads the copies of the protected data across the parts of the North Europe region, so every copy stays inside Germany and the recovery points remain reachable if part of that region becomes unavailable, which satisfies both the records law and the availability goal. Geo-redundant storage would place a copy in the region paired with North Europe, which lies outside Germany, and locally-redundant storage keeps the copies in one region only. Independently of the replication choice, Azure Backup provisions and manages the vault's storage for you and holds the backup data in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant, so no storage account is created or administered by your team and external users have no direct access to the data.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Geo-redundant (GRS): Geo-redundant storage keeps a second copy in the region paired with North Europe, and that paired region is outside Germany, so the copies would breach the requirement that every copy of the protected data stays inside the country.
- Locally-redundant (LRS): Locally-redundant storage keeps the copies in a single region, so a partial failure of that region could make the recovery points unavailable, which does not meet the stated availability goal.

context:
Your company uses Azure Backup to protect three production virtual machines and one Azure file share, and you are creating a new Recovery Services vault to hold their recovery points. The copies of the virtual machines are the company's only off-premises copy of the production data, and the business wants a copy of that data to exist in a second Azure region so a region-level incident leaves the copies intact. The vault is empty at the moment, so you can still pick its storage settings on the Backup Configuration pane. The exhibit lists the workloads that will be protected.

- Item: corp-prod-vault; Type: Recovery Services vault; Region: North Europe; Current state: To be created; nothing protected yet
- Item: app-prod-01; Type: Virtual machine; Region: North Europe; Current state: Planned for Azure Backup
- Item: app-prod-02; Type: Virtual machine; Region: North Europe; Current state: Planned for Azure Backup
- Item: design-share; Type: Azure file share; Region: North Europe; Current state: Planned for Azure Backup
prompt: The backup snapshots for the Azure file share are stored _____, and the vault's storage replication type is set to [...].

options.text: in the file share's own storage account, where the vault's redundancy setting has no effect
in the storage that Azure Backup provisions for the vault, where the vault's redundancy setting applies
in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant, where the vault's redundancy setting applies
in the file share's own storage account, where the vault's redundancy setting applies

explanation:
Both choices follow from how a new Recovery Services vault handles storage. For an Azure file share, Azure Backup takes snapshots that are kept in the same storage account as the backed-up file share, so the vault's storage replication setting is irrelevant for those snapshots; the copies of the protected virtual machines are the ones held in the storage that Azure Backup provisions and manages for the vault. Because Azure Backup holds the company's primary copy of the production data and the business wants that data to exist in a second Azure region, the vault's storage replication type should be the Geo-redundant (GRS) option, which is the default and keeps a replicated copy in the Azure paired region.

Why the other options are wrong:
- in the storage that Azure Backup provisions for the vault, where the vault's redundancy setting applies: This describes where the copies of the protected virtual machines are kept: Azure Backup provisions and manages the vault's storage automatically, and the vault's replication setting governs that copy. File share snapshots are the exception, because they are kept in the file share's own storage account.
- in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant, where the vault's redundancy setting applies: The backup data of protected virtual machines is held in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant that external users and guests cannot reach directly, but file share snapshots are not stored there; they stay in the storage account of the file share itself.
- in the file share's own storage account, where the vault's redundancy setting applies: The location is right, yet the vault's replication setting does not govern those snapshots. Because the snapshots live in the file share's own storage account, the vault's storage replication choice has no effect on them.

Azure Advisor is reporting virtual machines in your subscription that have never been put under protection, and the platform team wants to act on those findings from the Advisor screen itself instead of opening each machine one by one. The exhibit shows the machines that are in scope. Which behavior does the Advisor recommendation for those machines support?

- Virtual machine: web-01; Region: West Europe; Protection state: Protected by Azure Backup; Advisor finding: None
- Virtual machine: api-02; Region: West Europe; Protection state: No protection configured; Advisor finding: Raised
- Virtual machine: sql-03; Region: West Europe; Protection state: No protection configured; Advisor finding: Raised
- Virtual machine: api-04; Region: West Europe; Protection state: No protection configured; Advisor finding: Raised
prompt: Azure Advisor refreshes its findings for the virtual machines that have no backup _____, and its recommendation for each of those machines lets you {{advisor-action}}.

options.text: Every hour
Every day
Every week
Only when a virtual machine is created

explanation:
Azure Advisor analyzes your Azure usage and raises recommendations for virtual machines that have no backup, and it refreshes those recommendations hourly so newly deployed machines are flagged close to the time they appear. You can control those findings by snoozing the recommendation, and you can turn protection on for the machine directly from the recommendation by specifying the vault that will store the backups together with the backup policy that defines the schedule of backups and the retention of the backup copies. Therefore the supported behavior is an hourly refresh plus snoozing, with the inline action naming the vault and the backup policy.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Every day: The findings for unprotected virtual machines are refreshed every hour rather than once a day, so a machine deployed this morning is flagged without a day of delay.
- Every week: The recommendations are refreshed every hour rather than weekly; the interval is short so that unprotected virtual machines do not go unnoticed for days.
- Only when a virtual machine is created: The recommendations are a recurring hourly check on which virtual machines lack a backup. They are not a one-time event raised only at the moment a virtual machine is created.

- Property: Vault name; Value: rs-vault-prod-we
- Property: Location; Value: West Europe
- Property: Items protected today; Value: None
- Property: Workloads to be protected; Value: 3 Linux virtual machines and 1 SQL Server in an Azure VM

- Property: Retention for the protected data points; Value: 30 days
prompt: The audit team must be able to pull a copy of the protected data out of the Azure location paired with the vault's own location at any time, without waiting for Microsoft to declare a disaster.

options.text: Cross Region Restore
Soft delete
Enhanced soft delete
Immutability
Customer-managed key
Geo-redundant storage
Cross Subscription Restore
Cross-tenant restore (preview)

explanation: Each outcome maps to exactly one vault capability. The on-demand copy of the protected data from the Azure location paired with the vault's location is Cross Region Restore, which is switched on at vault level so you can recover the replicated data whenever you choose, for audit, compliance or a regional outage. The free safety net of roughly two weeks after data loss is Soft delete, which is enabled by default on new vaults and keeps any removed backup recoverable for 14 extra days at no charge. The business-chosen number of days plus the permanently-on, cannot-be-switched-off behaviour is Enhanced soft delete. The block on removing data points before their retention date, which can be made irreversible, is Immutability. Supplying your own encryption material and being able to cut off the vault's access to it later is the Customer-managed key option, where an RSA key from an Azure Key Vault protects the data through an AES 256-based DEK and the key can be disabled or revoked after assignment. Geo-redundant storage, Cross Subscription Restore and Cross-tenant restore (preview) satisfy none of the listed outcomes.

options.text: Cross Region Restore
Soft delete
Enhanced soft delete
Immutability
Customer-managed key
Geo-redundant storage
Cross Subscription Restore

explanation: Each outcome maps to exactly one vault capability. The on-demand copy of the protected data from the Azure location paired with the vault's location is Cross Region Restore, which is switched on at vault level so you can recover the replicated data whenever you choose, for audit, compliance or a regional outage. The free safety net of roughly two weeks after data loss is Soft delete, which is enabled by default on new vaults and keeps any removed backup recoverable for 14 extra days at no charge. The business-chosen number of days plus the permanently-on, cannot-be-switched-off behaviour is Enhanced soft delete. The block on removing data points before their retention date, which can be made irreversible, is Immutability. Supplying your own encryption material and being able to cut off the vault's access to it later is the Customer-managed key option, where an RSA key from an Azure Key Vault protects the data through an AES 256-based DEK and the key can be disabled or revoked after assignment. Geo-redundant storage, Cross Subscription Restore and Cross-tenant restore (preview) satisfy none of the listed outcomes.
