prompt: You have a single Azure VM named vm-orders01 that is protected by Azure Site Recovery, as shown in the exhibit. The East US region is entering a maintenance window, so you are moving the order-entry workload to the secondary region. You need the workload to resume in East US 2 without losing order transactions that have already been written to the replication cache, and the team accepts the extra minutes that this adds to the cutover. Which recovery point option should you select in the Failover pane?

options.text: Latest
Latest processed
Latest app-consistent
Custom

explanation:
Selecting Latest makes Site Recovery take all of the data it has received, including the writes still sitting in the cache storage account in the source region, and build a recovery point from it for the VM before the failover starts. Because every order transaction already sent to Site Recovery is captured, this is the choice that meets the requirement to avoid losing the transactions that are still in the cache, and it gives the lowest recovery point objective. The trade-off is that this extra work lengthens the cutover, which the team has explicitly accepted.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Latest processed: Selecting Latest processed uses the newest recovery point that Site Recovery has already produced, so no time is spent on the outstanding data and the recovery time objective is low. The 11 minutes of order transactions still in the cache are not part of that recovery point, so this choice would lose them and does not meet the requirement.
- Latest app-consistent: Selecting Latest app-consistent restores from an existing application-consistent recovery point, which is built from a snapshot taken at a particular moment. Writes still sitting in the cache were never captured in that snapshot, so the pending order transactions would be missing, and with app-consistent snapshots taken every 2 hours the point can also be close to two hours old.
- Custom: Selecting Custom lets you pick one of the recovery points that already exist, such as an application-consistent point or an older crash-consistent point. Those points do not contain the writes that are still in the cache, so picking one would lose the pending order transactions even though this option is available for a single-VM failover with no recovery plan.

prompt: You have an invoicing VM named vm-invoices05 that is protected by Azure Site Recovery and replicates from West Europe to East US 2. A regional outage in West Europe forced you to fail the VM over, and the workload is now running in East US 2. The exhibit shows the current protection state of that VM. The outage in West Europe has been resolved, and you want the workload running in West Europe again. Which action should you take next?

options.text: Select Re-Protect on the source VM in West Europe, then fail back to East US 2 once the reverse replication completes.
Select Re-Protect on the failed-over VM in East US 2, then fail back to West Europe once the reverse replication completes.
Select Commit on the failed-over VM in East US 2, then fail back to West Europe.
Select Change recovery point on the VM Essentials page in East US 2, then fail back to West Europe.

explanation:
The exhibit shows the failover to East US 2 is already committed, the primary region (West Europe) is available again, and you can create VMs there, but replication from East US 2 back to West Europe has not started. The way to return the workload is to start Re-Protect from the Overview page of the failed-over VM in East US 2: that begins reverse replication (secondary to primary), sending the initial data and then the deltas back to West Europe. Once that replication is running, you can fail back so the workload runs in its original region again.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Select Re-Protect on the source VM in West Europe, then fail back to East US 2 once the reverse replication completes: Re-Protect is started from the Overview page of the VM that is currently running in the secondary region, because that is the machine whose data has to be sent back to the primary region. Starting it from the source VM in West Europe would not send the East US 2 data back, and failing back to East US 2 would move the workload away from West Europe, which is the opposite of the goal.
- Select Commit on the failed-over VM in East US 2, then fail back to West Europe: Commit only finishes a failover: it deletes the recovery points that Site Recovery holds for that VM and does not start any replication toward the primary region. The exhibit shows the failover is already committed, so doing this again would only discard the remaining recovery points and the workload would stay in East US 2.
- Select Change recovery point on the VM Essentials page in East US 2, then fail back to West Europe: Change recovery point, on the Essentials page, only lets you pick a different recovery point for a VM that has already been failed over. It does not start replication toward West Europe and does not move the workload, so the VM would keep running in East US 2.

`Replication policy - vm-payroll01

Primary region:                      East US
Secondary region:                    West Europe
Recovery point retention:            24 hours
App-consistent snapshot frequency:   0 hours
Crash-consistent snapshot frequency: Every 5 minutes (fixed interval)`
prompt: You have a payroll VM named vm-payroll01 that is protected by Azure Site Recovery, as shown in the exhibit. When the workload is moved to the secondary region, the payroll database must never come back with a half-written transaction, so the recovery point used at failover has to include the data that was still held in memory together with the transactions that were in flight when that point was taken. Right now the only points you can pick at failover are the ones the service produces on its own every five minutes. You want a point that satisfies that requirement to be available the next time you fail this VM over. Which change should you make to the replication policy?

options.text: Increase the recovery point retention window and leave the app-consistent snapshot frequency unchanged.
Set the app-consistent snapshot frequency to a value that stays below the recovery point retention window.
Set the app-consistent snapshot frequency to a value that exceeds the recovery point retention window.
Reduce the recovery point retention window and leave the app-consistent snapshot frequency unchanged.

explanation:
The exhibit shows the app-consistent snapshot frequency at 0 hours, which means those snapshots are switched off, so the only points available for failover are the automatically produced crash-consistent ones that capture just what was on disk. Turning this frequency on requires setting it to a value that stays below the recovery point retention window, so the points built from those snapshots (in-memory data and in-flight transactions included) remain inside the 24-hour period for which recovery points are kept.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Increase the recovery point retention window and leave the app-consistent snapshot frequency unchanged: Lengthening the retention window only extends how long the points that already exist are kept. With the app-consistent snapshot frequency still at 0 hours, those snapshots stay disabled and no point that includes in-memory data and in-flight transactions is produced for the failover.
- Set the app-consistent snapshot frequency to a value that exceeds the recovery point retention window: A frequency set above the recovery point retention window is not a supported configuration: the app-consistent snapshot frequency must be set under the retention period, otherwise the points created would fall outside the window in which recovery points are kept.
- Reduce the recovery point retention window and leave the app-consistent snapshot frequency unchanged: Shortening the retention window reduces how long recovery points are kept, and with the app-consistent snapshot frequency still at 0 hours no app-consistent snapshots are taken at all, so the required point still would not exist at failover time.

You already moved the workload into the secondary region and it is serving traffic there, but the cutover has not been finalized. The application team reports that several transactions written shortly before the cutover are missing, and they want the workload brought up from a different point before anything is made permanent. Which action should you take?

options.text: Use Change recovery point on the vm-pay03 Essentials page in Central US to restart vm-pay03 from the point in time selected by the administrator.
Use Re-Protect on the vm-pay03 Overview page in Central US so you can start replication back to East US.
Run a test failover for vm-pay03 from East US and review the test instance it creates in Central US.
Raise the recovery point retention for vm-pay03 to 30 days in the replication policy, then re-enable replication from East US to Central US.

explanation:
The failover of vm-pay03 is still pending commit, so the recovery points that Site Recovery holds for the VM are still intact and the workload can be brought up from a different one. On the VM's Essentials page in the target region, Change recovery point lets you pick the point in time to restart from. Committing the failover first would delete those points permanently, so this must be done before the move is finalized.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Use Re-Protect on the vm-pay03 Overview page in Central US so you can start replication back to East US: Re-Protect sets up reverse replication from the secondary region back to the primary so the workload can be moved home later. It does not restart the already failed-over instance from a different point in time, and it only becomes available once the failover has been committed, which this VM has not been.
- Run a test failover for vm-pay03 from East US and review the test instance it creates in Central US: A test failover is a drill used to confirm that the replication setup works before an outage; it creates a separate test instance and leaves the live workload alone. It is not a way to bring the already failed-over VM up from a different point in time.
- Raise the recovery point retention for vm-pay03 to 30 days in the replication policy, then re-enable replication from East US to Central US: Recovery point retention controls how long the points that Site Recovery generates are kept. Raising it in the replication policy does not alter which point the running instance is using, and re-enabling replication from the primary is not what restores the workload from a chosen point.

prompt: You have a three-VM web tier that Azure Site Recovery protects, with the configuration shown in the exhibit. Before the scheduled maintenance window in East US, the business wants documented proof that this same tier can be brought up in East US 2. The live workload in East US must keep serving customer traffic throughout that proof. Which action should you take?

options.text: Run a test failover of the protected workload
Run a real failover of the protected workload to East US 2
Run a recovery plan failover of the protected workload to East US 2
Re-Protect the protected workload from East US 2 back to East US

explanation:
The requirement is to prove the replicated configuration works in the secondary region before the outage while the production VMs in East US remain live, which is exactly what a disaster recovery drill (test failover) is for: it verifies that everything works as expected without impacting the production environment. The exhibit also shows the workload is protected and healthy and that the target region has enough quota, so the validation can be carried out before the 12-day outage.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Run a real failover of the protected workload to East US 2: A real Failover is the action taken for an actual outage: it moves the production workload into the secondary region and the source location stops serving. That contradicts the requirement that the East US workload keep serving customer traffic while the proof is produced, and it leaves no opportunity to validate first.
- Run a recovery plan failover of the protected workload to East US 2: A recovery plan orchestrates the failover of the grouped VMs, but this is still the real failover of the production workload into East US 2, which is the action reserved for the outage itself. The plan is not what keeps production untouched while the setup is validated; the drill is.
- Re-Protect the protected workload from East US 2 back to East US: Re-Protect starts reverse replication from the secondary region back to the primary and is used after the workload has already been failed over into East US 2, where its status is Failover committed. It cannot be used to validate a setup whose VMs are still running only in East US.

`Virtual machine            : vm-billing01
Source region              : East US
Target region              : East US 2
Protection status          : Protected
Target availability type   : Single instance
Target resource group      : rg-billing-asr

prompt: You have a billing virtual machine named vm-billing01 that Azure Site Recovery protects, with the configuration shown in the exhibit. The business has decided that the copy of the VM that runs in East US 2 must be spread across three availability zones instead of running as a single instance. Which sequence of actions should you perform to make that change effective?

options.text: Disable replication for the VM, change the target availability type, then enable replication again
Change the target availability type in the protected VM's target settings, then keep replication running so the new value is used at the next failover
Run a test failover to East US 2, then choose the availability type for the instance the test creates
Complete the failover to East US 2, re-protect the VM there, then change the target availability type so it applies when you fail back

explanation:
The availability type of a protected VM is the one target setting that cannot be edited while replication is running. The only supported route is to take replication down for that VM, edit the target availability type (single instance, availability set or zone), and then bring replication back up, which recreates the target resources with the new type so a later failover spreads the VM across three availability zones in East US 2.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Change the target availability type in the protected VM's target settings, then keep replication running so the new value is used at the next failover: While replication is running you can freely change settings such as the target resource group, the target name and the SKU, but the availability type is excluded from that. Editing it with replication still running has no effect, and the existing single instance target remains in force.
- Run a test failover to East US 2, then choose the availability type for the instance the test creates: A test failover is useful for proving that the current configuration can start the workload in the secondary region, but it does not rewrite the target settings stored for the protected VM, so a real failover would still use the single instance target.
- Complete the failover to East US 2, re-protect the VM there, then change the target availability type so it applies when you fail back: Re-Protect followed by a fail back is how a workload that has already failed over is returned to the primary region; it does not alter the target availability type of the protected VM, which has to be edited while replication is down.

prompt: You have a Linux virtual machine named vm-orders02 that is covered by Azure Site Recovery, with the state shown in the exhibit. A regional outage is forcing the order-entry workload to move from East US to the secondary region, East US 2. The source machine is still powered on and serving customer traffic, and the operations team wants the service to attempt an orderly stop of that source machine first, so that the amount of data written shortly prior to the cutover is as small as possible. If the orderly stop cannot be completed, the move to the secondary region must still go ahead. Which action should you take to meet this requirement?

options.text: Shut down machine before beginning failover
Re-Protect the machine in the secondary region
Change the recovery point on the machine's Essentials page
Commit the failover for the machine

explanation:
Select "Shut down machine before beginning failover". This option tells Site Recovery to try to shut the source VM down first, which reduces the amount of data that can be lost during the cutover, and the failover continues even if that shutdown attempt fails — which matches the requirement that the move must go ahead regardless. The other choices govern different parts of the recovery lifecycle and do not affect how the source machine is handled while the cutover is being prepared.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Re-Protect the machine in the secondary region: Re-Protect on the VM Overview page starts reverse replication from the secondary region back to the primary region (sending the initial data and then deltas) so the workload is protected again once the primary region is healthy. It neither stops the source VM nor reduces the data lost at the cutover, so it does not meet the stated requirement.
- Change the recovery point on the machine's Essentials page: Change recovery point on the VM Essentials page is used after a failover has already happened, to bring the failed-over VM up from a different recovery point. It has no effect on how the source machine is handled during the failover itself.
- Commit the failover for the machine: Commit finalizes the failover: it deletes all available recovery points for that VM in Site Recovery, so the recovery point can no longer be changed. It does not attempt to stop the source machine, and it should only be used once the failed-over VM is confirmed to be running correctly.

prompt: You have a stateless web front-end virtual machine named vm-web02 that Azure Site Recovery protects, with the configuration and state shown in the exhibit. The workload was moved to East US 2 during a regional outage in East US and has been serving customer traffic from there since. The business has confirmed that the workload behaves correctly in East US 2 and wants the protection arrangement for that VM settled in the secondary region, because the monthly charges for keeping the recovery points of vm-web02 in the recovery service are no longer acceptable, and the outage in East US is still under investigation. Which action should you take?

options.text: Select Commit for vm-web02; this finalizes the failover and deletes the recovery points that Site Recovery holds for the VM.
Select Re-Protect for vm-web02 so that Site Recovery replicates changes made in East US 2 back to the primary region.
Select Change recovery point on the vm-web02 Essentials page so that Site Recovery restarts the VM from one of the other recovery points.
Select Test failover for vm-web02 so that Site Recovery validates the arrangement without affecting the live workload.

explanation:
Committing the failover is the action that finalizes the move to the secondary region: it deletes the recovery points that Site Recovery holds for the VM, which is exactly what the business is asking for, because those stored states and their associated storage cost are no longer acceptable. The failed-over VM has already been confirmed running and serving traffic in East US 2, so it is safe to commit now rather than earlier. The other actions do not remove the recovery points, and reverse replication cannot be started while the primary region is unavailable.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Select Re-Protect for vm-web02 so that Site Recovery replicates changes made in East US 2 back to the primary region: Re-Protect starts reverse replication from the secondary region back to the primary so that new changes are replicated again; it does not delete the recovery points. It also requires the primary region to be available, and East US is currently unavailable because of the ongoing regional outage, so it cannot be used in this situation.
- Select Change recovery point on the vm-web02 Essentials page so that Site Recovery restarts the VM from one of the other recovery points: Change recovery point restarts the failed-over VM from a different recovery point; it keeps the stored recovery points in place rather than removing them. Once the failover is committed, the recovery point of the VM can no longer be changed either.
- Select Test failover for vm-web02 so that Site Recovery validates the arrangement without affecting the live workload: Test failover is a disaster recovery drill that proves the setup works without touching production; it neither finalizes the failover nor removes the recovery points that are being held for the VM.

You have a virtual machine named vm-orders05 that Azure Site Recovery covers between East US and East US 2, and the exhibit lists what the readiness review recorded for it. A regional outage in East US forces the order-entry workload to move to the secondary region, and the business wants customer traffic restored as quickly as possible once the cutover happens, even though the last few seconds of orders written just before the outage may not be present afterwards. After the workload is running in East US 2, the operations team also wants to confirm that the copies of the source disks were set up correctly in the secondary region.

- Property: Virtual machine; Value: vm-orders05
- Property: Source region; Value: East US
- Property: Target region; Value: East US 2
- Property: Protection status; Value: Protected
- Property: Source virtual machine state; Value: Running
- Property: Source disk type; Value: Managed disks
- Property: Recovery point retention; Value: 24 hours
- Property: App-consistent snapshot frequency; Value: 0 hours
prompt: To restore service as fast as possible, you select _____ in the Failover pane, and the copies of the source disks in East US 2 are [...].

options.text: Latest processed
Latest
Latest app-consistent
Custom

explanation:
The keyed choice restores the workload from the newest recovery point that Site Recovery has already finished handling, so no extra work is needed before the workload can start and the recovery time is the lowest of the options in the Failover pane — which is exactly what the stated requirement (fastest possible restart) asks for. The exhibit also shows the app-consistent snapshot frequency at 0 hours, so app-consistent snapshots are disabled and there is no app-consistent recovery point to choose, and the team has explicitly accepted losing the last few seconds of writes. For the second slot, the copies of the source disks that Site Recovery maintains in the secondary region are managed disks named with the -ASRReplica suffix, and their disk state should show ActiveSAS; they also automatically carry a tag with the ASR-ReplicaDisk prefix.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Latest: This choice builds a recovery point for the virtual machine from all the data already sent to the recovery service before the cutover, so it adds time before the workload can start. It is the pick when the smallest possible data loss matters more than a fast restart, which is not the requirement in this scenario.
- Latest app-consistent: This choice fails over to the newest app-consistent recovery point. The exhibit shows the app-consistent snapshot frequency at 0 hours, so app-consistent snapshots are disabled and no such recovery point exists to select; it would also take longer to reach than the fastest choice.
- Custom: This choice lets you pick a recovery point yourself and is offered only when a single virtual machine is failed over outside a recovery plan. It requires the service to work with the replicated data before the workload starts, so it does not satisfy the requirement for the quickest restart.

options.text: Start the failover with the alternative size that the service recommends for the target region.
Start the failover with the size that the source machine uses for the target region, then resize the copy afterwards.
Start the failover with a size from a different generation family for the target region.
Resize the source machine first, then start the failover with a size that the target region offers.

explanation:
When the original size is not available in the target region, Site Recovery can surface a recommendation for a different size that the target region does offer, and the cutover should proceed with that size. The target size list only presents SKUs from the same generation family as the source VM (Gen 1 or Gen 2), so the team should accept the size the service proposes for East US 2 rather than trying to force the source size, pick something from another family, or alter the machine in the offline source region.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Start the failover with the size that the source machine uses for the target region, then resize the copy afterwards: The size the source machine runs with cannot be chosen for the copy because East US 2 does not offer it, so resizing the copy after the cutover is not a workable route; the recovery service proposes a size the target region does offer.
- Start the failover with a size from a different generation family for the target region: The size list offered for the failed-over copy contains only SKUs from the same generation family as the source VM, so a size from a different family is not available for the target VM.
- Resize the source machine first, then start the failover with a size that the target region offers: Changing the machine in the source region first is neither required nor workable while that region is offline; the recovery service determines the target size and proposes an alternative when the original size is unavailable in the target region.

options.text: create a replication group that includes both virtual machines
create an availability set that includes both virtual machines
create a replication policy that includes both virtual machines
create a recovery plan that includes both virtual machines

explanation:
A replication group bundles the protected virtual machines so that they fail over together to shared crash-consistent and app-consistent recovery points, which is what makes the two members of this tier come back at exactly the same point in time; the trade-off is some impact on workload performance, so this arrangement suits workloads that need consistency across machines. Because both machines are Linux, the traffic that members of such a group exchange with each other travels on TCP port 20004, and the documentation is explicit that this outbound rule must be opened manually for Linux and that no firewall appliance may block it. The two choices above therefore cover both halves of the request: grouping the machines for shared recovery points, and permitting the outbound port 20004 traffic between them.

Why the other options are wrong:
- create an availability set that includes both virtual machines: An availability set only controls fault-domain placement of the virtual machines; it has no effect on which recovery point each machine is restored from, so the front-end server and the session-state service could still come back at different points in time.
- create a replication policy that includes both virtual machines: A replication policy carries per-machine settings such as recovery point retention and app-consistent snapshot frequency; applying one policy to both machines does not make them fail over to shared recovery points, so the tier would not be restored from one identical point in time.
- create a recovery plan that includes both virtual machines: A recovery plan controls the sequence in which several machines are failed over and can drive automated failover; it does not create shared recovery points across the machines, so returning both to exactly the same point in time is still not guaranteed.

explanation:
After a failover and a re-protection, proximity placement group assignments can be lost and may need to be restored by hand, so the fix is to re-associate the virtual machine with the proximity placement group in the region where it is now running. the Azure Backup extension
the Azure Monitor agent extension
the Azure Site Recovery replication group service extension

explanation:
Turning on protection automatically installs the Site Recovery Mobility service extension on the protected virtual machine; that extension registers the machine with Azure Site Recovery and continuous replication starts. While replication runs, every disk write on that machine is sent immediately to the cache storage account in the source region, which is East US for this setup. That cache buffers the changes, which keeps the impact on the production application minimal, and the service later processes the cached data and delivers it to the target storage account or the replica managed disks in East US 2.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the Azure Backup extension: Azure Backup protects a virtual machine with its own snapshots and backup policies. It is not the component that Azure Site Recovery places on the machine when replication is enabled.
- the Azure Monitor agent extension: The Azure Monitor agent is installed to collect monitoring and telemetry data for a virtual machine. It plays no part in the replication data path and is not what Azure Site Recovery deploys when protection is turned on.
- the Azure Site Recovery replication group service extension: A replication group is a configuration that bundles virtual machines so that they fail over to shared crash-consistent and app-consistent recovery points. No such extension is placed on a virtual machine, and the exhibit shows that this machine is not grouped with other machines.

prompt: You have a three-tier application running on Windows Server 2022 virtual machines in East US, and you use Azure Site Recovery to protect them for Azure-to-Azure disaster recovery. The three tiers are configured for multi-VM consistency so that they come back at one shared recovery point. After protection starts, each virtual machine publishes only its own crash-consistent recovery points, and the tiers never publish a combined recovery point. The network security group on the subnet that hosts the tiers contains only the rules listed below. You need the tiers to fail over to a common, consistent recovery point. Which change should you make?

options.text: Add an outbound rule that allows TCP port 20004 to the other virtual machines in the deployment.
Add an outbound rule that allows TCP port 20004 to the Azure Site Recovery service tag.
Add an outbound rule that allows TCP port 20004 to the cache storage account.
Add an inbound rule that allows TCP port 20004 to the other virtual machines in the deployment.

explanation:
Members that share a recovery point exchange data with each other over TCP port 20004. The listed network security group permits only HTTPS 443 to the documented service tags and denies every other outbound flow, so the traffic between the tier members is dropped and each machine can publish only its own crash-consistent recovery point. Adding an outbound allowance for TCP port 20004 to the other virtual machines in the deployment restores the member-to-member exchange, letting the tiers publish a combined, consistent recovery point and fail over together.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add an outbound rule that allows TCP port 20004 to the Azure Site Recovery service tag: The service tag allowances in the documented pattern are HTTPS on port 443, and HTTPS 443 to the Azure Site Recovery service tag is already permitted in the exhibit. The consistency exchange between tier members is not sent to that service tag; it runs directly between the members on port 20004, so opening 20004 to the service tag does not fix the missing shared recovery point.
- Add an outbound rule that allows TCP port 20004 to the cache storage account: The cache storage account in the source region buffers replicated disk writes so production impact stays low; it is not the peer for the exchange between consistency members. Opening port 20004 to it therefore leaves the member-to-member exchange blocked and the combined recovery point unpublished.
- Add an inbound rule that allows TCP port 20004 to the other virtual machines in the deployment: Site Recovery requires outbound connectivity only and never needs inbound connectivity to the protected virtual machine, and the consistency exchange is outbound as well. An inbound allowance changes nothing about the blocked outbound flow, so the tiers would still not publish a shared recovery point.

prompt: You have a SQL Server virtual machine in West Europe that is protected with Azure Site Recovery for Azure-to-Azure disaster recovery. Your recovery objective requires that the database can be restored to a point no more than 30 minutes before the incident, and that transactions which were already committed but not yet written to the data files are still present in the recovered database. The replication policy that is currently assigned to the virtual machine is shown below. You need to update the policy so that both conditions are satisfied. Which change should you make?

options.text: Set the app-consistent snapshot frequency to 15 minutes and keep the recovery point retention at one day
Set the app-consistent snapshot frequency to 12 hours and keep the recovery point retention at one day
Set the recovery point retention to 30 minutes and leave the app-consistent snapshot frequency disabled
Set the crash-consistent recovery point interval to one minute and leave the app-consistent snapshot frequency disabled

explanation:
Setting the app-consistent snapshot frequency to 15 minutes creates an app-consistent recovery point every 15 minutes, so the worst-case gap between the incident and the newest usable recovery point stays inside the 30-minute recovery objective, and each of those points also captures the in-memory state through VSS, which is what carries the transactions that were committed but not yet written to disk. The snapshot frequency remains lower than the one-day recovery point retention, so the retention value can stay as it is and no extra recovery points need to be stored.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Set the app-consistent snapshot frequency to 12 hours and keep the recovery point retention at one day: Twelve hours is a legal value because it is still lower than the one-day retention, but it leaves the database up to 12 hours behind the incident, far outside the 30-minute recovery objective.
- Set the recovery point retention to 30 minutes and leave the app-consistent snapshot frequency disabled: Shortening the recovery point retention only limits how long recovery points are kept. With the app-consistent snapshot frequency still disabled, no recovery point contains the in-memory transaction data, so the requirement that committed transactions survive the failover is not met.
- Set the crash-consistent recovery point interval to one minute and leave the app-consistent snapshot frequency disabled: The five-minute crash-consistent interval is fixed and cannot be changed, and crash-consistent points hold only data that was already written to disk, so they never carry the committed-but-unflushed transactions that the recovery objective requires.

prompt: You protect a write-intensive Azure virtual machine in East US 2 with Azure Site Recovery for Azure-to-Azure disaster recovery. Since the protection was enabled, the replicated copy in the recovery region keeps falling behind the source, so an unplanned failover would recover a copy that is minutes stale. The application cannot be changed to write less, and the storage configuration for the replication can still be adjusted. Which change should you make?

options.text: Set churn for the VM to High Churn and use a Premium Block Blob cache storage account in the source region
Set churn for the VM to Normal Churn and use a Premium Block Blob cache storage account in the source region
Set churn for the VM to High Churn and use a Standard general-purpose v2 cache storage account in the source region
Set churn for the VM to Normal Churn and use a Standard general-purpose v2 cache storage account in the source region

explanation:
The virtual machine writes about 70 MB/s continuously, which is a data change rate above what the churn path currently in place sustains — that is why the replica keeps falling behind and the recovery points age behind the source data. The option intended for write rates beyond the default path is the higher churn level, and it is used together with a Premium Block Blob cache storage account, which buffers the writes in the source region; when that churn level is selected, the cache storage list offers only Premium Block Blob accounts. Site Recovery supports up to 100 MB/s per virtual machine with that option, and up to 500 MB/s in configurations that meet the documented requirements, so this workload's write volume is covered.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Set churn for the VM to Normal Churn and use a Premium Block Blob cache storage account in the source region: Normal Churn is the default setting and the cache storage list for it contains only Standard accounts, so a Premium Block Blob account is not a valid pairing for it. Keeping the default churn level also keeps the write volume that the replication path already fails to sustain for this workload, so the replica would stay behind the source.
- Set churn for the VM to High Churn and use a Standard general-purpose v2 cache storage account in the source region: When the higher churn level is selected, the cache storage list contains only Premium Block Blob accounts, so a Standard general-purpose v2 account cannot be paired with it. A Standard cache account also lacks the throughput needed to absorb this workload's sustained writes.
- Set churn for the VM to Normal Churn and use a Standard general-purpose v2 cache storage account in the source region: This repeats the configuration that is already in place — the default churn level with a Standard cache storage account — so the replica would keep lagging behind the source and recovery points would keep aging, which fails the requirement.

prompt: You have two Azure virtual machines that run a line-of-business application in East US 2. They are protected with Azure Site Recovery for Azure-to-Azure disaster recovery, and West Europe is the recovery region. The current replication configuration is shown below. The cloud provider has announced a regional outage window for East US 2 that starts on Saturday, and the business wants the application to run from West Europe during that window with no committed transactions lost. Which action should you take?

options.text: Run a planned failover to West Europe.
Run an unplanned failover to West Europe.
Wait for the next app-consistent recovery point, then run an unplanned failover to West Europe.
Restore the virtual machine disks with Azure Backup in West Europe and start the application manually.

explanation:
The outage window is announced in advance, so this is an expected event rather than an unexpected disaster, and a planned failover is the Site Recovery path for that situation. Running a planned failover moves the protected virtual machines into the recovery region and preserves everything captured in the replicated copy, so the application can run from West Europe during the window without losing committed transactions. The table confirms both virtual machines are protected and healthy, and that app-consistent snapshots are being taken every 30 minutes, so the move can be carried out as described.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Run an unplanned failover to West Europe: An unplanned failover is meant for unexpected disasters, where the recovered copy contains only the data captured up to the last recovery point. With app-consistent snapshots every 30 minutes, anything committed after that point can be lost, which does not meet the requirement of running in West Europe without losing committed transactions.
- Wait for the next app-consistent recovery point, then run an unplanned failover to West Europe: Waiting for a fresher app-consistent recovery point only narrows the gap. Because the move is still an unplanned failover, data accrued after the last recovery point can still be lost. The expected-outage path that keeps the copied data intact is the planned failover.
- Restore the virtual machine disks with Azure Backup in West Europe and start the application manually: Azure Backup in a Recovery Services vault protects and restores data only; it doesn't reproduce the protected virtual machines or orchestrate a virtual machine failover, and no backup policy is configured for these machines here. It therefore can't deliver the application running from West Europe with no committed transactions lost.

The current target configuration for the protected machine is shown in the exhibit. You need the next failover to produce a machine that meets that requirement. Which action should you take?

options.text: Update the target properties of the replicated virtual machine in the replication settings, change the target availability type to Availability set, and save the update.
Disable replication for the virtual machine, modify the target availability type to Availability set, and then enable replication again.
Stop the virtual machine and start it again, then set the target availability type to Availability set in the replication settings.
Create a recovery plan that adds a manual action which creates an availability set and moves the recovered virtual machine into it before failover.

explanation:
Most target resources for a replicated virtual machine can be changed while protection is running, for example the target VM SKU, the target resource group, and the target network. The availability type (single instance, availability set, or availability zones) is the exception: it cannot be updated in place. To move the machine from a single instance layout to an availability set, you must turn protection off for that virtual machine, change the target availability type to Availability set, and then start protection again so the new target layout is used the next time the machine is failed over.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Update the target properties of the replicated virtual machine in the replication settings, change the target availability type to Availability set, and save the update: Target resources such as the target VM SKU can be updated while the protected machine keeps replicating, but the availability type is the one target setting that cannot be changed in place. Saving a target properties update alone leaves the machine configured to fail over as a single instance, so this does not deliver the required layout.
- Stop the virtual machine and start it again, then set the target availability type to Availability set in the replication settings: Starting and stopping the virtual machine only changes its power state. It has no effect on the target resources that Site Recovery uses when it creates the machine in the recovery region, so the recovered machine would still come up as a single instance.
- Create a recovery plan that adds a manual action which creates an availability set and moves the recovered virtual machine into it before failover: A recovery plan orchestrates the order of failover steps and the actions that run around them; it does not set the target availability type of a replicated item. The availability type is configured on the protected item itself and, because it cannot be edited while protection is running, it has to be changed by turning protection off, adjusting the setting, and starting protection again.

options.text: Add the shared disk to each virtual machine in the cluster through the Add disks operation so that it is replicated with the machines, keeping the current protection.
Turn protection off and back on for the whole cluster setup so the shared disk is replicated with the cluster.
Enable replication for the cluster so that each node replicates the shared disk independently, keeping the current protection.
Turn off protection for one virtual machine in the cluster and turn protection back on for that node so the shared disk is replicated with it.

explanation:
A disk shared by the nodes of a Windows Server Failover Cluster workload (for example the disk that holds a SQL Server failover cluster instance) needs special handling. The documentation states that the generic Add disks operation should be skipped for such a disk and that protection should instead be turned off and back on for the whole cluster setup. Repeating the protection steps for the cluster setup re-establishes the replication of the shared disk as part of the cluster, which is what attaches it to the cluster nodes created in the recovery region.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add the shared disk to each virtual machine in the cluster through the Add disks operation so that it is replicated with the machines, keeping the current protection: The generic Add disks operation is precisely the flow that should be avoided for a shared cluster disk. Adding the disk as an ordinary data disk to each node treats it as a normal disk, and it ends up as a standalone replica managed disk in the recovery region that is not associated with the cluster nodes.
- Enable replication for the cluster so that each node replicates the shared disk independently, keeping the current protection: Protecting the nodes separately leaves every node replicating the same shared disk on its own, so the disk is still not linked to the cluster in the recovery region. A shared cluster disk has to be handled as part of the cluster setup rather than node by node.
- Turn off protection for one virtual machine in the cluster and turn protection back on for that node so the shared disk is replicated with it: Re-enabling protection for only one node leaves the other node unprotected and does not re-establish the cluster-wide setup that the shared disk requires. Both nodes of the cluster setup have to be turned off and back on together so the shared disk is replicated as part of the cluster.

options.text: Cache storage account in the source region
Replica managed disks in the target region
Replication policy
Recovery plan
Mobility service extension
Azure Backup service

explanation: Each responsibility in this Azure-to-Azure design is carried by a different building block. The cache storage account is created in the region where the machines run and holds their writes briefly, so the production workload is not slowed down while the data is forwarded. Replica managed disks are created in the recovery region and carry the copied data from which the new virtual machines are built during a failover. The replication policy holds the recovery point retention and the app-consistent snapshot frequency, so it is what determines how often recovery points are produced and how far back the history is kept. The recovery plan groups the protected machines and sequences multi-tier failover and recovery, and it can carry scripts, manual actions and Automation runbooks. The Mobility service extension installs itself on each protected virtual machine, registers it with Site Recovery and starts sending that machine's writes to the cache in the source region.

You use Azure Site Recovery to protect a small estate of Azure virtual machines for Azure-to-Azure disaster recovery. North Europe is the source region and West Europe is the target region. The protected estate is listed in the exhibit.

Operations has agreed on the outcomes that this setup must deliver, and you have to attach each configuration element that Site Recovery offers to the outcome it produces. Drag each configuration element to the outcome it delivers.

- Virtual machine: vm-web-01; Region: North Europe; Workload: Catalog web front end; Notes: Serves catalog pages from a read-only cache
- Virtual machine: vm-order-01; Region: North Europe; Workload: Order intake with SQL Server; Notes: Orders are frequently committed while the request is still being handled in memory
- Virtual machine: vm-order-02; Region: North Europe; Workload: Order intake with SQL Server; Notes: Runs the same workload as vm-order-01 and must never diverge from it
- Virtual machine: vm-batch-01; Region: North Europe; Workload: Nightly reconciliation jobs; Notes: Write rate peaks at about 90 MB/s every night
prompt: vm-order-01 can be brought back to any moment within the previous two days

options.text: App-consistent snapshot frequency
Recovery point retention
High Churn
Replication group
Recovery plan

explanation: Each configuration element produces a specific outcome in an Azure-to-Azure setup. Recovery point retention decides how far back in time a machine can be brought back, so the two-day history for vm-order-01 comes from that setting (its default is one day). The app-consistent snapshot frequency decides how often memory contents and transactions in progress are captured, which is what brings back the order that was still in RAM; it is disabled by default at zero hours, and its value must stay below the retention period. High Churn is the option for a workload whose write rate exceeds what the default storage setup absorbs — it uses a premium block blob storage account and covers data churn up to 100 MB/s, which suits the roughly 90 MB/s peak of vm-batch-01. A replication group gives its member machines shared crash-consistent and app-consistent recovery points, so vm-order-01 and vm-order-02 come back at one shared moment; it is only for machines running the same workload and it affects workload performance. A recovery plan groups machines and sequences multi-tier failover and recovery, adding scripts, manual actions and Azure Automation runbooks, which is what produces the ordered, partly automated return of the tiers.

context:
You have a line-of-business application that you want to protect with Azure Site Recovery for Azure-to-Azure disaster recovery, and the estate is listed in the exhibit. Your company rule is that every colleague receives only the access their own task requires. Four of the built-in roles are available to you, and you need to work out which one allows each person to carry out the work described below. Drag each role to the work it authorises.

- Item: Source workload; Value: Four virtual machines in East US 2 (two Windows, two Linux)
- Item: Secondary region; Value: West Europe
- Item: Protection container; Value: Not created yet
- Item: Change window; Value: A regional outage of the source region; the application has to run from the secondary region
- Item: Team; Value: One colleague per workstream, plus yourself
prompt: Create the vault that will hold the protection configuration for the estate.

options.text: Owner on the subscription
Site Recovery Contributor
Virtual Machine Contributor
Backup Contributor

explanation: Each workstream needs a different grant. The protection container has to be created first at subscription scope, which needs admin or owner permissions on the subscription, so Owner on the subscription covers the work of creating the vault. The replication and failover operations performed inside that vault are run with the Site Recovery Contributor built-in role, so that role covers enabling and managing replication and running the switch to the secondary region. When the failover happens, new instances and their disks are created in the secondary region, and that work is covered by the Virtual Machine Contributor role (or the equivalent permissions to create a VM in the selected virtual network, write to an Azure storage account, and write to an Azure managed disk). Backup Contributor is left over, because it belongs to the Backup service, which in Azure Recovery Services only keeps data safe and recoverable.

- Machine: dhcp-01; Region: East US; Workload: DHCP service for the branch offices; Requirement for the recovery design: The service runs no transactional workload of its own, so bringing back the data that sat on the disks is enough, and the team wants it usable again quickly after an outage.

- Machine: web-01, api-01, worker-01; Region: East US; Workload: Three tiers of one web application; Requirement for the recovery design: The three machines must always be brought back to one shared moment in time, and the team accepts the extra load that this places on the workload.
- Machine: vm-archive-01; Region: East US 2; Workload: Reporting server; Requirement for the recovery design: The team wants to be able to recover the machine from any point in a seven-day window, and accepts that keeping that many points will raise the storage bill.
- Machine: vm-invoice-01; Region: West Europe; Workload: Invoice generator; Requirement for the recovery design: The instance that is created in the recovery region must not go down together with the source when a single zone in that region fails.

options.text: Crash-consistent recovery point
App-consistent recovery point
Replication group
Recovery point retention
Target availability type: availability zones

explanation: Each row of the exhibit states a recovery requirement, and each Site Recovery setting or capability satisfies exactly one of them: the DHCP service only needs the on-disk data, so a crash-consistent recovery point fits; the order database must keep accepted but unwritten orders, so an app-consistent recovery point fits; the three tiers must return to one shared moment, so they belong to a replication group; the seven-day window of recoverable moments is set by the recovery point retention of the replication policy; and surviving the loss of a single zone in the recovery region requires the target availability type to be availability zones.

- Machine: vm-app-01; Region: East US 2; Operating system: Ubuntu 22.04; Source size: Standard_D4s_v5; Target region: West Europe; Role: Web front end
- Machine: vm-db-01; Region: East US 2; Operating system: Ubuntu 22.04; Source size: Standard_D8s_v5; Target region: West Europe; Role: Database server
- Machine: vm-inv-01; Region: East US 2; Operating system: Windows Server 2022; Source size: Standard_D4s_v5; Target region: West Europe; Role: Invoicing service
- Machine: vm-file-01; Region: East US 2; Operating system: Windows Server 2022; Source size: Standard_D8s_v5; Target region: West Europe; Role: File share
prompt: vm-app-01 and vm-db-01 never reach a protected state, and the service reports that the registration cannot be completed.

options.text: Update the trusted root certificates and the certificate revocation list on the affected machines.
Install the latest Windows updates on the affected machines.
Exclude 169.254.169.254 from the traffic that the proxy forwards.
Confirm that the recovery region and the subscription can host the required size, then select the matching entry from the target size list.
Replace the sign-in filter with an allow-list of destinations that replication is permitted to use.
Enable the Site Recovery authentication proxy for the affected machines.

explanation: vm-app-01 and vm-db-01 run Ubuntu, and registration with Site Recovery fails on machines whose certificates are out of date; on Linux the fix is to update the trusted root certificates and the certificate revocation list, so that action belongs to the first symptom. The agent on vm-inv-01 cannot determine the machine's security type because the proxy forwards the instance metadata address, and excluding 169.254.169.254 from the proxied traffic restores that call, so it belongs to the second symptom. The instance produced for vm-file-01 was smaller than the source instance because the target size defaults to the source size or the next best available one when the recovery region or the subscription cannot host the required size; confirming capacity and selecting the matching entry in the target size list restores the source size, so it belongs to the third symptom. Finally, Site Recovery needs plain outbound connectivity and does not support an authenticating proxy, so the sign-in filter has to be replaced with an allow-list of destinations, which belongs to the fourth symptom.

context:
You protect a group of Linux virtual machines in North Europe with Azure Site Recovery for Azure-to-Azure disaster recovery, and the Mobility service that Site Recovery installed on each machine is still running a build from several months ago. Refreshing each machine by hand would need a change window every time a new build is published, so the platform team wants the service to keep that component current on its own. You need to change the replication configuration and the outbound network rules so that this happens without further manual work. Which two changes should you make?

`Replicated item: vm-app-01  (North Europe -> West Europe)

  Update settings                : Not selected
  Account for the update option  : Not set

Outbound rules on the source subnet (HTTPS 443):
  *.blob.core.windows.net
  login.microsoftonline.com
  *.hypervrecoverymanager.windowsazure.com
  *.servicebus.windows.net
`
prompt: The correct configuration is to _____, and the outbound rules must permit [...].

options.text: select Update settings and specify the Automation account
select Update settings and specify the cache storage account
select Update settings and specify the Recovery Services vault
select Update settings and specify the replica managed disk

explanation:
The Mobility service on a replicated virtual machine can be kept current by the platform when the update option in the extension settings is switched on and pointed at an Automation account, which is the pair of values Site Recovery expects on the Manage tab when replication is enabled. The agent then fetches the new build from *.automation.ext.azure.com, so that destination must be reachable outbound over HTTPS from the protected machine; where the rules are written against IP ranges rather than URLs, the GuestAndHybridManagement service tag is the one that covers this path, and it is needed in both the source and the target region. The cache storage account, the Recovery Services vault and the replica managed disk all belong to the replication data path and cannot deliver a new build to the agent.

Why the other options are wrong:
- select Update settings and specify the cache storage account: The cache storage account in the source region is where disk writes are staged before they are processed and replicated; it plays no part in delivering a new build to the Mobility service, so pointing the update option at it would leave the component outdated.
- select Update settings and specify the Recovery Services vault: The Recovery Services vault holds the replication configuration, the policies and the recovery points for the protected machines; the update option does not take a vault, so nothing would be kept current automatically.
- select Update settings and specify the replica managed disk: A replica managed disk is the copy of a source disk that Site Recovery maintains in the recovery region; it is a storage target for the replicated data, not something the update option can be pointed at.

prompt: Replication for vm-app-01 cannot start until the _____ is created in the [...].

options.text: cache storage account
target storage account
premium block blob storage account
replica managed disk

explanation:
Azure-to-Azure disaster recovery depends on a cache storage account that sits in the source region, the region that hosts the virtual machine being replicated. Disk writes are staged in that account while replication runs and are only then passed on to the recovery region, so the enable-replication operation cannot complete until such an account exists. The cache account therefore belongs in East US, the region hosting vm-app-01, and not in the recovery region, the vault's region, or the region where the replicated disks are created.

Why the other options are wrong:
- target storage account: A target storage account holds the data once it has been processed and sent on to the recovery region; it does not provide the staging location in the source region that the missing prerequisite refers to.
- premium block blob storage account: A premium block blob storage account is what the High Churn storage configuration uses when a virtual machine's write rate exceeds the normal limits, so it is a churn choice rather than the component this validation error is about.
- replica managed disk: Replica managed disks are the replicated copies of the machine's managed disks that the service creates in the recovery region; they are produced by the replication process itself and are not provisioned by you in the source region beforehand.

The target virtual machine SKU defaults to the source SKU or, when that SKU cannot be placed in the recovery region, to the next best available one, and the SKU list offered for the target only contains SKUs of the same family (Gen 1 or Gen 2) as the protected machine. Because West Europe has no capacity for D8s_v5, the failed-over instance is created with the next best size in that family, not with a size from another family or an arbitrary large size. For the disks, Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disk are replicated as Premium SSD v1 replica disks, and the source disk type is only applied again when the instance fails over, so the copy kept in the recovery region is a Premium SSD v1 disk.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the same size as the protected machine, if the recovery region has capacity for it: This describes the default only when the recovery region can host the exact SKU of the protected machine. The scenario states that there is no spare capacity for that size in West Europe, so Site Recovery falls back to the next best available size in the same family instead of keeping the original size.
- the largest size the recovery region offers: Site Recovery does not pick the largest size in the recovery region. The target SKU defaults to the source SKU or to the next best available one, which may be a smaller size than the source.
- a size from the previous generation of virtual machines: The list of SKUs offered for the target contains only SKUs from the same family (Gen 1 or Gen 2) as the protected machine, so a size from the previous generation of virtual machines is not an option that can be selected for the target.

You are adding disaster recovery coverage to the Linux virtual machine shown in the exhibit, and the protection never starts. The machine's installed package revision is only three days old, so it is not missing routine operating system fixes. When you run the enable-replication operation, the Mobility service that Site Recovery installs on the machine reports a registration failure and the machine stays in an unprotected state. You need this machine to become protected so that it can be failed over to the recovery region later. Which action should you take?

`Machine: vm-app-01
Operating system: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS
Image build date: 2025-04-18
Installed package revision: 3 days old
Mobility service version: 9.48.0.0

09:12:03  Starting registration with the recovery service.
09:12:21  Registration failed: the host rejected the chain presented by the service.
09:12:21  Protection state: not protected.`
prompt: To let the machine register with the recovery service and reach a protected state, you should _____.

options.text: update the trusted root certificates and the certificate revocation list (CRL) on the virtual machine
install the latest Windows updates on the virtual machine and re-run the enable-replication operation
reinstall the Site Recovery Mobility service extension on the virtual machine and re-run the enable-replication operation
reissue the certificates held in the Recovery Services vault and re-run the enable-replication operation

explanation:
Site Recovery registration can fail on a guest whose trust material is out of date, and the machine then never reaches a protected state. For a Linux guest the documented remedy is to update the trusted root certificates and the certificate revocation list (CRL) on the machine. This machine runs Ubuntu and its image is 18 months old, so refreshing that material on the guest is what unblocks the registration and lets protection start.

Why the other options are wrong:
- install the latest Windows updates on the virtual machine and re-run the enable-replication operation: Installing the latest Windows updates is the remedy that applies to Windows virtual machines. This guest runs Ubuntu and its packages are already current, so this action would not resolve the registration failure.
- reinstall the Site Recovery Mobility service extension on the virtual machine and re-run the enable-replication operation: The Mobility service extension is already installed and is the component that reports the failure. Reinstalling it does not refresh the stale trust material on the guest, which is what blocks the registration.
- reissue the certificates held in the Recovery Services vault and re-run the enable-replication operation: Reissuing certificates in the Recovery Services vault does not address the stale material held by the guest. The vault and its configuration are already correct, and the failure happens on the machine side during registration.

explanation:
With every target setting left at its default, Site Recovery builds the recovery-side resources in the recovery region itself: a new target resource group and a new virtual network and subnet whose names carry the asr suffix, created in the same subscription as the source virtual machine (here Contoso-Production). If a target availability set whose name carries the asr suffix already exists in the recovery region, that existing set is reused rather than a second one being created. The replicated copy of each source disk is a replica managed disk whose name carries the -ASRReplica suffix and which carries a tag prefixed with ASR-ReplicaDisk, with its disk state shown as ActiveSAS.

Why the other options are wrong:
- new resources in the recovery region whose names carry the asr suffix, in the subscription that holds the Recovery Services vault: The subscription that holds the Recovery Services vault is not what the default target configuration uses. By default the target resources are created in the same subscription that already hosts the source virtual machine, which in this estate is Contoso-Production and not Contoso-Platform where the vault sits.
- resources in the recovery region whose names match the source resource group and virtual network, in the same subscription as the source virtual machine: The default target configuration does not copy the names of the source resources. Site Recovery creates new target resources whose names carry the asr suffix; it does not adopt rg-app-prod or vnet-app-prod as the target resource group and network.
- new resources in the recovery region whose names carry the asr suffix, in a new subscription that you create for the recovery region: Site Recovery does not create a new subscription for the recovery side. The default target resources are created in the subscription that already hosts the source virtual machine, so a purpose-built subscription is not part of the default setup.

You are writing the disaster recovery design for a business application that runs on six virtual machines pinned to an availability zone in East US 2. The estate must be recovered into West Europe inside an availability zone, and the design has to record how the zone in the recovery region is chosen, because the protection the business relies on depends on this choice. The draft of the design simply names zone 1 of West Europe, picked because it is the zone number the machines use today. Which statement should the design use?

- Property: Protected estate; Value: Six virtual machines running the business application
- Property: Availability zone in East US 2; Value: Zone 1
- Property: Recovery region; Value: West Europe
- Property: Target availability type in the draft; Value: Availability zones
- Property: Zone named in the draft for the recovery region; Value: Zone 1
prompt: The disaster recovery design should tell the operations team to _____.

options.text: recover into a logical zone of West Europe that maps to a physical zone other than the one reached by the zone number in East US 2
recover into zone 1 of West Europe, because the estate uses zone 1 in East US 2 and an equal zone number identifies the same physical zone across subscriptions and regions
recover the protected estate as a single instance in West Europe, because a standalone instance carries no zone placement and cannot be lost with an availability zone
recover the protected estate into zone 1 of West Europe with an availability set, because fault domains give the estate the separation that the design is looking for

explanation:
For zone-to-zone recovery the zone used in the recovery region has to be chosen from the zone-to-physical-zone mapping that applies to the target subscription. Equal logical zone numbers don't identify equal physical zones across subscriptions or regions, so a design that simply repeats the source zone number does not deliver the separation the business asked for. The design must name a logical zone whose mapped physical zone is not the one the current zone number reaches, and the target availability type (single instance, availability set or availability zones) has to be availability zones for this estate.

Why the other options are wrong:
- recover into zone 1 of West Europe, because the estate uses zone 1 in East US 2 and an equal zone number identifies the same physical zone across subscriptions and regions: Matching zone numbers in two subscriptions or regions do not point at the same physical zone, so repeating the number used in East US 2 in West Europe does not deliver the separation the design is looking for. The zone in the recovery region has to be picked from the mapping that applies to the target subscription.
- recover the protected estate as a single instance in West Europe, because a standalone instance carries no zone placement and cannot be lost with an availability zone: A single instance carries no zone placement at all, so it does not deliver the zone-level recovery the design calls for; the target availability type for this estate is availability zones.
- recover the protected estate into zone 1 of West Europe with an availability set, because fault domains give the estate the separation that the design is looking for: An availability set spreads the disks of the instance across fault domains, but it is a different availability type from a zone and does not give the zone-level placement the design calls for. On top of that, the target availability type cannot be changed while replication is running: replication has to be disabled, the setting changed, and replication enabled again.

prompt: You host contoso.com in Azure DNS and the domain is already delegated to the Azure name servers. Internet clients resolve api.contoso.com to the public address 52.142.18.7. Workloads inside vnet-app (10.1.0.0/16) need api.contoso.com to reach the internal address 10.1.0.20, and that internal address must not be handed out to internet resolvers. Which arrangement should you create?

options.text: Publish an A record for api with the internal address in the existing public zone, and keep the public address in the same record set.
Create a private zone whose name matches the public zone, publish the api record with the internal address there, and link vnet-app to that private zone.
Create a private zone whose name is api.contoso.com, publish the apex record with the internal address there, and link vnet-app to that private zone.
Publish a CNAME record for api in the public zone that targets a host record holding the internal address.

explanation:
Two zones carrying the same domain name give one query two different answers depending on where it is sent, which is the split-horizon pattern. Creating a private zone with the same name as the public zone, adding an A record for api that holds 10.1.0.20, and linking vnet-app to that private zone makes members of vnet-app resolve api.contoso.com to the internal address, while everybody else keeps using the public zone and its 52.142.18.7 record. The link is required: a virtual network must be linked to a private zone for its members to resolve the records published in that zone, and a linked network can resolve every record in the zone.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Publish an A record for api with the internal address in the existing public zone, and keep the public address in the same record set: Everything published in the public zone is resolved by internet resolvers, so 10.1.0.20 would be handed out to the internet, which the requirement forbids. On top of that, the api record set already holds the public address, so both addresses would be returned to every client rather than clients in the virtual network receiving a different answer.
- Create a private zone whose name is api.contoso.com, publish the apex record with the internal address there, and link vnet-app to that private zone: The private zone has to carry the same name as the public zone for one query to produce different answers inside and outside the virtual network. A private zone called api.contoso.com is a different domain, so it does not give a split view of contoso.com, and the relative record name published inside it would resolve as api.api.contoso.com.
- Publish a CNAME record for api in the public zone that targets a host record holding the internal address: Records placed in the public zone are returned to every resolver, so the internal address would be exposed on the internet. In addition, a CNAME record set cannot coexist with another record set of the same name, and the public zone already publishes an A record set named api, so the alias cannot be added alongside it.

`Contoso Registrar - Domain: contoso.com
Record type: NS
  ns1-37.azure-dns.com.
  ns2-37.azure-dns.net.`
prompt: Your company hosts contoso.com in Azure DNS for its public web properties. Since the domain was pointed at Azure, users report that lookups for contoso.com succeed for some internet resolvers but time out for others, depending on which resolver they use. You have not modified anything inside the zone itself; the registrar currently shows the following. Which change should you make?

options.text: Update the registrar's NS records so the domain is delegated to every name server listed for the zone in Azure DNS
Create the same zone name in a second Azure DNS resource group and delegate the domain to that zone's name servers
Point the registrar's NS records at the name servers of a different zone in the same Azure DNS subscription
Add an NS record set inside the zone for each name server that is absent and leave the registrar's NS records unchanged

explanation:
Azure DNS hands every new zone a set of four name servers drawn from a shared pool and writes the authoritative NS records into the zone automatically, but the domain only uses them once the registrar delegates to them. All of the zone's name servers should be delegated, no matter what the domain is called, and each address is entered with its trailing dot because that dot marks the end of a fully qualified name. The registrar above lists only two of them, so resolvers that query the other two cannot reach the authoritative servers for contoso.com, which explains why resolution succeeds for some clients and times out for others.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Create the same zone name in a second Azure DNS resource group and delegate the domain to that zone's name servers: A zone name may be reused in another resource group, but every instance is served by a different set of name servers and only one set can be configured at the registrar. Adding a second zone in a different resource group does nothing to repair the incomplete delegation of the zone you already have.
- Point the registrar's NS records at the name servers of a different zone in the same Azure DNS subscription: The name servers that must be delegated are the ones assigned to the contoso.com zone, because only they hold its records. Pointing the registrar at another zone's name servers would break lookups for contoso.com entirely rather than make them succeed for a subset of resolvers.
- Add an NS record set inside the zone for each name server that is absent and leave the registrar's NS records unchanged: The apex NS record set is created and deleted automatically together with the zone, and the name servers Azure pre-populates in it cannot be removed or edited. Delegation of the domain happens at the registrar, so adding records inside the zone changes nothing about how resolvers locate it.
