prompt: Your company hosts contoso.com in a public Azure DNS zone that is already delegated to the Azure name servers, and the zone contains the record sets listed below. The app service behind www.contoso.com is being retired, and clients must now receive the two static front-door addresses 203.0.113.10 and 203.0.113.24 when they look up that name. Which change should you make?

options.text: Keep the www CNAME record set and add a new A record set named www that contains 203.0.113.10 and 203.0.113.24.
Remove the www CNAME record set and create two separate A record sets named www, one holding 203.0.113.10 and the other holding 203.0.113.24.
Remove the www CNAME record set and create an A record set named www that contains 203.0.113.10 and 203.0.113.24.
Add a second record to the existing www CNAME record set so that it holds both addresses and retire the app-service hostname.

explanation:
Azure DNS groups records into record sets by name and type, and DNS standards don't permit a CNAME record set to coexist with any other record set of the same name. Because www currently holds a CNAME record set (pointing at the retired app-service hostname), that record set has to be removed before the name can publish address records. Once it is gone, one A record set named www can carry both 203.0.113.10 and 203.0.113.24 as two records inside the same record set, which is how Azure DNS serves a name from two addresses; the TTL of 3600 seconds then applies to both records in that set.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Keep the www CNAME record set and add a new A record set named www that contains 203.0.113.10 and 203.0.113.24: This keeps the www CNAME record set in place while adding an address record set for the same name, which is exactly what DNS standards forbid: a CNAME record set can't coexist with another record set of the same name, so the A record set at www can't be created while the CNAME is still there.
- Remove the www CNAME record set and create two separate A record sets named www, one holding 203.0.113.10 and the other holding 203.0.113.24: Removing the CNAME record set is the right starting point, but the two addresses belong in a single A record set. Azure DNS manages records as record sets, and to serve a second address you add the record to the existing record set instead of creating another record set with the same name and type.
- Add a second record to the existing www CNAME record set so that it holds both addresses and retire the app-service hostname: A CNAME record set can hold only a single record, and its value is a target hostname rather than an address, so it can't carry both addresses. The CNAME record set for www has to be removed and replaced by an A record set holding those addresses.

explanation:
A virtual network can be linked to only one private zone while autoregistration is turned on, so the existing vnet-app link to legacy.internal.contoso.com has to be detached before vnet-app can be linked to internal.contoso.com with autoregistration enabled. Detaching it also satisfies the requirement that the decommissioned legacy zone end up with no virtual network links. With autoregistration enabled on the new vnet-app link, Azure creates and maintains A records for the vnet-app VMs that point at their private IPs, and because a private zone can be linked by many virtual networks, vnet-hub keeps resolving the names published in internal.contoso.com and keeps its own VM registrations without any change.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add a vnet-app link to internal.contoso.com with autoregistration enabled and keep the existing vnet-app link to legacy.internal.contoso.com with autoregistration enabled: This keeps autoregistration turned on for two private zone links of the same virtual network. Azure allows a virtual network to link to only one private DNS zone when autoregistration is enabled, so the second autoregistration-enabled link cannot be created, and the legacy zone would still carry a virtual network link.
- Add a vnet-app link to internal.contoso.com with autoregistration disabled and keep the existing vnet-app link to legacy.internal.contoso.com with autoregistration enabled: With autoregistration disabled on the new vnet-app link to internal.contoso.com, Azure does not create or update A records for the vnet-app VMs in that zone, so the automatic registration requirement is not met, and the legacy zone also keeps its virtual network link with autoregistration enabled.
- Add a vnet-app link to internal.contoso.com with autoregistration enabled and disable autoregistration on the vnet-hub link to internal.contoso.com: Turning autoregistration off on the vnet-hub link stops Azure from creating and updating A records for the vnet-hub VMs, which breaks the requirement to keep those registrations. It also leaves the vnet-app link to legacy.internal.contoso.com with autoregistration enabled, so vnet-app would still be attached to two private zones with autoregistration turned on.

prompt: Your company hosts contoso.com in a public Azure DNS zone that is delegated to the Azure name servers. A partner operates a secondary DNS server that mirrors this zone for the benefit of its own users. Yesterday you added a TXT record set for a domain-verification challenge, and the partner's server keeps answering from the copy of the zone it already holds, so the new record is missing there. You need the partner's next scheduled refresh to pick up your change. Which change should you make?

options.text: Edit the SOA record set and set the serial number to a higher value
Edit the SOA record set and set the host value to the primary name server
Edit the TXT record set you added yesterday and set its TTL to a lower value
Delete the SOA record set and create a new one that carries a higher serial number

explanation:
Azure DNS does not refresh the serial number of the zone's SOA record set when other records in the zone are added or changed, so the serial the partner's secondary server holds is still the one being published and the mirror looks untouched. Raising the serial number yourself by editing the SOA record set is what tells the secondary server that the zone has been updated, so its next refresh reloads the zone including the new TXT record. The apex SOA record set can be edited in place, and every one of its properties except the host value can be changed, so the rest of the zone stays intact.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Edit the SOA record set and set the host value to the primary name server: The host value of the apex SOA record set is preconfigured by Azure to the primary name server name and is the one property that cannot be edited. Even if it could be changed, the partner compares the serial value rather than the host value, so the zone would still appear unchanged to it.
- Edit the TXT record set you added yesterday and set its TTL to a lower value: The TTL on a record set only controls how long resolvers cache that particular record. The partner decides whether to reload the zone by comparing the zone's SOA serial, so lowering the TTL on the TXT record set does not mark the zone as updated.
- Delete the SOA record set and create a new one that carries a higher serial number: The apex SOA record set is created and deleted automatically together with the zone and cannot be created or deleted on its own, so it cannot be swapped for a new one. The serial number has to be raised by editing the SOA record set that already exists.

prompt: Your company hosts contoso.com in a public Azure DNS zone that is already delegated to the Azure name servers, and the zone currently holds the record sets shown below. Your mail provider has sent you the string that defines which hosts are allowed to send mail on behalf of contoso.com, and it wants that string published for contoso.com itself rather than for any one of its hosts. Which change should you make?

options.text: Add a record set of type TXT that holds the supplied string as a single value
Add a record set of type MX that holds the supplied string as a single value
Add a record set of type CNAME that holds the supplied string as a single value
Add a record set of type SPF that holds the supplied string as a single value

explanation:
The string that lists the hosts allowed to send mail on behalf of a domain is a sender policy framework (SPF) policy. RFC 7208 requires SPF to be published with the TXT record type and deprecated the dedicated SPF type, and Azure DNS does not support that obsolete type. TXT records map a name to arbitrary text and are the type used for this kind of mail configuration (SPF and DKIM alike), so the supplied string belongs in a TXT record set for contoso.com, added alongside the existing A and MX sets at the root of the zone.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add a record set of type MX that holds the supplied string as a single value: An MX record set maps a name to the mail servers that accept mail for it, so its values are server host names with priorities, not the text of a sending policy. The policy text is published as a TXT record.
- Add a record set of type CNAME that holds the supplied string as a single value: A CNAME record set only makes one name an alias for another name, so it cannot carry the policy text, and it cannot be created at the root of the zone in any case: the root already holds the NS and SOA record sets that Azure creates with the zone, so a CNAME there would conflict with them.
- Add a record set of type SPF that holds the supplied string as a single value: The obsolete SPF record type was deprecated by RFC 7208 and is not supported by Azure DNS; policies of this kind are published with the TXT record type instead.

explanation:
A CAA record is the mechanism for naming the certificate authorities that are allowed to provide certificates for a domain, and it carries exactly the three properties used here: Flags (0-255, carrying the critical flag), Tag, and Value. Because the request covers every host name in contoso.com, including names whose first label is an asterisk, the Tag must be the one that permits certificates of all types rather than only wildcard ones, and the record must sit at the zone apex so it applies to the whole domain. Flags = 0 with Tag = issue and Value = ca.contoso-cert.example at contoso.com therefore matches the request.

Why the other options are wrong:
- A CAA record set for contoso.com with Flags = 0, Tag = issuewild, Value = ca.contoso-cert.example: This option uses the tag that restricts authorities only for wildcard certificates. It would leave certificates for ordinary host names in contoso.com unrestricted, so it does not satisfy a request that covers every name in the domain.
- A CAA record set for contoso.com with Flags = 0, Tag = iodef, Value = ca.contoso-cert.example: This tag names a contact address that certificate authorities use to report unauthorized certificate requests. It tells nobody which authority may provide certificates, so the stated restriction would not be enforced.
- A TXT record set for contoso.com whose value is ca.contoso-cert.example: A TXT record simply publishes arbitrary text in the zone. `{
  "publicZone": "contoso.com - delegated to the Azure name servers",
  "internalZone": "corp.contoso.com - linked only to vnet-app (10.1.0.0/16) in West US",
  "linkSettingsForVnetApp": "Automatic registration of virtual machines is turned off; the entry for app.contoso.com (10.1.0.25) was added by hand",
  "secondInternalNetwork": "vnet-dr (10.20.0.0/16) in East US - not linked to any zone yet",
  "sessionServiceForContoso": "sip-gw.contoso.com - sessions accepted over TCP 5060",
  "thirdPartyVoiceProvider": "publishes a mapping for sip2.partner.net that rewrites the name into a contact URI",
  "domainValidationData": "1,200 characters long, supplied for contoso.com and submitted through the portal",
  "requestedZoneForAcquiredCompany": "fabrikam.local"
}`
prompt: Clients must discover where the session server for contoso.com lives and how to reach it.

options.text: Add an SRV record set whose name starts with the service and protocol labels, and set Priority, Weight, Port and Target on each record.
Add a NAPTR record set and fill in Order, Preference, Flags, Service, Regexp and Replacement.
Supply the value as a single entry and let Azure split it into 255-character segments; one record set can hold 4,096 characters in total.
Add a PTR record set that covers the private address space of the linked network.
Keep the zone as a global resource and link every network that must reach it.
Choose a suffix for the zone other than .local so that every client can resolve it.

explanation: Each slot maps to one Azure DNS capability. SRV records exist to point clients at service locations, so the SRV record set (with the service and transport encoded in the record set name and Priority, Weight, Port and Target set per record) satisfies the session-server discovery requirement. NAPTR records rewrite a name into a service URI and carry Order, Preference, Flags, Service, Regexp and Replacement, which matches the third party's published mapping. TXT records carry arbitrary text, each string may be up to 255 characters, the portal/PowerShell/CLI split a single string into 255-character segments automatically, and a TXT record set holds up to 4,096 characters in total, so the TXT handling satisfies the long validation-data requirement. PTR records provide reverse lookups in private DNS, which work only for the private IP space of the linked virtual network and return the host/record name with the zone name as the suffix, satisfying the 10.1.0.25 lookup. Private zone data is stored as a global resource, so one zone can be linked to virtual networks in different regions and stays available if service is interrupted in one of them, satisfying the multi-region and outage requirement. Finally, .local is not supported by all operating systems, so the requested fabrikam.local zone must use a different suffix.

an additional virtual network link from the on-premises network to the corp.contoso.com Azure Private DNS zone
Azure Traffic Manager
DNS Resolver Policy

explanation:
Resolving names between Azure and on-premises networks in both directions is conditional forwarding, and in Azure DNS that is provided by Azure DNS Private Resolver; a plain private zone only answers for the virtual networks linked to it, and an on-premises network cannot be linked to a zone that way, so an extra link cannot make the two environments resolve each other's names. The time to live is a property of a record set rather than of each individual record, so all records in the set share it; reducing it to 60 seconds on the record set that holds the public web host makes clients re-query within about a minute after the address is changed.

Why the other options are wrong:
- an additional virtual network link from the on-premises network to the corp.contoso.com Azure Private DNS zone: A private zone is resolved from a virtual network that is linked to it, and an on-premises network is not something you can link, so an additional link cannot make the on-premises server answer for the names published in Azure or make the Azure workloads answer for the names held on premises.
- Azure Traffic Manager: Azure Traffic Manager is a DNS-based traffic load balancer for public-facing applications spread across Azure regions; it distributes traffic for internet endpoints rather than relaying queries between Azure and on-premises networks.
- DNS Resolver Policy: DNS Resolver Policy filters and logs DNS queries at the virtual network level and can block names listed in the Threat Intelligence feed; it does not relay queries to an on-premises DNS server.

The tooling that publishes the token calls the Azure DNS REST API directly, and it currently offers the whole token as a single text value, which the service will not accept. What should the request contain, and which record set name should the token be published under?

`Public zone:                 contoso.com - delegated to the Azure name servers

prompt: The request should carry _____, and the record set should be named [...].

options.text: Three text values of 255 characters or fewer each in a single TXT record set
One text value of 600 characters in a single TXT record set
Three text values of 600 characters each in a single TXT record set
Three text values of 255 characters or fewer each in a single CNAME record set

explanation:
The token is 600 characters long, while a single DNS text value may be at most 255 characters. The portal, PowerShell and CLI accept one long string and divide it into shorter segments for you, but a direct REST API call requires every string to be supplied separately, so the tooling has to send three values, none longer than 255 characters, inside one TXT record set. The total of 600 characters is well inside the 4,096-character allowance for a single TXT record set. Because the provider queries the domain contoso.com rather than a host beneath it, the token belongs in the zone's root record set, written @; writing contoso.com as the relative name would produce contoso.com.contoso.com.

Why the other options are wrong:
- One text value of 600 characters in a single TXT record set: This offers the whole 600-character token as one value, which is above the 255-character maximum for a single text value. Only the portal, PowerShell and CLI divide a long string into shorter segments for you; a direct REST API call must supply each string separately.
- Three text values of 600 characters each in a single TXT record set: Each of the three values would be 600 characters long, above the 255-character maximum allowed for one text value, so the token has to be divided so that every value stays within that limit.
- Three text values of 255 characters or fewer each in a single CNAME record set: A CNAME record set carries an alias target rather than the provider's verification text, and it cannot be created at the zone root, which already holds the NS and SOA record sets.

explanation:
For the duplicate hosted zone, a zone name only has to be unique within its resource group, and the same name may be reused in another resource group or in another subscription; each instance of the zone is handed its own four name servers, and only one set of them can be configured at the registrar. For the partner's subdomain, the delegation is done with a separate NS record set, because the zone's own top-level NS record set is created and deleted with the zone and the Azure name servers pre-populated inside it cannot be removed or edited — other NS record sets, used to delegate a subdomain, carry no such restriction. For the signed zone, the DNSSEC-managed types DNSKEY, RRSIG and NSEC3 appear automatically when the zone is signed, and they cannot be created or modified afterwards.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The second zone is created and receives the same name server addresses as the first, so either set can be pointed at the registrar: Each instance of a hosted zone is given its own four name server addresses, so the copy in subscription B does not reuse the addresses of the zone in subscription A. The registrar can also be configured with only one of the two sets, so the claim that either set may be used there is wrong as well.
- The second zone is created and receives its own name server addresses, so both sets can be pointed at the registrar at the same time: The zone instances do each get their own name server addresses, but only one set can be configured at the registrar, so the two sets cannot both be pointed at it at the same time.
- The second zone cannot be created because a zone name must be unique across the whole subscription: A zone name must be unique within its resource group, but the same name can be reused in another resource group or in another subscription, so the copy in subscription B under rg-dns-dr can be created.

options.text: cannot be edited or removed
can be edited in place by a zone administrator

can only be changed through the domain registrar

explanation:
Both of these entries live at the top of the zone and are managed by the platform. The name server entry at the top of the zone is created with the zone and disappears with it, and the Azure name servers that the platform prepopulates inside it cannot be removed or modified, so it is not the place where a team can hand the domain over to its own servers; only the entry's TTL and metadata can be changed, and extra name servers can be added for co-hosting. The start-of-authority entry follows the same pattern for its lifecycle: it is created with the zone and deleted with it and has no separate create or delete operation. Its properties are editable with exactly one exception, the host value, which the platform preconfigures to the primary name server name (ns1-37.azure-dns.com in the exhibit), so the server name shown there is fixed while other values, such as the responsible mailbox or the serial number, remain changeable.

Why the other options are wrong:
- can be edited in place by a zone administrator: Administrative permissions do not lift the restriction: the Azure name servers prepopulated in the top-level entry cannot be removed or modified. Only the entry's TTL and metadata can be changed, and additional name servers may be added.
- can be removed, or replaced with an entry naming the in-house servers: The entry has no separate delete operation - it is removed only together with the zone - and the Azure name servers inside it cannot be removed or edited to name in-house servers instead.
- can only be changed through the domain registrar: Registrar settings decide which servers are authoritative for the domain, but they do not change what this zone permits: the prepopulated Azure name servers in the top-level entry still cannot be removed or modified.

options.text: can be published in the public zone, because an Azure private zone accepts only the A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, PTR, SOA, SRV and TXT record types

explanation:
The record that names the permitted certificate authority is a CAA record. Azure Private DNS supports the A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, PTR, SOA, SRV and TXT record types, so a CAA record set cannot be created in the private zone corp.contoso.com, and the proposal to add it there fails. A public zone supports CAA alongside the other common types, so the restriction for contoso.com belongs in the public zone that holds the domain.

Why the other options are wrong:
- can be published in the private zone rather than the public zone, because an Azure private zone accepts every record type that a public zone accepts: This claim that a private zone takes every record type a public zone takes is not correct: the types an Azure private zone supports are A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, PTR, SOA, SRV and TXT, and CAA is not among them, so the record cannot be added to corp.contoso.com.
- can be published in the private zone rather than the public zone, because an Azure private zone accepts the A, AAAA, CAA, CNAME, MX, NS, PTR, SOA, SRV and TXT record types: The list given here wrongly adds CAA and NS to the capabilities of a private zone. An Azure private zone supports A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, PTR, SOA, SRV and TXT, so the record that names the permitted certificate authority has to be published in the public zone instead.
- can be published in the private zone rather than the public zone, because an Azure private zone accepts the A, AAAA, CAA, CNAME, MX, NS, PTR, SOA, SRV, TXT and TLSA record types: This list is broader still, because TLSA is not a record type an Azure private zone supports either, and the real private zone set is A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, PTR, SOA, SRV and TXT. options.text: Developer tier
Basic tier

Premium tier

explanation:
The combination of requirements here needs the top tier: a deployment with no public IP on the bastion host (private-only architecture), capture of graphical RDP and SSH sessions that are stored in a blob container for later review, plus the native client with Microsoft Entra ID authentication. Session recording and the private-only deployment without a public IP are both available only in the Premium tier, and Premium also includes everything the Standard tier offers.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Developer tier: The Developer tier runs on shared infrastructure at no charge, but it handles a single VM at a time, is limited to selected regions, and is intended for development and testing. It offers neither session recording nor the native client, and it does not provide the private-only architecture.
- Basic tier: The Basic tier is a dedicated deployment with a fixed capacity of two instances, but it lacks the native client, shareable links, IP-based connections, custom ports and file transfer. It has no session recording, and a dedicated Basic deployment still requires a Standard SKU, statically allocated public IP address, so it cannot be deployed without one.
- Standard tier: The Standard tier adds the native client, shareable links, IP-based connections, custom ports, file transfer and host scaling, but it still requires a public IP address on the bastion host and it does not include session recording. Because the environment must run without a public IP on the host and must retain playback of graphical sessions, Standard alone is not sufficient.

- Keep the host on the Basic tier and supply port 53389 at connection time: Supplying the custom port at connection time is right, but the host in the exhibit runs the Basic tier, and custom inbound ports are supported only from the Standard tier upward. Basic also lacks the native client, shareable links, IP-based connections and file transfer, so the tier has to be raised before the custom port can be used.
- Keep the host on the Basic tier and supply port 3389 at connection time: This fails for two reasons: a Basic tier host does not support custom inbound ports, and WinServer01's RDP service is not listening on 3389, so a session supplied with the default port cannot succeed either.

Your company operates two separate virtual networks, Contoso-Core-VNet and Contoso-Spoke-VNet, and an Azure Bastion host named core-bastion-01 already serves the workload machines in Contoso-Core-VNet. The operations team now wants to reach the workload machines in Contoso-Spoke-VNet through that same host, so the team keeps running a single remote access setup, and the administrators also want to start their sessions from home rather than from the office. The current environment is shown below.

- Property: Resource group; Contoso-Core-VNet: rg-core; Contoso-Spoke-VNet: rg-spoke
- Property: Address space; Contoso-Core-VNet: 10.1.0.0/16; Contoso-Spoke-VNet: 10.2.0.0/16
- Property: Azure Bastion host; Contoso-Core-VNet: core-bastion-01 (Standard tier); Contoso-Spoke-VNet: none
- Property: Public IP address of the Azure Bastion host; Contoso-Core-VNet: core-bastion-pip (Standard, static); Contoso-Spoke-VNet: not applicable
- Property: Workload machines; Contoso-Core-VNet: 3 Windows, 1 Linux; Contoso-Spoke-VNet: 2 Windows, 2 Linux
- Property: Public IP address on the workload machines; Contoso-Core-VNet: none; Contoso-Spoke-VNet: none
prompt: To let the operations team reach the workload machines in Contoso-Spoke-VNet through the single host that already runs in Contoso-Core-VNet, your team should _____; so that the administrators can start those sessions from home, the inbound rule for the host's public IP address must allow [...] traffic.

options.text: Peer Contoso-Core-VNet with Contoso-Spoke-VNet
Add a public IP address to each workload machine in Contoso-Spoke-VNet
Deploy a second Azure Bastion host in Contoso-Spoke-VNet
Widen the AzureBastionSubnet of Contoso-Core-VNet to cover 10.2.0.0/16

explanation:
A single Azure Bastion deployment can serve workload machines in other virtual networks once those networks are linked, so peering Contoso-Core-VNet and Contoso-Spoke-VNet lets the existing host core-bastion-01 reach the spoke machines over their private addresses, which keeps one remote access setup instead of two. Client sessions terminate on the bastion host itself and are encrypted with TLS on port 443, so 443 is the only port that has to be open inbound on the host's public IP address for administrators working from home; RDP 3389 and SSH 22 are used on the hop from the host to the target machine, not by the client against the host.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add a public IP address to each workload machine in Contoso-Spoke-VNet: Giving the spoke machines public IP addresses would expose them directly to the internet and bypass the centralized remote access setup; the requirement is to reach them over their private addresses through the existing host.
- Deploy a second Azure Bastion host in Contoso-Spoke-VNet: A second host would give the team a working setup, but it contradicts the stated goal of running a single remote access setup and adds another resource to maintain and another set of hourly charges, since one deployment can serve several linked networks.
- Widen the AzureBastionSubnet of Contoso-Core-VNet to cover 10.2.0.0/16: The subnet reserved for the host must sit in the same virtual network as the host and may hold no other resources; it cannot be widened to swallow an address range that belongs to a different virtual network, and that range belongs to a separate network that must be linked instead.

Administrators start their remote sessions from the office and from home, either in the Azure portal or with the remote desktop software already installed on their laptops. Sessions started in the office reach the host but the session window to WinSrv01 never opens, while sessions started at home cannot reach the host at all. The network team has attached one network security group to the AzureBastionSubnet and another one to the network interface of WinSrv01, and the inbound rules currently configured on them are listed below. prompt: To restore those sessions, the network team should add _____ to the network security group on the AzureBastionSubnet and [...] to the network security group on the network interface of WinSrv01.

options.text: Allow inbound TCP 443 from the Internet
Allow inbound TCP 3389 from the Internet
Allow inbound TCP 22 from the Internet
Allow inbound TCP 80 from the Internet

explanation:
A remote session to a virtual machine travels over two hops. On the first hop the administrator's browser or native client contacts the bastion host's public address, and that connection is encrypted with TLS on port 443, so the network security group on the AzureBastionSubnet must allow inbound TCP 443 from the Internet; without it, sessions started outside the office range never reach the host. On the second hop the host opens the remote desktop session to WinSrv01 over the private addresses of the virtual network, which requires inbound TCP 3389 (the default RDP port for Windows targets) from the virtual network on the network security group attached to the target's network interface. The current rules on both groups only admit the office range, which explains why home sessions fail before reaching the host and why office sessions never get a window to WinSrv01.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Allow inbound TCP 3389 from the Internet: The desktop protocol port is used on the hop from the host to the target machine inside the virtual network, not on the hop where remote users contact the host over the Internet, so opening it to the Internet is unnecessary and exposes the target's protocol directly.
- Allow inbound TCP 22 from the Internet: Port 22 carries SSH sessions to a target machine; users do not open a session straight to the host with SSH, and the encrypted channel to the host is established on port 443.
- Allow inbound TCP 80 from the Internet: Port 80 serves unencrypted HTTP and is not the port used for the encrypted remote access channel to the host, which runs over TLS on port 443.

A dedicated deployment needs an address of Standard SKU with a Static allocation method, so removing it breaks the remote access path, and it does nothing to the workload machines.

prompt: You have a Standard Azure Load Balancer in the subscription contoso-prod that fronts a three-instance Linux web tier. Its single load balancing rule references the health probe shown below, and that probe was deployed from an ARM template. Since the template was applied, the load balancer has not delivered a single new client connection to any of the three instances, the Health Probe Status metric reads 0 for every backend IP address, and clients that already had a session keep it. You need new connections to reach the backends again. The probe must poll as often as the portal schedules probes by default, and the number of consecutive results required before an instance changes state must stay as it is today. Which change should you make?

options.text: Set the probe interval to 5 seconds and leave the threshold unchanged
Set the probe interval to 5 seconds and raise the threshold to 10
Leave the probe interval at 120 seconds and raise the threshold to 10
Leave the probe interval at 120 seconds and change the probe protocol to TCP

explanation:
An HTTP probe request is subject to a built-in 30-second timeout. This probe's interval is 120 seconds, which is longer than that timeout, so each probe times out and is recorded as failed even though the application answers /health with HTTP 200 in milliseconds when called directly. A failed probe only stops the load balancer from sending new connections to that instance, and with all three probes failing the Standard load balancer delivers no new flows while established TCP sessions survive — exactly the reported symptoms. Lowering the interval to 5 seconds (the cadence the portal applies by default, and also the smallest value Azure allows) lets each probe finish inside the timeout window, and keeping the threshold as it is preserves the current behaviour for how many consecutive results flip an instance's state.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Set the probe interval to 5 seconds and raise the threshold to 10: Lowering the interval is the right direction, but the threshold was not to be changed. Raising it to 10 only alters how many consecutive failures or silent probes are needed to flip the instance state; it cannot turn a probe that never completes within the timeout into a valid answer, and it contradicts the requirement to leave the threshold as it is.
- Leave the probe interval at 120 seconds and raise the threshold to 10: Leaving the interval at 120 seconds keeps every probe running past the 30-second timeout that applies to HTTP probes, so the probes keep timing out and failing and the instances never re-enter rotation for new connections. Raising the threshold merely delays the state change instead of making the probe succeed.
- Leave the probe interval at 120 seconds and change the probe protocol to TCP: A TCP probe has no built-in request timeout of its own — it is judged once the interval elapses and the next probe is sent — and keeping the 120-second cadence does not satisfy the requirement to poll at the portal's default frequency. Changing the protocol also replaces the application's own health verdict with a plain check that a listener accepted the connection, which is not the signal this workload relies on.

Averaging over the five-minute window means a single zero sample no longer drives the rule to zero, so brief dips do not page the team, while the split dimensions tell the engineer exactly which frontend IP and port stopped delivering traffic or which backend instance on which port stopped answering its probe.

With Count, one zero sample inside the five-minute window is enough for the condition of less than or equal to 0 to fire, so the team is paged for a one-minute dip, which contradicts the requirement.

A data path availability rule split by backend IP address and backend port never identifies the frontend that stopped delivering traffic, and a health probe status rule split by frontend IP address and frontend port never identifies the backend instance that stopped answering its probe, so neither page carries the information on-call needs.

It fronts two FortiGate network virtual appliances in active-active mode, and each appliance forwards traffic onward to a web tier of four Linux VMs. The single load balancing rule references the health probe shown below, and since the web VM named web-04 was stopped, that probe has been failing on both appliances. New client connections to the application no longer reach the web tier, even though three of the four web VMs are healthy and serving traffic. You need new client connections to keep reaching the web tier while a single web VM is stopped. Which change should you make?

options.text: Change the health probe protocol to TCP and the probe port to 443, so that each FortiGate appliance is no longer judged by the HTTP status returned after forwarding the request to one of the web VMs.
Set the probe threshold to 1 and the probe interval to 5 seconds, so that an appliance whose forwarded health check fails leaves the backend pool sooner.
Add an NSG rule to the appliance subnet allowing inbound traffic from 168.63.129.16 to the probe port on each FortiGate NIC, so both appliances accept the probe instead of dropping it.
Reconfigure the FortiGate appliances so that each one replies to the health probe locally on the NIC where the probe arrives, rather than forwarding the probe to the web VMs.

explanation:
Both appliances are currently answering the probe by forwarding it to a host behind them (member web-04 only), so stopping that one web VM turned every probe into an HTTP 502. After two consecutive failures the threshold removes both appliances from the backend pool, and a single unhealthy server cascades into an application outage. When a load balancer fronts a network virtual appliance, the probe must be answered by the appliance itself on the NIC where the probe arrives, and the appliance must not forward the probe to the VMs behind it. Once each FortiGate serves the probe on that NIC, the probe stays healthy, the appliances stay in the pool, and new client connections keep reaching the web tier while web-04 is stopped.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Change the health probe protocol to TCP and the probe port to 443, so that each FortiGate appliance is no longer judged by the HTTP status returned after forwarding the request to one of the web VMs: Changing the protocol or the port does not help, because the appliances would still be answering the probe by forwarding it to web-04, which is stopped; a TCP check against a stopped host fails just as an HTTP one does. What decides the outcome is which component replies to the probe, not the protocol or port it uses.
- Set the probe threshold to 1 and the probe interval to 5 seconds, so that an appliance whose forwarded health check fails leaves the backend pool sooner: Threshold and interval only control how quickly an instance is taken out of the pool once its probe fails; they cannot turn a failing probe into a successful one. Lowering the threshold to 1 would remove the appliances from the pool sooner and widen the outage.
- Add an NSG rule to the appliance subnet allowing inbound traffic from 168.63.129.16 to the probe port on each FortiGate NIC, so both appliances accept the probe instead of dropping it: The probe is already reaching both appliances — each one returns HTTP 502 instead of dropping the packet — and the NSG already permits probe traffic by default through the AzureLoadBalancer service tag. An extra rule for 168.63.129.16 changes nothing, and blocking that platform address on a production system is unsupported in any case.

prompt: You have a Standard internal Azure Load Balancer named lb-web-in in the subscription contoso-prod. It sits in front of three Ubuntu virtual machines that run nginx, and its single load balancing rule maps frontend port 443 to backend port 8443 on those machines. That rule references the health probe and the server configuration shown below. Since the probe was created, the Health Probe Status metric has read 0 for every backend IP address, no new client connection reaches the servers, and the few sessions that were already established keep running. You need new connections to be spread over the three machines again, and the team is not allowed to add or change anything on the machines themselves. Which change should you make?

options.text: Set the probe protocol to HTTPS and the probe port to 8443
Set the probe protocol to HTTP and the probe port to 8443
Set the probe protocol to HTTPS and the probe port to 443
Set the probe port to 8443 and the probe interval to 5 seconds

explanation:
The probe has to talk to the port the virtual machines actually listen on, and it has to use the same transport that port expects. The only listener on each machine is nginx on 8443 with TLS enabled, while the probe is a plain HTTP probe aimed at port 80, where nothing is listening. A plain HTTP probe never adds TLS, so it can never obtain a 200 answer from that listener (the TLS handshake fails or the port answers with a non-200 status, and either outcome counts as a failed probe). Because every probe attempt fails, all three instances stay out of rotation and the load balancer stops handing out new connections, while the sessions that were already open survive because a failed probe only removes an instance from receiving new traffic. Switching the probe to HTTPS on port 8443 makes it complete the TLS session and receive the 200 response for path /, so the instances return to the pool and new client connections are distributed over them again.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Set the probe protocol to HTTP and the probe port to 8443: Changing only the port leaves the probe as a clear-text HTTP probe. The listener on 8443 expects TLS, so an HTTP GET sent without TLS cannot return 200; the probe still fails, the instances stay marked unhealthy, and new connections are still not delivered.
- Set the probe protocol to HTTPS and the probe port to 443: The port has to be one the virtual machines really listen on, and no process listens on 443 on the backends; the frontend port only belongs to the load balancer. An HTTPS probe aimed at 443 gets no answer, so the probe fails and no instance returns to the pool.
- Set the probe port to 8443 and the probe interval to 5 seconds: Shortening the interval only makes the same mismatched probe run more often, so every attempt still fails and the instances remain out of rotation. The threshold counts consecutive results and cannot make a probe succeed; the protocol and target port are what must match the listener.

The behaviour seen in the exhibit is a tier difference, not a probe configuration problem. When every probe in the pool is down, a Standard load balancer keeps established TCP flows alive as long as the pool holds more than one backend instance, and it simply stops sending new flows, which matches the requirement that in-flight sessions finish while no new client connections are accepted. Basic behaves differently: all TCP flows expire when the probes are down, which is why every open session was cut during the simultaneous reboot. Moving the workload onto a Standard load balancer satisfies the requirement and also leaves behind the retired Basic tier.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Keep the Basic load balancer and add a second health probe with a lower threshold so established client sessions survive the outage: Adding another probe or lowering the threshold only affects how quickly an instance is marked up or down and how quickly it recovers; it does not change how the tier handles already-established TCP flows when every probe is down. On Basic those flows still expire, so the in-flight client sessions would still be cut.
- Keep the Basic load balancer and change the health probe protocol from HTTP to TCP so established client sessions survive the outage: HTTP and TCP probes are both supported on Basic, so switching the protocol only changes what the probe checks and the response it accepts. Neither protocol alters the treatment of established flows during a full probe outage, so the sessions would continue to be terminated.
- Keep the Basic load balancer and enable HA Ports on the load balancing rule so established client sessions survive the outage: HA Ports is a Standard-only capability and cannot be enabled on a Basic load balancer. It also changes how inbound ports are distributed across backends rather than controlling what happens to connections that are already established.

prompt: Available

options.text: The data path availability metric has reported 90% health or better
The data path availability metric has reported less than 90% but more than 25% health for at least two minutes
The data path availability metric has reported less than 25% health for at least two minutes
No data path availability information has reached the load balancer for the last 10 minutes

explanation: The Resource health entry for a Standard load balancer is recalculated every two minutes from the load balancer's data path availability reading. A reading of 90% or better means the resource is healthy, so the entry reads Available. A reading below 90% but above 25% that has held for at least two minutes means the entry reads Degraded, which points to platform or user-initiated events worth investigating. A reading below 25% held for at least two minutes means the entry reads Unavailable, with inbound connectivity largely lost. When no data path availability information has reached the load balancer for ten minutes the entry reads Unknown, which is a transient state that corrects itself as soon as data arrives.

prompt: You operate a Standard internal Azure Load Balancer named lb-app that fronts three Linux web VMs in the app VNet. An operations engineer must get a direct SSH session (TCP 22) into exactly one chosen VM, while HTTPS traffic on port 443 must keep being spread across the whole pool exactly as it is today. Which object should you add to the load balancer?

options.text: Add an inbound NAT rule that maps the frontend IP and port 22 to one backend instance in the app-pool.
Add a load balancing rule that maps frontend port 22 to backend port 22 across every instance in the app-pool.
Add an outbound rule that maps the frontend IP and port 22 to one backend instance in the app-pool.
Add a second load balancing rule for frontend port 22 and lower the health probe's unhealthy threshold until only the desired instance stays in rotation.

explanation:
An inbound NAT rule forwards a frontend IP and port to one named VM or scale set instance rather than to the whole pool. That matches the requirement: the SSH session reaches the chosen web VM on TCP 22 while the existing https-443 rule keeps distributing traffic across every instance in app-pool.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add a load balancing rule that maps frontend port 22 to backend port 22 across every instance in the app-pool: A load balancing rule spreads traffic across every healthy instance of the target pool, so SSH connections would land on whichever VM answers the probe rather than on the chosen one.
- Add an outbound rule that maps the frontend IP and port 22 to one backend instance in the app-pool: An outbound rule applies source network address translation to the instances a backend pool identifies so they can reach the internet; it does not forward a frontend port to one chosen instance.
- Add a second load balancing rule for frontend port 22 and lower the health probe's unhealthy threshold until only the desired instance stays in rotation: A second load balancing rule still distributes port 22 traffic across all healthy instances, and lowering the unhealthy threshold only removes instances from rotation; it never pins traffic to one instance.

prompt: You have deployed a Standard Azure Load Balancer named lb-web in the app VNet to front two Linux web VMs that serve an internet-facing portal. Since the deployment, external browsers hang on the HTTPS connection, even though the load balancer health probes report both VMs as healthy. You need external clients to reach the portal on port 443 again, without changing the application or the VMs. Which configuration change should you make?

options.text: Add a network security group rule that allows inbound traffic from the internet to the load balancer's public IP address on port 443
Add a network security group rule that allows inbound traffic from the virtual network to the load balancer's public IP address on port 443
Add a network security group rule that allows outbound traffic from the backend virtual machines to the internet on port 443
Remove the network security group from the subnet so that traffic to the load balancer's public IP address on port 443 is no longer filtered

explanation:
The Standard SKU behaves differently from the retired Basic SKU: Standard load balancers and their public IP addresses reject inbound connections unless a network security group explicitly permits them, and inbound is still blocked when no NSG exists on the subnet or NIC. In this deployment the only inbound permissions on nsg-app-subnet are for traffic sourced from the virtual network and from the AzureLoadBalancer service tag, followed by a deny-all for every other source, so connections from internet clients to 20.61.132.19:443 are dropped while the health probes (which originate from the platform, not from a client) keep succeeding. Adding an explicit allow rule for internet-sourced inbound traffic to the load balancer's public IP address on port 443 opens the path from external browsers to the backend pool without touching the application or the VMs.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add a network security group rule that allows inbound traffic from the virtual network to the load balancer's public IP address on port 443: This rule only opens the path for sources inside the virtual network. The subnet NSG already permits that traffic through AllowVnetInBound, and external browsers originate outside the virtual network, so they would still be stopped by the deny-all inbound rule. It therefore does not address the reported symptom.
- Add a network security group rule that allows outbound traffic from the backend virtual machines to the internet on port 443: An outbound permission governs connections leaving the virtual machines. The reported problem is with inbound connections from external browsers, so allowing egress on port 443 changes nothing for those clients.
- Remove the network security group from the subnet so that traffic to the load balancer's public IP address on port 443 is no longer filtered: Removing the NSG does not open the frontend. With the Standard SKU, inbound is closed unless an NSG permits it, and when no NSG exists at all on the subnet or NIC the traffic is still blocked, so detaching the NSG leaves external clients unable to connect.

Those VMs now also need to call a partner's SaaS API over the internet, and the partner's firewall only accepts requests that originate from the load balancer's public IP address 20.60.30.40. Which object should you add to lb-edge so the pool members can reach the partner API with that source address?

options.text: Add an inbound NAT rule to lb-edge that maps frontend port 22 to one VM in pool-app
Add a load balancing rule to lb-edge that maps frontend port 443 to all VMs in pool-app
Add an HA ports rule to lb-edge with protocol All and port 0 for pool-app
Add an outbound rule to lb-edge that covers all VMs in pool-app

explanation:
An outbound rule on a Standard load balancer applies outbound network address translation (NAT) to every instance the backend pool identifies, so traffic the pool members send to the internet leaves with the load balancer's public IP address as its source. Here lb-edge is already Standard with a Standard static public IP (20.60.30.40), the pool is IP-based, and no NAT gateway exists on the subnet, so adding an outbound rule for pool-app gives the VMs a source address the partner's firewall will accept while the existing port 443 rule continues to serve inbound clients. Outbound rules are a Standard SKU capability, which this deployment already satisfies.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add an inbound NAT rule to lb-edge that maps frontend port 22 to one VM in pool-app: An inbound NAT rule pins one frontend port to one specific instance and forwards incoming connections to that instance; it does not rewrite the source address of traffic the pool members originate, so the partner API would still see the VMs' private addresses.
- Add a load balancing rule to lb-edge that maps frontend port 443 to all VMs in pool-app: Load balancing rules apply to inbound traffic only, mapping a frontend IP and port to a backend port so connections are spread across the pool; they never translate the source address of traffic leaving the pool.
- Add an HA ports rule to lb-edge with protocol All and port 0 for pool-app: HA ports (protocol All, port 0) balance every TCP and UDP port of an internal Standard load balancer for network virtual appliances, and HA ports are not supported on a public load balancer; they also provide no address translation for internet-bound traffic.

prompt: You operate an internal Standard load balancer named lb-nva in the hub virtual network vnet-hub. It fronts two firewall appliances that run as an active-active pair; each one terminates encrypted tunnels to the on-premises network and forwards traffic to the workload virtual machines. Both appliances must keep receiving every TCP and UDP flow that arrives at the shared front end, so either one can carry the load and take over from the other, and the on-premises monitoring appliance sends ICMP echo requests to that front end and expects replies. Which component should you configure on lb-nva?

options.text: An HA ports rule, with protocol set to All and port set to 0
A load balancing rule, with protocol set to TCP and port set to 0
An inbound NAT rule, with protocol set to All and port set to 0
An outbound rule, with protocol set to All and port set to 0

explanation:
An HA ports rule is the component built for this scenario. It is a load balancing rule configured with protocol set to All and port set to 0, and a single rule then balances every TCP and UDP flow arriving on every port of an internal Standard load balancer, distributing traffic per flow across the pool members that the health probe reports as healthy. It also carries ICMP, which is what the on-premises monitoring appliance expects from 10.20.5.10, and it is the recommended pattern for network virtual appliances such as firewalls, VPNs and SD-WAN devices where defining a separate rule for each port is impractical. Because lb-nva is an internal Standard load balancer, this configuration is supported; HA ports is not available on public load balancers or on the retired Basic SKU.

Why the other options are wrong:
- A load balancing rule, with protocol set to TCP and port set to 0: A load balancing rule with protocol set to TCP and port set to 0 does not meet the requirement. A standard rule maps one frontend protocol and port to a backend pool and balances only traffic for that protocol and port; it would not distribute the appliance traffic on every TCP and UDP port, and load balancing rules do not carry ICMP except on an internal Standard load balancer with HA ports enabled.
- An inbound NAT rule, with protocol set to All and port set to 0: An inbound NAT rule forwards a frontend address and port to one specific virtual machine or scale set instance rather than spreading traffic across the pool, so it cannot give both appliances an equal share of the incoming flows. Inbound NAT rules also support only TCP and UDP, so they cannot carry the ICMP echo traffic the on-premises monitor relies on.
- An outbound rule, with protocol set to All and port set to 0: An outbound rule configures outbound network address translation so that pool instances can reach the internet or other endpoints. It governs egress from the pool members and has no effect on how inbound flows are distributed or on ICMP handling, so it does not satisfy the failover behaviour required for the appliance pair.

You are creating the load balancer with the Standard SKU (the Basic SKU is retired), and the subscription contains the following unused address resources. Which resource should you attach to the load balancer's front end?

options.text: pip-checkout-prod, assigned to the load balancer's frontend IP configuration

pip-legacy-checkout, assigned to the load balancer's frontend IP configuration
pip-checkout-dr, assigned to the load balancer's frontend IP configuration

pip-checkout-prod is a Standard SKU public IP with the fixed address 20.62.14.8, which is the address the fraud-scoring provider allows, so it can be used as the frontend IP configuration of the Standard load balancer. prompt: You operate a Standard internal Azure Load Balancer named lb-api in the virtual network vnet-app. It fronts six Linux VMs (vm-api-01 through vm-api-06) that serve an internal order API. After the last release, every backend instance is reported as unhealthy and no client traffic reaches the pool, even though the application team confirms that all six VMs are running normally. The only endpoint the application exposes on each VM is its encrypted listener on port 443; the plaintext listener was removed and you are not allowed to change the VMs or the application. You need the probe to exercise that encrypted endpoint itself and validate the application's health path, so that an instance whose application path is broken is pulled out of rotation while healthy instances stay in. Which change should you make to the health probe on lb-api?

options.text: Change the probe protocol to HTTPS and set the probe port to 443
Change the probe protocol to TCP and set the probe port to 443
Keep the probe protocol as HTTP and set the probe port to 443
Keep the probe protocol as HTTP on port 80 and increase the unhealthy threshold

explanation:
On the Standard SKU a health probe can use TCP, HTTP or HTTPS. Only an HTTP or HTTPS probe actually validates the application's health path, and because the VMs expose just one listener that speaks TLS on port 443, the probe has to speak the same encrypted protocol to reach the /healthz path. Setting the probe protocol to HTTPS with port 443 therefore exercises the same endpoint clients use, restores the pool, and still removes an instance whose application path is broken. A TCP probe would only confirm that the port accepts a connection, and an HTTP probe would fail against a TLS-only listener, so neither meets the requirement.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Change the probe protocol to TCP and set the probe port to 443: A TCP probe is only a connectivity check: it proves that something is listening on 443 but never exercises the application's health path on the encrypted endpoint, so it would report the instances as healthy without giving the required path validation.
- Keep the probe protocol as HTTP and set the probe port to 443: An HTTP probe sends a plaintext request and expects a plaintext response. The VMs expose only a TLS listener on port 443, so the request never completes successfully and every instance would continue to be reported as unhealthy.
- Keep the probe protocol as HTTP on port 80 and increase the unhealthy threshold: Port 80 no longer has a listener on any of the backend VMs, so a probe to that port cannot succeed no matter how the threshold is set. Raising the unhealthy threshold only changes how quickly an instance is removed from rotation; it does not make the probe reach the application.

The published contract is fixed: callers inside the network connect to the private address 10.20.5.15 on TCP 443, and a request must be able to be answered by any of the four VMs. The application on each VM accepts connections only on TCP 8443. Health probes report all four pool members as healthy, yet callers get an empty reply and the connection is closed as soon as it is accepted. You may not change the application or the callers. Which change should you make to lb-api?

options.text: Set the backend port of the load-balancing rule to 8443 so that traffic is sent to the application port on the backend instances
Set the frontend port of the load-balancing rule to 8443 so that the client traffic is sent to the application port on the backend instances
Set the backend port of the load-balancing rule to 443 and change the health probe to TCP 443 so that the probe traffic and the client traffic use the same port
Add an inbound NAT rule that forwards the frontend address and TCP 443 to one backend instance on port 8443

explanation:
A load-balancing rule maps a frontend IP configuration and frontend port to the backend addresses and ports of every instance in the target pool, so the rule's backend port has to be the port the application actually uses. Here the instances look healthy because the probe already queries TCP 8443, but the rule's backend port is still 443, so each flow is delivered to a port where nothing is listening and the connection is dropped. Add an outbound rule for the lb-web backend pool
Enable HA ports on the lb-web frontend

explanation: Each need is satisfied by one configuration change. options.text: Create a load balancer in the Global tier that has lb-book and lb-book-we in the backend pool.
Set the frontend IP configurations of lb-book and lb-book-we to zone-redundant.

explanation: Each keyed change answers one need. - Resource: lb-legacy; Details: Basic SKU; public address 20.71.9.9; fronts pool-legacy with 1 Windows server in vnet-edge; rule maps TCP 443 to backend port 443
- Resource: pip-modern; Details: Standard SKU; public address 20.71.9.12; not attached to any load balancer
- Resource: pip-legacy; Details: Basic SKU; public address 20.71.9.9; attached to lb-legacy
- Resource: lb-track; Details: Standard SKU; internal address 10.40.2.15; fronts pool-track with 4 Windows servers in vnet-ship; rule maps TCP 443 to backend port 8443; TCP probe on port 8443

prompt: Requirement A — the customer portal must stay reachable while one of the region's data centers is out of service

options.text: Enable a zone-redundant frontend IP configuration
Create a Standard load balancer with a Standard SKU public IP instead of the Basic public IP
Set Admin State to disabled on the affected backend member
Enable Private Link on the Standard internal load balancer
Attach the existing Basic public IP to the Standard load balancer
Create a Gateway SKU load balancer in front of the internal backend appliances

explanation: Requirement A is met by enabling a zone-redundant frontend IP configuration on the Standard public load balancer lb-shop: on the Standard tier a frontend IP configuration can be zone-redundant or zonal for inbound and outbound traffic, so the customer portal keeps serving traffic when one availability zone is lost, while the retired Basic tier offers no availability zone support. Requirement B is met by creating a Standard load balancer and pairing it with a Standard SKU public IP (pip-modern, 20.71.9.12): the Basic tier was retired on 30 September 2025 and a Basic public IP cannot be attached to a Standard load balancer, so the legacy deployment must be replaced rather than re-addressed. Requirement C is met by setting Admin State to disabled on the one server that needs maintenance: Admin State overrides health probe behaviour for an individual backend instance, so it stops taking new traffic while staying in the pool. Requirement D is met by enabling Private Link on the Standard internal load balancer lb-track: Private Link is a supported platform integration for Standard internal load balancers, which lets the branch office reach the internal service over a private connection instead of exposing it to the internet.

You operate a Standard internal Azure Load Balancer named lb-orders in the virtual network vnet-orders. It balances four Linux VMs — vm-orders-01, vm-orders-02, vm-orders-03 and vm-orders-04 — that host the internal order API. A failing disk means vm-orders-03 has to be patched during a maintenance window of about three hours. While that window is open, vm-orders-03 must not receive any new client connections, the other three VMs must keep serving every request exactly as before, and vm-orders-03 must stay registered with the load balancer. You may not change the application, the servers, or their network security rules; the change has to be made on the load balancer resource itself. Which setting should you change?

`{
  "loadBalancerName": "lb-orders",
  "sku": "Standard",
  "loadBalancerType": "internal",
  "frontendIpConfiguration": { "ipAddress": "10.20.7.12", "protocol": "TCP", "frontendPort": 443 },
  "backendPoolName": "pool-orders",
  "backendPoolServers": ["vm-orders-01", "vm-orders-02", "vm-orders-03", "vm-orders-04"],
  "healthProbe": { "name": "probe-orders", "protocol": "HTTP", "port": 8080, "path": "/healthz", "intervalSeconds": 15, "threshold": 3 },
  "loadBalancingRule": { "name": "rule-orders", "protocol": "TCP", "frontendPort": 443, "backendPort": 443 },
  "currentProbeResult": "all four VMs reporting healthy"
}`
prompt: To keep vm-orders-03 from taking new client connections during its patch window, you should change _____.

options.text: the Admin State of the affected backend pool instance
the health probe of the affected backend pool
the load balancing rule of the affected backend pool
the frontend IP configuration of the affected load balancer

explanation:
The Admin State setting is the per-instance override used for maintenance work: it overrides the load balancer's health probe verdict for one backend pool instance. Setting the Admin State of vm-orders-03's entry in pool-orders to Down stops the load balancer from delivering new connections to that single VM even though its probe still reports it as healthy, while the probe configuration, the load balancing rule, the frontend address and the other three VMs are left untouched and vm-orders-03 stays in the pool. Admin State only takes effect where a health probe is attached to the rule, which is the case for rule-orders. Afterwards the instance can be returned to service by clearing that Admin State or setting it back to None.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the health probe of the affected backend pool: This health probe belongs to the whole backend pool, so any change to it changes the health verdict for vm-orders-01 through vm-orders-04 together. It cannot single out one machine to stop taking new connections while the others keep serving.
- the load balancing rule of the affected backend pool: The load balancing rule maps the frontend address and port onto every VM in the pool, so changing it alters the delivery of traffic to all four machines rather than to the single machine being patched.
- the frontend IP configuration of the affected load balancer: The frontend IP configuration is the address that clients connect to; changing it would affect reachability of the whole order API and the traffic of all four VMs, not the routing to one machine.

The three backend VMs of the payment pool are placed one in each of the three availability zones of the region where the load balancer is being created. You need the frontend to keep accepting client connections and keep delivering traffic to healthy backends while a single availability zone in that region is unavailable. options.text: Zone-redundant

Zonal, pinned to availability zone 3

explanation:
On the Standard SKU the availability zone support type is set on the frontend IP configuration, and it can be either zone-redundant or zonal. A zone-redundant frontend IP configuration is served from infrastructure in the region's availability zones instead of being tied to one of them, so losing a single zone does not stop the load balancer from receiving and distributing traffic, while the health probes keep traffic only on healthy instances (here the pool has one VM per zone, so the VM in the failed zone is dropped and the others keep serving). A zonal frontend belongs to a single availability zone, so it offers no protection when that zone is unavailable and does not meet the requirement.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Zonal, pinned to availability zone 1: This option binds the frontend IP configuration to availability zone 1 only, so the frontend depends on that single zone and the requirement of staying reachable during one zone outage is not met.
- Zonal, pinned to availability zone 2: This option binds the frontend IP configuration to availability zone 2 only, so the frontend depends on that single zone and the requirement of staying reachable during one zone outage is not met.
- Zonal, pinned to availability zone 3: This option binds the frontend IP configuration to availability zone 3 only, so the frontend depends on that single zone and the requirement of staying reachable during one zone outage is not met.

- Property: Backend pool; Value: vm-web-01, vm-web-02, vm-web-03, vm-web-04 (NIC based)

prompt: To have every inbound request inspected by the appliance before it reaches the web servers, you should _____.

options.text: Create a Gateway SKU load balancer with the appliance VM in its backend pool, and chain lb-portal to it.
Create a Standard SKU load balancer with the appliance VM in its backend pool, and keep lb-portal in front of the web servers.
Create an inbound NAT rule on lb-portal that forwards the frontend IP and port 443 to the appliance VM.
Create a Gateway SKU load balancer with the appliance VM and the web servers in one backend pool, and keep lb-portal as it is.

explanation:
fw-vendor-01 is a third-party network virtual appliance, and Gateway is the Azure Load Balancer SKU dedicated to those appliances, while Standard is the general-purpose Layer 4 service. A Standard load balancer and a Gateway load balancer can be chained: the Standard public load balancer's frontend references the frontend IP configuration of the Gateway load balancer, so inbound traffic is handed to the appliance first and is then delivered onward to the consumer load balancer and its web servers, while clients keep using 20.61.14.9. The appliance VM belongs in the Gateway load balancer's backend pool, and the four web servers stay in lb-portal's pool.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Create a Standard SKU load balancer with the appliance VM in its backend pool, and keep lb-portal in front of the web servers: A Standard SKU load balancer spreads inbound traffic across every instance in its backend pool, so registering the appliance as one more pool member means some requests reach the web servers without ever passing through the appliance. The SKU dedicated to network virtual appliances is the Gateway one, and chaining a Standard load balancer to a Gateway load balancer is what inserts the appliance into the traffic path.
- Create an inbound NAT rule on lb-portal that forwards the frontend IP and port 443 to the appliance VM: An inbound NAT rule forwards a frontend IP and port to one specific instance in the backend pool. It is for single-instance access such as SSH or RDP, not for placing an appliance in the traffic path, and requests it sends to the appliance would not then be balanced on to the four web servers.
- Create a Gateway SKU load balancer with the appliance VM and the web servers in one backend pool, and keep lb-portal as it is: The Gateway SKU is dedicated to network virtual appliances, so the application web servers do not belong in its backend pool; they must stay behind the Standard public load balancer. This option also leaves lb-portal unchanged, so no reference from the public frontend points at the appliance load balancer and inbound requests are never inspected.

context:
You publish a home-improvement retailer's customer portal to the internet through a Standard public load balancer named lb-storefront. The four backend VMs behind that portal sit in the availability set aset-web and are added to lb-storefront's backend pool by their network interfaces. The business now wants a second, separate service — a returns portal — built on three new Windows VMs that are already deployed and that must remain in aset-web. The returns portal has to be reachable on its own public address through its own load balancer, while the customer portal keeps serving traffic exactly as it does today, and the portal VMs cannot be moved, removed or repurposed. Which configuration should you apply to the new load balancer and its backend pool?

`Resource              Type                             Details
-------------------  -------------------------------  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
lb-storefront        Standard public load balancer    Backend pool type: NIC based; frontend public address 20.10.4.7; publishes the customer portal
aset-web             Availability set                Contains vm-store-01 to vm-store-04 and vm-returns-01 to vm-returns-03
vm-returns-01..03    Windows Server 2022 VMs          No public addresses; must remain members of aset-web
lb-returns           Standard public load balancer    Not created yet; must publish the returns portal on its own public address`
prompt: To publish the returns portal from its own load balancer while leaving the customer portal untouched, the team must _____.

options.text: set lb-returns backend pool type to IP-based
set lb-returns backend pool type to NIC-based
set lb-returns backend pool type to NIC-based and move the returns VMs to another availability set
set lb-returns backend pool type to NIC-based and place the returns VMs in a separate resource group

explanation:
Load balancers are counted against an availability set according to how their backend pool is built: only one public load balancer with a network-interface-based backend pool is permitted per availability set (and likewise one internal one), and that restriction does not apply to load balancers whose backend pool is built from the addresses of the instances. Because lb-storefront already occupies the single public NIC-based slot for aset-web, the new load balancer lb-returns has to use an IP-based backend pool to be created alongside it for the returns VMs, which stay in aset-web.

Why the other options are wrong:
- set lb-returns backend pool type to NIC-based: This produces a second public load balancer for aset-web whose backend pool is network-interface based, exceeding the limit of one public NIC-based load balancer per availability set that lb-storefront already occupies.
- set lb-returns backend pool type to NIC-based and move the returns VMs to another availability set: Moving the returns VMs to another availability set contradicts the requirement that they remain in aset-web, and as long as lb-returns keeps a network-interface-based backend pool it still counts against the per-availability-set limit.
- set lb-returns backend pool type to NIC-based and place the returns VMs in a separate resource group: Changing resource groups does not change availability set membership, and the returns VMs are required to stay in aset-web, so lb-returns would still be a second public load balancer with a network-interface-based pool tied to that availability set.
