A retail group publishes the same ordering service from two Azure regions. Each region already has its own public load balancer in front of the virtual machines that serve the application, and customers today must use a different address for each region. The business now wants one static public address that every customer uses, with each customer session served by the nearest regional deployment and a region that fails dropped from service automatically. The two regional load balancers must keep their current addresses and rules, and no virtual machine or application may be changed. Which configuration should you create?

`Current deployments

lb-west   (West US)       Public Standard load balancer
                           frontend address 20.61.8.24
                           backend pool: 4 virtual machines in vnet-west

lb-eu     (North Europe)  Public Standard load balancer
                           frontend address 20.60.115.9
                           backend pool: 4 virtual machines in vnet-eu

Customer requirement
                           One static public address for every customer
                           Each session served by the nearest regional deployment
                           A failed region leaves service automatically`
prompt: To give all customers a single address that spans both regions, _____.

options.text: Create a new public Standard load balancer with the Global tier and place the two regional load balancers in its backend pool
Create a new public Standard load balancer in West US and add the virtual machines from the North Europe deployment to its backend pool
Create a new internal load balancer with the Global tier and place the two regional load balancers in its backend pool
Change the SKU of the two regional load balancers to the Global tier so their existing frontend addresses serve all customers

explanation:
A single public entry point that sends each customer to the nearest regional deployment and drops a failed region from service is what the Global tier of Azure Load Balancer provides for public Standard load balancers. You create a new load balancer in the Global tier and add the two existing regional load balancers to its backend pool, so their addresses, rules and virtual machines stay exactly as they are. The regional deployments themselves are never converted; they are linked from the new global one.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Create a new public Standard load balancer in West US and add the virtual machines from the North Europe deployment to its backend pool: A regional public Standard load balancer balances only virtual machines or scale set instances from a single virtual network in its own region, so the North Europe virtual machines cannot join the backend pool of a load balancer in West US, and a plain Standard load balancer does not distribute traffic between regions.
- Create a new internal load balancer with the Global tier and place the two regional load balancers in its backend pool: Global tier front ends are public only; an internal front end is not supported on such a load balancer, so it could never give customers the public address they must use.
- Change the SKU of the two regional load balancers to the Global tier so their existing frontend addresses serve all customers: Regional load balancers cannot be upgraded to the Global tier - a Global tier load balancer has to be created as a separate resource - and each of the two regional load balancers would keep serving only its own region instead of one shared entry point.

prompt: The frontend should be created with _____, and the health probe should be adjusted with [...].

options.text: The Basic SKU public IP on a Standard SKU load balancer
The Standard SKU public IP on a Standard SKU load balancer
The Standard SKU public IP on a Basic SKU load balancer
The Basic SKU public IP on a Basic SKU load balancer

explanation:
The new load balancer has to be a Standard SKU public load balancer: the Basic SKU was retired on 30 September 2025 and never supported outbound rules, so only Standard can publish the portal to the internet and at the same time give the checkout VMs outbound connectivity through the load balancer's own address. A public Standard load balancer requires a Standard public IP address, so pip-store-b is the only address resource in the subscription that can be attached to the frontend, while pip-store-a uses the Basic SKU and is rejected as a SKU mismatch. For the probe, the unhealthy threshold is the setting that decides when an instance is pulled out of rotation. Raising it keeps a VM in the pool while it is briefly restarting, and a VM whose application never returns is still removed once the higher number of consecutive probe failures is reached.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The Basic SKU public IP on a Standard SKU load balancer: A Basic SKU public IP cannot be attached to a Standard SKU load balancer, so the frontend would still be rejected because the public IP SKU and the load balancer SKU must match.
- The Standard SKU public IP on a Basic SKU load balancer: A Standard SKU public IP cannot be attached to a Basic SKU load balancer, and the Basic SKU was retired on 30 September 2025, so it is not an option for this deployment.
- The Basic SKU public IP on a Basic SKU load balancer: The Basic SKU was retired on 30 September 2025 and it never supported outbound rules, so this combination cannot satisfy both the internet-facing publishing and the outbound requirements for the checkout VMs.

prompt:
You have a three-tier application running in the virtual network vnet-prod. The network security group nsg-tier is associated with subnet app-subnet, which holds every virtual machine of the application: vm-web (its network interface is a member of asg-web), vm-api (member of asg-api), vm-db (member of asg-db), and vm-tools, whose network interface belongs to no application security group. The rules currently configured in nsg-tier are listed in the exhibit.

You need internet clients to reach vm-web on TCP 443, and you need vm-api to call vm-web on TCP 8443, while no other source - including virtual machines inside vnet-prod that are not members of an application security group - may open TCP 8443 to vm-web. Today vm-tools can still open TCP 8443 to vm-web.

Which single change to nsg-tier meets all of these requirements?

options.text: Add an inbound deny rule with source Any, destination asg-web, and destination port 8443, using a priority number greater than 110.
Add an inbound deny rule with source Any, destination asg-web, and destination port 8443, using a priority number lower than 110.
Add an outbound deny rule with source Any, destination asg-web, and destination port 8443, using a priority number greater than 110.
Add an inbound deny rule with source Any, destination asg-web, and destination port 443, using a priority number greater than 110.

explanation:
Custom rules are inspected in priority order and processing stops at the first rule that matches, while the platform defaults occupy 65000-65500 and are therefore always evaluated after custom rules. Placing a new inbound deny rule for source Any, destination asg-web and destination port 8443 at a priority above 110 (for example 120) keeps the required asg-api to asg-web path working, because that traffic still matches the allow rule at 110 first. Any other source, including vm-tools inside vnet-prod, no longer falls through to the built-in AllowVNetInBound rule at 65000 and is instead rejected by the new deny rule. The rule is scoped to port 8443, so the internet path to vm-web on 443 is unaffected, and scoping the destination to asg-web keeps the rule limited to the web tier's members.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add an inbound deny rule with source Any, destination asg-web, and destination port 8443, using a priority number lower than 110: A deny rule at a priority below 110 is inspected before the allow rule at 110, so it would also reject the traffic from asg-api to asg-web on 8443 and break the required API-to-web path. The deny must be evaluated after that allow rule, not before it.
- Add an outbound deny rule with source Any, destination asg-web, and destination port 8443, using a priority number greater than 110: Outbound rules govern traffic leaving the protected resources, so an outbound deny does not stop vm-tools from opening an inbound 8443 session to vm-web. Network security groups are stateful, so restricting the outbound side does not close the inbound connection either.
- Add an inbound deny rule with source Any, destination asg-web, and destination port 443, using a priority number greater than 110: The unprotected path is on TCP 8443, so scoping the deny to 443 leaves 8443 open; vm-tools still matches the built-in AllowVNetInBound rule at 65000 for that port and keeps reaching the web tier.

The network security group nsg-app is associated with app-subnet, and the virtual machine vm-app1, which runs an order-processing application, has its network interface in that subnet. The custom and built-in rules that nsg-app currently contains are listed in the exhibit.

The partner that processes the orders exposes its API at 203.0.113.10, listening on TCP 8443. Every call from vm-app1 to that endpoint fails today, while the application's package downloads over TCP 443 keep working. Once the calls succeed, the partner's responses have to reach vm-app1, and traffic from this subnet to any other destination on TCP 8443 must stay blocked.

Which single rule should you add to nsg-app?

options.text: An outbound Allow rule with priority 120 that permits TCP 8443 to 203.0.113.10.
An inbound Allow rule with priority 120 that permits TCP 8443 from 203.0.113.10.
An outbound Allow rule with priority 500 that permits TCP 8443 to 203.0.113.10.
An outbound Allow rule with priority 120 that permits TCP 443 to 203.0.113.10.

explanation:
The call to the partner is blocked today because the request from vm-app1 to 203.0.113.10:8443 is evaluated against the outbound rules: Allow-Package-Repo (priority 110) only covers TCP 443, so evaluation continues and Deny-Other-Outbound (priority 200) matches and drops it, ahead of the built-in AllowInternetOutBound default. Adding an outbound Allow rule for TCP 8443 to 203.0.113.10 with priority 120 - a lower number, so it is evaluated before 200 - permits the call, and naming the partner address keeps other outbound traffic on 8443 blocked. Why the other options are wrong:
- An inbound Allow rule with priority 120 that permits TCP 8443 from 203.0.113.10: This rule only governs traffic arriving at the resource. The request that vm-app1 sends to the partner is evaluated against the outbound rules, where Deny-Other-Outbound at priority 200 still matches and stops it, so the calls continue to fail.
- An outbound Allow rule with priority 500 that permits TCP 8443 to 203.0.113.10: Rules are evaluated in priority order and evaluation stops at the first match. With priority 500 the new rule is evaluated after Deny-Other-Outbound at priority 200, so the deny rule matches first and the request is dropped before the new rule is considered.
- An outbound Allow rule with priority 120 that permits TCP 443 to 203.0.113.10: The partner API listens on TCP 8443, so a rule for TCP 443 never matches the request traffic and Deny-Other-Outbound at priority 200 still blocks it. A recent audit found that a separate virtual machine inside vnet-hub, which has no connection to the corporate network, can also open RDP sessions to the management virtual machines. You need RDP over TCP 3389 to keep working for the corporate range, and you need all other sources, including virtual machines inside vnet-hub, to be unable to open TCP 3389 to the management virtual machines. Which single change to nsg-mgmt meets both requirements?

options.text: Add a deny rule for TCP 3389 from all sources at priority 200, so the existing allow rule at priority 100 is evaluated first for the corporate range.
Add a deny rule for TCP 3389 from all sources at priority 50, so the deny is evaluated before the existing allow rule at priority 100 for the corporate range.
Change the existing allow rule at priority 100 so its source for TCP 3389 becomes * instead of the corporate range, which keeps RDP available to every source.
Change the priority of the existing allow rule for TCP 3389 from 100 to 66000, so it is evaluated after the default rules for the corporate range.

explanation:

- Add a deny rule for TCP 3389 from all sources at priority 50, so the deny is evaluated before the existing allow rule at priority 100 for the corporate range: A deny rule at priority 50 carries a lower priority number than the allow rule at priority 100, so it is evaluated first and drops the corporate traffic as well, breaking the administrator access that must keep working. The new rule needs a higher priority number than the existing allow rule so that the allow rule is the one that matches for the corporate range.
- Change the existing allow rule at priority 100 so its source for TCP 3389 becomes * instead of the corporate range, which keeps RDP available to every source: Changing the source of the existing allow rule from the corporate range to * (Any) opens TCP 3389 to every source, which is the opposite of what is required. That rule already limits RDP to the corporate range; the extra access comes from the default rule permitting traffic between resources in the same virtual network, which is evaluated later and cannot be edited.
- Change the priority of the existing allow rule for TCP 3389 from 100 to 66000, so it is evaluated after the default rules for the corporate range: Custom rule priorities must be unique and fall between 100 and 4096, so 66000 is not a usable value; the 65000 to 65500 range belongs to the platform's default rules, which cannot be edited or deleted. options.text: One augmented rule containing several explicit source IP addresses and several destination ports
One augmented rule containing several source service tags and several destination ports
One augmented rule containing several source application security groups and several destination ports
One augmented rule containing several source service tags and several source application security groups

explanation:
An augmented security rule can combine several explicit source addresses (or ranges) and several ports into a single custom rule, so nsg-edge can hold the two partner allowances for TCP 443 and TCP 8443 in one inbound rule. Augmented rules are available here because the exhibit shows nsg-edge was created with the Resource Manager deployment model. Service tags and application security groups cannot be multiplied within a single rule, which is what disqualifies the other combinations.

Why the other options are wrong:
- One augmented rule containing several source service tags and several destination ports: This option asks for several service tags in the source of one rule. A single rule can't specify multiple service tags, so they can't be bundled together, augmented or otherwise.
- One augmented rule containing several source application security groups and several destination ports: This option asks for several application security groups in the source of one rule. The same restriction applies to application security groups: one rule can't specify multiple of them, so they can't be packed into a single rule.
- One augmented rule containing several source service tags and several source application security groups: This option asks for multiple service tags and multiple application security groups in the same rule. Neither multiple service tags nor multiple application security groups can be specified in a single rule, so no augmented rule can hold these values.

Two virtual machines run in app-subnet: vm-web, whose network interface is a member of the application security group asg-web, and vm-api, whose network interface is not a member of any application security group. The rules currently defined in nsg-shop are listed in the exhibit.

The team needs shoppers on the internet to reach the storefront that runs on vm-web over TCP 443, and vm-web has to be able to answer them.

Which statement about the traffic that nsg-shop permits is correct?

options.text: A shopper on the internet can open a TCP 443 session to vm-web, and vm-web can send the responses for that session.
A shopper on the internet can open a TCP 443 session to vm-web, but vm-web cannot send the responses for that session.
A shopper on the internet cannot open a TCP 443 session to vm-web, and vm-web cannot send the responses for that session.
A shopper on the internet can open a TCP 443 session to vm-api, and vm-api can send the responses for that session.

explanation:
The custom inbound rule at priority 100 uses the Internet service tag as source, asg-web as destination, and TCP 443 as the service, so it is evaluated before the default rules and permits a shopper to open a session to vm-web, whose network interface is a member of asg-web. The answers are not blocked afterwards: network security groups are stateful, so the reply to an allowed inbound connection is permitted without an extra rule, and the default AllowInternetOutBound rule at priority 65001 also allows outbound traffic to the Internet destination.

Why the other options are wrong:
- A shopper on the internet can open a TCP 443 session to vm-web, but vm-web cannot send the responses for that session: The replies are not blocked. Because the group is stateful, once the inbound session has been allowed the reply traffic for that session is permitted without a separate outbound rule, and the default AllowInternetOutBound rule at priority 65001 permits outbound traffic to the Internet destination in any case.
- A shopper on the internet cannot open a TCP 443 session to vm-web, and vm-web cannot send the responses for that session: The custom allow rule at priority 100 is processed before the default DenyAllInbound rule at priority 65500, and its source, destination and service all match the shopper's request to vm-web, so the session is established and the responses are returned.
- A shopper on the internet can open a TCP 443 session to vm-api, and vm-api can send the responses for that session: The allow rule at priority 100 targets the asg-web destination, and vm-api's network interface is not a member of that group, so the rule does not apply to it. No other inbound rule allows the Internet source to reach vm-api on TCP 443, so the default DenyAllInbound rule blocks that traffic.

You run an internal Azure Load Balancer named ilb-web that sends client traffic to the virtual machines vm-app1 and vm-app2, which live in subnet svc-subnet of the virtual network vnet-scale. The load balancer is configured with a health probe on TCP 8080, and the Azure portal currently reports both backend instances as unhealthy. The network security group nsg-web is associated with svc-subnet, and its inbound rules are listed in the exhibit.

You need the health probes to succeed so that the backends start receiving traffic, and clients outside the virtual network must not be able to open TCP 8080 directly to vm-app1 or vm-app2.

Which single change to nsg-web restores the health probes?

options.text: Add a custom inbound rule with a priority lower than 200 that allows TCP 8080 from the AzureLoadBalancer service tag.
Edit the built-in rule AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound at priority 65001 so that its destination port becomes 8080.
Add a custom inbound rule with a priority of 4096 that allows TCP 8080 from the AzureLoadBalancer service tag.
Add a custom inbound rule with a priority lower than 200 that allows TCP 8080 from Any source.

explanation:
Rules are processed in priority order, and processing stops at the first rule whose attributes match the traffic. The custom deny for TCP 8080 at priority 200 is therefore evaluated before the built-in AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound rule at 65001, so probe traffic is dropped before the built-in allowance is ever reached, which is why both backends are reported unhealthy. Adding a new custom inbound rule that allows TCP 8080 from the AzureLoadBalancer service tag, with a priority number lower than 200, makes that allowance the first match for probe traffic, so the probes succeed. Every other source on TCP 8080 still fails to match the new rule and continues to the deny at priority 200, so clients outside the virtual network remain unable to open that port directly to the backends.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Edit the built-in rule AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound at priority 65001 so that its destination port becomes 8080: The built-in default rules cannot be opened, changed, or removed in the portal; only custom rules can be edited or deleted. In addition, a change made at priority 65001 would still be evaluated after the custom deny at priority 200, so probe traffic would be dropped before reaching that rule and the probes would stay unhealthy.
- Add a custom inbound rule with a priority of 4096 that allows TCP 8080 from the AzureLoadBalancer service tag: A priority of 4096 is inside the permitted 100-4096 range, but the lower number is processed first, so evaluation reaches the deny rule at priority 200 and stops there. The new allowance at 4096 is never consulted for this traffic, so the probes remain blocked.
- Add a custom inbound rule with a priority lower than 200 that allows TCP 8080 from Any source: Allowing TCP 8080 from Any source opens that port to every address, including clients outside the virtual network, so the requirement that only the load balancer's probe traffic may reach the backends on 8080 is broken. The source of the allowance has to be restricted to the load balancer.

prompt: You manage the virtual networks vnet-hub and vnet-spoke with Azure Virtual Network Manager. The subnet app-subnet in vnet-spoke is protected by the network security group nsg-spoke, and the exhibit lists the security admin rule configuration that applies to vnet-spoke together with the rules defined in nsg-spoke. A host on the internet tries to open a TCP 22 session to the virtual machine vm-app1, whose network interface is in app-subnet. The team needs to document which control decides the result of that attempt. Which statement correctly describes the outcome?

options.text: The security admin rule stops the traffic, so none of the rules in nsg-spoke are evaluated.
The security admin rule hands the traffic to nsg-spoke, where Allow-SSH-From-Any at priority 100 permits the session.
The security admin rule hands the traffic to nsg-spoke, where DenyAllInbound at priority 65500 blocks the session.
The security admin rule is superseded by Allow-SSH-From-Any at priority 100, because custom rules in a network security group are evaluated ahead of built-in rules.

explanation:
Security admin rules pushed down by Azure Virtual Network Manager are evaluated ahead of network security group rules. When the matching admin rule carries the Deny action, evaluation of that connection ends at the admin rule and the packets are discarded without ever being handed to the NSG on the subnet. The custom allow rule at priority 100 in nsg-spoke therefore has no bearing on this attempt. Handing a connection on to NSG evaluation is the behavior of an admin rule whose action is Allow, and Always allow bypasses the NSG altogether by delivering the traffic straight to the destination.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The security admin rule hands the traffic to nsg-spoke, where Allow-SSH-From-Any at priority 100 permits the session: Passing a connection on to the NSG is what an admin rule with the Allow action does. The rule in the exhibit uses the Deny action, so evaluation ends at the security admin rule and nsg-spoke is never consulted, which means Allow-SSH-From-Any at priority 100 plays no part in the result.
- The security admin rule hands the traffic to nsg-spoke, where DenyAllInbound at priority 65500 blocks the session: The built-in DenyAllInbound rule at priority 65500 can only decide the outcome if the NSG is evaluated, and the security admin rule with the Deny action ends evaluation before that happens. Even if the NSG were evaluated, the custom rule at priority 100 would match first and permit TCP 22 from any source.
- The security admin rule is superseded by Allow-SSH-From-Any at priority 100, because custom rules in a network security group are evaluated ahead of built-in rules: Custom rules being evaluated ahead of built-in rules is correct within an NSG, but it does not apply here: the security admin rule ends the evaluation before the NSG is consulted, so the allow rule at priority 100 cannot influence this attempt and cannot supersede the admin rule.

You have a virtual network vnet-corp with a single subnet, mail-subnet, that holds the virtual machine vm-biz. The network security group nsg-mail is associated with mail-subnet, and the configuration that is currently in place is shown in the exhibit. The application on vm-biz sends transactional email to customers, and company policy requires that every message be submitted through the authenticated SMTP relay at 198.51.100.45, which accepts submissions on TCP 587; direct submission to outside mail servers is not permitted. Today vm-biz downloads packages over TCP 443 without trouble, but every attempt to reach 198.51.100.45 on TCP 587 times out, and the team does not want outbound traffic to the rest of the internet opened up along the way.

Which change to nsg-mail should you make?

options.text: Add an inbound security rule with source 198.51.100.45, destination Any, service Custom, destination port 587, protocol TCP, action Allow, priority 100.
Add an outbound security rule with source Any, destination 198.51.100.45, service Custom, destination port 587, protocol TCP, action Allow, priority 100.
Add an outbound security rule with source Any, destination 198.51.100.45, service Custom, destination port 587, protocol TCP, action Allow, priority 250.
Add an outbound security rule with source Any, destination Any, service Custom, destination port 25, protocol TCP, action Allow, priority 100.

explanation:
The mail submission is a connection that vm-biz itself opens, so the new rule has to be an outbound rule whose destination is the relay address and whose destination port is the port the relay listens on. The custom rule at priority 210 denies all other internet-bound outbound traffic, and rules are processed in ascending priority order with evaluation stopping at the first match, so the new allowance must sit at a lower priority number than 210 - priority 100 is unused and is evaluated first, while every other internet destination stays denied by the rule at 210. Because network security groups are stateful, the relay's replies are permitted automatically once the outbound flow is allowed, so no inbound rule is needed for the response traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add an inbound security rule with source 198.51.100.45, destination Any, service Custom, destination port 587, protocol TCP, action Allow, priority 100: This grants permission to traffic arriving at vm-biz, but the session towards the relay is started by vm-biz. An inbound allowance does not permit the outbound request, so every submission to the relay keeps timing out.
- Add an outbound security rule with source Any, destination 198.51.100.45, service Custom, destination port 587, protocol TCP, action Allow, priority 250: Priority 250 is evaluated after the custom deny on all other internet-bound outbound traffic at priority 210, and processing stops at the first matching rule, so this allowance is never reached for traffic on TCP 587. The submissions keep failing, and 100 (or any other unused number below 210) is what has to be used.
- Add an outbound security rule with source Any, destination Any, service Custom, destination port 25, protocol TCP, action Allow, priority 100: This opens outbound TCP 25 to every internet destination instead of limiting traffic to the relay on TCP 587, which breaks the company requirement to submit only through the relay. It also would not deliver mail anyway, because Azure blocks direct outbound SMTP on TCP 25 for Pay-as-you-go subscriptions, and a network security group rule cannot lift that platform restriction.

The standard outbound rules still permit sessions to public services, and the new block covers only that one address on that one port, so the update sessions over TCP 443 keep working with no extra rule.

Creating or updating a network security group is governed by the create-or-update action for the group itself, Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/write, and creating or updating a rule inside it is governed by the separate rule action, Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/securityRules/write. The role in the exhibit carries only the read actions for both, which is why the portal displays the group and its rules but rejects every attempt to save; in addition, the account performing the change needs read access on the resource group. - Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/read: The read action only lets the team open the group and look at its rules; it never authorizes a change, so every save in the portal still fails with an authorization error.
- Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/delete: This action removes an existing group. It does not authorize creating one or changing one, so the team would still be unable to save the groups it is asked to manage.
- Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/join/action: This action associates an existing group with a subnet or a network interface. It does not authorize creating or updating the group itself, so it does not fix the rejected saves.

context:
You have a virtual network vnet-lab with one subnet, lab-subnet, that holds the virtual machines vm-a and vm-b. The network security group nsg-lab is associated with lab-subnet, and the exhibit lists what nsg-lab contains today. A corporate policy states that the workloads in this subnet must not use the name resolution service that the platform provides. The team tried to enforce this with a custom outbound rule that denies UDP port 53 to every destination, but vm-a still resolves host names, and its package downloads over TCP 443 keep working.

The team now wants to add one more rule that stops those lookups. That rule has to block them whatever transport they travel on, because the resolver also answers over TCP when a reply does not fit into a single datagram, and it must leave the way package downloads are handled exactly as it is today.

Which values should the new rule use?

`Item                           Value
Network security group         nsg-lab, associated with subnet lab-subnet of virtual network vnet-lab
Machines in lab-subnet         vm-a, vm-b
Custom outbound rule in nsg-lab  Block-Lookups: source *, destination *, protocol UDP, destination port 53, priority 200
Observed today                 vm-a resolves host names for its partner API; package downloads over TCP 443 succeed`
prompt: The new rule's destination should be _____ and its protocol should be [...].

options.text: AzurePlatformDNS
AzurePlatformIMDS
AzurePlatformLKM
VirtualNetwork

explanation:
Traffic that the platform itself uses, including the name resolution traffic the workloads send to the platform's resolver, is not evaluated by the rules of the network security group unless one of the platform service tags is named. That is why the existing Block-Lookups rule, which denies UDP 53 to every destination, never touches those queries and vm-a keeps resolving host names. Naming AzurePlatformDNS as the destination is what brings that resolver traffic into scope for evaluation, and choosing the Any protocol makes the rule match the lookups over UDP as well as over the TCP fallback, so no lookup path stays open. Because the destination is limited to the name resolution service tag, the rule does not affect the TCP 443 package downloads.

Why the other options are wrong:
- AzurePlatformIMDS: That tag covers the instance metadata address 169.254.169.254, so a rule naming it would only pull the metadata traffic into scope for evaluation. The lookups that vm-a sends to the platform's resolver would keep being delivered, because that address is not part of this tag.
- AzurePlatformLKM: That tag names a different platform address, so a rule that uses it would not put the name resolution traffic in scope either. The resolver would continue to answer vm-a and the policy would stay unmet.
- VirtualNetwork: That service tag collects the addresses that belong to the virtual network, and the platform's resolver address is outside the virtual network, so the lookups are not part of that group. A rule built on it neither reaches nor filters the resolver traffic.

The subnet holds two virtual machines: vm-front, which carries the storefront and has a public address, and vm-admin, which handles administration only. Corporate users on 203.0.113.0/24 report that they cannot open sessions to the storefront on TCP 443. The team wants that range to reach the storefront, while vm-admin must stay unreachable on TCP 443 from the same range, and the new rule has to be evaluated ahead of the default rules without reusing a priority number that is already taken in the same direction.

The exhibit lists the resources and the rules that nsg-shop contains today.

Which values should the new rule use?

- Resource: Subnet shop-subnet; Detail: Address range 10.4.0.0/24
- Resource: Virtual machine vm-front; Detail: Network interface nic-front; private IP address 10.4.0.6; public IP address 20.55.4.19; storefront listener on TCP 443
- Resource: Virtual machine vm-admin; Detail: Network interface nic-admin; private IP address 10.4.0.9; no public IP address
- Resource: Network security group nsg-shop; Detail: Associated with subnet shop-subnet

prompt: Set the Source to 203.0.113.0/24, the Destination to _____, the Destination port ranges to 443, the Protocol to TCP, the Action to Allow, and the Priority to [...].

options.text: the private IP address of vm-front
the public IP address of vm-front
the private address range of the subnet that holds vm-front and vm-admin
the service tag Internet

explanation:
The destination has to be the private IP address of vm-front, 10.4.0.6. Inbound rules are evaluated only after Azure translates a public IP address to the private address assigned to the resource, and the guidance for the rule editor says that when the address belongs to an Azure virtual machine you enter its private address rather than its public one, so a rule that names the public address never matches the arriving traffic and the storefront stays unreachable. A subnet range would also open TCP 443 to vm-admin, which the requirement forbids, and the Internet service tag stands for public address space and does not match the translated destination. The priority has to satisfy three conditions at once: it must fall in the 100 to 4096 range that custom rules accept, it must not collide with a priority already used by another rule in the same direction, and it must be lower than the 65000 to 65500 band in which the default rules sit, because the defaults are given the lowest priority so custom rules are processed first. 200 is the only offered value that meets all three. Because a network security group is stateful, the replies from vm-front back to the corporate clients are permitted automatically, so no extra outbound rule is required.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the public IP address of vm-front: The public address is translated to the address assigned inside the virtual network before inbound rules are evaluated, so a rule whose destination is the public address never matches the arriving traffic and the storefront stays unreachable.
- the private address range of the subnet that holds vm-front and vm-admin: That range covers 10.4.0.9 as well, so the rule would open TCP 443 to vm-admin, which the requirement rules out. The destination has to name only vm-front.
- the service tag Internet: The Internet service tag stands for public address space. Once the public address is translated, the destination of the inbound traffic is the address assigned inside the virtual network, so the tag does not match, and it would in any case be much wider than the requirement.

explanation:
Once the rule at priority 120 that allows SSH from 203.0.113.0/24 is deleted, nothing in nsg-ops matches that range for TCP 22 any more, so new sessions from the corporate range fall through to the blanket deny at priority 130 and are refused. An edit to a rule, however, only shapes sessions that are started after the change, so the session the engineer already holds keeps running and has to be closed from the machine itself, for example by signing the user out. The replacement rule that permits SSH from the approved jump host 203.0.113.25 to vm-ops1 must be evaluated before the blanket deny at priority 130, so it needs a lower number; 100 is the only offered value that is unused, sits inside the 100-4096 range allowed for custom rules, and comes before 130.

Why the other options are wrong:
- new connections from that range are refused and the session that is already open is dropped: The second half is wrong: an edit to a rule never terminates a connection that is already established, so the open session stays up.
- new connections from that range are still accepted while the session that is already open keeps running: The first half is wrong: after the allow rule at priority 120 is gone, new sessions from the corporate range no longer match any allow rule and are refused by the deny at priority 130.
- new connections from that range are still accepted and the session that is already open is dropped: Both halves are wrong: new sessions from that range are refused once rule 120 is deleted, and the established session is not dropped by a rule change.

You have an internal load balancer named ilb-api in the virtual network vnet-svc. It listens on TCP 443 on the address 10.0.1.10 and passes connections on to the virtual machines vm-api1 and vm-api2, which run in subnet svc-subnet. The network security group nsg-svc is associated with svc-subnet, and the exhibit lists the resources and the inbound rules that nsg-svc holds today.

A member of the corporate network opens a session to 10.0.1.10 on TCP 443, and the load balancer passes it on to one of the two machines; this traffic is not a health probe. The team added the rule at priority 120 expecting it to let corporate sessions through, yet those sessions are still refused, and the team needs to work out which addresses Azure weighs against the inbound rules. It plans to correct the rule that is already in place rather than add another one.

Which pair of addresses does Azure evaluate, and which change to the rule at priority 120 should the team make?

`RESOURCE OR RULE                    DETAIL
---------------------------------  --------------------------------------------------
Virtual network                     vnet-svc
Subnet                              svc-subnet, associated with nsg-svc
Load balancer                       ilb-api, internal, frontend address 10.0.1.10, TCP 443
Machines behind ilb-api             vm-api1 (10.0.1.21) and vm-api2 (10.0.1.22)
Health probe                        ilb-api-probe, TCP 8080, sent by ilb-api to the machines behind it
Corporate network range             203.0.113.0/24
Inbound rule Allow-Probe-8080       Priority 110, source AzureLoadBalancer, destination Any, service Custom, port 8080, action Allow
Inbound rule Allow-Lb-Source-443    Priority 120, source 10.0.1.10, destination Any, service Custom, port 443, action Allow
Inbound rule DenyAllInbound         Priority 65500, source Any, destination Any, action Deny (built-in default)`
prompt: Azure weighs the inbound rules of nsg-svc against _____, and the team should [...].

options.text: the address of the party that opened the session and the private address of the machine that receives the forwarded traffic
the private address of ilb-api and the private address of the machine that receives the forwarded traffic
the frontend address of ilb-api and the address of the party that opened the session
the addresses covered by the AzureLoadBalancer service tag and the frontend address of ilb-api

explanation:
For traffic that arrives through a load balancer, the network security group compares the rules against the address of the machine that started the connection as the source and the address of the machine that ultimately receives it as the destination; the load balancer's own addresses are not what the rules are matched on. That is why the rule whose source is 10.0.1.10 never matches the corporate session, and why the source of that rule has to become the corporate range 203.0.113.0/24 while its existing destination and port settings can stay as they are. The AzureLoadBalancer service tag in the rule at priority 110 only covers the health probes that the load balancer sends to the backends, which are a different flow from the session in this scenario, and the built-in deny of all inbound traffic at priority 65500 is what refuses the session today.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the private address of ilb-api and the private address of the machine that receives the forwarded traffic: This option puts the load balancer's private address on the source side of the comparison. Traffic forwarded by a load balancer keeps the address of the machine that started the session as its source, so a rule written with the load balancer's address can never match the corporate user.
- the frontend address of ilb-api and the address of the party that opened the session: This option puts the load balancer's frontend address on the destination side. The destination address and port that Azure matches for forwarded traffic belong to the machine that receives the connection, not to the frontend address of the load balancer.
- the addresses covered by the AzureLoadBalancer service tag and the frontend address of ilb-api: This option describes the flow of the health probes, which are sent by the load balancer service itself and therefore match the AzureLoadBalancer service tag. The corporate session does not come from the probe.

prompt:
You have a Linux virtual machine named web-vm that runs a public-facing web application. The VM sits in the app-subnet of the hub-vnet virtual network, has a public IP address, and its network interface is named web-vm-nic. Two network security groups are associated with it: nsg-app-subnet is linked to the subnet, and nsg-web-nic is linked to the network interface.

Since the last change to nsg-web-nic, external clients report that they can no longer reach the web application over HTTP, although the application itself is healthy and serving requests locally. The merged effective rules view for web-vm-nic lists the following rows.

The team must restore external HTTP access to the application and wants to keep an NSG associated at both the subnet and network interface levels. Which action should you take?

options.text: Add an inbound allow rule for TCP 80 in the subnet NSG, and keep the existing allow rule in the NIC NSG.
Add an inbound allow rule for TCP 80 in the NIC NSG, and keep the existing rule set in the subnet NSG.
Add an inbound deny rule for TCP 80 in the subnet NSG, and keep the existing allow rule in the NIC NSG.
Add an outbound allow rule for TCP 80 in the subnet NSG, and keep the existing allow rule in the NIC NSG.

explanation:
Inbound rules from the subnet NSG and the NIC NSG are combined with AND: a connection is admitted only if both levels permit it. The merged view shows that nsg-web-nic already permits inbound TCP 80 (securityRules/Allow-HTTP, priority 100, source Any), but nsg-app-subnet carries only the built-in defaults, so the Internet-sourced request is stopped by defaultSecurityRules/DenyAllInBound (priority 65500) at the subnet level and never reaches the NIC rules. Creating the same inbound allow rule (source Any, source port Any, destination the VM address, destination port 80, protocol TCP, access Allow, a priority such as 100 that outranks the default deny) in nsg-app-subnet makes the flow permitted at both levels; the NIC-level allow rule is retained because both NSGs stay attached.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add an inbound allow rule for TCP 80 in the NIC NSG, and keep the existing rule set in the subnet NSG: A single allow is not sufficient for inbound traffic: the connection must also be permitted by the subnet NSG. The NIC NSG already contains securityRules/Allow-HTTP for destination port 80 at priority 100, so adding another allow there changes nothing, and the subnet NSG's defaultSecurityRules/DenyAllInBound still blocks traffic from the Internet.
- Add an inbound deny rule for TCP 80 in the subnet NSG, and keep the existing allow rule in the NIC NSG: This makes the block explicit rather than removing it. Inbound traffic must be permitted by both the subnet NSG and the NIC NSG, so a deny on the subnet side stops the flow regardless of the allow that exists on the interface side.
- Add an outbound allow rule for TCP 80 in the subnet NSG, and keep the existing allow rule in the NIC NSG: Outbound rules govern traffic leaving the VM, not the inbound connection from the client, and the built-in AllowInternetOutbound default already permits egress to the Internet. Adding an outbound allow for TCP 80 therefore has no bearing on the failing request.

prompt:
You have a Windows Server virtual machine named sql-vm that hosts an internal line-of-business application. The machine sits in the mgmt-subnet of the core-vnet virtual network, its network interface is sql-vm-nic, and the merged view of the rules that apply to that interface is shown below.

Administrators on the corporate network can no longer open Remote Desktop to the machine, even though the application is healthy and listening on TCP 3389. Corporate security requires that an NSG stay associated with both the subnet and the network interface, and that Remote Desktop remain reachable only from the corporate source range 203.0.113.0/24. You need to restore administrator access while meeting those requirements. Which action should you take?

options.text: Create an inbound allow rule for TCP 3389 from the source range 203.0.113.0/24 with priority 120 in nsg-mgmt-subnet, the NSG associated with the subnet.
Change the priority of the default DenyAllInBound rule in nsg-sql-nic from 65500 to 120.
Create an inbound allow rule for TCP 3389 with source address prefix Any and priority 120 in nsg-sql-nic, the NSG associated with the network interface.
Create an inbound allow rule for TCP 3389 from the source range 203.0.113.0/24 with priority 120 in nsg-sql-nic, the NSG associated with the network interface.

explanation:
Effective rules are the merge of the rules of the NSG on the network interface and the rules of the NSG on the subnet, and inbound traffic must be permitted by both of them. In the merged view the only rule permitting TCP 3389 from 203.0.113.0/24 sits at the subnet level (nsg-mgmt-subnet, priority 110); the interface-level NSG (nsg-sql-nic) contains only the built-in defaults, whose DenyAllInBound at priority 65500 blocks the flow. Adding an inbound allow rule for TCP 3389 from 203.0.113.0/24 in nsg-sql-nic with a priority such as 120 (which outranks the default deny) supplies the missing permission at the interface level, keeps the source restricted to the corporate range, and leaves both NSG associations in place as the baseline requires.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Create an inbound allow rule for TCP 3389 from the source range 203.0.113.0/24 with priority 120 in nsg-mgmt-subnet, the NSG associated with the subnet: This adds a duplicate of the rule that already exists at the subnet level. The interface-level NSG still has no rule permitting TCP 3389, so the built-in DenyAllInBound at priority 65500 continues to block the connection; when both levels carry an NSG, the permission has to exist in both of them for inbound traffic to flow.
- Change the priority of the default DenyAllInBound rule in nsg-sql-nic from 65500 to 120: The built-in default rules are fixed: their priorities cannot be changed and the rules themselves cannot be edited or deleted, so the default deny at the interface level stays at 65500 and still blocks inbound TCP 3389.
- Create an inbound allow rule for TCP 3389 with source address prefix Any and priority 120 in nsg-sql-nic, the NSG associated with the network interface: This would restore the connection, but a source prefix of Any exposes Remote Desktop to every source, including the internet, which violates the requirement that it be reachable only from the corporate source range 203.0.113.0/24.

You have a Linux virtual machine named batch-vm that runs a log-collection agent. The machine sits in the app-subnet of the prod-vnet virtual network, and its network interface is named batch-vm-nic. Two network security groups apply to it: nsg-app-subnet is linked to the subnet, and nsg-batch-nic is linked to the network interface.

Since the agent was upgraded, every attempt to send its logs to an Azure Storage account over HTTPS (TCP 443) times out, while inbound administration from the corporate range still works normally. The outbound rows of the merged effective security rules view for batch-vm-nic are shown below.

The uploads must succeed again, security policy requires that egress to the internet stay blocked for every destination other than Azure Storage over TCP 443, and both network security groups must remain associated. Which action should you take?

options.text: Add an outbound allow rule to nsg-app-subnet for TCP 443 to the Storage service tag, using a priority number lower than 200.
Add an outbound allow rule to nsg-batch-nic for TCP 443 to the Storage service tag, using a priority number lower than 110.
Edit the outbound deny rule in nsg-app-subnet so that its action allows outbound traffic.
Add an outbound allow rule to nsg-app-subnet for TCP 443 to the Storage service tag, using a priority number higher than 200.

explanation:
The merged view shows that the network interface NSG already permits outbound TCP 443 to the Storage service tag (priority 110), while the subnet NSG carries a deny rule for all outbound traffic at priority 200. For outbound traffic the rules of the network interface NSG are processed first and the subnet NSG rules afterwards, and a deny in either of the two groups stops the flow, so the interface-level allow never carries the upload through. The permit therefore has to exist in nsg-app-subnet as well, and it has to outrank that group's deny rule, which means giving it a priority number lower than 200. Because the deny rule is kept and only the storage exception is added, egress to every other internet destination stays blocked, and both groups remain associated.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add an outbound allow rule to nsg-batch-nic for TCP 443 to the Storage service tag, using a priority number lower than 110: The network interface NSG already permits outbound TCP 443 to the Storage service tag at priority 110, so another allow rule there changes nothing. The upload is still stopped by the deny rule in nsg-app-subnet, because a deny in either of the two groups blocks outbound traffic regardless of an allow in the other.
- Edit the outbound deny rule in nsg-app-subnet so that its action allows outbound traffic: Turning that deny rule into an allow would let the uploads through, but it would also open egress to every destination on the internet, breaking the policy that only Azure Storage over TCP 443 may be reached. The deny rule should stay in place and a narrow exception should be added above it.
- Add an outbound allow rule to nsg-app-subnet for TCP 443 to the Storage service tag, using a priority number higher than 200: A priority number higher than 200 ranks below the deny rule in nsg-app-subnet, so that deny rule still matches first and the upload remains blocked. The new rule needs a lower number than the deny rule to take precedence over it.

Neither interface has a network security group of its own; a single network security group named nsg-payout is associated with the payout-subnet. Since nsg-payout was associated with the subnet, requests sent from ledger-vm to order-vm time out, although the API is healthy and answers locally on the machine. The merged effective rules view for order-vm-nic lists the rows below. You need order intake to work again between the two virtual machines while nsg-payout stays associated with the payout-subnet. Which action should you take?

options.text: Edit the custom rule in nsg-payout so that it stops blocking traffic that originates inside the virtual network.
Associate a new network security group with order-vm-nic that allows inbound TCP 8080 from the ledger-vm address range, leaving nsg-payout in place.
Raise the priority number of the custom rule in nsg-payout so that it is processed after the built-in rule that permits traffic from all sources inside the virtual network.
Add an outbound rule to nsg-payout that allows all response traffic from order-vm back to ledger-vm on TCP 8080, leaving the inbound rows untouched.

explanation:
The merged view shows that the only user-created rule, securityRules/DenyEast-West-Traffic, sits at priority 100 in the network security group associated with the subnet and denies inbound traffic whose source is the VirtualNetwork service tag. ledger-vm is inside that virtual network, so its calls to order-vm match this rule. Because lower priority numbers are processed first, that deny is evaluated before defaultSecurityRules/AllowVnetInBound, the built-in rule that normally permits traffic originating inside the virtual network and between virtual machines in the same subnet. The blocking rule lives in the network security group associated with the subnet, so that group has to be adjusted for the flow to succeed. Editing the custom rule so it no longer matches traffic originating inside the virtual network (or adding an allow rule with a priority number lower than 100 for the ledger-vm address range in the same group) restores order intake while nsg-payout stays associated with the payout-subnet.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Associate a new network security group with order-vm-nic that allows inbound TCP 8080 from the ledger-vm address range, leaving nsg-payout in place: A network security group associated with the interface cannot override the one associated with the subnet. Inbound traffic is evaluated against the subnet's network security group first and then the interface's, and the port has to be permitted by both, so the priority 100 deny in nsg-payout keeps dropping the calls from ledger-vm no matter what an interface-level group allows.
- Raise the priority number of the custom rule in nsg-payout so that it is processed after the built-in rule that permits traffic from all sources inside the virtual network: User-created rules accept priorities from 100 to 4096, while the built-in rules carry the lowest priority, so a custom rule can never be processed after defaultSecurityRules/AllowVnetInBound. Moving the rule to a higher number therefore cannot make it yield to the built-in allow, and the calls stay blocked.
- Add an outbound rule to nsg-payout that allows all response traffic from order-vm back to ledger-vm on TCP 8080, leaving the inbound rows untouched: The connection is refused on the inbound side before any response is generated, and outbound rules are evaluated in the opposite direction, with the interface's group first and the subnet's group second. The built-in outbound rules already permit the reply traffic, so an extra outbound rule for TCP 8080 changes nothing for the requests coming from ledger-vm.

The machine sits in the svc-subnet of the prod-vnet virtual network, has a public IP address assigned, and its network interface is api-vm-nic. After a recent hardening review, the security team recorded that every port of the machine can be reached from the internet.

The properties of the machine and the result of the rules review are shown below.

The team must reduce the internet-facing surface of every virtual machine in svc-subnet, and the audit needs a listing of all the rules that govern api-vm-nic, including the built-in defaults. Which action should you take?

options.text: Associate a new network security group with svc-subnet, add the inbound and outbound rules the API needs, and then review the effective security rules for api-vm-nic to confirm what applies to the interface.

Associate a new network security group with api-vm-nic, add the inbound and outbound rules the API needs, and then review the effective security rules for api-vm-nic to confirm what applies to the interface.

Associate a new network security group with svc-subnet, add the inbound and outbound rules the API needs, and then review only the custom rules stored in the network security group to confirm what applies to the interface.

Associate a new network security group with svc-subnet, add the inbound and outbound rules the API needs, and then use IP flow verify in Azure Network Watcher to confirm what applies to the interface.

explanation:
The machine has a public IP address and no network security group on either level, so nothing filters its traffic and all of its ports stay exposed to the internet. Putting the new network security group on svc-subnet gives every interface in that subnet a filtered path, which is the scope the team asked for and the attachment level recommended over per-interface associations; the allow rules needed by the API are then added so the service keeps working. The audit listing comes from the effective security rules view for api-vm-nic, because that view merges the rules of the network security group on the subnet with those on the interface and shows the built-in defaults, such as the inbound deny and the outbound allow, alongside the custom rules.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Associate a new network security group with api-vm-nic, add the inbound and outbound rules the API needs, and then review the effective security rules for api-vm-nic to confirm what applies to the interface: Attaching the network security group to api-vm-nic filters only that one interface. Every other virtual machine in svc-subnet would remain unfiltered and exposed, so the requirement to reduce the surface of the whole subnet is not met, and an interface-level association is the scope to avoid when a subnet-wide filter is needed.
- Associate a new network security group with svc-subnet, add the inbound and outbound rules the API needs, and then review only the custom rules stored in the network security group to confirm what applies to the interface: Looking only at the custom rules stored in the network security group omits the built-in defaults and shows only one level of the configuration, so it cannot produce the listing of everything that governs api-vm-nic that the audit requires. The merged effective rules view for the interface is the source for that listing.
- Associate a new network security group with svc-subnet, add the inbound and outbound rules the API needs, and then use IP flow verify in Azure Network Watcher to confirm what applies to the interface: IP flow verify answers a yes/no question for one specific flow and names the rule responsible for it; it does not enumerate every rule that governs the interface. It is useful after the rules are in place to confirm one flow, not to build the audit listing.

explanation:
The merged view shows an allow for TCP 22 from 198.51.100.0/24 at priority 100 under both the NetworkInterface and the Subnet association. Inbound traffic is evaluated against the subnet's rules first and then the interface's rules, and the port has to be allowed by both, so this flow already passes NSG filtering; the built-in DenyAllInBound at priority 65500 is evaluated later and never applies, and no other row denies it. Remove the association between the subnet and the network security group, keeping the association to the network interface.

explanation:
The repeated rows are a side effect of the same network security group being linked at two levels: when one group is linked to both the network interface and the subnet, the merged listing shows its built-in defaults and its custom rules once per association. Dropping the network interface level leaves a single association, so each rule of nsg-shop is listed once, and filtering stays in place because the subnet-level association applies to every network interface in web-subnet, including app-vm-nic, api-vm-nic and worker-vm-nic. It also contradicts the recommendation to attach the group to the subnet rather than to individual interfaces.
- Keep both associations and delete the repeated entries from the rule list of the network security group so the merged listing shows each rule once: The network security group does not store two copies of a rule: the repeated rows exist only in the merged listing, produced by the two associations. Nothing can be deleted from the rule list to remove them, and the built-in default rules are present in every group and cannot be removed at all.
- Keep both associations and lower the priority number of the custom rules on the network interface so the merged listing applies each rule once: A priority number only decides which matching rule wins for a given flow; it does not collapse repeated rows in the merged listing. context:
You have two Linux virtual machines in the shared-subnet of the acme-vnet virtual network. billing-vm, whose network interface is billing-vm-nic, hosts an internal billing service that listens on TCP 8443, and reporting-vm, whose network interface is reporting-vm-nic, sends nightly end-of-day reports to that service across the private addresses of the subnet. One network security group, nsg-shared, is associated with shared-subnet, and neither interface carries a network security group of its own.

The deny rule below was introduced to keep the billing service from being reached by other workloads that share the subnet. Since the billing service moved to its new build, every report sent from reporting-vm times out before the service replies, although the service is healthy and answers requests locally. The merged effective security rules view for billing-vm-nic lists the rows below.

Report delivery from reporting-vm to billing-vm has to work again, the existing inbound deny rule for TCP 8443 must stay in nsg-shared exactly as written, and nsg-shared has to remain associated with shared-subnet. Which action should you take?

- Rule name: securityRules/Allow-BillingSsh; Direction: Inbound; Priority: 110; Source: 203.0.113.0/24; Destination: Any; Destination port: 22; Access: Allow; Association: Subnet
- Rule name: securityRules/Deny-SubnetIngest; Direction: Inbound; Priority: 120; Source: 10.20.0.0/24; Destination: Any; Destination port: 8443; Access: Deny; Association: Subnet
- Rule name: defaultSecurityRules/AllowVnetInBound; Direction: Inbound; Priority: 65000; Source: VirtualNetwork; Destination: Any; Destination port: Any; Access: Allow; Association: Subnet
- Rule name: defaultSecurityRules/DenyAllInBound; Direction: Inbound; Priority: 65500; Source: 0.0.0.0/0; Destination: Any; Destination port: Any; Access: Deny; Association: Subnet
- Rule name: defaultSecurityRules/AllowInternetOutBound; Direction: Outbound; Priority: 65000; Source: Any; Destination: Internet; Destination port: Any; Access: Allow; Association: Subnet
prompt: The change that restores the report flow while respecting the stated constraints is to _____.

options.text: Add an inbound allow rule to nsg-shared for TCP 8443 from reporting-vm to billing-vm with a priority number lower than the number on the deny rule.
Add an inbound allow rule to nsg-shared for TCP 8443 from reporting-vm to billing-vm with a priority number higher than the number on the deny rule.
Add an inbound allow rule for TCP 8443 from reporting-vm to billing-vm to a new network security group associated with reporting-vm-nic, and keep the deny rule on nsg-shared with its priority number.
Add an inbound allow rule to nsg-shared for TCP 8443 from reporting-vm to billing-vm with a priority number, and remove the deny rule on nsg-shared.

explanation:
Inside a single network security group the rules are evaluated by priority, and the rule with the lower priority number takes precedence. The custom deny rule for TCP 8443 sits at priority 120 in nsg-shared, so it wins over the built-in AllowVnetInBound default at 65000 and blocks the reports arriving from reporting-vm in the same subnet. Putting an allow rule for TCP 8443 from reporting-vm to billing-vm into the same network security group with a priority number below 120 makes that rule take precedence for this flow only, while the deny rule stays in place for the other workloads in the subnet and nsg-shared remains associated with shared-subnet. Because no network security group is attached to billing-vm-nic, the subnet association is the only level that filters this inbound traffic, so the new rule in nsg-shared is sufficient on its own.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add an inbound allow rule to nsg-shared for TCP 8443 from reporting-vm to billing-vm with a priority number higher than the number on the deny rule: A priority number above 120 is evaluated after the deny rule, so the deny at priority 120 still blocks the report traffic and the added rule never takes effect for that flow.
- Add an inbound allow rule for TCP 8443 from reporting-vm to billing-vm to a new network security group associated with reporting-vm-nic, and keep the deny rule on nsg-shared with its priority number: The flow into billing-vm is filtered by the rules of the network security group associated with the subnet that holds billing-vm-nic, and inbound traffic has to be permitted by the subnet group and the network interface group at the same time. A group attached to reporting-vm-nic filters traffic entering reporting-vm and cannot override the subnet deny, so the reports stay blocked.
- Add an inbound allow rule to nsg-shared for TCP 8443 from reporting-vm to billing-vm with a priority number, and remove the deny rule on nsg-shared: This breaks the stated constraint that the inbound deny rule for TCP 8443 must remain in nsg-shared exactly as written, and it would also reopen the billing service to every other workload in the shared subnet that the deny rule was created to block.

options.text: create an inbound allow rule for TCP 443 from Any in nsg-app with a priority number lower than the default deny rule
create an inbound deny rule for TCP 443 from Any in nsg-app with a priority number lower than the default deny rule
create an outbound allow rule for TCP 443 from Any in nsg-app with a priority number lower than the default deny rule
create an inbound allow rule for TCP 443 from Any in nsg-app with a priority number higher than the default deny rule

explanation:
Nothing in the listing allows inbound TCP 443: the only custom rule in nsg-app opens port 8080, and the built-in default rule DenyAllInBound (priority 65500 in the listing, source 0.0.0.0/0, which includes the internet) denies everything else that arrives from outside. That is why external calls to port 443 time out while calls from inside the virtual network still succeed through AllowVnetInBound. Rules are processed in priority order and a lower number wins, so a new inbound allow rule for TCP 443 from Any whose priority number is lower than the default deny rule is evaluated first and opens the port; custom priorities run from 100 to 4096, so a value such as 100 outranks the default rules. Because nsg-app is the group associated with app-subnet and no group is attached to the interface, that one rule is enough. For the second step, IP flow verify in Azure Network Watcher returns a yes/no verdict for one specific flow and identifies the security rule responsible for allowing or denying it, which is exactly what the team asked for.

Why the other options are wrong:
- create an inbound deny rule for TCP 443 from Any in nsg-app with a priority number lower than the default deny rule: A deny rule for TCP 443 keeps blocked exactly the traffic the team wants to permit. The symptom already comes from a deny, so adding another deny cannot open the port.
- create an outbound allow rule for TCP 443 from Any in nsg-app with a priority number lower than the default deny rule: The failing connections are inbound, and outbound rules are never consulted for traffic arriving at the interface, so the default deny rule would still stop TCP 443.
- create an inbound allow rule for TCP 443 from Any in nsg-app with a priority number higher than the default deny rule: A lower priority number wins, so a custom rule numbered above the default deny rule is never reached for this traffic. Custom rule priorities are in fact limited to the range 100 to 4096, which all sit below the default rules.

The machine runs in the app-subnet of the prod-vnet virtual network, its network interface is web-vm-nic, and the network security group nsg-app is associated with app-subnet. A custom inbound rule in nsg-app at priority 110 allows TCP 443 from the VirtualNetwork service tag to any destination, and the built-in default rules are present alongside it.

prod-vnet was peered with partner-vnet, whose address space is 10.40.0.0/16, three days ago. Since that peering was created, the security team has seen machines in partner-vnet open HTTPS sessions to web-vm, which the business did not intend to allow. The team wants to establish exactly which source addresses the VirtualNetwork service tag matches today for web-vm-nic, so that the rule can be narrowed to corporate ranges only. Which should the team do?

The rules that apply to web-vm-nic are listed below.

- Rule name: securityRules/Allow-Internal-Https; Direction: Inbound; Priority: 110; Source: VirtualNetwork; Destination: *; Port: 443; Access: Allow
- Rule name: defaultSecurityRules/AllowVnetInBound; Direction: Inbound; Priority: 65000; Source: VirtualNetwork; Destination: VirtualNetwork; Port: *; Access: Allow
- Rule name: defaultSecurityRules/AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound; Direction: Inbound; Priority: 65001; Source: AzureLoadBalancer; Destination: VirtualNetwork; Port: *; Access: Allow

options.text: the expanded source address prefixes for the VirtualNetwork service tag
the destination address prefixes for the custom rule that allows TCP 443 from the VirtualNetwork service tag
the source address prefixes for the built-in default rule that denies all inbound traffic
the priority numbers for the custom inbound rules that use a service tag

explanation:
The listing that applies to web-vm-nic is the merged view of every rule that governs that interface, and for a rule whose source is a service tag the listing also reports the individual address prefixes behind that tag in the expanded source address prefixes. The VirtualNetwork service tag automatically picks up the address space of a peered virtual network, so once partner-vnet was peered, its 10.40.0.0/16 range began matching the allow rule, which is why machines in partner-vnet can now open HTTPS sessions to web-vm. Reading that expansion tells the team exactly which source addresses satisfy the rule today, so it can then narrow the rule to corporate ranges.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the destination address prefixes for the custom rule that allows TCP 443 from the VirtualNetwork service tag: The destination side of the allow rule describes where matching traffic is delivered (any destination in this rule), not which sources satisfy the tag, so it cannot reveal the partner range that now matches.
- the source address prefixes for the built-in default rule that denies all inbound traffic: The built-in default deny rule carries the fixed source 0.0.0.0/0 and no service tag, so the prefixes attached to it say nothing about which addresses the VirtualNetwork service tag matches.
- the priority numbers for the custom inbound rules that use a service tag: Priority numbers only decide which rule is evaluated first when several rules match; they carry no address information and therefore cannot show what the service tag resolves to.

hosts inside trade-vnet, but not hosts inside the peered partner-vnet
hosts inside the peered partner-vnet and hosts on the public internet
any host that can route to the machine, because the custom rule in the subnet group matches every source

explanation:
Inbound traffic reaches the machine only when both the subnet group and the interface group allow it, and the built-in defaults admit traffic that originates inside the virtual network. The VirtualNetwork service tag expands automatically to include the address prefixes of peered virtual networks, so partner-vnet traffic is covered by that built-in allow, and the rule exists in both nsg-orders-subnet and nsg-orders-nic. Hosts inside trade-vnet are allowed as well, through the built-in default rule and, for the API port, through the custom rule in the subnet group. Hosts on the public internet match the built-in default deny whose source is 0.0.0.0/0 in the subnet group, and the interface group also carries a custom deny for the Internet source on TCP 8080, so internet traffic is stopped.

Why the other options are wrong:
- hosts inside trade-vnet, but not hosts inside the peered partner-vnet: The VirtualNetwork service tag automatically expands to include the prefixes of peered virtual networks, so hosts in partner-vnet match the built-in default rule that admits traffic coming from inside the virtual network, and that rule is present in both nsg-orders-subnet and nsg-orders-nic. Partner traffic is therefore permitted, so the rules in force do not confine the API to trade-vnet.
- hosts inside the peered partner-vnet and hosts on the public internet: Hosts in the peered partner-vnet are indeed allowed, but hosts on the public internet are not: their traffic matches the built-in default deny with source 0.0.0.0/0 in the subnet group, and the interface group holds a custom deny for the Internet source on TCP 8080. Inbound traffic must be allowed by both groups, so internet traffic never reaches the API.
- any host that can route to the machine, because the custom rule in the subnet group matches every source: The custom rule in the subnet group permits TCP 8080 only from 10.20.3.0/24, so it does not match every source, and the remaining inbound traffic is filtered by the built-in default deny with source 0.0.0.0/0 that exists in both groups. context:
You support a subscription that contains a Linux machine named data-vm and a Windows machine named jump-vm, each with a single NIC. The NIC of data-vm (data-vm-nic) sits in data-subnet of prod-vnet, and the NIC of jump-vm (jump-vm-nic) sits in admin-subnet of corp-vnet. The rules that govern a NIC are the merged set of the rules of the network security group (NSG) attached to that NIC and of the group attached to its subnet, and the same merged listing can be produced in more than one place.

Your colleagues work from Windows machines that have PowerShell and the Az module installed, from Linux machines that have the Azure CLI installed, and one reviewer works only in the Azure portal in a browser.

You need to match each of the five deliverables below to the tool or command that produces it. Drag the appropriate choice onto each deliverable.

- Machine: data-vm (Linux); NIC: data-vm-nic; Subnet: data-subnet of prod-vnet; Network security groups that apply: nsg-data-subnet, nsg-data-nic
- Machine: jump-vm (Windows); NIC: jump-vm-nic; Subnet: admin-subnet of corp-vnet; Network security groups that apply: nsg-admin-subnet
prompt: Confirm whether one inbound connection from a known source address and port is permitted, and identify the rule that decided it

options.text: Get-AzEffectiveNetworkSecurityGroup -NetworkInterfaceName <nic-name> -ResourceGroupName <rg-name>, run in PowerShell with the Az module, returning the rules as JSON
az network nic list-effective-nsg --name <nic-name> --resource-group <rg-name>, run with the Azure CLI, returning the rules as JSON
The Effective security rules pane in the Azure portal (Networking > Network settings > the network interface > Help), with its Download button for the complete output
IP flow verify in Azure Network Watcher
The network verifier in Azure Virtual Network Manager

explanation: Each deliverable maps to a different way of inspecting the rules that apply to a NIC. IP flow verify in Azure Network Watcher returns a yes/no verdict for one specific flow and names the rule that allowed or denied it, so it belongs with the first deliverable. The network verifier in Azure Virtual Network Manager explains reachability between machines, the internet and other Azure resources, taking NSG rules and other policies into account, so it belongs with the second. Get-AzEffectiveNetworkSecurityGroup is the PowerShell cmdlet that returns the merged rule set as JSON for the Windows colleague, while az network nic list-effective-nsg is the Azure CLI command that returns the same JSON for the Linux colleague. The portal's Effective security rules pane is the browser-based view, and because it displays only the first fifty rules, its Download button is what produces the complete file for archiving.
