- Resource: stmodern01; Setting: Virtual networks; Value: vnet-warehouse/snet-modern
prompt: You have a virtual network named vnet-warehouse in the East US region with two subnets. The subnet snet-legacy runs a Linux virtual machine for a reporting job that reads data files from the classic storage account stclassic01, and the subnet snet-modern runs a web application that uploads blobs to the general purpose v2 storage account stmodern01. A service endpoint policy named sep-storage is associated with both subnets, and the current configuration is shown in the exhibit. Since sep-storage was associated with these subnets, the reporting job fails with 403 responses returned by the storage service, while the web application keeps working. You need the reporting job to read from stclassic01 once more, and snet-modern must keep the account restriction that sep-storage gives it. Which action should you take?

options.text: Remove the service endpoint policy from snet-legacy.
Copy the resource ID of stclassic01 into the serviceResources array of the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint policy on snet-legacy.
Associate an additional service endpoint policy with snet-legacy that lists stclassic01 in its serviceResources array.
Set the Public network access setting of stclassic01 to Enabled from all networks and leave the service endpoint policy associated with snet-legacy.

explanation:
A service endpoint policy is an allow-list: once it is associated with a subnet, only the storage accounts named in its serviceResources array are reachable from compute in that subnet, and everything else is denied. Only accounts created with the Azure Resource Manager resource model can be listed, and classic storage accounts are not supported in endpoint policies at all, so stclassic01 can never be named in sep-storage. That is why the reporting job in snet-legacy is denied while the web application in snet-modern, whose account is listed, still works. Policies filter only the traffic originating in the subnets they are associated with, so detaching sep-storage from snet-legacy restores the legacy account access and leaves the restriction on snet-modern untouched.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Copy the resource ID of stclassic01 into the serviceResources array of the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint policy on snet-legacy: The classic storage account's resource ID cannot be placed in the serviceResources array, because only accounts that use the Azure Resource Manager model can be listed and classic storage accounts are not supported in endpoint policies. The policy would therefore continue to deny the reporting job's traffic.
- Associate an additional service endpoint policy with snet-legacy that lists stclassic01 in its serviceResources array: Adding a second policy on the same subnet does not help. Several policies on one subnet are combined as a union, and the classic account still cannot be named in any of them, so the traffic from snet-legacy stays denied.
- Set the Public network access setting of stclassic01 to Enabled from all networks and leave the service endpoint policy associated with snet-legacy: Widening the account's own public network access does not override an endpoint policy. A policy denies every storage account that is not on its allow-list, so stclassic01 remains blocked, and the account would additionally be reachable from any internet source.

prompt: You have a virtual network named vnet-data that runs the ingestion virtual machines in the subnet snet-ingest, and the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint is already enabled on that subnet. The security team wants those virtual machines to reach only the storage accounts st-ingest-a and st-ingest-b, and a service endpoint policy named sep-ingest has been created to express that restriction. When the team tries to associate sep-ingest with snet-ingest, the portal reports that the policy cannot be attached to the subnet. The current state of the objects is shown below. Which action should you take?

options.text: Recreate the service endpoint policy in subscription sub-contoso-prod in the West Europe region so that it can be associated with snet-ingest.
Recreate the service endpoint policy in subscription sub-contoso-security in the West Europe region so that it can be associated with snet-ingest.
Recreate the service endpoint policy in subscription sub-contoso-prod in the East US region so that it can be associated with snet-ingest.
Recreate the service endpoint policy in subscription sub-contoso-security in the East US region so that it can be associated with snet-ingest.

explanation:
A service endpoint policy can only be attached to a subnet whose virtual network sits in the same subscription and the same region as the policy, and policies can only be used with virtual networks deployed through the Azure Resource Manager deployment model. In the exhibit vnet-data satisfies the deployment-model requirement (it was created from an ARM template) and snet-ingest already has the Microsoft.Storage endpoint, but sep-ingest currently lives in subscription sub-contoso-security in the East US region while the virtual network lives in sub-contoso-prod in West Europe. Recreating the policy in subscription sub-contoso-prod in the West Europe region satisfies both placement constraints, so it can then be associated with snet-ingest and limit that subnet to the listed storage accounts (st-ingest-a and st-ingest-b), with every other storage account denied.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Recreate the service endpoint policy in subscription sub-contoso-security in the West Europe region so that it can be associated with snet-ingest: Recreating the policy in the West Europe region fixes only one of the two placement rules: the policy would still live in sub-contoso-security while the virtual network is in sub-contoso-prod. A policy must be in the same subscription as the virtual network whose subnets it filters, so the attachment to snet-ingest would still be rejected.
- Recreate the service endpoint policy in subscription sub-contoso-prod in the East US region so that it can be associated with snet-ingest: Recreating the policy in sub-contoso-prod fixes only the subscription rule: the policy would still be in the East US region while vnet-data is in West Europe. Because the policy must be in the same region as the virtual network it filters, it still cannot be associated with snet-ingest.
- Recreate the service endpoint policy in subscription sub-contoso-security in the East US region so that it can be associated with snet-ingest: Leaving the policy in sub-contoso-security in the East US region matches neither the subscription nor the region of vnet-data, so neither of the two placement conditions is met and the policy still cannot be attached to the subnet. The storage accounts listed in the policy can sit in another subscription, but the virtual network and the policy cannot.

context:
You have a virtual network vnet-prod in the East US region with one subnet, snet-app, that hosts the Linux virtual machines of an internal reporting application. Those virtual machines upload blobs to a general purpose v2 storage account named streports01. The account currently accepts requests from any source, and the network security group nsg-reporting associated with the subnet contains only its default rules. The current configuration is shown below.

The security team wants the reporting traffic to travel over the Azure backbone, wants streports01 to accept connections only from vnet-prod, and wants the virtual machines in snet-app to reach only the storage accounts the team has signed off. Five configuration changes are on the table. Drag each change to the requirement it satisfies.

- Object: vnet-prod; Setting: Region; Current value: East US
- Object: vnet-prod; Setting: Address space; Current value: 10.20.0.0/16
- Object: snet-app; Setting: Address space; Current value: 10.20.1.0/24
- Object: snet-app; Setting: Routing toward Azure platform services; Current value: Only the default platform route
- Object: snet-app; Setting: Per-account filtering of Azure platform traffic; Current value: None in place
- Object: streports01; Setting: Account type; Current value: General purpose v2
- Object: streports01; Setting: Public network access; Current value: Enabled from all networks
- Object: streports01; Setting: Allowed address ranges and networks; Current value: None listed
- Object: nsg-reporting; Setting: Security rules; Current value: Platform defaults only
prompt: Traffic to the platform service keeps the provider's public address as the destination, while the provider sees the caller's internal address instead of a public one.

options.text: Enable the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on snet-app
Attach the service endpoint policy to snet-app that allows the named storage accounts
Add the virtual network rule on streports01 that trusts snet-app
Create the private endpoint for streports01 on snet-app
Add outbound rules to nsg-reporting that allow the Storage service tag and deny the Internet

explanation: Each slot states an outcome, so match the change that produces that outcome. Enabling the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on snet-app keeps the account's public address as the destination and sends the traffic over the Azure backbone with the virtual machine's private IPv4 as the source address, which is the requirement about keeping the provider's public address as the destination while the provider sees an internal address. Attaching the service endpoint policy to snet-app is an allow-list of named accounts: once it is attached, only the accounts it names can be reached and everything else is denied, which matches the requirement about approved targets being the only reachable ones. Adding the virtual network rule on streports01 lets the storage resource compare the caller's internal address range against the ranges the account trusts and accept traffic only from the designated subnet, which matches the requirement about the storage resource checking that range. Creating the private endpoint for streports01 puts the service behind an address of its own inside the subnet, which matches the requirement about reaching the platform service through such an address. Adding outbound rules to nsg-reporting that allow the Storage service tag and deny the Internet keeps traffic toward the storage service working while refusing every other destination, which matches the remaining requirement.

context:
You have a virtual network named vnet-tickets in the West Europe region. The ticketing application's Linux virtual machines run in subnet snet-agent, where they upload report files to a storage account, read application secrets from a key vault, and query a database server. The administrators' Linux virtual machines run in a separate subnet named snet-ops. The current configuration is shown below.

The operations team has drafted seven configuration changes. Drag each change into the box that describes the result it produces for the ticketing application. One of the drafted changes produces none of the listed results.

- Object: Virtual network vnet-tickets; Setting: Region; Value: West Europe
- Object: Subnet snet-agent; Setting: Workload; Value: Ticketing application's Linux virtual machines
- Object: Subnet snet-ops; Setting: Workload; Value: Administrators' Linux virtual machines
- Object: Subnets snet-agent and snet-ops; Setting: Service endpoints; Value: None enabled
- Object: Storage account sttickets; Setting: Region; Value: West Europe
- Object: Storage account sttickets; Setting: Public network access; Value: Enabled from all networks
- Object: Key vault kv-tickets; Setting: Region; Value: West Europe
- Object: Key vault kv-tickets; Setting: Public network access; Value: Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses
- Object: Key vault kv-tickets; Setting: Allowed virtual networks; Value: vnet-tickets with subnet snet-agent
- Object: SQL server sqltickets; Setting: Region; Value: West Europe
- Object: SQL server sqltickets; Setting: Firewall; Value: Azure services and resources disabled; no virtual network rules
- Object: Storage services cleared for the ticketing application; Setting: List; Value: sttickets, starchive01
prompt: Storage uploads reach the storage service across the Microsoft Azure backbone, and the source the service sees comes from the application's subnet range.

options.text: Enable the storage service endpoint (Microsoft.Storage) on subnet snet-agent.
Enable the key vault service endpoint (Microsoft.KeyVault) on subnet snet-agent.
Enable the SQL service endpoint (Microsoft.Sql) on subnet snet-agent and register a virtual network rule for vnet-tickets/snet-agent on the sqltickets firewall.
Create an Azure Private Link private endpoint for the key vault kv-tickets in subnet snet-agent and reserve a dedicated private IP for it.

Create a service endpoint policy for Azure Storage whose service resources name the storage accounts sttickets and starchive01, and associate it with subnet snet-agent so only the named accounts remain reachable.
Enable the storage service endpoint (Microsoft.Storage) on subnet snet-ops, which receives traffic only from the administrators' virtual machines.

Set the public network access of storage account sttickets to Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses, and add vnet-tickets with subnet snet-agent to the allowed virtual networks of the storage account.

explanation: Enabling a service endpoint on the application's subnet (the storage endpoint for uploads, the key vault endpoint for secret lookups) gives the PaaS service a direct route over the Microsoft Azure backbone and changes the source address the service sees to the vnet's private range, so those two items deliver the backbone and source-identity results. The SQL item both enables the SQL endpoint and registers the application subnet on the database firewall, which is what makes the database accept that subnet and reject every other source. The policy item names the cleared storage accounts and attaches the policy to the application subnet, so that subnet reaches only those accounts and all other storage services are denied. The private endpoint item puts the key vault's own network interface and dedicated private IP inside the deployment, which is the dedicated-interface result rather than the backbone result. The account network access item switches the storage account to selected virtual networks and IP addresses and adds the application subnet, which is what limits the origins the account accepts. The endpoint enabled on the administrators' subnet affects only that subnet and delivers none of the listed results.

context:
You have a storage account named st-archive01 in the East US region that holds the company's compliance archives. The account is reachable only from an Azure application subnet that appears in the account's virtual networks, and the Linux virtual machines in that subnet upload and download files without any problem. The corporate data center is connected to Azure through an ExpressRoute circuit, and staff in that data center upload audit files to the same account; those uploads fail with HTTP 403 responses while the virtual machines in Azure keep working. You need the data center uploads to succeed again, and you must not let any other source on the internet reach the account. Which action should you take?

- Item: Storage account; Value: st-archive01 (East US), general purpose v2
- Item: Public network access; Value: Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses
- Item: Virtual networks; Value: vnet-app / snet-app
- Item: Service endpoint on snet-app; Value: Microsoft.Storage, enabled
- Item: Allowed IP addresses; Value: none
- Item: On-premises connectivity; Value: ExpressRoute circuit er-circuit-01 with private peering to the virtual network vnet-app; data center egress uses the public IP 20.240.10.5
- Item: Upload from the virtual machines in snet-app; Value: Succeeds
- Item: Upload from the data center; Value: HTTP 403 (Request authorization failed)
prompt: To let the data center uploads succeed again without exposing the account to any other source, you should _____.

options.text: Add the on-premises public IP addresses to the IP firewall of st-archive01.
Add the on-premises public IP addresses to the virtual networks list of st-archive01.
Attach a service endpoint policy that lists st-archive01 to the subnet snet-app.
Enable the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on every subnet of vnet-app so that on-premises uploads also travel over the backbone.

explanation:
The account is locked to the virtual network, and on-premises access to a resource that is secured to a virtual network is only possible when the on-premises NAT or ExpressRoute public IPs are placed in that resource's IP firewall. The storage account's public network access is already set to accept selected virtual networks and IP addresses, so putting the data center's egress public IP 20.240.10.5 into the account's IP address rules lets the data center uploads succeed while every other source stays blocked.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add the on-premises public IP addresses to the virtual networks list of st-archive01: The virtual networks list of a storage account only accepts virtual networks and their subnets — you pick the subscription, the virtual network and the subnet. Raw public IP addresses cannot be placed there, so this change does not let the data center uploads through.
- Attach a service endpoint policy that lists st-archive01 to the subnet snet-app: A service endpoint policy filters only the traffic that originates in the subnets it is attached to. The failing uploads come from the corporate data center over the ExpressRoute connection, so a policy on snet-app has no effect on them.
- Enable the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on every subnet of vnet-app so that on-premises uploads also travel over the backbone: Service endpoints are switched on per service and per subnet, and they change the path for traffic from the instances in that subnet. Traffic that starts in the data center and reaches Azure over the ExpressRoute connection is not sourced from a subnet inside vnet-app, so enabling an endpoint on the subnets of vnet-app does not change how those uploads are authorized.

The team has already switched on the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint for snet-invoice, and now the general purpose v2 storage account stbilling01 must accept traffic only from vnet-billing/snet-invoice with every other network excluded. A developer on the team holds only the custom role shown in the exhibit, and she can turn service endpoints on for a subnet without any trouble. When she tries to save the account's list of allowed networks, which has to include snet-invoice, the portal refuses the request with an authorization error. You need her to complete the account-side change without granting her Owner or Contributor on the subscription.

- Setting: Virtual network; Value: vnet-billing
- Setting: Subnet; Value: snet-invoice
- Setting: Service endpoint on snet-invoice; Value: Microsoft.Storage
- Setting: Storage account; Value: stbilling01, general purpose v2
- Setting: Custom role held by the developer; Value: Billing Network Onboarding
- Setting: Role permission: Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/read; Value: Granted
- Setting: Role permission: Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/subnets/write; Value: Granted
- Setting: Role permission: Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/write; Value: Granted
- Setting: Saving the account's list of allowed networks; Value: Failed with an authorization error
prompt: You should add the _____ permission to the Billing Network Onboarding custom role so that the developer can save the account's list of allowed networks.

options.text: Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/subnets/joinViaServiceEndpoint/action
Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/subnets/join/action
Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/write
Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/write

explanation:
Turning a service endpoint on needs write access to the virtual network, and that is what the developer already has. Securing the Azure service resource to that virtual network — that is, adding the subnet to the account's list of allowed networks — additionally requires the Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/subnets/joinViaServiceEndpoint/action permission on the subnets being added. Built-in service administrator roles carry that permission by default, and a custom role can be extended with it, which is the change that removes the authorization error.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/subnets/join/action: Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/subnets/join/action covers joining a subnet to a virtual network; it does not cover registering the subnet with an Azure service resource, which is what the account-side change does.
- Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/write: Write access on the virtual network is what allows service endpoints to be configured on its subnets, which the developer already has. It does not authorize adding the subnet to the service resource's list of allowed networks.
- Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/write: Write access to the storage account lets the developer change account properties and data, but the request that adds the subnet to the account's allowed networks is authorized against the subnet, so this permission does not clear the error.

prompt: The administrator should _____.

options.text: Add stbatch01 to the allow-list of sep-jobs and keep sep-jobs on snet-batch.
Attach a second policy that names only stjobs01 and associate it with snet-batch and snet-report.
Detach sep-jobs from snet-batch and associate it with snet-report.
Set stjobs01 to allow connections from all networks and keep sep-jobs on snet-batch.

explanation:
The policy sep-jobs is attached to the subnet that hosts the Azure Batch account. Endpoint policies are not supported for that managed Azure service, and the pool virtual machines in that subnet can no longer reach the storage account that the Batch service manages, so the Batch jobs fail with 403 responses. Taking the policy off snet-batch removes the filtering that breaks the Batch account, and attaching it to snet-report, where the Microsoft.Storage endpoint is already enabled and where the reporting traffic originates, restores the account-level restriction the security team asked for and leaves only stjobs01 reachable from the reporting machines.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add stbatch01 to the allow-list of sep-jobs and keep sep-jobs on snet-batch: Adding the storage account that the Batch service creates to the allow-list cannot help: managed storage accounts are not supported by endpoint policies and are denied by default whenever a policy is attached to the subnet, so the Batch workload keeps failing.
- Attach a second policy that names only stjobs01 and associate it with snet-batch and snet-report: Policies attached to one subnet are unioned, so adding a second policy that names stjobs01 to snet-batch does not undo the filtering sep-jobs applies there; traffic from that subnet to the Batch-managed account stays denied and the jobs still fail.
- Set stjobs01 to allow connections from all networks and keep sep-jobs on snet-batch: Public network access on the storage account does not override the filtering an endpoint policy applies to traffic leaving the subnet the policy is attached to, and allowing connections from all networks would also break the requirement that only the approved network may reach the account.

prompt: The virtual machines in snet-pos can reach _____, while the virtual machines in snet-ops can reach [...].

options.text: st-a and st-b, but not st-c
st-a and st-c, but not st-b
st-b and st-c, but not st-a
st-a, st-b, and st-c, but not another storage account

explanation:
Each service endpoint policy is an allow-list that filters only the traffic originating in the subnets it is attached to, and when several policies are attached to one subnet the resources named in any of them are allowed. The subnet snet-pos carries sep-a and sep-b, whose lists name st-a and st-b, so those accounts are reachable there and every other account, including st-c, is denied. The subnet snet-ops carries sep-b and sep-c, whose lists name st-b and st-c, so those two accounts are reachable there, while sep-a is attached only to snet-pos and therefore does not make st-a reachable from snet-ops.

Why the other options are wrong:
- st-a and st-c, but not st-b: st-c is named only by sep-c, which is attached to snet-ops, and st-b is named by sep-b, which is attached to snet-pos; from snet-pos the reachable accounts are st-a and st-b.
- st-b and st-c, but not st-a: sep-a is attached to snet-pos and names st-a, so st-a is reachable from snet-pos, while st-c is named only by sep-c, which is attached to snet-ops, so st-c is not reachable from snet-pos.
- st-a, st-b, and st-c, but not another storage account: st-c is not named by any policy attached to snet-pos, so the policies on that subnet deny it; the subnet reaches st-a and st-b only.

context:
You have a virtual network named vnet-report in the East US region with a subnet snet-app that hosts a Linux virtual machine named vm-report01. That machine uploads blobs to the storage account streport01. A user-defined route in vnet-report sends 0.0.0.0/0 to a network virtual appliance at 10.0.1.4 so that outbound traffic from the subnet is inspected, and a BGP connection to the corporate network also advertises 0.0.0.0/0 to the virtual network. An administrator then switched on the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint for snet-app and re-ran the upload job. The observations recorded after that change are shown below.

The team needs to understand why the appliance no longer captures the upload traffic. Which statement best explains the recorded behavior?

- Observation: Service endpoint enabled on snet-app; Recorded value: Microsoft.Storage
- Observation: Address space of vnet-report; Recorded value: 10.1.0.0/24
- Observation: User-defined route in vnet-report; Recorded value: 0.0.0.0/0 to 10.0.1.4 (network virtual appliance)
- Observation: BGP routes advertised to vnet-report; Recorded value: 0.0.0.0/0
- Observation: Packets captured at the appliance from vm-report01; Recorded value: 0
- Observation: Source address in the streport01 access log for the uploads; Recorded value: 10.1.0.24 (the address assigned to vm-report01)
- Observation: Upload job result; Recorded value: Success (HTTP 201)
prompt: The most likely explanation for the recorded behavior is that _____.

options.text: Azure's route for the storage service prefix, whose next hop type is VirtualNetworkServiceEndpoint, takes precedence over the user-defined route and the BGP route for that traffic.

The user-defined route to the network virtual appliance takes precedence over the VirtualNetworkServiceEndpoint route that Azure adds for the storage service prefix, so the traffic should have reached the appliance.
The BGP route takes precedence over the VirtualNetworkServiceEndpoint route that Azure adds for the storage service prefix, so the traffic should have followed the on-premises 0.0.0.0/0 path.

Azure's route for the storage service prefix, whose next hop type is VirtualNetworkServiceEndpoint, takes precedence over the user-defined route but not over the BGP route, so the traffic should have followed the on-premises 0.0.0.0/0 path.

explanation:
When a service endpoint is enabled on a subnet, Azure adds a default route for each supported service address prefix, and the next hop type of that route is VirtualNetworkServiceEndpoint. The storage service prefix is more specific than the 0.0.0.0/0 routes in the virtual network, and the route created for the endpoint wins over any user-defined route or BGP route that matches the same prefix. The upload traffic therefore goes straight to the storage service over the Azure backbone instead of being sent to the appliance, which is why the appliance captured nothing while the job still succeeded. The source address recorded for the uploads is the virtual machine's private address, which is the expected result once the endpoint is active, because traffic to the service leaves the machine with its private IPv4 address instead of its public address.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The user-defined route to the network virtual appliance takes precedence over the VirtualNetworkServiceEndpoint route that Azure adds for the storage service prefix, so the traffic should have reached the appliance: A user-defined route never takes precedence over the route that Azure creates for a service endpoint prefix. The endpoint route matches the storage service prefix, which is more specific than 0.0.0.0/0, so the appliance route is not used for the upload traffic and the appliance captures nothing.
- The BGP route takes precedence over the VirtualNetworkServiceEndpoint route that Azure adds for the storage service prefix, so the traffic should have followed the on-premises 0.0.0.0/0 path: The route created for the service endpoint wins over a BGP route that matches the same prefix as well, so the on-premises 0.0.0.0/0 path is not used for the upload traffic. In addition, the user-defined route for 0.0.0.0/0 covers the same prefix and would be preferred over the advertised BGP route.
- Azure's route for the storage service prefix, whose next hop type is VirtualNetworkServiceEndpoint, takes precedence over the user-defined route but not over the BGP route, so the traffic should have followed the on-premises 0.0.0.0/0 path: The route created for the service endpoint takes precedence over the BGP route as well as over the user-defined route, so the traffic could not have followed the on-premises path. This statement therefore does not match how the platform routes traffic to the storage service.

context:
You have a virtual network named vnet-gallery in the West Europe region, and its subnet snet-web runs the Linux virtual machines of a picture gallery application. Those virtual machines upload images to the general purpose v2 storage account stgal01, whose network settings accept requests only from vnet-gallery/snet-web. The Microsoft.Storage service endpoint is enabled on snet-web. A developer runs a name lookup from one of the virtual machines and then checks the storage account's diagnostic log for the same upload; both results are captured in the exhibit.

The team wants to confirm that the gallery traffic reaches the account over the Azure backbone and that the account keeps rejecting requests from every other network. Which statement best accounts for the observations in the exhibit?

`$ nslookup stgal01.blob.core.windows.net
Server:          168.63.129.16
Address:         168.63.129.16

Name:    stgal01.blob.core.windows.net
Address: 52.142.224.14

Storage account diagnostic log entry for the upload of logo.png:
  client_ip     = 10.0.1.7      (vm-gallery01)
  status_code   = 201
  auth_method   = StorageServiceAccessKey`
prompt: The observations in the exhibit are best explained by the fact that _____.

options.text: Enabling the endpoint leaves name resolution unchanged, so the hostname still returns the service's public addresses, while the route and the source address of the traffic change.
Enabling the endpoint leaves name resolution unchanged, so the hostname still returns the service's public addresses, while the route and the source address of the traffic do not change.
Enabling the endpoint changes name resolution, so the hostname returns the service's private addresses, while the route and the source address of the traffic change.

Enabling the endpoint leaves name resolution unchanged, so the hostname still returns the service's public addresses, while the route and the source address of the traffic change for reasons unrelated to the endpoint.

explanation:
A service endpoint leaves name resolution alone: the DNS entries for the service stay as they are and keep resolving to the public addresses that Azure assigns to the storage service, which is why the lookup from the virtual machine still returns 52.142.224.14. What the endpoint changes is the path and the source address of the traffic. Azure adds a more specific default route for the service's address prefixes whose next hop type is VirtualNetworkServiceEndpoint, and requests leave the virtual machine with its private IPv4 address, which is why the account's diagnostic log records 10.0.1.7 (vm-gallery01) as the client address. The account can therefore keep refusing every source outside vnet-gallery/snet-web while the traffic stays on the Azure backbone.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enabling the endpoint leaves name resolution unchanged, so the hostname still returns the service's public addresses, while the route and the source address of the traffic do not change: This denies the effect the endpoint actually has. Once the endpoint is deployed, service traffic from the subnet switches from the virtual machine's public IPv4 address to its private IPv4 address and takes the more specific service route over the Azure backbone, which is exactly what the diagnostic log entry shows with 10.0.1.7 as the client address.
- Enabling the endpoint changes name resolution, so the hostname returns the service's private addresses, while the route and the source address of the traffic change: This claims that name resolution changes, which a service endpoint does not do; the service hostname keeps resolving to the public addresses of the service. To have the service name resolve to private addresses inside the virtual network you would deploy a private endpoint (Azure Private Link), not a service endpoint.

options.text: In snet-pipeline, turn on the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint.
On stlogs01, change public network access to Enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses and add vnet-insights/snet-pipeline to the list of virtual networks.
Create a service endpoint policy whose serviceResources array lists stlogs01 and stlogs02, and associate that policy with snet-pipeline.
In the network security group on snet-pipeline, add an outbound rule allowing destination service tag Storage on port 445 and a rule denying destination service tag Internet on port *.
Create a private endpoint for stlogs01 in snet-pipeline.

explanation: Each drafted change produces a different effect. Turning on the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on snet-pipeline gives the pipeline an optimized path to the account over the Azure backbone; the account keeps its own public IP address, and the traffic leaves the virtual machine with its private address instead of a public one, which is what the account records as the caller (it1 -> sl1). The account-side network settings on stlogs01 are what make that account answer only the listed virtual network and subnet and refuse every other source (it2 -> sl2). A service endpoint policy attached to the subnet acts as an allow-list of resources: only stlogs01 and stlogs02 remain reachable from that subnet and every other storage account refuses the traffic (it3 -> sl3); such a policy only filters traffic on a subnet where the matching service endpoint is enabled, so it pairs with it1. The network security group rules let the subnet reach the Storage service tag on port 445 while the deny rule for destination service tag Internet on port * overrides the default AllowInternetOutBound rule, so everything else leaving Azure is dropped (it4 -> sl4). A private endpoint places a dedicated IP address and a network interface for the account inside the virtual network (it5 -> sl5).

prompt: You run an Azure environment where the virtual machine web-01, in the spoke virtual network app-spoke, must open TCP sessions on port 443 to a partner application at 203.0.113.10 reached over ExpressRoute. Users report that the sessions fail intermittently, while other outbound connections from the same machine succeed. You need to identify the network security group rule responsible for the failures so the team can adjust it, and the partner agreement does not allow probes to be sent to their production endpoint. Which Network Watcher capability should you use for this investigation?

options.text: IP flow verify, because it reports the matching network security group rule for the traffic without contacting the destination
Connection troubleshoot, because it reports the matching network security group rule after running live probes
NSG diagnostics, because it reports the matching network security group rule for virtual machine scale set instances
Next hop, because it reports the next hop type, its IP address, and the route table for the destination

explanation:
IP flow verify statically evaluates the rules that apply to the virtual machine's network interface and subnet, combining the rules of every attached network security group with the Azure Virtual Network Manager admin rules in force on the virtual network. It returns whether the connection is allowed or denied together with the name of the rule that decided it and the group holding that rule, and it supports TCP and UDP on an individual virtual machine. Because it only simulates rule evaluation and never opens a connection to the destination, it also satisfies the partner's restriction on probes.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Connection troubleshoot, because it reports the matching network security group rule after running live probes: Connection troubleshoot runs live probes toward the destination to measure latency and draw the hop-by-hop topology, which the partner agreement in this scenario forbids. It also checks TCP or ICMP connections only and is aimed at end-to-end reachability rather than a rule-level evaluation, so it is not the right choice here.
- NSG diagnostics, because it reports the matching network security group rule for virtual machine scale set instances: NSG diagnostics is the tool to reach for when rules apply to a virtual machine scale set or when ICMP rules have to be evaluated. In this case the endpoint is an individual virtual machine, the protocols in scope are TCP and UDP, and admin rules from Azure Virtual Network Manager are in force on the virtual network, which NSG diagnostics does not weigh.
- Next hop, because it reports the next hop type, its IP address, and the route table for the destination: Next hop answers where a destination address would be routed: it returns the next hop type, that hop's IP address, and the route table involved. It never evaluates network security group rules or admin rules, so it cannot identify the rule responsible for the failed sessions.

prompt: You support a workload running in the virtual network app-spoke. The scale set ss-app must reach a partner API by hostname api.partner.example over TCP 443 in the outbound direction, but those sessions time out. The team wants a single diagnostic run that reports measured round-trip latency, renders the path from source to destination step by step, and tells them whether the failure sits in their own configuration or in the platform. The images used by ss-app are frozen, so nothing may be added to the instances. Which Network Watcher capability should you use?

options.text: IP flow verify
Next hop
Connection troubleshoot
NSG diagnostics

explanation:
Connection troubleshoot is the only Network Watcher capability that performs an end-to-end reachability run and returns measured latency (minimum, maximum, average), a step-by-step topology from source to destination, and per-hop issues with origin, severity and type — for example GuestFirewall, DnsResolution, NetworkSecurityRule, UserDefinedRoute, CPU or Memory — so the team can tell whether the fault is in their own configuration or in the platform. It also accepts the inputs in this scenario: a virtual machine scale set is a supported source, a fully qualified domain name is a supported destination, and TCP is a supported protocol. Its agentless experience (currently preview) runs the diagnostics over Azure platform APIs, so no extension has to be added to the frozen ss-app images. IP flow verify only simulates the security and admin rules that would apply to a single virtual machine's traffic and reports no live test, latency or listener state; next hop reports where traffic would be routed and never evaluates rules or measures reachability; NSG diagnostics reports which rules apply to subnets and scale sets but gives no latency measurement and no attribution to the guest operating system firewall, name resolution or resource saturation.

Why the other options are wrong:
- IP flow verify: This option is a static rule simulation: it reports whether the rules in force would permit or block the traffic and names the matched rule and the group holding it, but it never opens a session, so it produces no latency figures, no step-by-step path and no evidence that a process is listening at the destination. It also exercises only TCP and UDP rules for a single virtual machine, and rules attached to a scale set fall outside its scope, so it cannot answer the end-to-end question raised here.
- Next hop: This option reports the forwarding target for a destination address, that target's address and the routing table that supplied the entry. It answers where traffic would go, not whether traffic actually arrives: it measures no latency, opens no session, and reports no issues that can be attributed to the guest operating system firewall, name resolution or CPU and memory pressure. It therefore cannot satisfy the latency, topology and root-cause attribution the team asked for.
- NSG diagnostics: This option reports which rules apply to subnets and to virtual machine scale sets and how each rule was matched, which is the right tool for rule questions such as an ICMP rule or a scale-set rule set. It does not run a reachability test, does not measure latency, and does not report DNS, guest firewall or resource-saturation issues, so it cannot deliver the end-to-end diagnosis described in the scenario.

explanation:
Next hop is the capability built for route resolution. Given a destination address, it reports the type of routing device the platform would use (such as VirtualAppliance, VirtualNetworkGateway or Internet), the IP address of that device, and the identifier of the route table that contains the matching route; when the matching route comes from no user-created table, the table is reported as System Route. It evaluates the platform's routing configuration only, so nothing is probed at 10.60.5.20 and the on-premises team's restriction is respected. That is exactly the three-part answer the team asked for: device type, device address, and route table holding the applied route — and it explains why traffic for 10.60.5.20 follows the 10.0.0.0/8 prefix in rt-spoke-udr toward the virtual appliance rather than the ExpressRoute gateway.

Why the other options are wrong:
- IP flow verify: IP flow verify simulates whether traffic would be permitted or blocked by network security group rules and Virtual Network Manager admin rules, and it names the security rule that matched. It never reports a routing device for a destination address or the route table involved, and it does not evaluate user-defined routes, so it cannot answer a routing question.
- Connection troubleshoot: Connection troubleshoot runs live probes and returns reachability, latency and a hop-by-hop topology, which is not permitted here because the on-premises team forbids probes to the destination. It may flag a route as a contributing cause, but it is not the tool that hands back the routing device type, its IP address and the route table as a routing report.
- NSG diagnostics: NSG diagnostics inspects network security group rules and their logs for traffic to a specific virtual machine or network interface and reports which security rule matched. It says nothing about where the platform routes a destination address, so it cannot produce the routing report that was requested.

options.text: The next hop check confirms that no route you created matches traffic to 10.70.9.5, so the traffic leaves the virtual network via the public Internet path rather than reaching the ExpressRoute gateway.
The next hop check confirms that a route you created sends 10.70.9.5 to the virtual appliance in the hub virtual network, so the traffic takes the appliance path instead of the ExpressRoute gateway.
The next hop check confirms that a security group rule denies the traffic, so open port 443 in the network security group attached to snet-app before the sessions can reach the Internet.
The next hop check confirms missing ARP entries on the ExpressRoute circuit, so the fault lies with the on-premises network rather than in your own routing of that prefix.

explanation:
The stored output combines two well-known fields of a next hop result: the next hop type (Internet) and the route table (System Route). The route table is reported as System Route when no route you created applies to the destination, so nothing in your own route tables redirects 10.70.9.5 toward the ExpressRoute gateway. Traffic therefore falls back to the platform's built-in egress over the Internet, which is why the on-premises server never sees the sessions, and the routing design has to be corrected with an appropriate route for that prefix. A next hop result describes only where traffic would be sent; it says nothing about whether security group or Virtual Network Manager admin rules would allow it.

Why the other options are wrong:
- The next hop check confirms that a route you created sends 10.70.9.5 to the virtual appliance in the hub virtual network, so the traffic takes the appliance path instead of the ExpressRoute gateway: A route you created that matched the destination would have been reported together with the route table holding it, not as System Route, and a virtual appliance destination would appear with the VirtualAppliance next hop type plus the appliance address. Neither appears in the stored output, so this reading does not match the result.
- The next hop check confirms that a security group rule denies the traffic, so open port 443 in the network security group attached to snet-app before the sessions can reach the Internet: A next hop result never evaluates network security group rules or Virtual Network Manager admin rules, so it cannot confirm that a rule denies the traffic, and it does not name a rule to open. Rule-level answers for TCP or UDP traffic on a single virtual machine come from IP flow verify, while end-to-end reachability with root-cause detail comes from connection troubleshoot.
- The next hop check confirms missing ARP entries on the ExpressRoute circuit, so the fault lies with the on-premises network rather than in your own routing of that prefix: Missing ARP entries on an ExpressRoute circuit are surfaced by connection troubleshoot as a routing error, not by a next hop check. A next hop result only reports the next hop type, its IP address and the route table that matched, so it cannot confirm an ARP condition.

prompt: You have a workload that runs as the virtual machine app-01 in subnet snet-app of the virtual network vnet-app. Traffic from app-01 that is bound for the on-premises server 10.60.4.25 is handed to the network virtual appliance fw-01 in subnet snet-nva, and the sessions never complete, although the appliance itself is powered on and healthy. A Network Watcher connection troubleshoot run between app-01 and 10.60.4.25 produced the result below. You need the sessions from app-01 to the on-premises server to be established. Which change should you make?

options.text: Enable IP forwarding on the network interface of the network virtual appliance that forwards traffic to the on-premises network.
Enable IP forwarding on the network interface of the source virtual machine that originates the traffic.
Enable IP forwarding on the network interface of the network virtual appliance in the hub virtual network.
Enable IP forwarding on the network interface of the destination virtual machine in the on-premises network.

explanation:
The run reports the session as Unreachable, the next hop for the destination as a VirtualAppliance (10.20.7.9), and an issue on that appliance hop with error code IPForwardingNotEnabled, Origin Local and Severity Error. Origin Local means the condition sits on the hop itself, so the fault is on the network virtual appliance that sits in the path of the on-premises prefix. IPForwardingNotEnabled is the routing condition reported when the network interface of such an appliance is not enabled for IP forwarding: the appliance receives the traffic from app-01 but will not route it onward to the on-premises network, which is why the sessions never complete. Turning on IP forwarding for the network interface of the appliance that handles this traffic restores the path.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enable IP forwarding on the network interface of the source virtual machine that originates the traffic: app-01 only originates the sessions; it is not a device that relays traffic between segments, so switching on IP forwarding for its own network interface cannot change what the appliance does with it. The recorded condition belongs to the hop that plays the virtual appliance role, and no issue is reported on the source hop.
- Enable IP forwarding on the network interface of the network virtual appliance in the hub virtual network: The result identifies the appliance hop in the application virtual network (NextHopType VirtualAppliance, resource id of fw-01) and reports no condition on any interface in the hub virtual network. Enabling forwarding on an interface that is not on the reported path leaves the reported error untouched.
- Enable IP forwarding on the network interface of the destination virtual machine in the on-premises network: The condition concerns an Azure network interface inside the virtual network. The host in the on-premises network does not relay this traffic, and enabling forwarding on its interface has no bearing on the behaviour of the appliance that received it.

options.text: IP flow verify
Next hop
Connection troubleshoot

explanation: Case A asks which rule produced a refusal and whether that rule comes from Virtual Network Manager administrator configuration or from a security group entry, and it forbids live probes. Case C needs an end-to-end check that reports whether anything is listening on the target port, which stage of the path carries the problem and on which side of that stage it appears, and the number of failed probes, with nothing installable on the source; those per-stage results and probe counters come from a connection troubleshoot run, whose agentless experience also allows an Application Gateway v2 source.

You need to record the error code that the tool reported for each investigation, so the team can act on the right problem. Which error code belongs to each run? Drag each error code into the matching slot.

`Run R1
  Start virtual machine: vm-app-01
  End point: vm-db-02
  Test performed: TCP 443 outbound
  Outcome reported by the run: The run could not start. The Network Watcher extension installed for vm-app-01 was not responding, and zero probes were sent.

Run R2
  Start virtual machine: vm-app-02
  End point: vm-web-03
  Test performed: TCP 8080 outbound
  Outcome reported by the run: The run reached vm-web-03, but the check confirmed that nothing there accepted connections for 8080.

Run R3
  Start virtual machine: vm-app-03
  End point: 10.70.9.5 (on-premises via ExpressRoute)
  Test performed: TCP 443 outbound
  Outcome reported by the run: The run reported that traffic for 10.70.9.5 is handed to a next hop of None instead of leaving through the ExpressRoute gateway, so every session fails.

Run R4
  Start virtual machine: vm-app-04
  End point: vm-api-05
  Test performed: TCP 443 outbound
  Outcome reported by the run: The run failed to open a local socket: the socket it needed was still lingering in the TIME_WAIT state left over from an earlier check.`
prompt: Error code for R1 (vm-app-01 to vm-db-02)

options.text: AgentStopped
NoListenerOnDestination
UserDefinedRoute
SourcePortInUse
RouteMissing
UDRLoop

explanation: Each run's outcome matches the error code that connection troubleshoot reports for that condition. R1 is AgentStopped, because the run could not start once the Network Watcher extension on the starting virtual machine stopped responding. R2 is NoListenerOnDestination, because the target was reached but the check confirmed that nothing there accepted connections for 8080. R3 is UserDefinedRoute, because a route in the customer's own configuration sends the traffic to a next hop of None, which is the blackhole the tool reports. R4 is SourcePortInUse, because the probe could not bind since the local socket it needed was still in the TIME_WAIT state from an earlier check.

explanation: Every code in the slots points at one specific configuration detail. A user-defined route that sends traffic to the address of the hop already handling it produces UDRLoop. Two network interfaces of one virtual machine sharing an address range produce MultiNICsInSameSubnet, which is reported because that setup can lead to asymmetric routing and unpredictable traffic. options.text: ConnectionStatus
AvgLatencyInMs
ProbesFailed
SecurityRuleAccessResult
AppliedTo
DestinationPortStatus

explanation: Each request describes one specific piece of evidence carried by a stored Network Watcher connection troubleshoot run. ConnectionStatus holds the overall verdict of the check (Reachable or Unreachable), so it answers whether the far end answered. AvgLatencyInMs holds the average round-trip delay and, together with the minimum and maximum values, is returned only when the check succeeded, so it answers the request for mean round-trip delay. ProbesFailed counts the probes that did not complete and is capped at 100, matching the request about how many issued attempts did not complete. SecurityRuleAccessResult reports Allow or Deny once the entries in force on the interface and subnet have been evaluated, so it produces the allow-or-block outcome. AppliedTo records whether the group holding the matched entry sits on the network interface or on the subnet, which answers the attachment-level question. DestinationPortStatus reports the state of the destination port (Unknown, Reachable, Unstable, NoConnection or Timeout), which is the condition of the far endpoint during the attempt, including timeouts and no-answer cases.

context:
You have a service that runs as the virtual machine srv-02 at 10.20.6.44 in the subnet snet-app of the virtual network vnet-app. A client virtual machine client-01 at 10.20.4.19 opens TCP sessions to srv-02 on port 443, and every attempt is refused. You ran a Network Watcher IP flow verify check for the inbound traffic from client-01 and stored the result below. The result reports the rule that produced the refusal, but it points to no network security group. You need the sessions from client-01 to be accepted. Which interpretation and change should you apply?

- Property: Network Watcher region; Value: East US
- Property: Virtual machine region; Value: East US
- Property: Local IP; Value: 10.20.6.44
- Property: Remote IP; Value: 10.20.4.19
- Property: Direction; Value: Inbound
- Property: Protocol; Value: TCP
- Property: Local port; Value: 443
- Property: Remote port; Value: 51234
- Property: Result; Value: Access denied
- Property: Rule that matched; Value: DenyAllInBound
- Property: Network security group; Value: No link returned
prompt: The stored result shows that _____, so you should [...].

options.text: a default security rule produced the refusal, and no network security group is named
a custom rule that belongs to a scale set produced the refusal, and no network security group is named
a custom rule in the network security group applied to the client produced the refusal, so that group should be opened
the check ran in a region other than the virtual machine's, so no rule can be named for it

explanation:
The stored result reports Access denied, names the rule DenyAllInBound and returns no link to a network security group. The documentation states that the result omits the link when a default security rule is the one deciding the outcome, so the missing link tells you that no custom rule in force permits this traffic and that the built-in rule named in the result is what refuses it. The other explanations do not survive the stored facts: rules that belong to a scale set are not evaluated by this check at all, a custom rule always comes back with the group that holds it, and the check cannot even run for a virtual machine that sits in a different region from the Network Watcher instance. Because the groups evaluated for the checked virtual machine are the network security groups applied to its network interface or its subnet, the correction is a custom allow rule for the inbound TCP traffic in one of the groups applied to the machine that runs the service.

Why the other options are wrong:
- a custom rule that belongs to a scale set produced the refusal, and no network security group is named: Rules applied to virtual machine scale sets are outside this check, so a scale set rule cannot be the one named in the result; those rules have to be examined with NSG diagnostics instead.
- a custom rule in the network security group applied to the client produced the refusal, so that group should be opened: A custom rule is always reported together with the network security group that holds it, so the missing link rules this out; for inbound traffic the groups in force are the ones applied to the machine that runs the service, not the client's.
- the check ran in a region other than the virtual machine's, so no rule can be named for it: The check needs a Network Watcher instance in the same subscription and region as the virtual machine, so a result could not have been produced from another region; both regions in the stored result are the same.

options.text: Set the next hop type of a route to None
Remove the route table from GatewaySubnet
Turn on Enable IP forwarding for the network virtual appliance's interface
Turn off virtual network gateway route propagation on the route table
Set the next hop IP of the route to the private IP of the network virtual appliance

explanation: Each issue points at a different part of the route configuration. The decommissioned range 10.30.0.0/16 currently matches the catch-all route and must be discarded, which is what a route whose next hop type is None does. The site-to-site link refuses to come up because rt-ops, which contains a 0.0.0.0/0 route, is associated with the gateway subnet of a VPN-connected virtual network; the association has to go, not the propagation setting, because propagation must never be switched off on that subnet. Packets that reach the appliance but are never delivered onward point at the NIC setting of a virtual machine that forwards traffic to an address other than its own, Enable IP forwarding. The requirement to ignore whatever the corporate router advertises means the prefixes learned from the gateway must stay out of the subnet, so virtual network gateway route propagation has to be switched off. Finally, a route with next hop type Virtual appliance only works when the appliance's private IP address is supplied, and the partner route in the table has no next hop IP, so that traffic never reaches the appliance.

options.text: Virtual network peering
Global virtual network peering
Subnet peering
Azure Virtual Network Manager connectivity configuration

explanation: Each requirement matches a different Azure connectivity design. edge-vnet and core-vnet both sit in East US and must exchange their whole address ranges, which is the same-region virtual network peering. core-vnet and eu-reporting-vnet sit in different regions (East US and West Europe) and need their complete address ranges exchanged, which is the cross-region global virtual network peering. The partner link must carry only the address range that holds the file-transfer service in edge-vnet, which is the added flexibility of subnet peering, where a chosen list of subnets is peered instead of the entire address space. Finally, 600 spoke environments attached to core-vnet without administering each peer one by one calls for the Azure Virtual Network Manager connectivity configuration, which scales to a hub-and-spoke topology with up to 1,000 spokes on one hub.

- Virtual network: branch-vnet; Address space: 10.2.0.0/16; Region: East US; Cloud: Public; Microsoft Entra tenant: contoso.onmicrosoft.com; Notes: One of 240 branch networks; subnet AppSubnet; no gateway of its own
- Virtual network: prod-vnet; Address space: 10.3.0.0/16; Region: East US; Cloud: Public; Microsoft Entra tenant: contoso.onmicrosoft.com; Notes: Production network; subnets AppSubnet and DataSubnet; linked to the partner network
- Virtual network: partner-vnet; Address space: 10.6.0.0/16; Region: West Europe; Cloud: Public; Microsoft Entra tenant: fabrikam.onmicrosoft.com; Notes: Partner network; subnet AppSubnet

options.text: Refuse the request: a peering never joins networks that run in separate clouds.

Configure summarizedGatewayPrefixes on the network that holds the gateway, so its VPN and ExpressRoute gateways advertise summarized prefixes instead of the address space of that network and of the networks peered to it.
Add a guest user from each tenant as an administrator in the opposite tenant.
Use subnet peering so that only the listed subnets are peered, instead of the whole address space.
Move the design to Azure Virtual Network Manager connectivity configurations.

explanation: Each design maps to one capability of virtual network peering and its surroundings. The request from the 21Vianet-operated network cannot be met, because a peering never joins networks that run in separate clouds. The corporate routers can be given a single aggregated range by populating summarizedGatewayPrefixes on the network that holds the gateway, so the VPN and ExpressRoute gateways there advertise summarized prefixes rather than the address space of the hub and of the networks peered to it. The cross-organization link to partner-vnet needs a user from each tenant added as a guest user in the opposite tenant, which is what allows both sides to choose and manage the other side's networks. Keeping the partner's reach limited to the application server network calls for subnet peering, since ordinary virtual network peering connects the whole address space and all subnets. Attaching several hundred branch networks to one shared hub calls for Azure Virtual Network Manager connectivity configurations, which scale beyond hand-built peerings.

explanation:
A peering carries traffic only; it never resolves host names across the linked networks, and default Azure name resolution cannot look up names in a peered network. The supported way to resolve names across a peering is Azure Private DNS or a custom DNS server. Creating a private zone for contoso.internal, publishing a record that points at the orders service address 10.2.0.20, and linking the zone to app-vnet and to services-vnet satisfies both requirements: a private zone is only consulted by the networks that are linked to it, so the storefront web servers resolve orders.contoso.internal and the orders team resolves the storefront server names.

- create an Azure Private DNS zone for contoso.internal and link it to only services-vnet: Linking the private zone only to services-vnet leaves the storefront web servers outside the zone, so their lookup for orders.contoso.internal still fails. options.text: resize the address space of one of the networks
keep the address space of one of the networks and add a subnet peering link for the chosen subnets
keep the address space of one of the networks and enable gateway transit on the peering
keep the address space of one of the networks and connect them with a gateway-to-gateway VPN connection

explanation:
The two networks share part of the same IP space: test-vnet's 10.20.5.0/24 sits inside app-vnet's 10.20.0.0/16. Azure only accepts a virtual network peering when the two networks use non-overlapping IP address spaces, so the blade refused the combination and no peering was created. Editing the address space of one of the networks removes the collision — for example, move test-vnet and its subnet to a range that sits outside 10.20.0.0/16, or shrink app-vnet's range so that it no longer covers 10.20.5.0/24 while app-subnet (10.20.1.0/24) stays inside it. A virtual network's address space can be edited by changing a prefix length, adding ranges or deleting ranges, and once the two plans no longer collide the peering can be created and then brought to Connected on both sides.

Why the other options are wrong:
- keep the address space of one of the networks and add a subnet peering link for the chosen subnets: Subnet peering is an extra option built on top of virtual network peering that lets you pick specific subnets to peer instead of the whole address space. It does not relax the rule that the two networks being peered must use non-overlapping IP address spaces, so the same conflict remains and the blade would refuse the combination again.
- keep the address space of one of the networks and enable gateway transit on the peering: Gateway transit is a routing option that lets one network use a gateway hosted in the other network. It has no bearing on the IP plan requirement that blocked the creation, and neither network hosts a gateway or route server, so the option could not be enabled here.
- keep the address space of one of the networks and connect them with a gateway-to-gateway VPN connection: A gateway-to-gateway VPN would carry traffic between the two networks over an IPsec tunnel instead of over an Azure virtual network peering, and it would need a gateway plus public IP in each network, which neither network has today. It therefore does not deliver the requested peering link.

explanation:
When the two subscriptions sit in different Microsoft Entra tenants, each side must be able to see and administer the other's virtual network before the peering can be created. The documented way to do that is to add a person from each tenant as a guest in the opposite tenant's directory and give that account administrator rights there. Only then can each team select the remote virtual network from the Subscription and Virtual network pickers and configure its own side of the peering, so that both entries reach Connected and traffic flows.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the partner team must create the peering for their side only, and your side must stay in the Initiated state: A peering that is configured on one side only stays in the Initiated state and carries no traffic at all; the link only works when a matching peering exists on the remote virtual network as well.
- the partner network must be added by entering its resource ID on the peering blade instead of choosing it from the subscription list: The resource ID field is the fallback for a remote virtual network you cannot read in your own tenant; it does not grant access across tenants. Permissions still have to be assigned in both directories before either side can create the peering, so supplying the ID alone leaves the authorization error in place.
- the partner network must be moved into a subscription that belongs to your own Microsoft Entra tenant: Resources cannot be relocated into a subscription that belongs to a different Microsoft Entra tenant, and the partner network is owned by the partner organisation in its own tenant. Changing subscription ownership would not create the cross-tenant connectivity that the link needs.

The spoke virtual networks have no gateway subnet, so populating the property on them does not change what the hub gateway sends to the corporate device.
- set the summarizedGatewayPrefixes property on the VPN gateway resource gw-hub-01 in hub-vnet: summarizedGatewayPrefixes is a property of a virtual network, not of the VPN gateway resource. It has to be populated on the virtual network that contains the gateway, which is hub-vnet.

to move one network to a different resource group so that the address ranges no longer clash

explanation:
Virtual networks can only be peered when their address ranges do not collide — the documentation states that the virtual networks you peer must have nonoverlapping IP address spaces. Here both networks claim 10.5.0.0/16, so the peering is refused and no entry is created on either side. The fix is to edit the address prefix of one network (the address space of a virtual network can be resized by editing a prefix such as 10.1.0.0/16, adding or deleting ranges) so that the two networks hold distinct ranges, and then create the peering again. A peering must be configured on each of the two virtual networks: when the first side is created its status is Initiated, and only when the second side is created does the status become Connected for both. A peering that exists on one side only carries no traffic, so until the support team adds its own side the link reports Initiated and passes nothing.

Why the other options are wrong:
- to add a second address prefix on one network so that the address space covers both ranges: Adding a further address prefix leaves 10.5.0.0/16 claimed by both networks, so the two address ranges still collide and the peering is still refused.
- to enable gateway transit on one network so that the traffic is carried by the gateway: Gateway transit only decides where traffic is sent once a peering exists and a gateway is present; it does not remove the requirement that the two networks hold nonoverlapping address ranges, so the peering still cannot be created.
- to move one network to a different resource group so that the address ranges no longer clash: The resource group a virtual network lives in has no bearing on its address range, so relocating one network does not resolve the duplicate range and the peering remains refused.

explanation:
Two settings have to change. On spoke-vnet you turn on the option that lets the virtual network rely on the gateway or route server that lives in the peer: that option is what makes spoke-vnet exchange routes with the remote route server, so rs-hub-01 in hub-vnet hands over the prefixes it learned from fwa-hub-01, including 192.168.0.0/16, and the application servers finally get a route to the corporate network. The hub side has to grant the matching permission, 'Allow gateway or route server in 'hub-vnet' to forward traffic to the peered virtual network', because the spoke-side option can only be switched on when the peer allows its own gateway or route server to forward traffic across the link, and this permission is what lets the route server in the hub send anything to the spoke.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Allow gateway or route server in the peered virtual network to forward traffic to 'spoke-vnet': This setting only lets the gateway or route server in the peer forward traffic into spoke-vnet. It does not open a route exchange between rs-hub-01 and the spoke, so the application servers still have no entry for 192.168.0.0/16; it is the hub-side permission that must be granted for this.
- Allow 'spoke-vnet' to receive forwarded traffic from the peered virtual network: This setting covers traffic that an appliance in another network forwards across the link. It does not hand the prefixes that rs-hub-01 learned from fwa-hub-01 to the spoke, so the missing route stays missing.
- Allow 'spoke-vnet' to access the peered virtual network: This setting decides whether the peer may reach spoke-vnet at all and it is on by default. It says nothing about route exchange between the two sides, so it cannot put the corporate prefix into the route tables of the spoke's virtual machines.

- Set the data-tier address range to 10.30.9.64/30: A /30 range is smaller than the smallest subnet range Azure accepts, which is /29, so this request is rejected outright before any capacity question arises.
- Set the data-tier address range to 10.30.9.128/29: Relocating the subnet does not change its size: 10.30.9.128/29 is still eight addresses with five reserved by Azure, so only three usable addresses remain, which cannot hold the four planned workloads plus growth.

options.text: Enable network policies for private endpoints on the subnet so that the subnet's network security group and route table apply to every private endpoint in it.
Enable the service endpoints for Azure Storage and Azure Key Vault services on the subnet so that every resource of those services can accept traffic from it.
Enable subnet delegation to Microsoft.Network/privateEndpoints so that the platform creates and manages the private endpoint network interfaces inside the delegated subnet.
Move the private endpoints into a separate subnet that has its own network security group and route table, leaving the current subnet and its controls unchanged.

explanation:
Turning on the subnet's setting for network policies on private endpoints makes the network security group and route table assigned to that subnet apply to every private endpoint deployed in it. Because the requirement is that the existing controls in the `integration` subnet cover the private endpoints that live there, enabling this setting at subnet scope is the change that satisfies it.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enable the service endpoints for Azure Storage and Azure Key Vault services on the subnet so that every resource of those services can accept traffic from it: Service endpoints solve a different problem: the Azure service keeps its public endpoint and Azure restricts access to that public endpoint to your VNet, and each resource of the service (for example each Storage account) must separately be permitted to accept traffic from the subnet. They do not extend the subnet's network security group or route table to private endpoints, so they do not deliver the single set of rules the security team asked for.
- Enable subnet delegation to Microsoft.Network/privateEndpoints so that the platform creates and manages the private endpoint network interfaces inside the delegated subnet: Subnet delegation grants one service permission to create its own service-specific resources in the subnet during deployment; it is not a way of extending the subnet's network security group or route table to private endpoints. Delegation also cannot be added or removed while resources of the delegated service are already deployed in the subnet, so it is the wrong lever for this goal.
- Move the private endpoints into a separate subnet that has its own network security group and route table, leaving the current subnet and its controls unchanged: Relocating the private endpoints to another subnet that carries different controls leaves the network security group and route table in the `integration` subnet unchanged, so the endpoints still would not be covered by the protections already in force for that subnet. Moving resources also adds work without meeting the stated requirement.

explanation:
Virtual networks created through the portal, and by API versions released after March 31, 2026, are created with `defaultOutboundAccess` set to `false`, so their subnets are private by default and the virtual machines get no implicit outbound public IP. The output shows exactly that state for `app-vnet`: `defaultOutboundAccess` is false and the network interface of `nic-app-01` has no public IP address, which is why the machines can reach each other but nothing on the internet. Virtual machines in such a subnet need an explicit outbound method — a NAT gateway associated with the subnet, a public IP on the network interface, or a public load balancer with outbound rules. Because the requirement rules out public IP addresses on the virtual machines, associating a NAT gateway with the `app` subnet is the change that restores outbound connectivity; the NAT gateway must be created in the same subscription and region as the virtual network.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add a service endpoint for Azure Storage to the `app` subnet: Service endpoints leave the service's own public endpoint in place and simply restrict it to your virtual network; enabling the Azure Storage endpoint only affects traffic that is destined for Azure Storage. It does not give the virtual machines a general path out to internet-hosted services and does not change the subnet's lack of an outbound method.
- Create a virtual network peering from `app-vnet` to the `shared-services` virtual network: Virtual network peering links two virtual networks so the resources on either side can communicate with each other, in the same or different regions and even across subscriptions. It is not an outbound connectivity method for the virtual machines in the `app` subnet, so it does not restore their access to the internet.
- Enable the private endpoints network policy setting on the `app` subnet: The private endpoints network policy setting is what makes a subnet's network security group and route table apply to the private endpoints placed inside that subnet. The `app` subnet has no network security group, no route table and no private endpoints, and this setting has no effect on the outbound connectivity of ordinary virtual machines.
