You have a general-purpose v2 storage account, contosodata, that stores business files in named groups. After an audit, the compliance team listed four recovery situations that this account has to withstand, and they want each one mapped to the single mechanism that actually delivers it. Match each situation to its mechanism.

- Property: Account type; Value: General-purpose v2
- Property: Hierarchical namespace; Value: Disabled
- Property: Soft delete for blobs; Value: Enabled, 7 days
- Property: Soft delete for containers; Value: Disabled
- Property: Blob versioning; Value: Disabled
- Property: Resource locks; Value:
prompt: Situation 1 - A maintenance script removed an entire named group of files with everything in it, and that group has to be recoverable exactly as it was.

options.text: Blob soft delete
Container soft delete
A canNotDelete lock
Azure Backup

explanation: Each situation is answered by a different mechanism. Situation 1 is the risk of the whole named group being removed, which is what container soft delete retains and restores together with its contents (Restore Container returns the container with its blobs, versions and snapshots). Situation 2 is the risk of an individual file being deleted or overwritten while its group keeps running, which is what blob soft delete retains and restores with Undelete Blob, snapshots and versions attached. Situation 3 is about prevention rather than recovery: neither soft delete feature blocks deletion of the storage account itself, so a lock placed on that resource is what makes the deletion fail. Situation 4 goes beyond what the storage service retains, so it needs Azure Backup, which Microsoft recommends in addition to both soft delete features for wider risks such as accidental account deletion or ransomware.

`Account: contosodata
Account type: General-purpose v2

prompt: Overwriting an existing file with a different payload on this account

options.text: The replaced content is not kept at all, while a deleted file can still be brought back until the window closes
The directory and everything under it is kept, and its contents cannot be read until the directory itself is brought back
There is no way to enumerate them; the exact original name has to be known
The deleted files are disconnected from the directory and cannot be brought back under the new name
A replaced file is kept as an older copy that stays available until the window closes
The deleted directories are listed alongside the live ones, so each one can be found by name

explanation: Every item in the key belongs to a hierarchical namespace (Data Lake Storage Gen2) account, and the two unused items describe flat namespace accounts, which this account is not. On a hierarchical namespace account, soft delete protects deletes only: overwrites are not captured, so replacing a file leaves no earlier copy, while a deleted file stays in the service and can be brought back until the retention window closes (s1 = i1). Deleting a directory soft-deletes the directory together with everything inside it, and the contents stay inaccessible until the directory itself is undeleted (s2 = i2). Such an account cannot enumerate soft-deleted containers at all, so the exact original container name must be known to bring one back (s3 = i3). Renaming a directory disconnects its soft-deleted blobs from it, so files deleted inside it can no longer be brought back under the new name and the original name must be restored first (s4 = i4).

options.text: Turn off blob soft delete on the account
Raise the container soft delete retention period to 30 days
Turn on permanent delete on the account
Turn off blob versioning on the account

explanation: Each change matches the behaviour that follows from the account's current configuration. Turning off blob soft delete does not free anything early: the blobs and snapshots that were already retained keep the expiry schedule that was in force when they were deleted, so their space is still billed until then. Raising the container retention period is not retroactive, so only containers deleted afterwards get the longer window, while containers already soft-deleted keep the period that applied at their deletion. Turning on permanent delete lets an authorised caller remove retained snapshots and versions ahead of their retention window, which shortens the protection the account otherwise gives. Finally, with blob versioning switched off while blob soft delete stays on, this flat-namespace account again creates a retained copy of the previous content on every overwrite, and an undelete of the blob brings those retained copies back with it.

context:
You have a general-purpose v2 storage account, contosodata, where the finance group stores each month's close pack in a blob container called monthly-close. Two days ago a cleanup script took that container out of the account, and the window during which it can be brought back has not closed yet. The application has since created another container under the same name to write into, but nothing has been uploaded to it yet. Your runbook tries to bring the original container back and the request is rejected because of the name. You need the original container, together with the blobs it held when it was taken out of the account, to be restored under that same name. Which change should you make?

- Setting: Blob soft delete; Value: On, 14-day retention
- Setting: Container soft delete; Value: On, 14-day retention
- Setting: Blob versioning; Value: Off
prompt: The change you should make is to _____.

options.text: Remove the container that occupies that name, then restore the original container to the same name
Extend the account's retention period, then restore the original container to the same name
Turn on blob versioning for the account, then restore the original container to the same name
Grant the runbook identity the Storage Blob Data Contributor role, then restore the original container to the same name

explanation:
A soft-deleted container is always restored as a whole and only under its original name, and a restore cannot overwrite a live name: when the name has been reused, the restore is rejected until the live object holding that name is deleted or renamed. Here the application has taken the name monthly-close, so the container currently using it has to be removed (deleted, or its content copied elsewhere and the container deleted) before the restore is retried. Once the name is free, the original container comes back together with the blobs, blob versions and snapshots it held at the moment it was taken out of the account, and it can only come back under that same original name.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Extend the account's retention period, then restore the original container to the same name: Extending the retention period only changes how long a soft-deleted container stays recoverable; it does nothing about the name conflict, because the request is rejected because the name is already in use, not because the recovery window is too short. The restore would fail the same way.
- Turn on blob versioning for the account, then restore the original container to the same name: Blob versioning applies to individual blobs and their overwrites. It neither frees the container name nor changes how a soft-deleted container is brought back, so turning it on would not make the rejected restore succeed.
- Grant the runbook identity the Storage Blob Data Contributor role, then restore the original container to the same name: The request was rejected with a name conflict rather than an authorization error, so granting the runbook identity the Storage Blob Data Contributor role, which is already the least-privileged role able to restore a soft-deleted container, would not change the outcome.

context:
You have a general-purpose v2 storage account, contosodata, that holds each quarter's reporting data in a container named quarterly-reports. Three days ago a faulty script deleted that container, and it is still in the deleted state. Until this morning, the account kept deleted containers for 7 days; the compliance team has just asked for 30 days of protection, so you raised the retention period on the account to 30 days. The team expects quarterly-reports to be covered by the new 30 days as well, but that container will still be gone for good after 7 days counted from the moment it was deleted. You need quarterly-reports to stay recoverable for a full 30 days from now. Which action should you take?

- Item: Storage account type; Value: General-purpose v2
- Item: Container soft delete retention, until this morning; Value: 7 days
- Item: Container soft delete retention, current; Value: 30 days
- Item: quarterly-reports container; Value: Deleted 3 days ago, still in the deleted state
prompt: The action you should take is to _____.

options.text: Undelete the container and then delete it again.
Wait until the current retention period ends and then delete the container again.
Change the retention period on the account again and leave the container as it is.
Undelete the container and leave it in place.

explanation:
The retention period is applied at the moment a container is deleted. Raising it from 7 to 30 days therefore only affects containers deleted after the change: quarterly-reports was deleted while the 7-day setting was in effect, so it stays on that schedule and is permanently deleted when its window ends, with no way to recover it afterwards. To give that container the longer window, bring it back into the account and delete it again, so the new deletion is recorded under the current 30-day setting and the container remains recoverable for the full 30 days.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Wait until the current retention period ends and then delete the container again: Waiting cannot work, because once the existing 7-day window elapses the soft-deleted container is permanently deleted and cannot be recovered; by then there is nothing left to delete a second time under the 30-day setting.
- Change the retention period on the account again and leave the container as it is: Retention changes are not retroactive. The new value governs only containers deleted after the update, so leaving quarterly-reports in its current deleted state keeps it on the period that applied when it was deleted.
- Undelete the container and leave it in place: Bringing the container back makes it an active container again rather than a deleted one, so it sits in no retention window at all and gains no protection until it is deleted once more under the current setting.

context:
You have a general-purpose v2 storage account, contosodata, with a hierarchical namespace enabled. The account's current recovery settings and the way the platform team reclaims space are shown below. The compliance team now wants every file that this automatic cleanup removes to stay recoverable for as long as the account already keeps other removed data, and the rest of the account's recovery settings must stay exactly as they are. Which change should you make?

`{
  "accountType": "General-purpose v2 with hierarchical namespace enabled",
  "blobSoftDelete": "On, 14-day retention",
  "blobVersioning": "Off",
  "containerSoftDelete": "Off",
  "reclaimingSpace": "The ingestion pipeline calls Set Blob Expiry on each file once processing finishes"
}`
prompt: The most suitable change for this account is to _____.

options.text: replace the expiry cleanup with a lifecycle management policy on the account
replace the expiry cleanup with a longer blob soft delete retention period on the account
replace the expiry cleanup with container soft delete at 30 days on the account
replace the expiry cleanup with blob versioning on the account

explanation:
Set Blob Expiry is an ADLS-only operation, and blobs removed that way never enter the soft-deleted state, so they cannot be undeleted; expiry on an existing blob in a hierarchical namespace account does not soft-delete it either. When a lifecycle management policy deletes a blob, snapshot, or version, soft delete still applies: the object moves to the soft-deleted state and stays recoverable for the account's retention period, which here is the 14 days already configured for blob soft delete. Moving the cleanup from the expiry call to a lifecycle management policy is therefore the only change that makes automatically removed files recoverable, and it leaves the account's other recovery settings untouched.

Why the other options are wrong:
- replace the expiry cleanup with a longer blob soft delete retention period on the account: Lengthening the retention period only changes how long the service keeps objects that already went into the soft-deleted state. Files removed by Set Blob Expiry never become soft-deleted and cannot be undeleted, so no retention length makes them recoverable.
- replace the expiry cleanup with container soft delete at 30 days on the account: Container soft delete covers the case where the container itself is deleted, bringing back the container together with the blobs it held. Here the container stays in place and individual files are removed by an expiry call, which never soft-deletes them, so this setting changes nothing for the cleanup job.
- replace the expiry cleanup with blob versioning on the account: Blob versioning keeps the earlier state of a blob that is overwritten as a version. The expiry operation takes the file out of the account outright and does not soft-delete it on a hierarchical namespace account, so turning versioning on does not make these removals recoverable.

context:
You have a general-purpose v2 storage account, contosodata, with a flat namespace, and its current data protection settings are shown below. Every morning a reporting job publishes a new build by replacing the blob daily-report.csv in place, and yesterday's build turned out to contain wrong figures that finance has already corrected in downstream reports. The finance team now needs the build that was live yesterday to be the file that users see, and the account's retention settings must stay exactly as they are. The container holding the blob was never deleted, and daily-report.csv itself has only ever been replaced, never deleted. Which sequence of operations should you run?

- Setting: Account type; Value: General-purpose v2, flat namespace
- Setting: Blob soft delete; Value: Enabled
- Setting: Retention for soft-deleted blobs; Value: 30 days
- Setting: Blob versioning; Value: Enabled
- Setting: Container soft delete; Value: Enabled, 7-day retention
prompt: You should _____.

options.text: Undelete the blob and copy the version from yesterday over the base blob
Undelete the blob and restore only the version from yesterday in the same operation
List the versions with include=deleted and download the version from yesterday as the live blob
Restore the container that holds the blob and copy the version from yesterday over the base blob

explanation:
With blob versioning enabled on this account, each replacement of daily-report.csv leaves a version behind, and the Undelete Blob operation brings back all of a blob's soft-deleted versions at once. There is no way to bring back a single version on its own, so the documented way to make one earlier state the live file is to undelete the blob first and then copy that version over the base blob, which is what the keyed option does. Because the blob itself was never deleted, the undelete call still restores the versions attached to it, and the account's retention settings are left untouched.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Undelete the blob and restore only the version from yesterday in the same operation: The recovery call for a blob brings back every soft-deleted version attached to it at once; the service offers no option to bring back just the one version you want, so the second step in this choice cannot be performed.
- List the versions with include=deleted and download the version from yesterday as the live blob: Data held in a soft-deleted state cannot be read or downloaded before it has been restored, so listing the versions with the deleted flag included and downloading one of them directly fails; the data has to be brought back first.
- Restore the container that holds the blob and copy the version from yesterday over the base blob: The container-level recovery operation applies to a container that was deleted, and this container was never deleted, so it has nothing to bring back; container recovery also cannot pick one earlier state of a live blob.

context:
You have a general-purpose v2 storage account, contosodata, that holds the legal department's case files inside a blob container. The account is configured so that a container removed by mistake can be brought back for 30 days, and the team has already confirmed that this works for a container that was deleted last month. The risk register now includes the possibility that the whole account is deleted, which would take the retained containers and every file in them with it and leave nothing that can be brought back. You need that kind of removal to be refused, and you do not want to change how long a deleted container stays recoverable. Which change should you make?

- Setting on contosodata: Account type; Current value: General-purpose v2
- Setting on contosodata: Namespace; Current value: Flat
- Setting on contosodata: Blob soft delete; Current value: Enabled, 30-day retention
- Setting on contosodata: Container soft delete; Current value: Enabled, 30-day retention
- Setting on contosodata: Blob versioning; Current value: Disabled
prompt: To meet that requirement, you should _____.

options.text: add a lock to the storage account resource
add a lock to the blob container resource
increase the container soft delete retention on the storage account to 365 days
grant the Storage Blob Data Contributor role to the account administrators

explanation:
Container soft delete only preserves a deleted container while the storage account itself is still in place. If the storage account is deleted, everything it held, including soft-deleted containers and their blobs, goes with it, and no setting inside the account can prevent that removal. The documented way to stop the account itself from being deleted is to place a lock on the storage account resource, and that leaves the 30-day recovery window for deleted containers untouched.

Why the other options are wrong:
- add a lock to the blob container resource: A lock applied only to an individual blob container prevents that container from being deleted, but it does not stop the storage account itself from being removed, and everything the account holds would be lost when the account goes.
- increase the container soft delete retention on the storage account to 365 days: A longer retention period only governs how long the service keeps a container that was deleted while the account remained in place; it cannot preserve anything once the account itself has been deleted, and it also changes the recovery window you asked to keep as it is.
- grant the Storage Blob Data Contributor role to the account administrators: The Storage Blob Data Contributor role grants data-plane permissions on the blobs of the account; it places no restriction on deleting the storage account resource, so the account could still be removed with everything in it.

context:
You have a general-purpose v2 storage account, contosopipe, that holds each night's pipeline output and is read by the data engineering team through Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2. A week ago you switched on the account's recovery window for removed files so that accidental removals could be undone. Since then every request through the account's dfs.core.windows.net endpoint fails with EndpointUnsupportedAccountFeatures and the pipeline has stopped, while the account still serves its other workloads normally. You need the pipeline working again and the 14-day protection for removed files to stay in force. Which change should the team make?

- Setting: Account type; Value: General-purpose v2 (flat namespace)
- Setting: Recovery window for removed files; Value: On, 14 days
- Setting: Recovery window for removed containers; Value: Off
- Setting: Object versioning; Value: Off
- Setting: Pipeline access method; Value: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 (dfs.core.windows.net)
- Setting: Error returned by every pipeline request; Value: EndpointUnsupportedAccountFeatures
prompt: The data engineering team should _____.

options.text: Point the pipeline at the *.blob.core.windows.net endpoint and keep the 14-day protection in place.
Upgrade the account to a hierarchical namespace and keep the 14-day protection in place.
Turn off the account's deleted-file protection so the *.dfs.core.windows.net endpoint works again.
Grant the pipeline's identity the missing data-plane role and keep the 14-day protection in place.

explanation:
On a flat-namespace account, turning on the recovery window for removed files makes the Data Lake Storage (DFS) endpoint unusable: calls to *.dfs.core.windows.net fail with EndpointUnsupportedAccountFeatures. The documented ways out are to send the workload to the account's blob endpoint (*.blob.core.windows.net) or to move the account to a hierarchical namespace. Because the namespace upgrade is itself blocked while that recovery feature is enabled (the documented sequence is to disable it, migrate, then re-enable it), a straight upgrade would leave the 14-day protection switched off in the meantime. Routing the pipeline to *.blob.core.windows.net restores the workload immediately and keeps the 14-day protection fully in force, which satisfies both requirements.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Upgrade the account to a hierarchical namespace and keep the 14-day protection in place: Converting the account to a hierarchical namespace is rejected while the recovery feature for removed files is turned on; the documented sequence is to disable it, run the migration, then re-enable it. That would leave the 14-day protection off during the change, so this single step does not meet the requirement as stated.
- Turn off the account's deleted-file protection so the *.dfs.core.windows.net endpoint works again: This unblocks the Data Lake endpoint, but it removes the guard against accidental removals that the team was explicitly asked to keep for 14 days. It trades the required protection for the endpoint, so it is not the right change.
- Grant the pipeline's identity the missing data-plane role and keep the 14-day protection in place: The failure is not an authorization problem. prompt: Your organization requires that every object held in the account be protected by two layers of encryption, each using its own key and a different algorithm. An audit of a production storage account found that only the standard service-side layer is active on it. The account is already in service and carries live customer workloads that must keep running. Which approach should you take to put the second layer in place?

options.text: Switch the setting on in the storage account itself, under Security + networking > Encryption, and confirm it reports Enabled.
Provision another storage account with infrastructure encryption enabled on the Encryption tab at creation time, then migrate the payload over to it.
Re-deploy the storage account's ARM template with infrastructure encryption set to Enabled, so the account picks up the property value.
Assign a built-in Azure Policy definition that requires infrastructure encryption, which brings the storage account into compliance.

explanation:
Infrastructure encryption is chosen only while the account is being provisioned, by setting Enable infrastructure encryption = Enabled on the Encryption tab of the create-account experience, and the account cannot be switched to it or away from it afterwards. Because this account has been in service since April with the setting off, the second layer cannot be added to it in place: a storage account of a kind that supports the setting (general-purpose v2 qualifies) has to be provisioned with it turned on, and the stored payload then moved across. Note that Microsoft also considers this extra layer unnecessary for most scenarios and recommends it only where compliance truly demands double encryption.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Switch the setting on in the storage account itself, under Security + networking > Encryption, and confirm it reports Enabled: The Encryption blade under Security + networking is where you verify the setting, not where you change it. The value is fixed when the account is created, so the portal cannot switch infrastructure encryption on for an account that already exists.
- Re-deploy the storage account's ARM template with infrastructure encryption set to Enabled, so the account picks up the property value: The property belongs to the account's creation-time configuration, so re-deploying the template against the running account cannot retroactively apply it; the setting stays disabled and the deployment cannot deliver double encryption for what is already stored.
- Assign a built-in Azure Policy definition that requires infrastructure encryption, which brings the storage account into compliance: A built-in policy definition that requires infrastructure encryption only evaluates and flags resources. It can keep accounts from missing the setting, but it cannot apply an immutable creation-time property to an account that is already running, so it does not put the second layer in place here.

prompt: You have a general-purpose v2 storage account whose blob data is protected by a key your own team manages in the Azure Key Vault vault kv-contoso. The account's key version setting is blank, so Azure Storage settles on the version by itself. Your compliance group now wants the superseded key version taken out of use. Which action should you take?

options.text: Leave the older version enabled until at least one day has passed since the newer version was created, then disable the older version in the vault.
Disable the older version in the vault now and rely on the account's regular check to switch it to the newer version.
Let the vault roll out a further version of the key on its own, and disable the currently active version once that happens.
Disable the older version in the vault now and re-save the account configuration to force it to pick up the newer version straight away.

explanation:
Because the account is configured without a specific key version, Azure Storage only looks in the key vault once a day and adopts the newest version it finds there. The newer version in this exhibit was created a few hours ago, so the account may still be working with the older one; switching that version off immediately would leave the account without a usable key, and blob reads and writes would start failing with HTTP 403. Keeping the older version enabled for at least a day after the newer one is created gives the account time to move over, and turning the older version off afterwards causes no downtime and no exposure of unencrypted data.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Disable the older version in the vault now and rely on the account's regular check to switch it to the newer version: The account's check happens only once a day, so it does not react the moment a new version appears. Disabling the older version right away can therefore break data operations before the account has moved to the newer version.
- Let the vault roll out a further version of the key on its own, and disable the currently active version once that happens: Azure Storage never creates or rotates key versions in your vault; the new version has to be created by you and the account pointed at it. Waiting for the vault to roll out a version by itself would leave the old one serving the account indefinitely.
- Disable the older version in the vault now and re-save the account configuration to force it to pick up the newer version straight away: Re-saving the account configuration does not force an immediate lookup; automatic tracking still happens on the daily schedule. To move across at once you would have to specify the newer version explicitly, which turns off automatic version tracking and makes future updates your job.

Your security policy requires that all data in the account be encrypted at rest with a key that your own team manages in Azure Key Vault, rather than one held by the platform vendor. Which statement correctly describes the data that the account's key protects?

options.text: Every data type in the account, including queues and tables, is protected with the key as soon as the key is assigned.
Blobs and file shares are protected with the key; queues and tables need an encryption scope before the key reaches them.
Blobs and file shares are protected with the key only after infrastructure encryption is turned on for the account.
Blobs and file shares are protected with the key; queue and table data are covered only if you chose them for the account when you created it.

explanation:
A key held by your own team in Azure Key Vault reaches Blob Storage and Azure Files only. Queue and Table data sits under that key solely when those two services are opted in during account creation; on an account that did not opt them in, they stay on Microsoft-managed keys. Nothing in the exhibit's other properties (account kind, redundancy, access tier) changes this scope of coverage.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Every data type in the account, including queues and tables, is protected with the key as soon as the key is assigned: Assigning a customer-managed key does not spread it to every service in the account. Queue and Table storage remain on Microsoft-managed keys unless those services were selected at account creation, so this statement promises protection that the account does not have.
- Blobs and file shares are protected with the key; queues and tables need an encryption scope before the key reaches them: Encryption scopes give per-container and per-blob key control for Blob Storage only; they are not a mechanism for bringing Queue or Table storage under the vault key.
- Blobs and file shares are protected with the key only after infrastructure encryption is turned on for the account: Infrastructure encryption is a second layer beneath the service layer that always relies on a Microsoft-managed key separate from the service key, and Microsoft states it is rarely needed. It is not a prerequisite for a vault key to protect blobs and file shares, and turning it on cannot extend that key to queues or tables.

prompt: You have a general-purpose v2 storage account that four business units share. Each unit's blobs sit under its own encryption scope so that the key boundary can be drawn per tenant, and the scope shown below belongs to a unit whose contract ended last week. You need both of these outcomes: the ongoing charges for that scope must stop, and nothing may be able to read or write the blobs that sit under it any more. Which action should you take?

options.text: Remove the encryption scope from the storage account so it is deleted together with its key
Revoke the key in the key vault kv-contoso and leave the encryption scope as it is
Turn off the encryption scope, then revoke the key it uses in the key vault kv-contoso
Add a new key version in kv-contoso and point the encryption scope at that version

explanation:
An encryption scope can never be deleted; the only lifecycle action available is to turn it off, and once it is off every later read and write against that scope fails with 403, which satisfies the second requirement. Turning the scope off also ends the ongoing charges for it. Because the scope was created well over 30 days ago, the minimum-billing window has already passed, so stopping it now stops the cost. Microsoft also recommends turning a scope off before withdrawing its key in the vault, otherwise the scope keeps being billed while its data is unreachable — so the correct sequence is to turn the scope off first and then revoke the key.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Remove the encryption scope from the storage account so it is deleted together with its key: There is no delete operation for an encryption scope. Scopes are permanent objects that can only be turned off and later turned back on, so the scope and its containers cannot be removed this way.
- Revoke the key in the key vault kv-contoso and leave the encryption scope as it is: Withdrawing the key alone leaves the scope switched on, so the account continues to be charged for a scope whose blobs nobody can reach. Microsoft advises switching off the scope first and only then revoking the key.
- Add a new key version in kv-contoso and point the encryption scope at that version: Adding a new version of the key does not retire the scope: the scope remains active, keeps being billed, and the blobs under it stay reachable under the new version. Azure Storage also never rotates a customer-managed key for you; a new version takes effect only if the account or scope is pointed at it.

The planned configuration for the new account is shown below. Which change must you make before the account is created?

options.text: Create the account with the system-assigned identity and grant it wrapkey, unwrapkey and get permissions on the key.
Create the account with the user-assigned identity and grant it wrapkey, unwrapkey and get permissions on the key.
Create the account with the user-assigned identity and grant it get and list permissions on the key.
Create the account without an identity, then attach a user-assigned identity after deployment and grant it wrapkey, unwrapkey and get permissions on the key.

explanation:
When a storage account is created with a key that the customer holds in Azure Key Vault, the account must be given a user-assigned managed identity as part of creation, and that identity must hold at least the wrapkey, unwrapkey and get permissions on the key so the service can wrap and unwrap the account encryption key. The planned configuration therefore has to swap the identity block to a user-assigned one and ensure those three permissions exist on contoso-storage-key before the account comes up.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Create the account with the system-assigned identity and grant it wrapkey, unwrapkey and get permissions on the key: The permissions listed are the right ones, but a system-assigned identity cannot back a customer-managed key at account-creation time; the system-assigned option only becomes available when the key is applied to an account that already exists.
- Create the account with the user-assigned identity and grant it get and list permissions on the key: get and list are read-style permissions and do not let the account protect or unprotect its own encryption key. wrapkey and unwrapkey are required in addition to get, so key access fails when the account is created.
- Create the account without an identity, then attach a user-assigned identity after deployment and grant it wrapkey, unwrapkey and get permissions on the key: The key has to work at the moment the account is created, and creation requires the user-assigned identity to be part of the account from the start. Bolting an identity on only after deployment leaves the account without a usable identity for its key.

prompt: You have a general-purpose v2 storage account, stgcontoso, whose blob data must be encrypted with a key that your own team maintains in the Azure Key Vault vault kv-contoso. The account, the vault, the key and the permissions granted to the account's identity are all configured as shown below. You need to finish the setup so that the account can actually use that key. Which change should you make first?

options.text: Enable soft delete and purge protection on kv-contoso
Enable purge protection on kv-contoso and re-create key-contoso as a 4096-bit RSA-HSM key
Enable soft delete on kv-contoso and grant the identity only the get permission on key-contoso
Enable soft delete on kv-contoso and change the account to a user-assigned managed identity

explanation:
The vault that holds a customer-managed key must have soft delete enabled and purge protection enabled, and the key itself must be an RSA or RSA-HSM key of 2048, 3072 or 4096 bits. In the exhibit the vault has both soft delete and purge protection turned off, while everything else already qualifies: key-contoso is an RSA 2048-bit key, and the account's identity holds wrapKey, unwrapKey and get. Turning on both vault protections is therefore the one change that must be made before stgcontoso can use the key.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enable purge protection on kv-contoso and re-create key-contoso as a 4096-bit RSA-HSM key: Purge protection by itself is not enough — soft delete must be enabled on the vault as well. The key also already qualifies: RSA at 2048 bits is one of the accepted key types and sizes, so replacing it with a 4096-bit RSA-HSM key changes nothing that was broken and forces the account to be pointed at a new key.
- Enable soft delete on kv-contoso and grant the identity only the get permission on key-contoso: Soft delete alone leaves purge protection off, so the vault still fails the requirement. The identity also already carries the minimum set of permissions it needs — wrapKey, unwrapKey and get — so narrowing it to get only would remove capabilities the account relies on rather than fix a problem.
- Enable soft delete on kv-contoso and change the account to a user-assigned managed identity: Soft delete alone leaves purge protection off, so the vault still fails the requirement. The identity choice is also already acceptable: only at account-creation time must a user-assigned managed identity be supplied for customer-managed keys, while an existing storage account may use either its system-assigned or a user-assigned identity, so no identity change is needed here.

A second business unit owns an encryption scope of its own, esc-marketing, and its data must live in that same container with each unit's blobs protected by a separate key. Every upload from that unit is currently rejected, and the finance unit's blobs must not be lost. Which change should you make?

options.text: Recreate the container with 'Use this encryption scope for all blobs in the container' cleared at creation time, then move the existing blobs into it.
Recreate the container with 'Use this encryption scope for all blobs in the container' selected at creation time, and the marketing uploads will succeed.

explanation:

- Clear 'Use this encryption scope for all blobs in the container' on the existing container from the Encryption pane, and the marketing uploads will succeed right away: The choice between requiring the container's default scope and permitting clients to override it is fixed when the container is created, so clearing it on the existing container has no effect and the uploads keep returning HTTP 403.
- Change the default encryption scope of the existing container to esc-marketing, and leave the checkbox as it is: Repointing the container's default at esc-marketing does not lift the restriction on overrides, would place the finance unit's data under the wrong scope, and the container's default scope is in any case decided at creation time rather than afterwards.

The scope is created, and Azure Storage keeps its key version aligned with the latest version in the vault, just as it does for the existing scopes.

- The request is rejected, because a storage account cannot hold more than 10,000 encryption scopes, so you would have to raise the quota first: The 10,000 figure is the ceiling for scopes whose key version Azure Storage keeps aligned with the vault, not a hard limit on how many encryption scopes an account may contain. The layout below shows where each object sits today. You need the design document to state the location rules accurately before the account configuration is finalized. Which statement is correct?

`Object                        Tenant     Region       Subscription
Storage account stgcontoso    Contoso    East US      sub-contoso-prod
Managed HSM holding the key   Fabrikam   West Europe  sub-fabrikam-sec`
prompt: Regarding where the vault that holds the key may sit, _____.

options.text: it may differ in tenant, region and subscription independently
it must match the account's region, but may differ in tenant and subscription
it must match the account's subscription, but may differ in tenant and region
it must match the account's tenant, but may differ in region and subscription

explanation:
The documentation states that the key vault or managed HSM supplying the key is allowed to sit in a different Microsoft Entra tenant, a different region and a different subscription than the storage account. So the Fabrikam managed HSM in West Europe under sub-fabrikam-sec is an acceptable arrangement for stgcontoso in Contoso's tenant in East US, and no relocation is needed; a managed HSM exposes the same APIs and management interfaces as a key vault. The rules that do apply concern the key itself (RSA or RSA-HSM of 2048, 3072 or 4096 bits, soft delete and purge protection on the vault or HSM) and the identity permissions (wrapkey, unwrapkey, get), not the vault's location.

- it must match the account's region, but may differ in tenant and subscription: The vault is allowed to sit in a different region from the storage account, so a region match is not a requirement and the West Europe HSM is fine.
- it must match the account's subscription, but may differ in tenant and region: The vault is allowed to sit in a different subscription from the storage account, so a subscription match is not a requirement.
- it must match the account's tenant, but may differ in region and subscription: The vault is allowed to sit in a different Microsoft Entra tenant from the storage account, so a tenant match is not a requirement either.

You have stgcontoso, a general-purpose v2 storage account that keeps seven years of legal records in the blob container legal-records. Every container in this account carries the encryption scope esc-legal, and that scope is protected by a key your own team manages in the Azure Key Vault vault kv-contoso. The legal team has asked for two things: the records older than seven years should be moved into the archive tier to reduce cost, and every new upload should be placed in the tier of the requester's choice at the moment it is written. The current configuration is shown below. Which outcome should you tell the legal team to expect?

- Object: Account stgcontoso; Property: Account kind; Value: General-purpose v2
- Object: Account stgcontoso; Property: Encryption scope on containers; Value: esc-legal
- Object: Encryption scope esc-legal; Property: Key type; Value: Customer-managed key in kv-contoso
- Object: Container legal-records; Property: Tier of the blobs stored today; Value: Cool
- Object: Container legal-records; Property: Blobs the legal team wants to move; Value: 12,500 records older than seven years
- Object: New upload request from the legal team; Property: Tier named in the request; Value: Archive
prompt: When the legal team carries out its two requests, _____.

options.text: the upload that names an access tier is rejected and the scoped blobs cannot be moved to the archive tier
the upload that names an access tier succeeds and the scoped blobs cannot be moved to the archive tier
the upload that names an access tier is rejected and the scoped blobs can be moved to the archive tier
the upload that names an access tier succeeds and the scoped blobs can be moved to the archive tier

explanation:
Blobs that sit under an encryption scope have two restrictions: Azure Storage will not accept an access tier on a new upload for such a blob, and an existing encryption-scoped blob cannot be moved into the archive tier. The legal team's upload that names the archive tier is therefore rejected, and the 12,500 older records in legal-records cannot be moved to the archive tier either. The archive tier itself is still covered by the account's normal at-rest encryption, so nothing about encryption coverage changes for blobs stored there; the blocks come from the encryption scope, not from a gap in encryption.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the upload that names an access tier succeeds and the scoped blobs cannot be moved to the archive tier: Wrong about the upload: an access tier cannot be set when uploading a new blob that is protected by an encryption scope, so that request is rejected even though the archive move is also blocked.
- the upload that names an access tier is rejected and the scoped blobs can be moved to the archive tier: Wrong about the archive move: an existing blob that is protected by an encryption scope cannot be moved to the archive tier, so the 12,500 records stay where they are.
- the upload that names an access tier succeeds and the scoped blobs can be moved to the archive tier: Wrong on both counts: naming an access tier at upload time is rejected for a blob under an encryption scope, and a scoped blob cannot be moved to the archive tier.

You look after stgcontoso, a general-purpose v2 storage account that a billing platform has been using for two years. Its current configuration is shown below. The auditors have asked for the queue and table data held in the account to be protected by the key that your team manages in Azure Key Vault, in the same way the blob and file share data is protected today. Which action should you take?

- Property: Account kind; Value: General-purpose v2
- Property: Service encryption; Value: Customer-managed key
- Property: Key store; Value: Azure Key Vault kv-contoso, key billing-key-1
- Property: Key version tracking; Value: Automatic
- Property: Blob service; Value: Protected by the customer-managed key
- Property: Azure Files service; Value: Protected by the customer-managed key
- Property: Queue service; Value: Protected by a Microsoft-managed key
- Property: Table service; Value: Protected by a Microsoft-managed key
prompt: To protect the queue and table data of a general-purpose v2 account that is already running with a customer-managed key, you must _____.

options.text: provision a replacement account that applies a customer-managed key to Queue and Table storage, then move the queues and tables across
reconfigure the existing account in place so that a customer-managed key applies to Queue and Table storage
move the queues and tables into containers in the existing account so that a customer-managed key applies to them as well
assign an encryption scope to each queue and table so that a customer-managed key applies to them as well

explanation:
A customer-managed key protects Blob Storage and Azure Files automatically, but the Queue and Table services are protected by such a key only when those services are opted in while the account is being created. Because stgcontoso has been running for two years, that opt-in can no longer be added to it, so the only way to bring its queue and table data under the vault key is to set up a replacement account with the customer-managed key enabled for Queue and Table storage and copy the queues and tables into it.

Why the other options are wrong:
- reconfigure the existing account in place so that a customer-managed key applies to Queue and Table storage: The opt-in that extends a customer-managed key to Queue and Table storage is only offered when the storage account is created, so an in-place change to an account that is already running cannot turn it on for those services.
- move the queues and tables into containers in the existing account so that a customer-managed key applies to them as well: Containers belong to the blob service. Copying the data into containers would change which service holds it rather than bring the Queue and Table services of the account under the vault key, and the messages and entities in those services would still be protected only by a Microsoft-managed key.
- assign an encryption scope to each queue and table so that a customer-managed key applies to them as well: An encryption scope sets the key scope for a container or a single blob in blob storage, so it does not extend a customer-managed key to the Queue and Table services.

You look after stgcontoso, a general-purpose v2 storage account that holds blob containers and an Azure Files share, with the content of both protected by a customer-managed key, contoso-content-key, that your team keeps in the Azure Key Vault vault kv-contoso. On 12 October the vault administrator disabled that key, and since then the applications that use this account's content report errors instead of returning data, although the account's managed identity still holds its permissions on the key. The service desk needs an accurate account of what the clients receive and which of the account's calls are affected. Choose the completion below that gives it.

`stgcontoso - storage account (general-purpose v2)

Item                                Value
---------------------------------   ------------------------------------------
Storage account                     stgcontoso (general-purpose v2)
Content held                        Blob containers and the Azure Files share 'reports'
Key protecting the content          Customer-managed key 'contoso-content-key' in vault kv-contoso
Key state in kv-contoso             Disabled on 12 October
Managed identity permissions        wrapkey, unwrapkey, get (unchanged)
Client symptom since 12 October     Requests for account content return an error instead of data`
prompt: While the key stays disabled in the vault, _____ is returned to the clients, and [...].

options.text: HTTP 403 (Forbidden)
HTTP 404 (Not Found)
HTTP 409 (Conflict)
HTTP 500 (Internal Server Error)

explanation:
Disabling a customer-managed key in the key vault withdraws the storage account's ability to use that key, and Microsoft documents the client-visible result: after the key is disabled, clients cannot call operations that read from or write to a resource or its metadata, and those calls fail with error code 403 (Forbidden) for all users. The affected calls are the Blob Storage reads and writes (Get Blob, Get Blob Properties, Get/Set Blob Metadata, Put Blob, Put Block, Append Block, Put Page, Copy Blob, Set Blob Tier and similar) and the Azure Files calls (Create File, Get File, Put Range, Copy File, Rename File, List Directories and Files, plus the directory and file property and metadata operations), so blob and Azure Files content and metadata reads and writes all fail with the same status code.

Why the other options are wrong:
- HTTP 404 (Not Found): HTTP 404 (Not Found) is wrong because the containers, blobs and file shares still exist; nothing was deleted. The documented outcome of a disabled customer-managed key is 403 (Forbidden) for the affected calls.
- HTTP 409 (Conflict): HTTP 409 (Conflict) would signal a request that clashes with the current state of the resource. The key being unusable is reported as 403 (Forbidden), not a conflict.
- HTTP 500 (Internal Server Error): HTTP 500 (Internal Server Error) would indicate a fault on the service side. The documented outcome is an authorization failure that the client sees as 403 (Forbidden) for every user.

You are creating the general-purpose v2 storage account stgcontoso, and the blobs it holds must be encrypted at rest with a key that your own team keeps in Azure Key Vault. You have already created the vault, the key and the access policy for the account's identity, but pointing the account at that key does not complete successfully. The configuration as it stands today is shown below. You need to correct it so that the account can actually use the key.

`Object: Storage account stgcontoso
  Type: general-purpose v2
  Encryption key source: customer-managed key in Azure Key Vault
  Key name: contoso-content-key
  Location: West Europe

Object: Key vault kv-contoso
  Soft delete: Disabled
  Purge protection: Disabled
  Location: West Europe

Object: Key contoso-content-key
  Key type: EC
  Key size: 521
  Key state: enabled

Object: Managed identity stgcontoso-identity
  Key permissions: get, wrapKey, unwrapKey
  Identity type: system-assigned
`
prompt: You should _____.

options.text: enable soft delete and purge protection on kv-contoso, create a new RSA-HSM key of size 4096 in that vault, and point stgcontoso at it
enable soft delete and purge protection on kv-contoso, create a new RSA-HSM key of size 1024 in that vault, and point stgcontoso at it
enable soft delete on kv-contoso but leave purge protection off, create a new RSA-HSM key of size 4096 in that vault, and point stgcontoso at it
enable soft delete and purge protection on kv-contoso, keep the existing EC key contoso-content-key, and point stgcontoso at it

explanation:
A vault that holds a customer-managed key must have soft delete and purge protection enabled, and the key itself must be an RSA or RSA-HSM key of size 2048, 3072 or 4096. In the layout shown, kv-contoso has neither protection switched on and contoso-content-key is an EC key of size 521, so stgcontoso cannot use it. Turning on both protections in the vault, creating an RSA-HSM key of an accepted size, and repointing the account at that new key resolves both blockers. The managed identity already holds get, wrapKey and unwrapKey, and the vault may sit in the same location as the account, so no other change is required.

Why the other options are wrong:
- enable soft delete and purge protection on kv-contoso, create a new RSA-HSM key of size 1024 in that vault, and point stgcontoso at it: A key size of 1024 is not accepted for customer-managed keys. The supported sizes are 2048, 3072 and 4096, so the account still cannot use the key.
- enable soft delete on kv-contoso but leave purge protection off, create a new RSA-HSM key of size 4096 in that vault, and point stgcontoso at it: Purge protection must be enabled on the vault that holds the key. Leaving it off keeps the setup from working even with a key of an accepted type and size.
- enable soft delete and purge protection on kv-contoso, keep the existing EC key contoso-content-key, and point stgcontoso at it: The key type is the blocker here. Customer-managed keys must be RSA or RSA-HSM keys, so an EC key cannot be used no matter which protections are switched on in the vault.

You have stgcontoso, a general-purpose v2 storage account whose blobs today are protected by the key that Microsoft manages for you. Contoso wants to hold the key itself, so the account is to be pointed at a key in the Azure Key Vault vault kv-contoso. The account holds about 40 TB of blobs and no outage has been approved for the application that writes to it. You need to know what happens to the blobs that are already in the account during this change. Which statement correctly describes Azure Storage's behavior?

- Item: Account; Value: stgcontoso (general-purpose v2)
- Item: Key type protecting the blobs today; Value: Microsoft-managed key
- Item: Blob data in the account; Value: About 40 TB across twelve containers
- Item: Approved application outage; Value: None
prompt: During this change, _____.

options.text: Azure Storage wraps the account key with the Contoso key, so the blobs already in the account are covered by it right away.
Azure Storage decrypts and re-encrypts every blob with the Contoso key, so the blobs already in the account are covered by it only after that work is finished.
Azure Storage leaves the account key with Microsoft, so the blobs already in the account are covered by the Contoso key only after each blob is uploaded again.

explanation:
A customer-managed key does not encrypt blob data directly. Azure Storage uses it to wrap the account encryption key, so only the protection of that key changes: the stored data stays encrypted throughout, the blobs that are already in the account are covered from the moment the account is pointed at the Contoso key, and no outage, no emptying of the account and no extra upload are needed. A storage account can also be moved between Microsoft-managed keys and customer-managed keys at any time.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Azure Storage decrypts and re-encrypts every blob with the Contoso key, so the blobs already in the account are covered by it only after that work is finished: Wrong: the Contoso key never encrypts blob data directly. Azure Storage uses it to wrap the account encryption key, so no blob is decrypted and re-encrypted, and the new protection applies from the moment the account is pointed at that key.
- Azure Storage leaves the account key with Microsoft, so the blobs already in the account are covered by the Contoso key only after each blob is uploaded again: Wrong: the account key does not stay with Microsoft once the account is pointed at the Contoso key. The account encryption key is re-wrapped under the Contoso key, so the blobs that are already stored are covered too, and no blob has to be uploaded again.

prompt: A nightly pipeline on a Linux runner uploads the contents of the folder /srv/reports into the reports container of storage account contososa. options.text: azcopy sync
azcopy copy
azcopy set-properties
azcopy jobs clean

explanation:
`azcopy sync` replicates the source location onto the destination and removes destination blobs that no longer exist in the source, which is exactly the mirroring behaviour the nightly job needs. It also honors the recursive flag so subfolders are included.

Why the other options are wrong:
- azcopy copy: `azcopy copy` is the command currently in the script. It writes new and updated blobs but deliberately leaves unrelated destination content untouched, so q2-summary.pdf would stay forever. It suits one-off or ad-hoc transfers where extra files on the destination are harmless.
- azcopy set-properties: `azcopy set-properties` changes blob access tier and replaces metadata and index tags after a transfer. It never deletes or adds blobs, so it cannot reconcile the container with the source folder.
- azcopy jobs clean: `azcopy jobs clean` deletes the log and plan files created by all transfer jobs; it operates on job metadata, not on the blobs in the container.

They have no identity in Contoso's tenant, their application runs unattended with no interactive sign-in, and their operators must create, read, and delete files in the share using one self-contained value that the app stores in its own configuration. Which action should you take to hand over that access?

options.text: Invite the partner's operators into the Contoso tenant and let them sign in with Microsoft Entra ID after adding the subscription in Storage Explorer.
Send the partner the storage account key from Settings > Access keys and have them connect with Account name and key in Storage Explorer.
Generate an account-level SAS for the storage account in Storage Explorer and send the partner the Connection string or Query string it produces.
Turn on public anonymous access for contractdocs in Storage Explorer and send the partner the plain share URL.

explanation:
Storage Explorer can mint an account-level SAS directly from the storage account node: right-click the account, choose Get Shared Access Signature, set the time frame and permissions, select Create, and copy the Connection string or the raw Query string. That is exactly the credential form the partner needs, because a SAS is the option for a party that cannot sign in interactively, and Azure Files shares are among the resources that accept Entra ID or a SAS. Requesting only the create/read/delete file permissions keeps the partner scoped to what its application actually does.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Invite the partner's operators into the Contoso tenant and let them sign in with Microsoft Entra ID after adding the subscription in Storage Explorer: Entra ID requires an identity that can actually authenticate to Contoso's tenant, and the partner has none. Adding a subscription through Account Management in Storage Explorer only surfaces accounts to principals who can sign in, so this leaves the partner's unattended application with nothing to use.
- Send the partner the storage account key from Settings > Access keys and have them connect with Account name and key in Storage Explorer: Account name and key is supported only when attaching a whole storage account. File shares, queues, and tables must be connected with Microsoft Entra ID or a SAS. An account key is also all-or-nothing, with no way to limit it to the share or to the specific file operations the partner requires.
- Turn on public anonymous access for contractdocs in Storage Explorer and send the partner the plain share URL: Public anonymous access is offered only for blob containers and for ADLS Gen2 containers or directories, never for a file share or a whole storage account, so it cannot be enabled as a way to reach contractdocs.

prompt: You are writing a one-off migration script, /opt/migrate/run.sh, that uploads a local folder into Blob storage in the storage account contososa. The script runs on the shared jump box whose properties are listed below, and it must reach the account on every run with no manual pre-step by an administrator. Which step should the script take?

options.text: Set AZCOPY_AUTO_LOGIN_TYPE=DEVICE in the script, then run the copy
Set AZCOPY_AUTO_LOGIN_TYPE=AZCLI in the script, then run the copy
Set AZCOPY_AUTO_LOGIN_TYPE=PSCRED in the script, then run the copy
Run azcopy login --tenant-id=<tenant-id> on the box once, then run the copy

explanation:
With AZCOPY_AUTO_LOGIN_TYPE=DEVICE, AzCopy prompts the operator for an interactive Microsoft Entra ID sign-in, holds the resulting token in memory only, and discards it when the operation completes. That matches the host exactly: no secret store is installed, nothing is written to disk, no prior session is reused, and an operator is present who can finish the sign-in in a browser. The copy command then works without any manual pre-step.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Set AZCOPY_AUTO_LOGIN_TYPE=AZCLI in the script, then run the copy: AZCLI makes AzCopy borrow the sign-in that already exists for the Azure CLI on that host. The table shows no CLI session exists, and any such session is itself a credential the CLI has stored, which the retention policy forbids.
- Set AZCOPY_AUTO_LOGIN_TYPE=PSCRED in the script, then run the copy: PSCRED is for a service principal: it expects a tenant ID together with the app's client ID and secret supplied through the environment. That would place a credential on the host, which policy forbids, and no such credentials are available on the box.
- Run azcopy login --tenant-id=<tenant-id> on the box once, then run the copy: azcopy login obtains an OAuth token and writes it to the OS secret store so later runs can reuse it. On a host with no secret store, such as this jump box, that command fails outright, so no reusable session is ever established; it also contradicts the rule that nothing may be kept for a later run.

prompt: You are moving seven years of scanned documents from a Windows file server into Blob storage in storage account contososa by using AzCopy. The job handling the 2020 folder was still running overnight when the host lost power, and the AzCopy process ended. The job's log and state files are still present on that host, and nothing in the source folder changed during the interruption. You want the remaining files of that folder to reach the destination while the ones already sent are left alone and not sent a second time. Which command should you run?

options.text: azcopy jobs resume with job ID 3b7d20
azcopy copy with the same source folder C:\Scans\2020 and destination container
azcopy sync with the same source folder C:\Scans\2020 and destination container
azcopy jobs remove with job ID 3b7d20

explanation:
AzCopy keeps each copy or sync operation as a job with its own log and state files on the machine, and the jobs command family is how you recover work from it. `azcopy jobs resume` with the job ID continues an interrupted job from that stored state, transferring only what has not already been sent. The listing shows job 3b7d20 stuck InProgress part-way through the 5.04 TB folder, so that is the job to continue.

Why the other options are wrong:
- azcopy copy with the same source folder C:\Scans\2020 and destination container: Starting a fresh `azcopy copy` run does not continue the recorded job: it begins a new transfer with its own plan and progress, so the work already done by 3b7d20 is not tracked or picked up by it. To pick up an interrupted transfer you use the jobs commands, not a new copy run.
- azcopy sync with the same source folder C:\Scans\2020 and destination container: `azcopy sync` replicates the source onto the destination and deletes destination content that no longer exists in the source. It is for keeping two locations mirroring each other, not for picking up a stopped transfer, and on a partially populated destination it can remove content it does not consider part of the source.
- azcopy jobs remove with job ID 3b7d20: `azcopy jobs remove` drops the files associated with a job, discarding the job's records so that transfer is no longer resumable. The already-uploaded blobs stay in the destination, but the remaining 3.4 TB of the 2020 folder would then have to be transferred from the beginning.

prompt: You have storage account contososa with hierarchical namespace enabled. Nobody on your team can be given Entra ID data roles in this subscription, so the team's reach comes only from the ACL entries shown below. A nightly AzCopy job uploads new blobs into the /finance/2026 directory of the account, and every run now fails with an access denied error. You need that nightly upload to succeed without changing where the blobs are placed. Which change should you make?

options.text: Add an ACL entry granting devgrp execute on /finance
Add an ACL entry granting devgrp write on /finance
Add an ACL entry granting devgrp execute on /finance/2026
Add an ACL entry granting devgrp read on /finance

explanation:
On an account with hierarchical namespace, ACL entries can carry authorization on their own, without a data role. The documented requirement for such a principal is write on the target directory plus execute on the container and on every parent directory of the target. devgrp already has write on the target /finance/2026 and execute on the container root, but the intermediate directory /finance carries no entry for the group at all, so the traversal down the path is broken. Granting execute on /finance supplies the missing link and the upload succeeds. Missing execute on parent directories is a documented cause of access denied even when the other permissions are correct.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add an ACL entry granting devgrp write on /finance: write on /finance would only let the group create entries under that directory; it grants no traversal. The path requirement calls for execute on the container and on every parent directory, and /finance currently has no entry, so this change leaves the broken traversal in place.
- Add an ACL entry granting devgrp execute on /finance/2026: /finance/2026 is the target directory, and the write entry the group already has there is exactly the permission the upload needs. The gap sits on an ancestor directory, /finance, so adding execute on the target itself does not make the whole path traversable and the run still fails.
- Add an ACL entry granting devgrp read on /finance: read on a directory does not stand in for the traversal the rule requires. The documented requirement is execute on the container and on every parent directory, so granting read on /finance leaves the same access denied error at run time.

explanation:

- Swap Azurite in the tests for the Azure Storage Emulator, which Storage Explorer starts automatically: Replacing Azurite does not help. explanation: Each report matches one distinct constraint of the tool. - Host: Host C - Windows service host; How the host is used: No person ever signs in; the copy runs as an app registration whose own credentials are issued to automation; What the runbook has to achieve: The copy must reach the account unattended as that app registration

options.text: export AZCOPY_AUTO_LOGIN_TYPE=DEVICE

export AZCOPY_AUTO_LOGIN_TYPE=AZCLI
export AZCOPY_TENANT_ID=<tenant-id>

$Env:AZCOPY_AUTO_LOGIN_TYPE="PSCRED"
$Env:AZCOPY_TENANT_ID=<tenant-id>
azcopy login

explanation: Each host is matched to the mechanism that fits how it runs. Host A needs a throwaway credential: with AZCOPY_AUTO_LOGIN_TYPE=DEVICE AzCopy returns a device code for the engineer to confirm, keeps the token only in the process memory, and discards it when the operation finishes, so nothing survives on the laptop. Host B needs to borrow the session already present: AZCOPY_AUTO_LOGIN_TYPE=AZCLI makes AzCopy use the operator's existing Azure CLI session, and AZCOPY_TENANT_ID pins it to the directory of that identity, so the scheduled script needs no prompt. Host C has no person at the keyboard: AZCOPY_AUTO_LOGIN_TYPE=PSCRED authenticates the copy as the app registration (service principal), with AZCOPY_TENANT_ID selecting its directory. Host D is prepared once and reused: azcopy login obtains an OAuth token and stores it in the operating system secret store, so every later copy on that workstation keeps working without a new sign-in.
