context:
Your platform team is standardising how AzCopy v10 is delivered to the three build hosts in the exhibit. On the two desktops a compressed file can simply be unpacked by hand, but build-agent-07 runs Linux and two rules apply there: AzCopy's own libraries must not be left for someone to chase by hand, and a version bump must arrive as an ordinary update rather than as a folder someone edits on disk. The runbook step for that host currently tells the engineer to unpack the archive and add its folder to the PATH. Which change should the team make to that runbook step?

- Host: win-build-21; Operating system: Windows 11; How the host is used: Interactive desktop session
- Host: mac-build-04; Operating system: macOS 14; How the host is used: Interactive desktop session
- Host: build-agent-07; Operating system: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS; How the host is used: Unattended runs only; version bumps handled by the platform team
prompt: On build-agent-07 the runbook step should instead _____.

options.text: install AzCopy from the distribution package manager
unpack the AzCopy zip archive into /opt/azcopy and add that folder to PATH
unpack the AzCopy tar archive into /opt/azcopy and add that folder to PATH
copy an AzCopy binary off another host and add that folder to PATH

explanation:
The two rules on build-agent-07 — AzCopy's dependencies being taken care of automatically and version bumps staying simple — are exactly the reasons Microsoft gives for putting AzCopy on Linux through the distribution's package manager, which is the documented Linux route. The portable compressed binary (zip on Windows and macOS, tar on Linux) is the route documented for the other operating systems, and unpacking it on the Linux host would leave the platform team responsible for dependencies and for every later bump. So the runbook step must switch to the distribution package manager.

Why the other options are wrong:
- unpack the AzCopy zip archive into /opt/azcopy and add that folder to PATH: The zip archive is the portable binary documented for Windows and macOS; unpacking it on the Ubuntu host leaves the platform team chasing AzCopy's libraries and handling each version bump by hand, which breaks both rules on build-agent-07.
- unpack the AzCopy tar archive into /opt/azcopy and add that folder to PATH: The tar archive is the correct artifact type for Linux, but unpacking it is still the manual portable-binary route: dependency resolution and later updates stay the platform team's problem, and the documented Linux route for automatic dependency resolution and simpler updates is the distribution package manager.
- copy an AzCopy binary off another host and add that folder to PATH: Copying a binary from another machine puts a file on disk but resolves none of AzCopy's dependencies on the target host, and every version bump then depends on whoever copied the file, so neither rule is satisfied.

context:
Your team is retiring the on-premises NAS at Contoso's Leipzig site and placing its archive in storage account contososa. Two entries in the cutover runbook are still blank, and the exhibit lists what the storage team has established so far. You need both entries filled in so the plan states what performs the transfer of the data set and so the engineer has a measured figure for how fast this site can actually transfer data before the window is signed off. Which pair of entries should you use?

- Property: Data set; Value: 1.4 TB of scanned documents held in roughly 6 million files
- Property: Source; Value: On-premises NAS, exposed to the migration host as a network share
- Property: Destination; Value: Blob container archive in storage account contososa
- Property: Window agreed with the business; Value: Three consecutive nights
- Property: Condition set by the storage team; Value: A measured speed figure for this site's network and disks before the plan is approved
prompt: The cutover plan should list _____ as the component that carries the data set across, and the pre-cutover test entry should call for [...] so the team has a speed figure for this site.

options.text: Azure Storage Mover
AzCopy v10
Storage Explorer
azcopy sync

explanation:
The data set is 1.4 TB, and for migrations of more than about 1 TB the documentation points to the managed Azure Storage Mover service rather than AzCopy, so that is what the plan should name as the component that carries the data. azcopy bench is the command that pushes or pulls test data to or from a location in order to measure throughput before a real migration, which is exactly the speed figure the storage team requires for this site; the other three commands only report on entities, on jobs and on environment settings.

Why the other options are wrong:
- AzCopy v10: AzCopy v10 is the general command-line utility for transferring data to, from and between storage accounts, but at this data set's size the guidance is to use the managed Azure Storage Mover service, so naming AzCopy v10 as the component that carries the data does not fit the plan.
- Storage Explorer: Storage Explorer is a standalone desktop app for visual, interactive work on a workstation, so it is not the component that performs a bulk transfer of 1.4 TB from a network share.
- azcopy sync: azcopy sync is a single command that mirrors a source onto a destination; it belongs to the AzCopy tooling and is not the service this plan should name for a data set above the roughly 1 TB guidance.

context:
You have a nightly AzCopy job that pushes a month of scans into the scans container of storage account contososa, and the upload line of the runbook already looks like the one shown below. The transfer succeeds every night, but the next morning the archive team finds that the freshly arrived blobs are still in the hot tier and still carry the previous season's index tag, so a separate system has to open the container and correct each blob individually. You need the blobs that are already in the container moved to a cooler tier and given new metadata and index tags where they sit, without sending the data again. Which command should the runbook use for that step?

`azcopy copy "/srv/scan" "https://contososa.blob.core.windows.net/scans" --recursive=true

Current state of the container after the job finishes:
  Tier of new blobs ............ Hot
  Index tag on new blobs ...... season=2025

Required end state for those same blobs:
  Tier ......................... Cool
  Index tag .................... season=2026`
prompt: The runbook's post-upload step should run _____ against the scans container.

options.text: azcopy set-properties
azcopy copy
azcopy make
azcopy bench

explanation:
Blobs that are already in the destination container need their settings changed where they sit, and set-properties is the command that changes blob access tier and replaces metadata and index tags after a transfer. Running it against the scans container moves the new blobs from hot to cool and rewrites the index tag to season=2026 without moving the data again.

Why the other options are wrong:
- azcopy copy: copy is the transfer command: it writes new and updated objects from a source to a destination and leaves unrelated destination content alone, so running it again would move data rather than change the tier, metadata or tags of the blobs that have already landed.
- azcopy make: make creates a container or a file share. The scans container already exists, so this command would do nothing for the blobs inside it and would not change their tier, metadata or index tags.
- azcopy bench: bench uploads or downloads test data to measure throughput before a real migration. It leaves test objects behind and does not adjust the tier, metadata or index tags of the blobs already in the container.

context:
Your nightly pipeline for Contoso's finance group puts each night's CSV exports into the container named nightlycsv in storage account contososa, and the finance application reads only ordinary files from the Azure Files share named archive in that same account. The table shows what the pipeline does today. Last night's exports never reached the share, and the pipeline has to deliver them by itself with no person involved. Using AzCopy v10 on that pipeline runner, which approach should the pipeline take?

- Item: Runner; Detail: Scheduled Linux agent that starts itself nightly and cannot prompt anyone for a sign-in
- Item: What it does now; Detail: Uploads the night's CSV exports into the nightlycsv container of storage account contososa
- Item: Where the files must land; Detail: The archive Azure Files share of the same account, readable by the finance application
- Item: Last night's outcome; Detail: All exports are present in the container; nothing arrived in the share
prompt: The pipeline should use _____.

options.text: a single azcopy copy whose source is the nightlycsv container and whose destination is the archive share
azcopy jobs resume against the previous attempt, which had already copied part of the nightlycsv container into the archive share
a Storage Explorer session that drags the nightlycsv container over into the archive share by hand
two azcopy invocations, one to bring the nightlycsv container down to the runner and one to push the local copy into the archive share

explanation:
AzCopy v10 is not limited to account-to-account or on-premises-to-cloud moves; it can also move data between services, for example from a Blob Storage container into an Azure Files share and back. So one azcopy copy run whose source is the nightlycsv container and whose destination is the archive share places the night's CSV exports in the share as ordinary files in a single unattended step. AzCopy is also the tool intended for scripted, scheduled and batch work such as this nightly pipeline, whereas Storage Explorer is an interactive desktop application.

Why the other options are wrong:
- azcopy jobs resume against the previous attempt, which had already copied part of the nightlycsv container into the archive share: azcopy jobs resume continues an interrupted job using the plan and log files that job saved earlier. The scenario describes no earlier transfer job and nothing that ever started moving into the share, so there is nothing to resume and no data would reach the share.
- a Storage Explorer session that drags the nightlycsv container over into the archive share by hand: Storage Explorer is a desktop application for visual, interactive, one-off work on a workstation; it cannot serve as an unattended pipeline step, and AzCopy already performs the container-to-share transfer on its own.
- two azcopy invocations, one to bring the nightlycsv container down to the runner and one to push the local copy into the archive share: AzCopy moves data between a Blob Storage container and an Azure Files share directly, so staging the files on the runner's local disk first is an unnecessary extra hop; a single copy operation takes them straight to the share.

context:
You are standing up a new media archive in storage account contososa. The account holds nothing yet, and the transfer job you already wrote copies the two source folders shown in the exhibit into the destinations beside them. On its first run the job stops immediately, before a single file is transferred, because neither destination is present. You need both destinations to exist first. Which command should you add to the runbook?

- Source folder on the Linux runner: /srv/media; Destination name in contososa: media; Destination type: Blob container
- Source folder on the Linux runner: /srv/replays; Destination name in contososa: replays; Destination type: Azure Files share
prompt: Before the transfer job is started, the runbook must call _____ once for each destination listed in the exhibit.

options.text: azcopy make
azcopy copy
azcopy sync
azcopy remove

explanation:
The two destinations listed are a blob container and an Azure Files share, and azcopy make is the command whose purpose is to create a container or a file share. Running it once for media and once for replays gives the existing transfer job somewhere to write, which is exactly what the failing first run needs.

Why the other options are wrong:
- azcopy copy: azcopy copy writes new and updated objects from the source into the destination. It moves data into places that already exist and does not create an empty blob container or file share, so it cannot clear the failure reported here.
- azcopy sync: azcopy sync replicates the source onto the destination and removes destination files that no longer exist at the source. It is a data movement command, not one that establishes the container or the share.
- azcopy remove: azcopy remove deletes blobs or files that already exist in a container or share. Nothing is in place yet, so there is nothing to delete and this command will not bring the two destinations into being.

context:
Contoso's payroll team keeps an Azure Files share named payrolldocs in storage account contososa that staff keep changing all day, and the group wants that share's whole contents sitting in Blob storage in the same account. AzCopy v10 is the tool they chose, and every run so far has ended without placing a single file at the destination. You need the transfer to actually complete. Which change should the team make?

- Property: Tool; Value: AzCopy v10
- Property: Source; Value: Azure Files share payrolldocs, roughly 3 TB
- Property: Destination; Value: Blob container payrollarchive in the same account
- Property: Activity on the source; Value: About 200 staff create and edit documents during every working day
- Property: Current run pattern; Value: Runs during business hours and ends with an error before anything is transferred
prompt: The payroll team should _____ so the transfer completes.

options.text: Hold all activity on the source and destination still for the duration of the transfer
Sign in with a shared access signature appended to the source and destination URLs
Add the AzCopy install folder to the system PATH on the transfer runner
Wait about five minutes for the data role assignment to propagate, then start the transfer again

explanation:
AzCopy does not run a transfer whose source or destination is being actively changed while the job executes. The payroll share changes continuously during business hours, so every run started in that window is refused before any data moves. Freezing activity on both ends for the length of the run is what lets the transfer proceed; any other authentication or installation change leaves the conflict in place.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Sign in with a shared access signature appended to the source and destination URLs: A shared access signature only supplies credentials for the source and destination URLs; it has no effect on the restriction that stops a transfer whose endpoints keep changing, so the runs would still end early.
- Add the AzCopy install folder to the system PATH on the transfer runner: Putting the install folder on the PATH only matters when the azcopy command is not recognised from another directory. Here the command is recognised and runs, then ends early, so the PATH is not the problem.
- Wait about five minutes for the data role assignment to propagate, then start the transfer again: The short wait for a newly assigned data role to propagate applies only to role assignments. No role is being granted in this situation, and five minutes of waiting cannot quiet a share that staff edit all day.

prompt: You have an existing storage account that is shown below. An HPC team needs a share today that Linux nodes reach over NFSv4.1 with single-digit millisecond latency, and next quarter the same account must also hold a large, low-cost departmental share for Windows clients. You need a single billing model that covers both shares. Which File share billing model should you select on the file share creation blade?

options.text: Pay-as-you-go
Provisioned v1
Provisioned v2
Provisioned v1 for the NFS share now, Pay-as-you-go for the departmental share later

explanation:
Provisioned v2 is the billing model recommended for new deployments, and it is the only one that covers both SSD and HDD media in a single FileStorage account. It serves the NFSv4.1 share on Premium media now and the planned HDD SMB share later, and it requires Primary service to be set to Azure Files, which this account already has. Its SKUs here would be PremiumV2_ZRS or StandardV2_ZRS (note that ZRS for SSD is offered only in a subset of regions).

Why the other options are wrong:
- Pay-as-you-go: Pay-as-you-go is an HDD-only model and requires a StorageV2 account, so it cannot deliver the SSD media the NFS share needs and cannot be used in this FileStorage account.
- Provisioned v1: Provisioned v1 serves SSD media, so it would work for the NFS share, but it is the older model and cannot host HDD shares, which breaks the plan for the departmental share in the same account.
- Provisioned v1 for the NFS share now, Pay-as-you-go for the departmental share later: Pay-as-you-go shares need a StorageV2 account and are unavailable in this FileStorage account; the departmental share should be created with the same provisioned v2 model using a StandardV2 or PremiumV2 SKU instead.

prompt: You have a FileStorage account set up as shown below and are creating a file share for an engineering team. The original plan put the workload on SSD with LRS because latency mattered most. That has changed: the share's data must now be recoverable from a second Azure region, and per-GiB cost has become the priority over latency. Which combination of Performance and Redundancy should you select on the file share creation blade?

options.text: Set Performance to Premium (SSD) and Redundancy to ZRS
Set Performance to Standard (HDD) and Redundancy to GZRS
Set Performance to Standard (HDD) and Redundancy to LRS
Set Performance to Premium (SSD) and Redundancy to GRS

explanation:
Recovering the share in a second Azure region requires a redundancy option that replicates asynchronously across regions, which only the geo-redundant choices (GRS or GZRS) provide. File shares on SSD are limited to LRS and ZRS, so keeping the share on Premium leaves no cross-region option at all; the media tier has to move to Standard (HDD), where all four redundancy options are supported. GZRS then gives zone-redundant copies in the primary region plus async replication to a second region, and Standard/HDD is the cost-effective tier the team has agreed to accept.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Set Performance to Premium (SSD) and Redundancy to ZRS: ZRS keeps three copies inside the primary region, spread across availability zones; it protects against a zone failure but creates no copy in a second region, so it cannot satisfy the new recovery requirement.
- Set Performance to Standard (HDD) and Redundancy to LRS: Standard (HDD) is the right media tier for this requirement, but LRS is single-region only — three copies in one storage cluster — so there is still nothing to recover from in a second region.
- Set Performance to Premium (SSD) and Redundancy to GRS: SSD file shares support only LRS and ZRS, so GRS cannot be deployed on the Premium tier; the deployment would fail rather than produce a cross-region copy.

prompt: You have a classic file share created on a FileStorage storage account with the NFS protocol, and you granted access to a virtual network where Linux virtual machines run. You need those machines to mount the share, but every mount attempt stalls and then fails, and the subnet's network security group currently contains only the rules shown below. Which change should you make?

options.text: Allow TCP port 2049 outbound from the clients, and allow inbound TCP port 2049 for the virtual networks granted access
Allow UDP port 2049 outbound from the clients, and allow inbound UDP port 2049 for the virtual networks granted access
Allow TCP port 445 outbound from the clients, and allow inbound TCP port 445 for the virtual networks granted access
Allow TCP port 443 outbound from the clients, and allow inbound TCP port 443 for the virtual networks granted access

explanation:
NFSv4.1 traffic runs on TCP port 2049. Clients must be able to send that traffic outbound, and any network security groups associated with virtual networks that have been granted access to the share must not block it coming in on the same port. The group shown ends in a catch-all deny for both directions with no rule for 2049, so every mount attempt is dropped, which matches the observed stall and timeout.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Allow UDP port 2049 outbound from the clients, and allow inbound UDP port 2049 for the virtual networks granted access: Wrong transport. A share created with the NFS protocol serves NFSv4.1 clients, which carry their traffic over TCP; permitting the same port number over UDP leaves the mount blocked by the outbound deny rule.
- Allow TCP port 445 outbound from the clients, and allow inbound TCP port 445 for the virtual networks granted access: Wrong service port. Port 445 is the SMB port used by Windows-style shares; this share was created with the NFS protocol and its Linux clients never send SMB traffic, so this rule changes nothing for the failing mount.
- Allow TCP port 443 outbound from the clients, and allow inbound TCP port 443 for the virtual networks granted access: Wrong service port. Port 443 carries HTTPS traffic such as FileREST calls to the share; NFS client traffic does not use it, and it is already permitted here, which shows the failure has a different cause.

Keep this FileStorage storage account and add the share with the Provisioned v2 billing model at Standard performance using the StandardV2_LRS SKU

explanation:

- Keep this FileStorage storage account and add the share with the Provisioned v2 billing model at Standard performance using the StandardV2_LRS SKU: Provisioned v2 does work on this FileStorage account, and StandardV2_LRS is a valid provisioned v2 SKU that covers HDD. Microsoft Entra Domain Services with Kerberos
AD-based Kerberos authentication for Linux clients
Keep the storage account key and reinforce share-level permissions

explanation:

You need the on-premises servers that reach Azure over an existing ExpressRoute circuit, and the virtual machines in a hub virtual network in a second Azure region, to mount the share. The address the clients use must keep working through an availability-zone outage without manual changes on each client. Which network configuration should you deploy for this share?

options.text: Deploy a service endpoint in the client virtual network subnets and mount the share by the storage account name.
Deploy a private endpoint for the storage account, and have clients mount the share over its address in the virtual network.
Deploy allowlist entries on the storage account firewall for the on-premises address space and the peered virtual network.
Deploy a site-to-site VPN from the branch offices into the virtual network and keep mounting the share over the public endpoint.

explanation:
A private endpoint gives the share a static IP address inside your own virtual network, and it is reachable across peered networks, other regions, and ExpressRoute, which covers both client groups in the exhibit. It also avoids the SMB-over-internet path on port 445 that many ISPs block, so on-premises mounts work without manual changes when an availability-zone event occurs.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Deploy a service endpoint in the client virtual network subnets and mount the share by the storage account name: A service endpoint restricts access to specific virtual network subnets at no extra charge, but the IP address it assigns can change during a zone outage, forcing clients to remount, and it does not serve clients arriving from the corporate LAN over ExpressRoute.
- Deploy allowlist entries on the storage account firewall for the on-premises address space and the peered virtual network: Firewall allowlists apply to the public endpoint and match public address ranges. Traffic arriving from the ExpressRoute-connected LAN and from the peered hub virtual network does not carry the allowed corporate public range, so those mounts keep failing and no address inside the network is handed to the clients.
- Deploy a site-to-site VPN from the branch offices into the virtual network and keep mounting the share over the public endpoint: A VPN only changes the path into Azure; the share is still mounted from the public endpoint, so the mounts keep depending on the public endpoint and on SMB to port 445 over the outbound internet path, which many ISPs block.

prompt: You have a storage account and its file share configured as shown below. A long-standing on-premises application mounts the share over SMB by passing the account name and one of the account's access keys, and since these settings were applied every mount attempt returns an authentication error. People browsing the share in the Azure portal see its folders normally, and that behaviour has to stay as it is. The application itself cannot be rebuilt to use a different credential method this quarter. Which setting should you change?

options.text: Select Enable storage account key access on the storage account, leaving the portal's Microsoft Entra browsing unchanged.
Clear Default to Microsoft Entra authorization in the Azure portal on the storage account, so that browsing the share falls back to the access key the application already stores.
Rotate the storage account access keys and redeploy the application's mount definition with the newest key, because authentication failures usually mean an expired credential.
Enable soft delete for file shares on the storage account and raise Days to retain deleted file shares to 90, so anything the application removes by mistake stays recoverable.

explanation:
Enable storage account key access is the switch that decides whether the account's shared keys may be used at all — for SMB mounts and for FileREST calls. While it is unchecked, no access key can authenticate, so a mount that supplies the account name plus a key fails regardless of which key it uses, and rotating the keys changes nothing. Default to Microsoft Entra authorization in the Azure portal only decides whether the portal browses the share with the user's Entra identity instead of a shared key, which is why portal users still see their folders and why that setting should stay as it is. Selecting Enable storage account key access therefore restores key-based mounts while identity-based browsing in the portal continues to work.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Clear Default to Microsoft Entra authorization in the Azure portal on the storage account, so that browsing the share falls back to the access key the application already stores: That setting governs only how the Azure portal browses share contents (user identity instead of a shared key). It has no effect on SMB or NFS mounts, so it cannot fix the mount failures, and clearing it would remove the identity-based portal browsing that must be kept.
- Rotate the storage account access keys and redeploy the application's mount definition with the newest key, because authentication failures usually mean an expired credential: Rotating keys cannot help because the account currently blocks shared key credentials altogether — the key is not being treated as an expired credential, key-based mounting is simply refused, so reissuing the keys and redeploying the mount produces the same authentication error.
- Enable soft delete for file shares on the storage account and raise Days to retain deleted file shares to 90, so anything the application removes by mistake stays recoverable: Soft delete governs how long deleted shares stay recoverable, and soft-deleted content is still billed for its used capacity. It neither issues nor accepts credentials, so extending the retention period cannot repair a mount that is failing authentication.

explanation: Each request maps to a different file share capability. The REST-only refusal is governed by Minimum TLS version, because SMB and NFS traffic never uses TLS; setting it to TLS1_2 rejects clients that negotiate an older handshake. Finally, the snapshot ceiling documented for a file share is 200 read-only, point-in-time, incremental copies retained for up to 10 years, so 10 years is the longest span the compliance team can be promised.

prompt: Classic file share inside a storage account

options.text: R1 - SMB share for domain users with per-folder permissions, protected by Azure Backup
R2 - NFSv4.1 share with its own networking and billing, created without a storage account
R3 - NFS share encrypted at rest with a key from the company's own Key Vault
R4 - One share that Windows clients mount over SMB and Linux clients mount over NFSv4.1

explanation: R1 and R3 both belong on classic file shares: SMB with domain identities, Windows-style folder permissions, and Azure Backup is only available inside a storage account, because the top-level Microsoft.FileShares provider is NFS only today, and a customer-managed key at rest is not an option there either, since those shares must use Microsoft-managed keys. R2 is exactly what Microsoft.FileShares exists for: an NFSv4.1 share with its own billing, networking, and security and no parent storage account. R4 fits neither slot, because one share exposes either SMB or NFS and never both; in a classic account the two client groups would need two separate shares that sit side by side in the same account.

You have the storage account and the file shares shown below. Four requests have come in from the teams that use them. Three can be met by the mechanisms listed here and one cannot. Drag each request to the mechanism that delivers it.

- Resource: Storage account contosofiles01; Configuration: FileStorage, StandardV2_GZRS, primary service Azure Files, region East US
- Resource: Share teamdocs; Configuration: SMB, Standard (HDD), Provisioned v2
- Resource: Share buildartifacts; Configuration: SMB, Premium (SSD), Provisioned v2
- Resource: Share hpcscratch; Configuration: NFSv4.1, Premium (SSD), Provisioned v2
- Resource: Recovery Services vault contoso-rsv; Configuration: East US, same subscription as the storage account
prompt: Share snapshots

options.text: Compliance must be able to open teamdocs exactly as it stood at 09:00 on a chosen morning, read from it, and know that nobody can alter that copy. A storage administrator raises one whenever the auditors ask for it.

Legal wants buildartifacts recovered on daily, weekly, monthly and yearly cycles, each cycle with its own retention period, and no one may shorten or switch off that protection once the repository is registered. This repository uses SMB.

A support engineer removed hpcscratch by mistake an hour ago and it has to come back before the retention period ends; the same automatic protection has to cover future accidental removals on every share in this account, including the NFS one.

Once buildartifacts is registered, the HPC team wants hpcscratch to receive exactly the same scheduled daily, weekly, monthly and yearly protection, with the same per-cycle retention, and nobody may switch that protection off.

explanation: teamdocs is an SMB share and the request is for an on-demand, unalterable, point-in-time copy: share snapshots are read-only point-in-time copies, are created manually in the portal or by PowerShell/CLI, are incremental, and each share supports up to 200 of them retained for up to 10 years — so i1 goes to Share snapshots. Legal's request for scheduled daily, weekly, monthly and yearly cycles with per-cycle retention and a guard that stops anyone removing the protection is Azure Backup, which handles the scheduling and retention with grandfather-father-son policies and takes a delete lock on the storage account as soon as a share in it is configured for backup; it works for SMB shares and uses a Recovery Services vault in the same region and subscription, which the exhibit already provides — so i2 goes to Azure Backup. The request to recover an accidentally removed share inside a retention period, on every share in the account including the NFS one, is soft delete: it is a storage-account level setting that is on by default (7 days by default), keeps a removed share recoverable until the retention period ends, and applies regardless of protocol, whereas Azure Backup is SMB-only — so i3 goes to Soft delete. Finally, hpcscratch is an NFSv4.1 share, and Azure Backup cannot protect NFS shares at all, so nothing in the list delivers the last request.

- Consumer: A — Windows workstations and servers; Environment and constraints: Staff sign in with Microsoft Entra ID accounts only. The machines are not joined to any directory, and no server directory will be deployed for them.

- Consumer: C — Non-Windows build servers; Environment and constraints: The servers are members of the organization's own Active Directory forest and must prove who they are with those directory accounts before they can reach the data.

options.text: Storage account key
Microsoft Entra Kerberos for hybrid and cloud-only identities
Microsoft Entra Domain Services
AD-based Kerberos authentication for Linux clients

explanation: Each consumer's environment rules out the other three options. Consumer C runs a non-Windows operating system and authenticates against Active Directory with its directory accounts, which is AD-based Kerberos authentication for Linux clients. Consumer D's host is not joined to any directory and its application can only supply a stored secret, so it mounts with the storage account key.

Change Performance of the existing file share from HDD to SSD
Change File share billing model of the existing file share to Provisioned v2

explanation:
The tier a share is deployed on is fixed when the share is created, so an existing HDD share cannot be turned into an SSD share in place. The supported route to SSD latency is to provision a separate share on the SSD tier in the same FileStorage account, migrate the files into it, and repoint the application.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Change Redundancy of the existing file share from LRS to ZRS: ZRS keeps three copies spread across availability zones, which is a durability improvement only; the share stays on the same tier, so response times would not improve.
- Change Performance of the existing file share from HDD to SSD: The tier is chosen when the share is created and cannot be changed afterwards, so editing Performance on an existing share does not move it to SSD.
- Change File share billing model of the existing file share to Provisioned v2: The File share billing model only decides how a share is charged and provisioned. Switching an existing share to Provisioned v2 leaves its files on the tier they were deployed with.

The other shares in this account show up in the vault's backup policies, but this one has never once been reported as protected, and the team assumed the portal's automatic backup step had covered every new share in the account. The share's protocol was fixed when it was created and recreating the share this quarter is not an option, so you need this share's data to be brought back if it is lost. Which action should you take?

- Property: Primary service; Value: Azure Files

prompt: You should _____ so that this share's data can be brought back if it is lost.

options.text: Remove the backup configuration from the share and use snapshots for recovery
Re-run the backup configuration so that the policy starts picking up the share
Enable soft delete on the account so that the backup can restore deleted share content
Add a second backup schedule to the existing vault for this share

explanation:
The vault-based backup service for file shares protects only shares that use SMB; a share created with NFS can never be included, which is why this share is missing from every policy while its SMB siblings are listed. Because the protocol is fixed for the life of the share, the workable way to bring this data back is point-in-time, incremental copies of the share, of which up to 200 per share can be kept for up to 10 years. Stripping the unusable backup configuration and using those copies gives the team a mechanism that actually captures the data.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Re-run the backup configuration so that the policy starts picking up the share: This share uses NFS, a protocol that the vault-based backup service does not cover for file shares, so re-running the configuration or letting the policies rescan cannot add it to any policy.
- Enable soft delete on the account so that the backup can restore deleted share content: Soft delete keeps a deleted share and its files in a recoverable state for the configured retention period, but it does not copy data anywhere and plays no part in bringing back a share's contents.
- Add a second backup schedule to the existing vault for this share: Extra schedules still depend on the same vault-based backup service, which covers only SMB shares, so a second schedule changes nothing for an NFS share.

options.text: have no effect on this file share; both settings only apply to Blob data
change this file share to POSIX-style permissions and host-based access on every mount
allow this file share to serve NFSv4.1 on the same endpoint as its SMB protocol
have to be in place on any account before a provisioned file share can be created

explanation:
Enable hierarchical namespace and Enable network file system v3 are Blob-oriented options. They are disabled on FileStorage accounts, and on a StorageV2 account they can still be ticked even when Primary service is Azure Files, but in neither case do they alter a file share. The share keeps the semantics of the protocol it was created with, so its permissions and connectivity behave exactly as before.

Why the other options are wrong:
- change this file share to POSIX-style permissions and host-based access on every mount: POSIX-style, host-based permissions are what an NFS share uses. A share's permissions model is fixed by the protocol chosen at creation, and neither Configuration-tab option changes it for an existing SMB share.
- allow this file share to serve NFSv4.1 on the same endpoint as its SMB protocol: A single file share exposes either SMB or NFS, never both, and the protocol is chosen when the share is created. Ticking these options does not add NFSv4.1 to an SMB share.
- have to be in place on any account before a provisioned file share can be created: Creating a provisioned file share depends on the account kind and on Primary service being Azure Files, not on these two checkboxes. Leaving them ticked neither blocks nor enables share deployment.

Its redundancy setting keeps the data in the primary region and also writes it asynchronously to a paired Azure region, and the setting that exposes that paired copy has been switched on. Contingency planners asked what staff could open from the paired region if the primary region became unavailable, without any change to the account. Which statement describes what they would get?

- Property: Storage account name; Value: contosofiledata01
- Property: Storage account kind; Value: StorageV2
- Property: Primary service; Value: Azure Files
- Property: Redundancy; Value: RA-GZRS
- Property: Read access (secondary); Value: Enabled
- Property: File share; Value: appdata (Protocol: SMB)
prompt: Given the configuration shown, the correct conclusion is that _____.

options.text: the file share can be mounted directly from the secondary region before the account is failed over
the file share's data cannot be read from the secondary region until the account is failed over
the file share's data can be read from the secondary region only through the FileREST API
the file share's data can be read from the secondary region by clients holding a storage account key

explanation:
Azure Files does not support read access to the secondary region on an account that uses geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS or RA-GZRS) before a failover is performed, so switching on the read access option has no effect on a file share. The share's data is therefore only reachable through the secondary region after the account has been failed over, which makes that the accurate statement.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the file share can be mounted directly from the secondary region before the account is failed over: Incorrect. Mounting is served from the primary region; nothing exposes a mounted SMB share through the secondary region while the account is still serving the primary region.
- the file share's data can be read from the secondary region only through the FileREST API: Incorrect. The FileREST API reaches whichever region is currently serving the account, so switching APIs does not unlock the secondary copy for file share data before a failover.
- the file share's data can be read from the secondary region by clients holding a storage account key: Incorrect. A storage account key grants full administrative access to the share through the primary endpoint; it has no bearing on the secondary region before a failover.

explanation:
The Microsoft.FileShares deployment model is the one where a file share is created as its own top-level Azure object, with billing, networking, and security set on the share itself and no parent storage account to create first, which is exactly what this team asked for. Shares created that way, however, always use Microsoft-managed keys, so the request for keys held in the studio's own key vault cannot be granted in this model. Customer-managed keys are available only to classic file shares that live inside a storage account, and that deployment is precisely what the platform team wanted to avoid. One of the two stated wishes therefore has to be given up: per-share administration without a parent account, or key-vault-controlled encryption, not both.

Why the other options are wrong:
- a share inside a new StorageV2 storage account: A StorageV2 account is where classic file shares live (it is the required kind for pay-as-you-go HDD shares), but it is a parent storage account that the platform team would have to own, size, and keep running, so the per-share object they asked for still does not exist.
- a share inside a new FileStorage storage account: FileStorage is the classic account kind used for provisioned SSD and HDD file shares; it also requires a storage account to be created and operated first, so it does not satisfy the requirement for a single object that carries its own billing, networking, and access settings.

Storage File Data SMB Share Elevated Contributor

explanation:
Share-level Azure RBAC and NTFS-style folder ACLs do not stack up for a user: the two intersect and the more restrictive of the two governs. Here the migrated folder's ACL grants the finance group nothing, and the ACLs may not be changed, so the only way to give the group working write access from the share level is Storage File Data SMB Share Privileged Contributor. It delivers the same read/write/delete data access as the regular share contributor role but is not limited by the ACLs already present on files and folders, so it succeeds even where the folder ACL is None.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Storage File Data SMB Share Reader: This role maps to read-only access at the share level, so it can never let the finance group create or modify workbooks, regardless of the folder ACL. It is the role the group holds today, which matches the access-denied symptom.
- Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor: It grants read, write and delete on the share, but the existing folder ACL still applies and the most restrictive of RBAC and ACL wins. With the folder ACL set to None for the group, members would still be denied.
- Storage File Data SMB Share Elevated Contributor: Its added value is the permission to change the share ACL, which is the one action you are not allowed to perform here; it does not loosen an ACL that already denies access. Because the finance group's effective folder entry is None, this role would still return access denied.

From a domain-joined Windows server the mount fails right away with error 1396, "The target account name is incorrect", and the security log shows KRB_AP_ERR_MODIFIED. You need the appliance to mount the share with its directory identity. Which change to the directory account should you make?

options.text: Set userPrincipalName on the service logon account to cifs/contosofs.file.core.windows.net@contoso.local
Set userPrincipalName on the service logon account to cifs/contosofs@contoso.local
Set servicePrincipalName on the service logon account to svc_azurefiles@contoso.local
Set sAMAccountName on the service logon account to cifs/contosofs.file.core.windows.net

explanation:
When the directory account used for the storage account is a user-type (service logon) object, Kerberos must be able to find the service principal through the account's userPrincipalName, so the UPN has to be the service principal plus the UPN suffix: cifs/<StorageAccountName>.file.core.windows.net@<UPN-suffix>. Here the object still carries the short svc_azurefiles@contoso.local value, so ticket requests fail with 1396 / KRB_AP_ERR_MODIFIED — especially once AES256 encryption is in play. Join-AzStorageAccount sets this value automatically, which is why hand-built setups miss it.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Set userPrincipalName on the service logon account to cifs/contosofs@contoso.local: This shortens the principal to the storage account name only. The UPN has to be built from the full service principal plus the domain suffix, not a trimmed principal, so the lookup still fails.
- Set servicePrincipalName on the service logon account to svc_azurefiles@contoso.local: The service principal is already in the required form for Azure Files and doesn't change when the account type is user. Overwriting it with an email-style value breaks the request for a service ticket, so the mount keeps failing.
- Set sAMAccountName on the service logon account to cifs/contosofs.file.core.windows.net: sAMAccountName is the NetBIOS logon name and is limited to 20 characters or fewer (15 or fewer under NETBIOS restrictions), supplied without a trailing $; it can't hold a principal name, and it isn't what Kerberos consults for a service ticket.

prompt: Your company is moving file workloads into storage account contosofs and wants every workstation and server in the estate below to reach the shares with its signed-in user identity rather than an account key. You are not changing the on-premises domain or how your company manages identities there. You need to settle on one directory source to use for this account. Which identity source should you configure for contosofs?

options.text: On-premises Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS)
Microsoft Entra Domain Services
Microsoft Entra Kerberos
On-premises Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) plus Microsoft Entra Kerberos

explanation:
Microsoft Entra Kerberos is the only single source that serves the whole estate as described. It removes the requirement that clients reach on-premises domain controllers, supports Entra-joined clients and macOS clients such as the designer laptops, and is the recommended choice when FSLogix profiles are involved, which covers the Windows 11 session hosts. The hybrid-joined servers also qualify as long as their users are synced from the on-premises domain to Microsoft Entra ID, because share-level permissions target the Entra object. Linux user authentication isn't supported with this source, but that isn't a blocker here because the build agents authenticate with a managed identity, which is a separate mechanism that can coexist with this source. Whichever source is chosen, Kerberos must be enabled under Authentication methods in the account's SMB security settings.

Why the other options are wrong:
- On-premises Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS): AD DS authorizes from SIDs the client already holds, so every client has to be able to reach a domain controller of the on-premises domain. The designer laptops have no network path to those controllers and are Entra joined rather than domain joined, so this source can't serve the estate as listed. AD DS remains the right pick when an existing on-premises domain is in place and clients can reach its domain controllers.
- Microsoft Entra Domain Services: Entra Domain Services is a managed domain you deploy in Azure and that clients must be able to join or at least reach; non-Azure clients can't join that managed domain, so the macOS laptops and the hybrid-joined servers would have no way to authenticate to it with their existing identities. It also still depends on connectivity to its domain controllers, and it manages synchronization from Microsoft Entra ID for you rather than removing the domain-joined requirement.
- On-premises Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) plus Microsoft Entra Kerberos: Only one identity source can be configured per storage account, and that source governs every file share in the account, so AD DS and Entra Kerberos cannot be run side by side on contosofs. Choose one and cover the remaining clients with managed identity or other mechanisms.

explanation:
Access to Azure Files requires passing two gates: a share-level Azure RBAC role and a Windows ACL at the file or directory level. In this case the ACL gate already passes, because the folder grants the object Modify. The failing gate is RBAC, and a computer account such as CONTOSO\SVC-BUILD$ has no Microsoft Entra ID object that a role assignment can target. The route the documentation provides for computer accounts (and sMSAs and gMSAs) is the storage account's default share-level permission, which applies to every share inside the account. It starts as None, which denies all file and directory access, so you turn it on under Step 2: Set share-level permissions and choose a role; Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor gives read, write and delete without changing ACLs, which is what this task needs. Keep in mind that the change can take up to about 30 minutes to propagate before you retest.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Assign the Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor role to CONTOSO\SVC-BUILD$ on the storage account's build share: Role assignments are made against Microsoft Entra ID objects, and a computer account such as CONTOSO\SVC-BUILD$ has no Entra object, so this assignment cannot be created for it. Computer accounts are handled through the storage account's default share-level permission instead.
- Assign the Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor role to a Microsoft Entra group that has the computer account as a member on the storage account's build share: Adding the computer account to a Microsoft Entra group does not help: the group only carries identities that have an Entra object, and the computer account still has none to assign to. The documented route for computer accounts is the storage account's default share-level permission.
- Assign the Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor role to the on-premises group CONTOSO\BUILD-WRITERS on the storage account's build share: An on-premises group has no Microsoft Entra ID object to assign a role to, and even when such a group is synced, its membership by a computer account does not make that computer account assignable. options.text: Add Kerberos to Authentication methods in the SMB security settings of the storage account
Restrict Kerberos ticket encryption to RC4-HMAC only in the SMB security settings of the storage account

explanation:
Azure Files authorizes an SMB request from the Kerberos ticket that the directory service issues, and all three supported identity sources require that ticket-based method to be turned on under Authentication methods in the storage account's SMB security settings. With only NTLMv2 in the allowed list there is nothing to evaluate for a domain credential: NTLMv2 covers account-key mounts, which is exactly why the key mount still works. Adding Kerberos to Authentication methods is the change that unblocks the session. The share-level role and the inherited ACL only come into play once a caller is authenticated, so neither can compensate for a session that never starts.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Restrict Kerberos ticket encryption to RC4-HMAC only in the SMB security settings of the storage account: Ticket encryption governs how an already-issued ticket is encrypted, not whether ticket-based authentication is accepted, so narrowing it to RC4-HMAC changes nothing while Kerberos is missing from Authentication methods. AES-256 is the recommended setting for the encryption type anyway, so this would move the account the wrong way twice.
- Remove NTLMv2 from Authentication methods in the SMB security settings so key-based mounts are rejected: NTLMv2 is the account-key path, and Azure Files doesn't use NTLM to authenticate domain credentials, so deleting it from Authentication methods would leave no usable method in the list and block every client, key-based mounts included. It does not turn on the ticket flow the users need.
- Restrict the allowed SMB versions to 3.1.1 only in the SMB security settings of the storage account: The SMB version setting only decides which dialect a client may negotiate for the session, and the affected workstations already speak SMB 3.x. Restricting versions changes nothing while Kerberos is absent from Authentication methods.

options.text: Contributor on the storage account
Reader on the storage account
Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor on the storage account
Storage File Data Privileged Contributor on the storage account

explanation:
Registering a storage account with on-premises AD DS changes properties on the storage account itself, so the documented least-privilege pairing is Reader on the resource group plus Contributor on the storage account. The Reader half is already in place here, so Contributor on contosofs is the single addition that lets the join complete without handing out anything broader.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Reader on the storage account: Reader grants no permission to write account properties, so the join would still be refused with the same authorization error. Reading the account is not what the cmdlet does.
- Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor on the storage account: This is a data-plane role scoped to file data in the shares. It gives users rights over SMB file shares but no rights to modify the storage account's configuration, which is exactly what the failing write targets.
- Storage File Data Privileged Contributor on the storage account: Also a data-plane role for file data, and the privileged variant additionally overrides existing ACLs. Neither capability lets you update the storage account resource, so the join stays unauthorized.

explanation:
The designer holds an account that exists only in Microsoft Entra ID, and for such cloud-only identities the Windows-side ACL tooling cannot apply the entry: File Explorer and icacls are usable only for hybrid identities under Microsoft Entra Kerberos, and for identities from AD DS or Entra Domain Services. The route that works is the Azure Files REST-based ACL tooling, for example Add-AzFileAce from the RestSetAcls module (the file browser in the Azure portal is the other working path), which can resolve the cloud-only object and write the folder's permission entry, typically with inheritable flags so new files below the subfolder are covered. Adding a share-level role would not achieve the goal on its own, because the role and the folder entry intersect and the more restrictive of the two governs, so a write-capable role cannot override an entry that grants only read.

options.text: AzFilesHybrid supports only AES-256 Kerberos, and registrations created with a version below v0.2.2 used RC4, so moving them forward means clearing the client Kerberos cache with klist purge and remounting.

Service logon account passwords expire at the domain's maximum password age, whereas computer account passwords are driven by the client machine (by default about every 30 days) and never expire in the directory.
The directory identity created to represent a storage account never has to be synced to Microsoft Entra ID.

Turning the feature off stops identity-based access to the account's shares but leaves the computer or service logon account behind in the domain as an orphaned object, and removing it isn't automatic.

explanation: Row A is explained by the statement that AzFilesHybrid supports only AES-256 Kerberos and that registrations made with a version older than v0.2.2 fell back to RC4. Because the tickets clients hold were issued under RC4, mounts keep failing until the cache is purged (klist purge) and the share is remounted after the switch to AES-256. Row B is explained by the difference in how the two account types handle password age: a computer account (the default from the join cmdlet) has its password renewed by the client machine about every 30 days and never expires in the directory, whereas a service logon account follows the domain's password expiration policy and therefore stops working once the maximum password age elapses. Row C is explained by the fact that the Active Directory identity created to represent a storage account does not need to be synchronized to Microsoft Entra ID, so an empty result in the tenant is expected. Row D is explained by the documented consequence of disabling AD DS: the shares lose identity-based access and the computer or service logon account stays in the on-premises directory as an orphaned object, because its removal isn't automatic.

prompt: Row 1 - mchen

options.text: Read, write and delete, but the folder's permissions cannot be changed
Read, write and delete even where the folder grants nothing
Every request is refused
Read, write, delete and change the folder's permissions

explanation:
The two gates combine rather than add up: Azure RBAC and the folder's own permission entry are intersected, and the more restrictive of the two wins in both directions. On top of that, Storage File Data Privileged Contributor and Privileged Reader bypass the folder's entries, and when an identity has both an account-level default permission and a specific assignment, the higher of the two roles applies.

Row 1: Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor plus a Modify folder entry yields read, write and delete with no ability to alter the folder's permissions, because that share role works on data without touching the ACL.
Row 2: Storage File Data Privileged Reader behaves like the Contributor role but ignores existing ACLs, so it still reads, writes and deletes in a folder whose entries say None.
Row 3: Storage File Data SMB Share Reader combined with a None folder entry means the most restrictive side wins and every request is refused.
Row 4: The account default is Storage File Data SMB Share Elevated Contributor while the explicit assignment is only Reader, so the identity ends up with the Elevated Contributor role, which adds the modify-permissions capability on top of the read, write and delete its Modify folder entry already allows.

Because the identity source is an account-level property, any later switch of that source on contosofs briefly breaks identity-based access to all of its shares, which is what the finance users must be told.

Why the other options are wrong:
- configure the second identity source on the storage account contosofs beside its current one: Only one identity source can be configured per storage account, so a second one cannot sit beside the current one; whichever source is configured governs every share in that account.
- reconfigure the storage account contosofs so the second identity source covers all eight shares: Switching the source on contosofs would also move the six finance shares onto the platform team's source, which is not allowed, and the switch interrupts identity-based access on all shares while it happens.

`PS C:\> Get-AzStorageAccount -Name contosofs | Select-Object -ExpandProperty AzureFilesIdentityBasedAuth

prompt: Set the directory object's Kerberos encryption type to _____ and have each client [...].

options.text: AES256
RC4-HMAC
RC4
DES-CBC-CRC

explanation:
AES256 is the supported and recommended Kerberos encryption type for identity-based access over SMB: AzFilesHybrid supports AES-256 only, and older module versions defaulted the storage account's directory object to RC4, which is why it still shows RC4-HMAC. The object is a computer account, so you set the cipher on it with Set-ADComputer -KerberosEncryptionType "AES256". Once the cipher changes, every client still holds tickets issued under the old one, so those cached tickets must be discarded (klist purge) and the share remounted so a ticket under the new cipher is requested.

- RC4-HMAC: RC4-HMAC is exactly the legacy value already in place, which is what fails once the domain tightens its cipher policy; the tooling supports AES-256 only, so the object has to move off it.

explanation:

- assign a share-level role to the cluster's group so the NFS clients sign in with their identities: Share-level Azure RBAC roles such as Storage File Data SMB Share Reader or Contributor are only evaluated once a directory identity has been authorized for an SMB share. prompt: The step that gets the appliance mounting the share again with its own identity is _____.

explanation:

options.text: enabled for all authenticated users and groups, with Storage File Data SMB Share Reader
enabled for all authenticated users and groups, with Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor

left at its current deny-everything value, with the existing entries on each share root deciding who can open what

explanation:
The account-wide default share permission applies to every share inside the storage account and, at its starting value, blocks all file and directory content, which is why domain users hit access denied even though their group is listed on the share root. Turning on the option that covers all authenticated users and groups and choosing the read-only share role lets every domain user clear the account-level gate, while the entries already on each folder still decide what those users can open, so nothing can be rewritten or deleted beyond what those entries allow. Share-level permission changes normally settle within about 30 minutes but can take longer than that, so the service desk must allow the change to propagate before treating a failed attempt as a fault.

Why the other options are wrong:
- enabled for all authenticated users and groups, with Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor: Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor adds write and delete on top of read, so it grants more than the stated need and would let people alter content where their folder entries are meant to limit them to viewing.
- enabled for all authenticated users and groups, with Storage File Data Privileged Reader: Storage File Data Privileged Reader grants access on its own instead of honouring the entries on the folders, so it breaks the requirement that those entries keep deciding who may open what.
- left at its current deny-everything value, with the existing entries on each share root deciding who can open what: While the account-wide default stays at its deny-everything starting value, the account-level gate blocks every user regardless of what the share roots list, so the folder entries on their own cannot get anyone in.

On a domain-joined Windows server you mapped \\contosofs.file.core.windows.net\reports to a drive letter and tried to take ownership of the workbook and to read its permissions, but both commands report that the path cannot be found, and the share never shows up in File Explorer on that server. `PS C:\> icacls Z:\q3-report.xlsx
ERROR: The system cannot find the path specified.

PS C:\> takeown /f Z:\q3-report.xlsx
ERROR: The system cannot find the path specified.

PS C:\> Get-PSDrive Z

Name  Provider      Root
----  --------      ----
Z     FileSystem    \\contosofs.file.core.windows.net\reports`
prompt: You should _____.

options.text: mount the share with net use and assign it a drive letter
mount the share with a PowerShell drive and point the native permission tools at the drive-qualified path
mount the storage account root with net use and reach the share through it
mount the share with net use and assign it a drive letter using the storage account key

explanation:
Share mounts used for Windows ACL work have to be created with the Windows net use command, as the documentation requires, so the mapping is visible to File Explorer, cmd.exe and the native tools such as icacls and takeown. A drive created only inside PowerShell stays inside that session, so native commands report the path as missing - exactly what the session log shows even though Get-PSDrive lists Z. Because identity-based access is already enabled against the on-premises domain and the Storage File Data SMB Admin role is held, mounting with the admin's own domain identity and then running takeown is the supported way to take ownership of a workbook whose existing ACL blocks the change, after which the ACL can be edited. This keeps the storage account key out of the picture.

Why the other options are wrong:
- mount the share with a PowerShell drive and point the native permission tools at the drive-qualified path: A drive created with New-PSDrive exists only inside the PowerShell session and is not exposed to File Explorer, cmd.exe or native tools such as icacls and takeown. That is precisely why those commands reported the path as missing even though Get-PSDrive listed the mapping, and aiming the same tools at the drive-qualified path does not change it.
- mount the storage account root with net use and reach the share through it: Azure Files mounts are made per file share, so the mapping has to point at \\contosofs.file.core.windows.net\reports rather than at the account root; the account root is not a mountable share and gives the permission tools nothing to operate on.
- mount the share with net use and assign it a drive letter using the storage account key: This is the documented but less secure fallback: a key mount grants immediate full access to everything on the share without any need to take ownership, and this scenario rules it out by platform policy. The Storage File Data SMB Admin role is the supported alternative for taking ownership of a file whose existing ACL blocks you.

Microsoft Entra ID itself is not an identity source for Azure Files sign-in, so it fills none of the three slots.

prompt: You have an NFS file share named nfsdata, created with the Microsoft.FileShares resource provider in storage account stcontoso. Immediately after the share was created, you created two snapshots from the CLI; both calls reported success. You now need the stored recovery points on this share to be browsable, but listing them returns nothing. Which action should you take?

options.text: Mount the share from a Linux client first, then delete the early snapshots and take new ones
Register the share with Azure Backup, then delete the snapshots that show nothing and let the service create new ones
Replace the listing command with the file data plane APIs (AzStorageShare) so the existing snapshots show up
Wait 24 hours after the share was created, then run the listing command again to see the snapshots

explanation:
For NFS file shares, the share should be mounted before snapshots are captured. If a new NFS share is snapshotted before it has ever been mounted, listing its snapshots returns an empty list even though the creation calls succeeded. The fix is to mount the share (for example from an NFS client on a Linux VM), delete the snapshots that were taken before that first mount, and capture them again; afterwards the list is populated.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Register the share with Azure Backup, then delete the snapshots that show nothing and let the service create new ones: Azure Backup does not support NFS file shares, so it cannot be registered for this share or used to manage its recovery points. Snapshots are the only in-service protection option for NFS shares.
- Replace the listing command with the file data plane APIs (AzStorageShare) so the existing snapshots show up: Only the file management APIs (AzRmStorageShare) are supported for NFS share snapshots; the file data plane APIs (AzStorageShare) are not supported, so switching to them will not surface the stored snapshots.
- Wait 24 hours after the share was created, then run the listing command again to see the snapshots: There is no waiting period after creation that makes the snapshot list populate; the empty result comes from capturing snapshots before the share was mounted. The early snapshots must be deleted and re-created after mounting.

explanation:

- 2 June 2026, thirty days after the share was deleted: This uses the current 30-day value, but 30 days was not in effect on 3 May 2026 when payroll was deleted, so it does not govern this share.
- 4 June 2026, thirty days after the retention change was saved: Changing the retention period does not retroactively re-date existing soft-deleted shares. The new 30-day period was only in effect from 5 May 2026 and applies to shares deleted after that point.
- 12 May 2026, seven days after the retention change was saved: This applies the correct 7-day duration but starts the clock on the wrong date. The retention clock starts when the share is deleted (3 May 2026), not when the retention setting is saved, so the share expires on 10 May 2026, not 12 May 2026.

prompt: You have a classic SMB file share named archive in storage account stcontoso. Your nightly batch job rewrites thousands of files in that share, and last week it corrupted several of them. You need a point-in-time copy of the share's files from before tonight's run so you can roll the bad writes back one file at a time. The attempt to capture it has failed. Which action should you take first?

options.text: Delete the oldest snapshots of the file share archive, then create the new snapshot
Delete the file share archive and create a new share with the same name, then create the new snapshot
Raise the file share soft delete retention period on storage account stcontoso, then create the new snapshot
Reduce the redundancy of the file share archive from geo-redundant to locally redundant, then create the new snapshot

explanation:
A file share can hold a maximum of 200 snapshots, and the existing snapshots are never overwritten or replaced by a new one, so the request is rejected while the share is already at that count. Removing the snapshots with the oldest timestamps frees the slots that a new point-in-time copy needs, while the share itself and the files in it are left untouched, so you can still restore individual files afterwards.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Delete the file share archive and create a new share with the same name, then create the new snapshot: Deleting the file share removes its snapshots along with it and erases the share's data, so the point-in-time versions you still need would be destroyed; a freshly created, empty share also contains none of the files the job is about to overwrite.
- Raise the file share soft delete retention period on storage account stcontoso, then create the new snapshot: Soft delete governs how long a deleted file share can be undeleted. It does not control how many snapshots an existing share may hold, so changing the retention period frees no snapshot slot and the next request still fails.
- Reduce the redundancy of the file share archive from geo-redundant to locally redundant, then create the new snapshot: Snapshots inherit the redundancy of the base share, but redundancy has no bearing on how many snapshots a share may contain. Changing it neither removes the existing snapshots nor raises the cap, so the request would still be rejected.

prompt: You have a classic SMB file share named contracts in storage account stcontoso. A compliance officer has asked that the share's contents be removed before the current recovery window ends, and the share was already deleted yesterday. You need to purge it now. Which sequence of steps should you follow?

options.text: Undelete the share, disable soft delete for file shares on the storage account, delete the share again, and then re-enable soft delete for the account.
Leave soft delete for file shares enabled on the storage account and delete the share again, so the data is removed right away.
Disable soft delete for file shares on the storage account and wait for the retention period to expire, so the share is removed permanently.
Undelete the share, delete the snapshots it contains, and then disable soft delete for file shares on the storage account.

explanation:
Soft delete cannot be bypassed. While it is enabled for file shares, a delete request against the share is captured again as a soft-deleted share, so the data stays recoverable until the retention window that was in force at deletion expires. The only way to remove the share permanently before that window ends is to undelete it first (which brings back the share with its files and its snapshots), turn off soft delete for the account, delete the share so the deletion is permanent, and then turn soft delete back on so the account's other shares stay protected.

Why the other options are wrong:

The extra data held by those snapshots is appearing as a monthly charge, and finance wants it reduced. You must keep the ability to restore the entire share to its most recent point in time. Which action should you take?

options.text: Delete the four oldest snapshots and keep only the newest one
Delete the newest snapshot and keep only the oldest one
Delete every snapshot on the share and rely on file share soft delete for the recovery point
Keep all snapshots and reduce the snapshot frequency from nightly to weekly instead

explanation:
Share snapshots are incremental: each one stores and bills only the data that changed since the preceding snapshot, and removing a snapshot frees only the data that was unique to it. Every snapshot that remains still carries everything needed to browse and restore its own point in time, so retaining only the newest copy (22 October 2026) preserves a full restore of the latest state while releasing the unique data billed for the four older copies — including the 812.4 GiB charged for the 25 September bulk import. Soft delete has no bearing on this: it only covers a deleted share, and this share is still active.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Delete the newest snapshot and keep only the oldest one: Because each snapshot carries only its own increment, the earliest copy cannot reproduce anything written after the bulk import, so the most recent state would no longer be restorable. It also leaves the other copies in place, so the billed data for them is not released.
- Delete every snapshot on the share and rely on file share soft delete for the recovery point: Soft delete is the recovery path for a share that has been deleted: it holds the share and its contents for the configured retention so the share can be undeleted. It does not produce point-in-time versions of files inside a share that still exists, so removing every snapshot would leave no way to recover earlier contents of this active share.
- Keep all snapshots and reduce the snapshot frequency from nightly to weekly instead: Taking snapshots less often only limits the unique data added by future snapshots; the data already stored for the existing snapshots stays on the account and keeps being billed, so the current monthly charge is unchanged. It also reduces the number of recovery points available and widens the exposure between runs.

prompt: You administer two NFS file shares in storage account stcontoso, and both were created with the Microsoft.Storage resource provider. Your operations lead wants two standing safeguards in place: a file that someone accidentally deletes inside a share that stays online must be recoverable, and a share that gets deleted must be recoverable with all of its contents. Which combination of features should you put in place?

options.text: Enable soft delete for all file shares at the account level; capture share snapshots of the shares
Enable soft delete for all file shares at the account level only
Capture share snapshots of the shares only
Configure an Azure file share backup policy for the account

explanation:
The two safeguards need two different mechanisms. A file deleted while its share is still active can only be brought back from a point-in-time copy of that share, and on NFS shares Azure file share backup is not supported, so share snapshots are the option (soft delete works at share level only and cannot recover an individual file from a share that was never deleted). A share that gets deleted needs soft delete, which retains the share with all of its contents for the retention window and undeletes it in its pre-deletion state; share snapshots cannot cover this because deleting a file share removes its snapshots with it. Soft delete for file shares is configured once at the storage account level and covers the classic Microsoft.Storage shares in stcontoso, so the correct option is the only combination that satisfies both requirements.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enable soft delete for all file shares at the account level only: Soft delete for all file shares, enabled at the account level, only covers the case where the whole share is deleted. It cannot bring back a single file that was removed while the share stayed active, because it operates at the share level only and no deleted share exists to undelete.
- Capture share snapshots of the shares only: Capturing share snapshots covers the file-level safeguard, but it does not satisfy the share-level safeguard: when a file share is deleted its snapshots are deleted along with it, so nothing would remain to restore the deleted share.
- Configure an Azure file share backup policy for the account: Azure file share backup is not supported for NFS file shares, so a backup policy in this account would deliver neither safeguard for the two NFS shares listed.

Mount the share, then list the stored recovery points in the hidden .snapshots directory under the mount path and take the files out with cp -r.
Open the file share's Snapshots tab, right-click the file and choose Restore, then Overwrite original file.

explanation: The Windows workstation uses the Previous versions tab reached through the item's Properties, where Open browses one point in time and Restore copies the entire directory recursively back to its original location. The Linux server mounts one point in time by passing snapshot=@GMT-year.month.day-hour.minutes.seconds to mount -t cifs together with a credentials file, an option the kernel supports from version 4.19. The NFS host lists the stored points in the hidden .snapshots directory under its mount path, enters the one it wants, and copies the files out with cp -r. The portal path is the file share's Snapshots tab, then right-click the file, Restore, and Overwrite original file. The Recovery Services vault policy and the undelete operation belong to neither client path.
