context:
You have classic file shares in storage account stcontoso. You have recorded the results of four routine checks, shown in the exhibit. You need to determine what caused each result. Which statement accounts for each finding?

- Finding: Finding A — budget share; Observed result: The share budget was deleted on 5 Oct 2026. At that moment the account's soft delete retention period was 7 days; on 8 Oct it was changed to 30 days. The share's expiry still shows 12 Oct 2026.
- Finding: Finding B — sales share; Observed result: A share snapshot of sales was created on 1 Oct and another on 8 Oct. The 8 Oct snapshot increased the monthly storage bill by 35 GB, although the share holds 2 TB of files whose contents and metadata were identical on both dates.
- Finding: Finding C — inventory share; Observed result: Creating a new share snapshot for inventory failed and no snapshot was added. The files in inventory remain readable and writable.
- Finding: Finding D — contracts share; Observed result: After the share contracts was deleted, the three snapshots previously listed for it disappeared from the portal and support cannot retrieve them.
prompt: Finding A — budget share

options.text: A change to the soft delete retention period applies only to shares deleted after the change; shares deleted earlier keep the retention period that was configured when they were deleted.
Each new share snapshot is incremental: only the data that differs from the previous snapshot is stored and billed, so repeated content is not charged again.
Each file share supports a maximum of 200 share snapshots; once that limit is reached, an older snapshot must be deleted before another one can be created.
Deleting the base file share also deletes all of its snapshots, so snapshots cannot be kept after the share is gone.
A share snapshot can be retained for up to 10 years before it has to be deleted.

explanation: Finding A is explained by the rule that a retention-period change is not retroactive: the share budget was deleted on 5 Oct while the period was 7 days, so it expires on 12 Oct, while the later change to 30 days only affects shares deleted from 8 Oct onward. Finding B is explained by incremental snapshots: because the files and metadata were the same on 1 Oct and 8 Oct, only the changed data (35 GB) is stored and billed for the second snapshot. Finding C is explained by the per-share snapshot ceiling: a share can hold at most 200 share snapshots, and after that limit is reached an older snapshot must be deleted before a new one can be created, which is why the new snapshot failed while the share itself stayed usable. Finding D is explained by the lifecycle rule that snapshots live only as long as their base share, so deleting the share contracts removed its three snapshots and they cannot be retained independently.

context:
You administer the file shares in storage account stcontoso. The exhibit lists four jobs you need to complete today. Match each job to the command or portal location you should use for it. One of the listed options is not usable for any of the jobs.

- Job: A; Share: media — classic SMB, created with the Microsoft.Storage provider; What the job requires: Capture a point-in-time copy of the share's data using the Azure CLI.
- Job: B; Share: analytics — NFS, created with the Microsoft.Storage provider; What the job requires: Capture a point-in-time copy of the share's data using Azure PowerShell.
- Job: C; Share: metrics — NFS, created with the Microsoft.FileShares provider; What the job requires: Read the mount endpoint hostName value that the portal's JSON view displays for this share.
- Job: D; Share: metrics — NFS, created with the Microsoft.FileShares provider; What the job requires: Change the metadata of a point-in-time copy that already exists on this share.
prompt: Job A

options.text: az storage share snapshot
New-AzRmStorageShare
az fileshare show
Operations > Snapshots > Properties
AzStorageShare (file data plane API family)

explanation: Job A covers a classic SMB share, and share snapshots for classic shares can be created with the portal, Azure PowerShell or the Azure CLI, so az storage share snapshot is the right tool. Job B covers an NFS share, where snapshot operations only work through the file management API family (AzRmStorageShare, for example New-AzRmStorageShare); the file data plane family (AzStorageShare) is explicitly not supported for NFS snapshots, so that leftover option fits no job here. Job C needs the mount endpoint hostName of a Microsoft.FileShares NFS share, which can be read with az fileshare show (or Get-AzFileShare). Job D needs the metadata of an existing point-in-time copy on a Microsoft.FileShares NFS share, which is updated in the portal under Operations > Snapshots > Properties.

context:
You have carried out the four administrative actions listed in the exhibit against the file shares in storage account stcontoso. You need to know what each action actually produced. Match each step to the outcome that follows from it.

- Step: S1; Action carried out: Deleted the oldest of the five snapshots of the classic file share 'ledger'
- Step: S2; Action carried out: Tried to copy a whole snapshot of the share 'ledger' into a different storage account all at once
- Step: S3; Action carried out: Copied a file out of a snapshot back onto the same path in the live share 'ledger'
- Step: S4; Action carried out: Deleted a provisioned file share while soft delete was enabled
prompt: S1 — first step in the exhibit

options.text: Only the content that existed solely in that snapshot was removed; every remaining snapshot still holds everything needed to browse and restore its point in time.
There is no single operation that does this; the content has to be moved one file at a time, for example with AzCopy.
The share now shows the earlier content, the snapshot itself stays unchanged, and later snapshots count that file as changed content.
The share keeps consuming its quota until the recovery window ends, when it is finally removed.

explanation: Each step produces exactly one of the listed outcomes. Deleting one snapshot of a share (S1) discards only the data that was unique to that snapshot; every other snapshot still contains everything required to browse and restore its point in time. A snapshot can never be promoted into a whole share, so it cannot be copied to a different storage account in one operation (S2); the data has to be transferred file by file, for example with AzCopy. Copying a file out of a snapshot back over the same path in the live share (S3) replaces that file in the base share while the snapshot itself remains intact, and the restored content counts as changed content for subsequent snapshots. Finally, deleting a provisioned share while soft delete is enabled (S4) leaves the share consuming its quota until the soft delete retention window expires, at which point it is fully removed.

The share now shows the earlier content, the snapshot itself stays unchanged, and later snapshots count that file as changed content.

explanation: Each step produces exactly one of the listed outcomes. Deleting one snapshot of a share (S1) discards only the data that was unique to that snapshot; every other snapshot still contains everything required to browse and restore its point in time. A snapshot can never be promoted into a whole share, so it cannot be copied to a different storage account in one operation (S2); the data has to be transferred file by file, for example with AzCopy. Copying a file out of a snapshot back over the same path in the live share (S3) replaces that file in the base share while the snapshot itself remains intact, and the restored content counts as changed content for subsequent snapshots. Finally, deleting a provisioned share while soft delete is enabled (S4) leaves the share consuming its quota until the soft delete retention window expires, at which point it is fully removed.

prompt: To place the captured version into the destination share, the transfer must run _____, and the destination share ends up with [...].

options.text: one file at a time with AzCopy, because a snapshot cannot be moved to another storage account as a single unit
as one snapshot with AzCopy, because a snapshot already holds every file in the share at that point in time
by promoting the snapshot to replace the source share, and then copying the replaced share to the destination
by capturing a new snapshot of the source share inside the destination storage account

explanation:
A share snapshot is never promoted to replace its base share, and a whole-share restore is done file by file; an entire snapshot also cannot be copied to another storage account in one operation. The captured version therefore has to be moved out file by file with AzCopy (or another copy mechanism), which is the first slot's keyed option. Content taken out of a snapshot and written to a different destination is written as an ordinary writable file rather than as a new snapshot, and copying it out leaves the base share's own contents untouched, which is the second slot's keyed option.

Why the other options are wrong:
- as one snapshot with AzCopy, because a snapshot already holds every file in the share at that point in time: Wrong: there is no single-unit copy of a snapshot into a different storage account. The captured content must be transferred per file (for example with AzCopy), because an entire snapshot cannot be copied to another storage account in one operation.
- by promoting the snapshot to replace the source share, and then copying the replaced share to the destination: Wrong: a snapshot is never promoted to replace the base share, so no promotion step exists. Restoring a whole share from a captured version is done file by file, not by turning the capture into the live share.
- by capturing a new snapshot of the source share inside the destination storage account: Wrong: snapshots are created inside a file share in the account where that share lives, so a snapshot of the source share cannot be captured from the destination account, and nothing of the captured version would be transferred by doing so.

You deleted that share on 22 October 2026, yet the account's quota report still shows the same amount of space in use as before the deletion. Which statement explains the quota result?

prompt: The deleted share _____.

options.text: keeps consuming its provisioned capacity until the retention period ends
stops consuming its provisioned capacity as soon as the deletion completes
keeps consuming its provisioned capacity until the retention period is changed
keeps consuming its provisioned capacity until the share is undeleted

explanation:
For a provisioned file share, soft delete keeps the deleted share in the account's quota calculation: the share continues to consume its provisioned capacity until its soft-delete expiry, when it is finally fully deleted and the capacity is released. Deleting invoices on 22 October 2026 therefore leaves the account showing 900 GiB of the 900 GiB provisioned quota in use rather than freeing the 100 GiB immediately. Share snapshots do not change this, because deleting the base share also removes its snapshots.

Why the other options are wrong:
- stops consuming its provisioned capacity as soon as the deletion completes: Capacity is not handed back at the moment of deletion. A soft-deleted provisioned share keeps counting toward the account's total quota until its soft-delete expiry, so the reported usage stays at 900 GiB.
- keeps consuming its provisioned capacity until the retention period is changed: Changing the recovery setting does not restart or cancel the clock for a share that has already been deleted. Shares deleted before a retention change expire according to the retention period that was in force when they were deleted, so the share keeps consuming capacity until that original window completes.
- keeps consuming its provisioned capacity until the share is undeleted: Undeleting the share brings it back as an active share; it has no bearing on when the account's quota is relieved. The provisioned capacity stops counting only when the soft-delete window completes and the share is fully deleted.

Soft delete for file shares in the storage account
An Azure Resource Manager lock on the storage account

explanation:
Requirement R1 applies to designdata, which is an NFS share. Azure file share backup is supported for SMB file shares only, and Azure Backup does not support NFS file shares, so the only in-service protection available for an NFS share is share snapshots; these can be created for a schedule with the REST API, client SDKs, Azure PowerShell (New-AzRmStorageShare) or the CLI (az storage share snapshot), and the earlier version of a file can then be restored from them. Requirement R2 applies to policies, a classic SMB share. A scheduled, policy-driven service that automates the taking of copies and manages their retention exists for SMB shares: Azure file share backup, which is supported for SMB file shares only.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Azure file share backup for the file share: Azure file share backup supports SMB file shares only, and Azure Backup does not support NFS file shares, so it cannot protect the NFS share designdata.
- Soft delete for file shares in the storage account: Soft delete retains a file share after it has been removed and can return it with all of its contents; it does not create point-in-time copies of the files in a share that is still online, so it cannot satisfy R1.
- An Azure Resource Manager lock on the storage account: An Azure Resource Manager lock prevents changes to or removal of the storage account it is placed on; it stores no copies of the data and provides no way to restore an earlier version of a file.

stores the data in a separate storage account in the paired region and not in the primary region

explanation:
A share snapshot inherits the redundancy of the base share, so in a geo-redundant storage account such as stcontoso the snapshot's data is held in the account's primary region and is also stored redundantly in the paired region (West US 2); no second storage account is involved. The snapshot also carries the files' system properties and the file share metadata with the values they had when the snapshot was taken, and because no separate metadata was supplied at creation in this scenario, those are the values that come back on restore.

Why the other options are wrong:
- stores the data in the primary region and not in the paired region: The snapshot inherits the redundancy of the base share, so in a geo-redundant account its data is also stored in the paired region; it is not confined to the primary region.
- stores the data in a separate storage account in the paired region and not in the primary region: A snapshot is held inside the same storage account as the base share. No separate storage account is created to hold snapshot data, so the data is never written to another account in the paired region.
- stores the data in the paired region and in the primary region, but only after the base share is deleted: A snapshot is created alongside the share and its data is protected from that moment onward; it is not held back until the base share is deleted.

Which change should you make so the failover subnet keeps working while access stays limited to selected networks?

options.text: Replace the service endpoint on the failover subnet with a Microsoft.Storage.Global endpoint
Add an IP network rule for the public address range that the failover virtual network's subnets egress through, and leave the service endpoint as is
Set public network access on stcont001 to Enabled from all networks so the public endpoint answers every request
Enable the "Allow trusted Microsoft services to access this storage account" network security exception

explanation:
Azure Storage service endpoints come in two types. Microsoft.Storage only reaches storage accounts located in the same region as the virtual network, whereas Microsoft.Storage.Global reaches accounts in any region, which is what a geo-redundant account needs when clients operate from the paired region. Because a subnet can carry only one storage service endpoint, the existing Microsoft.Storage endpoint on app-subnet-failover must be removed before the global one is added. Both subnets are already listed in the account's virtual network rules, so after the swap the failover subnet is authorized and region-agnostic. This preserves the "Enabled from selected networks" restriction rather than opening the account to the internet.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add an IP network rule for the public address range that the failover virtual network's subnets egress through, and leave the service endpoint as is: Wrong: a service endpoint makes traffic from that subnet reach storage with a private source IP, so an IP network rule built around the subnet's public address never matches. IP rules are the tool for clients outside a virtual network, not for subnets that already route through a service endpoint.
- Set public network access on stcont001 to Enabled from all networks so the public endpoint answers every request: Wrong: this makes the account reachable from any network, which removes the network filtering the account is supposed to keep and exposes it to the internet. It solves the 403 by deleting the security boundary rather than by authorizing the failover subnet.
- Enable the "Allow trusted Microsoft services to access this storage account" network security exception: Wrong: that exception exists for Azure platform services that connect from outside your network boundary and cannot be expressed as a virtual network or IP rule, such as a logging or diagnostics service reading resource logs or metrics tables. Traffic from your own subnets is handled by virtual network rules and service endpoints.

Add an IP network rule for the public NAT IP addresses used for Microsoft peering

explanation:
When an on-premises network reaches Azure through an ExpressRoute circuit, the addresses the storage account actually sees are the translated public addresses used on the Microsoft peering path, because on-premises private addresses are translated before the traffic enters Microsoft's network. IP network rules filter on public IP ranges, so the rule must list those Microsoft peering translation addresses, which are supplied either by the service provider or by the customer. Adding them authorizes nothing, so the backup job would still be denied.
- Add an IP network rule for the public IP address range of the on-premises firewall's Internet-facing interface: The Internet-facing address of the on-premises firewall is what Azure sees when traffic reaches Azure over the ordinary Internet, not over an ExpressRoute circuit. With a circuit in place, the source presented to the service is the translated address on the peering path, so this range would not match and the uploads would still fail.
- Add an IP network rule for the private IP address range of the circuit's private peering: Private peering carries on-premises traffic to Azure virtual networks over a private link; it does not deliver traffic to the public endpoint that IP network rules govern. Listing its private range therefore cannot authorize the backup source.

Copying out of stsrc01 has worked for months, but since last night's change every run now fails on the destination leg: the client logs show the destination host cannot be resolved from vnet-backup and the job reports HTTP 403 when it writes to stdst02. The accounts and that network are described below. You need tonight's copy to complete, and neither account may be opened up to traffic from any network. Which action should you take?

options.text: Add an IP network rule to stdst02 that allows the public address range of vnet-backup.
Create a blob private endpoint for stdst02 in vnet-backup.
Create an additional blob private endpoint for stsrc01 in vnet-backup.
Enable a network security exception on stdst02 that allows trusted Azure services.

explanation:
The job runs in a network where it reaches stsrc01 over Private Link, and vnet-backup has the privatelink.blob.core.windows.net private zone linked. A copy client needs a working path to every account it touches, so leaving only the source side privatised breaks the destination leg: inside that network the destination name has no private address to resolve to. Giving stdst02 its own blob private endpoint in vnet-backup supplies that address, the ordinary connection string for the destination then resolves correctly, and the existing virtual network rules and selected-networks setting can stay in place.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add an IP network rule to stdst02 that allows the public address range of vnet-backup: An IP network rule matches the public source address ranges of clients that reach the public endpoint, which suits office networks, on-premises hosts and scanners. Traffic sent from vnet-backup does not present that range to storage — once a subnet carries a service endpoint its traffic arrives with a private source IP — so an address range would neither resolve the destination name nor give the job a path to it.
- Create an additional blob private endpoint for stsrc01 in vnet-backup: stsrc01 already has a blob private endpoint in vnet-backup and reads from it succeed, so a second one for the same account in the same subnet adds nothing. The failing leg is the destination: the copy client needs a private path to the destination account as well, and only one side is currently privatised.
- Enable a network security exception on stdst02 that allows trusted Azure services: A network security exception is for Azure platform services that run outside your network boundary, such as a diagnostics or logging service reading resource logs or metrics tables. AzCopy running inside vnet-backup is not such a service, so the exception would not restore the destination connection and would weaken the account for no benefit.

Add a resource instance rule that authorizes the platform services that run in your tenant.
Add an IP network rule that lists the public address ranges of the platform services.
Add a virtual network rule that authorizes the subnet where the platform services run.

explanation:
A network security exception for trusted services is the mechanism for Azure services that run outside your network and cannot be expressed as a virtual network or IP rule, such as a service that only needs to write resource log files or metrics tables; these services authenticate strongly before they connect. Switching on the Azure services list for stdiag01 lets the log and metrics writes through, while every other source still has to match an explicit virtual network, IP or resource instance rule, so no other network gains access.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add a resource instance rule that authorizes the platform services that run in your tenant: A resource instance rule covers Azure resources you can point at individually: the resource must live in the same Microsoft Entra tenant as the storage account, and its role assignments decide which operations it may run. The platform services writing these logs are not resource instances in your tenant, so there is nothing to select for them.
- Add an IP network rule that lists the public address ranges of the platform services: IP network rules work by matching the client's public IP address against a range you supply. The callers here originate from addresses you do not control and cannot express as a stable range in your own address space, so no correct range can be listed, and a range broad enough to try would expose the account to unrelated networks.
- Add a virtual network rule that authorizes the subnet where the platform services run: Virtual network rules authorize named subnets of your own virtual networks, and each such subnet must also have a storage service endpoint enabled on it. The platform services writing these logs do not run in a subnet you can select, so such a rule never matches their traffic.

You have storage account stmesh01, a general-purpose v2 account in East US. Overnight your infrastructure pipeline deleted vnet-app and its application subnet, then rebuilt both with identical names. Since the rebuild, the batch job that runs in that subnet receives HTTP 403 for every request it sends to stmesh01, while unrelated workloads are unaffected. You need the job working again with no source beyond the application subnet able to reach the account. Which action should you take?

- Item: Storage account; Observed state: stmesh01 (general-purpose v2, East US)
- Item: Public network access; Observed state: Enabled from selected networks

- Item: Service endpoint on the rebuilt application subnet; Observed state: Not present

options.text: Enable the storage service endpoint on the rebuilt application subnet, then add that subnet to the account's virtual network rules and save
Enable the storage service endpoint on the rebuilt application subnet, then add the 10.20.0.0/24 range to the account's IP network rules and save
Enable the storage service endpoint on the rebuilt application subnet, then add the rebuilt subnet to the account's trusted services exception and save
Enable the storage service endpoint on the rebuilt application subnet, then set the account's public network access to Enabled from all networks and save

explanation:
A subnet is authorized by a virtual network rule, and every subnet in such a rule must also carry a storage service endpoint, which supplies the direct route to the account. Deleting a subnet that a rule referenced removes it from the account's rules as well, and a replacement created under the same name inherits nothing, so both steps must be repeated for the rebuilt application subnet: enable the service endpoint and add the subnet as a rule, then save. The account stays on Enabled from selected networks, so nothing beyond the listed source can connect.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enable the storage service endpoint on the rebuilt application subnet, then add the 10.20.0.0/24 range to the account's IP network rules and save: IP network rules match a public address range and suit clients outside Azure, while a source inside vnet-app belongs in a virtual network rule. Once the service endpoint is enabled on the subnet, its traffic reaches storage with a private source address, so a range rule built for the public address no longer matches anything.
- Enable the storage service endpoint on the rebuilt application subnet, then add the rebuilt subnet to the account's trusted services exception and save: The trusted services exception is the escape hatch for Azure platform services that run outside your boundary and cannot be expressed as a subnet or IP rule, such as a diagnostics or logging writer. Your own application subnet is not such a service, so listing it there authorizes nothing and the requests stay blocked.
- Enable the storage service endpoint on the rebuilt application subnet, then set the account's public network access to Enabled from all networks and save: Enabled from all networks removes network filtering and lets any client reach the public endpoint, which contradicts the requirement that only the application subnet may connect. The account should stay on Enabled from selected networks with the rebuilt subnet listed.

With only privatelink.blob.core.windows.net and privatelink.dfs.core.windows.net linked, the name stvault09.file.core.windows.net still leads to the public endpoint, which is Disabled, and the mount never reaches the account. Creating a private endpoint for the file sub-resource and linking privatelink.file.core.windows.net to vnet-hub gives the share an address inside the network while the public endpoint stays shut. From inside that network the client keeps using the ordinary mount path \\stvault09.file.core.windows.net\shares and lets DNS supply the address; the privatelink name is the endpoint's own DNS record, not a host a client dials directly.

Why the other options are wrong:

explanation:
Once ci-snet carries a storage service endpoint, requests originating in that subnet arrive at the storage account with a private source address, so 203.0.113.10 is no longer the caller and the existing IP network rule can never match; every upload therefore gets HTTP 403. Because the subnet already has the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint in place, the fix is to authorize the subnet itself with a virtual network rule for ci-snet of vnet-dev. That restores the CI job's uploads and keeps the account closed to every source that is not listed, while the job keeps a private source address instead of hairpinning through a public IP.

Why the other options are wrong:
- An IP network rule for the public address the subnet used before the endpoint was enabled: An IP network rule matches the source address exactly as the storage service sees it. After the service endpoint was enabled on ci-snet, traffic from that subnet is delivered with a private source address, so listing the subnet's old public address — or adding it again — changes nothing and the job keeps receiving HTTP 403.
- A resource instance rule for the virtual machine that hosts the job: A resource instance rule authorizes a specific Azure resource by its identity, and it is intended for resources that no subnet or IP range can isolate, with role assignments on the resource deciding which data operations it may run. Here the client is an ordinary subnet whose source is already isolable by service endpoint, so authorizing the VM identity is not the change that restores these uploads.
- Public network access changed to Enabled from all networks: Enabled from all networks removes network filtering from stbuild09 altogether. That contradicts the requirement that no unlisted source gain access and leaves the account reachable from any network on the internet.

After you save settings that allow access, the rules that block access stay in force for up to one more minute, which covers the 08:00 and 08:01 runs; from 08:03 the saved rule is in force and the agent works. Because the account's configuration is already right, nothing further should be done to it — rewriting the rule, adding an IP network rule for the agent's address, or issuing credentials would either be pointless or would widen or duplicate access rather than fix anything.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Network rules decide which networks may reach an account but never check credentials, so these HTTP 403 responses come from the agent's missing credential rather than from where it sits: Network rules are network filtering only and never authenticate, but that does not explain the timing: the account was returning HTTP 403 before the rule existed and began succeeding minutes later with no credential change, which matches the delay after an allow change instead.

A colleague opens the storage account in the portal, goes to Lifecycle management under Data management, and starts adding a rule that moves unused log files to the cool tier after 30 days. options.text: Enable access time tracking on the storage account and change the rule's blob type to Block blobs
Enable access time tracking on the storage account and change the rule's blob subtype to Previous versions and snapshots
Enable access time tracking on the storage account and change the rule's blob type to Append blobs

explanation:
A read-based condition on the Base blobs page appears only when both prerequisites are met: access time tracking is turned on for the account (Enable access tracking on the Lifecycle management blade under Data management) and the rule's blob type is Block blobs. With tracking disabled there is no last accessed time to evaluate, and with Append blobs selected the option is still hidden. Turning tracking on and switching the blob type to Block blobs makes the Last accessed condition available; this also matches the tiering limitation, since moving data to cool applies only to block blobs and never to append or page blobs.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Enable access time tracking on the storage account and change the rule's blob subtype to Previous versions and snapshots: Changing the blob subtype only changes which versions of a blob a rule targets (current version, previous versions, snapshots). It does not affect whether a read-based condition is offered. Because access tracking would still be enabled but the blob type would remain Append blobs, the Last accessed condition would continue to be unavailable.
- Enable access time tracking on the storage account and change the rule's blob type to Append blobs: This changes nothing that the condition depends on: the blob type stays Append blobs, and the Last accessed option is offered only for Block blobs. Cool-tier tiering actions also do not apply to append blobs, so the rule could not move these files to cool.
- Enable access time tracking on the storage account and change the rule's blob type to Page blobs: With the blob type set to Page blobs, the read-based condition is still not offered, because it is limited to Block blobs. Page blobs are also excluded from tiering actions, so the cool-tier move would not apply.

options.text: Split the rule into two rules: one that filters on the path prefix alone and one that filters on the blob index tag alone.
Add the blob index tag to the filter set of the current rule, so the path prefix and the tag both have to match.
Remove the path prefix from the filter set, so the rule matches only blobs carrying the blob index tag alone.
Add a second action to the rules in the policy so that blobs carrying the expire tag move to the cool tier, and leave the filters in place.

explanation:
Filters inside a single rule are combined with a logical AND, so the saved rule only reaches blobs that carry the releases/ path prefix and the expire=true tag at the same time. The packages stored under releases/ without the tag, and the tagged renditions sitting outside that path, are therefore never processed. Splitting the rule into a rule filtered on the path prefix and a rule filtered on the blob index tag brings both groups under management, and a blob that satisfies both characteristics is simply picked up by each rule.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add the blob index tag to the filter set of the current rule, so the path prefix and the tag both have to match: Stacking more filters in one rule keeps the AND behaviour, so the rule still matches only the intersection of the prefix and the tag. Nothing changes for the two groups that match a single characteristic, and stacking filters can never widen a rule's reach; that requires separate rules.
- Remove the path prefix from the filter set, so the rule matches only blobs carrying the blob index tag alone: This narrows the rule down to tagged blobs only, which leaves the packages stored under releases/ without the expire tag unmanaged — the opposite of what the team needs. It solves the tag side of the requirement by abandoning the path side.
- Add a second action to the rules in the policy so that blobs carrying the expire tag move to the cool tier, and leave the filters in place: Actions decide what happens to blobs a rule already matches; they do not change which blobs match. The filter set still requires the path prefix and the tag together, so adding another tiering action adds no coverage for either group.

options.text: Replace the tierToCool action with a delete action for base blobs.

The 24-hour pause has to come before the policy is removed, because only disabling the rules stops the in-flight execution.

Every blob in the container was written with the account's default encryption scope, and after that run the packages are still in the hot tier, so the storage bill for the container has not dropped. The packages must remain retrievable for audit for several more years, and the team wants the policy to lower the per-blob cost of these packages. Which change should be made to the policy?

options.text: Keep the archive action and add a blob index tag filter so the rule selects only the blobs written with the encryption scope.

explanation:
A lifecycle management policy cannot change the tier of a blob that uses an encryption scope to the archive tier. Swapping the archive action for a cool-tier action keeps the packages online and retrievable for audit while lowering their per-blob cost, which is what the team asked for.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Keep the archive action and add a blob index tag filter so the rule selects only the blobs written with the encryption scope: Selecting the scoped blobs more precisely cannot help: the restriction applies to the archive tier itself, no matter how the rule picks its blobs, and the rule already carried no filters, so it was already evaluating these packages. The action still has no effect on them.
- Change the delete action so that blobs using the encryption scope are removed 90 days after their last modification instead of being moved to a tier: Removing the packages would reduce storage consumption, but the packages must stay retrievable for audit for several more years, so deleting them contradicts the stated requirement and discards data that is still needed.
- Keep the archive action but base it on the creation time rather than the last modified time, so the policy moves the blobs to the archive tier sooner: Switching the age basis from last modified time to creation time only changes when the rule fires. The packages are already well past any threshold the policy uses, yet they never reached the archive tier, so the timing of the condition is not the cause.

Which change should the team make to the policy?

options.text: Add all of the listed path prefixes and blob index tag conditions to the existing rule, so the service evaluates every filter together each time the policy runs.
Split the intended matches across multiple rules, keeping each rule within the number of path prefixes and blob index tag conditions that one rule supports.
Replace the path prefixes with a single prefix that matches the container root, and rely on the blob index tag conditions to select the artifacts.
Add the values through the portal's Add a rule form instead of Code View, so the portal distributes the path prefixes and blob index tag conditions among the saved rules.

explanation:
A single lifecycle rule can carry at most 10 case-sensitive path prefixes and at most 10 blob index tag conditions. The planned configuration needs 14 path prefixes and 12 tag conditions, so one rule cannot hold it and the service will reject the policy with those filters. Because the team must govern every listed artifact set while leaving other blobs in the account untouched, the intended values have to be distributed across several rules, each staying within the per-rule filter limits.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add all of the listed path prefixes and blob index tag conditions to the existing rule, so the service evaluates every filter together each time the policy runs: Adding all 14 path prefixes and all 12 blob index tag conditions to the existing rule exceeds the per-rule maximums of 10 path prefixes and 10 blob index tag conditions, so the policy cannot be saved in that form.
- Replace the path prefixes with a single prefix that matches the container root, and rely on the blob index tag conditions to select the artifacts: Widening the prefix to the container root would make the rule apply to blobs the team did not list, and the 12 tag conditions still exceed the per-rule maximum of 10 tag conditions.
- Add the values through the portal's Add a rule form instead of Code View, so the portal distributes the path prefixes and blob index tag conditions among the saved rules: The portal's Add a rule form creates one rule at a time and does not redistribute filters across rules; the same per-rule limits on path prefixes and blob index tag conditions apply to every rule it creates.

prompt:
You have three storage accounts that hold data for the same platform team, and each account carries its own lifecycle policy with a single rule that moves blobs to the cool tier 30 days after their last modification.

The three policies keep drifting apart, because every time someone adjusts the aging rules, three separate policies have to be edited. The team needs one scheduled mechanism that applies the same tiering operation to blobs in all three accounts, so that the operation can be maintained and audited in a single place. The blobs must stay in the accounts where they are today: data residency rules and the sheer volume rule out copying or relocating them.

Which approach should the team take?

options.text: Add path prefix filters for the containers in the other two Azure Storage accounts to the rule in contosotelemetry, so that the tier operation runs across the other accounts.
Use the whole account rule scope in the policy on contosomedia, so that the tier operation runs across the other accounts.
Use Azure Storage Actions so that the tier operation runs across the three accounts.
Enable access time tracking on each of the three accounts and add a last accessed condition to every rule, so that the tier operation runs across the three accounts based on read activity.

explanation:
A lifecycle policy always belongs to the storage account in which it is defined: its rule scope can be the whole account, selected containers, or a subset of that account's blobs picked out by name prefix or blob index tag, and prefix and tag filters only narrow the blobs inside that same account. No scope or filter choice therefore reaches objects that live in another account. Azure Storage Actions is the supported way to carry out the same data operation on objects across multiple storage accounts at once, and it works on the data where it already sits, which fits the residency and volume constraints in this scenario.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Add path prefix filters for the containers in the other two Azure Storage accounts to the rule in contosotelemetry, so that the tier operation runs across the other accounts: Path prefix filters match blob names inside the account where the policy is saved, so prefixes naming containers in the other two accounts never select their blobs; the rule in contosotelemetry still operates only on that one account.
- Use the whole account rule scope in the policy on contosomedia, so that the tier operation runs across the other accounts: The rule scope choices are the whole account, selected containers, or a subset of the account's blobs selected by prefix or blob index tag, so a whole-account scope in contosomedia covers only contosomedia and nothing in the other two accounts.
- Enable access time tracking on each of the three accounts and add a last accessed condition to every rule, so that the tier operation runs across the three accounts based on read activity: Access time tracking is switched on per account and only makes a last accessed condition available to a rule; it changes which condition is tested, not which accounts a policy can act on, and the team would still have to edit a separate rule in each of the three accounts.

context:
You have a general-purpose v2 storage account named contosofiles that stores quarterly financial workbooks. The account already runs a lifecycle policy with two enabled rules, and you need to add a third rule that moves workbook blobs to the cool tier based on the time since their last modification.

A colleague opens the storage account in the portal, goes to Lifecycle management under Data management, switches to Code View, and pastes a JSON fragment that holds just the new rule. The portal rejects the save, and the colleague expects the new rule to start moving blobs right after the policy is accepted.

Which approach should the colleague take?

`Storage account type: General-purpose v2
Rules already saved on the account: CoolStaleWorkbooks (enabled), ExpireClosedPeriods (enabled)
Rule to add: TierCurrentWorkbooks - moves block blobs to the cool tier based on the time since their last modification
Pasted into Code View: a JSON fragment containing only TierCurrentWorkbooks
Save outcome: the portal reported that the request was rejected`
prompt: The colleague should _____, and should expect the new rule to [...].

options.text: submit the whole policy document with every rule, including the new one
submit only the new rule and let the service keep the policy it already has
submit the new rule in one document and the remaining rules in a second document
submit the new rule with the remaining rules turned off so that only the new rule runs

explanation:
A lifecycle policy is read and written as one complete document, and the service rejects partial submissions. That is why the fragment holding only TierCurrentWorkbooks was refused: the colleague has to resubmit the whole policy document with every rule, including the new one, so the rules already saved on the account travel in that same document. Even after the save succeeds, a rule change is not applied instantly - the service runs an active policy once per day, and a newly added or edited rule can take up to 24 hours to take effect and for the first execution to start. So the colleague should expect the new rule to start moving workbooks later, not right after the save.

Why the other options are wrong:
- submit only the new rule and let the service keep the policy it already has: Submitting only the new rule is exactly the partial update the service refuses; the account's policy must be resubmitted with all of its rules present in the same document.
- submit the new rule in one document and the remaining rules in a second document: A storage account carries a single policy, so there is no second document to submit; every rule has to travel in the one document that replaces the saved policy.
- submit the new rule with the remaining rules turned off so that only the new rule runs: Turning the existing rules off does not make the submission complete - the document still has to carry every rule - and switching all rules off also leaves the policy inactive.

It stores partner exports spread across 14 containers, and it also stores unrelated application blobs that the platform team must leave untouched. The team needs the account's lifecycle policy to move every partner export to the cool tier 30 days after its last modification, and it wants the policy to select some exports by blob index tag as well. A colleague drafted a single rule that lists one path prefix for each container plus one tag condition for each export family. Which change should the team make?

`Storage account type: General-purpose v2
Containers holding partner exports: 14
Unrelated application blobs in the same account: Yes
Path prefixes in the drafted rule: 14
Blob index tag conditions in the drafted rule: 12`
prompt: The team should _____, with each rule listing at most [...] path prefixes and at most [...] blob index tag conditions.

options.text: divide the drafted rule into several rules
keep the drafted rule and express the extra prefixes as tag filters
keep the drafted rule and widen its scope to the whole storage account
keep the drafted rule and leave the remaining containers unmanaged

explanation:
A single rule in a lifecycle policy can hold at most 10 case-sensitive path prefixes and at most 10 blob index tag conditions. The colleague's one rule carries 14 path prefixes and 12 tag conditions, so it cannot express what the team needs, and the team must divide that drafted rule into several rules, each staying within the 10-prefix and 10-tag-condition limits. Dividing is also the only way to keep the unrelated application blobs out of scope, because filters inside one rule are combined with a logical AND and a whole-account scope would age out those blobs too. The extra rules are added to the same policy document, which the service runs once per day.

Why the other options are wrong:
- keep the drafted rule and express the extra prefixes as tag filters: A path prefix cannot be turned into a blob index tag condition: tag conditions match on blob index tags, so the 10-prefix limit for one rule would still be exceeded and every blob would first have to be tagged.
- keep the drafted rule and widen its scope to the whole storage account: A whole-account scope would also move the unrelated application blobs to the cool tier, which the team must leave untouched, and the 12 tag conditions would still exceed the 10-condition limit for one rule.
- keep the drafted rule and leave the remaining containers unmanaged: Leaving the remaining containers out of the policy means those partner exports never move to the cool tier, so the team's requirement is not met.

One enabled rule in the account's lifecycle policy moves block blobs to the cool tier 30 days after their last modification. The first policy execution took more than twenty hours and moved only part of the account, and later executions take the longest on working days when the application's traffic is heaviest. The platform team wants every eligible object to reach the cool tier eventually without holding back the application's own activity.

Which statement best explains what the team is seeing?

`Account type:            General-purpose v2
Objects held:            About 75 million, spread across 210 containers
Workload on the account: Line-of-business application issuing a steady stream of read and write requests
Lifecycle policy:        One enabled rule: move block blobs to the cool tier 30 days after last modification
Observed:                First execution took 22 hours and moved only part of the account; later executions take longest on the busiest working days`
prompt: The behaviour the platform team is seeing is best explained by the fact that _____.

options.text: The execution shares the account's request-rate limit with the application's traffic, and application requests are prioritised, so the execution slows when the account approaches that limit and the total duration grows with the number of objects evaluated.
Each execution can act on only a fixed number of objects, and the objects it does not reach are never managed when the application's requests keep the account busy.
The duration of an execution depends on the volume of data the policy copies between tiers, and the application's requests are served with that work in progress.
Every execution must wait through the 24-hour delay that follows a policy change before it can start, so the account stays a day behind the application's traffic.

explanation:
Policy processing and the workload draw on the same per-second request budget of the account, and workload requests are prioritised over policy requests. As the account approaches its request-rate limit, policy evaluation slows down, and the length of an execution also grows with the number of blobs that are evaluated. With roughly 75 million objects and heavy application traffic, the first execution therefore ran for many hours and progressed only part way through the account, and later executions behave the same way, taking longest on the busiest working days.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Each execution can act on only a fixed number of objects, and the objects it does not reach are never managed when the application's requests keep the account busy: There is no fixed per-execution cap on the number of blobs a run evaluates. Run duration scales with the number of blobs evaluated, so every eligible blob is eventually processed, just more slowly on a busy account.
- The duration of an execution depends on the volume of data the policy copies between tiers, and the application's requests are served with that work in progress: The length of a run is not set by the volume of data moved between tiers. A tier change is a Set Blob Tier operation on each blob, and the factor that changes with the account's traffic is the shared per-second request limit.
- Every execution must wait through the 24-hour delay that follows a policy change before it can start, so the account stays a day behind the application's traffic: The up-to-24-hour delay applies after a policy is added or edited, so the change can take effect and the first execution can start. It is not a wait that precedes every execution, and it does not vary with how busy the workload is.

no charge for the policy itself, a charge for deletions, a charge for each Set Blob Tier operation, and a charge for each last access time update as an other transaction billed at most once every 24 hours per object

explanation:
A lifecycle policy document itself is not billed, and the delete action it performs is free of charge. The billable work is the operation charge for the Set Blob Tier calls a policy run makes, plus each last access time update, which counts as an 'other transaction' billed at most once every 24 hours per object and separately from read transactions (which is why access time tracking is enabled on this account). On top of that, add-on services such as Microsoft Defender for Storage can charge for the operations a lifecycle policy performs, so the forecast must allow for charges from that service as well.

Why the other options are wrong:
- no charge for the policy itself, no charge for deletions, a charge for each Set Blob Tier operation, and no charge for last access time updates: Last access time updates are not free. With access time tracking enabled, every update counts as an 'other transaction' billed at most once every 24 hours per object, separately from read transactions.
- a charge for the policy itself, no charge for deletions, a charge for each Set Blob Tier operation, and a charge for each last access time update as an other transaction billed at most once every 24 hours per object: The policy document itself generates no charge; only the work it performs (Set Blob Tier calls and last access time updates) is billed.
- no charge for the policy itself, a charge for deletions, a charge for each Set Blob Tier operation, and a charge for each last access time update as an other transaction billed at most once every 24 hours per object: Deletions are free of charge, so the delete action in the rule does not add a charge to the bill.

prompt: The team should update the saved policy by _____, and the expected billing effect of the revised policy is [...].

options.text: replacing the tierToCool action with a delete action on the existing age threshold
replacing the tierToCool action with a tierToArchive action on the existing age threshold
replacing the tierToCool action with a tierToHot action on the existing age threshold
replacing the tierToCool action with a delete action on a last-accessed threshold

explanation:
For a general-purpose v2 account, tiering actions such as tierToCool and tierToArchive apply only to block blobs; tiering is not supported for append blobs or page blobs. Because every opsfeed blob is an append blob, the saved tierToCool action never moves anything, so the rule completes without effect and the feed blobs keep their hot-tier charges. The retained copies are past their usefulness once the 45-day window passes, so the policy should end their lifecycle rather than change their tier: replace the tierToCool action with a delete action that uses the rule's existing age threshold. Delete operations are free of charge and the policy itself is free, so the revised policy adds no charge of its own to the account bill, and with access time tracking turned off there are no last access time update charges either.

Why the other options are wrong:
- replacing the tierToCool action with a tierToArchive action on the existing age threshold: Archiving is also a tiering action, and tiering is allowed only on block blobs, so this replacement would leave the rule just as ineffective for the append blobs in opsfeed.
- replacing the tierToCool action with a tierToHot action on the existing age threshold: A lifecycle management policy cannot rehydrate a blob to an online tier, although a policy can move a blob from cool back to hot when it is accessed, and tiering does not apply to append blobs in the first place.
- replacing the tierToCool action with a delete action on a last-accessed threshold: A last-accessed condition requires access time tracking to be enabled and is offered only when the blob type is Block blobs; this account has access time tracking turned off and the feed blobs are append blobs.

Following the policy through its own event, metrics, and logs answers both of the team's requirements at a scale of 400,000 objects, which an item-by-item inspection cannot reach.

Why the other options are wrong:
- list every blob in the account each day and compare the tier it reports with the tier recorded the day before: Walking every blob each day and comparing the tier it reports with the previous day's value is the manual approach the team already ruled out, and a tier difference only shows that a file was left behind; it never explains why the policy skipped it.
- enable Microsoft Defender for Storage and work from the alerts it raises about blobs that were not moved: Microsoft Defender for Storage raises alerts about risky or suspicious activity on the account, not about the objects a lifecycle policy acted on, and it can even add charges for operations carried out through a lifecycle policy. It gives the team no visibility into what an execution did or why it failed.
- check the Activity log for the policy definition and confirm that the rule is saved and enabled: The Activity log records control-plane operations such as saving or enabling the policy definition. prompt: Your team must replicate 24 container pairs of block blobs from contosoordersprod in East US to contosoreplicas in West Europe. Both accounts are general-purpose v2 in the same Microsoft Entra tenant, were created in the past week (so AllowCrossTenantReplication is false on them), and already have blob versioning plus the change feed switched on. Because of the number of container pairs involved, you build the policy on the destination account from a JSON definition file and then apply it to the source account. Your draft file is shown below. Which change must you make before any blob is copied?

options.text: Replace each account value with the full Azure Resource Manager resource ID of that account.
Keep both account values but set policyId to an empty string and assign your own unique ruleId to every rule.
Keep both account values but add a "prefix" of "*" to every rule so each source account container matches all of its blobs.
Keep both account values but set minCreationTime to 1601-01-01T00:00:00Z on every rule so blobs already in each account are included.

explanation:
The two account properties in a replication policy must carry the full Azure Resource Manager resource ID of each account (for example /subscriptions/<subscriptionId>/resourceGroups/<resource-group>/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/<name>). Azure Storage needs the complete ID to resolve the account, and it reads those IDs to confirm both accounts belong to the same Microsoft Entra tenant — which is exactly why a bare account name is not enough when AllowCrossTenantReplication is false, as it is by default on accounts created from December 15, 2023 onward. Supplying the full ID is recommended practice even when cross-tenant replication is permitted.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Keep both account values but set policyId to an empty string and assign your own unique ruleId to every rule: In a hand-written policy file you leave policyId set to "default" and leave every ruleId as an empty string, so the service generates the policy and rule identifiers itself. Choosing your own values is not what the service expects, and this change does nothing about how the two accounts are referenced.
- Keep both account values but add a "prefix" of "*" to every rule so each source account container matches all of its blobs: A rule prefix can name a container and a virtual directory, but it never supports wildcard characters, so "*" is invalid. Besides that, a prefix does not influence how the source and destination accounts are resolved.
- Keep both account values but set minCreationTime to 1601-01-01T00:00:00Z on every rule so blobs already in each account are included: Setting minCreationTime to 1601-01-01T00:00:00Z is how you ask for every existing blob to be backfilled, so it changes the copy scope rather than fixing anything required here. Leaving the accounts as bare names still prevents the service from resolving them in this configuration.

options.text: Turn on the change feed for contosomediaprod and turn on versioning for contosomediadr.
Turn on the change feed for contosomediadr and turn on versioning for contosomediadr.
Turn on the change feed for contosomediaprod and turn on versioning for contosomediaprod.

explanation:
Object replication needs two features switched on: the change feed on the source account, because Azure Storage reads the source account's change feed to discover writes to copy, and blob versioning on both accounts, because the service copies the blob plus its current and previous versions. In the exhibit the source already has versioning but its change feed is off, while the destination has the change feed but no versioning, so you must turn the change feed on for contosomediaprod and versioning on for contosomediadr.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Turn on the change feed for contosomediadr and turn on versioning for contosomediadr: Turning the change feed on for contosomediadr accomplishes nothing for replication: the destination account is never the account whose change feed the service polls, so the writes in contosomediaprod remain invisible to it. The versioning part of this option is right, but the change feed must be switched on at the source end.
- Turn on the change feed for contosomediaprod and turn on versioning for contosomediaprod: This fixes the change feed but leaves the destination without versioning. Versioning has to be enabled on both accounts because the service replicates the blob's versions to the destination, and with versioning off there contosomediadr still can't receive the copies.
- Turn on the change feed for contosomediadr and turn on versioning for contosomediaprod: Both changes land on the wrong accounts: versioning is already enabled on contosomediaprod, and the change feed belongs on the source rather than on the destination, so with this combination replication still has nothing to poll and the destination still cannot accept versions.

prompt:
You have an object replication policy that copies block blobs from contosobacksrc (West Europe) into contosobackdr (West US 2). A retention script in the source account moves blobs older than 90 days to the Archive tier to cut cost. After its first run, three of the 2024 blobs report a replication failure and nothing reached the destination container, while blobs that are still in Hot keep replicating normally. Your runbook has already rehydrated two of those three back to the Hot tier, yet a day later the destination container still holds neither of them. The current state of sample blobs is below.

Which change should you make so the two rehydrated blobs reach contosobackdr?

options.text: Wait it out: once a rehydrated blob is back in the Hot tier, the policy copies it automatically without any further change.
Delete the replication policy on both accounts, create it again with the same container pairs, and rehydrate the blobs once more.
Call Set Blob Tier on the blob in the destination container so the replica matches the source tier, which triggers the transfer.
Overwrite each rehydrated blob on the source once rehydration has finished, so a new version is created and the policy copies it to the destination.

explanation:
Archiving a blob on either side of a replication policy stops replication for that blob, and moving it back out of the Archive tier on its own does not restart it: the blob data has to be written again before the policy picks it up. That is why audit-2024-06.log and audit-2024-07.log are back in Hot but still show Failed with nothing in the destination, while the untouched Hot blob audit-2024-11.log replicated normally. Overwriting the two rehydrated blobs on the source produces a new version that the policy then copies to contosobackdr, which is the only way to get them replicated again.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Wait it out: once a rehydrated blob is back in the Hot tier, the policy copies it automatically without any further change: Simply waiting is not enough. The replication policy ignores a blob that was archived until the blob data on the source is written again, so the two rehydrated blobs stay uncopied indefinitely no matter how long you wait.
- Delete the replication policy on both accounts, create it again with the same container pairs, and rehydrate the blobs once more: Deleting and re-creating the policy does not restart replication for these blobs. The new policy gets a brand-new policy ID and cancels outstanding replication tasks, and existing blobs only re-replicate when the destination still holds a previous version for them, which is not the case here.
- Call Set Blob Tier on the blob in the destination container so the replica matches the source tier, which triggers the transfer: Access tier changes on a source blob are never carried across to the replica, so changing the tier of a blob in the destination container has no effect on whether the source blob is replicated. To archive a replica you call Set Blob Tier on the destination blob yourself, and that still does not copy the missing source blobs.

Your operations lead now wants a single view of how much replication work is still outstanding, because the replication state of a source blob only fills in once the copy finishes and never shows progress while the copy is in flight. You need to set up ongoing monitoring of the backlog. Which action should you take?

options.text: Turn on the Operations pending for replication and the Bytes pending for replication metrics for the replication policy logship.
Turn on only the Operations pending for replication metric for the policy logship, and infer the outstanding data volume from the Blob operations metric of the destination account.
Turn on the Bytes pending for replication metric at the contosologsprod account level instead of on the policy, and use the change feed metrics on the source container to see what is still queued.

explanation:
Object replication ships two per-policy metrics — Operations pending for replication and Bytes pending for replication — and each of them is emitted as a series of buckets by age (0-5, 5-10, 10-15, 15-30 minutes, 30 minutes-2 hours, 2-8 hours, 8-24 hours and more than 24 hours). Enabling both on policy logship is exactly how you see how much work is still outstanding, and it is the right answer because neither metric is on by default (the policy currently shows 'None').

Why the other options are wrong:
- Turn on only the Operations pending for replication metric for the policy logship, and infer the outstanding data volume from the Blob operations metric of the destination account: Enabling only the operations count leaves the byte backlog invisible, and the destination account's Blob operations metric counts all destination requests, not the objects and bytes still queued for replication, so it cannot stand in for the per-policy breakdown.
- Turn on the Bytes pending for replication metric at the contosologsprod account level instead of on the policy, and use the change feed metrics on the source container to see what is still queued: The two backlog metrics are configured on the replication policy, not as account-level settings, so switching them on at the contosologsprod account level does nothing for this policy. Change feed metrics report change feed records and reads, not objects queued for replication, so they do not answer the backlog question either.
- Leave monitoring at the individual blob level: poll the replication state property on each source blob until it reports Complete or Failed, and count the failures: A source blob's replication state is only populated once replication finishes, showing Complete or Failed together with the policy ID and rule ID, and it offers no percentage while the copy is in flight. Polling it therefore reports nothing while the backlog actually exists, which is precisely why the policy-level metrics are the monitoring mechanism to use.

prompt: You have an object replication policy that copies block blobs from contosoappsrc into contosoappdr so a partner application running near its users can read the data locally. A new partner agreement commits your organization to making newly written blobs readable on the replica within 15 minutes of the write, yet the observed lag is far beyond that and nothing in the current setup commits you to any delivery window at all. You need to close the gap. Which action should you take?

options.text: Turn on blob index tags replication for each rule so tags arrive with the replicas
Set minCreationTime to 1601-01-01T00:00:00Z so blobs already in the container also flow through replication
Enable priority replication on the replication policy
Add rules until the policy holds the maximum 1,000, so more containers benefit from replication

explanation:
Priority replication is the opt-in performance mode of object replication. When it is turned on and the source and destination accounts sit in the same continent, Azure commits under an SLA to replicating 99.0% of objects within 15 minutes. Sweden Central and Norway East are both in Europe, so these two accounts satisfy that geographic condition and the mode can be enabled on the policy. All other prerequisites are already met: both accounts are general-purpose v2, both have blob versioning enabled, and the source account has the change feed turned on.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Turn on blob index tags replication for each rule so tags arrive with the replicas: Blob index tags replication is a preview capability that copies blob index tags to the replicas, and it requires the EnableObjectReplicationTags preview feature to be registered on the source account. It changes what metadata travels with a blob, not how quickly the blob arrives, so it delivers no delivery-window commitment.
- Set minCreationTime to 1601-01-01T00:00:00Z so blobs already in the container also flow through replication: minCreationTime controls which blobs fall within the copy scope. Setting it to 1601-01-01T00:00:00Z backfills every blob that already exists in the source container, but it does not speed up new writes and would add cost by copying data that already exists.
- Add rules until the policy holds the maximum 1,000, so more containers benefit from replication: A policy can hold up to 1,000 rules, but that ceiling is about how many source containers can each be mapped to one destination container. This policy already maps its single container pair correctly, so adding rules neither changes how quickly blobs are copied nor adds any commitment on delivery timing.

options.text: Remove the retention policy and the legal hold from the destination container.
Reduce the retention period configured by the destination container's policy from 30 days to 1 day.

explanation:
Immutability set on the destination — a container- or version-level retention policy or legal hold — does not stop source writes from replicating, but it does block the matching updates and erasures from being applied on the replica. That matches the evidence: all 412 writes arrived, while all 37 erasures stayed visible in contosoarchived. Because the destination container holds a 30-day retention policy (unlocked) plus an active legal hold, the fix is to take both off the destination container so erasure events can be replicated.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Reduce the retention period configured by the destination container's policy from 30 days to 1 day: Shortening the window does not lift the protection: while the retention period applies, the protected versions still refuse the erasure, so the replica keeps the data. The setting has to be removed from the destination container, not merely made shorter.
- Add a legal hold at the blob version level on the destination container: A version-level legal hold is another form of the same protection. Adding it would leave the destination container blocking the erasures, exactly as it does today, and it is harder to clear than a retention period.
- Disable blob versioning on the destination account and remove the replication policy from both accounts: Blob versioning is required by object replication, and it cannot be switched off while a replication policy exists on the account, so the disable operation would be refused. Deleting the policy also ends replication entirely, which is the opposite of what the records team needs.

You have a new object replication design for the block blobs your media team writes to contosomedia (general-purpose v2, East US 2), and several teams want copies of that data read from other locations while one far account is meant to serve several teams at once. Nothing is configured on any account yet. You need to know how far the service actually stretches before the build starts, because some of the requested volumes exceed what is accepted. Match each request below to the limit that applies to it.

- Request: Regional read capacity; What the plan needs: The block blobs in contosomedia copied out to three separate locations
- Request: Shared replica; What the plan needs: One far account receiving copies from three teams, each with its own copy definition
- Request: Portal onboarding; What the plan needs: A definition covering 24 mapped folders, added one at a time through the portal
- Request: Full mirror; What the plan needs: A single definition covering 900 mapped folders, each mapped separately
prompt: The most far accounts that can hold copies of one account's blobs

options.text: Two destination accounts per source account
Two policies into one destination account
Ten container pairs per policy
One thousand rules per policy

explanation: The two request types about far accounts are both capped at two, but on opposite sides of the relationship: a single source account can feed at most two destination accounts (one policy each), and a single destination account can accept policies from at most two sources. That is why the regional read request (three locations fed from contosomedia) is bound by the source-side limit and the shared replica request (three teams pointing definitions at one far account) by the destination-side limit. The two mapping requests are governed by different ceilings: configuring container pairs one at a time through the portal stops after 10 pairs, so the 24-pair onboarding cannot be done that way, while a policy authored as a JSON definition file can carry up to 1,000 rules, each rule mapping exactly one container pair, which is enough for the 900-folder full mirror.
