context:
Block blobs that your team writes to the 'ledger' container in contosofinprod (general-purpose v2, East US) are mirrored asynchronously into the same container of a second general-purpose v2 account in West Europe, and the arrangement has been running for months. Finance now wants contosofinprod to stop keeping older blob versions so that storage charges fall, so an administrator submits the request shown below and the service turns it down. Which change should you make so that finance's request can be carried out?

- Setting or object: Source account; Current value: contosofinprod (general-purpose v2, East US)
- Setting or object: Container being mirrored; Current value: ledger (block blobs only)
- Setting or object: Receiving container; Current value: ledger, in a general-purpose v2 account in West Europe
- Setting or object: Blob versioning on contosofinprod; Current value: Enabled
- Setting or object: Change feed on contosofinprod; Current value: Enabled
- Setting or object: Request submitted by the administrator; Current value: Turn off blob versioning on contosofinprod
- Setting or object: Outcome; Current value: Turned down by the service; older versions keep accumulating
prompt: To make the request succeed, you _____ and only afterwards submit the change for contosofinprod.

options.text: Delete the object replication policies from the storage accounts taking part in the copy
Delete the 'ledger' container in the storage account that sends the copies
Archive the older blob versions in the storage account that sends the copies
Limit the copy scope of the object replication rules to new blobs only

explanation:
Blob versioning is a required building block of object replication, and the service refuses to switch versioning off on an account that still carries a replication policy; those policies have to be deleted first. Once the policies are removed from the accounts involved in the copy, the version-removal request can be submitted and blob versioning can be disabled on contosofinprod.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Delete the 'ledger' container in the storage account that sends the copies: Removing a container does not remove the object replication policy itself, so a policy is still attached to the account and the service keeps refusing the change.
- Archive the older blob versions in the storage account that sends the copies: Archiving versions changes only where the blob data is held, and archived blobs stop being replicated, so this neither clears the block on the account setting nor keeps copies flowing.
- Limit the copy scope of the object replication rules to new blobs only: Narrowing the copy scope only changes which blobs later runs pick up; the policy stays on the account, so blob versioning remains locked.

context:
Your analytics platform writes block blobs into the 'reports' container of contosoreports (general-purpose v2, East US), and an object replication policy is meant to copy them into the same container of contosoreportsdr (general-purpose v2, West Europe). Blob versioning is enabled on both accounts, the change feed is enabled on the source, and the policy is attached on both sides, yet the destination container is still empty. The blobs sit in folders named after the reporting year, and only the blobs in those folders should be copied; anything else in the container has to stay at the source. Which change should you make to the rule, and how many prefix matches can a single rule hold when you configure it in the portal?

- Item: Source account; Value: contosoreports (general-purpose v2, East US)
- Item: Destination account; Value: contosoreportsdr (general-purpose v2, West Europe)
- Item: Source container; Value: reports
- Item: Destination container; Value: reports (already created, holds no blobs)
- Item: Policy created through; Value: Azure portal, on the source account
- Item: Rules in the policy; Value: 1 (reports to reports)
- Item: Prefix filter on that rule; Value: 202* (the asterisk is meant to stand for any reporting year)
- Item: Blob versioning; Value: Enabled on source and destination
- Item: Change feed; Value: Enabled on source
- Item: Content of the source container; Value: reports/2024/..., reports/2025/..., reports/2026/..., plus files sitting directly in the container root
prompt: The team should _____ in the replication rule, and a single rule can hold [...] prefix matches when the policy is configured in the portal.

options.text: replace the wildcard with literal prefixes, one for each year folder
keep the wildcard prefix and add one more rule for each year folder
replace the wildcard with one literal prefix that names the container
drop the prefix filter so that one copy of every blob in the container is made

explanation:
A rule's prefix value may include a virtual directory but must not contain wildcard characters, so the current '202*' value can never match the year folders. The prefix has to spell out the real folder names, so the rule should carry one literal prefix per year folder (for example 2024/, 2025/, 2026/). A rule configured in the portal accepts up to five prefix matches, and three year folders fit easily inside that allowance, so no extra rules are needed. Keeping the wildcard, using a single prefix that names the container, or removing the filter altogether would respectively fail to match, miss the other year folders, or also move the files that must remain at the source.

Why the other options are wrong:
- keep the wildcard prefix and add one more rule for each year folder: Wildcard characters are never accepted in a rule's prefix string, so splitting the pattern across several rules leaves every rule equally invalid and nothing gets copied.
- replace the wildcard with one literal prefix that names the container: A single prefix that names the container does not line up with the blob names inside it, so the year folders would not be picked up; the prefix has to name the actual folder path.
- drop the prefix filter so that one copy of every blob in the container is made: Without a prefix filter every blob in the source container is replicated, including the files at the container root that the business wants kept at the source.

context:
You copy the 'casefiles' block blobs from contosocases (East US) into the 'casefiles' container of contosocasesdr (West Europe) with object replication, and files created after the policy went live arrive in the far account within minutes. A records officer now corrects a typo inside an existing file: contosocases accepts the change and shows the corrected text, while the copy in contosocasesdr still serves the original text. Erasing a file at the source behaves the same way — it is gone from contosocases but is still returned by contosocasesdr. Because the far copy is what the regulators and the archive team read, every correction and every erasure made at the source has to appear there as well. The current state of both accounts and of the copied container is listed below.

Which change should you make?

- Item: Account type; contosocases (source): General-purpose v2; contosocasesdr (destination): General-purpose v2
- Item: Blob versioning; contosocases (source): Enabled; contosocasesdr (destination): Enabled
- Item: Change feed; contosocases (source): Enabled; contosocasesdr (destination): Not applicable
- Item: Replication policy attached; contosocases (source): rp-case-001; contosocasesdr (destination): rp-case-001
- Item: Immutability policy on the 'casefiles' container; contosocases (source): None; contosocasesdr (destination): Active (container scope, time-based)
- Item: New file created at the source; contosocases (source): Present; contosocasesdr (destination): Present
- Item: Existing file corrected at the source; contosocases (source): Corrected content; contosocasesdr (destination): Original content
- Item: Existing file erased at the source; contosocases (source): Removed; contosocasesdr (destination): Still present
prompt: To make corrections and erasures made at the source show up in the far account, you need to _____.

options.text: remove the immutability policy from the destination container
remove the immutability policy from the source container
extend the immutability policy on the destination container to a longer period
add a legal hold to the destination container's blob versions

explanation:
The far account keeps serving stale content because the destination container is protected by a container-level immutability policy. When such a policy is in effect on the destination container, updates and deletes performed on the source container still succeed, but those changes fail to replicate to the destination container because of the immutability restriction. Object replication therefore requires that the destination container or blob not be protected by an immutability policy, so the protection has to be lifted on the destination container for corrections and erasures to be carried across.

Why the other options are wrong:
- remove the immutability policy from the source container: The source container is exactly where the writes already succeed — the corrected and erased blobs are accepted there — so nothing at the source is blocking the copy. The change fails when it is applied in contosocasesdr, so altering (or adding) protection on the source cannot make corrections and erasures reach the replica.
- extend the immutability policy on the destination container to a longer period: Lengthening the protection window on the destination container keeps the destination blobs protected for even longer, so updates and deletes continue to fail to replicate. This makes the stale-replica symptom worse rather than fixing it.
- add a legal hold to the destination container's blob versions: A legal hold on the destination blob versions adds a further restriction at the destination. An active version-level immutability policy also makes replication of the matching update or delete fail, so it does not restore the missing changes.

context:
Your media team uploads finished clips as block blobs to the 'clips' container in contosomediain (East US), and an object replication policy copies that container into the 'clips' container of contosomediaout (West Europe). Clips uploaded earlier this month reached the replica within minutes, but every clip uploaded since the pipeline was upgraded is missing from contosomediaout, and the replication status of those source blobs shows Failed. The business needs each newly uploaded clip to reach the replica. The current configuration is shown below.

Which change should you make?

- Item: Source account; Value: contosomediain — general-purpose v2, East US
- Item: Destination account; Value: contosomediaout — general-purpose v2, West Europe
- Item: Blob versioning; Value: Enabled on both accounts
- Item: Change feed; Value: Enabled on contosomediain
- Item: Replication policy; Value: rp-media-001 attached to both accounts; one rule maps container 'clips' to container 'clips'
- Item: Key supplied on each write request since the pipeline upgrade; Value: Customer-provided key
- Item: Clips uploaded before the pipeline upgrade; Value: Present in contosomediaout
- Item: Clips uploaded after the pipeline upgrade; Value: Absent from contosomediaout; replication status on the source shows Failed
prompt: The change that lets every newly uploaded clip reach the replica is _____.

options.text: Stop passing the customer-provided key on the write requests.
Keep passing the customer-provided key on the write requests and enable the change feed on the destination account.
Keep passing the customer-provided key on the write requests and rotate the key in Azure Key Vault.
Keep passing the customer-provided key on the write requests and add a second destination account to the policy.

explanation:
Object replication doesn't copy blobs that are encrypted with a customer-provided key, which is exactly the symptom here: the clips written after the upgrade carry a customer-provided key, they never reach contosomediaout, and their source-side replication status shows Failed. Object replication works with accounts and blobs protected by Microsoft-managed keys or customer-managed keys, so removing the customer-provided key from the write requests makes each upload fall back to the account's own supported encryption key, and the new clips are then replicated.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Keep passing the customer-provided key on the write requests and enable the change feed on the destination account: The change feed is required on the source account, where it is already enabled, and turning it on for the destination account has no effect here. Blobs encrypted with a customer-provided key are never replicated, so the new clips would still be missing from contosomediaout.
- Keep passing the customer-provided key on the write requests and rotate the key in Azure Key Vault: Rotating the key in Azure Key Vault only produces a new version of the key; the uploads still supply a customer-provided key, and object replication doesn't support blobs encrypted that way. The way the blobs are encrypted on write has to change, not just the key version.
- Keep passing the customer-provided key on the write requests and add a second destination account to the policy: Adding a second destination account doesn't change how the source blobs are encrypted. Blobs encrypted with a customer-provided key fail to replicate to any destination, so the new clips still wouldn't arrive anywhere.

context:
You have an object replication setup that is meant to copy the block blobs your media team writes to the 'clips' container of contosomediain (East US 2) into the 'clips' container of contosomediaout (West Europe), so that a partner in Europe can serve the clips locally. Blob versioning is enabled on both accounts, the change feed is enabled on contosomediain, and the same replication policy ID is configured on both accounts, yet no clip ever reaches contosomediaout and every new source blob reports a replication status of Failed. The current configuration of the two accounts is listed below.

You need the clips to reach contosomediaout while both accounts stay encrypted with a customer-managed key. Which change should you make?

`Property                 | contosomediain (source) | contosomediaout (destination)
Account type             | General-purpose v2       | General-purpose v2
Encryption at rest       | Customer-managed key    | Customer-managed key
Account failover         | Customer-managed failover | Not configured
Blob versioning          | Enabled                 | Enabled
Change feed              | Enabled                 | Disabled
Replication policy ID    | med-clips-001           | med-clips-001`
prompt: To make the new clips reach contosomediaout, you should _____.

options.text: remove the customer-managed failover configuration on contosomediain so the replication policy can copy the blobs
enable customer-managed failover on contosomediain and contosomediaout so both replication policies can copy the blobs
replace the customer-managed key of contosomediain with a customer-provided key so the replication policy can copy the blobs
disable blob versioning on contosomediain so the customer-managed failover configuration can be changed

explanation:
Object replication supports accounts encrypted with Microsoft-managed keys or customer-managed keys, but customer-managed failover isn't supported for either the source or the destination account in an object replication policy. contosomediain currently has customer-managed failover configured, so it can't take part in a replication policy that is supposed to copy the 'clips' container, which is why nothing arrives in contosomediaout and the source blobs report a replication status of Failed. Taking away the customer-managed failover configuration on contosomediain clears the blocking setting while both accounts keep their customer-managed key encryption, and the policy can then copy the block blobs to the destination container.

Why the other options are wrong:
- enable customer-managed failover on contosomediain and contosomediaout so both replication policies can copy the blobs: Enabling customer-managed failover on both accounts makes the deployment unusable: the feature isn't supported for either the source or the destination account in an object replication policy, so turning it on in contosomediaout would disqualify the destination account as well.
- replace the customer-managed key of contosomediain with a customer-provided key so the replication policy can copy the blobs: Replacing the customer-managed key with a customer-provided key doesn't address the account configuration, and it also breaks replication the other way: blobs encrypted with a customer-provided key fail to replicate, while customer-managed key encryption is supported. The requirement is to keep the customer-managed key, so this change is wrong on both counts.
- disable blob versioning on contosomediain so the customer-managed failover configuration can be changed: Blob versioning is a prerequisite for object replication and must be enabled on both the source and destination accounts; it also can't be disabled while any replication policy exists on the account, so this request would be refused. Changing it wouldn't affect the customer-managed failover configuration either.

context:
You have a general-purpose v2 storage account, contosoglobal, that currently replicates data to a destination account in a different Microsoft Entra tenant. Its current settings are listed below. Your security team requires that this account must no longer take part in copies that cross tenant boundaries, and that its AllowCrossTenantReplication property end up set to false. An administrator has already tried to set that property to false, and the service rejected the request. Which change should you make?

- Property: Account type; Value: General-purpose v2
- Property: AllowCrossTenantReplication; Value: true
- Property: Attached replication policies; Value: 1 (rp-glob-004)
- Property: Destination account; Value: In a different Microsoft Entra tenant
- Property: Blob versioning; Value: Enabled
prompt: To meet the requirement, you should _____.

options.text: delete the cross-tenant replication policy, then set AllowCrossTenantReplication to false
set AllowCrossTenantReplication to false, then delete the cross-tenant replication policy
delete only the replication rule, then set AllowCrossTenantReplication to false
disable blob versioning, then set AllowCrossTenantReplication to false

explanation:
Azure Storage refuses to set AllowCrossTenantReplication to false on an account that still takes part in cross-tenant object replication policies; the existing cross-tenant policies must be deleted first. Removing the cross-tenant replication policy from contosoglobal and only then setting its AllowCrossTenantReplication property to false meets the security requirement and blocks future cross-tenant policies on that account.

Why the other options are wrong:
- set AllowCrossTenantReplication to false, then delete the cross-tenant replication policy: Performing these two steps in this order leaves the first request denied, because the service rejects a change to false while the account still carries cross-tenant replication policies.
- delete only the replication rule, then set AllowCrossTenantReplication to false: Removing only the rule leaves the cross-tenant replication policy itself attached to the account, and the property change stays refused while any such policy remains.
- disable blob versioning, then set AllowCrossTenantReplication to false: Turning off blob versioning is not possible on an account that still has a replication policy, and disabling versioning in any case would not remove the cross-tenant policies that block the property change.

prompt: The exhibit lists the configuration of a storage account you own. Its data must keep serving traffic after the loss of an entire datacenter in the primary region and after a region-wide disaster, and application access must not be interrupted while the account is changed. Which change should you make?

options.text: Start one customer-initiated conversion to GZRS and let it run to completion
Start a customer-initiated conversion to ZRS now, then start the conversion to GZRS the following day
Open a support request for a support-initiated conversion to GZRS performed by support in a single step
Provision a new GZRS account in the same region and copy the existing containers into it with AzCopy

explanation:
Because this change alters zone redundancy as well as geo-redundancy, it cannot be done as a single conversion — it must be split into two conversions, which may run in either order. Starting from LRS, the first conversion moves the account to ZRS and the second moves it to GZRS. Leave a full day between the two so the background work of the finished conversion can settle. Both steps run without data loss and without application downtime, and the account's endpoints, keys and SAS tokens stay the same, which satisfies the no-interruption requirement.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Start one customer-initiated conversion to GZRS and let it run to completion: A conversion that also changes zone redundancy has to be performed as two separate operations, so GZRS cannot be reached in one pass from LRS; the second step has to be submitted later.
- Open a support request for a support-initiated conversion to GZRS performed by support in a single step: Support-initiated conversions follow the same rules as customer-initiated ones — a support request does not allow the two changes to be combined. Nothing in the exhibit blocks a conversion anyway (boot diagnostics is off, no archive-tier blobs, no object replication, change feed or point-in-time restore), so opening a request adds no value.
- Provision a new GZRS account in the same region and copy the existing containers into it with AzCopy: Copying to a second account is a manual migration, which is reserved for cases the conversion path cannot serve, such as a legacy block blob account, moving regions, or avoiding rehydration of archived blobs. It also takes the application offline, which the exhibit rules out.

prompt: You own the storage account described below. You need everything it holds to stay available if an availability zone in its primary region goes down, and you also want a copy of the data maintained in the paired region. Because a single redundancy setting governs the whole account, you must pick one option that works for every service it contains. Which setting should you choose?

options.text: GRS
GZRS
RA-GRS
RA-GZRS

explanation:
The account contains Azure Files shares, and Azure Files supports only LRS, ZRS, GRS and GZRS — it never supports the read-access-to-secondary variants. Of the four geo options offered, GZRS is therefore the only one that meets the zone-failure requirement while remaining selectable for the whole account: it writes synchronously to three or more availability zones in the primary region, so file shares stay mounted through a zone outage, and then copies asynchronously to the paired region. Both Blob Storage and Azure Files support it.

Why the other options are wrong:
- GRS: GRS replicates with LRS in the primary region before copying to the paired region, so the primary copies all sit in one datacenter in the primary region. Losing an availability zone there is not tolerated, and file shares on such an account must be remounted.
- RA-GRS: RA-GRS adds a readable secondary endpoint, but the primary region is protected only with LRS, so a zone failure in the primary region is not covered. Azure Files also does not support the read-access-to-secondary options, so this setting cannot serve the shares in the account.
- RA-GZRS: RA-GZRS would give zone resilience plus a readable secondary copy, but Azure Files never supports RA-GRS or RA-GZRS, so it cannot be applied to an account whose file shares must keep working.

options.text: Run one conversion that adds zone redundancy and the geographic copy in a single change.
Run a conversion that adds zone redundancy, wait a full day, then run a second conversion that adds the geographic copy.
Run a conversion that adds zone redundancy, then run a second conversion that adds the geographic copy without waiting a full day in between.
Copy the data to a new account with AzCopy and repoint the application, leaving redundancy on the existing account as it is.

explanation:
The account is a general-purpose v2 account in a zone-capable region with a paired region, none of its services are blocked, and no feature on it prevents conversion, so the change can be done in place with a customer-initiated conversion. Any change that also touches zone redundancy has to be a separate two-step conversion, so you first convert the account to keep copies across availability zones in the primary region, let a full day pass so background work can settle, and only then run the second conversion that adds the geographic copy. Both conversions cause no application downtime, and endpoints, keys and SAS tokens stay the same throughout.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Run one conversion that adds zone redundancy and the geographic copy in a single change: Zone redundancy cannot be folded into a single portal change together with the geographic copy. Geo-redundancy and read access can be toggled in one operation, but any change that also adds or removes zone redundancy must be a separate two-step conversion, so this jump cannot be applied in one go.
- Run a conversion that adds zone redundancy, then run a second conversion that adds the geographic copy without waiting a full day in between: The order and the two separate conversions are right, but the steps must not be run back to back. After a zone-redundancy conversion completes you should let a full day pass before touching redundancy again, which is why moving from a purely local setup to a zone-plus-geographic end state takes two operations on separate days.

This account is general-purpose v2 in a suitable region with no blocking features, so a conversion is the right route; copying to a new account can cause application downtime that this scenario's online requirement rules out.

Every time you start a customer-initiated conversion, the request is rejected and the Redundancy page reports the status as failed. Which action should you take first?

Turn off boot diagnostics for the virtual machines and open a Microsoft support request for the conversion
Turn on boot diagnostics for the virtual machines, then submit the conversion again
Turn on boot diagnostics for the virtual machines and open a Microsoft support request for the conversion

explanation:
While boot diagnostics is enabled on virtual machines that write their logs into the account, every attempt to add zone redundancy fails — the account stays as it is and each conversion request is rejected. The blocking feature has to be removed on the virtual machines first; once it is, the customer-initiated conversion can be submitted again. The conversion itself needs no downtime and no data loss (a brief pause of under 30 seconds is possible for HNS-enabled accounts), and the endpoints, keys and SAS tokens stay the same.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Turn off boot diagnostics for the virtual machines and open a Microsoft support request for the conversion: Removing the feature is the right half of the fix, but the route is wrong. A support request (Issue type Technical, Service type Storage Account Management, Problem type Data Migration, Problem subtype Migrate to ZRS, GZRS, or RA-GZRS) is the fallback for when a customer-initiated conversion isn't available; it is not what clears the blocking feature. Turn boot diagnostics off and resubmit the conversion yourself.
- Turn on boot diagnostics for the virtual machines, then submit the conversion again: This reverses the required action. Boot diagnostics is precisely the feature that stops any attempt to add zone redundancy from succeeding, so turning it on keeps the conversion rejected.
- Turn on boot diagnostics for the virtual machines and open a Microsoft support request for the conversion: Both parts fail: the feature that blocks the conversion remains active, and the support request is only the fallback route to consider after the blocking feature is removed.

A region-wide outage in its original home region forced an unplanned failover, so it is now serving from the region that used to be its pair and nothing is left behind in the original region. Management of the account still has to run in that original region. Your compliance team now wants the stored data protected again against the loss of a single availability zone. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Submit a customer-initiated conversion that takes the account from LRS to ZRS and wait for it to complete.
Run a migration: copy the contents into another account that already uses the setting you need, then repoint the application at it.
Open a support request with issue type Technical, service type Storage Account Management, problem type Data Migration and problem subtype Migrate to ZRS, GZRS, or RA-GZRS.
Run a customer-managed planned failover back to the original region so the account returns to its previous configuration.

explanation:
An unplanned failover leaves the account in LRS in the region that becomes its primary, and that state cannot be converted to a zone-redundant option: adding zone resilience to a post-failover LRS account has to be done by moving the data. Copying the contents into a second account that already uses the setting you need and repointing the application is therefore the supported path, for example with AzCopy or Azure PowerShell. Because a copy of this kind can interrupt application access, schedule it carefully.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Submit a customer-initiated conversion that takes the account from LRS to ZRS and wait for it to complete: This is the usual route for an account that has never failed over, but it is not available for an account sitting in LRS after an unplanned failover: that account cannot be converted to ZRS or GZRS in place.
- Open a support request with issue type Technical, service type Storage Account Management, problem type Data Migration and problem subtype Migrate to ZRS, GZRS, or RA-GZRS: The support-initiated route relies on the same in-place conversion, so it cannot rescue this account state either; even if the account passes the eligibility check, the request will not deliver zone resilience and you still have to move the data.
- Run a customer-managed planned failover back to the original region so the account returns to its previous configuration: A planned failover swaps the regions with no data loss and leaves the account geo-redundant, but it does not add protection against the loss of an availability zone, and failover is not a way to move or reconfigure stored data.

Run a customer-managed unplanned failover
Submit a request for Microsoft to initiate a failover
Use AzCopy to copy every container to a new storage account in the paired region and repoint the workload at that account

explanation:
A customer-managed planned failover swaps the primary and secondary locations on demand at the account level, without data loss, and the account then continues to hold copies in both regions — it comes back as GRS and keeps geo-redundancy. That matches both requirements: your team schedules and starts it for this account, and protection against a second regional failure survives the exercise. options.text: Rehydrate or relocate the archived blobs, then resubmit the conversion
Delete the archived blobs, then resubmit the conversion
Change the tier of the archived blobs to cool, then resubmit the conversion
Raise a support case of problem type Data Migration, then resubmit the conversion

explanation:
The archived blobs are what blocks the work: the archive tier is available only on accounts set to LRS, GRS or RA-GRS, so an LRS account that still holds archived blobs cannot be moved to a zone-redundant option. Getting that data out of the archive tier first, either by rehydrating it in place or relocating it, is the prerequisite, and once it is gone the conversion can be submitted again and completes without application downtime.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Delete the archived blobs, then resubmit the conversion: Destroying the data would breach the seven-year retention requirement, and the documented remedy for archived blobs is to relocate or selectively rehydrate them, not to remove them.
- Change the tier of the archived blobs to cool, then resubmit the conversion: A blob cannot be moved out of the archive tier without being rehydrated first, so this step cannot be carried out on its own and does not avoid the rehydration work that has to happen anyway.
- Raise a support case of problem type Data Migration, then resubmit the conversion: A support case is the route for diagnosing a conversion that has failed, but it does not lift the restriction that the archive tier is unsupported on these targets; the archived blobs have to leave the archive tier before the conversion will be accepted.

- Property: Storage account name; Value: contosearchlogs

- Property: Redundancy setting; Value: Locally redundant storage (LRS)

prompt: The account should be set to _____, and after a home-region outage the team must run [...] before the application can write to the account again.

options.text: RA-GRS
RA-GZRS
GRS
GZRS

explanation:
The application must be able to read while the home region is offline, which requires the RA- form so the paired-region copy stays readable; and the home region for this account offers no availability zones, so the zone-based settings are not offered there, leaving RA-GRS as the only option that satisfies both conditions. Once the home region is gone, restoring writes always requires an account failover: only promoting the surviving copy moves the primary endpoints to data the account can accept writes on, and even a plain geo-redundant setup cannot write without it.

Why the other options are wrong:
- RA-GZRS: RA-GZRS needs the primary region to support availability zones; the fixed home region for this account does not, so the setting cannot be offered there.
- GRS: GRS keeps a copy in the paired region but leaves it unreadable during a primary outage, so the application would lose access while the home region is offline.
- GZRS: GZRS has the same zone requirement as RA-GZRS and so is unavailable in the fixed home region; it also leaves the paired-region copy unreadable until it is promoted.

prompt: Your team must first _____, and then apply the replication setting [...] to the account.

options.text: bring the archived blobs back online from the archive tier
delete the blobs that sit in the archive tier before submitting the change
move the blobs that sit in the archive tier to a premium page blob storage account
add geo-redundancy first and add zone redundancy afterwards

explanation:
The account currently holds blobs in the Archive access tier, and that tier is supported only on accounts replicated with LRS, GRS or RA-GRS, so nothing can be moved to a zone-redundant setting while those blobs sit in Archive. Because the data must stay on this account, the archived blobs have to be rehydrated back into the hot or cool tier first (rehydration is slow and costly, but it is the only route that keeps everything in place), and only then can the account move to the strongest setting. RA-GZRS is the only option that meets all three stated goals at once: data is written synchronously to availability zones in the home region (survives losing one zone), it is replicated to the paired region (survives a region-wide disaster), and read access to the secondary copy lets the application keep reading through a home-region outage. Note that adding zone redundancy is a conversion and is done as a separate step from the geo and read-access change, with at least a day between the two operations, and both steps can be started by your own team without a support request.

Why the other options are wrong:
- delete the blobs that sit in the archive tier before submitting the change: Deleting the records is not a remedy: the invoices are retained business data and the account must keep serving them. The real constraint is that the Archive access tier cannot coexist with a zone-redundant setting, which is resolved by rehydrating the blobs (or by relocating them), not by destroying them.

explanation:
GRS replicates with LRS in the primary and then copies asynchronously to the paired region, so a region-wide disaster is survivable, and the archive tier is one of the settings that supports archived blobs, so nothing has to be relocated or brought back online. the version in the primary region is removed first, and the version in the paired region follows at the next synchronization
every version of the container is removed at once, but a recoverable version stays in the paired region for 30 days

explanation:
All replicas of a geo-replicated account always hold the same current state, and deletes and overwrites are applied to every copy at the same time. Replication therefore protects against node, datacenter, zone and regional failures, not against accidental deletion: with RA-GZRS the container is gone from the primary and the paired region at the same moment, so bringing it back requires a data-protection mechanism outside replication, such as blob soft delete, versioning, point-in-time restore or a separate copy of the data.

Why the other options are wrong:
- only the version in the primary region is removed, while the version in the paired region stays intact: There is no state in which the paired region keeps an independent, untouched copy after a delete. Every replica tracks the same current state, so the delete reaches the secondary as well; this option contradicts how replication works.
- the version in the primary region is removed first, and the version in the paired region follows at the next synchronization: Deletes are not applied to the primary region and then delayed to the paired region by a later synchronization cycle. All copies receive the delete together, so the team cannot wait and find the container still present in the other region.
- every version of the container is removed at once, but a recoverable version stays in the paired region for 30 days: No retention period is applied to deleted data by a replication setting. Deleting the container removes it from every copy at the same moment, and there is no 30-day window in which a copy in the paired region could still be used.

Raise the upper limit for the SAS expiration interval to 30 days so the current token keeps its validity

- Raise the upper limit for the SAS expiration interval to 30 days so the current token keeps its validity: Raising the upper limit for the SAS expiration interval only changes what the account accepts. - Attach the token to a stored access policy on the container so its validity can be extended or revoked later: Stored access policies exist only for a service SAS. A user delegation SAS is always ad hoc, so there is no stored policy to attach this token to, extend, or revoke through.

explanation:

Per the documentation, an account SAS can span one or more services, enables service-level operations such as Get/Set Service Properties and Get Service Stats, and carries the read, write and delete permissions a service SAS cannot grant. A service SAS stays inside a single service, so it cannot reach the file share, table or queue nor the resource-level calls. It also carries none of the resource-level property and statistics operations the automation must run.
- A service SAS bound to a stored access policy on the archive container: Wrong: attaching a stored access policy only lets you manage the token's expiry and revoke it later without rotating keys; it does not widen the token beyond the single service it was created for, so the file share, table, queue and whole-resource calls still fail.

options.text: Generate the token with the signed start time set at least 15 minutes in the past.
Generate the token with the signed expiry time extended 15 minutes beyond the value set now.
Generate the token with the signed start time set 15 minutes into the future.

explanation:
The command issues the token with no explicit start, so the service signs a start equal to the moment the job runs. The exporter's clock runs about 14 minutes behind, so requests arrive carrying a moment that is still inside the token's beginning, and the service refuses them with 403. Microsoft documents clock skew of up to 15 minutes in either direction and advises setting the start time at least 15 minutes in the past (or omitting it) so every recipient falls inside the window, with the same tolerance expected at the expiry.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Generate the token with the signed expiry time extended 15 minutes beyond the value set now: Lengthening the far end of the window cannot repair requests that are refused at the beginning of it, and the skew tolerance that matters here is at the start of the validity period, not past the expiry.
- Generate the token with the signed start time set 15 minutes into the future: Moving the start into the future makes the problem worse: a recipient already behind would have to catch up by a further 15 minutes before the token became usable, so requests would fail for longer, not less.
- Raise the upper limit for SAS expiry interval on the storage account from 1 hour to 24 hours: The upper limit for SAS expiry interval only caps how long newly created tokens may live on the account. It does not shift the beginning of a token's validity window and it cannot influence requests already rejected for arriving outside that window.

options.text: Reporting export — the scheduled AzCopy run fails on every object, and the tool rejects the schedule expression it is given.
Partner portal — the links partners receive keep working for about a week, and every later download is refused.
Web front end — every download fails with HTTP 403 immediately, even though the signature was produced seconds earlier.
Batch analytics — every request is refused and StorageBlobLogs shows SasExpiryStatus = 'Policy violated'.

explanation: Each integration fails for a different documented reason, so each lands in its own change. The reporting export feeds AzCopy an expression that lacks the seconds it requires, so the copy fails before any object moves (slot about +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ). The partner portal mints a user delegation SAS whose signing key only lives for seven days, so access ends after about a week no matter what window the request asked for (slot capping the lifetime at seven days). The web front end concatenates the signature onto the blob address without the leading ? delimiter, so the service answers with HTTP 403 (slot about inserting the ? character). Batch analytics issues access carrying an expiry and no start value; once the account's expiration policy is enabled the start value is mandatory, the signature is treated as out of policy, and the Block action refuses every request while StorageBlobLogs logs the SasExpiryStatus violation (slot about adding the signed start parameter).

You have a storage account whose delegated links must never be served beyond your company's maximum validity, and you find that the console page enforcing that ceiling is greyed out while the equivalent command returns an error. The account's current key metadata is shown in the exhibit. Which action should you take first?

- Access key: key1; keyCreationTime: ; Permissions: FULL
- Access key: key2; keyCreationTime: 2026-09-30T08:12:04Z; Permissions: FULL
prompt: The first action to take is to _____.

options.text: Regenerate the account access keys
Create a stored access policy on each container
Revoke the user delegation keys
Upgrade the installed Azure CLI

explanation:
key1 reports a null keyCreationTime in the exhibit, and the shared access signature (SAS) expiration policy cannot be configured while keyCreationTime is null for key1 or key2 — that is why the portal control is greyed out and the command errors. Regenerating the account access keys gives both keys a creation time, after which you can switch the expiration policy on and set the upper limit for SAS expiry interval and the Log or Block action.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Create a stored access policy on each container: Stored access policies only supply start time, expiry, and permissions for a service SAS on a container, table, queue, or file share; they do not populate a missing key creation time, so the setting stays unavailable.
- Revoke the user delegation keys: Revoking user delegation keys ends the user delegation keys and every token they signed, but it leaves key1's creation time empty, so configuring the policy still fails.
- Upgrade the installed Azure CLI: The Azure CLI version influences which commands and parameters exist (generating a user delegation SAS needs 2.0.78 or later); it cannot change what the account reports for its own keys.

A vendor's monitoring agent runs on the vendor's own hosts and has no identity in your directory. The exhibit lists every call it makes on each cycle, and you want it to hold one delegated credential that covers all of them. Separately, no token issued on this account may stay usable for longer than 12 hours, and a request that presents a longer-lived one must stop being served. Which type of shared access signature (SAS) should the agent receive, and which change should you make on the account's configuration settings page?

- Call the agent makes on each cycle: Read and overwrite reports/2026-q3.csv; Where it runs: Blob Storage, reports container
- Call the agent makes on each cycle: Read and delete queued messages; Where it runs: Queue Storage, events queue
- Call the agent makes on each cycle: Read the current service properties and request the latest service statistics; Where it runs: The storage resource as a whole
prompt: The agent should be handed a _____, and on the configuration settings page you should [...].

options.text: user delegation SAS
service SAS
account SAS
account SAS bound to a stored access policy

explanation:
The agent's list spans Blob Storage and Queue Storage and includes service-level work, so it needs the broad kind of signature: only an account SAS can span more than one service, carry the extra read, write and delete rights, and enable Get/Set Service Properties and Get Service Stats. The agent has no directory identity, so a user delegation SAS is impossible as well. For the lifetime rule, the upper limit for SAS expiry interval caps every new SAS created on the account, so setting it to 12 hours enforces the ceiling, and choosing the Block action makes the service reject out-of-policy requests instead of serving them and only writing them to logs.

Why the other options are wrong:
- user delegation SAS: A user delegation SAS is authorized against Microsoft Entra ID because it is signed with a user delegation key derived from Entra credentials, and the agent has no identity in your directory, so no such key can be obtained for it. Such a signature also tops out at 7 days.
- service SAS: A service SAS stays inside a single storage service, so it cannot cover the blob container and the queue in one token, and it cannot perform the service-level operations the agent needs at the resource level.
- account SAS bound to a stored access policy: Stored access policies can only be attached to a service SAS; an account SAS must always be ad hoc, so this combination does not exist.

You run a marketing site that links straight to every image file in the assets container of your storage account. The page will stay online for years and nobody on your side will refresh anything, so any visitor, signed in or not, must be able to fetch those images. The invoices container on the same account must keep refusing anyone who presents nothing. Which change should you make?

- Container: assets; Who can fetch its files today: Holders of a valid token; Stored access policies on it: 0; What it holds: Product and campaign images
- Container: invoices; Who can fetch its files today: Holders of a valid token; Stored access policies on it: 2; What it holds: Customer PDF invoices
prompt: On this storage account, you should _____.

options.text: Set the assets container's access level to Public
Set the invoices container's access level to Public
Issue one read-only service SAS and embed its query string in the page
Add a read-only stored access policy to the assets container and embed its link in the page

explanation:
When the goal is simply to let every visitor read every file in one container, the documented approach is to set that container to Public rather than to hand out tokens. A container set to Public keeps serving those images indefinitely with no signing key, no expiry and nobody having to renew anything, and because the change is scoped to a single container the rest of the account, including the invoices container, still refuses requests that carry no credential.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Set the invoices container's access level to Public: This opens the wrong container. Customer PDF invoices would become readable by anyone who guesses the name, which is exactly the resource that must stay closed.
- Issue one read-only service SAS and embed its query string in the page: A service SAS is a temporary token: its permissions and validity live in the token itself, so it stops working at the end of its signed window and someone has to mint a replacement. That does not give long-lived anonymous reads with nobody refreshing links, and it also means publishing a bearer query string on a web page.
- Add a read-only stored access policy to the assets container and embed its link in the page: A stored access policy is not a link in itself. It only supplies the permission and expiry constraints that a service SAS inherits, so any token built on it still stops being served at the end of its signed validity and must be reissued.

You have a nightly replication job that copies the day's export folder into the archive container of your storage account with AzCopy. The job builds the shared access signature (SAS) itself in code, appends it to the destination URL, and since the code was rewritten every run aborts before a single object is transferred, as the log shows. The container, the account key used to sign the token, the granted permissions and the resource path are all unchanged, and the scheduler's clock is correct. Which change should you make?

`# nightly replication job  (AzCopy 10.24.0 on Linux)
token="sv=2022-11-02&ss=b&srt=sco&sp=racw&sr=c&st=2026-10-22T01:00&se=2026-10-22T05:00&sig=REDACTED"
azcopy copy "./exports/*" "https://archstore.blob.core.windows.net/archive?${token}"

# job log
FATAL: job failed, 0 files transferred

prompt: To make the replication job transfer files again, _____.

options.text: write the st and se values of the shared access signature as +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ, with the seconds included
write the st and se values of the shared access signature as +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S, with the Z suffix left out
write the st and se values of the shared access signature as %Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ, with the leading + left out
write the st and se values of the shared access signature as +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%MZ, with the seconds left out

explanation:
Utilities such as AzCopy require the signed start and expiry of a shared access signature to be written as +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ, seconds included. The job writes both time values without the leading + and without seconds, so the utility cannot read them and aborts before any transfer. Rewriting the st and se values in that exact layout, seconds included, resolves the failure while leaving permissions, scope and signing key untouched.

Why the other options are wrong:
- write the st and se values of the shared access signature as +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S, with the Z suffix left out: The value still lacks the UTC Z designator that the expected layout includes, so the expiry cannot be read and the job still stops before copying.
- write the st and se values of the shared access signature as %Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ, with the leading + left out: Keeping the trailing Z but dropping the leading + leaves the value in a layout the utility does not read; seconds and the UTC designator alone are not enough.
- write the st and se values of the shared access signature as +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%MZ, with the seconds left out: Omitting the seconds truncates the time to whole minutes in a layout that expects seconds, so the utility again rejects the token and nothing is transferred.

`$ az storage container generate-sas --account-name contosoreports \

options.text: Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/generateUserDelegationKey
Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listkeys/action
Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listServiceSas/action
Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/regenerateKey/action

explanation:
The token is signed with a user delegation key derived from the signed-in identity's Microsoft Entra credentials, and creating that key requires an Azure RBAC role that contains Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/generateUserDelegationKey. With --auth-mode login and --as-user the command calls exactly that action on behalf of the signed-in developer, which is why a data-plane role scoped to the reports container is not enough and the call is refused. Granting a role that includes generateUserDelegationKey lets the developer produce the link while the account access key stays out of their hands.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listkeys/action: listkeys/action returns the account access keys, which is exactly the credential this design forbids. It is what a caller needs in order to sign a service or account SAS with the shared key, and it does not satisfy the delegation-key requirement behind this command.
- Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listServiceSas/action: listServiceSas/action lets an identity list the SAS credentials already stored on the account. It only reads existing tokens, it cannot create a delegation key, so the command would still be refused.
- Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/regenerateKey/action: regenerateKey/action rotates the account access keys. It does not create a delegation key, so it does not make this command succeed, and rotating keys would disrupt every other integration on the account.

You already switched on the account's shared access signature (SAS) expiration policy, set its upper limit to six hours and its action to refuse anything longer; those values are correct and must stay as they are. Six weeks later, a compliance scan reports that one producer's clients are still working with a credential that stays valid for a full month, and every request made with it is served. That producer and its consumers must keep running, and the credential it hands out must never outlive six hours; the other two producers must keep the credentials they already hold. Which change should you make?

- Item: Shared access signature (SAS) expiration policy; Value: Enabled
- Item: Upper limit for SAS expiry interval; Value: 6 hours
- Item: SAS expiration action; Value: Block
- Item: Producer A - vendor mobile app; Value: sv=2019-02-02&sr=b&sp=r&st=2026-09-01T08:00:00Z&se=2026-09-01T09:00:00Z&sig=...
- Item: Producer B - partner batch uploader; Value: sv=2019-02-02&sr=c&sp=racw&si=monthly-batch&sig=...
- Item: Producer C - back-office export job; Value: sv=2019-02-02&sr=c&sp=rw&st=2026-10-20T00:00:00Z&se=2026-10-20T01:00:00Z&sig=...
prompt: Because that producer and its consumers have to keep working while nothing they hold may last beyond six hours, you should _____.

options.text: Shorten the lifetime of the stored access policy that its token names, then reissue the tokens
Rotate the account access keys and delete the stored access policy that its token names, then reissue the tokens
Shorten the upper limit of the account's SAS expiration policy to 1 hour, then reissue the tokens
Shorten the lifetime of the account access key that signs its tokens, then reissue the tokens

explanation:
Producer B's query string names a container-level stored access policy (si=monthly-batch) and carries no signed start or signed expiry of its own, so that token inherits its start time, expiry and permissions from that stored access policy. The account's expiration action is not supported for a service SAS associated with a stored access policy, which is why a month-long credential is still served even though the account ceiling is six hours and the action is Block. Shortening the lifetime recorded in that stored access policy and reissuing the tokens therefore both caps producer B at six hours and leaves producers A and C, whose tokens carry their own signed start and expiry, untouched.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Rotate the account access keys and delete the stored access policy that its token names, then reissue the tokens: Rotating the account access keys would invalidate every token signed with them, which breaks producers A and C that must keep the credentials they already hold, and deleting the stored access policy would stop producer B's requests from being authorized at all rather than capping them, because its tokens keep naming that policy. The stored access policy itself is the right lever: it is where the constraints inherited by producer B's tokens live.
- Shorten the upper limit of the account's SAS expiration policy to 1 hour, then reissue the tokens: The account's upper limit and expiration action are not applied to a service SAS that references a stored access policy, so lowering the ceiling to 1 hour leaves producer B's month-long credential working exactly as before. The account setting also may not be changed in this scenario.
- Shorten the lifetime of the account access key that signs its tokens, then reissue the tokens: The account access key is the credential that signs new tokens, not something that shortens the validity of tokens already handed out. Producer B's window comes from the named stored access policy, so changing the key does not cap it and would force every producer to rebuild its tokens.

prompt: You hand SAS tokens to an external partner so its applications can upload and read files in a Blob Storage container. If the contract ends you must shut that partner off within minutes, and you cannot regenerate the storage account keys because unrelated workloads also use them. You review the tokens already sitting in the partner's configuration, as listed below. Which token design should you adopt going forward?

options.text: Hand out a service SAS that references a stored access policy on the container, and revoke by changing or deleting that policy
Hand out an account SAS that references a stored access policy on the container, and revoke by changing or deleting that policy
Hand out a user delegation SAS that references a stored access policy on the container, and revoke by changing or deleting that policy
Hand out a service SAS with a short expiry that is reissued on a schedule, and revoke by waiting for the current token to lapse

explanation:
A stored access policy can only be attached to a service SAS. Because the start time, expiry and permissions live server side on the container, the token inherits them, so editing or deleting that policy instantly stops every service SAS bound to it — and the account keys never have to be regenerated. A service SAS is also the narrower token here: it is signed with the account key and delegates to a resource in only one storage service (Blob Storage, in this case), which is all the partner needs.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Hand out an account SAS that references a stored access policy on the container, and revoke by changing or deleting that policy: An account SAS spans one or more storage services and adds service-level operations such as Get/Set Service Properties, but it must always be an ad hoc token. Stored access policies are not supported for account SAS, so editing or deleting a policy on the container would have no effect on it and the partner would keep access.
- Hand out a user delegation SAS that references a stored access policy on the container, and revoke by changing or deleting that policy: A user delegation SAS is signed with a user delegation key derived from Microsoft Entra credentials instead of the account key. Microsoft recommends it for security, but it also must always be an ad hoc token and cannot reference a stored access policy, so the on-demand revocation described here is not achievable with it.
- Hand out a service SAS with a short expiry that is reissued on a schedule, and revoke by waiting for the current token to lapse: Near-term expiry on an ad hoc token only limits how long a leaked token is useful; it does not let you cut the partner off when you need to. Revocation here would depend on the reissue schedule, not on any action you take at the time of the incident, so the requirement to shut access off within minutes is not met. Near-term expiry is the recommended fallback when a stored access policy cannot be referenced.

prompt: You have an ASP.NET service running on AKS that uses a system-assigned managed identity. On start-up it calls CreateIfNotExistsAsync for the reports container and then SetAccessPolicyAsync to define the policy that the service SAS tokens it hands out depend on. Blob reads and writes through the same identity work all day, and the container call succeeds, but the policy definition fails every time with HTTP 403 and ErrorCode AuthorizationFailure. You need the policy to be defined automatically at start-up with no operator step. Which change should you make?

options.text: Build the container client from a connection string that holds an account access key, so the SetAccessPolicyAsync request is authorized with Shared Key
Assign Storage Blob Data Owner to the app's managed identity so the identity is authorized to change the container's policies
Acquire an Entra access token for the managed identity and pass that token to SetAccessPolicyAsync as the credential
Grant the app the Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/generateUserDelegationKey action and sign the request with the resulting delegation key

explanation:
The REST operation behind stored access policy creation is Set Container ACL, and that operation must be authorized with Shared Key using the account access keys supplied in a connection string; Microsoft Entra credentials are explicitly not supported for it. That is why the same managed identity can read and write blobs yet receives 403 when SetAccessPolicyAsync tries to define the policy. Supplying the account access key in a connection string so the request is signed with Shared Key is the change that makes the policy definition succeed.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Assign Storage Blob Data Owner to the app's managed identity so the identity is authorized to change the container's policies: No role assignment, however broad, makes this work. The failure is not a permissions-scope problem: the operation that creates the stored access policy cannot be authorized with Microsoft Entra credentials at all, so widening the managed identity's data-plane role still returns 403.
- Acquire an Entra access token for the managed identity and pass that token to SetAccessPolicyAsync as the credential: Handing an Entra token to the SDK makes the call an Entra-authorized request, and an Entra-authorized Set Container ACL is rejected. The credential type itself is the problem here, not its scope.
- Grant the app the Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/generateUserDelegationKey action and sign the request with the resulting delegation key: A user delegation key is what signs a user delegation SAS, and stored access policies apply to a service SAS only. It is not a credential that can authorize Set Container ACL, so the call would still fail.

prompt: Five internal teams each need their own read/write access to the blobs in a single Blob Storage container, and each team must be able to have its access cancelled without disturbing the others. Every team's token is a service SAS that names a signed identifier on that container, so that you can change or cancel one team's access without regenerating the storage account keys. The container currently holds the entries listed below, and a sixth team starts on Monday needing the same read/write access. You must keep the five running teams working. Which change should you make?

options.text: Reassign a signed identifier that its present user no longer needs, then issue the new team's service SAS against that identifier.
Define a new signed identifier on a second container in the same storage account and issue the new team's service SAS against it.
Move the signed identifiers up to the storage account so the new team's entry does not compete for a slot on the container.
Add the new signed identifier as an extra entry on the container and let the service retire the oldest entry automatically.

explanation:
A container can hold at most five stored access policies, and defining a sixth is not supported, so a request carrying an extra entry is rejected. Because the new team needs access it can lose without rotating keys, it must stay on a service SAS that names a signed identifier, and the only way to supply one is to take over an identifier slot whose previous user no longer needs it. The five running teams are unaffected because their identifiers and their start, expiry and permission values are left alone.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Define a new signed identifier on a second container in the same storage account and issue the new team's service SAS against it: A stored access policy lives on the container whose resources it protects, so an identifier kept on a different container can only yield a service SAS for that other container's resources. The new team would still have no access to the shared container, and the five-entry limit still applies to whichever container holds the entries.
- Move the signed identifiers up to the storage account so the new team's entry does not compete for a slot on the container: There is no account-level collection of stored access policies that a service SAS can reference. They are held on the container resource and the maximum of five applies to that container, so moving the identifiers up to the storage account is not something the service supports.
- Add the new signed identifier as an extra entry on the container and let the service retire the oldest entry automatically: Nothing is retired automatically on your behalf. The Set Container ACL request that creates policies sets the container's policy collection from the list you send, and going past five entries on a container is unsupported, so the call fails instead of silently dropping the oldest one.

prompt: You support a Blob Storage container of scanned invoices that three client applications read directly, each using a service SAS that points at a signed identifier on that container. Every client takes its token once during installation, stores it in its own configuration, and only asks for a replacement after a call fails. The client teams cannot be redeployed on demand, so the tokens they hold must keep working for months without a manual reissue. You must change how the constraints on the container are configured. Which change should you make?

options.text: Set ExpiresOn far in the future (or infinite) and move it further out on a recurring basis
Leave ExpiresOn at its current value and add a second signed identifier carrying the same dates for new clients
Set ExpiresOn to the date the supplier contract ends and change nothing on the container after that
Set ExpiresOn to one hour and have each client fetch a replacement token every hour

explanation:
The start time, the expiry time and the permissions are held on the container and are enforced on every request, so a token that names the signed identifier can never be more permissive or longer-lived than the values shown in the exhibit. Because the clients here reuse one token until a call fails, the expiry has to be pushed out to a point they will never reach, and kept moving outward over time; that is the documented approach for long-lived tokens. That keeps the outage on 2026-09-15 from repeating when the current 2026-10-30 date arrives, without any client-side change.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Leave ExpiresOn at its current value and add a second signed identifier carrying the same dates for new clients: Adding a second signed identifier with the same dates changes nothing for the three existing clients, whose tokens already name scanonapp. They will fail the moment the current date passes, because the policy is checked on each request and there is no automatic replacement.

Clients that only reissue after a failure will simply keep failing.

prompt: You have an ASP.NET service that issues service SAS tokens for a Blob Storage container, where each token names a signed identifier that the service writes to the container with SetAccessPolicyAsync. Field reports say that a token a user has just pasted into a request is rejected for the first several minutes and then works, with nothing changed on the user's side, and your monitoring shows HTTP 403 on only those early requests. You need to correct how the constraints on the container are defined so that a token is usable the moment it is handed out. Which change should you make?

options.text: Set the start time on each signed identifier about 15 minutes earlier than the moment the entry is written
Set the start time on each signed identifier about 15 minutes later than the moment the entry is written
Set the expiry on each signed identifier about 15 minutes later than the moment the entry is written
Leave the start time and expiry on each signed identifier as they are, and have the issuing code put its own start time into every token

explanation:
The storage service and the calling client can disagree about the current time by roughly a quarter of an hour in either direction. Because both entries use DateTimeOffset.UtcNow as the start time, requests that reach the service before its clock has reached that instant are rejected, and the 403 errors stop once the service's clock passes the recorded value. Writing the start time about 15 minutes in the past absorbs that discrepancy so a token bound to the identifier is accepted immediately by every client.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Set the start time on each signed identifier about 15 minutes later than the moment the entry is written: Moving the start time into the future widens rather than removes the window in which early requests are refused, so the first calls after issuance would keep failing for a longer period.
- Set the expiry on each signed identifier about 15 minutes later than the moment the entry is written: The failures happen at the beginning of the validity window, not the end, so moving the expiry has no effect on them; as written here it would also cut the usable lifetime of every token down to about a quarter of an hour.
- Leave the start time and expiry on each signed identifier as they are, and have the issuing code put its own start time into every token: A service SAS that references a signed identifier inherits the start time, expiry and permissions held on the container, so values placed in the token itself do not override the entry; the early rejections would continue.

prompt: A nightly job in your release pipeline writes the access policy entries for the blob container 'vendor-dropbox' by calling SetAccessPolicyAsync with the list shown below. Last week someone trimmed that list so it carries only the newest vendor entry. Since that run, the four partner applications whose tokens name the entries that were on the container before the trim fail on every request with HTTP 403, and a portal check of the container's access policies now reports a single entry. None of those partners' tokens or settings changed. You must correct the job so the next nightly run leaves the tokens other teams depend on working. Which change should you make?

options.text: Have the job read the signed identifiers currently on the container and pass them together with the new entry to SetAccessPolicyAsync.
Replace the single call with one SetAccessPolicyAsync call per signed identifier, so that each entry is written separately.
Keep the trimmed list but move the call into a runbook step that an operator executes after inspecting the container by hand.
Drop the call from the job and hand each partner a token that carries its own start time, expiry and permissions rather than naming an entry.

explanation:
SetAccessPolicyAsync sets the container's whole access policy collection from the list of signedIdentifiers you pass: the entries you omit are removed. Trimming the list therefore deleted the four entries that the partner tokens name, and because a service SAS bound to a stored access policy is checked against that policy on every request, those tokens started failing with HTTP 403 the moment the entries went. Reading the identifiers already on the container and passing them together with the new entry preserves every token other teams depend on while still adding the new one.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Replace the single call with one SetAccessPolicyAsync call per signed identifier, so that each entry is written separately: Each call still sets the entire collection to whatever single identifier that call contains, so the earlier entries are removed one after another and only the last one survives — the same loss of tokens, just spread across several calls.
- Keep the trimmed list but move the call into a runbook step that an operator executes after inspecting the container by hand: The trimmed list still overwrites the container's policy collection whenever it runs, and a manual runbook step does not restore the entries that were already removed, so the broken tokens stay broken and the next run repeats the damage.
- Drop the call from the job and hand each partner a token that carries its own start time, expiry and permissions rather than naming an entry: A token that embeds its own start time, expiry and permissions holds no server-side constraints, so nothing on the container can edit or cancel it afterwards; this abandons the control you need and still leaves the four failing tokens unfixed.

prompt: You have a licensing portal that hands each retail kiosk a service SAS so the kiosk can read its licence file from the blob container 'license-files' without ever holding an account key. Kiosks refresh their own token through the portal once a year, so the signed identifier on that container is written to stay valid for roughly one year. Your compliance team has reviewed the settings and issuance output below and asked for the generation-time warnings and log entries to stop, while the kiosks keep exactly the access length they have today. Which change should you make?

options.text: Set the SAS expiration policy on the storage account to 365 days.
Set the SAS expiration policy on the storage account to 30 days and leave the container's signed identifier as it is.
Rewrite the container's signed identifier so it expires in 24 hours, and keep issuing kiosk tokens against it.
Hand the kiosks account SAS tokens that carry the same one-year expiry instead.

explanation:
The account-level SAS expiration policy defines a recommended upper validity interval, and it applies to service SAS tokens as well as account SAS tokens. Each kiosk token inherits the roughly one-year validity of the container's signed identifier, which is far longer than the 24 hours the account currently recommends, so every issuance exceeds the recommendation and produces the warning plus the storage log entry you see. Raising the account's SAS expiration policy to 365 days aligns the recommendation with the longest token you intend to issue, so the generation-time warnings and log entries stop while the kiosks keep the same year-long access and nothing has to be redeployed. Remember that this setting is only a recommendation: exceeding it never blocks a token, which is exactly why the mismatch shows up as noise rather than as an error.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Set the SAS expiration policy on the storage account to 30 days and leave the container's signed identifier as it is: Thirty days is still far shorter than the roughly one-year validity that the signed identifier gives every kiosk token, so each issuance would continue to exceed the recommended upper interval and keep producing the same warning and log entry — and it would only make the gap worse for any token issued today.
- Rewrite the container's signed identifier so it expires in 24 hours, and keep issuing kiosk tokens against it: A service SAS that references the signed identifier inherits that entry's start time, expiry time and permissions. Rewriting 'kiosk-read' to expire in 24 hours would cut off kiosks that can only refresh once a year, so those devices would begin receiving HTTP 403 (Forbidden), and it still leaves the account-level recommendation untouched.
- Hand the kiosks account SAS tokens that carry the same one-year expiry instead: Account SAS tokens are covered by the account's SAS expiration policy in exactly the same way as service SAS tokens, so a one-year account SAS would keep triggering the same warning and log entry. It would also grant the kiosks broader multi-service and service-level access (including operations such as Get/Set Service Properties) than reading a single licence file requires.
