prompt: You have a general-purpose v2 storage account with blob versioning enabled. A blob named invoices.pdf was written as a block blob and then overwritten twice, so the account now keeps a current version plus two earlier versions. An application requires invoices.pdf to be a page blob. You need to complete the conversion successfully. Which action should you take?

options.text: Delete the blob and all of its versions, then create the page blob again.
Overwrite the current version with page blob content and leave the two earlier versions unchanged.
Use Set Blob Metadata on the current version to change its type and leave the two earlier versions unchanged.
Copy the current version to a new blob in another container and remove only the current version.

explanation:
Every version of a blob must have the same blob type, so a block blob cannot be overwritten as a page blob while earlier versions still exist. With versioning enabled, deleting the blob does not remove its earlier versions, and the deleted current state itself becomes another version. The blob and all of its versions must therefore be deleted first, after which the file can be created again as a page blob.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Overwrite the current version with page blob content and leave the two earlier versions unchanged: An overwrite cannot change the blob type while earlier versions of the same blob exist, because the type must stay consistent across the whole version history; that request would be rejected.
- Use Set Blob Metadata on the current version to change its type and leave the two earlier versions unchanged: Set Blob Metadata records a new version of metadata, but it does not convert a block blob into a page blob, so the application would still be working with a block blob.
- Copy the current version to a new blob in another container and remove only the current version: Copy Blob keeps the source blob's type, and this option also places the result under a different name in a different container. It neither converts invoices.pdf nor clears the earlier versions of the original blob.

prompt: You have a general-purpose v2 storage account named contosoarchive with blob versioning turned on for the account and soft delete turned on for the 'reports' container. A cleanup script issued a delete request for every file in that container, and the service returned 202 Accepted for each request. The container now lists no files, yet the storage capacity attributed to it has not fallen and the finance invoice still includes the same volume. The team needs the space the deleted files occupied to be released and the account to end up holding no copies of that data. Which action should the team take?

options.text: Delete each version of those files separately, specifying which version to remove.
Wait for the container's soft delete retention period to expire, because the delete request also left the current version of each file in that recoverable state.
Set the access tier of the remaining versions in the container to archive, so that the account pays less for the data it still holds.
Turn off blob versioning for the account, because that immediately releases the versions left behind by the delete request.

explanation:
Once blob versioning is turned on, a delete request changes the meaning of delete: the current version of the file becomes a previous version instead of being freed, and that version stays in the account and keeps being billed. That is why the container lists no files while the capacity shown for it did not fall and the invoice is unchanged. To actually release the space you have to remove the versions themselves, one version at a time, passing the identifier of the version you want removed (the service lets you delete a specific version by its version ID). Soft delete does not change this: when a blob is deleted while versioning is on, no soft-deleted entry is created for the blob, so the retention window does not apply to that deletion.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Wait for the container's soft delete retention period to expire, because the delete request also left the current version of each file in that recoverable state: With versioning enabled, deleting a blob turns its current version into a previous version and does not create a soft-deleted entry for the blob, so the soft delete retention period never starts for that request and waiting for it to expire frees nothing. The content has to be removed by deleting the versions that are still there.
- Set the access tier of the remaining versions in the container to archive, so that the account pays less for the data it still holds: Moving a version to another access tier does not free the capacity that the data occupies; the content is still stored in the account and still billed. Moving versions to the archive tier also bills the full content length of every version and snapshot of that blob, and once a tier is set explicitly on a version it cannot be undone, so this both fails to release the space and makes the bill larger.
- Turn off blob versioning for the account, because that immediately releases the versions left behind by the delete request: Turning the setting off does not delete existing versions, snapshots or blobs. They remain in the account and continue to be billed, and afterwards they can still be read, listed and deleted, so disabling versioning on its own leaves the space in use.

prompt: A file replaced last week still opens with its earlier content, and the application keeps no copy of its own

options.text: Blob versioning
Snapshots
Lifecycle management policy
Azure Storage Actions task

explanation: The four observations map one-to-one onto four different configurations. The earlier content of a replaced file is kept automatically by the service, with no application code involved, which is what Blob versioning does on every write or delete. An account that holds only the replacement while the application had saved its own copy beforehand reflects manual, application-managed snapshots rather than an automatic history. For the cleanup observations, a lifecycle management policy counts a version's age with the day-based daysAfterCreationGreaterThan property, so an entry is removed 30 days after it was written even if it stayed live for much of that time, whereas an Azure Storage Actions task can key on when a version became noncurrent, so the 30 days are counted from the day it stopped being the live state even when it was written years earlier.

prompt: Contracts

options.text: Blob versioning
Snapshots
Soft delete for blobs
Lifecycle management policy
Azure Storage Actions task
Azure Resource Manager lock
Immutability (WORM) policy

explanation: Each workload asks for a different outcome, and each outcome has its own mechanism. Keeping earlier copies of every file with no application change is what blob versioning does automatically on every write or delete. A copy that the application takes at a moment it selects is a snapshot. Bringing one individually removed file back inside a retention window is the job of soft delete for blobs. Age-based cleanup measured from the date a copy was written belongs to a lifecycle management policy, whose version rules use the day-based daysAfterCreationGreaterThan property and count from the version's creation time. Cleanup that starts when a copy stops being the live one belongs to an Azure Storage Actions task, which can key on when a version became noncurrent. Preventing the account itself from being deleted or renamed needs an Azure Resource Manager lock, because versioning protects blob content only and offers no protection for the account resource. The immutability (WORM) policy item supports none of the six outcomes.

context:
You have a general-purpose v2 storage account named contosomedia. The account holds a video library, nightly reports, and log files, and blob versioning is enabled at account level. Finance flagged several surprises on the monthly invoice, and operations reported that fetching previous versions of one log file now runs far slower. You need to match each observation to the storage behavior responsible, so the team can pick the right configuration change next.

- Ref: A; Observation recorded during the monthly review: A nightly job rewrites report.csv using unchanged bytes each night, and the monthly amount billed for that file keeps growing.
- Ref: B; Observation recorded during the monthly review: The cool tier was set on one version, and the monthly amount billed for that file stays at the full content length of the file regardless of where the file resides now.
- Ref: C; Observation recorded during the monthly review: One old version of a video was moved to the cheapest storage tier, and the monthly amount billed for the whole account jumped by an amount far above the size of that one file.
- Ref: D; Observation recorded during the monthly review: Fetching the versions of one log file started running slower after the file was rewritten several times a day for months.
- Ref: E; Observation recorded during the monthly review: The account keeps hundreds of manual snapshots of the same block blobs, and the monthly amount billed for that data shows them counted twice.
prompt: Observation A

options.text: No tier was set on the versions, so the account is billed for the unique blocks across versions, and re-committing a block with identical data adds a billable block.
A tier was set on the version, so the version is billed for its full content length, and that tier choice is permanent even when the blob is moved to a different tier.
Moving a version into the archive tier charges the full content length of every version and snapshot of that blob, not only the version that was moved.
The blob has more versions than the recommended maximum of 1,000, and that slows down listing the versions of that blob.
The account still takes block blob snapshots, which duplicate data that the version history already captures, and adds cost.

explanation: Each observation is produced by one specific billing or performance behavior of versioned blobs. A: when no tier is explicitly set for the versions of a blob, the account is billed for the unique blocks across all versions, and a block that is replaced is billed as a unique block even when its ID and data are unchanged, so a nightly rewrite of identical bytes keeps adding charge for report.csv (i1). B: when a tier is explicitly set on a version, that version is billed for its full content length, and explicitly setting the tier cannot be undone, so a file whose tier was set stays billed at full content length wherever it sits afterwards (i2). C: when a blob or version is moved to the archive tier, the account is billed for the full content length of all of that blob's versions and snapshots, so archiving one old video version pushed the amount billed for that file far beyond the size of that single version (i3). D: a large number of versions per blob degrades blob listing performance, and Microsoft recommends maintaining fewer than 1,000 versions per blob, which explains the slower retrieval of previous versions of the frequently rewritten log file (i4). E: once versioning is enabled, versions already capture every update and delete of block blobs, so continuing to take manual snapshots adds no protection, duplicates data and increases cost (i5).

context:
You manage a general-purpose v2 storage account named contosoarchive, where the service keeps a history of every file change for you. A quarterly review produced the four observations below, each recorded against a different file. Match each observation to the behavior of the stored history that explains it.

- File: ledger-2025.csv; What the team recorded: A restore tool captured the string that came back with each write. Twelve months later it sent the same string again, and the service returned that same copy.
- File: policy.docx; What the team recorded: An editor changed the descriptive properties stored with last year's copy. The service rejected the request, and the stored properties stayed as they were.
- File: legacy.log; What the team recorded: This file was uploaded before the account began keeping any history, and it showed no string at all. After the first update it displayed one, and the earlier content was still retrievable.
- File: media-2019.bin; What the team recorded: A rarely opened copy from last year was moved to a cheaper storage option by naming its string. The copy that clients read today kept its current storage class.
prompt: Observation 1 (ledger-2025.csv)

options.text: For a file that predates the change, nothing is assigned until its first write; that write then stamps the identifier from the file's creation time and retains the earlier state as a previous copy.
Any single copy, current or not, can be placed in a different access tier by passing its identifier to the tiering operation.
Every stored copy carries the UTC time at which it was written, and that identifier keeps working for the whole life of the copy.
Copies that are no longer the live one are frozen: their content and their metadata cannot be altered after they are created.

explanation: Observation 1 (ledger-2025.csv) goes with the item stating that every stored copy carries the UTC time at which it was written and that the identifier stays valid for the life of the copy, because the service handed back the same copy when the saved string was reused a year later. Observation 2 (policy.docx) goes with the item about copies that are no longer the live one being frozen, because an earlier copy's content and metadata cannot be modified once created. Observation 3 (legacy.log) goes with the item about a file that predates the change receiving no identifier until its first write, with that write stamping one from the file's creation time and keeping the earlier state as a previous copy. Observation 4 (media-2019.bin) goes with the item about moving any single copy, current or not, to another access tier by passing its identifier, because only the named copy changed storage class while the live copy was unaffected.

The cleanup rule already in the account is not delivering the requested outcome: for the quarterly report, the replaced copy disappeared only a few days after the replacement, even though the rule is configured to retain copies for 30 days. Which configuration should you use to meet the retention the business wants?

- Item: Account; Value: contosoreports (general-purpose v2)
- Item: Blob versioning; Value: Enabled for the account
- Item: Cleanup mechanism in place; Value: Lifecycle management policy
- Item: Version cleanup property; Value: daysAfterCreationGreaterThan = 30
- Item: Retention the business asked for; Value: Remove a replaced copy 30 days after a newer copy takes its place
prompt: To meet the retention the business wants, the team should _____.

options.text: raise the daysAfterCreationGreaterThan value in the lifecycle management policy so previous versions are kept longer
enable soft delete for the container so the Azure Storage service removes previous versions after the retention window
move previous versions to the archive tier and delete them later with a scheduled script
create an Azure Storage Actions task that deletes previous versions by tracking how long each version has been superseded

explanation:
The requirement is to time the removal of a replaced copy from the moment it stopped being the live copy, not from the moment its data was originally written. A lifecycle management policy cannot express that: daysAfterCreationGreaterThan is anchored to the version's creation timestamp, so the quarterly report's replaced copy was already older than the 30-day threshold the moment it entered the version history, which is why it vanished days after the replacement. An Azure Storage Actions task can key on when a version became noncurrent, so it removes a replaced copy exactly 30 days after it was replaced regardless of how old the copy itself was.

Why the other options are wrong:
- raise the daysAfterCreationGreaterThan value in the lifecycle management policy so previous versions are kept longer: Raising daysAfterCreationGreaterThan changes only the length of the measurement window, not its starting point. The property is still counted from the time the version's data was written, so every replaced copy is retained for the configured number of days from its own write date rather than 30 days after it was replaced, and copies of files that are replaced often would be kept far longer than the business wants.
- enable soft delete for the container so the Azure Storage service removes previous versions after the retention window: Soft delete is a recovery mechanism for deleted blobs and deleted versions, not an automatic cleanup mechanism for previous versions. With blob versioning enabled, the data of a replaced copy persists as a previous version until it is explicitly removed, and soft delete retention only controls how long a deliberately deleted version stays recoverable.
- move previous versions to the archive tier and delete them later with a scheduled script: Archiving the replaced copies and deleting them with a scheduled script makes cleanup a manual, script-driven process and does not deliver the automatic removal 30 days after a replacement. Moving a version to the archive tier also changes billing for the whole account, since setting the archive tier on a version bills the full content length of every version and snapshot of that blob, not only the one that was moved.

context:
You have a general-purpose v2 storage account that has stored customer documents for several years. Blob versioning was switched on for the account earlier this week, and a scheduled job has since rewritten one of those documents for the first time since the switch. The support team asks whether the content from before the switch can be brought back, and whether anyone is allowed to edit a stored copy in place. You need to describe what the account now holds for that document and what may be done with the copies that predate the switch. Which statements are correct?

- Timestamp (UTC): 2024-03-14T09:00:00Z; Event: reports.txt stored in the 'documents' container
- Timestamp (UTC): 2026-10-20T08:00:00Z; Event: Blob versioning switched on for the account
- Timestamp (UTC): 2026-10-21T11:22:07Z; Event: reports.txt written again by the nightly reporting job
prompt: After the scheduled job's rewrite, _____. For the stored copies that predate the switch, [...].

options.text: the content from before the switch is kept as a previous version of the document, and the rewritten document is the current version
the content from before the switch is discarded, because only writes made after the switch are recorded
the content from before the switch becomes the current version, and the rewritten document is kept as a previous version
the content from before the switch is kept as a previous version of the document, and the rewritten document is also kept as a previous version

explanation:
reports.txt was written on 2024-03-14, before versioning was switched on, so it had no version ID. On the first write after the switch (2026-10-21), the modified blob becomes the new current version and the state of the blob before that update becomes a previous version, so the content from before the switch is kept and can be brought back. Previous versions are immutable: their content and metadata cannot be modified, so an old copy can only be read, deleted (by supplying its version ID), or copied elsewhere (for example with Copy Blob) to be used again.

Why the other options are wrong:
- the content from before the switch is discarded, because only writes made after the switch are recorded: Wrong: the service does keep the state that existed before the update. For a blob created before versioning was enabled, the state before the update becomes a previous version, so the earlier content is not discarded.
- the content from before the switch becomes the current version, and the rewritten document is kept as a previous version: Wrong: the order is reversed. On a write operation the modified blob becomes the new current version, and the earlier state becomes a previous version; the content from before the switch does not become the current version.
- the content from before the switch is kept as a previous version of the document, and the rewritten document is also kept as a previous version: Wrong: after a write there is always one current version. The rewritten document is the live state, and only the earlier state becomes a previous version, so the two cannot both be previous versions.

You have a general-purpose v2 storage account named contosofinance with blob versioning enabled for the account, and the table below shows the state of one blob stored in it. The team wants the copy written on 2026-08-14 kept in the cool tier so that its retrieval costs fall, while the copy that clients download today must stay as it is. The latest invoice shows a bigger charge for the older copy than the team expected, and the team also asks whether moving that copy back to hot would lower the bill again. You need to move the correct copy and describe how billing and tier behavior apply to it. Which statements are correct?

- Property: Account; Value: contosofinance (general-purpose v2)
- Property: Blob versioning; Value: Enabled for the account
- Property: Blob; Value: ledger.csv
- Property: Blob type; Value: Block blob
- Property: Versions of ledger.csv; Value: 3 (1 current, 2 previous)
- Property: Copy to place in the cool tier; Value: Version written 2026-08-14 09:12:44 UTC
- Property: Version ID of that copy; Value: 2026-08-14T09:12:44Z
- Property: Copy clients download today; Value: Version written 2026-10-02 08:03:11 UTC
- Property: Invoice observation; Value: Charge for the 2026-08-14 copy is larger than the team expected
prompt: To move that copy, you _____, and [...].

options.text: call Set Blob Tier with the version ID
call Set Blob Tier without the version ID
call Copy Blob with the source version ID
call Set Blob Metadata with the version ID

explanation:
The copy written on 2026-08-14 is a previous version of ledger.csv, so it is moved by calling Set Blob Tier and passing that copy's version ID (2026-08-14T09:12:44Z); a call that omits the version ID targets the current version, which is the copy clients already download. Once a tier is set explicitly on a version, that version is billed for its full content length rather than only for the unique blocks it added, and the tier decision cannot be undone: moving the copy back to hot still leaves it billed at full content length, so the expected fall in charges from a move back does not materialize.

Why the other options are wrong:
- call Set Blob Tier without the version ID: Set Blob Tier without the version ID applies the tier change to the current version of ledger.csv, which is the 2026-10-02 copy that clients download, and leaves the 2026-08-14 copy in its current tier.
- call Copy Blob with the source version ID: Copy Blob with the source version ID writes a new blob built from that copy instead of changing the tier of the stored version, so the 2026-08-14 copy keeps its present tier and the data is duplicated at extra cost.
- call Set Blob Metadata with the version ID: Set Blob Metadata writes metadata and never changes an access tier; on a previous version it cannot even change metadata, because previous versions are immutable.

context:
You have a general-purpose v2 storage account named contosologs that stores nightly log files. Blob versioning is enabled for the account, and the log ingestion app also takes a snapshot of its block blob after each upload. Finance reports that the storage charge for the account keeps climbing even though the file sizes have not changed. You need to bring that charge down and still be able to restore an earlier state of any log file. What should the team do?

- Account property: Account name; Value: contosologs
- Account property: Account type; Value: General-purpose v2
- Account property: Blob versioning; Value: Enabled
- Account property: Log ingestion app; Value: Creates a snapshot of the block blob after each upload
- Account property: Storage charge trend; Value: Up 22% over three months while file sizes stayed the same
prompt: The team should _____.

options.text: Stop taking the app's block blob snapshots, because the account already captures every write and delete of the blob.
Keep taking the app's block blob snapshots but move those snapshot copies to the archive tier so the older ones cost less to store.
Turn off blob versioning for the account and rely on the app's block blob snapshots alone, on the expectation that the stored versions will disappear from the account.
Enable container soft delete so that removed snapshot copies are reclaimed without an extra charge.

explanation:
Blob versioning records every write and delete of a blob automatically, so with versioning enabled on contosologs the history the team needs is already kept by the service itself. The app's own block blob snapshots are extra copies that add cost without adding recovery options the account does not already provide, and Microsoft recommends stopping block blob snapshots once versioning is enabled. Removing the app's snapshot step is therefore what lowers the charge while every earlier state of the log files stays restorable from the versions the account maintains.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Keep taking the app's block blob snapshots but move those snapshot copies to the archive tier so the older ones cost less to store: Moving the app's snapshot copies to the archive tier does not reduce the account's charge. When a version is moved to the archive tier, the full content length of every version and snapshot of that blob is billed, not only the one that was moved, so this change can raise the capacity cost for that blob's data instead of lowering it, and the snapshot copies remain billable storage either way.
- Turn off blob versioning for the account and rely on the app's block blob snapshots alone, on the expectation that the stored versions will disappear from the account: Turning off versioning moves the account in the wrong direction for the stated requirement. Snapshots are application-managed checkpoints taken on the app's schedule, so they do not record every update or delete the way the service's automatic history does, and disabling versioning does not remove the versions that are already stored, so the charge would not fall as expected.
- Enable container soft delete so that removed snapshot copies are reclaimed without an extra charge: Container soft delete governs recovering blobs that were deleted inside a container; it does not reduce the charge for copies that are still stored. The extra cost in this workload comes from the app creating a snapshot on every upload, so soft delete is not the setting that brings the charge down.

You have a general-purpose v2 storage account named contosoaudit that keeps one log blob per server. Blob versioning is turned on for the account. The log writer uploads each blob once and then calls Append Block every few seconds as new lines arrive, so the file is only ever appended to and never rewritten in full. A review of one blob shows a single live state and no earlier states, so the lines written earlier in the day cannot be examined once the next batch lands. You need every intermediate state of each log blob to be kept so that earlier content stays available for review. What should the log writer do?

- Step: 1; Client operation: Upload the blob; Content written: Lines 1-100
- Step: 2; Client operation: Append Block; Content written: Lines 101-200
- Step: 3; Client operation: Append Block; Content written: Lines 201-300
- Step: 4; Client operation: Append Block; Content written: Lines 301-400
prompt: To keep every earlier state of each log blob, the log writer should _____.

options.text: Call Create Snapshot on the blob after each batch of entries
Call Set Blob Tier on the blob after each batch of entries
Enable soft delete on the container that holds the log blobs
Add a lifecycle management rule with a version-age filter to the account

explanation:
For an append blob, the Append Block call does not create a new version, so with versioning enabled the service keeps only the live state of the file and the earlier content is lost. The documentation states that for page and append blobs the Append Block and Put Page operations do not create versions and that a manual snapshot is needed to capture those states. Calling Create Snapshot after each batch of appended entries therefore preserves every intermediate state; on a versioned blob the snapshot also produces a version holding identical data, so the states can be restored later.

Why the other options are wrong:
- Call Set Blob Tier on the blob after each batch of entries: Set Blob Tier only changes the access tier of a blob or version; it is not one of the operations that records a new state, so the content of each batch would still be discarded.
- Enable soft delete on the container that holds the log blobs: Soft delete protects blobs that were deleted from being permanently removed. It does not capture the content of a blob at each append, so the earlier states of the log file still would not be retained.
- Add a lifecycle management rule with a version-age filter to the account: A lifecycle management rule with a version-age filter only cleans up versions that already exist; it does not cause additional states to be recorded when data is appended.

context:
You have a general-purpose v2 storage account named contosodata that stores customer contracts in a container named contracts, and blob versioning is switched on for the account. The business requires that the contracts survive two accidents: the contracts container being removed by mistake, and the whole storage account being removed by mistake. You need to work out what the protection already switched on delivers for each accident and what has to be configured on top of it, so that both accidents are recoverable.

- Property: Account type; Value: General-purpose v2
- Property: Blob versioning; Value: Enabled
- Property: Versions kept; Value: All of them, no cleanup schedule
- Property: Container 'contracts'; Value: 1,480 blobs, 240 GB
- Property: Recovery of the container or the account after removal; Value: Not handled by the account's blob history
prompt: The protection already switched on _____, and [...] must be configured so that both accidents are recoverable.

options.text: keeps earlier copies of blobs that are replaced or deleted, but does not cover the removal of a container or of the whole account
keeps earlier copies of blobs that are replaced or deleted, and also covers the removal of a container or of the whole account
does not keep earlier copies of blobs that are replaced or deleted, but covers the removal of a container or of the whole account
keeps earlier copies of blobs that are replaced or deleted, but covers only the removal of a container and not the removal of the whole account

explanation:
Blob versioning is a per-blob history: the service stores a prior copy of a blob whenever that blob is written or deleted, so it protects individual files. It does nothing for the removal of a container or of the whole storage account, because those objects and their blobs disappear together and no version survives them. To cover the two accidents, an Azure Resource Manager lock protects the storage account from being removed, and container soft delete makes a removed container and its contents recoverable for the retention period.

Why the other options are wrong:
- keeps earlier copies of blobs that are replaced or deleted, and also covers the removal of a container or of the whole account: Wrong: the blob history only produces copies of individual blobs on write or delete. It cannot restore a container that was removed or an account that was removed, so claiming it also covers those cases is incorrect.
- does not keep earlier copies of blobs that are replaced or deleted, but covers the removal of a container or of the whole account: Wrong: the service does save earlier copies of blobs that are replaced or deleted, so the first half of this statement is false, and the second half is false as well.
- keeps earlier copies of blobs that are replaced or deleted, but covers only the removal of a container and not the removal of the whole account: Wrong: earlier copies of blobs are kept, but the removal of a container is not covered by that history either, and the removal of the whole account is likewise uncovered.
